The team needs an automated way to hold a new instance out of load balancer registration until that work succeeds. Which solution meets the requirement?
Correct: Add a launch lifecycle hook and complete its lifecycle action after the configuration script succeeds.
Why: The requirement is to gate traffic on successful startup work, not merely to detect a bad instance afterward. A launch lifecycle hook pauses the instance while its packages and configuration are installed; completing the action lets it proceed toward service and load balancer registration. Elastic Load Balancing health checks can drive replacement, but they do not provide this pre-registration wait. A longer health check grace period likewise does not confirm that the script succeeded.
Wrong options: Enable Elastic Load Balancing health checks so an unready instance can be replaced after a failed check. (Detecting an unhealthy instance after launch does not hold registration until the configuration work succeeds.); Extend the health check grace period to cover the expected package download time. (A grace period delays optional health checks but does not hold registration until the script succeeds.); Add a termination lifecycle hook to run the configuration script before the instance shuts down. (A termination hook runs at the wrong transition for preparing a newly launched instance.)

chunks.title: Amazon Athena serverless SQL on S3
chunks.text:
Amazon Athena serverless SQL on S3. Amazon Athena runs ad-hoc SQL directly against data in Amazon S3 without loading it into a database or managing query infrastructure. Choose it for occasional exploration of an S3 data lake; consider partitioning and columnar formats when scanned data and query cost matter.
When to use: Analysts need interactive SQL over logs or other existing S3 data.; Queries are occasional, and the team wants no query infrastructure to manage.; A query must combine S3 data with data in another supported source through Athena data source connectors.
Key facts: Athena for SQL is serverless; you pay for the queries you run.; Athena queries S3 data directly, without first loading it into Athena.; Athena supports formats including CSV, JSON, Parquet, and ORC.; Partitioning, compression, and columnar formats can reduce data scanned, improve performance, and lower cost.; Athena uses schema-on-read: table definitions do not change the underlying S3 objects.
Gotchas: Creating an Athena table does not convert or move the S3 data.; Athena can query data outside S3 through data source connectors; federation does not require copying every source into S3.; AWS Glue crawlers discover schemas, while Glue ETL jobs transform data; neither is required merely to run SQL on existing S3 files.
Confused with: AWS Glue: Choose Glue for schema discovery or ETL transformations; choose Athena to run interactive SQL over the data.; Amazon Redshift: Redshift is a data warehouse; Athena is a direct, serverless option for ad-hoc SQL on S3.; Amazon QuickSight: QuickSight creates BI visualizations; Athena runs SQL queries and can supply data to QuickSight.
ES: Amazon Athena ejecuta SQL ad-hoc directamente sobre datos de Amazon S3, sin cargarlos en una base de datos ni administrar infraestructura de consultas. Elígelo para explorar ocasionalmente un data lake en S3; considera particiones y formatos columnares cuando importen los datos escaneados y el costo. Athena for SQL es serverless; pagas por las consultas que ejecutas.; Athena consulta datos de S3 directamente, sin cargarlos primero en Athena.; Athena admite formatos como CSV, JSON, Parquet y ORC.; Las particiones, la compresión y los formatos columnares pueden reducir los datos escaneados, mejorar el rendimiento y bajar el costo.; Athena aplica schema-on-read: las definiciones de tablas no cambian los objetos subyacentes de S3.

chunks.title: Amazon Athena serverless SQL on S3
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional retailer keeps several years of checkout application logs as JSON files in Amazon S3. Investigators run SQL only when a discrepancy is reported, and the retailer does not want to load the files into a warehouse or maintain a query cluster. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Define a table over the S3 files and run the investigators' SQL with Amazon Athena.
Why: The deciding requirements are occasional SQL against existing S3 files, with neither a warehouse load nor a managed query cluster. Athena queries S3 directly and is serverless. Redshift would require the proposed data load, while the EMR design introduces a cluster to manage. Glue ETL addresses processing rather than the investigators' interactive SQL access.
Wrong options: Run AWS Glue ETL jobs to process each log file when an investigation begins. (Glue ETL processes and transforms data rather than providing the requested ad-hoc SQL query service.); Create an Amazon EMR cluster and use its SQL processing framework for investigations. (A query cluster introduces infrastructure management that the retailer wants to avoid.); Load the logs into Amazon Redshift and run SQL against warehouse tables. (Loading the logs into a warehouse conflicts with the requirement to query the existing S3 files without loading them.)

chunks.title: Amazon Athena serverless SQL on S3
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research team already queries compressed Parquet measurements in Amazon S3 with Athena. Files are organized into date partitions, but a monthly report still scans measurements from every date because its SQL does not restrict the date partition. The team must keep its current query service and reduce the amount of data scanned. Which change meets the requirement MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Add a filter on the date partition to the Athena report query.
Why: The files are already partitioned, but the report does not use the partition to limit its scan. Filtering on the date partition lets Athena scan less data and can lower query cost without changing services. A Glue crawler addresses metadata, not the missing query filter. Moving to Redshift would also violate the requirement to keep the current query service.
Wrong options: Create an AWS Glue crawler to infer the Parquet schema before every report. (Schema inference does not address a query that scans dates outside the requested month.); Use Amazon QuickSight to display the report without changing its Athena SQL. (Changing the visualization does not restrict which S3 partitions Athena scans.); Copy the measurements into Amazon Redshift for the monthly report. (Moving the report to Redshift does not keep the team's current query service.)

chunks.title: Amazon Athena serverless SQL on S3
chunks.text:
Scenario: A small museum receives weekly CSV exports in an Amazon S3 prefix. Curators want to run occasional SQL to count records by exhibit; the files need no cleaning or format conversion, and the originals must remain unchanged. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Define an Athena table for the S3 CSV files and query it as new files arrive.
Why: The curators need occasional SQL, not a transformation pipeline, and the original S3 files must stay unchanged. An Athena table applies its schema when queries run; defining it does not rewrite the CSV files. Glue ETL would introduce unnecessary processing, while loading into Redshift adds a step the scenario does not need. An EMR cluster adds infrastructure overhead.
Wrong options: Load each export into Amazon Redshift and query the loaded tables. (Loading exports into a warehouse adds a data-loading step unnecessary for occasional SQL on S3.); Run a scheduled AWS Glue ETL job to rewrite each CSV export before every query. (The files need no transformation, so the ETL job adds work without satisfying an unmet requirement.); Create an Amazon EMR cluster and run a SQL framework against the S3 exports. (Maintaining a cluster adds overhead for occasional queries that Athena can run without query infrastructure.)

chunks.title: Amazon Aurora architecture (shared storage, 6 copies across 3 AZs)
chunks.text:
Amazon Aurora architecture (shared storage, 6 copies across 3 AZs). Amazon Aurora is a managed, MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible relational database whose compute instances share a cluster storage volume spanning multiple Availability Zones. Choose it when an application needs familiar relational interfaces, distributed storage, and the option to fail over to a reader instance.
When to use: An existing MySQL or PostgreSQL application needs a managed relational database with little or no driver changes.; A workload needs readers that share the writer's cluster volume and can offload read traffic.; The database needs automatic failover to an Aurora Replica when the writer becomes unavailable.
Key facts: An Aurora cluster has one primary writer and can have up to 15 Aurora Replicas.; The writer and readers connect to the same cluster volume, which spans multiple Availability Zones.; Aurora Replicas are read-only; Aurora can fail over to a replica if the primary becomes unavailable.; Place Aurora Replicas in separate Availability Zones to maintain high availability.; Aurora storage scales automatically; the provided AWS FAQ states a maximum of 256 TiB per database instance.
Gotchas: A single-instance Aurora cluster has storage distributed across Availability Zones, but it has no Aurora Replica to take over its writer's compute role.; A read-only Aurora Replica cannot accept application writes until it becomes the primary through failover.; Do not treat distributed storage and a cross-AZ reader instance as the same high-availability feature.
Confused with: Amazon RDS: Choose Aurora when the requirement specifically calls for its shared cluster volume and Aurora Replicas; RDS also supports managed relational engines.; Amazon DynamoDB: DynamoDB is a NoSQL choice, not a replacement for an application that must keep MySQL or PostgreSQL compatibility.; Amazon DocumentDB: DocumentDB targets MongoDB-compatible document workloads, not MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible relational applications.
ES: Amazon Aurora es una base de datos relacional administrada, compatible con MySQL o PostgreSQL, cuyas instancias de cómputo comparten un volumen de almacenamiento que abarca varias Availability Zones. Elígela cuando necesites interfaces relacionales conocidas, almacenamiento distribuido y la posibilidad de hacer failover a una instancia lectora. Un clúster Aurora tiene un escritor principal y puede tener hasta 15 Aurora Replicas.; El escritor y los lectores se conectan al mismo volumen del clúster, que abarca varias Availability Zones.; Las Aurora Replicas son de solo lectura; Aurora puede hacer failover a una réplica si el principal deja de estar disponible.; Ubica Aurora Replicas en distintas Availability Zones para mantener alta disponibilidad.; El almacenamiento de Aurora crece automáticamente; la FAQ de AWS proporcionada indica un máximo de 256 TiB por instancia de base de datos.

chunks.title: Amazon Aurora architecture (shared storage, 6 copies across 3 AZs)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare analytics team has selected Aurora PostgreSQL for an existing relational application. It needs a cross-AZ failover target if the writer fails and wants to move read-only analysis queries away from that writer without maintaining a separate copy of the database for its readers. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Direct read-only analysis queries to Aurora Replicas in the cluster. + Add an Aurora Replica in a different Availability Zone from the writer.
Why: This design needs both a reader instance in another Availability Zone and a way to offload read-only analysis. An Aurora Replica provides a failover target, and Aurora Replicas can handle read queries while sharing the writer's cluster volume. Multi-AZ storage alone does not supply replacement writer compute, and reader instances cannot accept writes.
Wrong options: Place an RDS for PostgreSQL read replica outside the Aurora cluster for analysis. (It would not be an Aurora reader sharing the selected cluster volume.); Direct analysis queries and application writes to Aurora Replicas. (Aurora Replicas cannot perform application writes while they are readers.); Keep only the writer because the Aurora cluster volume spans multiple Availability Zones. (The multi-AZ volume does not create a reader instance to take over the writer's role.)

chunks.title: Amazon Aurora architecture (shared storage, 6 copies across 3 AZs)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company runs a MySQL application and wants to keep its existing drivers. Its database design calls for a writer and a read-only instance in another Availability Zone that share a storage volume; the reader must be available for automatic failover if the writer fails. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST application change?
Correct: Deploy an Aurora MySQL cluster with a writer and an Aurora Replica in another Availability Zone.
Why: The deciding requirements are MySQL compatibility, shared cluster storage, and a reader that can take over if the writer fails. An Aurora MySQL writer and an Aurora Replica use the same cluster volume, and Aurora can fail over to the replica. A single-instance Aurora cluster still has distributed storage, but it lacks the requested reader instance.
Wrong options: Deploy a single-instance Aurora MySQL cluster and send all queries to its writer. (Its storage spans Availability Zones, but it has no reader instance for the required failover.); Move the application to Amazon DocumentDB and place a reader in another Availability Zone. (DocumentDB targets MongoDB-compatible document applications rather than the required MySQL application.); Move the application to Amazon DynamoDB and store each ticket as an item. (DynamoDB would not preserve the application's MySQL interface or provide the requested shared Aurora cluster volume.)

chunks.title: Amazon Aurora architecture (shared storage, 6 copies across 3 AZs)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research publisher uses PostgreSQL drivers for a relational catalog. It wants a managed database whose storage grows automatically and whose reporting queries can run on several read-only instances connected to the writer's storage volume. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST application change?
Correct: Use Aurora PostgreSQL with a writer and Aurora Replicas for reporting.
Why: The existing PostgreSQL interface and the requirement that readers connect to the writer's storage volume identify Aurora PostgreSQL. Aurora separates DB instances from its shared cluster volume, and Aurora Replicas can offload reporting reads. RDS for PostgreSQL is a plausible relational choice, but it does not satisfy the specifically requested Aurora shared-volume design.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Keyspaces and issue the reporting queries through CQL. (Keyspaces uses a Cassandra-compatible interface rather than the required PostgreSQL drivers.); Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with read replicas for reporting. (Although it preserves PostgreSQL compatibility, this option does not provide the specified Aurora shared cluster volume.); Use Amazon Neptune and model catalog entries as graph vertices. (A graph model does not preserve the application's PostgreSQL relational interface.)

chunks.title: Aurora cloning and Backtrack
chunks.text:
Aurora cloning and Backtrack. Aurora cloning creates a separate cluster quickly using copy-on-write storage, making it useful for testing with production data. Aurora MySQL Backtrack rewinds an existing cluster after a bad change; choose it when recovery must happen in place and Backtrack was enabled when the cluster was created.
When to use: Create an independent test or development cluster from production data quickly, with minimal initial storage.; Rewind a Backtrack-enabled Aurora MySQL cluster after an accidental data change without restoring a new cluster.
Key facts: A clone initially shares data pages with its source; additional storage is used as their data changes.; The source and clone are separate clusters, so testing on the clone does not change the source.; Copy-on-write applies to up to 15 clones; the next clone is a full copy.; Backtrack must be enabled when an Aurora MySQL cluster is created or when a snapshot is restored; it cannot be enabled later on an existing cluster.; Backtrack affects the entire cluster, causes a brief disruption, and has a maximum target window of 72 hours. The actual window can be shorter.
Gotchas: A clone is not an in-place rewind of its source.; Backtrack is not available for Aurora PostgreSQL and cannot rewind only one table.; Aurora cannot create a clone in a different AWS Region from its source.; Backtrack does not replace backups.
Confused with: Snapshot restore: A snapshot restore creates a new cluster; cloning is faster and more space-efficient for an initial test copy.; Point-in-time restore: Point-in-time restore creates a new cluster, while Backtrack rewinds an eligible Aurora MySQL cluster in place.
ES: Aurora cloning crea rápidamente un clúster independiente con almacenamiento copy-on-write, útil para probar con datos de producción. Aurora MySQL Backtrack retrocede un clúster existente después de un cambio erróneo; elígelo si necesitas recuperar el clúster en el mismo lugar y Backtrack se habilitó al crearlo. Un clon comparte inicialmente las páginas de datos con el origen; se usa almacenamiento adicional a medida que cambian los datos.; El origen y el clon son clústeres independientes, por lo que las pruebas en el clon no modifican el origen.; Copy-on-write se aplica hasta a 15 clones; el siguiente clon es una copia completa.; Backtrack debe habilitarse al crear un clúster Aurora MySQL o al restaurar un snapshot; no puedes habilitarlo después en un clúster existente.; Backtrack afecta a todo el clúster, causa una breve interrupción y admite una ventana objetivo máxima de 72 horas. La ventana real puede ser menor.

chunks.title: Aurora cloning and Backtrack
chunks.text:
Scenario: A medical research company runs an Aurora production cluster and needs a separate cluster for testing a schema change against current production data. The test must not modify production, and the team wants to avoid initially storing a full physical copy of the data. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Create an Aurora clone of the production cluster and run the test on the clone.
Why: The deciding requirements are an independent test cluster and minimal initial storage. Aurora cloning creates a separate cluster that initially shares the source's data pages, allocating more storage as data changes. Snapshot and point-in-time restores can produce new clusters but do not offer the same copy-on-write advantage for this test. Backtracking production would not isolate the experiment.
Wrong options: Enable Backtrack on the production cluster and run the test there, then rewind it. (Backtrack does not isolate the schema test from production.); Create a point-in-time restored Aurora cluster and run the test there. (Point-in-time restore creates a separate cluster but does not provide the requested copy-on-write initial storage efficiency.); Restore a production snapshot into a new Aurora cluster for the test. (Snapshot restore provides a separate cluster but is less space-efficient initially than cloning.)

chunks.title: Aurora cloning and Backtrack
chunks.text:
Scenario: A game studio keeps an Aurora production cluster in one VPC and wants an independent cluster for load testing in another VPC in the same AWS Region. The subnets in the two VPCs map to the same Availability Zones. The studio wants the test cluster ready quickly with minimal additional storage at creation, while keeping production running. Which approach meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Create an Aurora clone in the test VPC using subnets mapped to the same Availability Zones.
Why: Different VPCs do not rule out Aurora cloning when their subnets map to the same Availability Zones. Because the clusters are in the same Region, a cross-VPC clone can give the studio an independent test cluster with minimal initial storage. Snapshot and point-in-time restores miss the copy-on-write storage requirement. Running tests on production, even with Backtrack, fails the isolation requirement.
Wrong options: Backtrack the production cluster before each test and run the load test on production. (Backtrack affects production and does not provide an independent cluster in the test VPC.); Restore production to a point in time into the test VPC using the matching Availability Zones. (Point-in-time restore creates a separate cluster but does not meet the requested copy-on-write efficiency.); Restore a production snapshot into the test VPC using the matching Availability Zones. (A snapshot restore can provide a separate test cluster but is less space-efficient at creation than cloning.)

chunks.title: Aurora Global Database
chunks.text:
Aurora Global Database. Aurora Global Database spans Regions with one writable primary cluster and read-only secondary clusters. Choose it when a relational application needs local reads worldwide and a path to recover from a Region-wide outage.
When to use: A relational application needs reads close to users in multiple Regions.; The database needs a secondary cluster in another Region for disaster recovery.; Writes can go to one primary Region.
Key facts: A global database has one primary Region and up to 10 read-only secondary Regions.; Aurora replicates changes to secondary Regions using dedicated infrastructure, typically with latency under a second.; The global database writer endpoint points to the primary writer, including after a switchover or failover.; Use switchover for a planned move of a healthy primary with no data loss; use failover after a primary-Region outage.
Gotchas: A secondary cluster does not independently accept writes; optional write forwarding sends its write requests to the primary.; Sub-second replication is typical latency, not a promise of zero data loss during an unplanned outage.; Aurora Global Database does not support Aurora Auto Scaling for secondary clusters.
Confused with: RDS Multi-AZ: Its standby addresses availability within one Region, not local reads and recovery across Regions.; RDS read replicas: Cross-Region replicas can serve reads, but DR requires promoting a replica rather than using an Aurora global database secondary.; DynamoDB global tables: They support multi-Region, multi-active writes for NoSQL; Aurora Global Database has one writable primary Region.
ES: Aurora Global Database abarca varias Regions con un clúster primario que acepta escrituras y clústeres secundarios de solo lectura. Elígelo cuando una aplicación relacional necesita lecturas locales en distintas partes del mundo y una ruta de recuperación ante la caída de una Region. Una base de datos global tiene una Region primaria y hasta 10 Regions secundarias de solo lectura.; Aurora replica los cambios a las Regions secundarias mediante infraestructura dedicada, normalmente con una latencia inferior a un segundo.; El global database writer endpoint apunta al escritor primario, incluso después de un switchover o failover.; Usa switchover para trasladar de forma planificada un primario en buen estado sin pérdida de datos; usa failover tras una caída de la Region primaria.

chunks.title: Aurora Global Database
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer operates an Aurora Global Database across two Regions. It will move production writes to the secondary Region during a scheduled relocation, while both Regions and their database clusters remain healthy. The database team requires no data loss during the move. Which operation should the team use?
Correct: Perform an Aurora Global Database switchover to the secondary Region.
Why: This is a planned relocation with healthy clusters and an explicit no-data-loss requirement. Aurora Global Database switchover is designed to move the primary under those conditions. Failover addresses an outage in the primary Region, while write forwarding leaves the primary where it is.
Wrong options: Promote an RDS read replica in the destination Region. (The deployment uses an Aurora global database secondary, and replica promotion is not its planned-move operation.); Enable write forwarding on the secondary cluster and redirect all writers to it. (Write forwarding sends requests to the existing primary; it does not relocate the primary cluster.); Perform a managed cross-Region failover to the secondary cluster. (Failover is the recovery operation for an outage of the primary Region, not the planned no-data-loss move.)

chunks.title: Aurora Global Database
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company has an Aurora Global Database and periodically switches its healthy primary cluster between Regions for operational reasons. Its application configuration should keep a single write connection target that follows the primary after each switch. Which endpoint should the application use?
Correct: The Aurora Global Database writer endpoint.
Why: The requirement is one write target that continues to identify the primary after a planned switch. The Aurora Global Database writer endpoint always points to the primary writer, including after switchover. Write forwarding is different: it can relay requests from a secondary cluster but does not make that secondary endpoint follow the primary.
Wrong options: A reader endpoint in the Region where the application currently runs. (A reader endpoint does not connect the application to the primary writer.); The primary Regional cluster's writer endpoint, updating configuration after each switch. (A Regional endpoint requires changing the configured target when the primary moves.); A secondary cluster endpoint with write forwarding enabled. (Forwarding sends writes to the primary but does not provide an endpoint that follows the primary writer.)

chunks.title: Aurora Global Database
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research publisher is designing an Aurora-based catalog for editors in two Regions. Editors in the secondary Region need local reads, and the publisher wants a database in that Region for recovery if the primary Region fails. The team also plans periodic, no-data-loss moves of the primary while both Regions are healthy. Which two choices meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Deploy an Aurora Global Database with a read-only secondary cluster in the editors' Region. + Use Aurora Global Database switchover for each planned move of the healthy primary.
Why: The architecture must provide local secondary-Region reads and a cross-Region recovery option; an Aurora Global Database secondary does both. Because the periodic moves are planned and both Regions remain healthy, use switchover to avoid data loss. RDS Multi-AZ does not supply the requested remote reads, and Aurora Global Database failover is intended for an outage rather than this planned operation.
Wrong options: Use Aurora Global Database failover for each planned move of the healthy primary. (Failover is for recovery from a primary-Region outage, not a planned no-data-loss move.); Use an RDS Multi-AZ standby in the primary Region as the editors' read target. (The standby is in the primary Region and does not serve reads in an instance deployment.); Use a cross-Region RDS read replica and rely on its automatic promotion for disaster recovery. (RDS read replicas do not provide automatic failover.)

chunks.title: Aurora Replicas, reader/custom endpoints and replica auto scaling
chunks.text:
Aurora Replicas, reader/custom endpoints and replica auto scaling. Aurora Replicas serve read-only queries and can be promoted if the primary instance fails. Use the reader endpoint for reads across replicas, a custom endpoint to route a workload to a selected subset, and Aurora Auto Scaling when reader demand changes.
When to use: Read traffic needs to use multiple Aurora Replicas without hardcoded instance addresses.; Analytics queries must connect to a different subset of instances than ordinary reads.; Reader capacity should increase and decrease with workload.
Key facts: An Aurora cluster can have up to 15 Aurora Replicas handling read-only queries.; The reader endpoint balances connections among Aurora Replicas; the cluster endpoint connects to the primary instance.; Custom endpoints connect to subsets of DB instances in a cluster.; Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes reader instances according to a scaling policy; it does not scale the writer's workload.; Auto Scaling's target metric averages all readers, including manually added readers and readers associated with custom endpoints.
Gotchas: An instance endpoint stays tied to a specific instance; cluster and reader endpoints handle instance failover better.; A custom endpoint changes connection routing, not which readers contribute to an Auto Scaling target metric.; If a cluster has no reader, the Auto Scaling target metric is not calculated and its policy alarms remain inactive.
Confused with: Reader endpoint: It balances connections among all Aurora Replicas, rather than selecting a subset for a particular workload.; Instance endpoint: It connects to one specific instance and does not automatically redirect connections when that instance becomes unavailable.
ES: Aurora Replicas atienden consultas de solo lectura y pueden promoverse si falla la instancia primaria. Usa el reader endpoint para lecturas entre réplicas, un custom endpoint para dirigir una carga a un subconjunto y Aurora Auto Scaling cuando cambia la demanda de lectura. Un clúster de Aurora puede tener hasta 15 Aurora Replicas que atienden consultas de solo lectura.; El reader endpoint distribuye conexiones entre Aurora Replicas; el cluster endpoint conecta con la instancia primaria.; Los custom endpoints conectan con subconjuntos de instancias de un clúster.; Aurora Auto Scaling agrega o elimina instancias lectoras según una política; no escala la carga del writer.; La métrica objetivo de Auto Scaling promedia todos los readers, incluidos los agregados manualmente y los asociados con custom endpoints.

chunks.title: Aurora Replicas, reader/custom endpoints and replica auto scaling
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company runs ordinary product queries and long-running analytics queries against the same Aurora cluster. It has provisioned readers with different capacities and wants analytics connections to use only a designated subset, without listing instance hostnames in the application. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a custom endpoint for the designated readers and connect analytics through it.
Why: The requirement is to select a subset of differently configured readers without maintaining their hostnames in application code. A custom endpoint provides a connection address for that subset. The reader endpoint instead balances among all Aurora Replicas, while instance endpoints identify individual instances and shift connection management to the application.
Wrong options: Send analytics to the instance endpoints of the designated readers and update the application when readers change. (Instance endpoints require the application to manage specific reader addresses.); Send analytics to the reader endpoint and ordinary queries to the cluster endpoint. (The reader endpoint balances connections among all replicas rather than isolating analytics on the designated subset.); Send analytics to the cluster endpoint and ordinary queries to the reader endpoint. (The cluster endpoint connects analytics to the primary instance, not the designated readers.)

chunks.title: Aurora Replicas, reader/custom endpoints and replica auto scaling
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics application uses an Aurora cluster with a primary instance and multiple Aurora Replicas. It sends updates and read-only tracking queries through separate connection pools. After an instance failure, both pools must reconnect to suitable available instances without discovering individual instance addresses. Which endpoint configuration is MOST appropriate?
Correct: Use the cluster endpoint for updates and the reader endpoint for tracking queries.
Why: Updates must reach the primary instance, and tracking queries should use the replicas. The cluster endpoint serves the primary and can reconnect to a new primary after failover; the reader endpoint serves read-only connections and can reconnect to available replicas. Instance endpoints do not automatically change which DB instance they connect to when one becomes unavailable.
Wrong options: Use the primary instance endpoint for updates and each replica's instance endpoint for tracking queries. (Instance endpoints remain tied to particular instances and do not provide the requested automatic redirection.); Use the cluster endpoint for both pools and add replicas when tracking demand grows. (The cluster endpoint routes tracking queries to the primary rather than distributing them among the replicas.); Use the reader endpoint for updates and the cluster endpoint for tracking queries. (Updates need the primary instance, whereas the reader endpoint is intended for read-only queries.)

chunks.title: Aurora Serverless v2
chunks.text:
Aurora Serverless v2. Aurora Serverless v2 automatically adjusts database compute and memory capacity as demand changes. Choose it for relational workloads with unpredictable peaks or idle periods when sizing and repeatedly resizing provisioned DB instances would add cost or operational work.
When to use: An application has sudden, unpredictable increases in database activity.; A new application has uncertain database capacity requirements.; Development, test, or tenant workloads alternate between busy and quiet periods.; Aurora readers must scale independently to handle periodic read spikes.
Key facts: Set a minimum and maximum capacity range; Aurora Serverless adjusts capacity within the configured range based on demand.; Capacity can change in increments as small as 0.5 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs).; Resource usage is measured per second, so reduced usage is reflected when an instance scales down.; Aurora Serverless supports reader DB instances, Multi-AZ clusters, Aurora global databases, and RDS Proxy.; Promotion tiers can be used to configure Aurora Serverless readers to scale independently of the writer.
Gotchas: A provisioned Aurora instance does not automatically gain Serverless v2 capacity scaling merely because it is in an Aurora cluster.; Setting the maximum capacity too low can prevent a Serverless v2 instance from scaling to meet an anticipated peak.; Adding Serverless v2 readers alone does not make a provisioned writer scale its capacity automatically.
Confused with: Provisioned Aurora DB instances: Provisioned capacity is selected through DB instance classes; Aurora Serverless v2 adjusts capacity automatically within a configured range.
ES: Aurora Serverless v2 ajusta automáticamente la capacidad de cómputo y memoria de la base de datos según cambia la demanda. Elígelo para cargas relacionales con picos impredecibles o períodos de inactividad cuando dimensionar y redimensionar instancias provisionadas aumentaría el costo o el trabajo operativo. Configuras un rango mínimo y máximo de capacidad; Aurora Serverless ajusta la capacidad dentro de ese rango según la demanda.; La capacidad puede cambiar en incrementos de tan solo 0.5 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs).; El uso de recursos se mide por segundo, por lo que la reducción se refleja cuando una instancia disminuye su capacidad.; Aurora Serverless admite instancias lectoras, clústeres Multi-AZ, Aurora global databases y RDS Proxy.; Los promotion tiers permiten configurar lectores de Aurora Serverless para que escalen independientemente del escritor.

chunks.title: Aurora Serverless v2
chunks.text:
Scenario: A software company provides separate Aurora databases to tenants whose busy periods rarely coincide. Some tenants also run occasional read-heavy reporting jobs while their write activity remains steady. The company wants each tenant's capacity to follow its own demand and wants reporting readers to scale without forcing their writers to scale. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use Aurora Serverless v2 readers with promotion tiers for independent scaling. + Use a separate Aurora Serverless v2 cluster and capacity range for each tenant.
Why: Two requirements drive the design: tenants have different busy periods, and reporting readers must scale separately from writers. A Serverless v2 cluster for each tenant lets capacity track that tenant's activity. Serverless v2 readers configured with promotion tiers can scale independently for reporting spikes. Peak-sized provisioned instances retain capacity during quiet periods, while changing reader instance classes after each job adds operational work.
Wrong options: Add provisioned reporting readers and change their instance classes after each job. (Repeated class changes do not meet the requirement for readers to follow demand automatically.); Add only Serverless v2 writers and send each reporting job to its writer. (It does not provide reporting readers that scale independently of steady writer activity.); Size every tenant's provisioned writer for the fleet's busiest reporting period. (This retains provisioned capacity across tenants even when their activity is low.)

chunks.title: Aurora Serverless v2
chunks.text:
Scenario: A game studio is building a new relational backend on Aurora and does not yet know its typical database capacity. Load tests occasionally place substantial demand on the database, while development environments spend long periods at low activity. The team wants capacity to follow demand without repeatedly selecting new instance classes. Which approach meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use Aurora Serverless v2 with a low minimum and a maximum that accommodates load tests.
Why: The studio needs room for occasional substantial tests without paying for peak-sized instances throughout quiet periods. Aurora Serverless v2 can scale within a configured minimum and maximum, making a low minimum and sufficiently high maximum appropriate. A maximum set at the low-activity level would defeat the peak requirement. Provisioned instances either retain excess capacity or require repeated resizing.
Wrong options: Use Aurora Serverless v2 with a maximum fixed at the expected low-activity capacity. (That maximum would not leave capacity for the substantial load-test demand.); Use provisioned Aurora instances and revise their classes after each load test. (Revising instance classes is the repeated capacity-management work the team wants to avoid.); Use provisioned Aurora instances sized for the highest load-test result. (Peak-sized provisioned instances remain allocated during long low-activity periods.)

chunks.title: Scaling policies: target tracking, step, scheduled, predictive
chunks.text:
Scaling policies: target tracking, step, scheduled, predictive. Choose an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling policy based on what tells you capacity must change. Use target tracking to maintain a metric target, scheduled scaling for a known time, predictive scaling for recurring demand patterns, and step scaling when different metric ranges require different responses.
When to use: Choose target tracking when a valid utilization or per-instance throughput metric should stay near a target as load changes.; Choose scheduled scaling when a capacity change is needed at a known time, including a one-time event.; Choose predictive scaling when demand follows a recurring pattern; choose step scaling when the size of the response must depend on the severity of a metric breach.
Key facts: Target tracking automatically creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms used for its scaling actions.; Target tracking supports predefined metrics including average Auto Scaling group CPU utilization and ALBRequestCountPerTarget, as well as suitable custom metrics.; A target tracking metric must describe instance utilization and change proportionally with group capacity.; With multiple target tracking policies, the group scales out if any policy is ready, but scales in only if all applicable policies are ready.; A target tracking policy scales out when its metric exceeds the target—not when it falls below it.
Gotchas: The raw Amazon SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric is not suitable for target tracking; queue messages per instance can be.; Load balancer RequestCount and Latency are not suitable target tracking metrics; ALBRequestCountPerTarget is a supported predefined metric.; Do not manually edit the CloudWatch alarms that Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling manages for target tracking.
Confused with: Scheduled scaling: Acts at a known time rather than maintaining a metric target.; Predictive scaling: Fits recurring demand patterns rather than a specified one-time capacity change.; Step scaling: Uses tiered responses to metric breaches rather than automatically maintaining one target value.
ES: Elige una política de Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling según la señal que indica cuándo debe cambiar la capacidad. Usa target tracking para mantener un valor objetivo, scheduled scaling para un momento conocido, predictive scaling para patrones recurrentes y step scaling para respuestas por niveles. Target tracking crea y administra automáticamente las alarmas de CloudWatch que usa para escalar.; Target tracking admite métricas predefinidas como la utilización promedio de CPU del Auto Scaling group y ALBRequestCountPerTarget, además de métricas personalizadas adecuadas.; Una métrica para target tracking debe representar la utilización de las instancias y cambiar proporcionalmente con la capacidad del grupo.; Con varias políticas de target tracking, el grupo escala hacia afuera si cualquiera está lista, pero escala hacia adentro solo si todas las políticas aplicables están listas.; Una política de target tracking escala hacia afuera cuando su métrica supera el objetivo, no cuando cae por debajo.

chunks.title: Scaling policies: target tracking, step, scheduled, predictive
chunks.text:
Scenario: A grocery delivery service runs its dispatch application in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. Order surges recur throughout the week, but their start times and sizes vary in a recognizable pattern. The service wants capacity to follow that recurring demand rather than setting a fixed capacity for each hour. Which approach best meets this requirement?
Correct: Use predictive scaling for the Auto Scaling group.
Why: The key requirement is to use a recognizable, recurring pattern while avoiding fixed hourly capacity settings. Predictive scaling is the appropriate choice for recurring demand. Scheduled scaling fits known times but the proposed fixed daily action misses the varying timing and size. Target tracking and step scaling respond to metrics instead of choosing capacity based on the recurring pattern.
Wrong options: Use scheduled scaling with the same desired capacity every afternoon. (A fixed daily capacity does not account for the stated variations in surge timing and size.); Use step scaling with CPU alarms for moderate and severe load. (Step scaling provides tiered reactions to metric breaches, not scaling based on the recurring pattern described.); Use target tracking with a CPU utilization target. (Target tracking maintains a utilization target as measured load changes, but it does not select capacity from the recurring demand pattern requested.)

chunks.title: Scaling policies: target tracking, step, scheduled, predictive
chunks.text:
Scenario: An insurer operates two EC2 Auto Scaling groups: one processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue, and the other serves requests through an Application Load Balancer. For each group, the team wants target tracking that maintains a meaningful per-instance or per-target workload level without managing CloudWatch alarms. Which TWO metric and policy choices meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use target tracking for the web group with ALBRequestCountPerTarget. + Use target tracking for the workers with a custom metric of queued messages per instance.
Why: Target tracking needs a metric that meaningfully reflects workload relative to the group's capacity. Messages per instance can work for the queue workers, and ALBRequestCountPerTarget is a supported predefined metric for the web group; target tracking also manages its own CloudWatch alarms. Raw queue depth and total load balancer RequestCount do not vary proportionally with group size. Load balancer Latency is likewise unsuitable because it does not necessarily change proportionally.
Wrong options: Use target tracking for the web group with load balancer RequestCount. (Total load balancer RequestCount does not change proportionally with the Auto Scaling group's capacity.); Use target tracking for the web group with load balancer Latency. (Load balancer Latency does not necessarily change proportionally with group capacity.); Use target tracking for the workers with Amazon SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible. (Raw visible queue depth might not change proportionally to the number of worker instances.)

chunks.title: Scaling policies: target tracking, step, scheduled, predictive
chunks.text:
Scenario: A veterinary booking application runs in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. Appointment traffic changes unpredictably throughout the day, and average group CPU utilization reliably reflects how busy the instances are. The team wants utilization to remain near a chosen target without maintaining scaling alarms. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use target tracking with average Auto Scaling group CPU utilization as the metric.
Why: The deciding requirements are a reliable utilization metric, unpredictable load, and no alarm maintenance. Target tracking adjusts group capacity around a selected target and creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms it uses. Step scaling is useful when the team wants distinct responses for different metric ranges, but that is not required here. Fixed schedules and recurring-pattern planning do not match the described traffic.
Wrong options: Use predictive scaling based on a recurring daily traffic pattern. (The scenario specifies unpredictable changes rather than a recurring pattern to plan around.); Use scheduled scaling to increase and decrease capacity at fixed times each day. (Fixed times do not address the stated unpredictable changes in traffic.); Use step scaling with CloudWatch alarms for several CPU utilization ranges. (Step scaling can react to CPU ranges, but the team would need to maintain the alarms and responses instead of setting one target.)

chunks.title: AWS Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling (DynamoDB, ECS, Aurora)
chunks.text:
AWS Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling (DynamoDB, ECS, Aurora). Application Auto Scaling adjusts supported resources beyond EC2 Auto Scaling, including ECS services, DynamoDB provisioned capacity, Aurora replicas, and Spot Fleet requests. Choose target tracking when a supported resource should scale toward a CloudWatch metric target; choose an AWS Auto Scaling scaling plan when related resources need discovery and a shared scaling strategy.
When to use: An ECS service’s desired task count must respond to changing demand.; Provisioned capacity for a DynamoDB table or global secondary index must adjust automatically.; An Aurora cluster needs its number of read replicas adjusted.; Related scalable resources need automatic discovery and scaling recommendations.
Key facts: Application Auto Scaling target tracking scales a resource based on a target value for a specific CloudWatch metric.; Application Auto Scaling also supports step, scheduled, and predictive scaling.; AWS Auto Scaling scaling plans can cover Aurora replicas, ECS desired task counts, DynamoDB provisioned capacity, Spot Fleet target capacity, and EC2 Auto Scaling groups.; Scaling plans use Application Auto Scaling and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to adjust capacity; they provide resource discovery and built-in scaling recommendations.; In scaling plans, predictive scaling is supported for Auto Scaling groups.
Gotchas: An EC2 Auto Scaling group adjusts EC2 instance capacity, not an ECS service’s desired task count or a DynamoDB index’s provisioned capacity.; Individual Application Auto Scaling policies do not provide the resource discovery and built-in recommendations described for scaling plans.; Scheduled scaling is a poor match when the requirement is to respond to unpredictable metric changes.
Confused with: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling: It adjusts EC2 Auto Scaling group capacity; Application Auto Scaling handles supported resources such as ECS services and DynamoDB indexes.; AWS Auto Scaling scaling plans: Scaling plans discover and coordinate related scalable resources; Application Auto Scaling policies can target an individual supported resource.
ES: Application Auto Scaling ajusta recursos compatibles más allá de EC2 Auto Scaling, incluidos servicios de ECS, capacidad aprovisionada de DynamoDB, réplicas de Aurora y solicitudes de Spot Fleet. Elige target tracking si un recurso debe seguir un objetivo de una métrica de CloudWatch; elige un scaling plan de AWS Auto Scaling si necesitas descubrir recursos relacionados y aplicarles una estrategia de escalado. Target tracking de Application Auto Scaling escala un recurso según un valor objetivo de una métrica específica de CloudWatch.; Application Auto Scaling también admite step scaling, scheduled scaling y predictive scaling.; Los scaling plans de AWS Auto Scaling pueden incluir réplicas de Aurora, número deseado de tareas de ECS, capacidad aprovisionada de DynamoDB, capacidad objetivo de Spot Fleet y grupos de EC2 Auto Scaling.; Los scaling plans usan Application Auto Scaling y Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling para ajustar capacidad; ofrecen descubrimiento de recursos y recomendaciones de escalado.; En los scaling plans, predictive scaling es compatible con grupos de Auto Scaling.

chunks.title: AWS Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling (DynamoDB, ECS, Aurora)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company runs an application with an ECS service, a provisioned-capacity DynamoDB table, and an Aurora cluster with read replicas. Its infrastructure team groups the related resources in a CloudFormation stack and wants automatic resource discovery plus recommendations for balancing performance and cost as demand changes. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an AWS Auto Scaling scaling plan for the scalable resources in the CloudFormation stack.
Why: The deciding requirements are automatic discovery of related stack resources and recommendations that balance performance and cost. AWS Auto Scaling scaling plans provide both and can scale ECS desired task count, DynamoDB provisioned capacity, and Aurora read replicas. Separate Application Auto Scaling policies could adjust those resources, but they miss the requested plan-level discovery and recommendations.
Wrong options: Configure Application Auto Scaling scheduled scaling for the ECS service, DynamoDB table, and Aurora replicas. (Schedules do not provide the requested resource discovery and recommendations for changing demand.); Configure separate Application Auto Scaling target tracking policies for each supported resource. (The individual policies can scale supported resources but do not provide the requested scaling-plan discovery and built-in recommendations.); Configure target tracking on an EC2 Auto Scaling group for the application. (An EC2 Auto Scaling group adjusts EC2 capacity, not the ECS, DynamoDB, and Aurora resources that must be discovered and scaled.)

chunks.title: AWS Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling (DynamoDB, ECS, Aurora)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research portal uses an Aurora cluster for reports. Report traffic arrives at unpredictable times, and the team wants the number of Aurora read replicas to adjust automatically toward a target value for a CloudWatch metric. The writers and all other application resources must remain outside this scaling configuration. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Apply Application Auto Scaling target tracking to the Aurora read replicas.
Why: The resource to scale is the number of Aurora read replicas, not compute instances or database write capacity. Application Auto Scaling supports Aurora replicas, and its target tracking mode uses a target value for a specific CloudWatch metric. Scheduled scaling can adjust a supported resource, but it does not satisfy the requirement to respond to unpredictable metric changes.
Wrong options: Apply Application Auto Scaling target tracking to the portal’s DynamoDB provisioned read capacity. (This targets a different resource and cannot change the number of Aurora read replicas.); Apply an EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking policy to the report application’s instances. (Scaling EC2 instances does not adjust the requested number of Aurora read replicas.); Apply Application Auto Scaling scheduled scaling to the Aurora read replicas. (Scheduled scaling follows a schedule rather than the requested CloudWatch metric target during unpredictable traffic.)

chunks.title: AWS Backup centralized backup plans
chunks.text:
AWS Backup centralized backup plans. AWS Backup centralizes backup plans, resource assignments, and monitoring across supported AWS services. Choose it when a scenario requires one policy-based approach across resource types or AWS accounts, scheduled cross-Region or cross-account copies, or retention protected by AWS Backup Vault Lock.
When to use: Apply consistent backup schedules and retention to supported resource types, including resources selected by tag.; Manage backup policies across accounts in an existing AWS Organizations structure.; Copy backups to another Region or account for disaster recovery.; Prevent early deletion of recovery points with AWS Backup Vault Lock.
Key facts: Backup plans define requirements and can be assigned to supported resources across services.; AWS Backup can automatically copy backups across Regions as part of a scheduled plan and can copy them across accounts in an AWS Organizations structure.; AWS Backup Vault Lock in Compliance mode cannot be removed after its grace time expires; Governance mode can be managed by users with sufficient IAM permissions.; Vault Lock retention limits apply to new backup and copy jobs, not recovery points already in the vault.; AWS Backup does not govern backups created outside AWS Backup.
Gotchas: Native service backups are not automatically covered by an AWS Backup plan or its centralized governance.; The relationship between AWS Backup and native backups varies by service; keeping both can create unintended duplicate costs.; Not every supported resource type offers incremental backups or cold-storage transitions.; A locked vault can retain backups until their configured lifecycle ends, creating storage costs if retention is set incorrectly.
Confused with: EBS snapshots and Data Lifecycle Manager: Use them for EBS-focused snapshot or AMI schedules, not centralized plans across multiple supported services.; RDS automated backups: They address RDS recovery, not one backup policy across RDS and other resource types.; DynamoDB PITR: It protects DynamoDB tables, not organization-wide backup plans and vault retention controls.
ES: AWS Backup centraliza backup plans, la asignación de recursos y el monitoreo de backups entre servicios AWS compatibles. Elígelo cuando necesites políticas para varios tipos de recursos o cuentas, copias programadas entre Regions o cuentas, o retención protegida con AWS Backup Vault Lock. Los backup plans definen requisitos y pueden asignarse a recursos compatibles de distintos servicios.; AWS Backup puede copiar backups automáticamente entre Regions como parte de un plan programado y entre cuentas de una estructura de AWS Organizations.; AWS Backup Vault Lock en Compliance mode no puede quitarse después del grace time; Governance mode puede ser administrado por usuarios con permisos IAM suficientes.; Los límites de retención de Vault Lock se aplican a nuevos trabajos de backup y copia, no a los puntos de recuperación que ya están en el vault.; AWS Backup no administra los backups creados fuera de AWS Backup.

chunks.title: AWS Backup centralized backup plans
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab adds supported EBS volumes, EFS file systems, and DynamoDB tables as new projects begin. Each resource is tagged with its project's protection class, and the lab wants new resources to receive the appropriate backup schedule without creating a service-specific schedule every time. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create AWS Backup plans for the protection classes and assign supported resources to the plans by tag.
Why: The lab needs backup schedules assigned by protection class across several supported services. AWS Backup plans can be applied to resources using tags, avoiding a separate backup configuration for each new resource. Data Lifecycle Manager and DynamoDB point-in-time recovery do not provide the required cross-service plan. Configuring native backups separately also fails the operational-overhead constraint.
Wrong options: Configure native backups separately for EBS, EFS, and DynamoDB whenever a new project is tagged. (Separate native configurations preserve the per-service work the lab explicitly wants to avoid.); Enable DynamoDB point-in-time recovery on each project table and use it to schedule backups for the other resources. (DynamoDB point-in-time recovery does not assign backup schedules to EBS or EFS resources.); Create Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies for the protection classes and select all tagged resources. (Data Lifecycle Manager is not the cross-service backup-plan solution needed for EFS and DynamoDB alongside EBS.)

chunks.title: AWS Backup centralized backup plans
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare network has an existing AWS Organizations structure with workloads in multiple accounts. It must centrally apply backup policies, keep copies in a separate account, and prevent even privileged users from removing the backup vault's retention protection after an approved review period. Which TWO actions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Apply AWS Backup Vault Lock in Compliance mode to the destination vault and allow its grace time to expire. + Use AWS Backup cross-account management policies and configure cross-account backup copies within the organization.
Why: There are two separate requirements: centrally managed cross-account protection and retention protection that privileged users cannot remove after review. AWS Backup cross-account policies and copies address the first; they require the organization's existing AWS Organizations structure. Vault Lock in Compliance mode addresses the second once its grace time expires. Governance mode is insufficient because users with sufficient IAM permissions can remove its lock.
Wrong options: Enable DynamoDB point-in-time recovery on tables in the workload accounts. (Table-level recovery does not meet the requirements for central policies, account copies, and vault protection.); Create Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager schedules independently in every workload account. (Independent account schedules do not provide the required centralized policy management.); Apply AWS Backup Vault Lock in Governance mode to the destination vault. (A user with sufficient IAM permissions can remove a Governance mode lock.)

chunks.title: AWS Backup centralized backup plans
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company runs supported Amazon EBS, Amazon EFS, and Amazon RDS resources in several accounts under AWS Organizations. Its recovery policy requires consistent backup schedules and copies in a second AWS Region, without maintaining separate automation for each service and account. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS Backup policies across the organization and backup plans with scheduled cross-Region copies for the supported resources.
Why: The deciding requirements are consistent protection across three resource types and multiple organization accounts, plus scheduled copies to another Region. AWS Backup provides centrally managed plans and policies for supported resources and can include cross-Region copies in a schedule. EBS-focused lifecycle schedules and RDS automated backups each cover too narrow a set of resources. Separate service-level schedules also retain the operational work the company wants to remove.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager schedules in each account and copy the resulting backups to the second Region. (Data Lifecycle Manager does not provide the required centralized backup plans across EBS, EFS, and RDS.); Create service-specific backup schedules in each account and collect their status in a central dashboard. (A dashboard does not eliminate the separate schedules and account-level automation the company wants to avoid.); Configure RDS automated backups in each account and use their schedules as the recovery policy for all three resource types. (RDS automated backups do not schedule protection for the EBS and EFS resources.)

chunks.title: AWS Batch
chunks.text:
AWS Batch. AWS Batch is a fully managed way to queue, schedule, and run batch workloads without building a batch scheduler. Choose it when the requirement is managed job scheduling and elastic compute, not merely a place to run containers.
When to use: Independent simulation, analytics, or ML jobs arrive in batches and need managed scheduling.; Compute capacity should adjust to submitted jobs, potentially using EC2 Spot Instances to reduce cost.; A team needs batch scheduling while running jobs on Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, or AWS Fargate.; SageMaker Training jobs need configurable queues and priorities.
Key facts: AWS Batch provisions compute resources in response to submitted jobs and optimizes workload distribution.; It runs containerized batch workloads on top of Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS.; Its compute options include EC2 instances and Fargate resources; batch workloads can use Spot or On-Demand Instances.; AWS Batch can queue SageMaker Training jobs according to configured priorities and resource availability.
Gotchas: Fargate supplies container compute; choosing Fargate alone does not address a requirement for managed batch queues and scheduling.; An existing Kubernetes workflow does not rule out AWS Batch: Batch can run workloads on Amazon EKS.; Choosing EC2 Spot capacity alone does not eliminate the work of building or managing a batch scheduler.
Confused with: AWS Fargate: Fargate provides container compute without managing servers; Batch adds managed batch queues and scheduling and can use Fargate resources.; Amazon EKS: EKS supports Kubernetes orchestration; Batch can run batch jobs on EKS while managing batch scheduling.; Amazon ECS on EC2: ECS on EC2 runs containers on EC2 capacity; Batch addresses the additional need to queue and schedule batch jobs.
ES: AWS Batch permite poner en cola, programar y ejecutar cargas de trabajo por lotes sin que tengas que crear un programador de trabajos. Elígelo cuando el requisito sea la programación administrada de trabajos y la capacidad de cómputo elástica, no solo ejecutar contenedores. AWS Batch aprovisiona recursos de cómputo según los trabajos enviados y optimiza la distribución de la carga.; Ejecuta cargas de trabajo por lotes en contenedores sobre Amazon ECS y Amazon EKS.; Sus opciones de cómputo incluyen instancias EC2 y recursos de Fargate; las cargas por lotes pueden usar Spot u On-Demand Instances.; AWS Batch puede poner en cola trabajos de SageMaker Training según prioridades configuradas y disponibilidad de recursos.

chunks.title: AWS Batch
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab runs thousands of independent, containerized climate simulations after each new dataset arrives. Jobs may wait for capacity, and the lab wants to use EC2 Spot Instances to reduce compute costs without operating batch scheduling software. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Submit the simulations to an AWS Batch job queue backed by an EC2 Spot compute environment.
Why: The deciding requirements are queued batch jobs, EC2 Spot capacity, and no self-managed batch scheduler. AWS Batch schedules submitted jobs and can run batch workloads using Spot Instances. ECS on EC2 Spot provides a plausible compute foundation, but the proposed design makes the lab build its own job queue and scheduler.
Wrong options: Deploy a worker application with AWS Elastic Beanstalk and have it poll a custom simulation queue. (A web application deployment platform does not remove the need to implement the specified batch queue and scheduling behavior.); Run the containers on an Amazon ECS cluster backed by EC2 Spot Instances and build a job queue and scheduler. (It can use the requested capacity, but the lab would still have to build and operate its batch scheduling components.); Run each simulation as an AWS Fargate task and build a queue to start tasks when capacity is available. (It leaves queue management to the lab and does not select the requested EC2 Spot Instances.)

chunks.title: AWS Batch
chunks.text:
Scenario: A genomics company has containerized analysis jobs and an established Kubernetes workflow on Amazon EKS. New sequencing runs arrive unpredictably; the company needs jobs queued and compute provisioned in response to submissions without administering batch scheduling software. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS Batch to queue the analysis jobs and run the batch workloads on Amazon EKS.
Why: The company needs both its established EKS workflow and managed scheduling for variable batches of jobs. AWS Batch can run batch workloads on Amazon EKS and provision resources in response to submitted jobs. Submitting Kubernetes Jobs directly to EKS is plausible, but the proposed solution adds a scheduler the company explicitly does not want to administer.
Wrong options: Use AWS Batch to queue the analysis jobs and run the workloads on Amazon ECS instead of EKS. (It supplies managed scheduling but does not preserve the stated EKS-based Kubernetes workflow.); Run the analysis containers on AWS Fargate and develop a queue to submit them as capacity becomes available. (It requires a custom queue and does not retain the stated EKS-based workflow.); Submit Kubernetes Jobs directly to Amazon EKS and develop a batch queue and scheduler for incoming runs. (It retains EKS but requires the company to administer the batch scheduling software it wants to avoid.)

chunks.title: AWS Budgets and budget actions
chunks.text:
AWS Budgets and budget actions. AWS Budgets tracks cost, usage, and RI or Savings Plans utilization and coverage against thresholds. Choose it when a scenario requires a threshold notification or a configured action, rather than analysis of spending trends.
When to use: Notify a team when actual or forecasted cost or usage approaches a budget.; Alert when RI or Savings Plans utilization or coverage falls below a target.; Apply an IAM policy or SCP after a cost or usage threshold is reached.
Key facts: Cost and usage budgets can notify on actual or forecasted amounts; RI and Savings Plans budgets can notify when utilization or coverage falls below a target.; Notifications can go to email, an Amazon SNS topic, or both.; Budget actions can run automatically or require manual approval. Available actions include applying an IAM policy or SCP and targeting specific EC2 or RDS instances.; A management account can apply an SCP to another account, but cannot target EC2 or RDS instances in another account.; AWS Budgets information is updated up to three times a day, typically 8–12 hours after the previous update.
Gotchas: A budget threshold is not a real-time spending cap: billing and notification delays can allow additional costs to accrue.; RI or Savings Plans utilization measures use of a commitment; coverage measures how much eligible usage the commitment covers.; A budget created in the management account is not automatically visible to users in the member account it tracks.
Confused with: AWS Cost Explorer: Use Cost Explorer to visualize or forecast spend; use AWS Budgets when a threshold must send an alert or trigger an action.; AWS Cost and Usage Report: Use the report for granular billing data and custom analysis, not a budget-threshold action.; Cost allocation tags: Tags attribute costs to teams or projects; they do not themselves issue budget alerts.
ES: AWS Budgets compara costos, uso y utilización o cobertura de RI y Savings Plans con umbrales. Elígelo cuando necesitas una notificación por umbral o una acción configurada, en lugar de analizar tendencias de gasto. Los presupuestos de costo y uso pueden notificar sobre valores reales o pronosticados; los de RI y Savings Plans pueden avisar cuando la utilización o cobertura cae por debajo de un objetivo.; Puedes enviar notificaciones por correo electrónico, a un tema de Amazon SNS o a ambos.; Las budget actions pueden ejecutarse automáticamente o requerir aprobación manual. Incluyen aplicar una política de IAM o un SCP y actuar sobre instancias EC2 o RDS específicas.; La cuenta de administración puede aplicar un SCP a otra cuenta, pero no puede actuar sobre instancias EC2 o RDS de otra cuenta.; La información de AWS Budgets se actualiza hasta tres veces al día, normalmente 8–12 horas después de la actualización anterior.

chunks.title: AWS Budgets and budget actions
chunks.text:
Scenario: A nonprofit uses an AWS Organizations management account to oversee a member account dedicated to a grant-funded project. It wants a forecasted monthly cost warning and, when the project's cost threshold is reached, an automatic restriction on provisioning new resources in the member account. The finance team will manage the controls from the management account rather than target individual instances. Which two configurations meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure an automatic AWS Budgets action in the management account to apply an SCP to the member account at the cost threshold. + In the management account, create an AWS Budgets cost budget that tracks the member account and sends a forecasted-cost notification.
Why: This scenario requires both a forecasted cost warning and an automatic cross-account restriction. A management-account budget can track a member account's costs and send a forecasted notification; its action can apply an SCP to another account. Targeting EC2 instances from the management account fails because budget actions cannot target EC2 instances in another account. The SCP action is threshold-driven, not a guarantee that spending stops immediately.
Wrong options: Create an AWS Budgets usage budget for the member account and notify on forecasted service usage. (A usage threshold does not meet the stated requirement for a forecasted monthly cost warning.); From the management account, configure a budget action to target EC2 instances in the member account. (A management account cannot target EC2 instances in another account with a budget action.); Use AWS Cost Explorer forecasts for the warning and cost allocation tags to restrict member-account provisioning. (Tags attribute costs but do not restrict provisioning, and this combination does not provide a budget-threshold action.)

chunks.title: AWS Budgets and budget actions
chunks.text:
Scenario: A small publisher expects its AWS costs to rise during a seasonal launch. The finance team wants an email before the month's forecasted spending exceeds a fixed target; it does not need a custom billing-data analysis. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an AWS Budgets monthly cost budget with a forecasted threshold and an email notification.
Why: The deciding requirement is an email tied to a forecasted monthly spending threshold. AWS Budgets supports forecasted cost notifications and can send them to an email address. Cost Explorer helps visualize forecasts, but reviewing one each morning misses the requested automatic alert. Neither a billing-data export nor cost allocation tags provides that alert on its own.
Wrong options: Export the AWS Cost and Usage Report to Amazon S3 for the finance team to query. (Granular billing data supports analysis but does not by itself send the requested threshold notification.); Activate cost allocation tags for the publisher's launch resources. (Tags help attribute costs but do not by themselves alert on forecasted spending.); Use AWS Cost Explorer to review its spending forecast each morning. (Cost Explorer can show a forecast, but manual review does not provide the requested budget-threshold email.)

chunks.title: AWS Config rules and configuration history
chunks.text:
AWS Config rules and configuration history. AWS Config records resource configurations and relationships over time, and AWS Config rules evaluate recorded resources for compliance. Choose it when the decision depends on historical configuration, compliance status, or remediation of a noncompliant resource—not on who made an API call.
When to use: An auditor needs to see how a resource was configured at a past point in time.; A team needs to evaluate resources against configuration policies and identify noncompliance.; A team wants a Config rule to trigger remediation through an AWS Systems Manager Automation document.; An organization needs a centralized inventory and compliance view across accounts and Regions.
Key facts: AWS Config records configurations and relationships for selected resource types.; Configuration snapshots and history are delivered to an Amazon S3 bucket.; AWS Config rules evaluate recorded resources and flag noncompliant resources.; Remediation uses AWS Systems Manager Automation documents associated with Config rules.; An AWS Config aggregator collects configuration and compliance data from multiple accounts and Regions into one account and Region.
Gotchas: CloudTrail answers who made an API call; Config answers how a resource was configured.; A configuration history is not, by itself, a compliance rule or an automatic fix.; An aggregator provides a centralized view; it does not replace recording and evaluation in the source accounts and Regions.
Confused with: AWS CloudTrail: Use CloudTrail for API activity attribution; use Config for resource configuration history and compliance.; Amazon CloudWatch: CloudWatch monitors metrics and operational signals; Config evaluates resource configurations against rules.; VPC Flow Logs: Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata, not historical security group configurations.
ES: AWS Config registra las configuraciones y relaciones de los recursos a lo largo del tiempo, y AWS Config rules evalúa si los recursos registrados cumplen las políticas. Elígelo cuando necesites conocer una configuración anterior, evaluar el cumplimiento o corregir un recurso no conforme, no cuando necesites saber quién hizo una llamada a la API. AWS Config registra las configuraciones y relaciones de los tipos de recursos que selecciones.; Las instantáneas y el historial de configuración se entregan a un bucket de Amazon S3.; AWS Config rules evalúa los recursos registrados y marca los que no cumplen.; La corrección utiliza AWS Systems Manager Automation documents asociados a Config rules.; Un AWS Config aggregator reúne datos de configuración y cumplimiento de varias cuentas y Regions en una cuenta y Region.

chunks.title: AWS Config rules and configuration history
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company records resource configurations and evaluates compliance in several AWS accounts and Regions. Its governance team now needs one place to view resource inventory and compliance results from all of them without building a separate collection system. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure an AWS Config aggregator for the accounts and Regions.
Why: The requirement is a centralized view of configuration inventory and compliance across accounts and Regions. An AWS Config aggregator collects that data into one account and Region. A CloudTrail trail centralizes a different kind of evidence—API activity—while manually combining snapshots adds operational work.
Wrong options: Use an AWS CloudTrail organization trail to consolidate API activity. (A trail consolidates API activity rather than AWS Config inventory and compliance data.); Use Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to display resource metrics from the accounts. (Metrics dashboards do not provide the requested centralized configuration and compliance view.); Export configuration snapshots from each account and manually combine the results. (Manual consolidation adds the collection work the company wants to avoid.)

chunks.title: AWS Config rules and configuration history
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company checks its EC2 security groups against an approved inbound-port policy. When a group becomes noncompliant, the company wants the corrective action to run automatically rather than wait for an engineer. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Evaluate the groups with an AWS Config rule and configure automatic remediation using an associated Systems Manager Automation document.
Why: The company needs both configuration-policy evaluation and an automatic corrective action. AWS Config rules flag noncompliant resources, and Config can remediate them using associated Systems Manager Automation documents. Recording history or sending a notification still leaves the correction to an engineer.
Wrong options: Monitor EC2 metrics with Amazon CloudWatch alarms and notify engineers when an alarm fires. (EC2 metrics do not evaluate the inbound-port policy, and notification is not automatic remediation.); Record security group history in AWS Config and have engineers correct each change after reviewing the history. (History supports investigation, but manual review does not meet the automatic-correction requirement.); Send AWS Config noncompliance notifications through Amazon SNS and ask engineers to update the groups. (Notifications identify a problem, but an engineer would still have to perform the correction.)

chunks.title: AWS Control Tower landing zone and controls
chunks.text:
AWS Control Tower landing zone and controls. AWS Control Tower sets up and governs a multi-account landing zone by orchestrating services such as AWS Organizations, AWS Service Catalog, and AWS IAM Identity Center. Choose it when an exam scenario requires standardized account provisioning and ongoing governance with minimal setup effort.
When to use: A central team needs to establish a secure, compliant multi-account environment.; Distributed teams need new accounts with pre-approved configurations.; Administrators need controls and a central view of noncompliant resources across accounts and OUs.
