Key facts: A landing zone contains the OUs, accounts, users, and other resources subject to enterprise-wide governance.; Account Factory provides configurable templates and automates account provisioning and enrollment.; Control Tower controls can be preventive, detective, or proactive.; The dashboard shows provisioned accounts, enabled controls, and noncompliant resources organized by account and OU.; Control Tower orchestrates other AWS services; AWS Organizations supplies underlying multi-account management capabilities.
Gotchas: AWS Organizations provides central account management and SCPs, but choosing it alone does not select Control Tower's orchestrated landing zone and Account Factory workflow.; AWS Service Catalog participates in Account Factory, but a Service Catalog product alone is not the complete Control Tower governance solution.; AWS IAM Identity Center is an integrated service, not a substitute for landing-zone governance.
Confused with: AWS Organizations: Organizations provides foundational multi-account management; Control Tower orchestrates a landing zone, Account Factory, controls, and oversight.; AWS Service Catalog: Account Factory builds on Service Catalog provisioned products, but Control Tower also automates account enrollment and application of controls.
ES: AWS Control Tower configura y gobierna una landing zone de múltiples cuentas mediante la coordinación de servicios como AWS Organizations, AWS Service Catalog y AWS IAM Identity Center. Elígelo cuando un escenario requiera aprovisionamiento estandarizado de cuentas y gobierno continuo con un esfuerzo de configuración mínimo. Una landing zone contiene las OU, cuentas, usuarios y otros recursos sujetos al gobierno de toda la empresa.; Account Factory ofrece plantillas configurables y automatiza el aprovisionamiento y la incorporación de cuentas.; Los controls de Control Tower pueden ser preventive, detective o proactive.; El dashboard muestra las cuentas aprovisionadas, los controls habilitados y los recursos no conformes organizados por cuenta y OU.; Control Tower coordina otros servicios de AWS; AWS Organizations aporta capacidades subyacentes de administración de múltiples cuentas.

chunks.title: AWS Control Tower landing zone and controls
chunks.text:
Scenario: A growing architecture firm is opening separate AWS accounts for its project teams. Its small cloud team needs a best-practice multi-account environment, standardized account creation, and ongoing governance without assembling each capability separately. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Set up an AWS Control Tower landing zone and provision accounts through Account Factory.
Why: The deciding requirements are a best-practice multi-account environment, standardized account creation, and minimal setup effort. AWS Control Tower establishes a landing zone and provides Account Factory for provisioning accounts with pre-approved configurations. AWS Organizations is an important underlying service, but using its APIs and SCPs directly leaves the team to put the broader workflow together.
Wrong options: Configure AWS IAM Identity Center for access to accounts created by each project team. (Identity Center addresses access but not the requested standardized account creation and landing-zone governance.); Publish AWS Service Catalog products for teams to use when configuring their accounts. (Service Catalog products alone do not provide the requested orchestrated landing zone and ongoing governance.); Create accounts with AWS Organizations APIs and manage SCPs directly. (Organizations provides account management and SCPs, but this option leaves the team to assemble the requested landing-zone and provisioning workflow.)

chunks.title: AWS Control Tower landing zone and controls
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research network already uses an AWS Control Tower landing zone. Its central administrators need to see which accounts and OUs contain resources that do not conform to enabled controls, without building a separate reporting view. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use the AWS Control Tower dashboard to view noncompliant resources by account and OU.
Why: The network already has a Control Tower landing zone, so the decision is about its built-in oversight capability. The Control Tower dashboard displays noncompliant resources organized by account and OU, along with information about enabled controls. Account Factory is a plausible Control Tower feature, but its role is account provisioning, not this reporting view.
Wrong options: Use Account Factory templates as the reporting view for existing resources. (Account Factory standardizes account provisioning rather than reporting noncompliant resources.); Review AWS Organizations account and OU listings as the compliance report. (An account and OU listing does not supply the requested Control Tower view of noncompliant resources.); Use AWS IAM Identity Center to review access to each research account. (Access management does not provide the requested view of noncompliant resources by account and OU.)

chunks.title: AWS Organizations, OUs and consolidated billing
chunks.text:
AWS Organizations, OUs and consolidated billing. AWS Organizations groups separate AWS accounts into organizational units (OUs) for central governance and provides a single consolidated bill. Choose it when a scenario needs account-level boundaries, policies applied to groups of accounts, and simplified payment across accounts.
When to use: Workloads need separate accounts for security, cost, or operational boundaries.; Several accounts should inherit a policy-based control from the same OU.; Accounts need one consolidated bill and a single payment method.
Key facts: An AWS account is a boundary for permissions, security, costs, and workloads.; An OU groups accounts for administration; accounts in an OU inherit a policy-based control attached to it.; OUs can be nested, and accounts can be moved between OUs.; AWS Organizations provides a single consolidated bill; AWS Cost Explorer can show usage and track costs across accounts.; Service control policies (SCPs) can control access to AWS resources, services, and Regions within an organization.
Gotchas: Tags can help classify resources, but they do not replace separate account boundaries.; AWS Cost Explorer tracks costs; it does not itself create the consolidated bill.; An OU organizes accounts and inherits controls; it is not a substitute for assigning users access through AWS IAM Identity Center.
Confused with: AWS Cost Explorer: Cost Explorer helps view usage and costs; AWS Organizations provides the consolidated bill.; AWS IAM Identity Center: IAM Identity Center provides access to accounts and resources; Organizations groups accounts and applies organization policies.
ES: AWS Organizations agrupa cuentas de AWS independientes en organizational units (OUs) para administrarlas de forma centralizada y proporciona una sola factura consolidada. Elígelo cuando necesites límites entre cuentas, políticas para grupos de cuentas y un pago simplificado. Una cuenta de AWS es un límite para permisos, seguridad, costos y cargas de trabajo.; Una OU agrupa cuentas para administrarlas; las cuentas de la OU heredan un control basado en políticas que se adjunte a ella.; Puedes anidar OUs y mover cuentas entre ellas.; AWS Organizations proporciona una factura consolidada; AWS Cost Explorer permite consultar el uso y seguir los costos entre cuentas.; Las service control policies (SCPs) pueden controlar el acceso a recursos, servicios y AWS Regions dentro de una organización.

chunks.title: AWS Organizations, OUs and consolidated billing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare analytics company is adding AWS accounts for new teams. Its finance group requires a single bill, while security requires a common policy-based control for all accounts handling regulated data, including accounts added later. Which two actions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Place regulated-data accounts in an AWS Organizations OU and attach the required control to the OU. + Use AWS Organizations consolidated billing for the company's accounts.
Why: The two independent requirements are an inherited control for a growing group of accounts and a single bill. Place regulated-data accounts, including new ones, in an OU with the control attached, and use AWS Organizations consolidated billing. AWS Cost Explorer helps analyze costs but does not itself create the consolidated bill; IAM Identity Center assigns access rather than the requested OU-level control.
Wrong options: Use AWS Cost Explorer to combine usage views for the teams' accounts. (Cost Explorer provides usage and cost visibility but does not produce the required single bill.); Use AWS RAM to share security resources with the regulated-data accounts. (Resource sharing does not attach an inheritable policy-based control to the accounts.); Use AWS IAM Identity Center to assign the same job-based access to users in each account. (Job-based user access does not make accounts inherit the requested OU-level control.)

chunks.title: AWS Organizations, OUs and consolidated billing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute uses AWS Organizations to group accounts by project stage. A pilot account is moving into a regulated stage, where accounts must inherit the same policy-based control without configuring that control separately on each account. Which action meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Move the pilot account into the regulated OU that has the required policy-based control attached.
Why: The deciding requirement is automatic inheritance of a control already associated with a group of accounts. AWS Organizations lets you move an account into an OU, and accounts in that OU inherit its attached policy-based control. Sharing resources through AWS RAM or viewing costs in Cost Explorer does not change which OU controls the account inherits.
Wrong options: Apply a tag policy to the pilot account and leave it in its current OU. (A tag policy does not place the account under the regulated OU's inherited control.); Use AWS Cost Explorer to group the pilot account's usage with the regulated accounts. (Grouping cost information does not apply a policy-based control to the account.); Use AWS RAM to share the regulated accounts' resources with the pilot account. (Sharing resources does not make the pilot account inherit an OU policy-based control.)

chunks.title: AWS Organizations, OUs and consolidated billing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A game studio has separate AWS accounts for its regional teams. It uses AWS IAM Identity Center to assign access by job role, but the security team also needs a central way to control which AWS Regions those accounts can access. Which solution best meets the additional governance requirement?
Correct: Group the accounts in an AWS Organizations OU and apply an appropriate service control policy (SCP).
Why: The studio already has job-based access; its new requirement is a central governance control over AWS Region access. AWS Organizations SCPs can control access to Regions, and attaching the control to an OU lets accounts in that OU inherit it. A tag policy classifies resources rather than meeting this access-control requirement.
Wrong options: Use AWS RAM to share approved resources across the regional accounts. (Sharing resources does not provide the requested central control over Region access.); Apply an AWS Organizations tag policy to classify each team's resources by Region. (Resource classification does not control which AWS Regions an account can access.); Use AWS Cost Explorer to track each regional team's usage across accounts. (Cost Explorer tracks usage and costs rather than controlling access to AWS Regions.)

chunks.title: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) and VPC sharing
chunks.text:
AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) and VPC sharing. AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) shares supported resources across accounts without creating a copy in each account. For VPC sharing, choose AWS RAM when accounts in the same AWS Organizations organization need to deploy their own application resources into centrally managed subnets.
When to use: Several accounts need to use one supported resource while the owning account retains ownership.; Accounts in an organization or OU need access without maintaining a list of account IDs.; Application teams in the same organization need separate accounts but shared VPC subnets.
Key facts: A VPC owner can share subnets with participants in the same AWS Organizations organization; participants manage their own application resources, not those of the owner or other participants.; After sharing within an organization is enabled, shares with its accounts do not require invitations. Shares with accounts outside the organization require recipient acceptance.; For cross-account shares, AWS RAM permissions set the maximum access; the consuming account must also grant its roles or users access through IAM identity-based policies.; A resource share containing Regional resources must be in the same Region as those resources. AWS RAM has no additional charge, though resource usage charges vary.
Gotchas: Sharing a subnet does not transfer ownership of the VPC or let participants manage another account's application resources.; An AWS RAM share alone does not grant every role in a consuming account permission to use the resource.; A general AWS RAM share can target specific external accounts, but VPC subnet sharing requires participants to be in the owner's organization.
Confused with: Resource-based policies: Some resources support cross-account resource policies, but AWS RAM can target an organization or OU without enumerating account IDs.; VPC peering: VPC peering connects separate VPCs; subnet sharing lets participating accounts deploy resources into subnets of the owner's VPC.
ES: AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) comparte recursos compatibles entre cuentas sin crear una copia en cada una. Para VPC sharing, elige AWS RAM cuando las cuentas de la misma organización de AWS Organizations deban implementar sus propios recursos de aplicación en subredes administradas centralmente. El propietario de una VPC puede compartir subredes con participantes de la misma organización de AWS Organizations; cada participante administra sus propios recursos de aplicación, no los del propietario ni los de otros participantes.; Una vez habilitada la opción de compartir dentro de la organización, las cuentas de esa organización no necesitan invitaciones. Las cuentas externas deben aceptar una invitación.; En una compartición entre cuentas, los permisos de AWS RAM fijan el acceso máximo; la cuenta consumidora también debe conceder acceso a sus roles o usuarios mediante políticas IAM basadas en identidad.; Un resource share que contiene recursos Regional debe estar en la misma Region que esos recursos. AWS RAM no tiene cargos adicionales, aunque los cargos por uso del recurso varían.

chunks.title: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) and VPC sharing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company keeps a supported network resource in a central AWS account. Several application accounts in one AWS Organizations OU need to use it, and the OU's membership changes regularly. The network team wants to avoid creating a copy in each account or updating access whenever an account joins the OU. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an AWS RAM resource share for the central resource and specify the OU as a principal.
Why: The deciding requirement is access for a changing OU without duplicating the resource or maintaining account IDs. AWS RAM supports sharing a resource with an OU as a principal, so the team can maintain one owned resource. Sharing by account ID or listing principals in a resource policy would require updates as accounts change; separate copies add maintenance.
Wrong options: Attach a cross-account resource-based policy that lists the current application account principals. (Listing current principals does not meet the requirement to avoid updates when OU membership changes.); Create an AWS RAM resource share and add each current application account by account ID. (Sharing by individual account ID would require updates as OU membership changes.); Create a copy of the resource in each application account and apply the same configuration to every copy. (Separate copies increase the provisioning and maintenance work the team wants to avoid.)

chunks.title: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) and VPC sharing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization uses separate AWS accounts for its analysis teams, all in the same AWS Organizations organization. The network team owns a centrally managed VPC, and each analysis team must launch its own EC2 instances into that VPC while remaining unable to manage another team's instances. The organization also wants to avoid maintaining a VPC for every team. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Use AWS RAM to share subnets of the central VPC with the teams' accounts.
Why: The teams need to deploy their own instances into one centrally managed VPC, not merely connect separate VPCs. VPC subnet sharing through AWS RAM allows accounts in the same organization to create application resources in shared subnets. Participants cannot manage resources belonging to the owner or other participants. Transit Gateway and peering can connect separate VPCs, but those options retain a VPC per team.
Wrong options: Give every team a VPC in its own account and connect each one to the central VPC with VPC peering. (Peering provides connectivity between VPCs rather than letting teams launch instances into the centrally managed VPC.); Give every team a VPC in its own account and connect the VPCs with AWS Transit Gateway. (This connects separate VPCs but still requires a VPC for every team.); Create all team instances in the network account's VPC and let teams administer the shared instances. (The teams must create and manage their own instances from their separate accounts.)

chunks.title: Selecting backup vs archival solutions
chunks.text:
Selecting backup vs archival solutions. Choose AWS Backup when the requirement is to schedule, manage, and restore protected resources through centralized backup plans. For backups that must be retained longer but are rarely needed, consider a plan that transitions eligible backups from warm to cold storage.
When to use: Several AWS resource types need consistent backup schedules and centralized monitoring.; Resources need recoverable backups now and lower-cost storage later.; Backup policies must be applied by resource tags or across accounts in an AWS Organization.
Key facts: AWS Backup uses backup plans to define requirements and apply them to resources.; Backup plans can be assigned to resources using tags.; Lifecycle policies can transition backups from warm to cold storage on a defined schedule; cold-storage eligibility depends on the resource type.; AWS Backup can back up and restore AWS Storage Gateway volumes.; Incremental backups are available for supported resource types, but not every resource type supports them.
Gotchas: An archive of exported data is not a substitute for a centralized plan that backs up the source resources.; Do not assume every AWS Backup resource type can transition to cold storage or use incremental backups.; AWS Backup does not govern backups created outside AWS Backup.
Confused with: Amazon S3 Glacier: Consider archival storage for retained objects; choose AWS Backup when the requirement is to schedule and govern backups of supported resources.; Native service backups: A service's own backup mechanism may protect that service, but AWS Backup provides centralized plans and monitoring across supported resources.
ES: Elige AWS Backup cuando necesites programar, administrar y restaurar recursos protegidos mediante planes de respaldo centralizados. Si debes conservar los respaldos por más tiempo, pero rara vez los necesitas, considera un plan que traslade los respaldos elegibles de almacenamiento warm a cold. AWS Backup usa backup plans para definir requisitos y aplicarlos a los recursos.; Puedes asignar backup plans a los recursos mediante etiquetas.; Las políticas de ciclo de vida pueden trasladar respaldos de almacenamiento warm a cold según un calendario; la elegibilidad para cold depende del tipo de recurso.; AWS Backup puede respaldar y restaurar volúmenes de AWS Storage Gateway.; Hay respaldos incrementales para los tipos de recursos compatibles, pero no todos los tipos los admiten.

chunks.title: Selecting backup vs archival solutions
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio runs applications on Amazon EC2 instances backed by EBS volumes and stores shared project files on Amazon EFS. Administrators currently maintain separate backup scripts and need one place to schedule protection and check backup activity. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create AWS Backup plans for the EBS-backed instances and EFS file systems, and monitor backup jobs in AWS Backup.
Why: The deciding requirement is centralized protection for two supported resource types, with less script maintenance. AWS Backup provides backup plans and a consolidated view of backup activity for supported resources, including EBS-backed EC2 instances and EFS file systems. Exporting files for archival does not establish a centrally managed backup plan for both sources.
Wrong options: Configure each resource type's native backup process independently and review backup activity in each service. (Service-by-service management misses the requirement for one place to schedule and monitor backups.); Keep separate backup scripts for EC2 and EFS, and combine their logs in an administrator-managed dashboard. (This retains the separate scripts and monitoring work the studio wants to eliminate.); Export project files to Amazon S3 Glacier and continue using separate scripts to protect the EC2 instances. (Archiving files does not provide the requested centralized schedules and activity view for both resource types.)

chunks.title: Selecting backup vs archival solutions
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research group uses AWS Backup plans to protect a set of resources whose backups are eligible for cold storage. The group expects to use recent backups for recovery, but older backups must be retained for a long time and are rarely needed. Which change meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively while keeping backup management centralized?
Correct: Add lifecycle policies that transition eligible backups from warm to cold storage after the recent-recovery period.
Why: The group needs backups for recent recovery and long retention, but older backups are rarely used. AWS Backup lifecycle policies can transition eligible backups from warm to lower-cost cold storage on a defined schedule without replacing the backup plans. Keeping everything warm misses the storage-cost objective; exporting files instead would not maintain managed backups of the resources.
Wrong options: Keep every backup in warm storage for its entire retention period. (This preserves the backup plans but does not use the available lower-cost cold storage for older backups.); Replace the centralized plans with independently managed native backups for each resource type. (Separate native processes abandon the required centralized backup management.); Stop the backup plans and export only the oldest research files to Amazon S3 Glacier. (An export of files does not preserve centralized backup-plan protection of the resources.)

chunks.title: Bastion hosts vs Systems Manager Session Manager
chunks.text:
Bastion hosts vs Systems Manager Session Manager. Session Manager provides shell access to managed EC2 instances without inbound SSH ports, bastion hosts, or SSH keys. Choose it when a scenario requires IAM-controlled access to private instances with optional session-activity logging.
When to use: Administrators need browser or CLI shell access to instances without public IP addresses.; Security policy requires closing inbound SSH ports and eliminating bastion and key management.; Access must be granted per user and managed node through IAM policies.
Key facts: Session Manager is a fully managed Systems Manager tool for connecting to managed nodes.; CloudTrail records Session Manager API calls; Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs can receive session log data.; Session content logging is unavailable for sessions that use port forwarding or SSH.; VPC endpoints for Systems Manager using AWS PrivateLink can keep traffic between managed nodes, Systems Manager, and Amazon EC2 on the Amazon network.
Gotchas: CloudTrail API records alone do not provide a record of commands run during a session.; Tunneling SSH through Session Manager does not make SSH session content available for Session Manager logging.; A bastion host still requires operating a jump box and does not eliminate inbound SSH access.
Confused with: SSH bastion host: A bastion is a host you maintain for jump access; Session Manager avoids bastions, inbound ports, and SSH keys.; CloudTrail logging: CloudTrail records Session Manager API calls; configure S3 or CloudWatch Logs for session log data.
ES: Session Manager ofrece acceso a una shell en instancias EC2 administradas sin puertos SSH de entrada, bastion hosts ni claves SSH. Elígelo cuando el escenario exige acceso a instancias privadas controlado mediante IAM y la opción de registrar la actividad de las sesiones. Session Manager es una herramienta totalmente administrada de Systems Manager para conectarte a nodos administrados.; CloudTrail registra las llamadas a la API de Session Manager; Amazon S3 o CloudWatch Logs pueden recibir los datos de registro de las sesiones.; El registro del contenido de la sesión no está disponible para sesiones que usan port forwarding o SSH.; Los VPC endpoints para Systems Manager mediante AWS PrivateLink pueden mantener el tráfico entre los nodos administrados, Systems Manager y Amazon EC2 dentro de la red de Amazon.

chunks.title: Bastion hosts vs Systems Manager Session Manager
chunks.text:
Scenario: A financial services team manages EC2 instances without public IP addresses. Engineers need shell access without opening inbound ports, and the team wants traffic between the managed instances and Systems Manager to stay on the Amazon network. Which design meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Use Session Manager with VPC endpoints for Systems Manager through AWS PrivateLink.
Why: The instances have no public IP addresses, inbound ports must stay closed, and the Systems Manager connection should remain on the Amazon network. Session Manager supports access to managed nodes without inbound ports; VPC endpoints for Systems Manager using AWS PrivateLink address the network-path requirement. A bastion or VPN with SSH fails the inbound-port constraint, while the NAT gateway design omits the requested PrivateLink path.
Wrong options: Use Session Manager with a NAT gateway instead of VPC endpoints for Systems Manager. (Session Manager avoids inbound ports, but this design does not use the documented PrivateLink option for keeping the specified traffic on the Amazon network.); Use a VPN for engineer access and permit SSH to the private instances from the VPN network. (This design still opens inbound SSH access to the instances.); Use a public bastion host to establish SSH connections to the private instances. (SSH from a bastion requires inbound SSH access to the managed instances.)

chunks.title: Bastion hosts vs Systems Manager Session Manager
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company is retiring its SSH bastion. On-call staff need keyless shell access to managed EC2 instances, with access limited to the instances each person supports. The company must also retain session log data for reviewing commands, without reopening inbound SSH. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use IAM policies to control which staff can start Session Manager sessions on each managed instance. + Use standard Session Manager shell sessions and send session log data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Why: The company needs both per-instance access control and retained data from keyless shell sessions. IAM policies govern who can initiate Session Manager sessions and which managed nodes they can access; standard Session Manager sessions can send session log data to S3. CloudTrail alone records API calls rather than command activity, and neither SSH nor port-forwarding sessions provide Session Manager session content logging.
Wrong options: Use Session Manager port forwarding and configure CloudWatch Logs to record the forwarded sessions. (Session Manager does not provide session content logging for port-forwarding sessions.); Enable CloudTrail for Session Manager API calls as the only source of command records. (CloudTrail records API calls but does not provide the requested session log data.); Start SSH sessions through Session Manager and configure Session Manager session logging. (Session Manager cannot log session content for SSH sessions, and SSH does not meet the keyless-shell requirement.)

chunks.title: Identifying metrics from business requirements (SLAs, availability targets)
chunks.text:
Identifying metrics from business requirements (SLAs, availability targets). Turn a business availability target into a measurement of whether the workload performs its agreed function when needed, over the specified period. If traffic may be absent, use CloudWatch Synthetics canaries to measure the customer journey rather than relying only on observed requests.
When to use: The SLA specifies an availability percentage and measurement period.; A customer-facing endpoint must be checked even when no customers visit.; A workload has hard dependencies whose failures affect its availability.
Key facts: Availability is the percentage of time a workload successfully performs its agreed function when required.; Under a strict availability measure, both scheduled and unscheduled interruptions reduce availability.; A 99.95% annual availability goal permits up to 4 hours 22 minutes of unavailability.; A request-based measurement can count a period with no requests as 100% available.; CloudWatch Synthetics canaries run scheduled customer-like checks and measure endpoint availability and latency.; Theoretical availability across independent hard dependencies is the product of their availabilities.
Gotchas: Healthy infrastructure does not prove that the agreed customer function works.; Excluding planned maintenance can overstate availability from a user's perspective.; Request-only measurements can miss an outage during a period with no traffic.
Confused with: 
ES: Convierte el objetivo de disponibilidad del negocio en una medición de si la carga de trabajo cumple su función acordada cuando se necesita, durante el período indicado. Si puede no haber tráfico, usa canaries de CloudWatch Synthetics para medir la experiencia del cliente en vez de depender solo de las solicitudes observadas. La disponibilidad es el porcentaje de tiempo en que una carga de trabajo cumple correctamente su función acordada cuando se requiere.; Con una medición estricta, tanto las interrupciones programadas como las no programadas reducen la disponibilidad.; Un objetivo anual de disponibilidad del 99.95% permite hasta 4 horas y 22 minutos de indisponibilidad.; Una medición basada en solicitudes puede contar un período sin solicitudes como 100% disponible.; Los canaries de CloudWatch Synthetics ejecutan comprobaciones programadas similares a las acciones de un cliente y miden la disponibilidad y latencia de los endpoints.; La disponibilidad teórica de un sistema con dependencias obligatorias independientes es el producto de sus disponibilidades.

chunks.title: Identifying metrics from business requirements (SLAs, availability targets)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company promises that its shipment portal will successfully return tracking results. The portal has two independent hard dependencies: a shipment-index service and an authorization service; a failure of either prevents a result. Each dependency and the portal itself has a 99.99% availability design goal. Which assessment should the architect use when setting a realistic end-to-end availability goal?
Correct: Use approximately 99.97%, accounting for the portal and both hard dependencies.
Why: A tracking result succeeds only if the portal and both hard dependencies work. For independent hard dependencies, the theoretical workload availability is the product of the component availabilities: 99.99% × 99.99% × 99.99%, or approximately 99.97%. Using the portal's goal alone misses dependency failures. The redundant-component calculation does not apply because neither dependency can substitute for the other.
Wrong options: Use 99.9999%, because the two dependencies provide redundant availability. (The dependencies are both required, not interchangeable redundant components.); Use 99.99%, because the portal's own design goal determines the customer-facing goal. (This ignores failures in either hard dependency.); Use 99.98%, because only the two dependency goals affect customer availability. (The portal's own availability must also be included in the hard-dependency calculation.)

chunks.title: Identifying metrics from business requirements (SLAs, availability targets)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional museum sells tickets through a website that receives almost no traffic overnight. Its SLA requires the ticket-search and checkout journey to remain available during those hours, and operators need a measurement that can reveal failures before visitors encounter them. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Schedule a CloudWatch Synthetics canary to perform the ticket journey and use its availability metrics.
Why: The SLA concerns whether visitors can complete a particular journey, including when nobody is visiting. A scheduled CloudWatch Synthetics canary can follow customer-like actions and produce availability metrics without customer traffic. Request-only availability can treat periods with no requests as 100% available, so it could conceal an overnight failure. Server uptime and home-page latency do not measure successful ticket search and checkout.
Wrong options: Measure only the response time of visitor requests to the website's home page. (Home-page requests do not verify the required ticket journey and may not occur overnight.); Calculate availability only from successful and failed visitor requests. (Periods without requests can be counted as fully available despite a broken ticket journey.); Calculate availability from the uptime of the servers hosting the ticket website. (Server uptime does not establish that ticket search and checkout succeed.)

chunks.title: Caching strategies: lazy loading, write-through, TTL
chunks.text:
Caching strategies: lazy loading, write-through, TTL. Use an application-side ElastiCache cache to reduce repeated database reads. Choose lazy loading when only requested data should occupy the cache, write-through when reads should find recently written data, and TTL when entries should expire and be refreshed.
When to use: Choose lazy loading when many records are rarely read and a slower first request is acceptable.; Add write-through when the application updates the database and subsequent reads should usually find the updated value in the cache.; Add TTL when cached entries should eventually expire, especially if writes can bypass the cache or rarely read entries accumulate.
Key facts: With lazy loading, the application checks the cache first; on a miss, it reads the database and populates the cache.; Lazy loading caches only requested data, but a miss adds latency and cached values can become stale after a database update.; Write-through updates the cache when the database is updated. It adds work to writes and can cache data that is never read.; Write-through is commonly paired with lazy loading so reads can refill an empty cache node.; An expired TTL key is treated as a miss. TTL limits how long an entry remains cached, but does not guarantee it was never stale before expiry.
Gotchas: Write-through alone does not refill entries missing from a newly empty cache node until those entries are written again.; Lazy loading alone does not update an existing cache entry when its database record changes.; TTL is not immediate invalidation: an entry can be stale before it expires.
Confused with: 
ES: Usa una caché de ElastiCache del lado de la aplicación para reducir lecturas repetidas de la base de datos. Elige lazy loading si solo quieres almacenar datos solicitados, write-through si las lecturas deben encontrar datos recién escritos y TTL si las entradas deben vencer y actualizarse. Con lazy loading, la aplicación consulta primero la caché; si no encuentra el dato, lee la base de datos y llena la caché.; Lazy loading almacena solo los datos solicitados, pero una ausencia agrega latencia y los valores pueden quedar desactualizados después de un cambio en la base de datos.; Write-through actualiza la caché cuando se actualiza la base de datos. Agrega trabajo a las escrituras y puede almacenar datos que nunca se leen.; Write-through suele combinarse con lazy loading para que las lecturas puedan volver a llenar un nodo de caché vacío.; Una clave cuyo TTL venció se trata como ausente. TTL limita cuánto permanece almacenada una entrada, pero no garantiza que nunca estuvo desactualizada antes de vencer.

chunks.title: Caching strategies: lazy loading, write-through, TTL
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher serves article metadata through an application backed by a database and ElastiCache. An independent editorial process sometimes updates the database without passing through the serving application; readers can tolerate an older value briefly, but cached values must eventually be refreshed. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST change to the editorial process?
Correct: Use lazy loading with a TTL so an expired entry is fetched again from the database.
Why: Editorial updates bypass the serving application's write path, so write-through implemented only there cannot refresh those entries. TTL makes an expired cache entry behave like a miss; lazy loading then retrieves the current database value on the next request. This meets the stated tolerance for briefly older values without changing the editorial writer. TTL does not guarantee that a cached value stays current before it expires.
Wrong options: Use lazy loading without expiry so requested metadata remains cached. (An entry can remain stale after an editorial database update.); Serve metadata from ElastiCache and refresh an entry only when the serving application writes it. (Editorial changes bypass that refresh path and can leave cached values stale.); Use write-through only in the serving application's write path. (It does not update the cache when the independent editorial process writes directly to the database.)

chunks.title: Caching strategies: lazy loading, write-through, TTL
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum publishes a large archive of exhibit descriptions that do not change after publication. Visitors repeatedly open a small subset of the archive, and the museum accepts a slower first request for each description. Which ElastiCache population strategy reduces repeat database reads MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use lazy loading: check the cache first, then fetch and cache a description on a miss.
Why: The archive is immutable, so the key decision is how to cache a small, frequently read subset without filling the cache with the rest. Lazy loading populates ElastiCache only after a requested description misses and serves later requests from the cache. The accepted first-request delay makes its miss penalty suitable. Write-through would also cache descriptions that may never be read.
Wrong options: Read the database for every request and place each result in ElastiCache afterward. (It continues to read the database even when a description is already cached.); Use write-through to cache every description as it is published. (It stores descriptions that visitors may never request, increasing cache use.); Use lazy loading and immediately expire each description after it is cached. (Immediate expiry prevents repeat requests from benefiting from the cached result.)

chunks.title: CDN and edge caching strategy for cost and performance
chunks.text:
CDN and edge caching strategy for cost and performance. Amazon CloudFront serves cached content from edge locations, improving viewer performance and reducing requests to the origin. For cost-focused scenarios, choose CloudFront for frequently requested content and tune the cache key and cache duration so identical responses can share a cached copy.
When to use: Viewers in multiple locations repeatedly request the same files, and the origin is handling too many requests.; A CloudFront distribution has a low cache hit ratio because requests include cookies, headers, or query parameters that do not change the response.; Requests from multiple CloudFront caching layers still place substantial load on one origin.
Key facts: CloudFront serves cached copies from edge locations and regional edge caches; an edge cache miss can be served from a regional edge cache or Origin Shield instead of the origin.; A longer practical Cache-Control max-age reduces how often CloudFront must check the origin for changed objects.; Forwarding unnecessary cookie, header, or query-string values can create separate cached copies of identical content.; Origin Shield adds a caching layer and consolidates requests to the origin through a single location.; AWS does not charge for data transfer out from an AWS origin to CloudFront; CloudFront usage still has its own pricing.
Gotchas: A long max-age is not appropriate merely to raise cache hits if objects must change sooner.; Forwarding every viewer cookie for static files can fragment the cache even when cookies do not affect those files.; Different query-parameter casing or ordering can cause CloudFront to cache identical responses separately.
Confused with: Direct delivery from Amazon S3: S3 can hold the definitive files; CloudFront adds edge caching and delivery close to viewers.; Origin Shield: Origin Shield is an additional CloudFront caching layer, not a replacement for choosing an appropriate cache key and duration.
ES: Amazon CloudFront entrega contenido en caché desde edge locations para mejorar el rendimiento de los usuarios y reducir las solicitudes al origen. En escenarios enfocados en costos, elige CloudFront para contenido solicitado con frecuencia y ajusta la cache key y la duración de caché para que las respuestas idénticas compartan una copia. CloudFront entrega copias en caché desde edge locations y regional edge caches; si no hay una copia en el edge, un regional edge cache u Origin Shield puede atender la solicitud sin consultar al origen.; Un Cache-Control max-age con el valor práctico más largo reduce la frecuencia con que CloudFront consulta al origen para detectar cambios.; Reenviar valores innecesarios de cookies, headers o query strings puede crear copias en caché separadas de contenido idéntico.; Origin Shield agrega una capa de caché y concentra las solicitudes al origen en una sola ubicación.; AWS no cobra la transferencia de datos de salida desde un origen de AWS hacia CloudFront; el uso de CloudFront sigue sujeto a sus propios precios.

chunks.title: CDN and edge caching strategy for cost and performance
chunks.text:
Scenario: A software publisher delivers popular installer files through CloudFront to viewers worldwide. Each published file remains unchanged for weeks, but repeated requests from multiple caching layers still place heavy load on its origin. The publisher wants to reduce origin requests without changing the files delivered to viewers. Which TWO changes meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Set a longer practical Cache-Control max-age for the published installer files. + Enable CloudFront Origin Shield for the distribution's origin.
Why: The files stay unchanged for weeks, so a longer practical max-age can increase cache hits without changing what viewers receive. Origin Shield adds another caching layer and channels requests from CloudFront caching layers through one location, reducing repeated origin fetches. Shortening the duration or creating unnecessary cookie and query variants works against the origin-load requirement.
Wrong options: Shorten the installer files' cache duration to check the origin more often. (A shorter duration increases the frequency of origin checks.); Cache installer files separately for every viewer cookie value. (Per-cookie caching creates extra variants of installer files that do not change by viewer.); Forward every query parameter when caching the installer files, including parameters ignored by the origin. (Parameters that do not change the file can needlessly split identical responses into separate cached copies.)

chunks.title: CDN and edge caching strategy for cost and performance
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing site uses one CloudFront distribution for personalized pages and shared CSS files. Every request carries a session cookie, but the CSS is identical for all customers; logs show frequent origin fetches for the CSS under different cookie values. Which change reduces origin requests while preserving personalized pages MOST effectively?
Correct: Add a separate cache behavior for CSS that does not cache based on cookie values, while retaining appropriate cookie handling for personalized pages.
Why: The deciding constraint is that CSS does not vary by session, while the pages do. A separate CSS cache behavior lets CloudFront share cached CSS across cookie values without changing how personalized pages are handled. Increasing max-age or adding Origin Shield without fixing the CSS cache key leaves its unnecessary variants in place.
Wrong options: Stop forwarding cookies for every path in the distribution. (The personalized pages still need their session cookie.); Increase the CSS max-age while continuing to cache each cookie value separately. (A longer duration does not prevent different session cookie values from fragmenting the CSS cache.); Enable Origin Shield while keeping the same cookie-based cache key for CSS and personalized pages. (Origin Shield adds caching but does not remove unnecessary per-cookie CSS variants.)

chunks.title: AWS Client VPN (remote users)
chunks.text:
AWS Client VPN (remote users). AWS Client VPN is a managed, OpenVPN-based service for individual users connecting from remote locations to AWS and on-premises resources. Choose it when the endpoint is a person's device rather than a network-to-network connection.
When to use: Employees need secure access from laptops to resources in a VPC.; Remote users need one VPN connection for reachable AWS and on-premises resources.; The organization wants managed remote access with group-based network authorization.
Key facts: Client VPN establishes encrypted TLS connections through an OpenVPN-based client.; A Client VPN endpoint terminates client sessions; its target network can be an associated VPC subnet or a direct Transit Gateway attachment.; Endpoint routes specify paths to destinations, and authorization rules control which users can access specified networks.; No authorization rules exist by default; configure them before users can access resources.; Client VPN supports Active Directory, federated, and certificate-based authentication.
Gotchas: A route to a network does not replace the authorization rule needed to grant users access.; Site-to-Site VPN connects networks; it is not the managed client-based connection for each employee's laptop.; Access to both VPC and on-premises resources requires the appropriate reachable paths and access configuration; creating an endpoint alone is not enough.
Confused with: AWS Site-to-Site VPN: Use Site-to-Site VPN for network-to-network connectivity; use Client VPN for individual remote clients.; AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect is a dedicated network connection, not an OpenVPN-based service for employee laptops.; AWS Transit Gateway: Transit Gateway can be a Client VPN target network, but Client VPN provides the remote users' VPN sessions.
ES: AWS Client VPN es un servicio administrado basado en OpenVPN para usuarios individuales que se conectan desde ubicaciones remotas a recursos de AWS y on-premises. Elígelo cuando el punto de conexión sea el dispositivo de una persona, no una conexión entre redes. Client VPN establece conexiones TLS cifradas mediante un cliente basado en OpenVPN.; Un Client VPN endpoint termina las sesiones de los clientes; su red de destino puede ser una subred de VPC asociada o una conexión directa a Transit Gateway.; Las rutas del endpoint indican los caminos a los destinos, y las authorization rules controlan qué usuarios pueden acceder a redes específicas.; De forma predeterminada no hay authorization rules; debes configurarlas para que los usuarios accedan a los recursos.; Client VPN admite autenticación mediante Active Directory, federación y certificados.

chunks.title: AWS Client VPN (remote users)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company has editors who work from hotels and home offices. Each editor needs an encrypted connection from a laptop to private applications in a VPC, and the company does not want to maintain remote-access VPN servers. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint and configure access for editors using an OpenVPN-based client.
Why: The deciding requirement is managed access for individuals connecting from different locations on their laptops. AWS Client VPN supports encrypted connections through an OpenVPN-based client without requiring the company to maintain remote-access VPN servers. Site-to-Site VPN is a network-to-network option and does not address the editors' individual client sessions.
Wrong options: Provision AWS Direct Connect for the publishing company's main office. (A dedicated connection to the main office does not give editors a client VPN connection from hotels and homes.); Create a VPC peering connection to a VPC used by the editors. (VPC peering connects VPCs, not individual editors' laptops to private applications.); Establish AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections for the editors' office networks. (Site-to-Site VPN connects networks rather than providing managed VPN sessions for editors connecting individually from changing locations.)

chunks.title: AWS Client VPN (remote users)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare company has configured a Client VPN endpoint with a VPC subnet association and a route to a private application network. Employees can establish VPN sessions, but none can access the application; the endpoint has no authorization rules. The company wants to permit only members of an existing identity provider group to reach that network. Which change meets the requirement MOST securely?
Correct: Add a Client VPN authorization rule for the application network that allows the identity provider group.
Why: The employees have VPN sessions and a route, but the endpoint lacks authorization rules. Client VPN requires an authorization rule to allow access to a specified network, and the rule can name an identity provider group. Adding another route or changing the target network does not provide the missing group-based permission.
Wrong options: Add another route for the application network to the Client VPN endpoint. (The route already exists, and another route does not grant users authorization to access the network.); Enable Client VPN connection logging to record employee sessions. (Connection logging provides visibility but does not authorize access to the application network.); Attach the Client VPN endpoint directly to an AWS Transit Gateway. (Changing the target network does not supply the missing group-specific authorization rule.)

chunks.title: CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge
chunks.text:
CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge. CloudFront Functions handles lightweight, short-running changes to requests and responses at viewer events. Choose Lambda@Edge when edge logic needs network access, request-body access, third-party libraries, or more memory.
When to use: Choose CloudFront Functions to normalize URLs, headers, cookies, or query strings for a cache key.; Choose CloudFront Functions for simple header changes, redirects, rewrites, or token validation using request metadata.; Choose Lambda@Edge when processing needs an external service, the request body, or an origin-request or origin-response event.
Key facts: CloudFront Functions runs at viewer request and viewer response events; Lambda@Edge also runs at origin request and origin response events.; CloudFront Functions has no network, file system, or request-body access; Lambda@Edge supports all three.; CloudFront Functions supports up to millions of requests per second; Lambda@Edge supports up to 10,000 requests per second per Region.; CloudFront Functions has 2 MB maximum memory. Lambda@Edge allows up to 128 MB at viewer events and 10,240 MB at origin events.; CloudFront Functions uses JavaScript; Lambda@Edge supports Node.js and Python.
Gotchas: A viewer-response function cannot normalize a request before the cache lookup.; CloudFront Functions can inspect authorization headers for token validation, but it cannot call an external authorization service.; Lambda@Edge memory limits differ between viewer and origin events.
Confused with: Lambda@Edge: It supports network calls, request bodies, libraries, and origin events; CloudFront Functions is for lightweight viewer-event logic.
ES: CloudFront Functions realiza cambios ligeros y de corta duración en solicitudes y respuestas durante eventos de viewer. Elige Lambda@Edge cuando la lógica en el edge necesite acceso a la red, al cuerpo de la solicitud, a bibliotecas de terceros o a más memoria. CloudFront Functions se ejecuta en eventos viewer request y viewer response; Lambda@Edge también admite origin request y origin response.; CloudFront Functions no tiene acceso a la red, al sistema de archivos ni al cuerpo de la solicitud; Lambda@Edge sí.; CloudFront Functions admite hasta millones de solicitudes por segundo; Lambda@Edge admite hasta 10,000 solicitudes por segundo por Región.; CloudFront Functions tiene un máximo de 2 MB de memoria. Lambda@Edge admite hasta 128 MB en eventos de viewer y 10,240 MB en eventos de origin.; CloudFront Functions usa JavaScript; Lambda@Edge admite Node.js y Python.

chunks.title: CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge
chunks.text:
Scenario: A news publisher serves articles through Amazon CloudFront. Tracking parameters create different cache entries for otherwise identical articles, and traffic can reach hundreds of thousands of requests per second in a Region. The publisher wants to remove those parameters before each cache lookup using short-running edge code. Which solution meets these requirements at the required scale?
Correct: Use CloudFront Functions at the viewer request event to remove the tracking parameters.
Why: The deciding requirements are normalization before the cache lookup and traffic far above 10,000 requests per second in a Region. CloudFront Functions at viewer request can change query strings for cache key normalization and supports up to millions of requests per second. Lambda@Edge at viewer request has the right timing but not the documented scale; response and origin-request events are too late for this cache lookup.
Wrong options: Use Lambda@Edge at the viewer request event to remove the tracking parameters. (It runs before cache lookup, but the stated traffic exceeds Lambda@Edge's documented scale of up to 10,000 requests per second per Region.); Use Lambda@Edge at the origin request event to remove the tracking parameters. (An origin request event occurs after CloudFront determines whether the request is a cache hit.); Use CloudFront Functions at the viewer response event to remove the tracking parameters. (A viewer response event occurs too late to change the request attributes used for the cache lookup.)

chunks.title: CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge
chunks.text:
Scenario: A streaming company uses CloudFront to deliver subscriber-only videos, including videos served from cache. Its security team requires an edge check on every viewer request that calls an external entitlement API before CloudFront returns content. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Use Lambda@Edge at the viewer request event to call the entitlement API.
Why: The check must both call an external service and apply before content is returned on every viewer request. Lambda@Edge provides network access, and its viewer request event has the required timing. CloudFront Functions can validate tokens from request metadata, but it cannot call the entitlement API; an origin request event would not check cache hits.
Wrong options: Use CloudFront Functions at the viewer request event to call the entitlement API. (CloudFront Functions cannot make network calls to the external API.); Use Lambda@Edge at the origin request event to call the entitlement API. (An origin request event does not provide a check on every viewer request, including cache hits.); Use CloudFront Functions at the viewer response event to call the entitlement API. (CloudFront Functions has no network access, and a response event is too late for the required pre-return check.)

chunks.title: Amazon CloudFront: distributions, origins, caching and TTLs
chunks.text:
Amazon CloudFront: distributions, origins, caching and TTLs. Amazon CloudFront delivers static and dynamic HTTP(S) content through edge locations, caching eligible content near viewers. Choose it when a scenario calls for lower global delivery latency and fewer requests to an S3 or HTTP origin; set cache expiration to match freshness requirements.
When to use: Viewers around the world repeatedly request website files or other HTTP(S) content.; An S3 bucket or HTTP server must serve as the definitive origin while edge caches handle repeat requests.; The origin needs fewer direct requests without sacrificing a stated content-freshness requirement.
Key facts: A CloudFront distribution identifies the origins from which CloudFront retrieves requested content.; An origin can be an S3 bucket or a custom HTTP server, including one running on EC2 or outside AWS.; A cache hit is served from an edge location; an edge miss may be satisfied by a regional edge cache or Origin Shield without contacting the origin.; Origin response headers can control cache duration. The documented default expiration is 24 hours, and the minimum is 0 seconds.; CloudFront Origin Shield can help minimize requests forwarded to an origin.
Gotchas: Do not assume the default cache duration meets a short freshness deadline.; A TTL of 0 seconds does not meet a goal of offloading repeated requests through caching.; CloudFront delivers cached HTTP(S) content; it is not a substitute for accelerating uploads into one S3 bucket.
Confused with: AWS Global Accelerator: Use CloudFront when edge caching of HTTP(S) content is the deciding requirement; Global Accelerator does not cache content.; S3 Transfer Acceleration: It addresses long-distance uploads to an S3 bucket, not cached delivery from an origin to viewers.
ES: Amazon CloudFront entrega contenido HTTP(S) estático y dinámico mediante edge locations y puede almacenarlo en caché cerca de los usuarios. Elígelo cuando necesites menor latencia global y menos solicitudes a un origen S3 o HTTP; ajusta la expiración de caché según el requisito de actualización. Una distribución de CloudFront identifica los orígenes de los que obtiene el contenido solicitado.; El origen puede ser un bucket S3 o un servidor HTTP personalizado, incluso en EC2 o fuera de AWS.; Si el contenido está en caché, se entrega desde una edge location; si no está en esa edge location, una regional edge cache o Origin Shield puede atender la solicitud sin contactar al origen.; Los encabezados de respuesta del origen pueden controlar la duración en caché. La expiración predeterminada documentada es de 24 horas y el mínimo es de 0 segundos.; CloudFront Origin Shield puede ayudar a minimizar las solicitudes enviadas al origen.

chunks.title: Amazon CloudFront: distributions, origins, caching and TTLs
chunks.text:
Scenario: An online magazine serves frequently requested article pages from an HTTP server that it manages outside AWS. Readers are spread across continents, and the publisher wants repeat page requests served near readers rather than repeatedly contacting that server. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a CloudFront distribution with the HTTP server as a custom origin.
Why: The publisher needs edge caching but must retain its existing HTTP server as the source of the pages. A CloudFront distribution can use that server as a custom origin and serve cached requests from edge locations. Global Accelerator does not cache pages, and S3 Transfer Acceleration does not address delivery from an HTTP origin. Operating more servers adds work instead of providing a managed cache.
Wrong options: Put AWS Global Accelerator in front of the existing HTTP server. (Global Accelerator does not cache repeated article requests near readers.); Deploy copies of the HTTP server in more locations and direct readers to the nearest copy. (Operating additional servers does not provide the requested managed edge cache and increases overhead.); Use S3 Transfer Acceleration to deliver the article pages from the existing server. (S3 Transfer Acceleration is for uploads to S3 and does not cache pages from this HTTP server.)

chunks.title: Amazon CloudFront: distributions, origins, caching and TTLs
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher uses CloudFront to deliver the same popular images to viewers worldwide from an on-premises HTTP origin. Even with edge caching, the publisher wants to minimize how many requests reach that origin as demand grows. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable CloudFront Origin Shield for the distribution.
Why: The deciding requirement is to further minimize requests to an existing HTTP origin while continuing to use CloudFront. CloudFront Origin Shield is specifically identified as an option for reducing requests forwarded to an origin. Setting expiration to zero undermines caching, and Global Accelerator provides no content cache. S3 Transfer Acceleration addresses a different traffic direction and destination.
Wrong options: Replace CloudFront with AWS Global Accelerator for image delivery. (Global Accelerator does not cache images to reduce repeat origin requests.); Set the images' CloudFront cache expiration to 0 seconds. (A zero-second expiration works against serving repeat requests from cache.); Use S3 Transfer Acceleration for requests to the on-premises origin. (S3 Transfer Acceleration addresses uploads to S3, not requests to this HTTP origin.)

chunks.title: Amazon CloudFront: distributions, origins, caching and TTLs
chunks.text:
Scenario: A learning platform has downloadable lesson images in S3 and frequently requested HTML pages on an existing HTTP server. Students across continents repeatedly access both kinds of content; the platform wants nearby cached responses while keeping each existing source as the definitive origin. Which two solutions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use a CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as an origin for the lesson images. + Use a CloudFront distribution with the existing HTTP server as a custom origin for the HTML pages.
Why: Both content types need nearby cached delivery while their current sources remain definitive. CloudFront can use S3 as the image origin and a custom HTTP server as the page origin, so A and D address the two sources. S3 Transfer Acceleration does not cache downloads, and Global Accelerator does not cache pages. Deploying more servers adds operational overhead rather than using managed edge caching.
Wrong options: Deploy additional HTTP servers near students and have them serve copies of both content types. (Additional servers increase operational work and replace the requested managed edge-caching approach.); Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for students downloading lesson images. (S3 Transfer Acceleration targets uploads and does not cache the requested image downloads.); Use AWS Global Accelerator for the HTTP pages to cache them near students. (Global Accelerator does not cache HTML pages.)

chunks.title: CloudFront geo restriction, HTTPS and field-level encryption
chunks.text:
CloudFront geo restriction, HTTPS and field-level encryption. Use CloudFront geographic restrictions to allow or block countries for every file in a distribution. Configure HTTPS separately for viewers and the origin; encrypting one connection does not establish that the other is encrypted.
When to use: Every file in a distribution must be available only in approved countries.; Different files need different geographic rules while remaining in one distribution.; Traffic must be encrypted both from viewers to CloudFront and from CloudFront to the origin.
Key facts: CloudFront geographic restrictions use a country-level allowlist or denylist and apply to the entire distribution.; For different restrictions on different files, use separate distributions or a third-party geolocation service.; CloudFront returns HTTP 403 when its geographic restrictions block a request.; If CloudFront cannot determine a viewer’s location, it serves the requested content.; On an HTTPS cache miss, CloudFront decrypts the origin response and re-encrypts it for the viewer.
Gotchas: A country allowlist on one distribution cannot exempt a subset of its files.; A viewer HTTPS requirement alone does not establish HTTPS between CloudFront and the origin.; Do not infer protection of individual form fields merely from HTTPS transport encryption.
Confused with: Third-party geolocation service: Use it with CloudFront when restrictions must vary by file or be more precise than country level.; Separate CloudFront distributions: They can support different geographic rules, but do not meet a requirement to retain one distribution.
ES: Usa CloudFront geographic restrictions para permitir o bloquear países en todos los archivos de una distribución. Configura HTTPS por separado para los clientes y el origen; cifrar una conexión no significa que la otra esté cifrada. CloudFront geographic restrictions usa una lista de países permitidos o bloqueados y se aplica a toda la distribución.; Para aplicar distintas restricciones a distintos archivos, usa distribuciones separadas o un servicio de geolocalización de terceros.; CloudFront devuelve HTTP 403 cuando sus restricciones geográficas bloquean una solicitud.; Si CloudFront no puede determinar la ubicación de un cliente, entrega el contenido solicitado.; Si hay un cache miss con HTTPS, CloudFront descifra la respuesta del origen y vuelve a cifrarla para el cliente.

chunks.title: CloudFront geo restriction, HTTPS and field-level encryption
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher has licensed its entire video catalog for viewing in three countries. Every file is served through one CloudFront distribution, and the publisher wants requests from all other countries blocked without maintaining application-based location checks. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Add the three countries to a CloudFront geographic restrictions allowlist on the distribution.
Why: The deciding requirements are country-level access for every file and the least operational overhead. A CloudFront geographic restrictions allowlist covers the entire distribution with the three approved countries. A third-party geolocation service is better suited to finer-grained rules, while a denylist naming the approved countries would block the wrong viewers.
Wrong options: Create a separate CloudFront distribution for each licensed country and configure a country allowlist on each. (Multiple distributions add overhead and do not meet the requirement to serve every file through one distribution.); Check each viewer’s country with a third-party geolocation service before issuing a CloudFront signed URL. (This can provide geographic control, but adds an application and third-party service when distribution-wide country rules suffice.); Add the three licensed countries to a CloudFront geographic restrictions denylist. (A denylist blocks the countries it names, which would block the publisher’s approved viewers.)

chunks.title: CloudFront geo restriction, HTTPS and field-level encryption
chunks.text:
Scenario: A booking company serves its web application through CloudFront with a custom HTTP/S origin. Its security policy requires encrypted connections from customers to CloudFront and from CloudFront to the origin, including requests that miss the cache. Which configuration meets these requirements?
Correct: Require HTTPS from viewers to CloudFront and configure CloudFront to use HTTPS with the origin.
Why: The policy explicitly covers two connections: customer to CloudFront and CloudFront to the custom origin. Requiring viewer HTTPS and configuring HTTPS to the origin encrypts both, including the origin request on a cache miss. Securing only one connection leaves the other requirement unmet; merely making the origin HTTPS-capable does not change a CloudFront connection configured to use HTTP.
Wrong options: Require HTTPS from CloudFront to the origin, and continue accepting HTTP connections from viewers. (The origin connection is encrypted, but customer connections to CloudFront can remain unencrypted.); Configure HTTPS at the origin and continue allowing CloudFront to use HTTP to contact it. (An HTTPS-capable origin does not encrypt requests that CloudFront sends to it over HTTP.); Require HTTPS from viewers to CloudFront, and leave the connection from CloudFront to the origin configured for HTTP. (The viewer connection is encrypted, but cache misses can reach the origin over HTTP.)

chunks.title: CloudFront origin access control (OAC) for private S3 origins
chunks.text:
CloudFront origin access control (OAC) for private S3 origins. CloudFront origin access control (OAC) lets a distribution make signed requests to a private, regular S3 bucket origin. For private object delivery, attach OAC and grant s3:GetObject to the CloudFront service principal in a bucket policy scoped to that distribution.
When to use: Viewers must retrieve S3 objects through CloudFront but not directly through S3 URLs.; A private S3 origin uses SSE-KMS or needs dynamic requests through CloudFront.
Key facts: Use the CloudFront service principal, cloudfront.amazonaws.com, with an AWS:SourceArn condition identifying the distribution in the bucket policy.; The recommended OAC setting always signs origin requests; with this setting, CloudFront-to-S3 communication is always HTTPS.; SSE-KMS objects also require a KMS key policy that permits the CloudFront distribution to use the key.; OAC requires a regular S3 bucket origin, not an S3 website endpoint.
Gotchas: Attaching OAC alone does not grant access to a private bucket; the bucket policy must allow it.; Do not sign requests requires the S3 origin to be publicly accessible.; An S3 website endpoint is a CloudFront custom origin and cannot use OAC.
Confused with: Origin access identity (OAI): OAI is the legacy option; OAC is recommended and supports SSE-KMS and dynamic requests.
ES: CloudFront origin access control (OAC) permite que una distribución envíe solicitudes firmadas a un origen de bucket S3 privado y normal. Para entregar objetos privados, asocia OAC y concede s3:GetObject al principal de servicio de CloudFront mediante una política de bucket limitada a esa distribución. En la política de bucket, usa el principal cloudfront.amazonaws.com y una condición AWS:SourceArn que identifique la distribución.; La configuración recomendada de OAC siempre firma las solicitudes al origen; con ella, la comunicación de CloudFront a S3 siempre usa HTTPS.; Los objetos con SSE-KMS también requieren una política de clave KMS que permita a la distribución usar la clave.; OAC requiere un origen de bucket S3 normal, no un endpoint de sitio web de S3.

chunks.title: CloudFront origin access control (OAC) for private S3 origins
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio accepts asset uploads through CloudFront and stores them in a private, regular S3 bucket origin. Its distribution must send PUT requests to S3, and only that distribution should be permitted to upload objects through the origin access configuration. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Attach an OAC to the S3 origin and configure it to always sign origin requests. + Allow cloudfront.amazonaws.com s3:PutObject on the objects in the bucket policy, conditioned on AWS:SourceArn matching the distribution.
Why: The origin is private and must accept PUT requests specifically from this CloudFront distribution. An always-signing OAC supports dynamic requests, while a bucket policy granting s3:PutObject to the CloudFront service principal with a distribution-specific AWS:SourceArn authorizes the upload. OAI does not meet the dynamic-request requirement, and unsigned OAC requests require a publicly accessible origin.
Wrong options: Create an OAI for the distribution and use it for dynamic PUT requests to the bucket. (OAI does not support dynamic PUT requests in this scenario.); Grant public s3:PutObject access in the bucket policy so uploads can reach S3. (Public upload permission violates the requirement to limit uploads to the distribution.); Attach an OAC to the S3 origin and configure it to never sign origin requests. (Never signing requests requires a publicly accessible S3 origin.)

chunks.title: CloudFront origin access control (OAC) for private S3 origins
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher uses an S3 website endpoint as a CloudFront origin for a library of downloadable PDFs. The site does not need S3 website-specific behavior, and the publisher now requires the bucket to remain private while readers download through CloudFront. Which change meets the requirement?
Correct: Replace the website endpoint with a regular S3 bucket origin, attach an always-signing OAC, and grant distribution-scoped s3:GetObject in the bucket policy.
Why: The existing website endpoint is the key constraint: CloudFront treats it as a custom origin, which cannot use OAC or OAI. Because website-specific behavior is unnecessary, the publisher can switch to a regular S3 bucket origin and use OAC with a distribution-scoped read policy. Keeping the website endpoint and adding an origin access mechanism will not work.
Wrong options: Replace the website endpoint with a regular S3 bucket origin and enable public read access for the PDFs. (Public read access violates the requirement that the bucket remain private.); Keep the website endpoint as a custom origin, attach OAC to it, and grant the distribution s3:GetObject. (OAC cannot be used with an S3 website endpoint configured as a custom origin.); Keep the website endpoint as a custom origin, configure an OAI, and grant that identity s3:GetObject. (An S3 website endpoint cannot use OAI either.)

chunks.title: CloudFront origin access control (OAC) for private S3 origins
chunks.text:
Scenario: A medical imaging portal serves files from a private S3 bucket through CloudFront. After the team changes the objects to SSE-KMS encryption, the distribution must continue serving them without granting public access to the bucket. The distribution already has an always-signing OAC and a distribution-scoped bucket policy allowing s3:GetObject. Which additional change meets the requirement?
Correct: Add a KMS key policy statement permitting the CloudFront service principal to use the key, scoped by AWS:SourceArn to the distribution.
Why: The S3 read permission already exists; the new requirement is access to objects encrypted with SSE-KMS. CloudFront also needs permission to use the KMS key, which can be granted in the key policy to its service principal and scoped to the distribution. Broadening the bucket policy does not supply KMS key permission, and OAI is not the recommended solution for SSE-KMS.
Wrong options: Replace OAC with an OAI and leave the existing S3 bucket policy unchanged. (OAI does not support this SSE-KMS scenario, and the existing policy is scoped to the OAC distribution.); Change the OAC to Do not sign requests so that S3 handles decryption independently. (Unsigned origin requests cannot access this private bucket.); Add another bucket policy statement granting s3:GetObject to cloudfront.amazonaws.com without a SourceArn condition. (A broader S3 read permission does not grant the distribution permission to use the KMS key.)

chunks.title: CloudFront origin groups and failover
chunks.text:
CloudFront origin groups and failover. A CloudFront origin group pairs a primary origin with a secondary origin for a cache behavior. On a cache miss, CloudFront can retry an eligible request against the secondary when the primary returns a configured failure code or encounters a qualifying connection or timeout failure.
When to use: Cached content must remain available when its primary origin fails.; A distribution has two origins, and requests should normally go to one primary origin.; Specific primary-origin errors should trigger a fallback without changing the viewer URL.
Key facts: The distribution needs at least two origins; create an origin group and assign it to the relevant cache behavior.; Failover occurs only for GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS; OPTIONS must also be configured as a cached HTTP method.; Selectable failover codes are 400, 403, 404, 416, 429, 500, 502, 503, and 504.; A connection failure can trigger failover when 503 is selected; a primary-origin timeout can trigger it when 504 is selected.; Cache hits are served without contacting either origin; for each eligible request that reaches the origin, CloudFront tries the primary first, even after an earlier request failed over.
Gotchas: Adding a second origin alone does not enable failover; the cache behavior must use the origin group.; POST and PUT requests do not fail over through CloudFront origin failover.; CloudFront does not permanently switch to the secondary after one failed request.
Confused with: 
ES: Un origin group de CloudFront vincula un origen primario y uno secundario a un cache behavior. Ante un cache miss, CloudFront puede enviar una solicitud elegible al origen secundario si el primario devuelve un código de error configurado o presenta una falla de conexión o timeout que cumpla las condiciones.
