La distribución necesita al menos dos orígenes; crea un origin group y asígnalo al cache behavior correspondiente.; El failover solo aplica a GET, HEAD y OPTIONS; además, OPTIONS debe estar configurado como cached HTTP method.; Los códigos de failover disponibles son 400, 403, 404, 416, 429, 500, 502, 503 y 504.; Una falla de conexión puede activar failover si seleccionas 503; un timeout del origen primario puede activarlo si seleccionas 504.; Los cache hits se sirven sin contactar a ningún origen; para cada solicitud elegible que llega al origen, CloudFront intenta primero con el primario, aunque una solicitud anterior haya usado el secundario.

chunks.title: CloudFront origin groups and failover
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer uses CloudFront to serve a catalog from a primary origin and has placed a copy at a secondary origin. Its application makes OPTIONS requests for catalog paths, and the team wants an uncached OPTIONS request to reach the secondary if the primary returns HTTP 502. Both origins are already members of an origin group assigned to the catalog cache behavior. Which configuration meets the failover requirement?
Correct: Select 502 as a failover code and include OPTIONS in the cache behavior's cached HTTP methods.
Why: Two details decide this case: the primary returns 502, and the viewer request uses OPTIONS. Select 502 among the origin group's failover codes and configure OPTIONS as a cached HTTP method for the cache behavior. Allowing OPTIONS without caching it is insufficient for CloudFront origin failover, even though the origin group is already assigned.
Wrong options: Include OPTIONS in cached HTTP methods and select 504, but not 502, as a failover code. (The stated primary response is 502, which will not trigger failover unless 502 is selected.); Select 502 as a failover code and allow OPTIONS as a viewer method without adding it to cached HTTP methods. (CloudFront will not fail over OPTIONS unless OPTIONS is configured as a cached HTTP method.); Select 502 as a failover code and configure a custom error page for the primary origin instead of caching OPTIONS. (A custom error page does not replace the cached-HTTP-method requirement for OPTIONS failover.)

chunks.title: CloudFront origin groups and failover
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum serves exhibit images through a CloudFront distribution backed by an S3 bucket. It has prepared a second origin containing the same images, and wants uncached requests to use that origin if the primary returns HTTP 503. The museum wants viewers to keep using the same distribution. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an origin group with the image bucket as primary and the second origin as secondary, select 503 for failover, and assign the group to the image cache behavior.
Why: The deciding requirements are fallback on HTTP 503 and continued use of the existing CloudFront distribution. Configure both origins in an origin group, select 503, and assign that group to the image cache behavior. Simply adding an origin—or creating a group without assigning it to the behavior—does not make requests use failover.
Wrong options: Add the second origin to the distribution and leave the image cache behavior pointed at the primary origin. (CloudFront will not use the second origin for this cache behavior merely because it exists.); Create the origin group and select 503 for failover, but keep the image cache behavior pointed directly at the primary origin. (The origin group cannot perform failover for requests routed by a cache behavior that does not use it.); Point the image cache behavior directly at the second origin and retain the original bucket as another origin. (This makes the second origin the normal destination rather than using it only when the primary returns 503.)

chunks.title: CloudFront signed URLs vs signed cookies
chunks.text:
CloudFront signed URLs vs signed cookies. CloudFront signed URLs and signed cookies both control access to private content served through CloudFront. Choose a signed URL for an individual file or a client that cannot use cookies; choose signed cookies for multiple restricted files when existing URLs should stay unchanged.
When to use: Use a signed URL for a restricted download of one file.; Use a signed URL when the viewer's client does not support cookies.; Use signed cookies for many restricted files, such as HLS video files, without changing their URLs.
Key facts: Signed URLs take precedence over signed cookies for the same file: if a viewer requests a file using a signed URL, CloudFront evaluates access based only on that URL.; If existing unsigned URLs contain Expires, Policy, Signature, Key-Pair-Id, or Hash-Algorithm as query parameters, neither signed URLs nor signed cookies can be used with those URLs as they are.; CloudFront signed URLs and signed cookies control access to content served through CloudFront.
Gotchas: Do not choose signed URLs for a collection of files when preserving every existing URL is a requirement.; A signed cookie does not override a signed URL supplied in the same file request.; Check existing query parameter names before selecting either CloudFront signing method.
Confused with: s3-presigned-urls: An S3 presigned URL grants temporary access to an S3 object; CloudFront signed URLs control access to content served through CloudFront.; s3-bucket-policies-block-public-access: A bucket policy sets bucket access rules; it is not the viewer-facing choice between one restricted CloudFront file and many.; s3-access-points: S3 Access Points separate access policies for applications or teams sharing a bucket, rather than controlling viewer access to CloudFront content.
ES: Las signed URLs y las signed cookies de CloudFront controlan el acceso a contenido privado servido mediante CloudFront. Elige una signed URL para un archivo individual o un cliente que no admite cookies; elige signed cookies para varios archivos restringidos cuando debes conservar las URL existentes. Las signed URLs tienen prioridad sobre las signed cookies para el mismo archivo: si el usuario solicita un archivo con una signed URL, CloudFront evalúa el acceso únicamente con esa URL.; Si las URL existentes sin firma contienen Expires, Policy, Signature, Key-Pair-Id o Hash-Algorithm como parámetros de consulta, no puedes usar signed URLs ni signed cookies con esas URL tal como están.; Las signed URLs y las signed cookies de CloudFront controlan el acceso al contenido servido mediante CloudFront.

chunks.title: CloudFront signed URLs vs signed cookies
chunks.text:
Scenario: A streaming publisher serves subscriber-only HLS video through CloudFront. Each video requires requests for multiple restricted files, and the publisher must keep the existing URLs used by its player. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Use CloudFront signed cookies for the video files.
Why: The publisher needs access to many restricted HLS files while keeping the player's URLs unchanged. CloudFront signed cookies are the documented choice for that combination. Per-file signed URLs change the URLs, and S3 access mechanisms do not address the stated CloudFront viewer-access requirement.
Wrong options: Create separate S3 Access Points for subscribers and non-subscribers. (Access Points organize bucket access policies, not viewer access to the existing CloudFront URLs.); Generate an S3 presigned URL for each video file. (This grants access to S3 objects rather than preserving the CloudFront player URLs.); Generate a CloudFront signed URL for each video file. (Signing each file's URL does not preserve the existing player URLs.)

chunks.title: CloudFront signed URLs vs signed cookies
chunks.text:
Scenario: A news site uses CloudFront signed cookies to grant subscribers access to multiple articles. During a migration, some article links also include CloudFront signed URLs that no longer authorize access, and subscribers report that those links fail despite having valid signed cookies. The site can remove the signed-URL parameters from those links while retaining its cookie-based access flow. Which change restores the intended access?
Correct: Remove the signed-URL parameters from those links and continue using signed cookies.
Why: The failing requests contain signed URLs that do not authorize access, even though subscribers have valid signed cookies. When both methods apply to the same file and a viewer requests it with a signed URL, CloudFront bases its decision only on the URL. Removing the signed-URL parameters allows the site to use its intended cookie-based flow; changing the cookies alone does not resolve the precedence problem.
Wrong options: Replace the signed cookies with new signed cookies, leaving the article links unchanged. (CloudFront evaluates a request containing a signed URL based only on that URL, not the replacement cookies.); Create an S3 Access Point for article requests, leaving the links unchanged. (An Access Point does not change how CloudFront evaluates the signed article links.); Add a bucket policy permitting subscriber access, leaving the article links unchanged. (A bucket policy does not change CloudFront's precedence for signed URLs over signed cookies.)

chunks.title: AWS CloudHSM
chunks.text:
AWS CloudHSM. Choose AWS CloudHSM when an application needs single-tenant HSMs and direct control of cryptographic keys, algorithms, and HSM users. If the requirement is simply managed encryption keys without operating HSMs, consider AWS KMS instead.
When to use: A compliance requirement calls for single-tenant, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs.; An application needs direct control over generating, storing, importing, exporting, or using cryptographic keys.; An existing PKCS #11, JCE, CNG, or KSP workload must move to AWS with fewer application changes.
Key facts: CloudHSM offers single-tenant HSMs; HSMs in FIPS-mode clusters are validated at either FIPS 140-2 Level 3 or FIPS 140-3 Level 3.; FIPS mode permits only FIPS-validated keys and algorithms; non-FIPS mode offers all CloudHSM-supported keys and algorithms.; CloudHSM's end-to-end encrypted data plane is not visible to AWS.; Customers manage CloudHSM users outside IAM roles, gaining control but taking on more responsibility than with a managed service.; CloudHSM automates HSM tasks including backups, provisioning, configuration, and maintenance.
Gotchas: Selecting FIPS mode alone does not establish that the HSMs are FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated; the documentation also describes FIPS 140-2 Level 3 HSMs.; Single-tenant HSM control does not mean zero customer responsibility: CloudHSM users are managed outside IAM roles.; Do not choose CloudHSM solely because an application needs managed encryption keys and explicitly does not need to operate HSMs.
Confused with: kms-key-types: Choose AWS KMS for managed key creation and control when operating HSMs is unnecessary; choose CloudHSM for direct control of single-tenant HSMs.; kms-multi-region-keys: A requirement for single-tenant HSMs and direct control of their cryptographic operations points to CloudHSM, not a regional key-availability decision.
ES: Elige AWS CloudHSM cuando una aplicación necesite HSM single-tenant y control directo de claves, algoritmos y usuarios criptográficos. Si solo necesita claves de cifrado administradas sin operar HSM, considera AWS KMS. CloudHSM ofrece HSM single-tenant; los HSM de clústeres en FIPS mode están validados según FIPS 140-2 Level 3 o FIPS 140-3 Level 3.; FIPS mode solo permite claves y algoritmos validados por FIPS; non-FIPS mode ofrece todas las claves y algoritmos compatibles con CloudHSM.; El plano de datos con cifrado de extremo a extremo de CloudHSM no es visible para AWS.; Tú administras los usuarios de CloudHSM fuera de los roles de IAM; esto te da control, pero también más responsabilidades que un servicio administrado.; CloudHSM automatiza tareas de los HSM, incluidos los respaldos, el aprovisionamiento, la configuración y el mantenimiento.

chunks.title: AWS CloudHSM
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company has an on-premises application that calls PKCS #11 to generate and use cryptographic keys. It wants to move the workload to AWS with fewer application changes while retaining direct control of its algorithms and keys. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Move the cryptographic workload to AWS CloudHSM using its PKCS #11 support.
Why: The existing PKCS #11 integration and the need for direct algorithm and key control decide the answer. AWS CloudHSM supports migration of PKCS #11 workloads with fewer application changes. A redesign around AWS KMS may be a valid managed-service approach, but it misses the stated migration constraint.
Wrong options: Use AWS Payment Cryptography for the application’s key operations. (The scenario is not a payment-processing workload, the use case identified for AWS Payment Cryptography.); Move the keys to AWS KMS and replace the application’s cryptographic integration. (Replacing the integration conflicts with the requirement for fewer application changes to the PKCS #11 workload.); Use AWS KMS and redesign the application to delegate its key operations to a managed service. (Redesigning the application misses the stated goal of migrating its existing PKCS #11 integration with fewer changes.)

chunks.title: AWS CloudHSM
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute is designing an AWS-based cryptographic service. Its policy requires single-tenant HSMs validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3, use of FIPS-validated keys and algorithms, and direct administration of cryptographic users by its security team. Which TWO design decisions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Select a CloudHSM FIPS-mode cluster with FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. + Have the security team manage CloudHSM users outside IAM roles.
Why: The design must meet separate HSM validation, algorithm, and user-administration requirements. Choose a FIPS-mode CloudHSM cluster with HSMs validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3, and manage CloudHSM users outside IAM roles. Non-FIPS mode misses the FIPS-key-and-algorithm restriction; IAM roles alone do not manage CloudHSM cryptographic users.
Wrong options: Use IAM roles as the sole way to manage cryptographic users on the HSMs. (CloudHSM customers manage their own users outside IAM roles.); Use AWS KMS in place of the single-tenant HSM cluster. (A managed key service does not address the explicit requirement to select single-tenant CloudHSM HSMs.); Use a CloudHSM non-FIPS cluster to make all supported algorithms available. (Non-FIPS mode does not restrict use to FIPS-validated keys and algorithms.)

chunks.title: AWS CloudTrail API auditing
chunks.text:
AWS CloudTrail API auditing. AWS CloudTrail records account activity so you can determine who or what made an API call and what resource it affected. For centralized auditing across AWS Organizations accounts, choose an organization trail that delivers logs to Amazon S3; configure data events when the requirement includes S3 object or Lambda function activity.
When to use: Investigators need to identify the user, role, or service behind an AWS action.; A security team needs one trail for management and member accounts, including newly added accounts.; Auditors need S3 object or Lambda function activity in addition to management events.
Key facts: Event history provides the past 90 days of management events for the account and Region being viewed; it does not show member-account events from the management account.; An organization trail logs events for the management account and member accounts and can deliver them to the same S3 bucket.; Only the management account or a delegated administrator can create or manage an organization trail; member accounts cannot change it.; New member accounts automatically receive the organization trail and begin logging.; A multi-Region organization trail covers enabled Regions, but an opt-in home Region prevents member accounts that have not enabled that Region from sending activity to it.; An incorrect S3 bucket policy can cause a trail delivery validation failure.
Gotchas: Do not use management-account Event history as a consolidated view of member-account events.; Management events alone do not satisfy a requirement to log S3 or Lambda data events.; Creating an organization trail does not guarantee successful delivery if its S3 bucket policy is incorrect.
Confused with: AWS Config: Choose Config for configuration history and compliance; choose CloudTrail to identify the actor and API action.; Amazon CloudWatch: CloudWatch monitors operational metrics and alarms; CloudTrail records account activity for auditing.; VPC Flow Logs: Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata, not the identity behind an AWS API call.
ES: AWS CloudTrail registra la actividad de una cuenta para identificar quién o qué hizo una llamada a la API y qué recurso afectó. Para auditar de forma centralizada cuentas de AWS Organizations, elige un organization trail que entregue registros a Amazon S3; configura data events si necesitas actividad de objetos de S3 o funciones de Lambda. Event history muestra los últimos 90 días de management events de la cuenta y Region que consultas; desde la cuenta de administración no muestra eventos de las cuentas miembro.; Un organization trail registra eventos de la cuenta de administración y las cuentas miembro, y puede entregarlos al mismo bucket de S3.; Solo la cuenta de administración o un delegated administrator puede crear o administrar un organization trail; las cuentas miembro no pueden modificarlo.; Las cuentas miembro nuevas reciben automáticamente el organization trail y comienzan a registrar eventos.; Un multi-Region organization trail cubre las Regions habilitadas, pero si su home Region es una opt-in Region, las cuentas miembro que no la habilitaron no le envían actividad.; Una política incorrecta del bucket de S3 puede provocar un error de validación de entrega del trail.

chunks.title: AWS CloudTrail API auditing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A health-tech company uses AWS Organizations and adds member accounts as teams expand. Auditors require a central S3 record of API activity across the organization and activity involving specified S3 objects and Lambda functions in member accounts. The company wants coverage to extend to new accounts without separate trail setup. Which TWO actions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Create an organization trail from the management or delegated administrator account and deliver its logs to S3. + Configure data events on the organization trail for the specified S3 and Lambda resources.
Why: Two distinct decisions matter: how to cover organization accounts and which activity to log. An organization trail delivers to a central S3 bucket and extends automatically to new member accounts. Configure data events for the specified S3 and Lambda resources to capture the activity the auditors requested. Event history is not a central member-account view, and individual trails add the per-account work the company wants to avoid.
Wrong options: Create an individual trail in each member account when the account is added. (Per-account setup fails the requirement to avoid separate trail configuration for new accounts.); Create AWS Config rules for the specified buckets and functions instead of logging their API activity. (Configuration evaluation does not record the requested S3 and Lambda data events.); Use Event history in the management account as the organization's central audit record. (It neither shows member-account events there nor delivers the requested central S3 record.)

chunks.title: AWS CloudTrail API auditing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company has several AWS Organizations accounts and adds accounts when it launches new imprints. Its security team needs a central S3 record of API activity from existing and newly added accounts, without configuring a trail in each account. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an AWS CloudTrail organization trail that delivers events to an S3 bucket.
Why: The deciding requirements are central S3 delivery and automatic coverage of new organization accounts. An organization trail logs activity for the management and member accounts, and logging begins automatically when an account joins. Individual account trails can deliver to S3, but maintaining them for each new account adds operational work. Event history in the management account is not a consolidated view of member-account events.
Wrong options: Use AWS Config in each account to record resource configuration changes. (Configuration history does not provide the requested central record of API activity.); Have the security team review CloudTrail Event history in the management account. (Management-account Event history does not show member-account events or provide the requested central S3 record.); Create a separate CloudTrail trail in each account and send each trail to S3. (Separate account trails require additional configuration as accounts are added.)

chunks.title: AWS CloudTrail API auditing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research consortium uses AWS Organizations. Several member accounts have not enabled the opt-in Region proposed as the home Region for a new audit trail, but the consortium needs API activity from every member account's enabled Regions. Which trail design meets this requirement MOST reliably?
Correct: Create a multi-Region organization trail with its home Region in a Region enabled for the member accounts.
Why: The trail must cover multiple enabled Regions without depending on members opting in to its home Region. A multi-Region organization trail whose home Region is enabled for the member accounts satisfies those constraints. If its home Region is an opt-in Region, members that have not enabled it do not send activity to that trail, even though it is multi-Region. A single-Region trail captures activity only in its own Region.
Wrong options: Create a multi-Region organization trail with its home Region in the proposed opt-in Region. (Member accounts that have not enabled that home Region will not send activity to the trail.); Use Event history in the management account to search all member accounts' enabled Regions. (Management-account Event history does not display member-account events.); Create a single-Region organization trail in a Region enabled for the member accounts. (A single-Region trail does not cover activity in each account's other enabled Regions.)

chunks.title: CloudWatch Logs, Logs Insights and metric filters
chunks.text:
CloudWatch Logs, Logs Insights and metric filters. CloudWatch Logs centralizes logs so teams can retain, search, and monitor them without building a separate log store. In an exam scenario, choose Logs Insights for interactive investigation and a metric filter with a CloudWatch alarm for ongoing alerts on matching log events.
When to use: Centralize application or AWS service logs and set a retention period for each log group.; Investigate incidents by querying existing log events with CloudWatch Logs Insights.; Count occurrences of a log pattern and alert when the resulting metric crosses a threshold.
Key facts: Log groups retain logs indefinitely by default; retention can be set per log group to a period from one day to 10 years.; CloudWatch Logs Insights provides interactive queries for searching and analyzing log data.; Metric filters can report matching log events to a CloudWatch metric, which can be used for an alarm.; Standard log groups support all CloudWatch Logs features; Infrequent Access log groups have lower ingestion charges but support only a subset.; CloudWatch Logs encrypts log data in transit and at rest.
Gotchas: Logs do not expire by default; a fixed retention requirement needs an explicit log-group retention setting.; An interactive Logs Insights query does not replace a metric and alarm for continuous threshold monitoring.; Do not assume every Standard-class feature is available in the Infrequent Access class.
Confused with: 
ES: CloudWatch Logs centraliza los registros para que los equipos puedan conservarlos, consultarlos y monitorearlos sin crear un almacén de logs aparte. En un escenario de examen, elige Logs Insights para investigar de forma interactiva y un metric filter con una alarma de CloudWatch para alertas continuas basadas en eventos coincidentes. De forma predeterminada, los log groups conservan los logs indefinidamente; puedes configurar por log group una retención de un día a 10 años.; CloudWatch Logs Insights permite buscar y analizar logs mediante consultas interactivas.; Los metric filters pueden enviar los eventos coincidentes a una métrica de CloudWatch que puedes usar en una alarma.; Los log groups de la clase Standard admiten todas las funciones de CloudWatch Logs; los de Infrequent Access tienen menores cargos por ingesta, pero admiten solo un subconjunto.; CloudWatch Logs cifra los datos de logs en tránsito y en reposo.

chunks.title: CloudWatch Logs, Logs Insights and metric filters
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company sends application logs from its EC2 instances to CloudWatch Logs. Its operations team must be notified when occurrences of a particular exception exceed a defined threshold, without changing application code or manually running queries. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter for the exception and a CloudWatch alarm on the resulting metric.
Why: The deciding requirement is automatic notification when a log pattern exceeds a threshold. A CloudWatch Logs metric filter reports matching events to a metric, and a CloudWatch alarm can monitor that metric. Logs Insights is useful for investigation, but running queries after an incident begins does not satisfy continuous monitoring. Deletion protection and field indexes address different needs.
Wrong options: Create a field index for the exception field and have operators query it after receiving customer reports. (A field index can improve applicable queries but does not create continuous alerts.); Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query for the exception whenever an operator starts an incident. (An on-demand query does not provide continuous threshold-based notification.); Enable deletion protection on the log group and review exception events in the console. (Deletion protection guards against log-group deletion but does not detect or notify on error rates.)

chunks.title: CloudWatch Logs, Logs Insights and metric filters
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company uses CloudWatch Logs for application events. During incidents, engineers must interactively investigate recent failures; separately, the operations team must receive an alert when a known error pattern crosses a threshold. The company wants to use the logs it already collects rather than modify the application. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Create a metric filter for the error pattern and a CloudWatch alarm for its metric. + Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to search and analyze the application events during incidents.
Why: The scenario distinguishes an interactive investigation from an ongoing alert. CloudWatch Logs Insights handles searches and analysis during incidents, while a metric filter and CloudWatch alarm handle threshold-based monitoring of a known pattern. A field index may make applicable queries more efficient, but it does not act as an alarm threshold. Retention and deletion protection manage log lifecycle and safety, not error notifications.
Wrong options: Set indefinite retention so engineers receive automatic notification of matching errors. (Retention determines when logs expire, not whether error matches produce alerts.); Enable deletion protection on the application log group to generate incident alerts. (Deletion protection prevents accidental deletion, not threshold-based notification.); Create a field index and use it as the alarm threshold for the error pattern. (Field indexes can improve applicable queries but are not metrics or alarm thresholds.)

chunks.title: Amazon CloudWatch metrics, alarms and dashboards
chunks.text:
Amazon CloudWatch metrics, alarms and dashboards. Amazon CloudWatch collects operational metrics, displays them on dashboards, and evaluates alarms that can notify teams or trigger supported resource actions. In an exam scenario, choose it when the decision depends on measured performance or an application KPI—not on API auditing or configuration history.
When to use: An EC2 workload needs memory or disk-usage monitoring: collect those system metrics with the CloudWatch agent.; A measured threshold must notify a team or trigger an EC2 Auto Scaling action.; An application must publish a business KPI as a custom metric and display it with infrastructure metrics.
Key facts: Many AWS services automatically report basic metrics to CloudWatch; applications can publish custom metrics.; A metric alarm evaluates a metric or metric-math expression against a threshold over specified periods.; Metric alarms can send Amazon SNS notifications or perform EC2 and EC2 Auto Scaling actions.; A composite alarm combines other alarm states to reduce alert noise, but cannot perform EC2 or Auto Scaling actions.; Dashboards present metrics and logs together and can be shared across accounts and Regions.
Gotchas: Do not assume an EC2 instance's memory and disk-usage metrics are covered by automatically reported basic metrics; use the CloudWatch agent.; A composite alarm can notify, but it cannot directly trigger an Auto Scaling action.; An alarm with missing metric data can enter INSUFFICIENT_DATA; that state does not necessarily indicate a resource failure.
Confused with: AWS CloudTrail: CloudTrail addresses who made an API call; CloudWatch evaluates operational metrics.; AWS Config: Config tracks configuration history and compliance; CloudWatch tracks performance metrics and alarms.; AWS X-Ray: X-Ray traces requests to find distributed latency bottlenecks; CloudWatch alarms evaluate metrics against thresholds.
ES: Amazon CloudWatch recopila métricas operativas, las muestra en dashboards y evalúa alarmas que pueden notificar a un equipo o activar acciones compatibles sobre recursos. En un escenario de examen, elígelo cuando la decisión dependa del rendimiento medido o de un KPI de la aplicación, no de la auditoría de llamadas API ni del historial de configuración. Muchos servicios de AWS envían automáticamente métricas básicas a CloudWatch; las aplicaciones también pueden publicar custom metrics.; Una metric alarm evalúa una métrica o una expresión de metric math frente a un umbral durante los períodos especificados.; Las metric alarms pueden enviar notificaciones de Amazon SNS o ejecutar acciones de EC2 y EC2 Auto Scaling.; Una composite alarm combina los estados de otras alarmas para reducir alertas innecesarias, pero no puede ejecutar acciones de EC2 ni de Auto Scaling.; Los dashboards reúnen métricas y logs y se pueden compartir entre cuentas y Regions.

chunks.title: Amazon CloudWatch metrics, alarms and dashboards
chunks.text:
Scenario: A photo-processing company runs workers in an EC2 Auto Scaling group. During large uploads, worker memory usage rises before CPU usage does, and the team wants capacity to increase when memory usage crosses its chosen threshold. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy CloudWatch agent to collect memory usage and create a metric alarm with an Auto Scaling action.
Why: The requirement is to scale on memory usage, which leads CPU usage for these workers. CloudWatch agent can collect EC2 memory metrics, and a metric alarm can perform an EC2 Auto Scaling action when its threshold is breached. An automatically reported CPU metric would react to a different signal. A composite alarm cannot perform the required Auto Scaling action.
Wrong options: Create a CloudWatch composite alarm on CPU alarms and assign it an Auto Scaling action. (It uses the wrong signal, and composite alarms cannot perform Auto Scaling actions.); Use AWS X-Ray traces to identify slow requests and initiate the capacity change. (Request tracing does not provide the required memory-threshold alarm for Auto Scaling.); Create a CloudWatch alarm on the instances' automatically reported CPU metric and use it for Auto Scaling. (CPU rises later than memory in this workload, so it misses the stated scaling signal.)

chunks.title: Amazon CloudWatch metrics, alarms and dashboards
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company sends application error events to CloudWatch Logs. Its operations team wants a numerical count derived from matching log events so it can graph the count beside other metrics and alert when the count crosses a threshold. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter, then graph and alarm on the resulting CloudWatch metric.
Why: The requirement is specifically to derive a metric from matching CloudWatch Logs events and then graph and alarm on it. A CloudWatch Logs metric filter extracts numerical values and generates a CloudWatch metric for dashboards and alerting. VPC Flow Logs describe IP traffic metadata, not application error events. Config and CloudTrail likewise answer different operational questions.
Wrong options: Create AWS Config rules for the application resources and add their compliance results to a dashboard. (Configuration compliance does not turn matching application log events into a numerical metric.); Enable CloudTrail for the account and use its API activity records as the application error metric. (API activity records do not extract a metric from the application's CloudWatch Logs events.); Enable VPC Flow Logs for the application's VPC and alarm on accepted and rejected traffic records. (IP traffic metadata does not supply the requested count of matching application error events.)

chunks.title: Amazon CloudWatch metrics, alarms and dashboards
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare software provider operates an application in several AWS accounts. Its central operations team needs to see metrics and logs from those accounts in one monitoring account and receive alerts based on metrics from the source accounts. Which TWO CloudWatch capabilities should the team use to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Create cross-account CloudWatch alarms that watch metrics in the linked source accounts. + Enable CloudWatch cross-account observability and link the application accounts to the monitoring account.
Why: The team needs both centralized visibility and metric-based alerting across accounts. CloudWatch cross-account observability links source accounts to a monitoring account for viewing metrics and logs, and enabled cross-account functionality permits alarms on metrics in other accounts. A cross-account composite alarm is an attractive but unsupported substitute. Config compliance and CloudTrail API auditing do not meet the operational-monitoring requirement.
Wrong options: Use AWS Config rules in the monitoring account to evaluate resource compliance in place of operational metrics. (Configuration compliance does not provide the requested cross-account metric and log monitoring.); Create CloudWatch composite alarms whose rules directly combine alarms from different AWS accounts. (CloudWatch does not support creating cross-account composite alarms.); Use CloudTrail activity records as substitutes for application metrics and logs in the monitoring account. (API audit records do not replace the requested operational metrics and logs.)

chunks.title: Amazon Cognito identity pools (temporary AWS credentials)
chunks.text:
Amazon Cognito identity pools (temporary AWS credentials). Amazon Cognito identity pools exchange app users’ identities for temporary AWS credentials, including for users who have not signed in. Choose an identity pool when a mobile or web app needs users to make IAM-authorized requests directly to AWS services.
When to use: App users need temporary credentials to sign requests to S3 or DynamoDB.; Guests need narrowly scoped access before signing in.; Permissions must differ by user claims or authentication status.
Key facts: Identity pools can issue temporary AWS credentials to authenticated and unauthenticated app users.; IAM roles and policies determine what those credentials can access.; An identity pool can exchange a Cognito user pool token or supported third-party identity-provider claims for AWS credentials.; Identity pools can use claims to select roles or create IAM session tags for granular access.
Gotchas: A user pool token authenticates a user; a user pool alone does not provide the temporary AWS credentials needed to sign direct AWS service requests.; Guest access still needs a narrowly scoped IAM role.; An identity pool can work with a user pool; the two are not mutually exclusive.
Confused with: cognito-user-pools: User pools handle app sign-in and tokens; identity pools exchange identities or tokens for temporary AWS credentials.; iam-identity-center-sso: IAM Identity Center is for workforce SSO; identity pools provide app users, including guests, with AWS credentials.
ES: Amazon Cognito identity pools intercambia las identidades de los usuarios de una aplicación por credenciales temporales de AWS, incluso si todavía no iniciaron sesión. Elige un identity pool cuando una aplicación móvil o web necesita que sus usuarios hagan solicitudes directas a servicios de AWS autorizadas mediante IAM. Identity pools puede emitir credenciales temporales de AWS para usuarios autenticados y no autenticados.; Los roles y las políticas de IAM determinan a qué pueden acceder esas credenciales.; Un identity pool puede intercambiar un token de Cognito user pools o claims de un proveedor de identidad compatible por credenciales de AWS.; Identity pools puede usar claims para seleccionar roles o crear IAM session tags para acceso granular.

chunks.title: Amazon Cognito identity pools (temporary AWS credentials)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A travel app lets guests read a limited set of itineraries from DynamoDB. After users sign in through the app’s existing Cognito user pool, they must make signed requests directly to DynamoDB with broader IAM permissions. The team does not want to distribute AWS credentials from its own servers. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure the identity pool to accept user pool tokens and assign an authenticated IAM role. + Configure an identity pool to issue narrowly scoped temporary credentials for guests.
Why: The app needs two levels of temporary AWS credentials: narrow guest access and broader access after user pool sign-in. An identity pool can issue guest credentials and accept user pool tokens to provide credentials under an authenticated IAM role. User pool tokens alone cannot serve as AWS credentials for signed DynamoDB requests, so option B misses both the credential and guest requirements.
Wrong options: Assign IAM Identity Center permission sets to guests and signed-in travelers. (Workforce permission sets do not address guest app users making direct signed DynamoDB requests.); Use user pool tokens as the credentials for both guest and signed-in DynamoDB requests. (User pool tokens are not AWS credentials, and guests do not sign in to receive them.); Use AD Connector to exchange the app’s user pool tokens for DynamoDB credentials. (AD Connector is not the identity-pool mechanism for exchanging user pool tokens for temporary AWS credentials.)

chunks.title: Amazon Cognito identity pools (temporary AWS credentials)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum’s mobile app lets visitors browse images stored in Amazon S3 without creating an account. The app must make signed requests directly to S3, and visitors must receive only the permissions needed to retrieve those images. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure a Cognito identity pool with guest access and a narrowly scoped IAM role.
Why: The deciding requirements are unsigned-in visitors and signed requests directly to S3. A Cognito identity pool can issue temporary credentials for guests, with IAM limiting access to the intended images. A user pool sign-in token does not meet the guest requirement or by itself supply credentials for those requests.
Wrong options: Configure IAM Identity Center for visitors and assign them access to the images. (Workforce SSO does not fit an app that must grant unsigned-in visitors temporary credentials.); Configure a Cognito user pool and require each visitor to obtain a sign-in token. (Requiring sign-in violates the guest-access requirement, and the token alone does not provide AWS credentials for signed S3 requests.); Federate a corporate SAML provider to IAM roles for the app’s visitors. (A corporate identity provider does not serve visitors who have not signed in.)

chunks.title: Amazon Cognito user pools (app sign-up/sign-in)
chunks.text:
Amazon Cognito user pools (app sign-up/sign-in). Amazon Cognito user pools provide a user directory and sign-in for web and mobile apps. Choose a user pool when customers need app accounts, external-provider sign-in, or tokens that the app uses to authorize requests; add an identity pool only when users need temporary AWS credentials.
When to use: Customers need to sign up for and sign in to a web or mobile app.; The app needs social, SAML, or OIDC sign-in and user pool tokens.; The team wants managed pages for sign-up, sign-in, MFA, or password reset.
Key facts: A user pool acts as an OIDC identity provider for the app.; User pools support native users and sign-in through social, SAML, and OIDC identity providers.; Managed login provides pages for sign-up, sign-in, MFA, and password reset.; Lambda triggers can customize workflows, including rejecting a sign-up request.; Identity pools provide credentials for users to access AWS services; user pools provide app authentication.
Gotchas: Do not enable self-service sign-up unless public registration is intended.; A user pool token is not, by itself, temporary AWS credentials for direct access to S3 or DynamoDB.; An external SAML provider can be a sign-in source for a customer app; it does not make workforce SSO the required solution.
Confused with: cognito-identity-pools: Identity pools issue temporary AWS credentials for access to AWS services; user pools handle app user sign-up and sign-in.; iam-identity-center-sso: IAM Identity Center fits centralized workforce SSO, not customer self-registration for an app.; identity-federation-saml-oidc: Federation to IAM roles addresses access through an existing IdP; a user pool can accept SAML or OIDC sign-in for app users.
ES: Amazon Cognito user pools ofrece un directorio de usuarios e inicio de sesión para aplicaciones web y móviles. Elige un user pool cuando los clientes necesiten cuentas en la aplicación, inicio de sesión con proveedores externos o tokens para autorizar solicitudes; agrega un identity pool solo si necesitan credenciales temporales de AWS. Un user pool actúa como proveedor de identidad OIDC para la aplicación.; Los user pools admiten usuarios propios e inicio de sesión mediante proveedores sociales, SAML y OIDC.; Managed login proporciona páginas de registro, inicio de sesión, MFA y restablecimiento de contraseñas.; Los Lambda triggers pueden personalizar los flujos, incluso rechazar una solicitud de registro.; Los identity pools proporcionan credenciales para que los usuarios accedan a servicios de AWS; los user pools autentican usuarios de la aplicación.

chunks.title: Amazon Cognito user pools (app sign-up/sign-in)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional theater is launching a ticketing app for the public. Visitors must create their own accounts, sign in, and reset forgotten passwords without the theater building those pages. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use a Cognito user pool with self-service sign-up and managed login.
Why: The deciding requirements are public self-registration and ready-made sign-in and password-reset pages. A Cognito user pool supports self-service sign-up, while managed login provides those pages. An identity pool serves a different purpose: issuing credentials for access to AWS services. Public self-registration is appropriate here because the theater explicitly wants anyone to be able to create an account.
Wrong options: Federate the theater's corporate SAML provider directly to IAM roles for visitors. (Corporate federation to IAM roles does not provide public app sign-up and managed password-reset pages.); Use a Cognito identity pool to issue AWS credentials to each visitor. (An identity pool supplies credentials for AWS service access, not the requested sign-up and password-reset pages.); Use IAM Identity Center for visitor sign-in and account creation. (IAM Identity Center targets workforce SSO rather than public customer registration.)

chunks.title: Amazon Cognito user pools (app sign-up/sign-in)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A recipe publisher's mobile app lets readers sign in with Google or with an account created in the app. Its backend needs app user tokens to distinguish signed-in readers, but readers will not call AWS services directly. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use a Cognito user pool with native accounts and Google sign-in.
Why: The app needs both native customer accounts and Google sign-in, followed by tokens for its backend. A Cognito user pool supports those app authentication paths. A Cognito identity pool is a tempting choice because it can work with external identities, but its purpose is to provide AWS service credentials, which this scenario does not require.
Wrong options: Federate the publisher's corporate IdP to IAM roles for readers. (Federation to IAM roles does not supply the requested native customer accounts.); Use IAM Identity Center with the publisher's workforce directory. (Workforce SSO does not address the stated customer accounts and Google sign-in.); Use a Cognito identity pool with Google as its provider. (An identity pool focuses on AWS credentials, which readers do not need, rather than native app sign-up.)

chunks.title: Amazon Cognito user pools (app sign-up/sign-in)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A medical equipment supplier is building a portal for approved repair shops. Shops need individual app accounts and sign-in, but the supplier must create each account after checking a contract; unknown visitors must not register themselves. Which solution meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Use a Cognito user pool with self-service sign-up disabled and create users through its admin workflow.
Why: The supplier needs app authentication but must control who receives an account. Cognito user pools support administrator-driven user creation, and self-service sign-up can remain disabled. Enabling self-service sign-up is the critical trap: it opens account registration to people on the internet, contrary to the approval requirement.
Wrong options: Use a Cognito identity pool and allow unauthenticated guests to obtain AWS credentials. (Guest AWS credentials do not enforce supplier-approved creation of app accounts.); Use a Cognito user pool with self-service sign-up enabled. (Self-service sign-up would allow unapproved visitors to create accounts.); Use IAM Identity Center and allow shops to enroll themselves as workforce users. (Workforce SSO does not meet the requirement for supplier-created customer app accounts.)

chunks.title: Compliance requirements, AWS Artifact and data classification
chunks.text:
Compliance requirements, AWS Artifact and data classification. AWS Artifact provides downloadable AWS security and compliance documents and lets you manage agreements with AWS. Use its documents as evidence about AWS controls, while your organization defines its own data classifications and documents its own controls.
When to use: An auditor requests an AWS SOC, ISO, or PCI compliance document.; An organization needs to review, accept, or track an agreement with AWS across its accounts.; A team must classify its data and determine which internal controls need supporting evidence.
Key facts: AWS Artifact provides on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents.; AWS Artifact supports reviewing, accepting, and tracking agreements for one account or multiple accounts in an organization.; Artifact documents can be submitted to auditors or regulators as evidence about AWS infrastructure and services.; Customers remain responsible for documents demonstrating their own company's security and compliance.; AWS recommends using internationally recognized standards and frameworks when developing data classification rules.
Gotchas: An AWS compliance report does not replace evidence for customer-managed controls.; An AWS Marketplace vendor's document is not a substitute for a document about AWS controls.; The supplied data classification whitepaper is marked historical; do not treat its examples as current mandatory rules.
Confused with: Internal compliance evidence: Artifact supplies documents about AWS controls; your organization must document its own controls.; AWS Marketplace vendor documents: Artifact can provide vendor documents too, but choose AWS documents when the request concerns AWS infrastructure and services.
ES: AWS Artifact ofrece documentos descargables de seguridad y cumplimiento de AWS y permite administrar acuerdos con AWS. Usa esos documentos como evidencia sobre los controles de AWS, mientras tu organización define sus propias clasificaciones de datos y documenta sus propios controles. AWS Artifact ofrece descargas bajo demanda de documentos de seguridad y cumplimiento de AWS.; AWS Artifact permite revisar, aceptar y dar seguimiento a acuerdos para una cuenta o varias cuentas de una organización.; Puedes presentar documentos de Artifact ante auditores o reguladores como evidencia sobre la infraestructura y los servicios de AWS.; Los clientes siguen siendo responsables de los documentos que demuestren la seguridad y el cumplimiento de su propia empresa.; AWS recomienda usar estándares y marcos reconocidos internacionalmente al desarrollar reglas de clasificación de datos.

chunks.title: Compliance requirements, AWS Artifact and data classification
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional bank is preparing for an audit of an application hosted on AWS. The auditor requests an AWS SOC report and documentation showing how the bank operates its own security controls. Which approach meets both requests with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Download the AWS SOC report from AWS Artifact and provide separate documentation of the bank's controls.
Why: The auditor asks for two kinds of evidence: a report about AWS and documentation about the bank's controls. AWS Artifact provides on-demand access to AWS SOC reports, so the bank can obtain that report there. The bank remains responsible for documenting its own controls; submitting the AWS report alone would leave that requirement unmet.
Wrong options: Download the AWS SOC report from AWS Artifact and use it as the complete evidence for both AWS and bank controls. (The AWS report does not replace documentation demonstrating the bank's own controls.); Prepare documentation of the bank's controls and omit the AWS SOC report because the application runs on AWS. (The auditor explicitly requested an AWS SOC report as well as the bank's documentation.); Download an AWS Marketplace vendor's compliance documents from AWS Artifact and submit the bank's control documentation. (The bank's documentation addresses its controls, but a vendor's documents do not supply the requested AWS SOC report.)

chunks.title: Compliance requirements, AWS Artifact and data classification
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company is designing a data classification program for a new AWS workload. Its governance team needs rules appropriate to the company's data, while an external reviewer also requests evidence about AWS security controls. Which approach meets both needs MOST effectively?
Correct: Develop company-specific classification rules using internationally recognized frameworks, and obtain AWS compliance documents from AWS Artifact.
Why: The company needs both its own data classification rules and evidence concerning AWS controls. AWS recommends internationally recognized standards and frameworks when customers develop classification rules, and AWS Artifact provides documents that can serve as audit artifacts about AWS. An AWS compliance report cannot stand in for the company's classification decisions. The provided classification whitepaper is marked historical, so its examples should not be treated as mandatory rules.
Wrong options: Develop company-specific classification rules using recognized frameworks, and submit AWS Marketplace vendor documents as evidence about AWS controls. (The classification approach fits, but vendor documents do not address the requested AWS controls.); Adopt example categories from the historical AWS data classification whitepaper as mandatory rules, and obtain AWS documents from AWS Artifact. (Artifact addresses the AWS evidence request, but a historical paper's examples are not mandatory company-specific rules.); Use an AWS compliance report as the company's classification rules, and present that report as evidence about AWS controls. (The report can serve as AWS evidence but does not define classification rules appropriate to the company's data.)

chunks.title: Cost-effective compute choice: Lambda vs Fargate vs EC2
chunks.text:
Cost-effective compute choice: Lambda vs Fargate vs EC2. Choose compute using measured utilization, workload requirements, and a cost model—not a blanket rule that one service is cheapest. Standard Lambda functions charge by requests and execution duration; steady workloads may justify evaluating EC2 purchasing options or Lambda Managed Instances, while an existing container workload may favor Fargate when the cost model and operational requirements support it.
When to use: Short, infrequent code executions with long idle periods: evaluate standard Lambda functions.; A containerized workload that should avoid managing EC2 instances: evaluate Fargate against the modeled alternatives.; Predictable, sustained demand: right-size resources and evaluate applicable EC2 purchasing options.; High-volume Lambda functions that must retain the Lambda programming model: evaluate Lambda Managed Instances.
Key facts: Standard Lambda functions are priced by request count and execution duration, measured in GB-seconds.; Lambda Managed Instances use EC2 instances managed by Lambda and retain the Lambda programming model; their charges include requests, EC2 instance charges, and a compute management fee.; The provided pricing documentation identifies Compute Savings Plans, EC2 Instance Savings Plans, and Reserved Instances as options for eligible EC2 instance charges.; AWS recommends cost modeling and selecting resource type, size, and number based on workload data.
Gotchas: Infrequent requests do not necessarily make Lambda cheapest if each execution consumes substantial duration and memory.; A steady workload does not, by itself, establish that EC2 beats Fargate; compare modeled costs for designs that meet the requirements.; Lambda Managed Instances are not billed like standard Lambda functions: EC2 instance and management charges apply.
Confused with: Standard Lambda functions vs. Lambda Managed Instances: Standard functions have request and execution-duration charges; Managed Instances add EC2 instance and management charges while retaining the Lambda programming model.; Fargate vs. EC2: For a container workload, use its operational constraints and measured cost model to decide rather than assuming either option is always cheaper.
ES: Elige el cómputo según la utilización medida, los requisitos y un modelo de costos; ningún servicio es siempre el más barato. Las funciones Lambda estándar cobran por solicitudes y duración de ejecución; para cargas sostenidas, evalúa opciones de compra de EC2 o Lambda Managed Instances, y para contenedores considera Fargate si el modelo de costos y los requisitos operativos lo respaldan. Las funciones Lambda estándar se cobran según la cantidad de solicitudes y la duración de ejecución, medida en GB-segundos.; Lambda Managed Instances usa instancias EC2 administradas por Lambda y conserva el modelo de programación de Lambda; sus cargos incluyen solicitudes, instancias EC2 y una tarifa de administración.; La documentación de precios proporcionada identifica Compute Savings Plans, EC2 Instance Savings Plans y Reserved Instances como opciones para cargos de instancias EC2 elegibles.; AWS recomienda modelar los costos y elegir el tipo, tamaño y número de recursos según los datos de la carga.

chunks.title: Cost-effective compute choice: Lambda vs Fargate vs EC2
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum runs code that validates small submissions from visitors. Requests arrive in brief bursts on event days, and the application does no work for weeks between events. The team has confirmed that each validation is a short execution and wants to avoid paying for provisioned compute throughout the idle periods. Which approach best meets these requirements with the MOST cost-effective compute billing model?
Correct: Run each validation as a standard AWS Lambda function invocation.
Why: The deciding constraints are short executions and weeks without requests. Standard Lambda functions are charged by requests and execution duration, making their billing model a strong fit for this pattern. Lambda Managed Instances can retain the Lambda programming model, but they also introduce EC2 instance and management charges, which undermine the stated idle-time objective.
Wrong options: Run the validator continuously on right-sized EC2 instances. (Continuously provisioned instances do not address the stated goal of avoiding provisioned compute during weeks without work.); Use Lambda Managed Instances backed by EC2 instances. (Its EC2 instance and management charges do not match the requirement to avoid provisioned compute during long idle periods.); Keep the validator running as a continuously provisioned Fargate service. (A continuously provisioned service does not satisfy the stated preference to provision compute only when validation work arrives.)

chunks.title: Cost-effective compute choice: Lambda vs Fargate vs EC2
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics firm already processes events with Lambda functions. Its high-volume workload is steady, and a cost model shows that moving those functions to Lambda Managed Instances would lower its total compute cost after accounting for instance charges and the management fee. The firm must retain its Lambda programming model and wants AWS to manage instance provisioning and patching. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Run the functions on Lambda Managed Instances.
Why: The firm needs both the Lambda programming model and managed instance operations. Lambda Managed Instances supplies those properties, and the scenario's cost model establishes the total-cost advantage for this particular workload. Standard Lambda functions avoid EC2 instance charges but can still cost more overall; moving to team-managed EC2 would violate the operational requirement.
Wrong options: Rebuild the functions as a continuously running Fargate container service. (Rebuilding them as a container service does not retain the required Lambda programming model.); Keep the functions on standard Lambda compute because it has no EC2 instance charge. (Avoiding an instance line item does not overcome the modeled lower total cost of the compliant alternative.); Move the event processing to team-managed EC2 instances with a purchasing commitment. (Team-managed instances fail the requirement for AWS-managed provisioning and patching.)

chunks.title: Cost-effective compute choice: Lambda vs Fargate vs EC2
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute is planning compute for two independent applications. One performs brief checks only when occasional samples arrive; the other keeps an EC2-based analysis engine continuously busy at a measured, appropriate instance size, with a predictable baseline. The institute wants to choose a cost approach suited to each usage pattern rather than impose one compute model on both. Which TWO choices best meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
Correct: Run the occasional sample checks as standard Lambda function invocations. + Keep the measured EC2 configuration for the analysis engine and evaluate a purchasing option for its stable baseline.
Why: The applications have different utilization patterns, so each needs its own cost decision. Standard Lambda function billing matches brief, occasional checks, while the continuously busy engine has a measured EC2 size and a predictable baseline suitable for evaluating purchasing options. Provisioning idle compute for the checks or increasing an already adequate instance size disregards the supplied usage data.
Wrong options: Keep EC2 instances continuously provisioned for the occasional sample checks. (Continuous provisioning does not suit the checks' long periods without work.); Increase the analysis engine's EC2 instance size to obtain more unused capacity. (The measured size already meets demand, so adding unused capacity works against right-sizing.); Move the busy analysis engine to standard Lambda functions without modeling its request and duration costs. (Continuous use alone does not justify a Lambda migration without a cost comparison.)

chunks.title: When to use containers and migrating apps into containers
chunks.text:
When to use containers and migrating apps into containers. Containers package an application with its dependencies to make deployment more consistent across compatible hosts. Choose them when portability, isolated workloads on a shared host OS, or a path from a legacy application to managed container deployment matters more than keeping each application in a separate VM.
When to use: The same application must move between compatible environments without rebuilding it for each host.; Multiple isolated applications or batch jobs should share a host OS.; An eligible legacy application must be containerized without requiring its source code.
Key facts: Containers use OS-level virtualization; VMs use hardware-level virtualization through a hypervisor.; Multiple isolated containers can run on one host OS without each needing a VM.; Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS are options for managing container deployments; Amazon ECR can hold container images.; AWS App2Container can generate images and deployment artifacts for supported existing applications without source code, but it is no longer open to new customers.
Gotchas: Portability still requires a host with suitable kernel components.; Moving an application into a container does not require splitting it into microservices first.; Do not propose a new App2Container signup: the tool is no longer open to new customers.
Confused with: Virtual machines: VMs use hypervisor-based hardware virtualization; multiple containers can instead share a host OS while remaining isolated.; AWS Lambda: For a requirement to preserve and deploy an existing application as a container image, rewriting it as functions is a different migration approach.
ES: Los contenedores empaquetan una aplicación con sus dependencias para que su implementación sea más consistente entre hosts compatibles. Elígelos cuando importen la portabilidad, el aislamiento de cargas que comparten un host OS o la migración de una aplicación heredada a un despliegue administrado de contenedores. Los contenedores usan virtualización a nivel de OS; las máquinas virtuales usan virtualización de hardware mediante un hipervisor.; Varios contenedores aislados pueden ejecutarse en un mismo host OS sin necesitar una máquina virtual para cada uno.; Amazon ECS y Amazon EKS permiten administrar despliegues de contenedores; Amazon ECR puede almacenar sus imágenes.; AWS App2Container puede generar imágenes y artefactos de despliegue para aplicaciones existentes compatibles sin código fuente, pero ya no admite clientes nuevos.

chunks.title: When to use containers and migrating apps into containers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer enrolled in AWS App2Container before it stopped accepting new customers. It has an existing ASP.NET application on a Windows server but no longer has the source code. The team wants to generate a container image from the running application, keep the image in an AWS container registry, and prepare for deployment on Amazon ECS with minimal manual packaging. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use AWS App2Container to analyze the running application and generate its container image and AWS deployment artifacts. + Store the generated container image in Amazon ECR for the planned Amazon ECS deployment.
Why: The company is already an App2Container customer, and the running ASP.NET application matches a type the tool can inventory and analyze. App2Container can generate a container image and AWS deployment artifacts without requiring the application's source code. Amazon ECR provides the requested image destination. Amazon EKS is an orchestration option, not a substitute for the image registry.
Wrong options: Create a separate VM image for the application and use it as the Amazon ECS container image. (A VM image does not meet the requirement to generate and store a container image.); Use Amazon EKS as the registry for the generated image and deploy the application on Amazon ECS. (Amazon EKS is a container orchestration option, not the requested container image registry.); Rebuild the application as AWS Lambda functions before creating an Amazon ECS deployment. (Rebuilding the application conflicts with the lack of source code and the minimal-packaging requirement.)

chunks.title: When to use containers and migrating apps into containers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company runs a rendering application in several environments whose hosts have suitable kernel components. Differences in software installed on those hosts cause inconsistent behavior, and the team wants to move the application without rebuilding it for each environment. The deployment artifact must include the application's dependencies. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Package the application and its dependencies in a container image, store it in Amazon ECR, and deploy the containers with Amazon ECS.
Why: The deciding requirement is to carry the existing application and its dependencies between compatible hosts without environment-specific rebuilds. A container provides an isolated package that shields the application from differences in software installed on the host; Amazon ECR can hold the image and Amazon ECS can manage deployment. Separate VM images or host-specific installation scripts preserve the per-environment work the company wants to eliminate.
Wrong options: Rewrite the rendering application as AWS Lambda functions and deploy a different version in each environment. (Rewriting and maintaining separate versions conflicts with moving the existing application without rebuilding it.); Install the application directly on each host and maintain a host-specific dependency installation script. (Host-specific installations leave the deployment dependent on differences between environments.); Create a separate VM image for each environment and install the application's dependencies in each image. (Separate VM images do not meet the requirement to avoid building an environment-specific deployment artifact.)

chunks.title: Cost allocation tags and multi-account billing
chunks.text:
Cost allocation tags and multi-account billing. Cost allocation tags attribute AWS charges to business categories such as teams or projects. Activate the tags in Billing and Cost Management to use them for cost reporting; use AWS Organizations consolidated billing when separate accounts need centralized payment and shared discounts.
When to use: Resources are tagged, but finance cannot break down costs by team, project, or application.; Multiple AWS accounts need centralized billing and combined usage for eligible discounts.; Finance needs both account-level charges and a tag-based view of shared workloads.
Key facts: AWS-generated and user-defined cost allocation tags must be activated separately before they appear in Cost Explorer or a cost allocation report.; Only an organization's management account, or a standalone account, can access the cost allocation tags manager in the Billing console.; A cost allocation report includes tagged and untagged costs.; With consolidated billing, the management account pays member-account charges and can obtain a cost report for each member account.; Consolidated billing combines usage across accounts to share volume pricing discounts, Reserved Instance discounts, and Savings Plans.
Gotchas: Applying a resource tag does not by itself activate it as a cost allocation tag.; Activating user-defined tags does not also activate AWS-generated tags.; Cost allocation tags attribute charges; they do not consolidate payment or pool usage across accounts.
Confused with: AWS Cost Explorer: Cost Explorer can filter views by activated tags; it does not replace applying and activating those tags.; AWS Budgets: Budgets addresses spending thresholds, not the activation of tags for chargeback.; AWS Cost and Usage Report: A detailed report can show cost allocation tags, but creating a report does not activate them.
ES: Las cost allocation tags atribuyen los cargos de AWS a categorías de negocio, como equipos o proyectos. Actívalas en Billing and Cost Management para usarlas en los informes de costos; usa consolidated billing de AWS Organizations cuando varias cuentas necesiten pagos centralizados y descuentos compartidos. Debes activar por separado las cost allocation tags AWS-generated y user-defined para que aparezcan en Cost Explorer o en un informe de asignación de costos.; Solo la management account de una organización, o una cuenta independiente, puede acceder al administrador de cost allocation tags en la consola de Billing.; Un informe de asignación de costos incluye los costos de recursos con y sin etiquetas.; Con consolidated billing, la management account paga los cargos de las cuentas miembro y puede obtener un informe de costos por cada una.; Consolidated billing combina el uso entre cuentas para compartir descuentos por volumen, descuentos de Reserved Instances y Savings Plans.

chunks.title: Cost allocation tags and multi-account billing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher operates production, testing, and analytics in separate standalone AWS accounts. It wants a central payer, a way to track charges by account, and combined usage that can share applicable volume pricing discounts. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Place the accounts in AWS Organizations and use consolidated billing.
Why: The publisher needs more than cost attribution: it requires one paying account and combined usage across accounts. AWS Organizations consolidated billing makes the management account responsible for member-account charges and allows account-level cost reporting. Combined usage can share volume pricing discounts, and consolidated billing has no additional fee. Tags alone can categorize costs but cannot satisfy the payment or discount requirements.
Wrong options: Review each standalone account separately in Cost Explorer. (Separate cost views do not centralize payment or combine account usage for discounts.); Create an AWS Budget in each standalone account for its expected charges. (Separate budgets do not provide consolidated payment or shared volume pricing discounts.); Apply the same CostCenter tag to resources in each standalone account. (Tags can categorize resource costs but do not create a central payer or combine usage across standalone accounts.)

chunks.title: Cost allocation tags and multi-account billing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company is moving three departments into separate AWS accounts while keeping some application resources shared across departments. Finance wants centralized payment, combined usage for applicable discounts, and a cost breakdown by project for resources tagged with a user-defined Project tag. Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Activate the user-defined Project cost allocation tag from the organization's management account. + Place the accounts in AWS Organizations with consolidated billing.
Why: Two distinct capabilities are required: multi-account payment and discount sharing, plus project-level cost attribution. Consolidated billing handles the first by combining charges and usage under the management account. Activating the user-defined Project cost allocation tag handles the second for tagged resources. A report alone does not activate Project, and a budget addresses neither missing capability.
Wrong options: Configure a Cost and Usage Report without activating cost allocation tags. (A detailed report without tag activation does not provide the requested breakdown by the Project cost allocation tag.); Create an AWS Budget for each department's account. (Budgets do not establish centralized payment or activate Project for cost allocation.); Use AWS Compute Optimizer to recommend smaller compute resources. (Compute right-sizing recommendations do not meet the payment or project-cost attribution requirements.)

chunks.title: AWS Cost and Usage Report / Data Exports
chunks.text:
AWS Cost and Usage Report / Data Exports. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) delivers detailed billing line items to an S3 bucket you own. Choose it when a scenario requires hourly cost and usage breakdowns for custom analysis with Athena or Quick, rather than a spend dashboard or threshold alert.
When to use: Analysts need billing line items in S3 for their own queries.; A report must break down costs by hour, product resource, or defined tags.; The team wants to analyze detailed billing data with Athena or Quick.
Key facts: CUR contains AWS’s most comprehensive set of cost and usage data.; You can configure reports with hourly, daily, or monthly granularity and deliver them to your S3 bucket.; Report line items identify combinations of AWS product, usage type, and operation.; The first report can take up to 24 hours to arrive; subsequent reports are updated at least once a day.; Updates during a billing month are cumulative estimates and can change before charges are finalized.
Gotchas: Hourly granularity describes the billing breakdown, not hourly delivery of new report files.; Cost allocation tags help attribute costs but do not, by themselves, deliver a line-item report to S3.; Cost Explorer is useful for visualizing and forecasting spend; it is not the choice when the requirement is detailed report files for custom Athena queries.
Confused with: AWS Cost Explorer: Use it to visualize or forecast spend; use CUR for detailed billing files in S3.; AWS Budgets: Use it for threshold alerts or actions, not line-item billing analysis.; Cost allocation tags: Tags attribute costs; CUR can include tag-based breakdowns in a delivered report.
ES: AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) entrega partidas detalladas de facturación en un bucket de S3 que te pertenece. Elígelo cuando necesites desgloses por hora para análisis personalizado con Athena o Quick, en lugar de un panel de gastos o una alerta por umbral. CUR contiene el conjunto más completo de datos de costos y uso de AWS.; Puedes configurar informes con granularidad por hora, día o mes y entregarlos en tu bucket de S3.; Las partidas del informe identifican combinaciones de producto de AWS, tipo de uso y operación.; El primer informe puede tardar hasta 24 horas en llegar; después, los informes se actualizan al menos una vez al día.; Las actualizaciones durante el mes son estimaciones acumulativas y pueden cambiar antes de que se finalicen los cargos.

chunks.title: AWS Cost and Usage Report / Data Exports
chunks.text:
Scenario: A video-streaming company wants its finance team to investigate AWS charges by hour, product, usage type, and operation. Analysts will run their own Athena queries against files stored in an S3 bucket the company owns. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure an hourly-granularity AWS Cost and Usage Report for delivery to the S3 bucket and use its Athena integration.
Why: The deciding requirement is detailed, hourly-granularity billing data in S3 for custom Athena queries. An AWS Cost and Usage Report provides line items and can be configured for Athena integration. Cost Explorer addresses spend visualization rather than delivery of the requested report files; tags alone do not produce those files.
Wrong options: Create AWS Budgets for each product and send threshold alerts to the finance team. (Threshold alerts do not provide billing line items for custom Athena queries.); Activate cost allocation tags for each product and query the tags with Athena. (Tags can help attribute costs but do not themselves deliver billing files to S3 for Athena.); Use AWS Cost Explorer to visualize hourly spending and export the results for the analysts. (Cost Explorer is suited to spend visualization and forecasting, not delivery of the requested detailed report files to S3.)

chunks.title: AWS Cost and Usage Report / Data Exports
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute has tagged AWS resources by laboratory and needs a reusable billing dataset for its own analyses. It wants to examine costs by those tags and by product resource, then analyze the delivered files with Quick. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Configure an AWS Cost and Usage Report with the needed resource and tag breakdowns, deliver it to S3, and use its Quick integration.
Why: The institute needs delivered billing files with resource and tag breakdowns, not just a way to label or forecast costs. CUR can provide those breakdowns in files delivered to S3 and supports integration with Quick. Cost allocation tags are useful for attribution, but activating them alone does not create the requested dataset.
Wrong options: Activate cost allocation tags and use them as the billing dataset in Quick. (Tags identify cost categories but do not by themselves deliver report files for analysis.); Create AWS Budgets for each laboratory and review the alerts in Quick. (Budgets provides threshold monitoring rather than the requested detailed billing dataset.); Use AWS Cost Explorer forecasts for each laboratory and load the forecasts into Quick. (Forecasts do not satisfy the need for a reusable, detailed billing dataset by resource and tag.)

chunks.title: AWS Cost Explorer
chunks.text:
AWS Cost Explorer. AWS Cost Explorer lets you visualize and analyze costs and usage, forecast future spending, and get Reserved Instance purchase recommendations. Choose it when the decision calls for exploring spending trends or planning purchases, rather than enforcing a spending threshold.
When to use: You need charts or reports to investigate changes in AWS costs and usage.; You need a spending forecast for planning.; You want recommendations for Reserved Instances to purchase.
