Key facts: Cost Explorer can show up to 13 months of historical data and forecast costs for the next 18 months.; It provides a main graph, cost and usage reports, and Reserved Instance reports.; Its cost data refreshes at least once every 24 hours, although upstream billing data can arrive later.; Viewing costs and usage in the Cost Explorer user interface is free; paginated Cost Explorer API requests incur a charge.
Gotchas: A forecast helps with planning; it is not a request to alert or take action when a threshold is crossed.; If the requirement is the most granular billing line items for custom analysis, choose a Cost and Usage Report instead of a visual Cost Explorer view.; Do not confuse Reserved Instance purchase recommendations with recommendations to change a resource's size.
Confused with: AWS Budgets: Choose Budgets for threshold alerts or actions; choose Cost Explorer to explore and forecast spending.; AWS Cost and Usage Report: Choose a Cost and Usage Report for granular line-item analysis; choose Cost Explorer for ready-to-use visual analysis.; AWS Compute Optimizer: Choose Compute Optimizer for resource right-sizing; choose Cost Explorer for cost trends and Reserved Instance purchase recommendations.
ES: AWS Cost Explorer te permite visualizar y analizar costos y uso, pronosticar gastos futuros y obtener recomendaciones de compra de Reserved Instances. Elígelo cuando necesites explorar tendencias de gasto o planificar compras, no aplicar un umbral de gasto. Cost Explorer puede mostrar hasta 13 meses de datos históricos y pronosticar costos para los próximos 18 meses.; Ofrece un gráfico principal, informes de costos y uso e informes de Reserved Instances.; Sus datos de costos se actualizan al menos una vez cada 24 horas, aunque los datos de facturación de origen pueden llegar después.; Consultar costos y uso en la interfaz de Cost Explorer es gratis; las solicitudes paginadas a su API tienen un cargo.

chunks.title: AWS Cost Explorer
chunks.text:
Scenario: A subscription publisher notices that its AWS bill has risen over several months. An architect needs to inspect visual cost trends, change the reporting dates, and group the results to identify where further investigation is warranted. The team does not need individual billing line items or automated responses to spending limits. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Explore cost and usage reports in AWS Cost Explorer.
Why: The architect needs exploratory visual analysis to find what warrants investigation. Cost Explorer provides graphs and reports for cost trends, with report parameters such as dates and groupings. A Cost and Usage Report suits granular custom analysis, but that extra detail and processing are unnecessary here.
Wrong options: Configure AWS Budgets with actions for spending thresholds. (Budget actions respond to thresholds rather than providing the requested exploratory views.); Review AWS Compute Optimizer's sizing recommendations. (Sizing recommendations do not provide the requested investigation of overall cost trends.); Analyze a Cost and Usage Report with custom queries. (Custom line-item analysis adds work and detail the team explicitly does not need.)

chunks.title: AWS Cost Explorer
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum runs several workloads on AWS and is preparing a quarterly cost review. The finance team wants to use AWS Cost Explorer directly, without building a separate billing-data pipeline. Which two requests can the team fulfill with Cost Explorer? (Choose two.)
Correct: View recommendations for Reserved Instances to purchase. + Review visual cost trends to identify areas for further inquiry.
Why: Cost Explorer directly supports both visual investigation of cost trends and recommendations for Reserved Instances to purchase. Those capabilities fit a quarterly review without a custom billing pipeline. Threshold actions belong to AWS Budgets, while granular line-item delivery is the Cost and Usage Report path.
Wrong options: Automatically apply an action when spending crosses a defined threshold. (Threshold-triggered actions are an AWS Budgets use case, not the requested Cost Explorer analysis.); Deliver granular billing line items to Amazon S3 for custom queries. (Delivering line-item data for custom analysis is a Cost and Usage Report use case.); Identify resources flagged by best-practice checks for open security groups. (Security best-practice checks are a Trusted Advisor use case, not Cost Explorer cost analysis.)

chunks.title: Amazon Data Firehose (delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch)
chunks.text:
Amazon Data Firehose (delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch). Amazon Data Firehose is a fully managed way to deliver streaming records to destinations such as S3, Redshift, OpenSearch Service, and Splunk without writing a delivery application. Choose it when the requirement is managed delivery rather than custom stream consumption, and account for buffering before delivery.
When to use: Producers must send streaming records to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch Service, or Splunk with little delivery infrastructure to manage.; An existing Kinesis data stream must also feed a managed delivery pipeline.; The destination is Redshift and the team wants Firehose to handle the S3 staging and COPY step.
Key facts: Firehose buffers records by size or time before delivering them.; A Firehose stream can read from an existing Kinesis data stream.; For Redshift delivery, Firehose first writes to S3, then issues a Redshift COPY command.; OpenSearch Service and Splunk deliveries can optionally be backed up to S3.; Firehose can be configured to transform data before delivery.
Gotchas: Do not assume delivery is immediate: Firehose buffers records.; A Redshift destination does not bypass S3 staging.; Selecting S3 as the destination does not also configure delivery to Splunk or OpenSearch Service.
Confused with: Kinesis Data Streams: Choose it for requirements such as multiple stream consumers, replay, or custom processing; Firehose is the managed destination-delivery choice.; Amazon MSK: Choose MSK when existing Apache Kafka producers or consumers require Kafka compatibility, not merely to deliver records to a Firehose-supported destination.; Amazon SQS: SQS is for queue-based message processing, not managed delivery of a streaming feed to these destinations.
ES: Amazon Data Firehose entrega registros de streaming a destinos como S3, Redshift, OpenSearch Service y Splunk sin que tengas que escribir una aplicación de entrega. Elígelo cuando necesitas entrega administrada en vez de consumidores de streaming personalizados, y considera el buffering previo a la entrega. Firehose acumula registros según el tamaño o el intervalo de tiempo antes de entregarlos.; Un Firehose stream puede leer de un Kinesis data stream existente.; Para entregar a Redshift, Firehose primero escribe en S3 y después ejecuta un comando COPY de Redshift.; Las entregas a OpenSearch Service y Splunk pueden tener un respaldo opcional en S3.; Puedes configurar Firehose para transformar los datos antes de entregarlos.

chunks.title: Amazon Data Firehose (delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A bicycle rental company sends trip events from its application servers throughout the day. Analysts need the events delivered to an S3 bucket, and the small platform team does not want to build or operate a delivery application. Buffered delivery is acceptable. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Send events to a Firehose stream configured with the S3 bucket as its destination.
Why: The deciding requirements are delivery to S3, acceptance of buffering, and no delivery application to manage. A Firehose stream accepts records from producers and delivers them to its configured S3 destination. Kinesis Data Streams could be part of a broader streaming design, but the proposed S3 consumer would still need to be built and operated.
Wrong options: Send events to Kinesis Data Streams and build a consumer that writes them to S3. (A custom consumer adds delivery code and operations that the team wants to avoid.); Send events to an SQS queue and run workers that delete messages after writing them to S3. (Queue workers introduce the delivery application the team explicitly wants to avoid.); Send events to an Amazon MSK topic and build a Kafka consumer that writes them to S3. (A Kafka consumer still requires the team to build and operate the delivery component.)

chunks.title: Amazon Data Firehose (delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch)
chunks.text:
Scenario: An online marketplace generates a stream of product-search events. Its operations team wants the events delivered to an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster and an optional copy stored in S3, without writing a delivery application. Buffered delivery is acceptable. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure a Firehose stream with OpenSearch Service as the destination and enable S3 backup.
Why: The destination is OpenSearch Service, with an optional S3 backup and no delivery code. Firehose supports that destination and can back up its records to S3 concurrently. An S3-destination Firehose stream alone does not meet the stated OpenSearch Service delivery requirement.
Wrong options: Configure a Firehose stream with S3 as the destination and expect it to populate OpenSearch Service. (Selecting S3 as the destination does not configure delivery to the OpenSearch Service cluster.); Write the events to an Amazon MSK topic and operate a consumer for OpenSearch Service and S3. (The consumer adds an application to build and operate for the required deliveries.); Write the events to Kinesis Data Streams and operate a consumer for OpenSearch Service and S3. (Operating a consumer conflicts with the requirement not to write a delivery application.)

chunks.title: Amazon Data Firehose (delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A concert venue sends entry-scan records throughout each event. Its security team needs the records delivered to Splunk and wants an optional S3 backup, while the venue's developers avoid maintaining a forwarding service. Some buffering before delivery is acceptable. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Send records to a Firehose stream with Splunk as the destination and S3 backup enabled.
Why: The venue needs managed delivery to Splunk plus an optional S3 copy, and it accepts buffering. Firehose supports Splunk as a destination with optional concurrent S3 backup. Choosing S3 as the Firehose destination instead misses the explicit Splunk delivery requirement.
Wrong options: Send records to Kinesis Data Streams and maintain a consumer that forwards them to Splunk and S3. (Maintaining the forwarding consumer violates the team's operational constraint.); Send records to an SQS queue and maintain workers that forward them to Splunk and S3. (The workers are a forwarding service the developers would have to maintain.); Send records to a Firehose stream whose destination is S3 and use that as the Splunk feed. (An S3 destination does not itself configure Firehose to deliver the records to Splunk.)

chunks.title: Transforming data formats (CSV/JSON to Parquet/ORC) and partitioning
chunks.text:
Transforming data formats (CSV/JSON to Parquet/ORC) and partitioning. Convert CSV or JSON data in Amazon S3 to columnar Parquet or ORC when Athena queries need to read data more efficiently. For existing data, choose Athena CTAS or an AWS Glue job; for incoming JSON, Amazon Data Firehose can convert records before delivering them to S3. Plan partitions around frequently filtered values as a separate data-layout decision.
When to use: Existing CSV or JSON files in S3 need conversion to Parquet or ORC.; Incoming JSON records should arrive in S3 in a columnar format.; Analytical queries repeatedly filter a large dataset or request only some columns.
Key facts: Parquet and ORC compress data by column and support predicate pushdown, helping Athena avoid reading unneeded blocks.; Athena CTAS and AWS Glue jobs can convert existing CSV or JSON data to Parquet or ORC.; Amazon Data Firehose converts JSON input to Parquet or ORC before storing it in S3; CSV input needs a Lambda transformation to JSON first.; Firehose format conversion uses a JSON deserializer, a matching AWS Glue Data Catalog schema, and a Parquet or ORC serializer.
Gotchas: Creating a catalog schema is not the same as rewriting existing files in a columnar format.; Firehose does not directly convert CSV input to Parquet or ORC without a preceding transformation to JSON.; A Firehose catalog schema that omits an input attribute will omit that attribute from the converted data.
Confused with: 
ES: Convierte datos CSV o JSON en Amazon S3 a los formatos columnares Parquet u ORC cuando las consultas de Athena necesiten leer los datos con mayor eficiencia. Para datos existentes, elige Athena CTAS o un trabajo de AWS Glue; para JSON entrante, Amazon Data Firehose puede convertir los registros antes de entregarlos a S3. Planifica las particiones según los valores que se filtran con frecuencia como una decisión aparte sobre la organización de los datos. Parquet y ORC comprimen los datos por columna y admiten predicate pushdown, lo que ayuda a Athena a evitar leer bloques innecesarios.; Athena CTAS y los trabajos de AWS Glue pueden convertir datos CSV o JSON existentes a Parquet u ORC.; Amazon Data Firehose convierte entradas JSON a Parquet u ORC antes de almacenarlas en S3; una entrada CSV requiere primero una transformación a JSON con Lambda.; La conversión de formatos en Firehose utiliza un deserializador JSON, un esquema correspondiente en AWS Glue Data Catalog y un serializador Parquet u ORC.

chunks.title: Transforming data formats (CSV/JSON to Parquet/ORC) and partitioning
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum stores years of visitor-event CSV files in Amazon S3. Analysts query the historical dataset with Athena and want the files rewritten in a columnar format to improve query efficiency. The team prefers to perform this one-time conversion with an Athena query rather than build an ingestion pipeline. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Run an Athena CTAS query over the CSV data and specify Parquet for the new table's stored data.
Why: The deciding requirement is a one-time rewrite of existing S3 files using an Athena query. CTAS can write query results as Parquet, providing the requested columnar conversion in one step. A Glue job is another valid conversion method but misses the stated preference. A catalog schema alone does not change the stored file format.
Wrong options: Run an AWS Glue job that reads the CSV files and writes Parquet files to S3. (A Glue job can convert the files, but it does not satisfy the team's preference to use an Athena query.); Create an AWS Glue Data Catalog schema for the CSV files and continue querying the original files. (A schema does not rewrite the existing CSV files into a columnar format.); Send new visitor events through Amazon Data Firehose with Parquet conversion enabled. (Converting newly ingested events does not perform the requested one-time conversion of historical S3 files.)

chunks.title: Transforming data formats (CSV/JSON to Parquet/ORC) and partitioning
chunks.text:
Scenario: A public-health research team has existing CSV and JSON datasets in Amazon S3. Researchers want new Parquet copies of these historical datasets for Athena analysis; they do not need to change how future records arrive. The team will consider either a query-based conversion or an ETL job. Which TWO solutions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Run AWS Glue jobs that read the existing datasets and write new Parquet files. + Run Athena CTAS queries over the existing datasets and specify Parquet for the new stored data.
Why: The team needs Parquet copies of data already stored in S3, not a change to future ingestion. Both Athena CTAS and AWS Glue jobs can convert existing CSV or JSON data to Parquet. Catalog definitions and read-only queries do not rewrite the source data or create converted copies. Firehose format conversion is not a direct conversion mechanism for existing CSV objects.
Wrong options: Query the CSV and JSON files in Athena without writing results to new files. (Queries that do not write converted output cannot produce the required Parquet copies.); Add Parquet table definitions to the AWS Glue Data Catalog without processing the source files. (Catalog definitions alone do not create Parquet copies of existing files.); Configure Firehose format conversion to read the existing CSV objects directly from S3. (Firehose's format converter does not directly accept CSV, and this does not describe converting stored S3 objects.)

chunks.title: Data ingestion patterns: batch vs streaming, frequency and size
chunks.text:
Data ingestion patterns: batch vs streaming, frequency and size. Choose ingestion by how data arrives and how soon it must be available. Amazon Data Firehose fits continuously generated records delivered to Amazon S3; AWS DataSync fits recurring transfers of existing on-premises files; AWS Glue fits scheduled transformation jobs.
When to use: Choose Amazon Data Firehose when applications continuously produce records that need streaming delivery to Amazon S3.; Choose AWS DataSync when existing NFS, SMB, object-store, or HDFS data must be transferred to Amazon S3 over the network.; Choose AWS Glue when the requirement is to clean or transform data in an on-demand or scheduled ETL job.
Key facts: Amazon Data Firehose is fully managed, scales with streaming throughput, and can deliver streaming records to Amazon S3.; Firehose can batch multiple incoming records into an S3 object and can transform data before delivery.; AWS DataSync automates transfers from supported on-premises storage systems to Amazon S3 and supports encryption and integrity validation.; AWS Glue jobs extract, transform, and load data; they can run on demand or on a schedule.
Gotchas: A large transfer of files is not a streaming-record workload merely because it runs frequently.; Firehose batching of incoming records does not make it the choice for a scheduled ETL job over existing files.; DataSync moves data; choose Glue when cleaning or transforming the data is the deciding requirement.
Confused with: AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway: File Gateway provides an on-premises NFS file share whose writes become S3 objects; DataSync transfers data from an existing supported storage source.; AWS Glue: Glue performs ETL jobs, while Firehose is a managed delivery path for incoming streaming records.
ES: Elige el patrón de ingesta según cómo llegan los datos y cuándo deben estar disponibles. Amazon Data Firehose sirve para entregar registros generados continuamente a Amazon S3; AWS DataSync, para transferir archivos existentes; y AWS Glue, para trabajos programados de transformación. Amazon Data Firehose es completamente administrado, escala según el volumen del flujo y puede entregar registros a Amazon S3.; Firehose puede agrupar varios registros entrantes en un objeto de S3 y transformarlos antes de la entrega.; AWS DataSync automatiza transferencias desde sistemas de almacenamiento locales compatibles a Amazon S3 y admite cifrado y validación de integridad.; Los trabajos de AWS Glue extraen, transforman y cargan datos; pueden ejecutarse bajo demanda o con una programación.

chunks.title: Data ingestion patterns: batch vs streaming, frequency and size
chunks.text:
Scenario: A transit operator's vehicles continuously send location records to an application. The operator wants the incoming records delivered to Amazon S3 for analysis throughout the day, rather than waiting for a scheduled file transfer. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Send the records to Amazon Data Firehose for managed delivery to Amazon S3.
Why: The deciding requirement is continuous delivery of incoming records to Amazon S3, not a scheduled transfer of stored files. Amazon Data Firehose provides managed streaming delivery to S3 and scales with streaming throughput. AWS Glue is useful for ETL jobs, but scheduling those jobs does not address the specified continuous ingestion pattern.
Wrong options: Write the records to an AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway share backed by Amazon S3. (File Gateway supplies a file-share interface, which the stated record-streaming application does not require.); Run AWS DataSync tasks to transfer record files from an on-premises share to Amazon S3. (DataSync transfers data from storage systems, while this application produces a continuous record stream.); Run scheduled AWS Glue ETL jobs to load the records into Amazon S3. (Scheduled ETL jobs do not match the requirement to ingest incoming records continuously.)

chunks.title: Data ingestion patterns: batch vs streaming, frequency and size
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab saves large sets of microscope images on an existing on-premises NFS server each week. It needs to transfer those files to its Amazon S3 data lake over the network, with integrity validation, without changing how researchers write files. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS DataSync to transfer files from the existing NFS server to Amazon S3.
Why: These are existing files on an NFS server, and the lab needs a network transfer that preserves its current write workflow. AWS DataSync supports NFS-to-S3 movement and data integrity validation. File Gateway is a plausible file-based alternative, but replacing the write location conflicts with the requirement not to change how researchers save files.
Wrong options: Send image data through Amazon Data Firehose to Amazon S3. (Firehose is for incoming streaming data, not transferring files from the existing NFS server.); Replace the NFS server's write location with an AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway share. (File Gateway would require changing the write location rather than transferring files from the existing NFS server.); Use scheduled AWS Glue ETL jobs to move the images into Amazon S3. (Glue is an ETL service, while the requirement is file transfer with integrity validation.)

chunks.title: Data lake architecture on Amazon S3
chunks.text:
Data lake architecture on Amazon S3. An Amazon S3 data lake centralizes varied data while allowing storage and compute to scale independently. In a scenario that requires preserving raw data, making it discoverable, and analyzing it with different tools, choose an S3-based lake with transformation and cataloging rather than a collection of isolated stores.
When to use: Structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data must be brought into a central repository.; Teams need to preserve raw assets and create optimized, usable versions.; Different users or tools need to find and analyze shared data without tying its storage to one compute environment.
Key facts: A data lake can store varied data centrally so it can be categorized, cataloged, secured, and analyzed.; Cloud-based data lakes decouple compute from storage, allowing each to scale independently.; An S3-based lake can transform raw assets into optimized formats and query data assets in place.; Data can be stored in separate buckets as it moves through extraction, transformation, and loading; separate buckets are an architectural option, not a universal requirement.
Gotchas: Centralizing files without cataloging them misses a requirement that users be able to find data assets.; Keeping only transformed output misses a requirement to retain raw inputs.; Moving every dataset into a single compute-bound analytics store misses independent storage and compute scaling.
Confused with: 
ES: Un data lake en Amazon S3 centraliza distintos tipos de datos y permite escalar el almacenamiento y el cómputo por separado. Si un escenario exige conservar datos originales, facilitar su descubrimiento y analizarlos con distintas herramientas, elige un lake basado en S3 con transformación y catalogación, no varios almacenes aislados. Un data lake puede almacenar distintos tipos de datos de forma centralizada para clasificarlos, catalogarlos, protegerlos y analizarlos.; Un data lake en la nube separa el cómputo del almacenamiento y permite escalar cada uno de forma independiente.; Un lake basado en S3 puede transformar datos originales en formatos optimizados y consultar los datos donde están almacenados.; Puedes almacenar datos en buckets separados durante la extracción, transformación y carga; es una opción de arquitectura, no un requisito universal.

chunks.title: Data lake architecture on Amazon S3
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional insurer receives documents, event records, and tabular exports from several business units. Analysts must retain the original inputs, find available datasets, and analyze them without first consolidating everything into one analytics engine. Which architecture meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Store original assets in an Amazon S3 data lake, catalog the datasets, and let analytics tools work with data in the lake.
Why: The deciding requirements are to retain varied originals, make datasets findable, and avoid dependence on a single analytics engine. An S3-based data lake provides a central repository whose assets can be cataloged and analyzed with different tools. Retaining only transformed results loses the originals, while separate repositories leave discovery fragmented.
Wrong options: Transform every incoming file into a single reporting format and retain only the transformed results in S3. (Discarding the inputs fails the explicit requirement to retain originals.); Store each business unit’s files in its existing repository and have analysts maintain a separate inventory for each repository. (Separate repositories and inventories do not provide the required centralized, discoverable collection.); Load every source into one analytics engine and require all teams to analyze data through that engine. (Requiring one engine conflicts with the stated need to analyze data without consolidating it into one engine first.)

chunks.title: Data lake architecture on Amazon S3
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company expects its collection of images, text records, and usage data to grow steadily. Different teams will apply different analytics tools, and demand for processing may change independently of the amount stored. Which approach best supports this growth while preserving flexibility for the teams?
Correct: Centralize the varied assets in an Amazon S3 data lake and use analytics tools separately from the lake’s storage.
Why: The key constraint is that stored data and processing demand will grow at different rates. A cloud-based S3 data lake separates compute from storage so each can scale independently, while providing a central collection for different analytics approaches. The single-environment option ties their growth together, and team-specific copies undermine centralization.
Wrong options: Store only text records in S3 and move images and usage data into separate, uncataloged repositories. (Splitting the data leaves the company without a central, discoverable collection of its varied assets.); Put all incoming assets into a single processing environment and expand storage only when processing capacity expands. (Linking storage growth to processing capacity conflicts with the requirement that their demand change independently.); Give each analytics team a separate copy of every dataset in a store dedicated to its chosen tool. (Tool-specific copies fragment the shared collection rather than providing a central repository.)

chunks.title: Data retention, lifecycle and deletion policies
chunks.text:
Data retention, lifecycle and deletion policies. Set retention by data classification: decide how long usable data and backups must be kept, then automate archiving or deletion. For S3 objects, use S3 Lifecycle transitions when a cheaper storage class fits and expiration when the required retention period ends; protect backups separately when the requirement calls for it.
When to use: S3 objects need automatic archiving or deletion after defined periods.; Different data classes have different access and retention requirements.; Backups need their own retention and protection strategy, separate from usable data.
Key facts: S3 Lifecycle transition actions change an object's storage class; expiration actions delete expired objects.; Lifecycle rules apply to both existing and newly added objects.; Lifecycle transition requests have costs, so a transition is not automatically worthwhile for short-lived data.; A bucket policy cannot prevent an S3 Lifecycle rule from deleting or transitioning objects in a general purpose bucket.; AWS Backup can automate backups across AWS services; AWS Backup Vault Lock and S3 Object Lock are protection mechanisms to consider for backups.
Gotchas: Do not give every data class the same retention period when its requirements differ.; Do not treat durable usable data as a substitute for backups.; Do not assume a bucket-policy deny overrides a configured S3 Lifecycle action.
Confused with: 
ES: Define la retención según la clasificación de los datos: decide cuánto tiempo conservar los datos utilizables y las copias de seguridad, y luego automatiza el archivado o la eliminación. Para objetos de S3, usa transiciones de S3 Lifecycle cuando convenga una clase de almacenamiento de menor costo y expiration cuando termine el período obligatorio; protege las copias de seguridad por separado si el requisito lo exige. Las acciones transition de S3 Lifecycle cambian la clase de almacenamiento; las acciones expiration eliminan objetos vencidos.; Las reglas de Lifecycle se aplican tanto a objetos existentes como a los nuevos.; Las solicitudes de transición de Lifecycle tienen costos; una transición no siempre conviene para datos de corta duración.; Una bucket policy no puede impedir que una regla de S3 Lifecycle elimine o traslade objetos en un bucket de uso general.; AWS Backup puede automatizar copias de seguridad entre servicios de AWS; AWS Backup Vault Lock y S3 Object Lock son mecanismos de protección que puedes considerar para ellas.

chunks.title: Data retention, lifecycle and deletion policies
chunks.text:
Scenario: A small publisher uploads temporary delivery logs to S3. The logs are consulted throughout their required 14-day retention period and must be deleted afterward; the team has no archival requirement. It wants an automated policy and wants to avoid unnecessary transition requests. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Configure an S3 Lifecycle expiration rule to delete the logs after 14 days without a transition.
Why: These logs remain in use during their short retention period and need deletion, not archiving. An S3 Lifecycle expiration rule automates deletion after the specified period. Adding a transition is not justified by the scenario and incurs transition-request costs; it also does not replace an expiration action. Retaining backups or merely restricting access would miss the deletion requirement.
Wrong options: Keep the logs indefinitely and restrict access with a bucket policy after day 14. (Restricting access does not delete logs when their required retention period ends.); Transition the logs to another S3 storage class during the retention period, then review them for deletion. (The extra transition has a request cost and leaves deletion as a manual task.); Use AWS Backup to retain copies of the logs after removing the originals at day 14. (Keeping backup copies beyond the required period conflicts with the stated deletion goal.)

chunks.title: Data retention, lifecycle and deletion policies
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research firm stores two classified datasets in one S3 bucket: temporary instrument output must be deleted after 60 days, while approved study records must remain available for a longer, separately defined period. The bucket contains older objects as well as new uploads, and the firm wants automatic enforcement for both groups. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create S3 Lifecycle expiration rules for the relevant groups of objects, using each group's required retention period.
Why: The deciding requirement is automatic deletion at different times for two classified groups, including objects already in the bucket. S3 Lifecycle expiration rules can act on groups of objects and apply to both existing and future objects. A single bucket-wide period would disregard the classification requirements, and a bucket policy cannot override Lifecycle deletion in a general purpose bucket. Backups and archiving address different parts of the data lifecycle, not the requested expiration rules.
Wrong options: Move all objects to an archival storage class and review them periodically for deletion. (Archiving does not automatically delete objects at their different required expiration times.); Apply one S3 Lifecycle expiration period to the entire bucket and use a bucket policy to exempt approved records. (A bucket-policy deny cannot stop a configured Lifecycle rule from expiring objects in a general purpose bucket.); Use AWS Backup for both datasets and remove objects from the bucket when each backup is created. (Creating backups does not implement the distinct retention periods required for usable objects in the bucket.)

chunks.title: Data transfer pricing: inter-AZ, inter-Region, internet egress
chunks.text:
Data transfer pricing: inter-AZ, inter-Region, internet egress. Data transfer cost depends on where traffic flows: between Availability Zones, between Regions, or out to the internet. In an exam scenario, identify the traffic path first, then remove unnecessary transfers without violating availability or placement requirements.
When to use: A workload sends substantial traffic between Availability Zones or AWS Regions.; An application can process data closer to where it is produced.; A team needs to identify network charges in its AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR).
Key facts: Inter-AZ transfer within a Region appears as Region-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes in AWS CUR. For each metered resource, both inbound and outbound traffic are charged; check service pricing because some in-Region traffic has no cost.; Inter-Region transfer has incoming and outgoing CUR line items. The incoming transfer to the destination Region has no charge; the charge is associated with transfer out of the source Region.; Internet egress typically appears as Region-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes (US East (N. Virginia) can omit the Region prefix, and CloudFront and some services use their own usage types). Transfer from the internet into AWS has no data transfer charge.; CloudFront egress can have a similar usage type to other internet egress. Use lineItem/ProductCode to distinguish AmazonCloudFront charges.; Data transfer charges vary by service and source Region, so confirm prices on the relevant service pricing page.
Gotchas: Two CUR line items for one inter-Region transfer do not mean both directions are charged.; A Regional-Bytes usage type does not prove that every in-Region transfer is billable; service-specific exceptions exist.; Do not identify CloudFront traffic from an Out-Bytes usage type alone.
Confused with: Inter-AZ transfer vs. inter-Region transfer: Inter-AZ traffic uses Regional-Bytes; inter-Region traffic has AWS-In-Bytes and AWS-Out-Bytes line items.; CloudFront egress vs. other internet egress: Their usage types can look similar; the product code identifies CloudFront.
ES: El costo de transferencia de datos depende de la ruta: entre Availability Zones, entre Regions o hacia internet. En un escenario de examen, identifica primero esa ruta y luego elimina transferencias innecesarias sin incumplir los requisitos de disponibilidad o ubicación. La transferencia entre Availability Zones de una misma Region aparece como Region-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes en AWS CUR. Para cada recurso medido se cobra el tráfico entrante y saliente; consulta los precios del servicio porque parte del tráfico dentro de una Region puede no tener costo.; La transferencia entre Regions genera registros de entrada y salida en CUR. La entrada a la Region de destino no tiene cargo; el cargo corresponde a la salida desde la Region de origen.; La salida hacia internet suele aparecer como Region-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes (en US East (N. Virginia) puede omitirse el prefijo de Region, y CloudFront y algunos servicios usan sus propios tipos de uso). La transferencia desde internet hacia AWS no tiene cargo por transferencia de datos.; La salida de CloudFront puede tener un tipo de uso parecido al de otras salidas hacia internet. Usa lineItem/ProductCode para distinguir los cargos de AmazonCloudFront.; Los cargos varían según el servicio y la Region de origen; confirma los precios en la página del servicio correspondiente.

chunks.title: Data transfer pricing: inter-AZ, inter-Region, internet egress
chunks.text:
Scenario: A video-production company runs a batch renderer in one Availability Zone and keeps its temporary source files on a processing server in another Availability Zone of the same Region. The files are transferred repeatedly during rendering, and the company can move the renderer without changing its availability requirements. Which change should the company make to reduce data transfer costs?
Correct: Run the renderer in the processing server's Availability Zone.
Why: The deciding requirement is to reduce repeated transfers without changing availability requirements. Placing the renderer with its temporary source files removes the stated inter-AZ transfer path. Moving it to another Region does not solve the placement problem, and assuming all in-Region traffic is free contradicts the documented inter-AZ charging behavior. Service-specific pricing should still be checked before estimating savings.
Wrong options: Keep the placement and budget only for transfers from AWS to the internet. (The stated transfer is between Availability Zones, not from AWS to the internet.); Move the renderer to a different AWS Region while keeping the processing server in place. (This replaces the inter-AZ path with an inter-Region path rather than removing the repeated transfer.); Keep the placement because transfers within a Region never incur data transfer charges. (Inter-AZ transfers can incur regional data transfer charges.)

chunks.title: Data transfer pricing: inter-AZ, inter-Region, internet egress
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization copies a dataset nightly from an application in one AWS Region to an analysis job in another. The analysis job can run in the application's Region, and no other process needs the remote copy. AWS CUR shows both an AWS-In-Bytes and an AWS-Out-Bytes line item for each copy. Which change MOST directly reduces the charged inter-Region transfer?
Correct: Run the analysis job in the application's Region and stop making the remote copy.
Why: The remote copy is unnecessary because the analysis job may run alongside the application. Stopping it removes the outgoing inter-Region transfer that determines the charge. The AWS-In-Bytes record does not carry the transfer charge, so excluding that record from a report does not reduce spending. Changing only the destination Availability Zone also leaves the cross-Region path intact.
Wrong options: Keep the nightly copy and move the analysis job to a different Availability Zone in its current Region. (Changing Availability Zones in the destination Region does not remove the inter-Region copy.); Keep both jobs in their current Regions and exclude the AWS-In-Bytes item from cost reports. (The incoming item has no charge, but the outgoing copy remains charged.); Reverse the direction of the nightly copy so the analysis Region becomes the source. (The source Region's outgoing transfer would still determine the charge.)

chunks.title: Data transfer pricing: inter-AZ, inter-Region, internet egress
chunks.text:
Scenario: An online publisher serves content through CloudFront and also operates an application that sends files directly to internet users. Its finance team sees DataTransfer-Out-Bytes usage in AWS CUR and must separate the two sources before proposing cost changes. Which report field should the team use to distinguish CloudFront egress from other internet egress MOST reliably?
Correct: lineItem/ProductCode, to identify records for AmazonCloudFront.
Why: The team must distinguish two types of outbound traffic before making a cost decision. CloudFront and other internet egress can have similar usage types, so lineItem/ProductCode is the reliable discriminator in AWS CUR. An Out-Bytes suffix alone cannot establish which product generated the traffic. The Region prefix alone does not resolve the ambiguity either.
Wrong options: The presence of AWS-In-Bytes, because that identifies CloudFront responses. (AWS-In-Bytes is described for inter-Region transfer, not as a CloudFront identifier.); Only the Out-Bytes suffix, because it uniquely identifies CloudFront traffic. (CloudFront and other internet egress can have similar Out-Bytes usage types.); Only the Region prefix, because CloudFront usage types never include one. (CloudFront egress usage types can have a prefix representing the edge location.)

chunks.title: Choosing the lowest-cost transfer method by size, bandwidth and deadline
chunks.text:
Choosing the lowest-cost transfer method by size, bandwidth and deadline. Estimate transfer time before choosing a transfer method: data size in bits divided by usable bandwidth in bits per second. If online transfer meets the deadline, compare its cost with the alternatives; if it cannot, consider AWS Snowball or an available higher-bandwidth connection, accounting for their full timelines and costs.
When to use: A scenario provides data volume, available bandwidth, and a migration deadline.; You must choose between an online transfer, an existing or proposed AWS Direct Connect connection, and AWS Snowball.; The lowest-cost choice must still meet the stated deadline.
Key facts: For decimal units, 1 TB is 8,000 Gb; at 100 Mbps, transferring 1 TB takes about 22 hours at sustained full bandwidth.; AWS DataSync supports efficient online transfers between on-premises environments and AWS storage services, including Amazon S3.; AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated private connection suited to ongoing, high-volume transfers.; Bandwidth limits can make online transfer insufficient for very large datasets; include the scenario's stated Snowball turnaround when comparing alternatives.; A transfer tool and a network connection solve different problems: AWS DataSync can move data over a connection, but it cannot remove that connection's bandwidth constraint.
Gotchas: Comparing costs before checking whether each option meets the deadline.; Treating an optimized transfer service as though it increases the site's available bandwidth.; Ignoring connection setup time or device turnaround time in a one-time migration.; Assuming AWS Direct Connect and AWS DataSync are interchangeable rather than potentially complementary.
Confused with: AWS DataSync vs. AWS Direct Connect: DataSync is an online data-transfer service; Direct Connect supplies a dedicated network connection.; AWS Snowball vs. online transfer: Compare the stated end-to-end Snowball timeline with the time required to transmit the data over the available connection.
ES: Antes de elegir el método de transferencia, estima el tiempo: tamaño de los datos en bits dividido entre el ancho de banda utilizable en bits por segundo. Si la transferencia en línea cumple el plazo, compara su costo con las alternativas; si no, evalúa AWS Snowball o una conexión disponible de mayor capacidad, incluidos sus tiempos y costos totales. Con unidades decimales, 1 TB equivale a 8,000 Gb; a 100 Mbps, transferir 1 TB tarda alrededor de 22 horas si se mantiene todo ese ancho de banda.; AWS DataSync permite transferencias eficientes en línea entre entornos locales y servicios de almacenamiento de AWS, incluido Amazon S3.; AWS Direct Connect ofrece una conexión privada dedicada adecuada para transferencias continuas de gran volumen.; Los límites de ancho de banda pueden hacer insuficiente una transferencia en línea para conjuntos de datos muy grandes; incluye el tiempo total de AWS Snowball indicado en el escenario.; Una herramienta de transferencia y una conexión de red cumplen funciones distintas: AWS DataSync puede mover datos por una conexión, pero no elimina el límite de ancho de banda de esa conexión.

chunks.title: Choosing the lowest-cost transfer method by size, bandwidth and deadline
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer must transfer a one-time 6 TB set of quality-control files to Amazon S3 within four days. It has a 50 Mbps internet uplink and an existing AWS Direct Connect connection with 500 Mbps of spare capacity. The estimated incremental cost is $250 to use the existing connection, compared with $600 for an AWS Snowball plan with a three-day end-to-end turnaround; use decimal units and assume full utilization. Which solution meets the deadline MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use AWS DataSync over the existing AWS Direct Connect connection.
Why: The 6 TB dataset is 48,000 Gb in decimal units. At 500 Mbps, its ideal transfer time is about 27 hours, whereas the 50 Mbps path takes about 11 days. Both the existing-connection plan and the quoted AWS Snowball plan meet the four-day deadline, but the existing-connection plan has the lower stated incremental cost.
Wrong options: Use AWS DataSync over the 50 Mbps internet uplink. (At 50 Mbps, transmitting 6 TB takes about 11 days and misses the deadline.); Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration over the 50 Mbps internet uplink. (The site's 50 Mbps uplink cannot transmit 6 TB within four days.); Use the quoted AWS Snowball plan for the file set. (Its three-day plan meets the deadline but costs more than the eligible existing-connection plan.)

chunks.title: Choosing the lowest-cost transfer method by size, bandwidth and deadline
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer is consolidating files from two branches into Amazon S3. Branch A must send 1 TB within three days over a 100 Mbps available internet uplink; its quoted internet transfer costs $50, while its AWS Snowball plan costs $400 and takes four days end-to-end. Branch B must send 40 TB within 12 days over a 40 Mbps available internet uplink; its AWS Snowball plan costs $700 and takes eight days end-to-end. A new AWS Direct Connect connection at either branch would take 20 days to establish. Using decimal units and assuming full uplink utilization, which two branch-specific choices meet their deadlines MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
Correct: For Branch A, use AWS DataSync over its existing internet uplink. + For Branch B, use its quoted AWS Snowball plan.
Why: Branch A's 1 TB takes about 22 hours at 100 Mbps, so its quoted internet transfer meets the three-day deadline at the lower stated cost. Branch B's 40 TB takes about 93 days at 40 Mbps, making its eight-day AWS Snowball plan the eligible choice. Branch A's Snowball turnaround and Branch B's proposed AWS Direct Connect setup each exceed their respective deadlines.
Wrong options: For Branch B, use AWS DataSync over its existing internet uplink. (At 40 Mbps, 40 TB requires about 93 days, exceeding Branch B's deadline.); For Branch A, use its quoted AWS Snowball plan. (Its stated four-day turnaround misses Branch A's three-day deadline.); For Branch B, establish AWS Direct Connect and transfer the files online. (The 20-day connection setup alone exceeds Branch B's 12-day deadline.)

chunks.title: Choosing the lowest-cost transfer method by size, bandwidth and deadline
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio needs to move a one-time 2 TB file archive to Amazon S3 within 48 hours. Its available internet uplink can sustain 200 Mbps for the transfer; for planning, use decimal units and assume full utilization. The studio's estimates are $40 for AWS DataSync over the internet, $300 and three days end-to-end for AWS Snowball, and at least five days to establish a new AWS Direct Connect connection. Which solution meets the deadline MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use AWS DataSync over the existing internet connection to transfer the archive to Amazon S3.
Why: At decimal units, 2 TB is 16,000 Gb; divided by 200 Mbps, the ideal transfer time is about 22 hours. AWS DataSync over the existing connection therefore meets the 48-hour deadline at the lowest stated price. The quoted AWS Snowball turnaround and AWS Direct Connect setup time each miss the deadline; AWS Storage Gateway addresses hybrid storage rather than the stated one-time transfer decision.
Wrong options: Transfer the archive with AWS Snowball using the quoted device plan. (The quoted three-day turnaround exceeds the 48-hour deadline.); Deploy AWS Storage Gateway as a hybrid-storage interface for the archive. (A hybrid-storage interface does not provide a faster connection than the available uplink for this one-time transfer.); Establish a new AWS Direct Connect connection and transfer the archive through it. (The stated connection setup time alone exceeds the deadline.)

chunks.title: Database cost optimization (reserved DB instances, serverless, retention)
chunks.text:
Database cost optimization (reserved DB instances, serverless, retention). Amazon RDS reserved DB instances discount eligible instance usage in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment; they are a billing discount, not separate physical databases. Choose them for predictable usage, but evaluate storage and backup costs separately because the reservation does not discount those charges.
When to use: An RDS database will run steadily for a one- or three-year period.; A team wants to reduce instance charges without changing its DB deployment.; A cost review shows substantial storage or backup charges that instance discounts alone will not address.
Key facts: A reserved DB instance discounts matching on-demand instance usage; matching includes AWS Region, DB engine, and instance type, with additional specifications for some engines.; Reservations have one- or three-year terms and cannot be canceled.; The discount applies to instance usage, not storage, backups, or I/O.; For supported engines, size flexibility applies within the same instance class type, AWS Region, and DB engine.; A Multi-AZ DB cluster can be only partially covered by reservations; uncovered instance usage remains on-demand.
Gotchas: Buying a reservation does not create a DB instance.; Deleting the DB instance does not cancel its reservation commitment.; A reservation for one instance class type does not provide size-flexible coverage for a different class type.; A lower instance bill does not necessarily resolve a backup-storage cost problem.
Confused with: On-demand RDS instance usage: On-demand usage avoids a reservation commitment; matching reserved usage receives a discounted instance rate during the term.
ES: Las reserved DB instances de Amazon RDS descuentan el uso elegible de instancias a cambio de un compromiso de uno o tres años; son un descuento de facturación, no bases de datos físicas separadas. Elígelas para un uso predecible, pero evalúa por separado el almacenamiento y los respaldos porque la reserva no descuenta esos cargos. Una reserved DB instance descuenta el uso on-demand que coincide con la reserva; la coincidencia incluye AWS Region, DB engine e instance type, además de otras especificaciones para algunos motores.; Las reservas tienen plazos de uno o tres años y no se pueden cancelar.; El descuento se aplica al uso de instancias, no al almacenamiento, los respaldos ni las operaciones de I/O.; Para los motores compatibles, la flexibilidad de tamaño se aplica dentro del mismo instance class type, AWS Region y DB engine.; Un Multi-AZ DB cluster puede tener cobertura parcial de reservas; el uso de instancias no cubierto sigue siendo on-demand.

chunks.title: Database cost optimization (reserved DB instances, serverless, retention)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research publisher has a steady RDS for MySQL workload and an existing reserved DB instance for db.r6i.large. Capacity testing shows that the database must move to db.r6i.xlarge in the same AWS Region, without changing its engine. The publisher wants to retain as much of its existing reservation benefit as possible. Which approach meets this requirement MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Move to db.r6i.xlarge and apply the existing reservation to the eligible portion of its usage.
Why: The required move stays within the db.r6i instance class type, the same engine, and the same AWS Region. RDS for MySQL supports size-flexible reservations under those conditions, though the existing reservation might cover only part of the larger instance's usage. Moving to db.r6id or db.r7g changes the class type and loses that size-flexible match. Reservation discounts also do not transfer to storage or backup charges.
Wrong options: Move to db.r6id.xlarge and rely on the existing reservation's size flexibility. (db.r6id is a different instance class type from db.r6i.); Move to db.r6i.xlarge and assume the existing reservation discounts storage and backup charges instead. (The reservation can discount eligible instance usage, not storage or backup charges.); Move to db.r7g.xlarge and rely on the existing reservation's size flexibility. (db.r7g is a different instance class type, so that size-flexible reservation does not apply.)

chunks.title: Database cost optimization (reserved DB instances, serverless, retention)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company operates an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster with three db.m6gd.large DB instances. It expects the cluster to run continuously for the next year in the same AWS Region and wants reservation discounts to cover all three instances. Which TWO purchase plans meet this coverage requirement MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
Correct: Purchase three db.m6gd.large Single-AZ reserved DB instances. + Purchase one db.m6gd.large Multi-AZ and one db.m6gd.large Single-AZ reserved DB instance.
Why: The cluster contains three DB instances, and the requirement is to cover all three with reservation discounts. AWS documents two equivalent purchase patterns: three matching Single-AZ reservations, or one matching Multi-AZ reservation plus one Single-AZ reservation. A single Multi-AZ reservation covers only two of the three instances. Plans that reserve fewer instances leave the remaining usage billed on-demand.
Wrong options: Purchase one db.m6gd.large Multi-AZ reserved DB instance. (This covers only two of the cluster's three DB instances.); Purchase one db.m6gd.large Single-AZ reserved DB instance and leave the other instances on-demand. (This deliberately leaves two DB instances without the requested reservation coverage.); Purchase two db.m6gd.large Single-AZ reserved DB instances. (One DB instance would remain without reservation coverage.)

chunks.title: AWS DMS and Schema Conversion (homogeneous vs heterogeneous migrations)
chunks.text:
AWS DMS and Schema Conversion (homogeneous vs heterogeneous migrations). AWS DMS moves database data and can replicate ongoing changes to keep a target in sync before cutover. For a change of database engine, convert and apply the schema with DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT, then use DMS to move the data; a same-engine move generally does not need schema conversion.
When to use: A database must move while source data continues to change.; A source and target use different database engines, requiring compatible schema and code objects.; A database is moving to AWS while retaining its current engine.
Key facts: AWS DMS supports one-time data migrations and ongoing change replication.; DMS Schema Conversion converts schemas, not data; DMS data migration features move the data.; DMS Schema Conversion can assess which objects convert automatically and which need manual work.; DMS Schema Conversion is fully managed and web-based; AWS SCT is a downloadable local tool.; DMS Schema Conversion can convert schemas for supported targets on Aurora, Amazon RDS, or Amazon Redshift.
Gotchas: Ongoing replication alone does not load existing rows; include an initial data load when the target starts empty.; DMS data movement is not a substitute for converting incompatible schema objects.; Do not choose a server-rehosting or disaster-recovery service when the requirement is a database-engine migration.
Confused with: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN): MGN rehosts servers to EC2; DMS moves database data and can pair with schema conversion for an engine change.; AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS): DRS replicates servers for recovery; it does not replace database schema conversion and data migration.
ES: AWS DMS mueve datos de bases de datos y puede replicar los cambios continuos para mantener sincronizado el destino antes del cambio. Si cambias de motor, convierte y aplica el esquema con DMS Schema Conversion o AWS SCT y luego usa DMS para mover los datos; un traslado al mismo motor normalmente no requiere conversión del esquema. AWS DMS admite migraciones de datos de una sola vez y replicación de cambios continuos.; DMS Schema Conversion convierte esquemas, no datos; las funciones de migración de DMS mueven los datos.; DMS Schema Conversion puede evaluar qué objetos se convierten automáticamente y cuáles requieren trabajo manual.; DMS Schema Conversion es una función web totalmente administrada; AWS SCT se descarga para usarlo localmente.; DMS Schema Conversion puede convertir esquemas para destinos admitidos en Aurora, Amazon RDS o Amazon Redshift.

chunks.title: AWS DMS and Schema Conversion (homogeneous vs heterogeneous migrations)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics firm will retire an on-premises PostgreSQL server and move its application data to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The target already has the required schema, but dispatch records will keep changing during the move. The firm wants to avoid running a database migration server itself and minimize the time the target falls behind. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS DMS to load the existing data and replicate ongoing changes to the RDS target.
Why: The existing schema removes the need for schema conversion, but changing dispatch records still require synchronization. AWS DMS can load existing data and replicate ongoing changes, and it manages the migration infrastructure. A one-time load is insufficient because records can change after they are copied. Disaster recovery of the server does not satisfy the requirement to populate the RDS target.
Wrong options: Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate the on-premises server and recover it when the firm retires the host. (Server recovery does not populate and synchronize the specified RDS database target.); Use AWS DMS for a one-time load to the RDS target and perform cutover after the load finishes. (A one-time load misses dispatch records changed during the move.); Use DMS Schema Conversion to recreate the PostgreSQL schema and then copy the data once. (The schema is already present, and a one-time copy does not keep up with changing dispatch records.)

chunks.title: AWS DMS and Schema Conversion (homogeneous vs heterogeneous migrations)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare analytics team is moving a SQL Server database to Aurora PostgreSQL. The team must adapt its stored procedures for the new engine and move existing patient records while keeping up with new records until cutover. Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Assess, convert, and apply the schema with DMS Schema Conversion. + Use AWS DMS to load existing records and replicate ongoing changes.
Why: This migration has two distinct jobs: adapting schema objects to Aurora PostgreSQL and transferring records that continue to change. DMS Schema Conversion handles the supported SQL Server-to-Aurora PostgreSQL conversion path; AWS DMS handles the initial data load and ongoing replication. Fleet Advisor inventories infrastructure rather than converting stored procedures. Server rehosting or disaster recovery would not produce the requested database-engine migration.
Wrong options: Use AWS Application Migration Service to rehost the SQL Server machine on EC2. (Rehosting the machine does not migrate its data into Aurora PostgreSQL.); Use DMS Fleet Advisor to inventory the source and treat its report as the converted target schema. (An infrastructure inventory does not convert or apply the target schema.); Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate the source server for recovery. (Server recovery does not adapt stored procedures or move records to the new database engine.)

chunks.title: AWS DMS and Schema Conversion (homogeneous vs heterogeneous migrations)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company is moving an on-premises MySQL database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. The target is empty, and agents must keep updating tickets while the initial data is copied. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS DMS for an initial data load and ongoing change replication, then switch the application to the target.
Why: The empty target needs the existing rows, and updates must continue while those rows are copied. An initial AWS DMS data load addresses the first requirement; ongoing change replication keeps the target synchronized before cutover. Replicating changes without the initial load misses the existing tickets. Changing to the same MySQL engine does not itself call for schema conversion.
Wrong options: Use AWS DMS to replicate ongoing changes only, then switch the application to the target. (Ongoing changes alone would not load the existing tickets into the empty target.); Use AWS Application Migration Service to rehost the database server on EC2 and direct agents to that server. (Rehosting a server on EC2 does not populate the specified RDS for MySQL target.); Use DMS Schema Conversion to convert the MySQL schema and apply it to the target instead of migrating data. (Schema conversion does not move the existing ticket data, and this move retains the same engine.)

chunks.title: AWS DataSync
chunks.text:
AWS DataSync. AWS DataSync moves files and objects online between supported storage locations, including on-premises NFS, SMB, HDFS, and object storage and AWS storage such as S3, EFS, and FSx. Choose it when a migration or recurring copy needs managed scheduling, integrity checks, or bandwidth control.
When to use: An active on-premises dataset needs an initial copy to AWS followed by scheduled incremental transfers.; Files or objects must move regularly into S3 for processing, or into EFS or FSx for a standby file system.; Transfers must be verified or kept within a limited network-bandwidth budget.
Key facts: Each task run scans the source and destination and copies data and metadata differences.; DataSync performs integrity checks during transfer; optional end-of-transfer verification can compare full-file checksums.; Tasks support scheduling, include and exclude filters, and a built-in bandwidth throttle.; Transfers involving on-premises storage require a DataSync agent; transfers between AWS storage services in the same account do not.
Gotchas: DataSync moves data over the network; it is not the offline-shipping choice for a site with inadequate connectivity.; A partner that must keep using an SFTP client needs a managed file-transfer endpoint, not a DataSync task.; Built-in integrity checks and optional end-of-transfer checksum verification are not the same setting.
Confused with: AWS Snow Family: Choose Snow Family for offline transfer when network transfer is impractical; choose DataSync for online migration or recurring copies.; AWS Transfer Family: Transfer Family provides endpoints for existing SFTP, FTPS, FTP, or AS2 clients; DataSync copies data between storage locations.
ES: AWS DataSync mueve archivos y objetos en línea entre ubicaciones de almacenamiento compatibles, como NFS, SMB, HDFS y almacenamiento de objetos local, y servicios de AWS como S3, EFS y FSx. Elígelo cuando una migración o copia recurrente necesite programación administrada, comprobaciones de integridad o control del ancho de banda. En cada ejecución, la tarea examina el origen y el destino y copia las diferencias de datos y metadatos.; DataSync comprueba la integridad durante la transferencia; una verificación opcional al final puede comparar checksums de archivos completos.; Las tareas admiten programación, filtros de inclusión y exclusión, y un límite de ancho de banda integrado.; Las transferencias con almacenamiento local requieren un agente de DataSync; las transferencias entre servicios de almacenamiento de AWS en la misma cuenta no lo requieren.

chunks.title: AWS DataSync
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retail analytics team is moving image objects from Azure Blob Storage to an Amazon S3 data lake. New objects arrive throughout the week, and the team wants scheduled online transfers without operating a transfer agent. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure a scheduled DataSync Enhanced mode task from Azure Blob Storage to S3.
Why: The source is cloud object storage, the destination is S3, and the copies must run online on a schedule. DataSync supports Azure Blob Storage and scheduled transfers; an Enhanced mode task can connect to cloud storage without an agent. Transfer Family provides a client-facing endpoint rather than a scheduled copy from the existing source. A custom application would increase operational overhead.
Wrong options: Give the source team an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint backed by S3 for its weekly uploads. (An SFTP endpoint requires a client upload workflow rather than scheduled copies from Azure Blob Storage.); Export the objects to AWS Snow Family devices for repeated offline delivery into AWS. (Repeated offline delivery does not meet the scheduled online-transfer requirement.); Build a scheduled application that lists Azure objects and writes changes to S3. (A custom application adds maintenance when a managed transfer task is available.)

chunks.title: AWS DataSync
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute keeps experiment records in an on-premises HDFS cluster. It must copy only the records selected for retention to Amazon S3 every weekend, limit use of a shared network link, and compare the copied files with the source after each transfer. The institute plans to use AWS DataSync. Which TWO task choices together meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Set a DataSync bandwidth throttle and enable optional end-of-transfer full-file verification. + Schedule the HDFS-to-S3 task for weekends and use an include filter for the selected records.
Why: The task must satisfy four constraints: weekend execution, selected records, bounded bandwidth, and comparison after copying. Scheduling with an include filter addresses the first two; a bandwidth throttle and optional full-file verification address the other two. Excluding the retention records would omit precisely the data the institute needs. Built-in transfer integrity checks do not replace the specifically requested end-of-transfer comparison.
Wrong options: Set up an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint for the HDFS cluster to submit records. (An SFTP endpoint does not configure the planned DataSync task to select and copy HDFS records.); Set an exclude filter that omits the records selected for retention. (Omitting the selected records prevents the required files from reaching S3.); Run the task manually after each weekend and copy the entire HDFS dataset. (Manual runs and copying everything miss the scheduled, selected-record requirements.)

chunks.title: AWS DataSync
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio stores active project files on an on-premises NFS server. It wants an initial copy in Amazon S3, followed by nightly copies of changes, but its shared internet connection must remain available for daytime collaboration. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy a DataSync agent, schedule an NFS-to-S3 task for off-hours, and set a bandwidth throttle.
Why: The deciding requirements are an online NFS-to-S3 migration, recurring copies of changes, and protection of a shared connection. A DataSync task can make the initial copy, run on a schedule, and limit its bandwidth. Snow Family is an offline transfer approach, so repeated shipments do not meet the nightly-copy requirement. A custom program could move data but would require more operational work.
Wrong options: Ship the initial files with AWS Snow Family and repeat shipments for nightly changes. (Offline shipments do not provide the required nightly online copies.); Run a nightly custom copy program from the NFS server to S3 and manage its network usage. (A custom program adds operational work compared with DataSync's built-in scheduling and throttle.); Provide an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint and have the NFS server submit files each night. (An SFTP endpoint does not itself scan the NFS share and copy its changes.)

chunks.title: DDoS-resilient architecture
chunks.text:
DDoS-resilient architecture. A DDoS-resilient architecture combines services that help absorb and filter external attacks rather than relying on capacity alone. In an exam scenario, distinguish a layered design from one that only scales the application during an attack.
When to use: A public application must remain available and responsive during external attacks.; The design must address both infrastructure-layer and application-layer attacks.; The business wants to avoid unnecessary scaling costs caused by attack traffic.
Key facts: DDoS attacks can affect application availability and responsiveness.; DDoS guidance distinguishes infrastructure-layer attacks from application-layer attacks.; Scaling infrastructure in response to an attack can create unnecessary direct costs.; A resilient design can combine Route 53, CloudFront, ELB, Auto Scaling, WAF, and Shield to absorb and filter external attacks.
Gotchas: Adding capacity alone does not meet a requirement to filter attack traffic.; Filtering application requests alone does not cover every type of DDoS attack.; Choosing a single service can miss a stated requirement for layered protection.
Confused with: 
ES: Una arquitectura resistente a DDoS combina servicios que ayudan a absorber y filtrar ataques externos, en vez de depender solo de la capacidad. En un escenario de examen, distingue un diseño por capas de uno que únicamente escala la aplicación durante un ataque. Los ataques DDoS pueden afectar la disponibilidad y la capacidad de respuesta de una aplicación.; La guía de DDoS distingue los ataques de capa de infraestructura de los de capa de aplicación.; Escalar la infraestructura en respuesta a un ataque puede generar costos directos innecesarios.; Un diseño resistente puede combinar Route 53, CloudFront, ELB, Auto Scaling, WAF y Shield para absorber y filtrar ataques externos.

chunks.title: DDoS-resilient architecture
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare scheduling service uses Route 53, CloudFront, an ELB, and Auto Scaling for its public application. Its team wants to keep those components while adding controls for hostile application requests and DDoS attacks that can affect availability beyond the application layer. Which TWO additions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Add WAF for application-request filtering. + Add Shield to the DDoS protection design.
Why: The existing architecture already has delivery and capacity components. The two missing additions are WAF for hostile application requests and Shield for broader DDoS protection. Adding more capacity instead can increase costs during an attack without supplying the requested filtering control.
Wrong options: Add another Route 53 configuration for the public domain. (A domain configuration does not provide the requested application-request filtering.); Increase the Auto Scaling range. (More capacity does not add a control for filtering hostile requests.); Add another ELB for application capacity. (Additional capacity does not meet either requested security-control addition.)

chunks.title: DDoS-resilient architecture
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company runs a public application behind an ELB with Auto Scaling. During an external attack, capacity increases while legitimate customers still experience slow responses. The company wants to address both infrastructure-layer and application-layer attacks without treating additional capacity as its only defense. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Place CloudFront in front of the application and combine Route 53, WAF, and Shield with the existing ELB and Auto Scaling.
Why: The deciding requirement is protection against both infrastructure-layer and application-layer attacks without relying solely on scaling. The layered design combines services for absorbing and filtering external attacks while retaining the existing ELB and Auto Scaling. Increasing capacity alone can create unnecessary direct costs during an attack and does not meet the filtering requirement.
Wrong options: Increase Auto Scaling capacity and retain the existing ELB. (More capacity does not satisfy the requirement to filter attack traffic.); Add Route 53 to the existing ELB and increase the Auto Scaling range. (This still relies on increased capacity rather than adding attack filtering.); Add WAF to the existing ELB and remove Auto Scaling to keep capacity fixed. (This adds filtering but removes the capacity component and does not provide the requested layered approach to both attack types.)

chunks.title: Dedicated Hosts vs Dedicated Instances (licensing, compliance)
chunks.text:
Dedicated Hosts vs Dedicated Instances (licensing, compliance). Both EC2 Dedicated Hosts and Dedicated Instances run instances on dedicated physical hardware. Choose Dedicated Hosts when licensing requires socket or core visibility, targeted placement, or host affinity; choose Dedicated Instances when the requirement is hardware isolation without those host-level controls.
When to use: Choose Dedicated Hosts for eligible BYOL licenses tied to physical sockets or cores.; Choose Dedicated Hosts when instances must be placed on, or return to, a specific host.; Consider Dedicated Instances when dedicated hardware is required but host visibility and placement control are not.
Key facts: Dedicated Hosts expose host IDs and physical socket and core counts; Dedicated Instances do not.; Dedicated Hosts support targeted placement and host affinity; Dedicated Instances support neither.; Dedicated Hosts are billed per host, while Dedicated Instances are billed per instance.; Dedicated Instances have limited BYOL support, including certain licenses with specific mobility rights.; Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to one AWS account, but might share hardware with other instances from that same account.
Gotchas: Dedicated hardware alone does not provide the socket or core visibility needed for some BYOL terms.; Stopping and starting a Dedicated Instance might place it on a different host.; Do not choose Dedicated Hosts on the assumption that they have an inherent performance or security advantage over Dedicated Instances.
Confused with: Dedicated Instances: Provide dedicated hardware without host visibility, targeted placement, or host affinity.; On-Demand Capacity Reservations: Reserve EC2 capacity in an Availability Zone; they do not provide Dedicated Host socket or core visibility.; Reserved Instances: A purchasing option does not, by itself, provide Dedicated Host placement and license visibility.
ES: Tanto EC2 Dedicated Hosts como Dedicated Instances ejecutan instancias en hardware físico dedicado. Elige Dedicated Hosts si la licencia exige visibilidad de sockets o núcleos, ubicación dirigida o host affinity; elige Dedicated Instances si solo necesitas aislamiento de hardware sin esos controles. Dedicated Hosts muestran el ID del host y la cantidad de sockets y núcleos físicos; Dedicated Instances no.; Dedicated Hosts admiten targeted placement y host affinity; Dedicated Instances no admiten ninguna de las dos.; Dedicated Hosts se facturan por host; Dedicated Instances, por instancia.; Dedicated Instances tienen compatibilidad limitada con BYOL, incluidas ciertas licencias con derechos específicos de movilidad.; Dedicated Instances usan hardware dedicado a una sola cuenta de AWS, pero podrían compartirlo con otras instancias de esa misma cuenta.

chunks.title: Dedicated Hosts vs Dedicated Instances (licensing, compliance)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company runs a licensed rendering tool on EC2 and stops its instance between projects. The vendor requires the tool to run on the same physical server when the instance starts again, and the operations team must be able to target that server for placement. Which approach meets these requirements?
Correct: Use a Dedicated Host with host affinity and targeted instance placement.
Why: The requirement is not merely dedicated hardware or available capacity: the instance must return to a particular physical server. Dedicated Hosts support host affinity and targeted placement. A Dedicated Instance might move to another host after a stop and start. Reserving instance capacity does not supply the missing host-level control.
Wrong options: Use a Dedicated Reserved Instance to reserve dedicated instance capacity. (Reserving Dedicated Instance capacity does not give targeted host placement or host affinity.); Use a Dedicated Instance and restart it when the next project begins. (A stopped and restarted Dedicated Instance might run on a different host.); Use an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the required Availability Zone. (Capacity in an Availability Zone does not identify or preserve the required physical host.)

chunks.title: Dedicated Hosts vs Dedicated Instances (licensing, compliance)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization is migrating two unrelated EC2 workloads. A simulation uses an existing per-socket software license and must report the physical socket count for audits. A variable-size data review workload requires hardware isolated from other AWS accounts, needs no host-level controls, and must be billed per instance rather than per host. Which two choices meet the respective requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Run the data review workload as Dedicated Instances. + Run the simulation on a Dedicated Host and use its socket visibility for audits.
Why: The workloads have different deciding requirements. The simulation needs physical socket visibility for its existing license, so it belongs on a Dedicated Host. The data review workload needs account-level hardware isolation and per-instance billing, which Dedicated Instances provide. Using Dedicated Hosts for data review would miss its billing requirement, while Dedicated Instances cannot supply the simulation's socket visibility.
Wrong options: Run the data review workload on default-tenancy instances with Capacity Reservations. (Capacity Reservations do not provide the required hardware isolation for default-tenancy instances.); Run the simulation on Dedicated Instances and record its EC2 instance type.
