(Dedicated Instances do not expose the host's physical socket count for the simulation audit.); Run the data review workload on Dedicated Hosts and allocate hosts as demand changes. (Dedicated Hosts are billed per host rather than per instance.)

chunks.title: Amazon Detective investigation
chunks.text:
Amazon Detective investigation. Amazon Detective helps investigators find the root cause and scope of suspicious activity by visualizing linked resource behavior and log data. Choose it when the task is to investigate a finding, rather than generate a threat alert or collect findings in one view.
When to use: A GuardDuty finding needs context about related API calls, network activity, and affected resources.; Investigators need to explore connections among multiple findings and entities.; A suspicious IAM user or role needs investigation for indicators of compromise.
Key facts: Detective extracts time-based events from AWS CloudTrail and Amazon VPC flow logs and ingests GuardDuty findings.; Its behavior graph links resource activity over time in interactive visualizations.; Finding groups help examine related activities and the root cause of high-severity GuardDuty findings.; Detective Investigation can examine IAM users and roles for indicators of compromise.; Detective provides access to up to a year of historical event data.
Gotchas: GuardDuty identifies potentially malicious activity; a GuardDuty finding can be the starting point for a Detective investigation.; Security Hub CSPM aggregates and prioritizes findings, but its cross-service view is not Detective's linked behavior investigation.; Security Lake centralizes security data; collecting raw logs is not the same as using Detective's prebuilt visualizations.
Confused with: Amazon GuardDuty: Use GuardDuty to identify suspicious activity; use Detective to investigate the activity and its connections.; AWS Security Hub CSPM: Security Hub CSPM brings findings together; Detective explores linked behavior to investigate root cause.
ES: Amazon Detective ayuda a investigar la causa raíz y el alcance de una actividad sospechosa mediante visualizaciones de datos de registros y comportamientos relacionados. Elígelo cuando debas investigar un hallazgo, no solo generar una alerta o reunir hallazgos en una vista. Detective extrae eventos de AWS CloudTrail y Amazon VPC flow logs e incorpora hallazgos de GuardDuty.; Su behavior graph relaciona la actividad de los recursos a lo largo del tiempo mediante visualizaciones interactivas.; Los finding groups ayudan a examinar actividades relacionadas y la causa raíz de hallazgos de GuardDuty de alta severidad.; Detective Investigation puede examinar usuarios y roles de IAM en busca de indicadores de compromiso.; Detective permite acceder a hasta un año de datos históricos de eventos.

chunks.title: Amazon Detective investigation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization is reviewing several high-severity GuardDuty findings that appear to involve the same AWS resources. The incident lead needs an interactive view showing how the findings and entities relate so the team can investigate a possible shared root cause. Which solution best meets this requirement?
Correct: Use Amazon Detective finding groups to examine the related findings and entities.
Why: The team already has multiple findings and needs to investigate how they connect. Detective finding groups display related findings and entities in an interactive visualization and support root-cause analysis of high-severity GuardDuty findings. Security Hub CSPM can prioritize findings, but that does not satisfy the request to explore their relationships.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Security Lake to collect the underlying security events in a central data lake. (Centralizing events does not itself provide the requested visualization of related findings and entities.); Use GuardDuty to identify more potentially unauthorized activity involving the resources. (Additional detection does not satisfy the need to visualize relationships among the findings already received.); Use AWS Security Hub CSPM to prioritize the GuardDuty findings in its security view. (Prioritizing findings does not show the connections and root cause requested for this investigation.)

chunks.title: Amazon Detective investigation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company is investigating a particular IAM role after noticing suspicious activity. Responders need to examine the role for indicators of compromise and understand whether it is involved in a security incident, rather than collect more findings from other accounts. Which solution best meets these requirements?
Correct: Run a Detective Investigation for the IAM role.
Why: The requirement centers on investigating a specified IAM role for indicators of compromise. Detective Investigation supports investigations of IAM users and roles and helps determine whether a resource is involved in a security incident. Security Hub CSPM aggregates findings, which the scenario explicitly distinguishes from the work responders need to do.
Wrong options: Use AWS Security Hub CSPM to aggregate findings across the accounts. (Cross-account findings aggregation misses the stated need to investigate indicators of compromise for this role.); Use Amazon Security Lake to centralize security data for the accounts. (Centralizing security data does not itself perform the requested investigation of the role.); Use GuardDuty to identify potentially malicious activity in AWS logs. (GuardDuty can identify suspicious activity, but the requirement is to investigate the specified IAM role for indicators of compromise.)

chunks.title: Direct Connect resiliency, VPN backup and encryption (MACsec/VPN over DX)
chunks.text:
Direct Connect resiliency, VPN backup and encryption (MACsec/VPN over DX). Direct Connect resiliency depends on redundant connections and where they terminate, not on adding Direct Connect gateways. Choose a resiliency model for the failure the business must survive, and assess encryption separately: these excerpts do not specify how to implement VPN backup, IPsec VPN over Direct Connect, or MACsec.
When to use: A critical workload must withstand a Direct Connect device, connection, or complete location failure.; A team needs to order redundant dedicated connections against a stated availability objective.; The business wants to verify that traffic uses a redundant virtual interface during a failover test.
Key facts: The maximum resiliency model uses separate connections on separate devices in more than one location and addresses device, connectivity, and complete location failures.; The high resiliency model uses two single connections in multiple locations.; The development and test model uses separate devices in one location; it does not protect against location failure.; The Resiliency Toolkit can guide connection ordering and test failover by bringing down a BGP peering session to check routing to a redundant virtual interface.; A Direct Connect gateway has built-in high availability; adding gateways does not replace redundant physical connections.
Gotchas: Two connections on separate devices at one location still share a location-failure risk.; A Direct Connect gateway connects networks; its built-in availability does not make a single connection resilient.; Do not treat a resiliency model as an encryption configuration. The supplied excerpts do not establish implementation details for VPN backup, VPN over Direct Connect, or MACsec.
Confused with: Direct Connect gateway: It connects Direct Connect to associated gateways or networks; it is not a second Direct Connect location.; Development and test resiliency: Separate devices in one location address device failure, not complete location failure.
ES: La resiliencia de Direct Connect depende de conexiones redundantes y de dónde terminan, no de agregar Direct Connect gateways. Elige un resiliency model según la falla que debe resistir el negocio y evalúa el cifrado por separado: estos extractos no especifican cómo implementar VPN backup, IPsec VPN over Direct Connect ni MACsec. El modelo maximum resiliency usa conexiones separadas en dispositivos separados y en más de una ubicación; contempla fallas de dispositivo, conectividad y ubicación completa.; El modelo high resiliency usa dos conexiones individuales en múltiples ubicaciones.; El modelo development and test usa dispositivos separados en una sola ubicación; no protege contra una falla de esa ubicación.; El Resiliency Toolkit guía la solicitud de conexiones y permite probar el failover al interrumpir una sesión BGP para comprobar el enrutamiento hacia una virtual interface redundante.; Direct Connect gateway tiene alta disponibilidad integrada; agregar gateways no sustituye las conexiones físicas redundantes.

chunks.title: Direct Connect resiliency, VPN backup and encryption (MACsec/VPN over DX)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A hospital is redesigning Direct Connect access for a critical application. Its acceptance criteria cover device, connectivity, and complete Direct Connect location failures; before sign-off, the network team must demonstrate that traffic takes a redundant virtual interface when a BGP peering session is brought down. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use the Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit failover test to check routing when BGP peering is brought down. + Use the maximum resiliency model for connections on separate devices in more than one location.
Why: This scenario requires both a design that covers location failure and a specific failover validation. The maximum resiliency model uses separate connections and devices in more than one location. The Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit supports a failover test that brings down BGP peering to verify routing to a redundant virtual interface. A one-location model misses the failure requirement, while checking ordinary gateway reachability misses the requested test.
Wrong options: Verify only that the Direct Connect gateway can reach each VPC. (Reachability alone does not demonstrate routing to a redundant virtual interface after BGP peering is brought down.); Order connections in the development and test model on separate devices at one location. (This model does not cover the required complete location failure.); Provision multiple Direct Connect gateways instead of redundant dedicated connections. (More gateways do not provide the physical connection and location redundancy required.)

chunks.title: Direct Connect resiliency, VPN backup and encryption (MACsec/VPN over DX)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab runs a non-critical development environment over Direct Connect. The lab wants connectivity to survive a device failure but accepts an outage if the entire Direct Connect location fails; it also wants to avoid ordering connections at another location. Which resiliency model best meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Development and test: separate connections on separate devices at one location.
Why: The lab requires device-failure protection but explicitly accepts location failure and does not want a second location. The development and test model provides separate connections on separate devices at one location for non-critical workloads. High and maximum resiliency both involve multiple locations, exceeding this stated need. Additional Direct Connect gateways do not substitute for separate connections.
Wrong options: Maximum resiliency: separate devices and connections in more than one location. (It protects against a location failure that the lab accepts and requires more than one location.); One connection at the existing location and two Direct Connect gateways. (Gateway redundancy does not address failure of the device serving the sole connection.); High resiliency: two single connections in multiple locations. (It introduces another location that the lab explicitly does not want to order.)

chunks.title: AWS Direct Connect
chunks.text:
AWS Direct Connect. AWS Direct Connect provides a private network connection from your facilities to AWS that bypasses internet service providers in the network path. Choose it for substantial, sustained hybrid traffic when more consistent bandwidth and network performance justify arranging a physical connection; do not assume the connection is encrypted or resilient by itself.
When to use: An on-premises network needs a private connection to VPC resources for sustained traffic.; A business values a more consistent network experience and can arrange connectivity through a Direct Connect location or partner.; Large outbound transfers make Direct Connect's data transfer pricing worth evaluating alongside port-hour charges.
Key facts: A private virtual interface accesses a VPC using private IP addresses; a public virtual interface accesses public AWS services, such as Amazon S3, using public IP addresses.; A Direct Connect gateway can extend private virtual interface access to multiple virtual private gateways across supported accounts and Regions.; Direct Connect billing includes port hours and outbound data transfer; a private connection can reduce costs in some circumstances, but is not automatically the cheapest choice.; For high availability, AWS recommends connections at multiple Direct Connect locations. An IPsec VPN can provide backup for VPC traffic.; Supported Direct Connect connections can use MACsec to encrypt traffic between an on-premises device and the Direct Connect point of presence.
Gotchas: A private network path does not, by itself, provide encryption.; One Direct Connect connection is not a highly available hybrid design.; A public virtual interface for Amazon S3 is not the private virtual interface used to reach VPC resources.; A link aggregation group can protect against a link failure but not a failure of its terminating device.
Confused with: AWS Site-to-Site VPN: Use an IPsec VPN when internet-based encrypted connectivity or a backup path fits; choose Direct Connect when the primary requirement is a private network path with more consistent performance.; AWS Transit Gateway: Transit Gateway connects and routes among multiple networks; it does not replace the physical connection from a facility to AWS.; VPC peering: VPC peering connects VPCs, not an on-premises facility to AWS over a dedicated private line.
ES: AWS Direct Connect proporciona una conexión de red privada desde tus instalaciones hacia AWS que evita a los proveedores de internet en la ruta. Elígelo para tráfico híbrido sostenido cuando una experiencia de red más constante justifique coordinar una conexión física; no supongas que la conexión está cifrada o que ofrece redundancia por sí sola. Una private virtual interface permite acceder a una VPC mediante direcciones IP privadas; una public virtual interface permite acceder a servicios públicos de AWS, como Amazon S3, mediante direcciones IP públicas.; Un Direct Connect gateway puede extender el acceso de una private virtual interface a múltiples virtual private gateways entre cuentas y Regions compatibles.; Direct Connect cobra por horas de puerto y transferencia de datos de salida; una conexión privada puede reducir costos en algunas circunstancias, pero no es automáticamente la opción más barata.; Para alta disponibilidad, AWS recomienda conexiones en varias ubicaciones de Direct Connect. Una IPsec VPN puede servir como respaldo para el tráfico de la VPC.; Las conexiones de Direct Connect compatibles pueden usar MACsec para cifrar el tráfico entre un dispositivo local y el punto de presencia de Direct Connect.

chunks.title: AWS Direct Connect
chunks.text:
Scenario: A film archive transfers a large volume of footage between its data center and an application in an Amazon VPC each day. The archive can arrange a connection through a Direct Connect location and wants a private network path that avoids internet service providers, with a more consistent network experience than its current internet link. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Establish AWS Direct Connect with a private virtual interface to the VPC.
Why: The deciding requirements are the private path from an on-premises facility and the desire to avoid internet service providers. Direct Connect supplies that connection, while a private virtual interface provides access to VPC resources using private IP addresses. A Site-to-Site VPN could connect the networks, but its internet-based path misses the stated requirement.
Wrong options: Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN from the data center to the VPC. (The VPN uses an internet-based path rather than the requested path that avoids internet service providers.); Peer the application's VPC with another VPC used by the archive. (VPC peering does not connect the archive's on-premises data center to AWS.); Attach the VPC to AWS Transit Gateway and route the data center's existing internet traffic to it. (Transit Gateway does not establish the required private connection from the data center to AWS.)

chunks.title: AWS Direct Connect
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer uses Direct Connect to exchange production data with an application in a VPC. It must keep a private connection to AWS available if a Direct Connect location or its terminating device fails; routing the production traffic over the internet is not permitted, even during failover. Which design meets these requirements with the HIGHEST availability?
Correct: Provision redundant Direct Connect connections at multiple Direct Connect locations.
Why: This scenario requires both location-level resilience and a private path during failover. AWS recommends connections at multiple Direct Connect locations for highly available connectivity. A link aggregation group at one location can help with a link failure but not a terminating-device failure. An IPsec VPN is a valid backup for VPC traffic only when an internet-based failover path is acceptable.
Wrong options: Aggregate multiple dedicated connections into one link aggregation group at a single location. (A link aggregation group does not protect against failure of the device where it terminates.); Keep one Direct Connect connection and add an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN for failover. (The VPN can back up VPC traffic but would route failover traffic over the internet, which is prohibited.); Keep one Direct Connect connection and attach the VPC to a Transit Gateway. (A Transit Gateway attachment does not create another physical path if the Direct Connect connection fails.)

chunks.title: AWS Direct Connect
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher is planning sustained data transfers between its office network and an application in a VPC. It can arrange a Direct Connect connection and wants the primary VPC traffic to bypass its internet provider, but it will accept an internet-based backup if that connection fails. Which TWO components should the publisher include? (Choose two.)
Correct: An IPsec Site-to-Site VPN connection to back up VPC traffic. + A Direct Connect private virtual interface for access to the VPC.
Why: The primary path must bypass the internet provider and reach private VPC resources, so it needs Direct Connect with a private virtual interface. The publisher explicitly permits an internet-based backup, making an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN suitable for VPC traffic during a Direct Connect failure. A public virtual interface targets public AWS services instead. A link aggregation group at one location is not an independent backup against a terminating-device failure.
Wrong options: A Direct Connect public virtual interface as the primary interface for private VPC resources. (A public virtual interface accesses public AWS services rather than private VPC resources.); A link aggregation group at one Direct Connect location as the sole backup path. (A link aggregation group at one location does not provide an independent backup if its terminating device fails.); VPC peering between the application VPC and another VPC as the office connection. (VPC peering does not connect the on-premises office network to AWS.)

chunks.title: AWS Directory Service: Managed Microsoft AD vs AD Connector vs Simple AD
chunks.text:
AWS Directory Service: Managed Microsoft AD vs AD Connector vs Simple AD. Choose the directory based on where Active Directory lives and which features the workload needs. AD Connector forwards requests to an existing on-premises AD; AWS Managed Microsoft AD provides actual Microsoft AD in AWS; Simple AD provides a basic, low-cost standalone directory.
When to use: Use AD Connector when compatible AWS applications must authenticate against an existing on-premises AD without caching directory information in the cloud.; Use AWS Managed Microsoft AD when a workload needs actual Microsoft AD features, such as trusts or schema extensions, in AWS.; Use Simple AD when a standalone, low-scale directory needs only basic AD compatibility.
Key facts: AD Connector forwards sign-in requests to on-premises domain controllers and can join EC2 Windows instances to the existing domain.; AD Connector does not support transitive trusts and is not compatible with RDS for SQL Server.; AWS Managed Microsoft AD supports trusts, schema extensions, and RDS for SQL Server workloads.; Simple AD is powered by Samba 4 and supports basic features including user accounts, group membership, domain join, and group policies.; Simple AD does not support MFA, trusts, schema extensions, or RDS for SQL Server.
Gotchas: AD Connector is a proxy, not a new Microsoft AD domain hosted in AWS.; Simple AD’s basic AD compatibility does not make it suitable for workloads that require actual Microsoft AD features.; An existing on-premises AD does not automatically make AD Connector the right choice: check whether the AWS workload supports it.
Confused with: IAM Identity Center: Use it for centralized workforce access across AWS accounts and applications, not as the AD domain needed by a Windows workload.; SAML/OIDC federation to IAM roles: Use federation for access through an existing identity provider; it does not provide AD domain services to an application.; Amazon Cognito user pools: Use user pools to authenticate application subscribers, not to supply AD features for Windows workloads.
ES: Elige el directorio según dónde reside Active Directory y qué funciones necesita la carga de trabajo. AD Connector reenvía solicitudes a un AD local existente; AWS Managed Microsoft AD proporciona Microsoft AD real en AWS; Simple AD ofrece un directorio independiente, básico y de bajo costo. AD Connector reenvía las solicitudes de inicio de sesión a los controladores de dominio locales y puede unir instancias EC2 Windows al dominio existente.; AD Connector no admite transitive trusts y no es compatible con RDS for SQL Server.; AWS Managed Microsoft AD admite trusts, schema extensions y cargas de trabajo de RDS for SQL Server.; Simple AD se basa en Samba 4 y admite funciones básicas como cuentas de usuario, pertenencia a grupos, unión al dominio y group policies.; Simple AD no admite MFA, trusts, schema extensions ni RDS for SQL Server.

chunks.title: AWS Directory Service: Managed Microsoft AD vs AD Connector vs Simple AD
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer is moving an AD-aware application to AWS. The application requires schema extensions and secure LDAP communications, and administrators must establish a trust with the company's on-premises AD so employees can use their existing credentials. Which directory option meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS Managed Microsoft AD and establish a trust with on-premises AD.
Why: The application needs actual AD capabilities in AWS, not just a way to forward sign-in requests. AWS Managed Microsoft AD supports schema extensions and secure LDAP communications, and a trust can allow use of credentials from on-premises AD. Simple AD lacks all three required features; AD Connector is a proxy rather than an AD domain in AWS.
Wrong options: Use AD Connector to redirect the application's directory requests. (AD Connector proxies to on-premises AD rather than providing the Microsoft AD in AWS with the requested features.); Use IAM Identity Center to provision workforce access to the application. (IAM Identity Center does not provide the AD schema, secure LDAP communications, and trust required by the application.); Use Simple AD and connect the application to its cloud directory. (Simple AD does not support schema extensions, LDAPS, or trust relationships.)

chunks.title: AWS Directory Service: Managed Microsoft AD vs AD Connector vs Simple AD
chunks.text:
Scenario: A small nonprofit is deploying a few Windows EC2 instances for an internal application that is compatible with Samba 4. It needs a standalone directory in AWS for user accounts, group memberships, and domain join, but does not need MFA, trusts, or schema extensions. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Create a Simple AD directory for the application and instances.
Why: The nonprofit needs a low-cost, standalone cloud directory with only basic AD-compatible features. Simple AD provides accounts, groups, and domain join, and the application is explicitly compatible with Samba 4. Managed Microsoft AD offers capabilities the scenario does not need, while AD Connector requires an existing on-premises directory to proxy.
Wrong options: Deploy AD Connector for the application and instances. (AD Connector redirects requests to an existing on-premises AD and does not provide the requested standalone directory.); Configure IAM Identity Center for the application and instances. (IAM Identity Center does not supply the standalone AD-compatible directory needed for domain join.); Create an AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory for the application and instances. (Managed Microsoft AD provides actual Microsoft AD features that this basic, low-cost scenario does not require.)

chunks.title: Distributed design patterns: retries with backoff, idempotency, circuit breakers
chunks.text:
Distributed design patterns: retries with backoff, idempotency, circuit breakers. Distributed calls can fail briefly or remain unavailable. Retry transient failures with bounded exponential backoff and jitter, make operations safe to repeat, and use a circuit breaker to stop calling a dependency that repeatedly fails.
When to use: A dependency has occasional timeouts, and retries could help it recover.; A consumer might repeat a mutating operation after an uncertain outcome.; A synchronous dependency repeatedly times out, threatening the caller’s responsiveness.
Key facts: Exponential backoff increases the interval between retries; jitter randomizes it to reduce coordinated traffic spikes.; Set a maximum retry count or elapsed time, and choose timeouts appropriate to the workload.; Retry transient failures at an appropriate layer; retries at multiple layers can compound into a retry storm.; Verify that an operation is idempotent before retrying it, or repeated calls can produce duplicate results.; An open circuit breaker stops routing calls to a failing service and can check later whether it has recovered.; An AWS example implements a circuit breaker with a Step Functions Express workflow and a DynamoDB table that tracks circuit status.
Gotchas: Retrying every error is not resilience: permission and configuration errors may require intervention.; Backoff without jitter can still synchronize retries; retries without a stopping point can create backlogs.; A circuit breaker is not simply a larger retry limit: it prevents further calls while the circuit is open.
Confused with: 
ES: Las llamadas distribuidas pueden fallar brevemente o permanecer indisponibles. Para fallas transitorias, usa reintentos limitados con exponential backoff y jitter; haz que las operaciones sean seguras de repetir y usa un circuit breaker para dejar de llamar a una dependencia que falla repetidamente. Exponential backoff aumenta el intervalo entre reintentos; jitter lo aleatoriza para reducir picos de tráfico coordinados.; Define un número máximo de reintentos o un tiempo máximo transcurrido, y elige timeouts adecuados para tu carga de trabajo.; Reintenta fallas transitorias en una capa apropiada; hacerlo en varias capas puede multiplicar los intentos.; Verifica que una operación sea idempotente antes de reintentarla; de lo contrario, las llamadas repetidas pueden producir resultados duplicados.; Un circuit breaker abierto deja de enviar llamadas a un servicio con fallas y puede comprobar más adelante si se recuperó.; Un ejemplo de AWS implementa un circuit breaker con un workflow Express de AWS Step Functions y una tabla de Amazon DynamoDB que registra su estado.

chunks.title: Distributed design patterns: retries with backoff, idempotency, circuit breakers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing platform calls a seating service that occasionally returns temporary errors during event launches. Several application layers currently retry the same request immediately, creating bursts of calls while the seating service is strained. The team wants successful requests to recover without amplifying the load. Which change meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use an applicable SDK retry capability at one chosen layer, with exponential backoff, jitter, and a retry limit.
Why: The deciding constraints are temporary failures and bursts caused by retries at several layers. Bounded exponential backoff gives the seating service time to recover, while jitter reduces synchronized spikes. Using applicable SDK behavior avoids unnecessary custom retry logic, but the team should verify and test its configuration. Increasing timeouts while retaining retries at every layer does not fix compounded attempts.
Wrong options: Keep retries at every layer, but increase each layer’s timeout. (Retries at multiple layers can compound attempts, and longer timeouts do not prevent traffic bursts.); Retry all errors at a fixed interval until the seating service responds. (Fixed, unbounded retries can synchronize traffic and repeatedly retry errors that will not resolve.); Disable retries and require customers to submit the request again after every temporary error. (This gives up the requested automatic recovery from occasional temporary errors.)

chunks.title: Distributed design patterns: retries with backoff, idempotency, circuit breakers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A meal-delivery company processes payment requests from an Amazon SQS-backed worker. If a payment call times out, the worker cannot tell whether the charge succeeded, but the business still needs to retry transient failures without charging a customer twice. Which design meets these requirements MOST safely?
Correct: Make the charge operation idempotent using a stable operation identifier, then apply bounded retries for transient failures.
Why: The timeout leaves the outcome of a mutating operation uncertain. Before retrying, the charge must be idempotent so that another attempt for the same operation cannot create an unintended duplicate result. Bounded retries can then help with transient failures. Exponential backoff and jitter alone address load, not duplicate charges.
Wrong options: Stop retrying timed-out calls and treat every timeout as a failed payment. (A timeout does not establish that the charge failed, and this design does not meet the retry requirement.); Retry each timed-out payment call immediately with a new request identifier. (A new identifier does not make a repeated charge recognizable as the same operation.); Apply exponential backoff and jitter to payment calls without changing how charges are processed. (Backoff controls retry traffic but does not prevent a timed-out, successful charge from being repeated.)

chunks.title: Amazon DocumentDB (MongoDB compatible)
chunks.text:
Amazon DocumentDB (MongoDB compatible). Amazon DocumentDB is a fully managed, MongoDB-compatible database for document workloads. Choose it when a migration must retain MongoDB application code, drivers, and tools rather than adopt a different database interface.
When to use: An existing MongoDB application must move to a managed database with minimal application changes.; A MongoDB-compatible workload needs read scaling through replicas.; A MongoDB-compatible workload needs to scale to millions of reads and writes per second with petabytes of storage.
Key facts: Applications can use the same code, drivers, and tools they use with MongoDB.; Instance-based clusters can have up to 15 replicas; a reader endpoint lets applications connect without tracking replica changes.; In instance-based clusters, all writes go through the primary instance, while the primary and replicas can serve reads.; For instance-based clusters, storage has six copies across three Availability Zones. Failover can use a provisioned replica in another Availability Zone.; Elastic clusters support millions of reads and writes per second and petabytes of storage.
Gotchas: Adding instance-based replicas scales reads; it does not move writes off the primary.; Replicated storage alone is not the same as having a provisioned replica available for failover.; A document data model alone does not establish MongoDB driver compatibility.
Confused with: Amazon DynamoDB: DynamoDB is also a NoSQL option, but DocumentDB is the choice when retaining MongoDB code and drivers is required.; Amazon Keyspaces: Keyspaces is Apache Cassandra compatible and uses CQL, not the MongoDB interface.; Amazon Aurora: Aurora is MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible; DocumentDB is MongoDB-compatible.
ES: Amazon DocumentDB es una base de datos de documentos totalmente administrada y compatible con MongoDB. Elígela cuando una migración deba conservar el código, los drivers y las herramientas de MongoDB en lugar de adoptar otra interfaz de base de datos. Las aplicaciones pueden usar el mismo código, los mismos drivers y las mismas herramientas que usan con MongoDB.; Los clústeres basados en instancias admiten hasta 15 réplicas; un reader endpoint permite conectarse sin rastrear los cambios en las réplicas.; En los clústeres basados en instancias, todas las escrituras pasan por la instancia primaria; tanto la primaria como las réplicas pueden atender lecturas.; En los clústeres basados en instancias, el almacenamiento mantiene seis copias en tres Availability Zones. El failover puede usar una réplica aprovisionada en otra Availability Zone.; Los elastic clusters admiten millones de lecturas y escrituras por segundo y petabytes de almacenamiento.

chunks.title: Amazon DocumentDB (MongoDB compatible)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media platform stores personalized content records in MongoDB and wants to keep using its MongoDB application code and drivers after migration. Its forecast calls for millions of reads and writes per second and petabytes of storage. Engineers propose adding read replicas, but write growth is also a primary constraint. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use an Amazon DocumentDB elastic cluster for the MongoDB-compatible workload.
Why: This migration requires both MongoDB compatibility and scale for writes as well as reads. Amazon DocumentDB elastic clusters support workloads with millions of reads and writes per second and petabytes of storage. Adding replicas to an instance-based cluster addresses read throughput, but its writes still go through the primary. DynamoDB and Keyspaces would also require changing away from the existing MongoDB interface.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Keyspaces and move the record operations to CQL. (Moving operations to CQL violates the requirement to retain MongoDB code and drivers.); Use a DocumentDB instance-based cluster and add replicas through its reader endpoint. (Instance-based replicas increase read throughput, but all writes still pass through the primary instance.); Use Amazon DynamoDB and redesign access to the records around partition keys. (Redesigning access for DynamoDB does not retain the existing MongoDB code and drivers.)

chunks.title: Amazon DocumentDB (MongoDB compatible)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher is moving its MongoDB-backed article catalog to AWS. Its application team must retain the existing MongoDB code and drivers, while a growing number of searches requires additional read capacity. The team does not want to update connection settings each time it adds a read replica. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use an Amazon DocumentDB instance-based cluster with replicas and connect searches through its reader endpoint.
Why: Retaining MongoDB code and drivers is the deciding migration constraint. Amazon DocumentDB provides that compatibility, and instance-based replicas add read throughput. Its reader endpoint also prevents the application from having to track replicas as they are added or removed. DynamoDB, Aurora PostgreSQL, and Keyspaces each require a different database interface.
Wrong options: Move the catalog to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and direct searches to its read replicas. (Aurora PostgreSQL does not meet the requirement to retain the MongoDB code and drivers.); Move the catalog to Amazon DynamoDB and redesign the application's data access around partition keys. (DynamoDB requires a different application access approach instead of retaining the MongoDB code and drivers.); Move the catalog to Amazon Keyspaces and access the articles through CQL. (Keyspaces uses the Apache Cassandra-compatible CQL interface rather than the existing MongoDB interface.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: backup and restore
chunks.text:
DR strategy: backup and restore. Backup and restore is the lowest-cost DR strategy when the business can tolerate recovery points and recovery times measured in hours. At failover, restore the data and redeploy the infrastructure, configuration, and application; choose a more active strategy when the workload must recover faster.
When to use: The workload can tolerate hours of lost data and hours to resume service.; Keeping a running recovery environment would cost more than the business requires.; Point-in-time recovery is important after accidental deletion or data corruption.
Key facts: Backup frequency determines the achievable recovery point and must align with the RPO.; AWS Backup centrally configures, schedules, and monitors backups for supported resources and can copy backups across Regions.; A regional recovery plan must restore backed-up data and redeploy infrastructure, configuration, and application code in the recovery Region.; Infrastructure as code, such as AWS CloudFormation, helps redeploy reliably; back up required code, configuration, and AMIs too.; AWS Backup provides restore capability but does not provide scheduled or automatic restoration; test backups and the DR plan.
Gotchas: Copying data to a recovery Region is not the same as having a workload ready to serve traffic.; Backups alone do not preserve the infrastructure and configuration needed to meet the RTO.; Continuous replication alone may be less useful than point-in-time backups for recovering from corruption or malicious changes.
Confused with: Pilot light: Core data and infrastructure are kept available in the recovery Region, while application servers must be switched on for recovery.; Warm standby: A scaled-down, fully functional workload is already running and can handle traffic at reduced capacity.; Multi-site active-active: Multiple Regions serve traffic simultaneously, with the greatest complexity and cost of these approaches.
ES: Backup and restore es la estrategia de DR de menor costo cuando el negocio tolera un RPO y un RTO medidos en horas. Durante la recuperación, debes restaurar los datos y volver a desplegar la infraestructura, la configuración y la aplicación; elige una estrategia más activa si la carga debe recuperarse antes. La frecuencia de los backups determina el punto de recuperación alcanzable y debe ajustarse al RPO.; AWS Backup permite configurar, programar y supervisar de forma centralizada los backups de recursos compatibles, y puede copiarlos entre Regions.; Para recuperarte en otra Region, debes restaurar los datos y volver a desplegar la infraestructura, la configuración y el código de la aplicación.; La infraestructura como código, por ejemplo AWS CloudFormation, facilita un redespliegue confiable; respalda también el código, la configuración y las AMIs necesarias.; AWS Backup permite restaurar, pero no programa ni ejecuta automáticamente las restauraciones; debes probar los backups y el plan de DR.

chunks.title: DR strategy: backup and restore
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research team uses an Amazon RDS database for a batch application. Its main concern is discovering hours later that a faulty import corrupted records; the application can be unavailable for several hours while the team recovers. Which approach meets the recovery requirement MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Schedule point-in-time-capable RDS backups, then restore an appropriate earlier backup and redeploy the application.
Why: The team must recover data from before the faulty import, not merely make a current copy available elsewhere. Point-in-time-capable RDS backups provide a restoration point, while the several-hour outage allowance permits restoration and redeployment. Continuous replication can propagate corruption, and keeping another application deployment running does not replace a point-in-time backup.
Wrong options: Run the application in multiple active Regions and replicate database changes between them. (An active-active deployment is costly and still needs backups to recover from a data-corruption disaster.); Continuously replicate the database to a live database in a recovery Region and rely on that copy for recovery. (Continuous replication alone may carry corrupted data to the recovery copy and does not provide the requested earlier recovery point.); Keep a scaled-down application and database running in a recovery Region, using replication as the recovery mechanism. (Warm standby adds running infrastructure but does not by itself address recovery to a point before corruption.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: backup and restore
chunks.text:
Scenario: A local ticketing company is documenting recovery of its application in another AWS Region. It accepts an RPO and RTO of several hours and wants to avoid paying for a running recovery stack. Its database and EC2-based application must both be recoverable. Which TWO actions best support a backup-and-restore plan that meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
Correct: Maintain infrastructure-as-code templates and preserve the AMIs, code, and configuration needed to redeploy. + Schedule backups at a frequency that meets the RPO and copy the needed backups to the recovery Region.
Why: The company can accept hours for both data loss and restoration, so it does not need a running DR stack. Backups copied to the recovery Region must be frequent enough for its RPO. Infrastructure-as-code templates and preserved AMIs, code, and configuration address the separate need to rebuild the application within its RTO; a live standby stack costs more, while database backups alone leave the application incomplete.
Wrong options: Keep a scaled-down application stack running in the recovery Region so it can receive traffic immediately. (A running warm standby stack adds ongoing cost that the hours-long recovery target does not require.); Store database backups, then recreate EC2 instances and application settings from memory during an outage. (Data backups alone leave the application rebuild error-prone and may cause the company to miss its RTO.); Rely only on continuous replication to a live recovery database and omit point-in-time backups. (A live replicated database adds resources and continuous replication alone can be insufficient for data-corruption recovery.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: backup and restore
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer runs a legacy application on Amazon EC2 and plans to recover in another Region. Its data backups already meet an hours-long RPO, and the business allows several hours to restore service. A recovery exercise showed that rebuilding servers and network settings manually took too long. Which change BEST supports the RTO while retaining a backup-and-restore strategy?
Correct: Maintain AWS CloudFormation templates and copy the required AMIs, code, configuration, and backups to the recovery Region.
Why: The backups already satisfy the data-loss target; the failed requirement is timely reconstruction of the workload. AWS CloudFormation can define resources for reliable redeployment across Regions, while copied AMIs, code, configuration, and backups supply what must be restored. Increasing backup frequency addresses RPO instead of the observed RTO problem, and data-volume snapshots alone leave the manual rebuild in place.
Wrong options: Copy the EC2 data-volume snapshots to the recovery Region and recreate instance configuration manually. (Copying data-volume snapshots still leaves the slow, error-prone configuration work identified in the exercise.); Keep a scaled-down, functional application environment running in the recovery Region. (Warm standby can shorten recovery, but it abandons the requested backup-and-restore approach and adds running resources.); Increase the frequency of data backups but continue rebuilding the application environment manually. (More frequent backups improve the recovery point but do not fix the slow infrastructure rebuild.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: multi-site active-active
chunks.text:
DR strategy: multi-site active-active. Multi-site active-active runs a workload in multiple AWS Regions and serves users from each of them. Choose it when continued service after a Region loss and recovery time near zero justify the highest cost and complexity of the DR strategies described.
When to use: Users must normally be served from multiple Regions, not just switch to a recovery Region during an outage.; The remaining Region or Regions must be ready to handle traffic when one Region is lost.; The business accepts greater cost and complexity to minimize recovery time.
Key facts: Unlike active/passive strategies, every deployed Region serves traffic during normal operation.; With appropriate technology and implementation, recovery time can be near zero for most disasters; it is not a guarantee of zero data loss.; Testing should verify that traffic moves away from a lost Region and that the remaining Regions can handle the load.; Backups and recovery testing are still necessary: corruption or deletion of data can require a non-zero recovery point.; Amazon Route 53 can route to regional endpoints and use health checks to send traffic only to healthy endpoints; DynamoDB global tables provide continuous, cross-Region asynchronous data replication.
Gotchas: A fully provisioned secondary Region that receives no normal traffic is hot standby, not multi-site active-active.; A scaled-down, running recovery stack is warm standby; needing to scale it up adds a recovery dependency.; Replicating data across Regions does not, by itself, make the application active-active.; Active-active does not replace point-in-time backups for data corruption or deletion.
Confused with: Warm standby: Its scaled-down recovery stack is running, but normal traffic goes to the primary Region and the recovery stack must scale up.; Pilot light: Core data and infrastructure are available, but application resources must be switched on before they can process requests.; Backup and restore: The recovery environment must be restored or redeployed rather than already serving users.
ES: Multi-site active-active ejecuta una carga de trabajo en varias AWS Regions y atiende usuarios desde cada una. Elígelo cuando mantener el servicio ante la pérdida de una Region y lograr un tiempo de recuperación cercano a cero justifique el mayor costo y complejidad de las estrategias de DR descritas. A diferencia de las estrategias active/passive, cada Region desplegada atiende tráfico durante la operación normal.; Con la tecnología y la implementación adecuadas, el tiempo de recuperación puede ser cercano a cero para la mayoría de los desastres; esto no garantiza cero pérdida de datos.; Las pruebas deben verificar que el tráfico deje de ir a una Region caída y que las demás puedan soportar la carga.; Todavía necesitas respaldos y pruebas de recuperación: la corrupción o eliminación de datos puede exigir un punto de recuperación distinto de cero.; Amazon Route 53 puede dirigir tráfico a endpoints regionales y usar health checks para enviarlo solo a endpoints saludables; DynamoDB global tables ofrece replicación continua y asíncrona entre Regions.

chunks.title: DR strategy: multi-site active-active
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research platform serves users from two Regions at the same time and has enough application capacity in either Region to continue serving them if the other is lost. Its operators now worry that an accidental deletion of shared data could affect what users see in both Regions. Which addition MOST directly addresses this remaining DR risk?
Correct: Keep point-in-time data backups and regularly test recovery from them.
Why: The platform already addresses regional application availability; the stated gap is accidental data deletion. AWS guidance says backups and recovery testing remain necessary with multi-site active-active, because a data disaster can require restoring an earlier point. More regional capacity does not recover deleted data, and continuous replication alone may not protect against deletion.
Wrong options: Add more application capacity in both Regions to increase tolerance of regional traffic shifts. (Application capacity addresses a Region loss, not recovery of deleted data.); Move normal traffic to one Region and reserve the other as a scaled-down warm standby. (Changing traffic to active/passive does not provide a recoverable version of accidentally deleted data.); Use continuous cross-Region replication as the sole data recovery mechanism. (Continuous replication alone may not protect against data deletion or corruption.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: multi-site active-active
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company is redesigning its application after a regional outage. Customers must be able to use the application in either of two Regions during normal operations, and losing one Region must not require starting application servers in the other. The company accepts higher ongoing costs to minimize recovery time. Which DR strategy meets these requirements?
Correct: Run the application in both Regions and direct customer traffic to both during normal operations.
Why: The deciding requirement is that both Regions serve customers before an outage. Multi-site active-active does that and can reduce recovery time to near zero for most disasters when implemented appropriately. Warm standby is already running, but it is scaled down and receives traffic only after recovery is initiated.
Wrong options: Keep cross-Region backups and redeploy the application in the recovery Region after an outage. (Backup and restore requires recovery-time deployment and does not serve customers from both Regions normally.); Replicate data to the second Region and provision its application servers only after an outage. (Pilot light must switch on application resources and does not serve customers from both Regions normally.); Run a scaled-down application in the second Region and send it traffic only after an outage. (Warm standby keeps a functional recovery stack but does not serve normal traffic from both Regions.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: multi-site active-active
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher operates a global article service from two Regions. It wants readers to reach the application in both Regions on ordinary days, while traffic to an unhealthy regional endpoint should stop if that Region fails. Article metadata is stored in DynamoDB, and the team accepts asynchronous cross-Region replication. Which design best meets these requirements?
Correct: Run the application in both Regions, use DynamoDB global tables, and configure Amazon Route 53 health checks for the regional endpoints.
Why: Normal traffic must reach both Regions, so the application must be active in each. DynamoDB global tables supplies continuous, asynchronous cross-Region replication, while Route 53 health checks can keep traffic away from unhealthy endpoints. A global table alone is insufficient if the second Region's application servers are not running.
Wrong options: Run the application in one Region, use DynamoDB global tables, and deploy application servers in the other Region during recovery. (Replicated data does not let readers use the second Region's application on ordinary days.); Copy DynamoDB backups to the second Region and restore the application there when the first Region fails. (Restoration after failure cannot satisfy the requirement to serve readers from both Regions ordinarily.); Run a scaled-down application in the second Region and configure Amazon Route 53 to send it traffic only when the primary Region fails. (This active/passive routing prevents both Regions from serving readers during normal operations.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: pilot light
chunks.text:
DR strategy: pilot light. Pilot light keeps replicated data and core recovery resources available in a second Region while leaving application-serving resources undeployed until failover. Choose it when the business needs a lower RPO than periodic backups offer, can allow time to provision compute, and wants to avoid running a functional standby application.
When to use: A regional outage is in scope, and data should already be replicated to the recovery Region.; The application can wait for servers to be deployed and scaled before serving traffic after failover.; Ongoing cost matters more than having a reduced-capacity application ready to accept requests immediately.
Key facts: Resources that support replication and backup, such as databases, remain on; application servers can remain undeployed until testing or failover.; Amazon RDS read replicas provide continuous cross-Region asynchronous replication. A read replica must be promoted to serve a read/write workload after failover.; AWS CloudFormation can define recovery infrastructure for consistent deployment across Regions; AMIs can be copied to the recovery Region for EC2 launches.; Pilot light cannot process application requests without first turning on servers and potentially deploying other non-core resources.; Continuous replication alone might replicate corruption or deletion; point-in-time backups provide a separate recovery option.
Gotchas: A recovery copy that can already handle requests at reduced capacity is warm standby, not pilot light.; Keeping only restorable backups in the second Region is backup and restore, even if deployment templates are ready.; An RDS read replica does not become the read/write primary merely because application servers are launched.
Confused with: Backup and restore: Recovery data remains in backups that must be restored; pilot light maintains replicated, live core data resources.; Warm standby: Warm standby can handle requests immediately at reduced capacity; pilot light must first turn on application resources.; Multi-site active/active: Active/active serves traffic from multiple Regions simultaneously; pilot light's recovery Region does not serve traffic before failover.
ES: Pilot light mantiene datos replicados y recursos centrales de recuperación disponibles en otra Región, pero deja sin desplegar los recursos que atienden solicitudes hasta el failover. Elígelo cuando se necesita un RPO menor que el de los respaldos periódicos, hay tiempo para aprovisionar cómputo y no se quiere mantener una aplicación de reserva funcional. Los recursos que respaldan la replicación y los respaldos, como las bases de datos, permanecen activos; los servidores de aplicación pueden quedar sin desplegar hasta una prueba o un failover.; Las réplicas de lectura de Amazon RDS proporcionan replicación asíncrona continua entre Regiones. Debes promover una réplica para atender una carga de lectura y escritura después del failover.; AWS CloudFormation permite definir la infraestructura de recuperación para desplegarla de forma consistente entre Regiones; puedes copiar las AMI a la Región de recuperación para lanzar EC2.; Pilot light no puede procesar solicitudes de la aplicación sin activar antes los servidores y, posiblemente, desplegar otros recursos no centrales.; La replicación continua por sí sola podría propagar corrupción o eliminaciones; los respaldos de un momento específico ofrecen otra opción de recuperación.

chunks.title: DR strategy: pilot light
chunks.text:
Scenario: A medical scheduling company uses a pilot light in another Region: its RDS data is replicated continuously, and its EC2 application servers are launched only for recovery. The company also needs a way to recover an earlier, uncorrupted version of its records if an accidental change is replicated. Which addition meets this requirement while preserving its pilot-light approach?
Correct: Add point-in-time backups of the replicated data in the recovery Region.
Why: The company needs both its existing live replication and a recovery point from before an accidental change. Continuous replication can carry corruption or deletion to the recovery Region, so add point-in-time backups of the replicated data there. Another replica has the same exposure, and switching to snapshot-only recovery would discard the pilot-light arrangement.
Wrong options: Add a running EC2 application tier in the recovery Region so staff can inspect replicated records continuously. (Running an application tier changes the standby posture but does not provide an earlier version of corrupted records.); Add another cross-Region RDS read replica that receives the same continuous changes. (A second continuously replicated copy does not by itself provide a point before the accidental change.); Replace continuous replication with periodic RDS snapshot copies to the recovery Region. (Replacing the live replica abandons the stated pilot-light data arrangement rather than adding corruption protection to it.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: pilot light
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional museum runs its ticketing application on Amazon EC2 with an Amazon RDS database. It wants changes replicated to a second Region and can allow time to launch application servers after a regional outage. The recovery Region must not run a ticketing application during normal operations. Which DR design meets these requirements with the LOWEST ongoing compute cost?
Correct: Maintain a cross-Region RDS read replica and recovery infrastructure definitions; launch EC2 application servers and promote the replica during failover.
Why: The deciding constraints are replicated changes, no running recovery application, and time to launch servers after an outage. Pilot light keeps the data resource available while leaving application compute off until failover; the RDS replica must then be promoted for writes. Snapshot restoration does not provide the requested live replicated database, while warm standby and active/active keep application compute running.
Wrong options: Run the ticketing application in both Regions and distribute customer requests between them. (Serving requests from both Regions violates the passive-recovery requirement and runs additional application compute.); Copy RDS snapshots to the recovery Region and restore the database and EC2 application during failover. (Snapshots require a database restore rather than keeping changes replicated to a live recovery database.); Maintain a cross-Region RDS read replica and a running, reduced-capacity EC2 application that can receive requests. (A running recovery application violates the requirement not to operate one during normal conditions and adds ongoing compute cost.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: pilot light
chunks.text:
Scenario: A small publisher is replacing a DR plan that restores its database from backups after a regional outage. It now requires continuously replicated data but accepts that its website will be unavailable while application servers are deployed in the recovery Region. It wants to avoid operating a request-serving website there before an outage. Which strategy is MOST cost-effective for these requirements?
Correct: Pilot light, with replicated data available and website servers deployed during failover.
Why: The publisher requires continuous data replication but explicitly allows a delay to deploy its website. Pilot light fits that combination by keeping core data resources available and turning on application resources for recovery. Backup and restore lacks the requested live replica; warm standby and active/active operate a website in the second Region before an outage.
Wrong options: Multi-site active/active, with the website serving visitors from both Regions. (Serving visitors from both Regions runs an additional website before an outage and adds unnecessary complexity.); Warm standby, with a reduced-capacity website running in the recovery Region. (A warm standby website can already serve requests, contrary to the requirement not to operate one before an outage.); Backup and restore, with periodic database backups copied to the recovery Region. (Periodic backups do not meet the requirement for continuously replicated data.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: warm standby
chunks.text:
DR strategy: warm standby. Warm standby keeps a scaled-down but fully functional copy of a workload running in a DR Region. Choose it when the recovery site must accept traffic immediately at reduced capacity, then scale up after failover.
When to use: A regional outage is in scope, and the DR site must already be able to process requests.; The business can pay for a small running environment but not full production capacity in both Regions.; Recovery can begin at reduced capacity while the DR Region scales out.
Key facts: Warm standby is active/passive: the DR workload is running, but normal traffic goes to the primary Region.; Unlike pilot light, warm standby can handle traffic at reduced capacity without first turning on application servers.; Amazon Route 53 health checks can support DNS failover to a healthy recovery endpoint.; Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can increase the DR Auto Scaling group's desired capacity; DR Region service quotas must permit the increase.; Scaling up depends on a control plane operation, so keep enough initial capacity running to handle the traffic expected at failover.
Gotchas: A replicated database alone does not make a functional warm standby application.; Warm standby does not mean both Regions serve users during normal operation.; Do not assume the DR site can handle full production traffic before scaling finishes.; Continuous replication does not replace point-in-time protection against data corruption or deletion.
Confused with: Pilot light: Its application servers must be turned on or deployed before the DR site can process requests; warm standby can process requests immediately at reduced capacity.; Backup and restore: Backups must be restored and the workload redeployed, rather than failing over to an already running application.; Multi-site active/active: Multiple Regions serve traffic simultaneously; warm standby normally serves traffic from only the primary Region.
ES: Warm standby mantiene una copia reducida, pero completamente funcional, de la carga de trabajo en una Región de DR. Elígela cuando el sitio de recuperación deba aceptar tráfico de inmediato con capacidad limitada y escalar después del failover. Warm standby es active/passive: la carga de DR está en ejecución, pero el tráfico normal va a la Región principal.; A diferencia de pilot light, warm standby puede atender tráfico con capacidad limitada sin encender primero los servidores de aplicaciones.; Los health checks de Amazon Route 53 pueden facilitar el DNS failover hacia un endpoint de recuperación saludable.; Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling puede aumentar la desired capacity del Auto Scaling group de DR; las service quotas de la Región de DR deben permitirlo.; Escalar depende de una operación de control plane, así que mantén capacidad inicial suficiente para el tráfico esperado al hacer failover.

chunks.title: DR strategy: warm standby
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional grocery platform replicates its application data into a second AWS Region. Its DR plan currently keeps the database available there but deploys web servers only after an incident; a test showed that deployment delays its first customer response. The platform can afford a small running web tier but not a second full-size site. Which change BEST addresses the test result?
Correct: Keep a smaller web tier running in the DR Region and scale it out when traffic moves there.
Why: The test identified a delay before the DR site can process its first request. Keeping a small but functional web tier running converts the design from pilot light to warm standby, so initial traffic can be handled before scale-out completes. Automating web-server deployment still leaves a period when the site cannot process requests. Full-capacity active/active would exceed the stated spending constraint.
Wrong options: Run both Regions at full capacity and direct grocery customers to both during normal operation. (Multi-site active/active conflicts with the stated limit on paying for a second full-size site.); Retain only cross-Region backups and restore the database and web tier during an outage. (Restoring and redeploying adds work before the first request can be handled.); Keep the web servers undeployed but automate their launch during a regional outage. (Automation may shorten deployment, but the site still cannot serve requests until the servers are launched.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: warm standby
chunks.text:
Scenario: A digital publisher serves readers from one AWS Region and needs a DR Region that can take initial requests immediately after a regional failure. Its team will pay for a small running copy, but not full capacity in both Regions, and plans to expand the copy after failover. Which TWO design choices support this plan MOST directly? (Choose two.)
Correct: Prepare an EC2 Auto Scaling group to increase DR capacity after failover. + Keep the complete application running at reduced capacity in the DR Region.
Why: The publisher needs a working DR application before a failure and more capacity after traffic moves. A reduced-capacity running copy satisfies the immediate-request requirement, and an EC2 Auto Scaling group supports subsequent scale-out. Deploying application servers during the incident is pilot light, which cannot process requests without that additional action. Full-capacity active/active conflicts with the stated spending limit.
Wrong options: Maintain only cross-Region backups and restore the workload after traffic switches. (Backups alone do not provide an application that can accept initial requests.); Keep the DR database running but deploy application servers when an outage occurs. (Application servers deployed only after an outage cannot handle the required initial requests immediately.); Serve normal reader traffic from full-capacity stacks in both Regions. (Full-capacity multi-site active/active does not meet the publisher's cost constraint.)

chunks.title: DR strategy: warm standby
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum runs its reservations application in one Region and keeps a smaller, functioning copy in a second Region. During a primary Region outage, the operations team wants to trigger a reviewed failover decision, route visitors to the copy without depending on a DNS configuration change, and then expand its EC2 capacity. Which approach meets these requirements MOST reliably?
Correct: Use Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) routing controls to switch Route 53 traffic after approval, then increase the recovery Auto Scaling group's desired capacity.
Why: The team needs a manual failover trigger without changing DNS routing configuration during the event. ARC routing controls can act as switches for Route 53 health checks through a data plane API, directing traffic to the already functioning standby. The recovery Auto Scaling group can then increase capacity. Editing Route 53 routing weights instead is a control plane operation and is less resilient as a failover dependency.
Wrong options: Configure automatic Route 53 DNS failover based on endpoint health checks, then scale the recovery application. (Automatic failover bypasses the team's requirement for a reviewed, manually triggered decision.); Restore backups into the second Region after approval, then change the primary application's DNS record. (Backup restoration discards the advantage of the already functioning recovery copy and delays traffic acceptance.); Change Amazon Route 53 weighted-routing values after approval, then increase the recovery Auto Scaling group's desired capacity. (Changing routing weights is a Route 53 control plane operation, contrary to the requested failover behavior.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB on-demand backups and point-in-time recovery
chunks.text:
DynamoDB on-demand backups and point-in-time recovery. DynamoDB point-in-time recovery (PITR) continuously backs up a table so you can restore it to a specific second within its configured recovery period, up to 35 days. Choose it for accidental writes or deletes; choose an on-demand backup when you need a snapshot to retain beyond that period.
When to use: A bad write or delete requires recovery to a specific time rather than to a scheduled snapshot.; One DynamoDB table needs continuous, fully managed backups.; A table needs a long-term snapshot for retention or archiving.
Key facts: PITR provides recovery points at per-second granularity for a configurable period of 1–35 days; the default is 35 days.; After PITR is enabled, you can restore to a time from five minutes before the present back through the configured recovery period.; PITR restores data to a new DynamoDB table, not over the source table.; Disabling and re-enabling PITR resets the start of the table's recoverable period.; An on-demand backup is a snapshot of the entire table at backup time and can be used for long-term retention.
Gotchas: A daily snapshot cannot restore the table to an arbitrary second between snapshots.; PITR does not provide recovery points older than its configured period or from before it was re-enabled.; Tags are not preserved on restored tables; add them before relying on tag-based policy conditions.
Confused with: aws-backup: AWS Backup can create and manage DynamoDB on-demand backups; DynamoDB PITR is the table-level continuous backup feature for per-second recovery.; rds-backups-pitr: RDS automated backups apply to RDS databases, not DynamoDB tables.; ebs-snapshots-dlm: EBS snapshot schedules protect EBS volumes, not DynamoDB tables.
ES: DynamoDB point-in-time recovery (PITR) respalda continuamente una tabla para que puedas restaurarla a un segundo específico dentro del período configurado, de hasta 35 días. Elígelo ante escrituras o eliminaciones accidentales; elige un on-demand backup si necesitas conservar una instantánea más allá de ese período. PITR ofrece puntos de recuperación con granularidad de un segundo durante un período configurable de 1 a 35 días; el valor predeterminado es 35 días.; Después de habilitar PITR, puedes restaurar desde cinco minutos antes del momento actual hasta el límite del período configurado.; PITR restaura los datos en una tabla nueva de DynamoDB; no sobrescribe la tabla de origen.; Deshabilitar y volver a habilitar PITR reinicia el comienzo del período recuperable de la tabla.; Un on-demand backup captura toda la tabla en el momento del respaldo y puede conservarse a largo plazo.

chunks.title: DynamoDB on-demand backups and point-in-time recovery
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company stores reservations in a DynamoDB table. A deployment script occasionally overwrites valid reservations, and operators must recover the table to a moment just before a bad run, which may occur between scheduled backups. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable DynamoDB PITR on the table and restore to a time before the bad run.
Why: The deciding requirement is recovery to a moment just before an unpredictable bad write. DynamoDB PITR continuously creates recovery points at per-second granularity and requires no on-demand backup schedule. Nightly on-demand backups and daily AWS Backup backups capture scheduled states, so either could miss the required moment.
Wrong options: Schedule daily EBS snapshots with Data Lifecycle Manager and restore the latest snapshot. (EBS snapshots protect EBS volumes rather than the DynamoDB table.); Schedule a daily DynamoDB backup using AWS Backup and restore the latest backup. (A daily scheduled backup cannot guarantee recovery to a moment between backups.); Create a DynamoDB on-demand backup every night and restore the latest backup after a bad run. (A nightly snapshot might not represent the table immediately before a bad run.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB on-demand backups and point-in-time recovery
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research team disabled PITR on a DynamoDB table last week and re-enabled it this morning. Investigators now need the table's state from a checkpoint taken three days ago, and an on-demand backup was created at that checkpoint. Which solution can recover the requested state?
Correct: Restore the on-demand backup created at the checkpoint to a new table.
Why: Disabling and re-enabling DynamoDB PITR resets the start of the recoverable period. Changing its configured length or waiting cannot make the three-day-old checkpoint recoverable through the newly enabled PITR. The on-demand backup taken at the checkpoint already contains the requested table state and can be restored.
Wrong options: Wait until PITR has been enabled for 35 days, then restore to the checkpoint time. (Waiting does not recreate recovery points from before PITR was re-enabled.); Set the PITR recovery period to 35 days and restore the table to the checkpoint time. (Increasing the period cannot recover PITR points from before PITR was re-enabled.); Create a new on-demand backup now and restore it as the checkpoint state. (A backup created now captures the current table, not its state three days ago.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned capacity (RCU/WCU)
chunks.text:
DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned capacity (RCU/WCU). DynamoDB on-demand manages throughput automatically and charges per read and write request, making it a strong choice when traffic is unpredictable. Provisioned mode charges for configured read and write capacity and fits workloads whose demand can be forecast; auto scaling can adjust that capacity within configured limits.
When to use: Choose on-demand when request rates are unpredictable or capacity planning and scaling policies would add unwanted work.; Choose provisioned when traffic is steady enough to forecast and controlling configured capacity is important.; Use provisioned auto scaling when a predictable workload changes over time and capacity should adjust within defined bounds.
Key facts: On-demand is the default throughput mode; it does not require specifying expected read or write throughput.; Provisioned mode is billed for hourly configured capacity, even when some of that capacity is unused.; For items up to 4 KB, one RCU supports one strongly consistent read or two eventually consistent reads per second.; One WCU supports one write per second for an item up to 1 KB; larger items require more capacity units.; Provisioned auto scaling uses minimum and maximum capacity settings and a target utilization percentage. Its alarms can take a few minutes to trigger scaling.
Gotchas: Auto scaling does not turn provisioned mode into pay-per-request billing.; Do not assume provisioned auto scaling reacts instantly to an unanticipated spike.; Capacity-unit calculations depend on item size and, for reads, consistency.
Confused with: 
ES: DynamoDB on-demand administra el throughput automáticamente y cobra por solicitud de lectura y escritura, por lo que conviene cuando el tráfico es impredecible. Provisioned mode cobra por la capacidad de lectura y escritura configurada y se adapta a cargas que puedes prever; auto scaling puede ajustar esa capacidad dentro de los límites configurados. On-demand es el modo de throughput predeterminado; no exige especificar el throughput esperado de lectura o escritura.; Provisioned mode se cobra según la capacidad configurada por hora, aunque no se utilice por completo.; Para elementos de hasta 4 KB, una RCU permite una lectura strongly consistent o dos lecturas eventually consistent por segundo.; Una WCU permite una escritura por segundo de un elemento de hasta 1 KB; los elementos más grandes requieren más unidades de capacidad.; Provisioned auto scaling usa valores mínimos y máximos de capacidad y un porcentaje objetivo de utilización. Sus alarmas pueden tardar unos minutos en activar el escalado.

chunks.title: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned capacity (RCU/WCU)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company stores reservation status in a DynamoDB table. Most days have few requests, but newly announced events cause unpredictable bursts, and the team does not want to plan throughput or maintain scaling policies. Which capacity mode meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use on-demand mode and let DynamoDB manage throughput.
Why: The deciding requirements are unpredictable bursts and no capacity planning or scaling policies. On-demand manages throughput automatically without requiring the team to specify expected read and write rates. Provisioned auto scaling can adjust capacity, but it still requires configuration and its alarms can take time to trigger.
Wrong options: Use provisioned mode with a fixed capacity based on a typical day. (Typical-day capacity does not address the unpredictable bursts.); Use provisioned mode and manually increase capacity when an event is announced. (Manual changes add operational work and cannot reliably anticipate every burst.); Use provisioned mode with auto scaling and a target utilization setting. (Auto scaling still requires a scaling policy and configured capacity bounds.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned capacity (RCU/WCU)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company uses a DynamoDB table for package scans. Its request volume follows a well-understood daily schedule, with gradual increases during business hours, and the company can forecast its capacity needs. It wants to adjust configured throughput as traffic changes instead of keeping peak capacity configured all day. Which approach best meets these requirements?
Correct: Use provisioned mode with auto scaling and configured capacity bounds.
Why: The company can forecast demand, making provisioned capacity suitable. Auto scaling adjusts configured throughput within minimum and maximum settings as traffic changes, avoiding a fixed peak setting throughout the day. On-demand does not use provisioned capacity bounds, while a fixed peak allocation leaves capacity configured during quieter periods.
Wrong options: Use provisioned mode and keep a fixed capacity sized for the daily peak.
