(Peak-sized fixed capacity remains configured during quieter hours.); Use on-demand mode and set minimum and maximum capacity units. (Minimum and maximum capacity-unit settings apply to provisioned auto scaling, not on-demand mode.); Use provisioned mode and manually update capacity whenever traffic changes. (Manual updates do not meet the goal of adjusting throughput as traffic changes without repeated intervention.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned capacity (RCU/WCU)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company operates two independent DynamoDB tables. The campaign table receives unpredictable bursts after creators publish links, while the internal reporting table has stable, forecastable traffic with gradual growth. The team wants to avoid throughput planning for campaigns but manage configured capacity for reporting. Which TWO choices meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Set the campaign table to on-demand mode. + Set the reporting table to provisioned mode with auto scaling.
Why: These tables have different access patterns, so they need not share a throughput mode. On-demand avoids planning capacity for unpredictable campaign bursts. Provisioned auto scaling lets the team manage configured capacity for the forecastable reporting workload while adjusting it as traffic changes. On-demand does not accept a provisioned RCU target, and leaving current provisioned capacity unchanged does not address growth.
Wrong options: Set the reporting table to on-demand mode and define an RCU target. (An RCU capacity target is not how on-demand throughput is configured.); Set the campaign table to provisioned mode at its usual request rate. (Usual-rate capacity does not account for unpredictable campaign bursts.); Set the reporting table to fixed provisioned capacity sized for its current traffic indefinitely. (An unchanged current-traffic setting does not accommodate the stated gradual growth.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
chunks.text:
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX). DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a managed, DynamoDB-compatible in-memory cache that can deliver microsecond responses for eventually consistent reads. Choose it when an existing DynamoDB application repeatedly reads the same items and needs faster reads or less load on the table with minimal application changes.
When to use: A read-heavy DynamoDB application repeatedly accesses the same keys.; Bursts of reads against hot items could otherwise require more provisioned read capacity.; The application accepts eventually consistent reads and needs microsecond latency.
Key facts: DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB and requires minimal functional changes to an existing application.; DAX can reduce eventually consistent read latency from single-digit milliseconds to microseconds.; Offloading repeated reads can reduce the need to overprovision DynamoDB read capacity units.; DAX performs best when cache hit rates exceed 90%.; DAX supports encryption at rest and TLS encryption in transit.
Gotchas: Do not choose DAX when reads must be strongly consistent.; Write-intensive workloads and workloads with few repeated reads are poor DAX fits.; DAX is a DynamoDB-specific cache, not a substitute for Redis/Valkey features such as pub/sub or sorted sets.
Confused with: ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey: Choose Redis/Valkey for needs such as pub/sub or sorted sets; choose DAX for DynamoDB-compatible caching of repeated, eventually consistent reads.; ElastiCache for Memcached: Memcached is a general-purpose simple cache; DAX is DynamoDB-compatible and needs minimal functional changes to an existing DynamoDB application.
ES: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) es un caché administrado en memoria, compatible con DynamoDB, que puede ofrecer respuestas en microsegundos para lecturas con consistencia eventual. Elígelo cuando tu aplicación DynamoDB lee repetidamente los mismos elementos y necesita lecturas más rápidas o menos carga en la tabla con cambios mínimos. DAX es compatible con la API de DynamoDB y requiere cambios funcionales mínimos en una aplicación existente.; DAX puede reducir la latencia de lecturas con consistencia eventual de milisegundos de un solo dígito a microsegundos.; Desviar lecturas repetidas al caché puede reducir la necesidad de aprovisionar capacidad de lectura adicional en DynamoDB.; DAX funciona mejor cuando la tasa de aciertos del caché supera el 90%.; DAX admite cifrado en reposo y cifrado en tránsito mediante TLS.

chunks.title: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company stores event availability in DynamoDB. During ticket releases, customers repeatedly request the same popular event records; the application accepts eventually consistent reads but needs microsecond responses. The team wants to change as little application functionality as possible. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Add a DAX cluster and use a DAX client for the event-record reads.
Why: The deciding constraints are microsecond reads of repeatedly accessed DynamoDB items and minimal application changes. DAX is a managed, DynamoDB-compatible cache for eventually consistent reads and can offload reads of hot keys. Redis/Valkey and Memcached would require the team to implement cache behavior in the application. Increasing read capacity addresses throughput rather than the requested read latency.
Wrong options: Place ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey in front of DynamoDB and implement application-managed cache lookups. (It introduces application-managed caching rather than using the DynamoDB-compatible cache that requires minimal functional changes.); Increase DynamoDB provisioned read capacity for ticket-release periods. (Additional read capacity does not address the stated need for microsecond read responses.); Add ElastiCache for Memcached and implement cache population for each event record. (This requires application-managed cache behavior instead of the minimal functional changes supported by DAX.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company keeps article metadata in DynamoDB. Its home page repeatedly reads a small set of featured articles, and editors accept eventually consistent results; the home page needs microsecond read responses. Security policy also requires encryption for traffic to the cache and for data the cache persists to disk. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST application change?
Correct: Use DAX with encryption in transit and encryption at rest enabled.
Why: Repeated reads of a few DynamoDB items with acceptable eventual consistency are a good fit for DAX's microsecond in-memory reads. DAX is DynamoDB-compatible, so adopting it requires minimal functional changes. It also supports TLS encryption in transit and encryption of data it persists to disk. Increasing read capacity does not target microsecond latency, while the other caches call for application-managed integration.
Wrong options: Use ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey and add application-managed metadata caching. (This requires application-managed cache integration instead of DAX's DynamoDB-compatible integration.); Use ElastiCache for Memcached and add application-managed metadata caching. (Application-managed caching misses the requirement for minimal application change.); Increase DynamoDB read capacity and keep the existing read path. (More read capacity does not provide the requested microsecond cache responses.)

chunks.title: Amazon DynamoDB fundamentals: keys, items, access patterns
chunks.text:
Amazon DynamoDB fundamentals: keys, items, access patterns. Amazon DynamoDB is a serverless, fully managed NoSQL database for key-value and document workloads that need consistent single-digit millisecond performance at scale. Choose it when the application can access data efficiently by key without relational JOINs.
When to use: The workload needs fast lookups of sessions, carts, or other items by a known key.; Traffic is unpredictable and the team wants to avoid database servers and capacity planning.; The application can design keys around its access patterns and denormalize data instead of using JOINs.
Key facts: DynamoDB supports key-value and document data models, but not a JOIN operator.; On-demand capacity charges for read and write requests and scales with traffic, including down to zero throughput when idle.; Secondary indexes support queries using alternate keys.; The maximum item size is 400 KB; store larger images in Amazon S3 and keep an object pointer in DynamoDB.; Time to Live (TTL) automatically deletes expired items without consuming write throughput.
Gotchas: Serverless scaling does not replace designing a partition key that spreads access across items.; Document data does not, by itself, mean the application needs MongoDB compatibility.; DynamoDB supports ACID transactions; a requirement for coordinated item changes does not automatically require a relational database.
Confused with: Amazon RDS: Choose RDS for a managed relational engine; choose DynamoDB for key-based NoSQL access without JOINs.; Amazon DocumentDB: DocumentDB is the MongoDB-compatible choice; DynamoDB supports document data without requiring MongoDB compatibility.; Amazon Aurora: Aurora is MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible; DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL database for key-based access.
ES: Amazon DynamoDB es una base de datos NoSQL serverless y completamente administrada para datos clave-valor y documentos, con rendimiento constante de milisegundos de un solo dígito a cualquier escala. Elígela cuando puedas acceder a los datos eficientemente por clave sin JOINs relacionales. DynamoDB admite modelos clave-valor y de documentos, pero no un operador JOIN.; La capacidad on-demand cobra por solicitudes de lectura y escritura y se ajusta al tráfico, incluso hasta cero rendimiento cuando no hay actividad.; Los índices secundarios permiten consultar con claves alternativas.; El tamaño máximo de un elemento es 400 KB; guarda imágenes más grandes en Amazon S3 y una referencia al objeto en DynamoDB.; Time to Live (TTL) elimina automáticamente los elementos vencidos sin consumir rendimiento de escritura.

chunks.title: Amazon DynamoDB fundamentals: keys, items, access patterns
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing startup stores a small record for each visitor session. Its API retrieves sessions by session ID, and traffic jumps sharply when new events go on sale. The team does not need relational JOINs and does not want to plan database throughput. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Store sessions in a DynamoDB on-demand table with session ID as the partition key.
Why: The deciding requirements are key-based session lookups, sharp traffic changes, and no throughput planning. DynamoDB provides serverless NoSQL access with consistent single-digit millisecond performance, while its on-demand mode adjusts capacity to request traffic. A relational engine might serve the lookups, but it does not provide the same fit for this stated access pattern and operational requirement.
Wrong options: Store sessions as documents in Amazon DocumentDB and retrieve them by session ID. (The scenario calls for serverless key-value access, not MongoDB compatibility.); Store sessions in Amazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition and retrieve each row by session ID. (Aurora provides a relational, MySQL-compatible database, but the workload does not need relational features.); Store sessions in Amazon RDS for MySQL and retrieve each row by session ID. (MySQL can retrieve a session by ID, but this design introduces a relational database when the team wants to avoid database throughput planning.)

chunks.title: Amazon DynamoDB fundamentals: keys, items, access patterns
chunks.text:
Scenario: A repair company stores job records in DynamoDB and usually retrieves a job by its job ID. A new support tool must also retrieve jobs by a unique external claim ID without replacing the existing job-ID lookup. The team wants to keep one operational table. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Add a global secondary index that uses the external claim ID as its key.
Why: The existing job-ID lookup must remain, but the support tool needs a second lookup key. DynamoDB secondary indexes allow queries using an alternate key without replacing the table's primary key. A separate RDS mapping adds a database, and a DynamoDB JOIN is not available.
Wrong options: Replace the table's job-ID key with the external claim ID. (Replacing the key would sacrifice the required job-ID lookup.); Add a JOIN between the DynamoDB job records and their external claim IDs. (DynamoDB does not support a JOIN operator.); Copy claim mappings into an Amazon RDS table and query it before reading DynamoDB. (A separate relational table adds an operational data store when a DynamoDB secondary index can provide the alternate lookup.)

chunks.title: Amazon DynamoDB fundamentals: keys, items, access patterns
chunks.text:
Scenario: A travel app stores temporary itinerary drafts by draft ID in DynamoDB. Draft requests are unpredictable, and each draft has a known expiration timestamp after which it no longer needs to be stored. The team wants to avoid both throughput planning and a scheduled cleanup application. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use DynamoDB on-demand and set a Time to Live (TTL) timestamp on each draft.
Why: This workload combines unpredictable requests with items that become unnecessary after a known time. DynamoDB on-demand avoids throughput planning, and TTL automatically deletes expired items to reduce storage usage without consuming write throughput. Standard-IA alone does not expire items, while a scheduled cleanup application adds operational work.
Wrong options: Use a DynamoDB Standard-IA table and retain drafts until users delete them. (Changing the table class does not remove drafts automatically after their expiration timestamps.); Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) with a DynamoDB table and retain drafts indefinitely. (DAX is a cache and does not meet the requirement to remove expired drafts from the table.); Use DynamoDB on-demand and run a scheduled application to delete expired drafts. (On-demand addresses variable traffic, but scheduled cleanup adds the operation the team wants to avoid.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB global tables
chunks.text:
DynamoDB global tables. DynamoDB global tables replicate a table across Regions so each replica can serve local reads and writes. Choose them when a NoSQL application needs multi-Region, multi-active access and the ability to shift traffic after a Region interruption.
When to use: Users in multiple Regions need fast local reads and writes to the same DynamoDB dataset.; The application must keep serving reads and writes from another Region if processing stops in one Region.; Separate AWS accounts need to own local replicas while sharing a replication group.
Key facts: Global tables are fully managed and automatically replicate DynamoDB data across Regions.; Any replica can serve reads and writes.; The default consistency mode is multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC); multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC) is also supported.; A table cannot mix consistency modes across replicas or change its mode after creation.; MRSC supports same-account global tables only.
Gotchas: A cross-Region replica intended only for reads does not satisfy a requirement for writes in every Region.; Do not assume the default MREC mode provides multi-Region strong consistency.; Choose the account model deliberately: MRSC cannot be used with multi-account global tables.
Confused with: Aurora Global Database: Choose global tables for multi-active writes to a DynamoDB dataset, not for a global relational database.; RDS Multi-AZ: Same-Region database availability does not provide local read and write replicas across Regions.; RDS read replicas: A read-focused replica does not meet a requirement for active writes in each Region.
ES: DynamoDB global tables replica una tabla entre Regions para que cada réplica atienda lecturas y escrituras locales. Elígelo cuando una aplicación NoSQL necesite acceso multi-Region y multi-active, además de poder desviar el tráfico si se interrumpe una Region. Global tables es una característica completamente administrada que replica automáticamente datos de DynamoDB entre Regions.; Cualquier réplica puede atender lecturas y escrituras.; El modo de consistencia predeterminado es multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC); también existe multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC).; No puedes combinar modos de consistencia entre las réplicas de una tabla ni cambiar el modo después de crearla.; MRSC solo admite global tables dentro de una misma cuenta.

chunks.title: DynamoDB global tables
chunks.text:
Scenario: A global retailer uses DynamoDB for a product-availability dataset. Regional business units operate in separate AWS accounts and require ownership of their local replicas, with distinct IAM, KMS, billing, and governance boundaries. Each unit must update the shared dataset from its own Region. Which design meets these requirements with the LEAST custom replication work?
Correct: Create a multi-account DynamoDB global table with a replica owned by each regional account.
Why: The separate account-ownership and governance boundaries determine the account model. Multi-account DynamoDB global tables allow each account to own its local replica while participating in shared replication and supporting writes across Regions. A same-account global table offers multi-Region access but misses the explicit requirement that separate accounts own their replicas.
Wrong options: Create a same-account DynamoDB global table and grant every business unit access to its regional replica. (The replicas would remain under one account rather than being owned by the separate business-unit accounts.); Create an Aurora Global Database and give each business unit access to a regional database. (This replaces the required DynamoDB dataset with a relational database design.); Place independent DynamoDB tables in the regional accounts and implement replication between them. (This retains separate ownership but requires the custom replication work the company wants to avoid.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB global tables
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization is creating a new DynamoDB table whose data must be readable and writable from two Regions. Its policy requires multi-Region strong consistency, and the organization can keep both replicas in one AWS account. Which configuration meets these requirements?
Correct: Create a same-account global table and select multi-Region strong consistency at creation.
Why: The deciding constraint is multi-Region strong consistency for a new table. DynamoDB global tables support MRSC, but only in a same-account configuration, so the organization must select that mode at creation. Leaving the mode unspecified selects MREC, and changing the mode later is not supported.
Wrong options: Create a multi-account global table and select multi-Region strong consistency. (Multi-Region strong consistency is supported only for same-account global tables.); Create a same-account global table and leave its consistency mode at the default. (The default mode is multi-Region eventual consistency, not the required strong consistency.); Create a same-account global table in the default mode and switch its mode after both replicas are active. (A global table's consistency mode cannot be changed after creation.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB global tables
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics platform keeps shipment state in DynamoDB and runs applications in two AWS Regions. Both applications must read and update shipment state locally, and the platform must be able to shift traffic to the remaining Region if processing stops in one. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements while avoiding custom table replication? (Choose two.)
Correct: Create a DynamoDB global table with a replica in each application Region. + Have each application read from and write to its local global table replica.
Why: The architecture must support writes in both Regions without application-managed replication. A global table supplies managed cross-Region replication, and each application can use its local replica for reads and writes. Sending updates to one Region misses local-write access; maintaining separate tables requires the custom replication the platform wants to avoid.
Wrong options: Use an RDS read replica in the second Region to receive that application's updates. (A read-focused replica does not meet the requirement for local updates to the DynamoDB dataset.); Keep one DynamoDB table in the first Region and route all updates there. (Updates from the second Region would not be served locally.); Keep independent regional DynamoDB tables and copy changes with application code. (Application-managed copying violates the requirement to avoid custom table replication.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB GSIs vs LSIs
chunks.text:
DynamoDB GSIs vs LSIs. DynamoDB secondary indexes support Query operations using keys other than the table’s primary key. Choose a GSI for a different partition key or an index added after table creation; choose an LSI at table creation when the partition key stays the same and a different sort key is needed.
When to use: Query items by an attribute that is not the table’s partition key: use a GSI.; Add a new query pattern to an existing table: add a GSI.; At table creation, query within one partition key by another sort key, with optional strongly consistent reads: use an LSI.
Key facts: A GSI can have a different partition key and an optional sort key; it can be added to an existing table.; An LSI uses the table’s partition key and a different sort key; it must be created with the table.; GSI queries support eventual consistency only; LSI queries can use eventual or strong consistency.; GSI queries return only projected attributes. An LSI can fetch nonprojected attributes from the base table.; For an LSI, indexed items for each partition key value must total no more than 10 GB; a GSI has no corresponding per-partition-key size restriction.
Gotchas: An LSI cannot be added to an existing table, even if the desired partition key matches.; A GSI is not an option when the index query must be strongly consistent.; Creating a GSI does not make unprojected attributes available in its query results.
Confused with: 
ES: Los secondary indexes de DynamoDB permiten consultas Query con claves distintas de la clave primaria de la tabla. Elige un GSI si necesitas otra partition key o debes agregar el índice después de crear la tabla; elige un LSI al crear la tabla si conservas la partition key y necesitas otra sort key. Un GSI puede tener otra partition key y una sort key opcional; puedes agregarlo a una tabla existente.; Un LSI conserva la partition key de la tabla y usa otra sort key; debes crearlo junto con la tabla.; Las consultas a un GSI solo admiten eventual consistency; las consultas a un LSI pueden usar eventual o strong consistency.; Una consulta a un GSI solo devuelve atributos projected. Un LSI puede obtener de la tabla atributos que no estén projected.; En un LSI, los elementos indexados por cada valor de partition key no pueden superar 10 GB en total; un GSI no tiene ese límite por valor de partition key.

chunks.title: DynamoDB GSIs vs LSIs
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company stores reservations in an existing DynamoDB table with reservationId as its partition key. Its support application must now retrieve reservations by customerEmail, which is stored on each item. The team wants to keep the table and use Query rather than Scan. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Add a GSI with customerEmail as its partition key and query the index.
Why: The deciding requirements are a new lookup by customerEmail and an existing table that the company wants to retain. A GSI can be added after table creation and can use customerEmail as its partition key for Query operations. An LSI cannot be added later and must retain the table’s partition key. Scanning fails the explicit Query requirement.
Wrong options: Add an LSI with customerEmail as its partition key and query the index. (An LSI must share the table’s partition key and cannot be added after table creation.); Scan the table with a filter on customerEmail. (A Scan does not meet the stated requirement to retrieve reservations using Query.); Create a new table keyed by customerEmail and query that table. (A second table does not meet the requirement to keep the existing table as the query solution.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB GSIs vs LSIs
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company is designing a DynamoDB table keyed by channelId and clipId. Its application must query clips for one channel ordered by publishTime; the same channel might eventually have more than 10 GB of indexed items. Eventual consistency is acceptable for these queries. Which index design meets these requirements?
Correct: Create a GSI with channelId as its partition key and publishTime as its sort key.
Why: The application needs to query by channelId and order results by publishTime, but indexed items for one channel could exceed 10 GB. A GSI can use those keys and has no per-partition-key size restriction of the kind imposed on LSIs. An LSI otherwise matches the query pattern, but its indexed items for each channelId value must total no more than 10 GB. Eventual consistency is acceptable, so the GSI’s consistency limitation does not prevent its use.
Wrong options: Create an LSI with channelId as its partition key and publishTime as its sort key. (An LSI limits indexed items for each channelId value to 10 GB.); Create an LSI with clipId as its partition key and publishTime as its sort key. (An LSI must retain channelId as its partition key.); Create a GSI with publishTime as its partition key and channelId as its sort key. (This reverses the requested access pattern, which queries items for one channel ordered by publishTime.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB Streams and event-driven processing
chunks.text:
DynamoDB Streams and event-driven processing. DynamoDB Streams records item-level changes so applications can react to table writes in near-real time. For an event-driven design with little shard-management work, enable the stream with the required record images and consume it through a Lambda event source mapping.
When to use: React to creates, updates, or deletes in a DynamoDB table.; Process changes in order for each individual item.; Trigger Lambda without writing a custom stream reader.
Key facts: Stream records are available for up to 24 hours.; StreamViewType can capture keys only, the new image, the old image, or both images.; Changes to the same item appear in modification order; there is no table-wide ordering guarantee.; A Lambda event source mapping reads shard records in sequence-number order and handles parent-before-child shard processing.
Gotchas: A record appearing once in the stream does not mean downstream processing happens exactly once.; You cannot edit StreamViewType on an existing stream; disable it and create a new stream to change the view.; A no-op PutItem or UpdateItem does not produce a stream record.
Confused with: 
ES: DynamoDB Streams registra cambios a nivel de elemento para que las aplicaciones reaccionen a las escrituras en una tabla casi en tiempo real. Para un diseño basado en eventos sin administrar shards por tu cuenta, habilita el stream con las imágenes necesarias y consúmelo mediante un event source mapping de Lambda. Los registros del stream están disponibles hasta por 24 horas.; StreamViewType puede capturar solo las claves, la imagen nueva, la imagen anterior o ambas.; Los cambios de un mismo elemento aparecen en orden; no hay garantía de orden para toda la tabla.; Un event source mapping de Lambda lee los registros de cada shard en orden de secuencia y procesa el shard padre antes que sus hijos.

chunks.title: DynamoDB Streams and event-driven processing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A clinic already has a DynamoDB stream configured with KEYS_ONLY for patient-appointment notifications. A new processor must compare appointment values before and after each change. The team wants the stream records themselves to contain both versions. What should the architect recommend?
Correct: Disable the existing stream and create a new one with NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES.
Why: The deciding requirement is that the records themselves contain both versions of an appointment. DynamoDB does not allow StreamViewType to be edited on an existing stream, so the team must disable it and create a new stream configured with NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES. Enabling another stream while the current one remains enabled is not an alternative.
Wrong options: Enable a second stream on the same table with NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES. (Enabling a stream on a table that already has one produces a ValidationException.); Keep KEYS_ONLY and have the processor read each appointment from the table after a change. (A later table read does not put the previous and current versions into the stream record.); Edit StreamViewType on the existing stream to NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES. (StreamViewType cannot be edited after the stream has been set up.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB Streams and event-driven processing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics platform writes shipment-status updates to DynamoDB. It needs to publish updates in modification order for each shipment, even as stream shards split, and its team does not want to maintain shard-discovery code. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable DynamoDB Streams and consume it using a Lambda event source mapping.
Why: The requirement is ordering for each shipment, not global ordering across the table. DynamoDB Streams preserves modification order for an individual item, while a Lambda event source mapping handles shard sequence and parent-before-child processing. A custom reader could also follow shard lineage, but it fails the stated goal of avoiding shard-discovery code.
Wrong options: Build a stream reader that discovers child shards and processes each parent before its children. (This can preserve the required ordering but requires the shard-discovery code the team wants to avoid.); Assign three custom reader processes to every stream shard to handle shard splits. (More than two simultaneous readers on a shard can cause throttling and does not remove shard-management work.); Build a stream reader that starts child shards as soon as they appear, before finishing their parents. (Processing a child before its parent conflicts with the required shard processing order.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL)
chunks.text:
DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL). DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL) marks individual items for automatic deletion using an expiration timestamp. Choose it for temporary data when deletion within a few days is acceptable, not when records must disappear at an exact deadline.
When to use: DynamoDB sessions or temporary records need per-item expiration without a cleanup job.; Expired records can remain stored briefly while DynamoDB deletes them automatically.; The initial TTL deletion should not consume write throughput in the Region where it occurs.
Key facts: Enable TTL on the table and designate an attribute containing a Number in Unix epoch seconds.; DynamoDB typically deletes expired items within a few days, not necessarily at expiration.; An expired item pending deletion can still be updated; moving its TTL timestamp into the future or removing the attribute prevents its TTL deletion.; Filter expressions can exclude expired items from Scan and Query results while deletion is pending.; With current-version global tables, TTL deletions replicate; replica Regions incur replicated write capacity usage and applicable charges.
Gotchas: A TTL value stored as a string is ignored, even if it looks like a timestamp.; TTL alone does not keep expired items out of query results immediately.; No write throughput for the initial TTL deletion does not mean free replicated deletions in global tables.
Confused with: 
ES: DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL) marca elementos individuales para su eliminación automática mediante una marca de tiempo de vencimiento. Elígelo para datos temporales cuando sea aceptable que la eliminación tarde unos días, no cuando los registros deban desaparecer en un momento exacto. Debes habilitar TTL en la tabla y designar un atributo de tipo Number con la hora Unix en segundos.; DynamoDB suele eliminar los elementos vencidos dentro de unos días, no necesariamente al vencer.; Todavía puedes actualizar un elemento vencido pendiente de eliminación; si cambias su marca TTL a una fecha futura o quitas el atributo, evitas su eliminación por TTL.; Puedes usar filter expressions para excluir elementos vencidos de los resultados de Scan y Query mientras esperan eliminación.; Con la versión actual de global tables, las eliminaciones TTL se replican; las Regiones réplica consumen capacidad de escritura replicada y generan los cargos correspondientes.

chunks.title: DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company stores short-lived checkout reservations in a DynamoDB table. Each reservation has its own expiration time, and removal within a few days is acceptable. The team wants to avoid a recurring cleanup process and avoid write throughput for the initial deletion. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable TTL and store each expiration as a Number containing Unix epoch seconds.
Why: The deciding requirements are per-item expiration, tolerance for deletion within a few days, and no recurring cleanup process. TTL automatically deletes items whose designated attribute contains a Number in Unix epoch seconds, without consuming write throughput for the initial deletion. A timestamp string is ignored by TTL, while filtering alone does not remove stored items.
Wrong options: Store numeric expiration times but leave TTL disabled and filter expired reservations from queries. (Filtering query results does not delete the stored reservations.); Enable TTL and store each expiration as a Unix epoch timestamp string. (DynamoDB ignores TTL values that are not of type Number.); Run a recurring Scan and issue DeleteItem requests for reservations past their expiration time. (A recurring deletion process adds operational work and uses writes for its deletes.)

chunks.title: DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A learning platform keeps temporary access grants in DynamoDB and has enabled TTL to remove them after expiration. A support dashboard uses Query to list grants, but an expired grant must stop appearing as soon as its expiration time passes, even if DynamoDB has not deleted it yet. The platform still wants automatic eventual cleanup. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Keep TTL enabled and add a Query filter expression that excludes grants whose expiration time has passed.
Why: TTL deletion is not immediate: expired items can remain in the table for a few days. A Query filter expression can exclude those items from dashboard results during that interval, while TTL eventually deletes them. Relying on TTL alone misses the visibility requirement, and filtering without TTL misses the cleanup requirement.
Wrong options: Keep TTL enabled and rely on DynamoDB Streams service-deletion records to suppress grants before they are deleted. (TTL deletion records enter the stream after deletion, not while an expired item is pending deletion.); Disable TTL and use only a Query filter expression to exclude grants past expiration. (The filter hides expired grants but does not provide automatic cleanup of stored items.); Keep TTL enabled and rely on TTL alone to remove grants from Query results at expiration. (An expired item can remain pending deletion for days and may still appear in Query results.)

chunks.title: EBS encryption with KMS
chunks.text:
EBS encryption with KMS. Amazon EBS encryption uses AWS KMS keys to encrypt volumes and snapshots. Enable encryption by default for future EBS resources; to replace an existing unencrypted volume, take a snapshot and create a new encrypted volume from it.
When to use: New EBS volumes must be encrypted without requiring encryption to be selected for each creation request.; An existing unencrypted EBS volume must be replaced with an encrypted one.; An unencrypted snapshot needs an encrypted copy, or a snapshot needs to be copied under a different KMS key.
Key facts: EBS encryption uses AWS KMS keys and protects data at rest and data in transit between an EC2 instance and its attached EBS storage.; Encryption by default automatically encrypts new empty volumes using the default KMS key for EBS encryption.; You cannot directly encrypt an existing unencrypted volume or snapshot.; To encrypt an unencrypted volume, create a snapshot and then create a new encrypted volume from it; to encrypt an unencrypted snapshot, create an encrypted snapshot copy.; You cannot change the KMS key associated with an existing volume or snapshot, but you can specify a different KMS key during a snapshot copy.; You cannot remove encryption from an encrypted volume or snapshot.
Gotchas: Enabling encryption by default does not retroactively encrypt existing unencrypted resources.; Creating a snapshot of an unencrypted volume is not, by itself, the step that produces an encrypted replacement volume.; Changing an existing snapshot's KMS key requires a copy; the key cannot be changed in place.
Confused with: 
ES: Amazon EBS encryption usa claves de AWS KMS para cifrar volúmenes y snapshots. Habilita encryption by default para los recursos EBS futuros; si necesitas reemplazar un volumen existente sin cifrar, crea un snapshot y, a partir de él, un volumen nuevo cifrado. EBS encryption usa claves de AWS KMS y protege los datos en reposo y en tránsito entre una instancia EC2 y su almacenamiento EBS adjunto.; Encryption by default cifra automáticamente los volúmenes vacíos nuevos con la clave predeterminada de KMS para EBS encryption.; No puedes cifrar directamente un volumen o snapshot existente sin cifrar.; Para cifrar un volumen sin cifrar, crea un snapshot y luego un volumen nuevo cifrado a partir de él; para cifrar un snapshot sin cifrar, crea una copia cifrada.; No puedes cambiar la clave de KMS asociada a un volumen o snapshot existente, pero sí puedes indicar otra clave al copiar un snapshot.; No puedes quitar el cifrado de un volumen o snapshot cifrado.

chunks.title: EBS encryption with KMS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company creates new, empty EBS volumes through several deployment workflows. The security team wants those future volumes encrypted even when a workflow does not explicitly request encryption, and it wants to avoid changing every workflow. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable EBS encryption by default for the account.
Why: The deciding requirement is to encrypt future volumes even when creation requests omit encryption settings. EBS encryption by default automatically encrypts new empty volumes using the default KMS key for EBS encryption. Setting encryption in each workflow could work, but it does not meet the stated operational-overhead constraint.
Wrong options: Add an encryption setting to each volume creation request. (This can encrypt new volumes, but it requires changes to every workflow and does not cover requests that omit the setting.); Create encrypted snapshot copies after each new volume is created. (Copying snapshots afterward does not ensure that each new volume is encrypted when created.); Specify a symmetric KMS key only when a deployment needs an encrypted volume. (Requests that do not specify encryption would still miss the requirement to encrypt future volumes automatically.)

chunks.title: EBS encryption with KMS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company has an encrypted EBS snapshot used to prepare recovery volumes. Its security policy now requires the recovery snapshot to use a different symmetric KMS key, while the original snapshot must remain available. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Copy the snapshot and specify the new KMS key for the copied snapshot.
Why: The recovery artifact must be a snapshot encrypted under a different KMS key, and the original must remain available. During a snapshot copy, a different KMS key can be associated with the resulting copy. The key on an existing snapshot cannot be changed in place, so changing the account default or editing the original does not meet the requirement.
Wrong options: Change the KMS key associated with the original snapshot in place. (The KMS key associated with an existing snapshot cannot be changed in place.); Enable EBS encryption by default with the new key and continue using the original snapshot. (Changing the default does not change the KMS key associated with the existing snapshot.); Create a volume from the original snapshot and change that volume's KMS key afterward. (The KMS key associated with an existing volume cannot be changed afterward, and this does not produce the required snapshot.)

chunks.title: EBS IOPS/throughput sizing, Elastic Volumes and EBS-optimized instances
chunks.text:
EBS IOPS/throughput sizing, Elastic Volumes and EBS-optimized instances. Size EBS performance at both ends of the connection: provision the volume for the workload’s IOPS and throughput, then check that the EC2 instance can sustain them. Elastic Volumes lets supported instances change volume size, type, or performance without detaching the volume or restarting the instance.
When to use: A workload needs more IOPS or throughput without a corresponding increase in storage capacity.; An application must remain running while its EBS volume is resized or reconfigured.; Provisioned EBS performance is higher than the throughput or IOPS observed by the instance.
Key facts: Elastic Volumes can increase size, change type, or adjust performance on supported instances without detaching or restarting.; After increasing volume size, extend the file system to use the additional space.; Changing gp2 to gp3 without specifying performance provisions the higher of the source volume’s equivalent performance and the gp3 baseline.; Effective EBS performance is bounded by the lower of the instance’s EBS limits and the aggregate performance of its attached volumes.; Consider both IOPS and throughput: depending on I/O size, either limit can be reached first.
Gotchas: Provisioning more volume throughput cannot overcome an EC2 instance’s EBS throughput limit.; A larger EBS volume does not automatically make its file system larger.; Omitting performance settings during a gp2-to-gp3 change does not necessarily produce the throughput the new workload requires.; Elastic Volumes can increase volume size, but cannot decrease it.
Confused with: 
ES: Dimensiona el rendimiento de EBS en ambos extremos: configura los IOPS y el throughput del volumen y verifica que la instancia EC2 pueda sostenerlos. Elastic Volumes permite cambiar el tamaño, el tipo o el rendimiento del volumen sin desconectarlo ni reiniciar una instancia compatible. Elastic Volumes puede aumentar el tamaño, cambiar el tipo o ajustar el rendimiento sin desconectar el volumen ni reiniciar una instancia compatible.; Después de aumentar el tamaño del volumen, debes extender el sistema de archivos para aprovechar el espacio adicional.; Si cambias de gp2 a gp3 sin especificar el rendimiento, se configura el mayor entre el rendimiento equivalente del volumen anterior y el rendimiento base de gp3.; El rendimiento efectivo de EBS está limitado por el menor valor entre la capacidad de EBS de la instancia y el rendimiento agregado de sus volúmenes.; Debes evaluar tanto IOPS como throughput: según el tamaño de las operaciones de E/S, puedes alcanzar primero cualquiera de los dos límites.

chunks.title: EBS IOPS/throughput sizing, Elastic Volumes and EBS-optimized instances
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media analytics company processes video metadata on an m5.4xlarge EC2 instance. Its attached EBS volumes already provide an aggregate 700 MB/s of throughput, but processing peaks require the instance to sustain 700 MB/s; the m5.4xlarge EBS throughput limit is 593.75 MB/s. An m5.8xlarge has an 850 MB/s EBS throughput limit, and the application does not need more volume capacity. Which change meets the peak-throughput requirement?
Correct: Move the workload and its existing EBS volumes to an m5.8xlarge instance.
Why: The attached volumes already provide the required aggregate throughput, so the m5.4xlarge instance is the limiting side of the connection. Moving the workload to the stated m5.8xlarge provides an EBS throughput limit above the 700 MB/s peak requirement. Adding or reconfiguring volumes on the m5.4xlarge cannot overcome that instance’s 593.75 MB/s limit.
Wrong options: Keep the m5.4xlarge and attach another EBS volume to increase aggregate provisioned throughput. (Additional volume throughput cannot raise the instance above its 593.75 MB/s EBS limit.); Keep the m5.4xlarge and increase the provisioned IOPS on its existing EBS volumes. (More provisioned IOPS does not remove the instance’s lower throughput limit.); Keep the m5.4xlarge and increase the size of its existing EBS volumes. (Increasing volume capacity does not remove the instance’s EBS throughput bottleneck.)

chunks.title: EBS IOPS/throughput sizing, Elastic Volumes and EBS-optimized instances
chunks.text:
Scenario: A clinic’s appointment application writes to an EBS data volume attached to an EC2 instance that supports Elastic Volumes. The volume is nearly full, and the application must remain running while the clinic adds usable storage space. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Increase the EBS volume size with Elastic Volumes while it remains attached, then extend the file system.
Why: The clinic needs usable file-system space without stopping its application. On an instance that supports Elastic Volumes, the EBS volume can be enlarged without detaching it or restarting the instance; the file system must then be extended. Increasing only the volume leaves the additional space unavailable to the file system, while stopping or detaching causes avoidable disruption.
Wrong options: Increase the EBS volume size with Elastic Volumes and leave the file system unchanged. (The application cannot use the added capacity until the file system is extended.); Detach the EBS volume, increase its size, extend the file system, and reattach it. (Detaching the application’s data volume interrupts access unnecessarily.); Stop the instance, increase the EBS volume size, extend the file system, and restart the instance. (Stopping the instance violates the requirement to keep the application running.)

chunks.title: EBS snapshots, Data Lifecycle Manager and Fast Snapshot Restore
chunks.text:
EBS snapshots, Data Lifecycle Manager and Fast Snapshot Restore. EBS snapshots are point-in-time, incremental backups of EBS volumes; AWS does not create them automatically. Choose Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) when an EBS-focused workload needs scheduled snapshots, retention, deletion, or a disaster recovery policy for an isolated Region or account.
When to use: EC2 workloads need regular backups of attached EBS volumes without manually creating each snapshot.; A policy must retain backups and delete outdated snapshots or EBS-backed AMIs.; An EBS-focused disaster recovery policy must back up data to an isolated Region or account.
Key facts: EBS snapshots save blocks changed since the most recent snapshot, rather than duplicating unchanged data.; Snapshot data is replicated across Availability Zones in its Region; a snapshot can restore a new volume in any Availability Zone in that Region.; DLM automates creation, retention, and deletion of EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs.; DLM cannot manage snapshots or AMIs created by other means.; Deleting one snapshot does not remove data still referenced by other snapshots.
Gotchas: Do not assume AWS automatically backs up EBS volumes.; Do not expect a DLM policy to apply retention or deletion rules to existing manually created snapshots.; Do not use the Amazon S3 console or API to access the underlying EBS snapshot data.
Confused with: AWS Backup: AWS Backup can automate EBS backups; DLM is the EBS-focused choice for snapshot and EBS-backed AMI lifecycle policies.; RDS automated backups: RDS backups protect a database, not the data on an EC2 instance's EBS volumes.; DynamoDB PITR: DynamoDB PITR protects a table, not an EBS volume.
ES: Los EBS snapshots son respaldos incrementales y de un momento específico de los volúmenes EBS; AWS no los crea automáticamente. Elige Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) cuando necesites programar snapshots, conservarlos, eliminar los antiguos o definir una política de disaster recovery para una Region o cuenta aislada. Los EBS snapshots guardan los bloques modificados desde el snapshot anterior, sin duplicar los datos que no cambiaron.; Los datos del snapshot se replican entre las Availability Zones de su Region; puedes restaurar un volumen nuevo en cualquier Availability Zone de esa Region.; DLM automatiza la creación, retención y eliminación de EBS snapshots y EBS-backed AMIs.; DLM no puede administrar snapshots ni AMIs creados por otros medios.; Eliminar un snapshot no elimina los datos que otros snapshots todavía referencian.

chunks.title: EBS snapshots, Data Lifecycle Manager and Fast Snapshot Restore
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer has a collection of EBS snapshots that engineers created manually during a migration. It now wants scheduled snapshots for the same volumes and automatic deletion of future backups after the required retention period. The existing manual snapshots must also be reviewed for deletion, without assuming the new policy will manage them. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a DLM policy for future snapshots and handle retention of the existing manual snapshots separately.
Why: The critical distinction is how each snapshot was created. DLM can automate creation and retention for its own future snapshots, but it cannot manage snapshots created by other means. The manufacturer therefore needs a separate process for its existing manually created snapshots. Creating future snapshots manually or through the EC2 API does not bring them under DLM's lifecycle policy.
Wrong options: Create future snapshots with the EC2 API and use a DLM policy to manage their retention. (Snapshots created through the EC2 API rather than by DLM are outside DLM's management.); Continue creating snapshots manually and use a DLM policy only to delete snapshots that exceed the retention period. (DLM cannot delete the manually created snapshots under its lifecycle policy.); Create a DLM policy and apply its retention schedule to both future and existing manual snapshots. (DLM cannot manage snapshots created by other means, including the existing manual snapshots.)

chunks.title: EBS snapshots, Data Lifecycle Manager and Fast Snapshot Restore
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab keeps experiment logs on EBS volumes attached to EC2 instances. It needs a recurring backup schedule, deletion of outdated policy-created backups, and a disaster recovery policy that backs up data to an isolated Region. The lab wants to use EBS snapshot lifecycle capabilities without managing the snapshots' underlying storage objects. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure a DLM policy to create scheduled EBS snapshots and manage their retention and deletion. + Configure a DLM disaster recovery policy to back up the data to the isolated Region.
Why: The lab needs two EBS-specific capabilities: automated snapshot lifecycle management and a disaster recovery policy for an isolated Region. DLM supports scheduled creation, retention, and deletion of its snapshots, as well as disaster recovery backup policies for isolated Regions or accounts. It cannot take over snapshots created manually. EBS snapshot data is also inaccessible through the Amazon S3 API, so moving underlying objects is not an option.
Wrong options: Use the Amazon S3 API to move the underlying EBS snapshot objects into the isolated Region. (The underlying snapshot objects cannot be accessed through the Amazon S3 API.); Enable DynamoDB PITR for the EC2 instances' EBS volumes. (DynamoDB PITR protects DynamoDB tables, not EBS volumes.); Create snapshots manually and let DLM automatically delete them when they become outdated. (DLM cannot manage snapshots created manually.)

chunks.title: EBS volume types: gp3, io2, st1, sc1
chunks.text:
EBS volume types: gp3, io2, st1, sc1. Choose an EBS volume type by its dominant I/O pattern and performance requirement. Use gp3 for general-purpose SSD workloads, io2 Block Express for demanding low-latency or sustained-IOPS workloads, st1 for throughput-heavy streaming, and sc1 for infrequently accessed data when lowest EBS storage cost matters.
When to use: An EC2 workload needs a boot volume or general-purpose transactional block storage: consider gp3.; A database requires sustained IOPS beyond gp3's limit or consistent sub-millisecond latency: consider io2 Block Express.; Large sequential reads or writes dominate: compare st1 for throughput with sc1 for colder, lower-cost storage.
Key facts: gp3 supports boot volumes and provides up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s per volume.; io2 Block Express supports up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s; it is designed for average latency under 500 microseconds with 16 KiB I/O.; st1 is a Throughput Optimized HDD volume for workloads such as big data, data warehouses, and log processing; its maximum throughput is 500 MiB/s.; sc1 is a Cold HDD volume for infrequently accessed, throughput-oriented data when lowest storage cost is important; its maximum throughput is 250 MiB/s.; st1 and sc1 cannot be boot volumes or use EBS Multi-Attach.
Gotchas: Do not choose an HDD volume for small-I/O transactional performance: SSD volumes are optimized for IOPS, while HDD volumes are optimized for streaming throughput.; sc1's cost-oriented use case does not make it suitable when the required per-volume throughput exceeds 250 MiB/s.; A volume's advertised limits do not guarantee application performance; instance configuration, I/O characteristics, and workload demand also matter.
Confused with: EC2 instance store: Instance store is temporary block storage; EBS is the choice when the data must remain available after an instance stops.; Amazon EFS: EFS provides shared Linux file storage, not an EBS block volume selected for one workload's I/O pattern.
ES: Elige el tipo de volumen EBS según el patrón de E/S dominante y el rendimiento requerido. Usa gp3 para SSD de propósito general, io2 Block Express para latencia baja o IOPS sostenidas exigentes, st1 para streaming de alto throughput y sc1 para datos de acceso infrecuente cuando importa el menor costo de almacenamiento EBS. gp3 admite volúmenes de arranque y ofrece hasta 80,000 IOPS y 2,000 MiB/s por volumen.; io2 Block Express admite hasta 256,000 IOPS y 4,000 MiB/s; está diseñado para una latencia promedio inferior a 500 microsegundos con E/S de 16 KiB.; st1 es un volumen Throughput Optimized HDD para cargas como big data, almacenes de datos y procesamiento de registros; su throughput máximo es de 500 MiB/s.; sc1 es un volumen Cold HDD para datos de acceso infrecuente orientados a throughput cuando importa el menor costo de almacenamiento; su throughput máximo es de 250 MiB/s.; st1 y sc1 no admiten volúmenes de arranque ni EBS Multi-Attach.

chunks.title: EBS volume types: gp3, io2, st1, sc1
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio is moving a medium-sized, single-instance application database to EC2. The database performs frequent small reads and writes, and the team needs an EBS volume type that can also serve as a boot volume. It has no requirement for sustained IOPS beyond general-purpose SSD capacity or consistent sub-millisecond latency. Which volume type meets these requirements without selecting a higher-performance tier the workload does not need?
Correct: gp3 General Purpose SSD
Why: Frequent small reads and writes point to SSD-backed EBS storage, and the boot-volume requirement rules out st1 and sc1. gp3 fits the stated medium-sized, single-instance database use case. io2 Block Express is a plausible SSD alternative, but the scenario explicitly lacks the demanding IOPS or latency requirement that would justify selecting it.
Wrong options: st1 Throughput Optimized HDD (st1 targets streaming throughput rather than small transactional I/O and cannot be a boot volume.); sc1 Cold HDD (sc1 targets infrequently accessed, throughput-oriented data and cannot be a boot volume.); io2 Block Express Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express targets more demanding sustained-IOPS and latency requirements that this scenario does not have.)

chunks.title: EBS volume types: gp3, io2, st1, sc1
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab keeps historical instrument output on an EBS data volume attached to an EC2 analysis server. Researchers access the data infrequently and read it in large streams when needed; they do not need the volume to boot the server. Among current EBS volume types, the lab prioritizes the lowest storage cost over higher throughput. Which volume type is the best fit?
Correct: sc1 Cold HDD
Why: This is still an EBS data-volume requirement, but access is infrequent and the dominant I/O pattern is streaming. sc1 is the Cold HDD type intended for throughput-oriented data when lowest storage cost matters. st1 is a plausible HDD choice if higher throughput is the priority, but that is not the lab's deciding constraint.
Wrong options: gp3 General Purpose SSD (gp3 targets general-purpose SSD workloads rather than the stated lowest-cost, infrequently accessed HDD use case.); st1 Throughput Optimized HDD (st1 favors higher streaming throughput, which the lab explicitly values less than lowest storage cost.); io2 Block Express Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express targets demanding IOPS and latency requirements that this cold, streaming workload does not have.)

chunks.title: EBS volume types: gp3, io2, st1, sc1
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare company is assigning EBS volumes to two separate EC2 workloads. An appointment service needs a bootable volume for frequent small transactional I/O, without exceptional latency or IOPS demands. A database on a Nitro-based instance needs its data volume to sustain 110,000 IOPS with 16 KiB operations. Which two volume assignments meet the respective workload requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use gp3 for the appointment service's boot volume. + Use io2 Block Express for the database's data volume.
Why: The two workloads have different I/O requirements, so each needs its own volume-type decision. gp3 fits the bootable, general-purpose transactional workload. io2 Block Express supports the database's 110,000-IOPS requirement on a Nitro-based instance, whereas gp3's maximum is 80,000 IOPS. Neither HDD option fits its proposed assignment.
Wrong options: Use gp3 for the database's data volume. (gp3 supports at most 80,000 IOPS, below the database's 110,000-IOPS requirement.); Use st1 for the appointment service's boot volume. (st1 does not support boot volumes and is optimized for streaming throughput rather than transactional I/O.); Use sc1 for the database's data volume. (sc1 is a throughput-oriented HDD volume, not a fit for the database's sustained small-I/O demand.)

chunks.title: AMIs, user data and golden images
chunks.text:
AMIs, user data and golden images. An AMI provides the software and configuration used to launch EC2 instances; pre-bake shared software into an AMI when repeated boot-time installation would slow launches. Use user data for tasks that must run when each instance starts, and copy an AMI to another Region before launching from it there.
When to use: Many instances need the same installed software and must launch without repeating a lengthy installation.; Instances need a small configuration task at launch while sharing the same base image.; A disaster recovery plan requires launching a matching EC2 configuration in another Region.
Key facts: An AMI is Region-specific and must be compatible with the chosen instance type.; You can create an AMI from an EC2 instance and copy an AMI to another Region.; User data can run configuration tasks after an instance starts; boot-time tasks add to launch time.; By default, Linux user data scripts run only during the first launch boot cycle.; An instance's user data attribute is not included when you create an AMI from that instance.
Gotchas: An AMI in one Region cannot be used directly to launch an instance in another; copy it first.; Creating an AMI does not preserve the source instance's user data attribute.; A user data script previously run on a Linux instance can remain as a file on disk; remove it before creating an AMI if it should not appear in new instances.
Confused with: EC2 user data: Use user data for launch-time tasks; pre-bake common software into an AMI when installing it at each boot would delay launches.
ES: Una AMI proporciona el software y la configuración para lanzar instancias EC2; incluye previamente el software común en una AMI cuando instalarlo durante cada arranque retrasaría los lanzamientos. Usa user data para tareas que deben ejecutarse al iniciar cada instancia y copia la AMI a otra Region antes de lanzar instancias allí. Una AMI es específica de una Region y debe ser compatible con el tipo de instancia elegido.; Puedes crear una AMI a partir de una instancia EC2 y copiar una AMI a otra Region.; User data puede ejecutar tareas de configuración después de que se inicie la instancia; las tareas de arranque aumentan el tiempo de lanzamiento.; Por defecto, los scripts de user data en Linux se ejecutan solo durante el primer ciclo de arranque del lanzamiento.; El atributo user data de una instancia no se incluye al crear una AMI a partir de ella.

chunks.title: AMIs, user data and golden images
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company has tested a configured EC2 AMI in its primary AWS Region. Its recovery plan calls for launching matching instances in a second Region after a regional disruption, without rebuilding the software there during recovery. Which approach meets this requirement?
Correct: Copy the tested AMI to the recovery Region and launch instances from the regional copy.
Why: The company needs its tested image available in the recovery Region before it launches instances there. AMIs are Region-specific, and EC2 supports copying an AMI to another Region for launches in that Region. Reusing the original AMI ID does not cross the regional boundary. Installing everything through user data would also violate the requirement to avoid rebuilding software during recovery.
Wrong options: Launch a base AMI in the recovery Region and install the software with user data during recovery. (This rebuilds the software at launch, contrary to the recovery requirement.); Use the primary Region's AMI ID when launching instances in the recovery Region. (An AMI is Region-specific, so the primary Region's AMI cannot be launched directly in the second Region.); Create another AMI from the primary instance and expect it to become available in both Regions. (Creating an AMI does not by itself make that image available in another Region.)

chunks.title: AMIs, user data and golden images
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research group launches Linux EC2 instances from one approved AMI. Each new instance must write a short, different experiment label into a local file when it first starts; the shared software image should remain unchanged. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Pass a user data shell script containing the experiment label when launching each instance.
Why: Each instance needs a different, short task at its initial launch, not a different software image. Passing a user data script at launch handles that task while preserving the shared AMI. A separate AMI per label adds image-management work. Editing user data after stopping an instance is not a substitute: Linux user data scripts run only on the first launch boot by default.
Wrong options: Create a separate AMI for each experiment label and launch its instances from that image. (Maintaining a separate image for each small label adds work when one shared AMI suffices.); Launch each instance, stop it, edit its user data, and restart it to write the label. (Updated Linux user data scripts do not run on restart by default.); Set user data on the source instance, create an AMI, and launch all experiments from it. (The source instance's user data attribute is not included in its AMI and would not supply different labels.)

chunks.title: EC2 Auto Scaling groups and launch templates
chunks.text:
EC2 Auto Scaling groups and launch templates. An EC2 Auto Scaling group (ASG) maintains an EC2 fleet at its desired capacity and can adjust capacity as demand changes. For a resilient application fleet, use an ASG across multiple Availability Zones with a launch template and connect it to a load balancer.
When to use: An EC2 fleet must replace terminated or impaired instances automatically.; Application demand varies, so instance count must grow and shrink within defined bounds.; Instances must be distributed across Availability Zones and added to a load balancer automatically.
Key facts: Minimum and maximum capacity bound the group; desired capacity is the number the group works to maintain.; Scaling policies can launch or terminate instances as demand changes.; An ASG can balance instances across multiple Availability Zones.; When connected to Elastic Load Balancing, the ASG automatically registers and deregisters instances.; Launch templates define instance configuration and support versioning; they are required for a single ASG using both Spot and On-Demand Instances or multiple instance types.
Gotchas: A load balancer distributes traffic but does not, by itself, replace failed EC2 instances.; Updating a launch template does not, by itself, roll the new configuration across existing instances; instance refresh provides rolling updates.; EC2 health checks might not detect an application that has stopped responding; a custom application health check can identify it.
Confused with: Launch configuration: Unlike a launch template, it cannot configure an ASG with both Spot and On-Demand Instances or multiple instance types.; Elastic Load Balancing: It distributes traffic to healthy instances; the ASG manages fleet capacity and replaces impaired instances.
ES: Un EC2 Auto Scaling group (ASG) mantiene una flota EC2 en su capacidad deseada y puede ajustar la capacidad cuando cambia la demanda. Para una flota de aplicaciones resiliente, usa un ASG en varias Availability Zones con un launch template y conéctalo a un load balancer. Las capacidades mínima y máxima delimitan el grupo; la capacidad deseada es la cantidad de instancias que el grupo procura mantener.; Las scaling policies pueden iniciar o terminar instancias cuando cambia la demanda.; Un ASG puede equilibrar las instancias entre varias Availability Zones.; Al conectarse a Elastic Load Balancing, el ASG registra y elimina automáticamente el registro de las instancias.; Los launch templates definen la configuración de las instancias y admiten versiones; son necesarios para usar Spot y On-Demand Instances, o varios tipos de instancia, en un mismo ASG.

chunks.title: EC2 Auto Scaling groups and launch templates
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company runs its web tier on an EC2 Auto Scaling group, but operators currently change its size and update load balancer registrations by hand. Demand rises and falls unpredictably, and new instances must receive application traffic without manual registration. Which TWO actions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Set minimum and maximum capacity for the ASG and add scaling policies based on demand. + Connect the ASG to Elastic Load Balancing so launched and terminated instances are registered and deregistered automatically.
Why: The scenario has two separate operational tasks: changing fleet size with demand and keeping load balancer registrations current. ASG scaling policies address the first task within minimum and maximum capacity, while Elastic Load Balancing integration automatically registers and deregisters instances. EC2 health checks support replacement of impaired instances but do not solve either demand-based scaling or manual registration on their own.
Wrong options: Create additional launch template versions whenever traffic changes. (Launch template versions define instance configuration, not automatic demand-based capacity or traffic registration.); Set the group's desired capacity manually whenever operators notice a traffic change. (Manual changes do not meet the requirement to respond to unpredictable demand with minimal operations.); Enable EC2 health checks and keep the group's desired capacity fixed. (Health checks help replace impaired instances but do not scale a fixed-size group with changing demand.)

chunks.title: EC2 Auto Scaling groups and launch templates
chunks.text:
Scenario: A clinic runs a stateless appointment application on EC2 instances behind a load balancer. Traffic varies during the day, and an instance or an Availability Zone might become unavailable. Which solution maintains application capacity across Availability Zones and responds to demand with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use an ASG with a launch template across two Availability Zones, set minimum, desired, and maximum capacity, add scaling policies, and connect it to the load balancer.
Why: The deciding requirements are automatic capacity adjustment and resilience across Availability Zones. A multi-AZ ASG with scaling policies maintains capacity within its minimum and maximum bounds, replaces impaired instances, and integrates with the load balancer. A fixed-size ASG addresses replacement but cannot respond to changing demand.
Wrong options: Use an ASG with a launch template and scaling policies in one Availability Zone, connected to the load balancer. (It can scale and replace instances but does not maintain capacity across multiple Availability Zones.); Deploy fixed EC2 fleets in two Availability Zones behind the load balancer and replace failed instances manually. (The fixed fleets require manual replacement and do not adjust capacity as demand changes.); Use an ASG across two Availability Zones with minimum, desired, and maximum capacity set to the same value, connected to the load balancer. (It can replace instances across zones, but identical capacity bounds prevent the fleet from growing or shrinking with demand.)

chunks.title: EC2 Auto Scaling groups and launch templates
chunks.text:
Scenario: A rendering company wants one EC2 Auto Scaling group for workers that can use several instance types. It also wants to combine Spot and On-Demand Instances in that group to optimize costs while maintaining the required capacity. Which configuration meets these requirements?
Correct: Create one ASG using a launch template and configure multiple instance types with Spot and On-Demand Instances.
Why: The requirement for several instance types and both purchase options within a single ASG determines the answer. A launch template is required to configure those features together. Launch configurations are a plausible alternative for simpler fleets, but they do not support this combination.
Wrong options: Create one ASG from a launch configuration and specify multiple instance types and both purchase options. (Launch configurations cannot support multiple instance types or a mix of Spot and On-Demand Instances in an ASG.); Create one ASG from a launch template, but configure only one instance type and On-Demand Instances. (The group would not use several instance types or combine Spot and On-Demand Instances.); Create separate Spot and On-Demand ASGs from launch configurations, each with one instance type. (Separate groups do not meet the requirement for one ASG using several instance types and both purchase options.)

chunks.title: EC2 hibernate vs stop
chunks.text:
EC2 hibernate vs stop. EC2 hibernation saves an instance’s RAM to its EBS root volume, then resumes its processes when the instance starts again. Choose it when a workload must retain its in-memory state through an idle period without paying for instance usage while it is stopped.
When to use: An application takes a long time to initialize or build its in-memory state.; The instance can be paused during idle periods but must resume its running processes.; The team wants to avoid instance usage charges during those stopped periods.
Key facts: Hibernation saves RAM contents to the EBS root volume.; On start, RAM contents are reloaded and previously running processes resume.; The EBS root volume and attached EBS data volumes persist; data volumes are reattached on start.; A hibernated instance retains its instance ID.; There is no instance usage charge while the hibernated instance is stopped, but EBS storage charges continue, including storage for RAM contents.; The instance must have hibernation enabled and meet the hibernation prerequisites.
Gotchas: A standard stop is not the choice when the requirement is to resume the prior contents of RAM.; Hibernation does not eliminate EBS storage charges.; Do not assume an existing instance can be hibernated unless hibernation is enabled and its prerequisites are met.
Confused with: EC2 stop: Choose hibernation when the instance must reload its saved RAM and resume its processes on start.; EC2 reboot: Hibernation is the choice when the instance must enter a stopped state yet later resume its saved in-memory work.
ES: EC2 hibernation guarda la RAM de una instancia en su volumen raíz de EBS y reanuda sus procesos cuando la instancia vuelve a iniciarse. Elígela cuando una carga de trabajo deba conservar su estado en memoria durante un período de inactividad sin pagar por el uso de la instancia mientras está detenida. Hibernation guarda el contenido de la RAM en el volumen raíz de EBS.; Al iniciar la instancia, se recarga la RAM y se reanudan los procesos que estaban en ejecución.; Persisten el volumen raíz y los volúmenes de datos de EBS adjuntos; los volúmenes de datos se vuelven a adjuntar al iniciar.; Una instancia hibernada conserva su ID de instancia.; No se cobra el uso de la instancia mientras está detenida por hibernation, pero se sigue cobrando el almacenamiento de EBS, incluido el espacio para el contenido de la RAM.; La instancia debe tener hibernation habilitada y cumplir sus requisitos previos.

chunks.title: EC2 hibernate vs stop
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio has an EC2 rendering workspace with attached EBS data volumes. Artists need to pause work between projects and later resume the same running processes on the same instance ID, with their data volumes available again. The studio wants no instance usage charges during the pause and accepts ongoing storage charges. The instance is eligible for hibernation. Which approach meets these requirements?
Correct: Hibernate the instance and start it when the next project begins.
Why: The studio needs more than persistent files: it needs the running processes and instance ID to survive a pause. Hibernation saves RAM to the EBS root volume; on start, processes resume, previously attached EBS data volumes are reattached, and the instance retains its ID. Keeping the instance running misses the cost requirement, and a standard stop misses the in-memory-state requirement. EBS storage remains billable while the instance is hibernated.
Wrong options: Stop the instance and start it when the next project begins. (A standard stop does not restore the RAM contents needed to resume the artists’ processes.); Keep the instance running and leave its EBS data volumes attached. (This keeps the workspace available but misses the requirement to avoid instance usage charges during the pause.); Terminate the instance and attach its data volumes to a replacement instance. (A replacement instance would not retain the original instance ID or resume its running processes.)

chunks.title: EC2 hibernate vs stop
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research team runs a simulation on an EC2 instance that spends hours building an in-memory model. The team does not need compute overnight, but researchers must continue from the running model the next morning. The instance can meet the prerequisites for hibernation. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Enable EC2 hibernation, build the model, and hibernate the instance overnight.
Why: The deciding requirements are to retain the built in-memory model and avoid paying for instance usage overnight. EC2 hibernation saves RAM to the EBS root volume and resumes processes when the instance starts. A standard stop does not satisfy the RAM-resumption requirement, while leaving the instance running misses the idle-period cost goal. EBS storage charges still apply during hibernation.
Wrong options: Terminate the EC2 instance overnight and launch a new instance each morning. (A newly launched instance does not resume the prior instance’s in-memory model.); Keep the EC2 instance running overnight so the model stays in memory. (Keeping it running preserves the model but does not avoid instance usage during the idle period.); Stop the EC2 instance overnight and start it each morning. (A standard stop does not meet the requirement to restore the running model from saved RAM.)

chunks.title: EC2 instance families and types
chunks.text:
EC2 instance families and types. Choose an EC2 instance family by the resource that constrains the workload, then choose a size within that family. For exam scenarios, distinguish balanced workloads from CPU-, memory-, storage-, and accelerator-focused workloads before considering processor compatibility.
When to use: A workload needs a particular balance of compute, memory, and storage.; A scenario calls for dense storage, GPU acceleration, deep learning training, or low-latency inference.; An application can run on Arm-based AWS Graviton processors.
Key facts: M is general purpose, C is compute optimized, and R is memory optimized.; D denotes dense storage; I denotes storage optimized.; P denotes GPU acceleration, Trn denotes AWS Trainium, and Inf denotes AWS Inferentia.; The g option identifies AWS Graviton processors, which are Arm-based.; The part after the period in an instance type name identifies its size.
Gotchas: Changing instance size does not change the resource emphasis of its family.; A Graviton option does not make a compute-optimized or memory-optimized family general purpose.; Deep learning training and inference have different purpose-built processors: Trainium and Inferentia.
Confused with: D versus I families: D denotes dense storage; I denotes storage optimized.; Trn versus Inf families: Trainium is purpose-built for deep learning training; Inferentia accelerates inference.
