ES: Elige una familia de instancias EC2 según el recurso que limita la carga de trabajo y después elige un tamaño dentro de esa familia. En escenarios de examen, distingue las cargas equilibradas de las que priorizan CPU, memoria, almacenamiento o aceleradores antes de considerar la compatibilidad del procesador. M es general purpose, C es compute optimized y R es memory optimized.; D indica dense storage; I indica storage optimized.; P indica aceleración por GPU, Trn indica AWS Trainium e Inf indica AWS Inferentia.; La opción g identifica procesadores AWS Graviton, basados en Arm.; La parte del nombre de la instancia después del punto indica su tamaño.

chunks.title: EC2 instance families and types
chunks.text:
Scenario: A telemetry team temporarily stages a large collection of raw device files on EC2 before transferring the processed results elsewhere. Its sizing priority is dense instance-local storage; CPU and memory requirements are ordinary. Which instance family best matches this priority?
Correct: D3 dense storage instances
Why: The requirement explicitly prioritizes dense instance-local storage. The D series denotes dense storage, so D3 is the closest family match. I4i is a plausible storage-focused alternative, but the naming distinction in this scenario is dense storage rather than storage optimization in general.
Wrong options: C7i compute optimized instances (C7i emphasizes CPU resources, which are not the sizing priority.); R7i memory optimized instances (R7i emphasizes memory rather than the requested dense instance-local storage.); I4i storage optimized instances (I4i is storage optimized, but D3 is the option specifically designated for dense storage.)

chunks.title: EC2 instance families and types
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer has rebuilt its web application for Arm-based processors and wants to evaluate AWS Graviton instances. Profiling shows a balanced mix of CPU and memory use, with neither resource dominating. Which instance family meets both requirements MOST directly?
Correct: M7g general purpose instances
Why: This choice must satisfy both the balanced workload profile and the Graviton processor requirement. M denotes general purpose, while the g option denotes AWS Graviton, making M7g the match. M7i matches the resource profile but its i option identifies Intel processors, so it misses the processor requirement.
Wrong options: C7g compute optimized instances (C7g provides Graviton processors but emphasizes compute rather than a balanced resource mix.); R7g memory optimized instances (R7g provides Graviton processors but emphasizes memory, which is not the dominant need.); M7i general purpose instances (M7i has the general-purpose emphasis but uses the Intel processor option rather than Graviton.)

chunks.title: EC2 instance families and types
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company is building two separate EC2 compute pools for a deep learning project. One pool will train models, while the other will serve low-latency predictions from trained models; the company wants purpose-built processors for each task. Which two instance families should it select? (Choose two.)
Correct: Trn2 AWS Trainium instances + Inf2 AWS Inferentia instances
Why: The two pools have different tasks, and the requirement calls for a purpose-built processor for each. AWS Trainium is purpose-built for deep learning training, while AWS Inferentia is designed for high-performance, low-latency inference. A general-purpose M instance might run application code, but it does not meet the stated processor requirement for either pool.
Wrong options: C7i compute optimized instances (C7i targets general compute-intensive work rather than either purpose-built deep learning processor requested.); M7i general purpose instances (M7i provides a general-purpose resource mix, not a purpose-built processor for either task.); R7i memory optimized instances (R7i prioritizes memory rather than purpose-built training or inference acceleration.)

chunks.title: Instance metadata service (IMDSv2)
chunks.text:
Instance metadata service (IMDSv2). IMDSv2 is the session-oriented way for an EC2 instance to access instance metadata, including the IAM-related metadata used by workloads with instance roles. When a scenario calls for reducing SSRF-related metadata exposure, require IMDSv2 on the instance rather than merely allowing applications to use it.
When to use: An EC2 workload needs instance metadata while the organization wants defense in depth against SSRF.; Unauthenticated IMDSv1 requests must fail without disabling metadata access.; A containerized workload needs IMDSv2 but cannot receive the token request's response at the default hop limit.
Key facts: By default, an instance can use IMDSv1, IMDSv2, or both; configuring IMDSv2 as required makes IMDSv1 calls fail.; IMDSv2 starts with a PUT request for a session token; subsequent metadata GET requests include that token.; A missing, invalid, or expired token receives HTTP 401 when tokens are required.; A token is specific to the instance that generated it and can last from one second to six hours.; The default IP response hop limit for token PUT requests is 1; it can be increased when a workload, such as a container service on the instance, needs it.
Gotchas: Using an IMDSv2-capable application does not by itself prevent IMDSv1 calls if the instance still permits them.; Requiring IMDSv2 can break a workload that uses an SDK version without IMDSv2 support.; Increasing the response hop limit is not a substitute for requiring IMDSv2.
Confused with: 
ES: IMDSv2 es la forma basada en sesiones con la que una instancia EC2 accede a instance metadata, incluidos los metadatos relacionados con IAM que usan las cargas de trabajo con roles de instancia. Si un escenario pide reducir la exposición de metadatos ante SSRF, exige IMDSv2 en la instancia en vez de solo permitir que la aplicación lo use. De forma predeterminada, una instancia puede usar IMDSv1, IMDSv2 o ambos; exigir IMDSv2 hace que fallen las llamadas IMDSv1.; IMDSv2 comienza con una solicitud PUT para obtener un token de sesión; las solicitudes GET posteriores incluyen ese token.; Cuando se exigen tokens, un token ausente, inválido o vencido produce HTTP 401.; El token solo es válido en la instancia que lo generó y puede durar desde un segundo hasta seis horas.; El hop limit IP predeterminado de la respuesta al PUT del token es 1; puedes aumentarlo si una carga de trabajo, como un servicio de contenedores en la instancia, lo necesita.

chunks.title: Instance metadata service (IMDSv2)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company runs an application on EC2 that needs access to instance metadata. A security review identifies an SSRF risk, and the company wants metadata requests without an IMDSv2 session token to fail. Which change meets this requirement MOST securely?
Correct: Configure the EC2 instance to require IMDSv2 and have the application obtain and include a session token.
Why: The deciding requirement is that metadata requests without an IMDSv2 token must fail. Configure the instance to require IMDSv2, then use a token obtained by PUT in subsequent metadata requests. Merely changing the application to use tokens leaves IMDSv1 available if the instance still accepts both versions. Increasing the hop limit addresses token-response delivery, not whether tokens are required.
Wrong options: Have the application request a new IMDSv2 token for every metadata lookup without changing the instance settings. (Generating tokens more often does not prevent other requests from using IMDSv1 when it remains allowed.); Increase the instance metadata response hop limit and leave both IMDS versions available. (A higher hop limit does not make tokenless IMDSv1 requests fail.); Update the application to use IMDSv2, but leave the instance configured to accept either IMDS version. (The application would use tokens, but the instance would still accept IMDSv1 requests without them.)

chunks.title: Instance metadata service (IMDSv2)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab is migrating an EC2-based analysis service to an IMDSv2-only configuration. Its current AWS SDK version does not support IMDSv2, but the service must continue retrieving instance metadata after the change. Which migration plan meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Upgrade to an SDK version that supports IMDSv2, verify metadata access, and then require IMDSv2.
Why: The service must keep accessing metadata, and the finished configuration must accept only IMDSv2. AWS states that an EC2 workload using an SDK needs an IMDSv2-supporting version to use IMDSv2. Upgrade and verify the SDK before requiring IMDSv2 on the instance. Requiring IMDSv2 while retaining the incompatible SDK would fail the continuity requirement.
Wrong options: Require IMDSv2 immediately and keep the current SDK version. (The current SDK does not support the metadata access method the instance would require.); Disable instance metadata access and keep the current SDK version. (Disabling metadata access prevents the service from continuing to retrieve it.); Leave IMDSv1 enabled and retry metadata requests when the current SDK receives an error. (Leaving IMDSv1 available does not achieve an IMDSv2-only configuration.)

chunks.title: EC2 placement groups: cluster, spread, partition
chunks.text:
EC2 placement groups: cluster, spread, partition. EC2 placement groups influence where related instances run. Choose cluster for low-latency communication within one Availability Zone, spread for a small set of instances that must use distinct hardware, and partition for large distributed workloads that need hardware separation between groups.
When to use: Tightly coupled compute nodes need low-latency node-to-node communication: choose cluster.; A small set of critical instances must be placed on distinct underlying hardware: choose spread.; A large distributed workload needs groups of instances isolated from other groups at the hardware level: choose partition.
Key facts: Cluster packs instances close together inside an Availability Zone.; Spread strictly places a small group of instances across distinct underlying hardware.; Partition separates logical partitions so instances in different partitions do not share underlying hardware.; Partition is commonly used for distributed and replicated workloads such as Hadoop, Cassandra, and Kafka.; An instance can belong to only one placement group at a time.
Gotchas: Default EC2 placement attempts to spread instances, but it is not the strict distinct-hardware placement provided by spread.; Partition separates groups from other groups; spread is the choice when each instance in a small set needs distinct hardware.; Cluster optimizes proximity and network latency, not hardware separation.
Confused with: Default EC2 placement: EC2 tries to spread instances by default; a spread placement group strictly places a small group on distinct hardware.; Precision time placement group: It provides supported hardware with direct access to high-precision time sources, not the node-to-node latency benefit of cluster.
ES: Los EC2 placement groups influyen en dónde se ejecutan las instancias relacionadas. Elige cluster para comunicación de baja latencia dentro de una Availability Zone, spread para un grupo pequeño que debe usar hardware distinto y partition para cargas distribuidas grandes que necesitan separación de hardware entre grupos. Cluster agrupa instancias cerca unas de otras dentro de una Availability Zone.; Spread coloca estrictamente un grupo pequeño de instancias en hardware subyacente distinto.; Partition separa particiones lógicas para que las instancias de particiones diferentes no compartan hardware subyacente.; Partition suele usarse con cargas distribuidas y replicadas como Hadoop, Cassandra y Kafka.; Una instancia solo puede pertenecer a un placement group a la vez.

chunks.title: EC2 placement groups: cluster, spread, partition
chunks.text:
Scenario: A payment company runs a small set of critical EC2 instances. It wants each instance placed on distinct underlying hardware to reduce correlated failures. Which approach meets this requirement MOST directly?
Correct: Launch the instances in a spread placement group.
Why: The company needs strict hardware separation for a small set of instances, so spread is the direct match. Default EC2 placement only tries to spread instances. Partition is designed to separate groups across logical partitions, and cluster serves low-latency communication instead.
Wrong options: Launch the instances in separate partitions of a partition placement group. (Partition separates groups of instances, whereas spread directly addresses strict placement of a small set of individual instances.); Launch the instances in a cluster placement group. (Cluster packs instances close together for low latency rather than placing each on distinct hardware.); Launch the instances without a placement group and rely on default EC2 placement. (Default EC2 placement tries to spread instances but does not provide the strict distinct-hardware placement requested.)

chunks.title: EC2 placement groups: cluster, spread, partition
chunks.text:
Scenario: A university is deploying two independent EC2 workloads: a small set of critical admission-service instances that must each use distinct underlying hardware, and a large Cassandra deployment whose node groups must not share hardware across groups. The university can use separate placement groups for the workloads. Which two placement decisions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Place the admission-service instances in a spread placement group. + Place the Cassandra node groups in different partitions of a partition placement group.
Why: The two workloads have different placement requirements, so each needs its own strategy. Spread strictly places the small admission-service set on distinct hardware. Partition separates the Cassandra node groups by underlying hardware; cluster does not meet either isolation requirement.
Wrong options: Place the Cassandra nodes in a cluster placement group. (Cluster packs instances close together and does not provide the requested separation between node groups.); Place the admission-service instances in a cluster placement group. (Cluster prioritizes proximity rather than distinct hardware for each critical instance.); Place the Cassandra nodes in a spread placement group. (Spread targets a small group of individually separated instances rather than hardware separation between groups in a large distributed workload.)

chunks.title: EC2 purchase options overview
chunks.text:
EC2 purchase options overview. Choose an EC2 purchase option by asking what the workload can commit to, whether it can be interrupted, and whether it needs reserved capacity or dedicated hardware. A predictable spend does not necessarily mean a predictable instance configuration.
When to use: Choose On-Demand when the workload cannot make a usage or configuration commitment and must not depend on interruptible capacity.; Choose Savings Plans for a 1- or 3-year usage-spend commitment; choose Reserved Instances when the instance configuration is also predictable.; Choose Spot for work that can run flexibly and tolerate interruption.; Choose Capacity Reservations for capacity in a specific Availability Zone; consider Dedicated Hosts when existing socket-, core-, or VM-based licenses require a dedicated physical host.
Key facts: On-Demand Instances are billed by the second.; Savings Plans commit to a consistent USD-per-hour usage amount for 1 or 3 years; Reserved Instances commit to a consistent instance configuration, including instance type and Region, for 1 or 3 years.; Spot Instances use unused EC2 capacity and suit applications that can be interrupted.; Capacity Reservations reserve EC2 capacity in a specific Availability Zone; Reserved Instances can also provide a capacity reservation when purchased for a specific Availability Zone.; Dedicated Hosts provide a fully dedicated physical host. Dedicated Instances run on single-tenant hardware and are billed by the hour.
Gotchas: A Savings Plans usage commitment is not a reservation of capacity in an Availability Zone.; A Capacity Reservation addresses capacity, not a request for a purchase-option discount.; Single-tenant instances and a fully dedicated physical host are not the same purchase.
Confused with: Savings Plans vs. Reserved Instances: Commit to a usage amount when the configuration may change; commit to a consistent configuration when it is predictable.; Dedicated Instances vs. Dedicated Hosts: The former are instances on single-tenant hardware; the latter provide a fully dedicated physical host.; Capacity Reservations vs. Spot Instances: The former reserve capacity in an Availability Zone; the latter use unused capacity for interruptible work.
ES: Elige una opción de compra de EC2 según el compromiso que puede asumir la carga, si tolera interrupciones y si necesita capacidad reservada o hardware dedicado. Un gasto predecible no implica necesariamente una configuración de instancia predecible. On-Demand Instances se facturan por segundo.; Savings Plans requieren un compromiso de uso en USD por hora durante 1 o 3 años; Reserved Instances requieren una configuración de instancia constante, incluidos el tipo de instancia y la Región, durante 1 o 3 años.; Spot Instances utilizan capacidad EC2 no utilizada y son adecuadas para aplicaciones que pueden interrumpirse.; Capacity Reservations reservan capacidad EC2 en una Availability Zone específica; Reserved Instances también pueden ofrecer una reserva de capacidad si se adquieren para una Availability Zone específica.; Dedicated Hosts proporcionan un host físico totalmente dedicado. Dedicated Instances se ejecutan en hardware de un solo inquilino y se facturan por hora.

chunks.title: EC2 purchase options overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: A software publisher expects a consistent amount of EC2 usage spending for the next year. Its teams regularly change instance types as they revise their applications, so the publisher cannot commit to a consistent instance configuration. Which purchase option reduces EC2 costs while matching the commitment the publisher can make?
Correct: Savings Plans
Why: The publisher can commit to a usage amount, but not to a stable instance configuration. Savings Plans match a consistent USD-per-hour usage commitment over a one-year term. Reserved Instances are the tempting alternative, but their configuration commitment conflicts with the publisher's changing instance types.
Wrong options: On-Demand Instances (They do not use the publisher's ability to make a usage commitment to reduce costs.); Capacity Reservations (They reserve capacity in an Availability Zone rather than addressing the stated usage-based cost commitment.); Reserved Instances (They require the consistent instance configuration that the publisher cannot commit to.)

chunks.title: EC2 purchase options overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio renders draft animations on EC2 whenever unused compute is available. Rendering can pause and resume later, and the studio accepts interruptions to minimize compute costs. Which purchase option is the MOST cost-effective match for this workload?
Correct: Spot Instances
Why: The studio explicitly accepts interruption and can be flexible about when rendering runs. Spot Instances use unused EC2 capacity and can significantly reduce costs under those conditions. A Capacity Reservation solves a different problem: ensuring capacity in a specific Availability Zone.
Wrong options: On-Demand Instances (They avoid an interruption-based purchasing choice but do not use the studio's stated flexibility to reduce costs.); Reserved Instances (They require a consistent configuration commitment that is not supported by the studio's flexible, occasional rendering need.); Capacity Reservations (They reserve capacity in an Availability Zone, which this flexible workload does not require.)

chunks.title: EC2 purchase options overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum is launching an interactive exhibit for an unknown number of days. Its EC2 application must remain available while the exhibit is open, but the museum cannot commit to a consistent usage amount or instance configuration. Which purchase option meets these requirements without a long-term commitment?
Correct: On-Demand Instances
Why: The deciding constraints are that the museum cannot make either kind of commitment and its application must not rely on interruptible capacity. On-Demand Instances meet those constraints and are billed for the instances launched. Spot may be less expensive, but its interruption tolerance does not match this exhibit.
Wrong options: Reserved Instances (They require a consistent instance-configuration commitment for 1 or 3 years.); Spot Instances (They can be interrupted, which conflicts with the availability requirement.); Savings Plans (They require a consistent USD-per-hour usage commitment for 1 or 3 years.)

chunks.title: Right-sizing with AWS Compute Optimizer
chunks.text:
Right-sizing with AWS Compute Optimizer. AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes resource configuration and CloudWatch utilization metrics to recommend right-sizing changes. Choose it when the decision is which resource size or configuration offers an appropriate price-performance trade-off, rather than simply how much the workload costs.
When to use: Choose an EC2 instance size using utilization history and projected utilization.; Evaluate whether an EBS volume or Lambda function configuration should change.; Review recommendations for EC2 Auto Scaling groups or ECS services on AWS Fargate.
Key facts: You must opt in before Compute Optimizer analyzes resources; resources also need sufficient metric data for recommendations.; The default analysis uses the last 14 days of CloudWatch utilization metrics.; Enhanced infrastructure metrics is a paid feature that extends the lookback period to 93 days for selected resources.; Recommendation pages show suggested changes; resource details include utilization history and projected utilization graphs.; Compute Optimizer supports EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda functions, and ECS services on AWS Fargate, among other resources.
Gotchas: A low average utilization figure alone does not establish that a smaller configuration will meet peak demand.; Compute Optimizer does not analyze resources until you opt in.; Do not assume the default 14-day window captures an important event that occurred earlier.
Confused with: AWS Cost Explorer: Cost Explorer focuses on spend analysis and can offer rightsizing recommendations; Compute Optimizer adds resource-specific utilization and projected-utilization views for evaluating changes.; AWS Budgets: Budgets tracks thresholds and alerts or actions; it does not serve as the resource-utilization view for choosing a size.; AWS Trusted Advisor: Trusted Advisor provides best-practice checks; Compute Optimizer provides resource-specific optimization recommendations and utilization graphs.
ES: AWS Compute Optimizer analiza la configuración de recursos y las métricas de uso de CloudWatch para recomendar cambios de tamaño. Elígelo cuando debas decidir qué tamaño o configuración ofrece una relación adecuada entre precio y rendimiento, no solo conocer el gasto. Debes activar Compute Optimizer para que analice recursos; estos también necesitan suficientes datos de métricas para recibir recomendaciones.; De forma predeterminada, analiza los últimos 14 días de métricas de uso de CloudWatch.; Enhanced infrastructure metrics es una función de pago que amplía a 93 días el período analizado para determinados recursos.; Las páginas de recomendaciones muestran cambios sugeridos; los detalles del recurso incluyen el historial y gráficos de uso proyectado.; Compute Optimizer admite instancias EC2, grupos de Auto Scaling, volúmenes EBS, funciones Lambda y servicios ECS en AWS Fargate, entre otros recursos.

chunks.title: Right-sizing with AWS Compute Optimizer
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company has opted in to AWS Compute Optimizer, and its Lambda functions have accumulated sufficient metrics. The team wants to reassess function memory configurations while considering the effect of a change on utilization and price-performance. Which approach meets these requirements MOST effectively?
Correct: Review Compute Optimizer's Lambda recommendations and utilization views before changing memory.
Why: The company needs a configuration decision informed by utilization, not merely a spending total. Compute Optimizer supports Lambda functions and provides recommendations and utilization views to help assess price-performance. A budget or billing export may expose costs, but neither option as proposed evaluates the effect of a memory change on utilization.
Wrong options: Set an AWS Budget on Lambda spending and choose a memory setting when the budget alerts. (A budget alert tracks a spending threshold rather than evaluating a function configuration.); Use cost allocation tags to separate Lambda charges by application before selecting memory. (Tags help attribute charges but do not assess the utilization effect of changing memory.); Export AWS Cost and Usage Report line items and choose memory based only on total Lambda charges. (Billing line items alone do not provide the requested utilization-based configuration evaluation.)

chunks.title: Right-sizing with AWS Compute Optimizer
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company wants to reduce costs for its EBS volumes and ECS services on AWS Fargate. It has not enabled resource-level optimization analysis, but both resource types have sufficient metrics. The team needs recommendations and utilization projections before deciding which configurations to change. Which two actions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Review Compute Optimizer's EBS and ECS-on-Fargate recommendations and projected-utilization graphs. + Opt in to AWS Compute Optimizer for the account.
Why: The team needs to enable analysis and then inspect resource-specific recommendations with utilization projections. Compute Optimizer requires opt-in, supports both EBS volumes and ECS services on AWS Fargate, and provides projected-utilization graphs for recommendations. Budgets and tags address spending controls or attribution, while the proposed Trusted Advisor check does not provide the requested comparison for both resources.
Wrong options: Activate cost allocation tags for the volumes and ECS services. (Cost attribution does not generate the requested resource-level optimization analysis.); Create AWS Budgets for EBS and Fargate spending thresholds. (Budget thresholds do not supply resource recommendations or utilization projections.); Review AWS Trusted Advisor best-practice checks for idle resources. (A best-practice check is not the requested recommendation and projected-utilization view for both resource types.)

chunks.title: ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere
chunks.text:
ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere. Use Amazon ECS Anywhere to run ECS tasks on customer-owned servers or VMs registered as external instances to an ECS cluster. Use Amazon EKS Anywhere for Kubernetes clusters on customer-owned infrastructure, including air-gapped environments; unlike regional Amazon EKS, its control plane and lifecycle are customer-managed.
When to use: Existing ECS workflows must schedule data-processing or outbound-traffic containers on on-premises servers.; A Kubernetes cluster must run on customer-owned infrastructure without a reliable connection to an AWS Region.; The team wants automated setup and lifecycle operations for an on-premises Kubernetes cluster and accepts responsibility for its maintenance.
Key facts: ECS Anywhere uses the EXTERNAL launch type for services and tasks on registered external instances.; ECS external instances require an IAM role and connectivity to the relevant AWS service endpoints.; ECS external instances do not support service load balancing, service discovery, or awsvpc task networking.; EKS Anywhere can run in air-gapped environments; customers manage its control plane and cluster lifecycle.; EKS Hybrid Nodes instead use customer-managed machines with an AWS-managed control plane in an AWS Region and require a reliable connection to that Region.
Gotchas: ECS Anywhere is a poor fit when the requirement depends on placing an on-premises web service behind an ECS service load balancer.; EKS Anywhere does not mean AWS manages the on-premises Kubernetes control plane.; Amazon EKS Distro supplies Kubernetes components, but it is not EKS Anywhere's cluster lifecycle automation.
Confused with: outposts: Outposts uses AWS-managed infrastructure at your site; ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere can use customer-owned machines.; local-zones-wavelength: Local Zones and Wavelength place compute near metro users or 5G devices, not on customer-owned on-premises servers.; vmware-cloud-on-aws: VMware Cloud on AWS preserves vSphere-based workloads and tooling; Anywhere options address running containers on customer-owned infrastructure.
ES: Usa Amazon ECS Anywhere para ejecutar tareas de ECS en servidores o VM propios, registrados como instancias externas en un clúster de ECS. Usa Amazon EKS Anywhere para clústeres de Kubernetes en infraestructura propia, incluso en entornos air-gapped; a diferencia de Amazon EKS regional, tú administras el plano de control y el ciclo de vida. ECS Anywhere usa el tipo de lanzamiento EXTERNAL para servicios y tareas en instancias externas registradas.; Las instancias externas de ECS necesitan un rol de IAM y conectividad con los endpoints correspondientes de AWS.; Las instancias externas de ECS no admiten balanceo de carga de servicios, descubrimiento de servicios ni el modo de red awsvpc para tareas.; EKS Anywhere puede funcionar en entornos air-gapped; tú administras su plano de control y el ciclo de vida del clúster.; En cambio, EKS Hybrid Nodes usa máquinas administradas por ti con un plano de control administrado por AWS en una región, y requiere una conexión confiable con esa región.

chunks.title: ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research laboratory runs Kubernetes workloads in a facility whose network must remain air-gapped. It owns the servers and accepts responsibility for maintaining its on-site clusters, but wants tooling that automates initial infrastructure setup and Kubernetes cluster lifecycle operations. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST cluster setup and lifecycle effort?
Correct: Deploy Amazon EKS Anywhere on the laboratory servers and manage the on-site cluster with its lifecycle tooling.
Why: The air-gapped network rules out EKS Hybrid Nodes, which needs a reliable connection to an AWS Region. EKS Anywhere can run in an air-gapped environment and simplifies infrastructure setup and Kubernetes cluster lifecycle operations. The laboratory still owns cluster maintenance; EKS Anywhere does not make the control plane AWS-managed. EKS Distro supplies Kubernetes components but leaves the choice and operation of management tooling to the customer.
Wrong options: Use Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes on the laboratory servers with an AWS-managed regional control plane. (EKS Hybrid Nodes requires a reliable connection to an AWS Region, which the air-gapped facility cannot provide.); Connect the laboratory's Kubernetes clusters with Amazon EKS Connector and manage their lifecycle in the EKS console. (EKS Connector provides console visibility but does not enable cluster management operations through the console.); Build self-managed Kubernetes clusters from Amazon EKS Distro components using tooling chosen by the laboratory. (EKS Distro provides components but leaves cluster management to the team's chosen tooling rather than supplying EKS Anywhere's lifecycle automation.)

chunks.title: ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere
chunks.text:
Scenario: A food manufacturer already uses Amazon ECS task definitions and wants to run containerized sensor-data processing on servers it owns at several plants. The tasks process local data and send results to AWS; they do not receive inbound application traffic. The company wants to retain its ECS workflows and avoid replacing the servers. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST infrastructure change?
Correct: Register the plant servers as Amazon ECS Anywhere external instances and run the tasks with the EXTERNAL launch type.
Why: The deciding constraints are customer-owned servers, existing ECS workflows, and tasks that do not need inbound traffic. ECS Anywhere registers those servers as external instances and runs tasks on them with the EXTERNAL launch type. Outposts would introduce AWS-managed infrastructure rather than reuse the servers. EKS Anywhere supports Kubernetes on customer-owned infrastructure, but it does not preserve the team's ECS workflow.
Wrong options: Install AWS Outposts at each plant and move the container workloads onto its AWS-managed infrastructure. (Outposts introduces AWS-managed infrastructure rather than using the company's existing servers.); Move the workloads to VMware Cloud on AWS and operate them with vSphere tooling. (This changes the workload location and tooling instead of running ECS tasks on the existing plant servers.); Deploy Amazon EKS Anywhere clusters on the plant servers and move the tasks into Kubernetes workloads. (EKS Anywhere can use those servers but requires a move from the existing ECS workflows to Kubernetes.)

chunks.title: Amazon EFS: shared NFS, performance/throughput modes, storage classes
chunks.text:
Amazon EFS: shared NFS, performance/throughput modes, storage classes. Amazon EFS is elastic, managed NFS file storage for shared access from Linux workloads, including EC2, containers, and Lambda. Choose a Regional file system when the shared files must remain available across Availability Zones; then match throughput and storage class to the access pattern.
When to use: Multiple Linux workloads need to read and write the same files using NFS or POSIX permissions.; Shared files must remain available if an Availability Zone becomes unavailable.; File-system throughput is unpredictable and should scale without provisioning capacity.; Infrequently accessed files can tolerate higher first-byte latency.
Key facts: EFS supports NFSv4.0 and NFSv4.1 and is accessible from EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda, and Fargate.; Regional EFS stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones; One Zone stores it in one Availability Zone.; General Purpose is the default performance mode and has lower per-operation latency than Max I/O.; Elastic throughput automatically scales with activity; Provisioned throughput specifies a level independently of file-system size; Bursting throughput scales with data stored in Standard.; Standard is intended for frequently accessed files needing the lowest latency. Infrequent Access and Archive have first-byte latencies of tens of milliseconds.; EFS does not support use with Windows-based EC2 instances.
Gotchas: One Zone EFS is not a substitute for Regional EFS when data must survive an Availability Zone loss.; Max I/O has higher per-operation latency than General Purpose and cannot be used with Elastic throughput.; Bursting throughput depends on the amount of data in Standard and uses burst credits; it is not the automatic, activity-based choice for unpredictable demand.; A shared NFS file system is not interchangeable with S3 object storage or an EBS block volume.
Confused with: s3-fundamentals: S3 stores objects; EFS provides shared NFS file-system access and POSIX permissions.; ebs-volume-types: EBS provides block volumes; EFS provides an elastic file system shared by many compute clients.; fsx-windows-file-server: Choose FSx for Windows File Server for Windows file-sharing requirements, not EFS for Windows-based EC2 instances.
ES: Amazon EFS ofrece almacenamiento de archivos NFS elástico y administrado para acceso compartido desde cargas Linux, incluidas EC2, contenedores y Lambda. Elige un sistema de archivos Regional si los archivos deben seguir disponibles entre Availability Zones; después ajusta el throughput y la clase de almacenamiento al patrón de acceso. EFS admite NFSv4.0 y NFSv4.1, y es accesible desde EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda y Fargate.; EFS Regional almacena los datos de forma redundante en varias Availability Zones; One Zone los almacena en una sola.; General Purpose es el performance mode predeterminado y tiene menor latencia por operación que Max I/O.; Elastic throughput se ajusta automáticamente a la actividad; Provisioned throughput establece un nivel independiente del tamaño; Bursting throughput depende de los datos almacenados en Standard.; Standard está orientada a archivos de acceso frecuente que necesitan la menor latencia. Infrequent Access y Archive tienen latencias de decenas de milisegundos para el primer byte.; EFS no admite su uso con instancias EC2 basadas en Windows.

chunks.title: Amazon EFS: shared NFS, performance/throughput modes, storage classes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher runs Linux web servers in several Availability Zones. Every server must read and update the same directory of uploaded files using the application's existing NFS file operations. The publisher does not want to manage file servers or provision storage capacity. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Mount a Regional Amazon EFS file system from the Linux web servers.
Why: The deciding requirements are shared NFS file operations across Linux servers and no storage-capacity management. Regional EFS provides an elastic, managed file system whose data is stored redundantly across Availability Zones. S3 is a plausible scalable alternative, but object access does not meet the application's NFS requirement.
Wrong options: Place the directory on EC2 instance store and replicate it between servers. (Instance-local storage and replication do not satisfy the requirement to avoid managing shared-file infrastructure.); Store uploads in Amazon S3 and have each server access them as objects. (S3 object access does not preserve the application's required NFS file operations.); Attach an Amazon EBS volume to each server and synchronize the directories. (Separate block volumes require synchronization and do not provide one managed shared NFS directory.)

chunks.title: Amazon EFS: shared NFS, performance/throughput modes, storage classes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization serves a Linux application whose users open and lock shared files during interactive sessions. The files are accessed frequently, and users notice added delay on individual file operations. Throughput demand is otherwise predictable. Which EFS configuration best meets the latency requirement?
Correct: Use General Purpose performance mode with Standard storage.
Why: This decision is about latency during frequent, interactive file operations, not maximizing a throughput setting. General Purpose has the lowest per-operation latency, and Standard is the EFS storage class for frequently accessed files needing the lowest latency. Max I/O is a tempting choice for parallel work, but it increases per-operation latency.
Wrong options: Use Max I/O performance mode with Archive storage. (Both Max I/O's per-operation latency and Archive's first-byte latency work against interactive access.); Use General Purpose performance mode with Infrequent Access storage. (Infrequent Access has higher first-byte latency and is not suited to frequently accessed interactive files.); Use Max I/O performance mode with Standard storage. (Max I/O has higher per-operation latency than General Purpose.)

chunks.title: Amazon EFS: shared NFS, performance/throughput modes, storage classes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A legal-services firm keeps older case files in a shared NFS directory used by Linux instances in multiple Availability Zones. Staff access these files infrequently and can tolerate tens of milliseconds of first-byte latency, but the files must remain available if an Availability Zone fails. The firm wants a storage class suited to this access pattern rather than the lowest-latency class. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use an EFS Regional file system with the files in Infrequent Access.
Why: The directory must retain NFS access and remain available through an Availability Zone failure, so Regional EFS is the appropriate file-system type. Infrequent Access matches files that are rarely opened and do not need Standard's lowest latency. One Zone misses the availability requirement, while S3 changes the required file-access model.
Wrong options: Use Amazon S3 for the older files and have the instances retrieve objects. (Retrieving S3 objects does not provide the required shared NFS directory.); Use an EFS Regional file system with all older files in Standard. (Standard targets frequently accessed, lowest-latency files rather than the stated infrequent-access pattern.); Use an EFS One Zone file system with the files in Infrequent Access. (One Zone stores data in one Availability Zone and does not meet the AZ-failure requirement.)

chunks.title: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
chunks.text:
AWS Elastic Beanstalk. AWS Elastic Beanstalk deploys web applications and provisions the resources needed to run them, including load balancing, health monitoring, and scaling. Choose it when developers want to deploy application code without configuring those resources individually, while the resources still run in their AWS account.
When to use: A team has a supported web application and wants a managed deployment workflow.; The application needs load balancing, health monitoring, and dynamic scaling without assembling each component separately.; Several application environments could benefit from sharing a managed cluster.
Key facts: Elastic Beanstalk Standard runs applications directly on Amazon EC2; it is cost effective for smaller or fewer applications and supports Windows applications.; Elastic Beanstalk Cluster runs applications on Amazon EKS and accepts a container image or source that Beanstalk builds into an image.; Cluster mode supports faster deployments and autoscaling, improved resource utilization across multiple environments, and managed OpenTelemetry integration.; Elastic Beanstalk supports Go, Java, .NET, Node.js, PHP, Python, Ruby, and Docker applications.; There is no additional charge for Elastic Beanstalk; you pay for the underlying AWS resources.
Gotchas: Managed provisioning does not mean the underlying resources disappear: Elastic Beanstalk creates them in your AWS account.; Do not assume every Beanstalk deployment runs directly on EC2; Cluster mode runs on EKS.; Do not choose Cluster solely because it sounds newer; Standard is suited to smaller or fewer applications and supports Windows applications.
Confused with: AWS Fargate: Choose Elastic Beanstalk for a managed web-application deployment workflow; Fargate is a choice for running containers without managing hosts.; Amazon EKS: Choose Elastic Beanstalk Cluster when you want Beanstalk to manage the application environment on EKS, rather than managing the EKS-based deployment yourself.
ES: AWS Elastic Beanstalk implementa aplicaciones web y aprovisiona los recursos necesarios para ejecutarlas, incluidos balanceo de carga, monitoreo de salud y escalado. Elígelo cuando quieras implementar código sin configurar esos recursos uno por uno, mientras los recursos permanecen en tu cuenta de AWS. Elastic Beanstalk Standard ejecuta aplicaciones directamente en Amazon EC2; es cost-effective para aplicaciones más pequeñas o menos numerosas y admite aplicaciones de Windows.; Elastic Beanstalk Cluster ejecuta aplicaciones en Amazon EKS y acepta una imagen de contenedor o código fuente que Beanstalk convierte en una imagen.; Cluster ofrece implementaciones y escalado más rápidos, mejor utilización de recursos entre varios entornos e integración administrada con OpenTelemetry.; Elastic Beanstalk admite aplicaciones en Go, Java, .NET, Node.js, PHP, Python y Ruby, además de Docker.; Elastic Beanstalk no tiene un cargo adicional; pagas los recursos subyacentes de AWS.

chunks.title: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional ticketing company has a Node.js web application ready to deploy. Its small development team wants AWS to provision load balancing, health monitoring, and dynamic scaling, but the resulting resources must reside in the company's AWS account. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy the application to an Elastic Beanstalk Standard environment.
Why: The deciding requirements are an existing Node.js web application and managed provisioning of load balancing, health monitoring, and scaling. Elastic Beanstalk supports Node.js and creates the environment's AWS resources in the customer's account. Standard is a suitable choice for this one application. Running on EC2 directly can work, but the team would have to configure the components that Beanstalk provisions.
Wrong options: Package the application as a container and deploy it as a service on AWS Fargate. (This introduces a container deployment rather than using Beanstalk's managed workflow for the existing Node.js application.); Package the application as a container and manage its deployment directly on Amazon EKS. (A direct EKS deployment adds container packaging and deployment work that the team wants to avoid.); Deploy the application on EC2 instances and configure load balancing, monitoring, and scaling separately. (This can meet the infrastructure requirements but makes the small team configure the components separately.)

chunks.title: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
chunks.text:
Scenario: A clinic runs a Windows-based .NET web application and wants to move it to AWS without first converting it into a container. The clinic expects to run only this application and wants managed environment provisioning rather than assembling its own scaling and health monitoring. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Deploy the application to an Elastic Beanstalk Standard environment.
Why: The deciding constraints are Windows support, no container conversion, and a single application. Elastic Beanstalk Standard supports Windows applications and is described as cost effective for smaller or fewer applications. It also provides managed environment provisioning. Cluster requires an image or source that Beanstalk builds into an image, so it is not the fit for a move that avoids container conversion.
Wrong options: Run the application on Windows EC2 instances and configure scaling and health monitoring independently. (This preserves the application but does not provide the requested managed environment provisioning.); Convert the application to a container image and deploy it with Elastic Beanstalk Cluster. (Cluster uses a container image, which conflicts with the requirement to move without container conversion.); Convert the application to a container image and manage its deployment directly on Amazon EKS. (This requires container conversion and puts deployment management on the clinic.)

chunks.title: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
chunks.text:
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS). AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) replicates supported on-premises or cloud-based servers to a low-cost staging area in a selected AWS Region. Choose it when the goal is to recover applications on AWS within minutes, rather than permanently migrate servers or migrate a database.
When to use: An existing server application needs disaster recovery on AWS without a permanent move.; The business needs recovery from the latest server state or an earlier point in time.; The team needs low-cost readiness and non-disruptive recovery drills.
Key facts: Replication goes to a staging area subnet in the selected AWS Region.; The staging area uses affordable storage and minimal compute during ongoing replication.; DRS converts servers to boot and run natively on AWS when instances are launched for a drill or recovery.; Recovery instances can launch within minutes from the latest server state or a previous point in time.; Teams can monitor replication, run non-disruptive drills, and replicate data back to the primary site for failback.
Gotchas: A requirement for ongoing disaster recovery is not the same as a one-time server migration.; Database migration alone does not recover an entire server application.; Keeping full-size recovery servers running continuously misses a requirement for minimal standby compute.
Confused with: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN): MGN is for rehosting servers on EC2; DRS is for ongoing disaster recovery with recovery drills and failback.; AWS Database Migration Service (DMS): DMS migrates databases; DRS recovers server-based applications.
ES: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) replica servidores compatibles, locales o en la nube, hacia un área de preparación de bajo costo en una AWS Region seleccionada. Elígelo cuando el objetivo sea recuperar aplicaciones en AWS en cuestión de minutos, no migrar servidores de forma permanente ni migrar una base de datos. La replicación llega a una subred de preparación en la AWS Region seleccionada.; Durante la replicación continua, el área de preparación usa almacenamiento asequible y recursos de cómputo mínimos.; DRS convierte los servidores para que arranquen y funcionen de forma nativa en AWS al lanzar instancias para simulacros o recuperación.; Puedes lanzar instancias de recuperación en cuestión de minutos desde el estado más reciente o desde un punto anterior en el tiempo.; Puedes supervisar la replicación, realizar simulacros sin interrupción y replicar datos de vuelta al sitio principal para el retorno.

chunks.title: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute keeps its primary application on supported servers outside AWS. It needs an AWS disaster recovery plan with low compute use during normal operation and regular recovery tests that do not interrupt researchers. The team wants to recover the application on AWS if the primary site becomes unavailable. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Monitor DRS replication and periodically launch recovery instances for non-disruptive drills. + Configure AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate the servers to a staging area subnet in the selected AWS Region.
Why: The institute needs both low-cost readiness and tests that do not interrupt its primary application. Configuring DRS replication to a staging subnet addresses readiness with minimal compute, while monitoring and non-disruptive drills validate recovery. Permanently migrating production misses the location constraint, and always-on full-size copies miss the compute constraint.
Wrong options: Use AWS DMS to migrate the application's database and treat the database migration as the server recovery plan. (Migrating a database does not recover the application servers.); Use AWS Application Migration Service to make EC2 the permanent production environment for the application. (A permanent migration conflicts with keeping the primary application outside AWS.); Run full-size copies of all application servers continuously on EC2 to keep the recovery environment ready. (Continuously running full-size servers conflicts with low compute use during normal operation.)

chunks.title: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company runs its editing application on servers in its own data center. It wants to keep production on premises but recover the application on AWS within minutes if the site fails. During normal operation, the AWS recovery environment must use minimal compute. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate the servers to a staging area in AWS and launch recovery instances when needed.
Why: The deciding requirements are recovery of existing servers within minutes and minimal compute during normal operation. DRS uses a low-cost staging area during replication and launches recovery instances when needed. MGN targets rehosting, while continuously running full-size copies misses the standby-compute constraint.
Wrong options: Use AWS Application Migration Service to rehost the servers on EC2 as the company's new production environment. (Rehosting production on EC2 does not satisfy the requirement to keep production on premises.); Use AWS DMS to migrate the application's database to AWS and retain the application servers on premises. (Migrating the database does not provide recovery of the application servers on AWS.); Maintain full-size copies of all application servers running on EC2 and switch to them after a site failure. (Continuously running full-size copies conflicts with the minimal-compute requirement.)

chunks.title: ElastiCache for Memcached
chunks.text:
ElastiCache for Memcached. Choose ElastiCache for Memcached for a simple, disposable object cache that benefits from multithreaded nodes and partitioning across nodes. If the cache needs replication, automatic failover, or Redis-style data structures, choose Valkey or Redis OSS instead.
When to use: Cached objects can be regenerated; cache replication and restore are not required.; The workload benefits from large nodes with multiple cores or threads.; Capacity must scale out and in by adding or removing cache nodes.
Key facts: Memcached is an in-memory key-value engine with a simple data model.; Memcached supports data partitioning and multithreading.; Memcached does not provide high availability through replication or automatic failover.; Memcached does not support Pub/Sub or sorted sets.; Backup and restore are available for serverless Memcached caches, but not for node-based Memcached clusters.
Gotchas: Do not choose Memcached when losing a cache node must trigger automatic failover to a replica.; Do not confuse partitioning across nodes with replication of cached data.; Do not claim Memcached never supports backups: serverless caches have backup and restore.; Memcached supports partitioning, but not online resharding.
Confused with: ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey: Choose Redis OSS or Valkey when replication, automatic failover, Pub/Sub, or sorted sets matter; choose Memcached for the simpler multithreaded cache.; DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX): DAX targets DynamoDB read caching; Memcached is the choice here for a simple, horizontally partitioned object cache.
ES: Elige ElastiCache for Memcached para una caché sencilla de objetos que puedes regenerar y que se beneficia de nodos multihilo y partición entre nodos. Si necesitas replicación, failover automático o estructuras de datos de Redis, elige Valkey o Redis OSS. Memcached es un motor en memoria de clave-valor con un modelo de datos sencillo.; Memcached admite partición de datos y ejecución multihilo.; Memcached no ofrece alta disponibilidad mediante replicación ni failover automático.; Memcached no admite Pub/Sub ni sorted sets.; Backup and restore está disponible para cachés Memcached serverless, pero no para clústeres Memcached basados en nodos.

chunks.title: ElastiCache for Memcached
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research portal uses a cache for computed chart objects that are recreated whenever they are missing. During enrollment periods, its engineers add cache nodes; afterward, they remove nodes. The team wants the simplest engine that supports this pattern and can use multiple threads on large nodes, and it does not need Pub/Sub, sorted sets, or cache replication. Which engine should the team select?
Correct: ElastiCache for Memcached
Why: The engineers explicitly prioritize a simple model, multithreaded large nodes, and the ability to add and remove cache nodes. AWS identifies these as reasons to choose Memcached. Redis OSS and Valkey with cluster mode enabled can partition data, but they do not meet the multithreaded-engine requirement. The portal also has no need for their Pub/Sub, sorted-set, or replication features.
Wrong options: ElastiCache for Valkey with cluster mode enabled (It can scale a partitioned cache, but does not match the specified need for multithreading on large nodes.); DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) (It targets DynamoDB read caching rather than the requested choice of a simple, multithreaded ElastiCache engine.); ElastiCache for Redis OSS with cluster mode enabled (It supports partitioning, but does not provide the multithreaded-engine characteristic the team requests.)

chunks.title: ElastiCache for Memcached
chunks.text:
Scenario: An architecture team is assigning cache engines to five new workloads. It wants to use ElastiCache for Memcached where a simple, multithreaded object cache can scale by adding nodes and where losing cached entries is acceptable. Which TWO workloads best fit that decision? (Choose two.)
Correct: A product catalog caches regenerable item objects and adds cache nodes during promotions. + A mapping service caches reproducible tile objects on large nodes and wants multiple threads.
Why: The team is looking for disposable object caches that benefit from Memcached's simple model, node scaling, and multithreading. The product catalog and mapping service satisfy those conditions without asking the cache to preserve data. The event dashboard and sports site require Pub/Sub and sorted sets, respectively, which Memcached lacks. The account portal requires replication and automatic failover, which Memcached also lacks.
Wrong options: A live event dashboard needs Pub/Sub to distribute updates to connected viewers. (Memcached does not support the Pub/Sub capability required by this workload.); An account portal requires cache replicas and automatic failover for its active cache. (Memcached provides neither high availability through replication nor automatic failover.); A sports site needs sorted sets to maintain live rankings in its cache. (Memcached does not support sorted sets, so Valkey or Redis OSS is a better match.)

chunks.title: ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey
chunks.text:
ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey. Choose ElastiCache for Valkey or Redis OSS when an in-memory cache or session store needs read replicas, Multi-AZ failover, or features such as sorted sets for leaderboards and pub/sub. For node-based deployments, pair a primary with a replica in another Availability Zone when the cache must remain available after a primary failure.
When to use: Sessions or cached data must remain available if a cache primary or Availability Zone fails.; Read-heavy traffic needs to be offloaded to cache read replicas.; The application needs Redis/Valkey features such as sorted sets for leaderboards or pub/sub.; A Valkey workload needs persistence beyond ordinary cache replication.
Key facts: Valkey and Redis OSS support read replicas; Memcached does not.; A read replica serves reads and can be promoted if the primary fails. Node-based replicas can be placed in different Availability Zones within the same Region.; ElastiCache Serverless manages cache capacity and maintains replicas automatically; node-based clusters give you control over nodes and placement.; Backup and Restore supports Valkey and Redis OSS snapshots. Node-based Valkey also offers durability through a Multi-AZ transactional log.; For Valkey durability, synchronous writes are designed for zero data loss; asynchronous writes prioritize write latency and can lose recent data during a failure.
Gotchas: A Memcached cluster is not a substitute when the requirement explicitly calls for read replicas or replica promotion.; A DAX cache targets DynamoDB reads; it does not replace a session store or leaderboard engine.; A read replica is a warm standby, not a guarantee of zero data loss: ordinary replication is asynchronous.; Snapshots support recovery but do not provide automatic failover for live traffic.
Confused with: ElastiCache for Memcached: Good for a simple cache without replication needs; choose Valkey or Redis OSS when read replicas and failover are required.; DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX): DAX accelerates DynamoDB reads with minimal application changes; Valkey or Redis OSS fits sessions and Redis-style data structures.
ES: Elige ElastiCache for Valkey o Redis OSS cuando una caché en memoria o un almacén de sesiones necesite réplicas de lectura, Multi-AZ failover o funciones como sorted sets para tablas de posiciones y pub/sub. En un despliegue basado en nodos, coloca una réplica en otra Availability Zone si la caché debe seguir disponible cuando falle el nodo primario. Valkey y Redis OSS admiten réplicas de lectura; Memcached no.; Una réplica atiende lecturas y puede ascenderse si falla el primario. En clústeres basados en nodos, puedes ubicarla en otra Availability Zone de la misma Region.; ElastiCache Serverless administra la capacidad y mantiene las réplicas automáticamente; un clúster basado en nodos te da control sobre los nodos y su ubicación.; Backup and Restore admite snapshots de Valkey y Redis OSS. Valkey basado en nodos también ofrece durabilidad mediante un registro transaccional Multi-AZ.; En la durabilidad de Valkey, las escrituras síncronas están diseñadas para evitar la pérdida de datos; las asíncronas priorizan la latencia y pueden perder datos recientes ante una falla.

chunks.title: ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media service caches results of expensive recommendation calculations and also keeps temporary user sessions. Traffic spikes unpredictably, and the team does not want to choose cache node sizes or manage replicas; the cache must remain highly available. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey to hold calculation results and temporary sessions.
Why: The decisive constraints are unpredictable demand, high availability, and avoiding node and replica management. ElastiCache Serverless monitors usage, scales capacity, and maintains replicas automatically. A node-based Valkey cluster could meet the availability requirement but still requires the team to choose nodes and plan capacity. DAX does not remove the need for a separate session store in this scenario.
Wrong options: Run a node-based ElastiCache for Memcached cluster and add nodes when traffic rises. (The team would still need to plan nodes and capacity, contrary to the stated operating constraint.); Run a node-based ElastiCache for Valkey cluster with replicas across Availability Zones. (It can provide availability, but the team must select node types and capacity.); Put DAX in front of the service’s database and manage a separate session store. (DAX is for DynamoDB reads and a separate session store adds work the team wants to avoid.)

chunks.title: ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey
chunks.text:
Scenario: A payment platform wants to keep tokenization state in ElastiCache for Valkey and retrieve it with microsecond read latency. Unlike disposable cache entries, an acknowledged write must be protected against data loss even if cache nodes fail; the platform accepts higher write latency for this protection. Which solution meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Enable synchronous durability on a node-based Valkey cluster to persist writes across Availability Zones before acknowledgement.
Why: The key requirement is protecting acknowledged writes from data loss, even at the cost of write latency. Node-based Valkey synchronous durability persists writes in a Multi-AZ transactional log before responding and is designed for zero data loss while retaining microsecond reads. Asynchronous durability responds before persistence and can lose recent data in a failure. Neither a read replica nor periodic snapshots provide the same acknowledged-write guarantee.
Wrong options: Enable asynchronous Valkey durability so writes return before persistence in the Multi-AZ transactional log. (Asynchronous durability can lose recently acknowledged writes during a failure.); Create a Valkey read replica in another Availability Zone and rely on ordinary replication for write durability. (Ordinary primary-to-replica replication is asynchronous and cannot guarantee the stated protection.); Configure recurring Valkey snapshots and restore the latest snapshot after cache node failures. (A periodic snapshot cannot protect every acknowledged write made since that snapshot.)

chunks.title: TLS termination on load balancers with ACM and SNI
chunks.text:
TLS termination on load balancers with ACM and SNI. An ALB HTTPS listener terminates client TLS at the load balancer and decrypts requests before sending them to targets. Choose it when the load balancer must handle HTTPS requests; choose an NLB TCP listener on port 443 when encrypted traffic must reach targets without load-balancer decryption.
When to use: Clients need HTTPS, and TLS should terminate at an Application Load Balancer.; An HTTPS listener needs a certificate available from ACM.; A listener needs a default certificate and additional certificates in its SNI list.
Key facts: An ALB HTTPS listener requires a server certificate and a security policy.; The listener uses the certificate to terminate the front-end connection and decrypt client requests.; You can select the default certificate from certificates available in ACM and add certificates to the listener’s certificate list.; The default certificate is also added to the SNI list.; An NLB TCP listener on port 443 passes encrypted traffic to targets without decrypting it.
Gotchas: An ALB HTTPS listener is not TLS passthrough: it decrypts the client connection.; A certificate alone is insufficient to configure a secure listener; a security policy is also required.; A forwarding default rule needs an available target group.
Confused with: NLB TCP listener on port 443: It passes encrypted traffic through without load-balancer decryption; an ALB HTTPS listener terminates the client TLS connection.
ES: Un HTTPS listener de ALB termina el TLS del cliente en el load balancer y descifra las solicitudes antes de enviarlas a los targets. Elígelo cuando el load balancer deba manejar solicitudes HTTPS; elige un TCP listener de NLB en el puerto 443 si el tráfico cifrado debe llegar a los targets sin que el load balancer lo descifre. Un HTTPS listener de ALB requiere un certificado de servidor y una security policy.; El listener usa el certificado para terminar la conexión frontal y descifrar las solicitudes de los clientes.; Puedes seleccionar el certificado predeterminado entre los disponibles en ACM y agregar certificados a la certificate list del listener.; El certificado predeterminado también se agrega a la SNI list.; Un TCP listener de NLB en el puerto 443 pasa tráfico cifrado a los targets sin descifrarlo.

chunks.title: TLS termination on load balancers with ACM and SNI
chunks.text:
Scenario: A community theater is updating its ALB so that visitors who arrive at its HTTPS endpoint receive a permanent redirect to a new URL. The ALB must terminate the visitors’ TLS connections, and the team has a server certificate available in ACM. Which two configurations meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Set the HTTPS listener’s default action to redirect to the new URL with HTTP 301. + Configure an ALB HTTPS listener with the ACM certificate and a security policy.
Why: The visitors need an HTTPS endpoint that terminates TLS and issues a permanent redirect. An ALB HTTPS listener needs a certificate and security policy, and its redirect action can use HTTP 301. Forwarding to a target group misses the redirect requirement, while TCP passthrough misses TLS termination at the load balancer.
Wrong options: Use an NLB TCP listener on port 443 to pass visitors’ encrypted connections through. (TCP passthrough does not terminate visitors’ TLS connections at the load balancer.); Configure an ALB HTTP listener with the new URL as its redirect destination. (An HTTP listener does not provide the required HTTPS endpoint for visitors.); Set the HTTPS listener’s default action to forward to an available target group. (A forward action sends requests to targets instead of redirecting visitors to the new URL.)

chunks.title: TLS termination on load balancers with ACM and SNI
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization sends encrypted connections to application targets. Its security rule prohibits the load balancer from decrypting client traffic; the encrypted traffic must pass through to the targets. The team does not need the load balancer to process HTTP requests. Which listener design meets the requirement?
Correct: Use an NLB TCP listener on port 443 to pass the encrypted traffic to targets.
Why: The security rule excludes TLS termination at the load balancer. An NLB TCP listener on port 443 passes encrypted traffic to targets without decrypting it. An ALB HTTPS listener, even with certificates in its SNI list, terminates the client connection and decrypts requests.
Wrong options: Use an ALB HTTPS listener with a redirect default action. (The HTTPS listener decrypts the front-end connection, and a redirect does not pass the connection through to targets.); Use an ALB HTTPS listener with certificates in its SNI list. (Adding certificates does not change the ALB HTTPS listener’s front-end decryption behavior.); Use an ALB HTTPS listener with an ACM certificate and a forward action. (An ALB HTTPS listener terminates the front-end TLS connection and decrypts client requests.)

chunks.title: Elastic Load Balancing: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB
chunks.text:
Elastic Load Balancing: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB. Choose an Application Load Balancer (ALB) for HTTP/HTTPS routing based on request content, a Network Load Balancer (NLB) for TCP/UDP traffic or a static IP address per Availability Zone, and a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) for virtual appliances. Check cross-zone behavior separately from the load balancer type.
When to use: Use ALB when HTTP hostnames, paths, headers, or other request attributes determine the target group.; Use NLB for transport-layer traffic, low-latency requirements, or static IP addresses per Availability Zone.; Use GWLB to distribute traffic to third-party virtual appliances.
Key facts: ALB operates at the application layer; NLB is recommended for Layer 4 TCP/UDP traffic.; GWLB routes each flow consistently to a target appliance and exchanges traffic with appliances using GENEVE on port 6081.; With cross-zone load balancing enabled, a node can route to targets in all enabled Availability Zones; without it, the node routes only to targets in its own zone.; ALB has cross-zone load balancing enabled at the load balancer level, although it can be disabled at the target group level. NLB and GWLB have it disabled by default.; A Network Load Balancer can forward to an Application Load Balancer-type target group when an application needs both an NLB static IP address per Availability Zone and ALB features.
Gotchas: An ALB does not become a Layer 4 load balancer merely because its listeners use TCP ports.; A static IP requirement does not mean giving up ALB request routing: an NLB can forward to an ALB.; NLB routing of an individual TCP connection to one target for its lifetime is not a reason to choose NLB for HTTP content-based routing.
Confused with: Network Load Balancer: Choose NLB for TCP/UDP or static IP addresses per Availability Zone; choose ALB when HTTP request content controls routing.; Gateway Load Balancer: Choose GWLB for a fleet of virtual appliances, not for ordinary HTTP path routing or a TCP application tier.
ES: Elige Application Load Balancer (ALB) para enrutar HTTP/HTTPS según el contenido de la solicitud, Network Load Balancer (NLB) para tráfico TCP/UDP o una dirección IP estática por Availability Zone y Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) para dispositivos virtuales. Evalúa cross-zone load balancing por separado del tipo de balanceador. ALB opera en la capa de aplicación; NLB se recomienda para tráfico TCP/UDP de Layer 4.; GWLB dirige cada flujo de forma consistente al mismo dispositivo de destino e intercambia tráfico con los dispositivos mediante GENEVE en el puerto 6081.; Con cross-zone load balancing habilitado, un nodo puede enviar tráfico a destinos de todas las Availability Zones habilitadas; sin él, solo envía tráfico a destinos de su propia zona.; ALB tiene cross-zone load balancing habilitado a nivel del balanceador, aunque puede deshabilitarse a nivel del grupo de destinos. NLB y GWLB lo tienen deshabilitado de forma predeterminada.; Un Network Load Balancer puede enviar tráfico a un grupo de destinos de tipo Application Load Balancer cuando se necesitan tanto una IP estática por Availability Zone como funciones de ALB.

chunks.title: Elastic Load Balancing: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB
chunks.text:
Scenario: A security team is deploying a fleet of third-party traffic inspection appliances. Packets belonging to the same flow must keep reaching the same appliance while the fleet scales across Availability Zones. Which load balancer meets this requirement MOST directly?
Correct: Use a Gateway Load Balancer with the inspection appliances as targets.
Why: The targets are inspection appliances, and packets in a flow must continue to reach the same appliance. GWLB uses a 5-tuple flow hash to select an appliance and consistently routes subsequent packets in that flow to it. An NLB keeps an individual TCP connection on one target, but that is not the specified appliance-flow solution. ALB rules operate on HTTP request attributes.
Wrong options: Use a Network Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener for the inspection appliances. (NLB connection routing is not the GWLB appliance-routing behavior required for packets in the same flow.); Use an Application Load Balancer with host-header rules for the inspection appliances. (ALB host-header rules process HTTP requests rather than keeping arbitrary packet flows on an appliance.); Use an Application Load Balancer with a target group for each inspection appliance. (ALB target groups do not supply the stated packet-flow routing to third-party appliances.)

chunks.title: Elastic Load Balancing: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB
chunks.text:
Scenario: A game studio uses a Network Load Balancer for a TCP service in two enabled Availability Zones. One zone currently has far fewer registered targets, and operators want each load balancer node to be able to use healthy targets in either enabled zone. Which change meets this requirement?
Correct: Enable cross-zone load balancing on the existing Network Load Balancer.
Why: The requirement is for every load balancer node to reach targets in both enabled zones. Cross-zone load balancing provides that routing scope, and it is disabled by default on an NLB. Adding listeners does not change which zones a node can route to. Disabling a zone prevents its registered targets from receiving traffic.
Wrong options: Leave the NLB at its default cross-zone setting and add a TCP listener in each zone. (With cross-zone balancing disabled, each NLB node routes only to targets in its own zone.); Disable the zone with fewer targets while keeping its targets registered. (Targets in a disabled zone receive no traffic even if they remain registered.); Replace the NLB with a Gateway Load Balancer and retain the TCP application targets. (GWLB is intended for virtual appliances and also has cross-zone balancing disabled by default.)

chunks.title: Elastic Load Balancing: ALB vs NLB vs GWLB
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher is splitting its HTTPS website into an article service and a subscription service. Both services will run on EC2 instances, and requests for /subscribe must reach a different target group than requests for /articles. Which load balancer meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use an Application Load Balancer with HTTPS listener rules that forward each path to its target group.
Why: The deciding requirement is routing HTTPS requests to different target groups by URL path. An ALB evaluates listener rules and supports path conditions, so one load balancer can make that decision. An NLB is appropriate for transport-layer connections but cannot use an HTTP path to select a target group. GWLB addresses virtual-appliance traffic rather than this website-routing need.
Wrong options: Use a Gateway Load Balancer with each service registered as a target appliance. (GWLB is intended for virtual appliances and does not provide the required HTTP path rules.); Use a Network Load Balancer with separate TCP target groups for each service. (An NLB selects targets for connections rather than routing requests by URL path.); Use one Network Load Balancer for each service and select between them in application code. (Application-side selection adds work and does not provide the requested path-based listener routing.)

chunks.title: Amazon EMR (Spark/Hadoop big data processing)
chunks.text:
Amazon EMR (Spark/Hadoop big data processing). Amazon EMR is a managed cluster platform for processing large amounts of data with big data frameworks such as Apache Spark and Apache Hadoop. Choose it when the requirement is to run a framework-based processing workflow, rather than simply query data or produce dashboards.
When to use: A large-scale workflow must run on Apache Spark or Apache Hadoop.; A team needs to process or transform large amounts of data involving Amazon S3 or Amazon DynamoDB.; The workload requires a managed cluster platform for big data analytics.
Key facts: Amazon EMR simplifies running big data frameworks on AWS.; Supported examples include Apache Hadoop and Apache Spark.; EMR can process data for analytics and business intelligence workloads.; EMR can transform and move large amounts of data into and out of stores such as Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB.
Gotchas: A requirement to query S3 data with ad-hoc SQL does not, by itself, call for an EMR cluster.; A requirement for business-user dashboards is not the same as a requirement to run a big data processing framework.; Do not choose a service solely because it can perform some transformation; check whether the workflow specifically requires Spark or Hadoop on a managed cluster.
Confused with: Amazon Athena: Athena fits ad-hoc SQL on S3; EMR fits framework-based big data processing.; AWS Glue: Glue fits serverless ETL and schema discovery; EMR fits a managed cluster for frameworks such as Spark and Hadoop.; Amazon Redshift: Redshift fits data warehousing and BI queries; EMR fits big data framework workflows.
ES: Amazon EMR es una plataforma de clústeres administrada para procesar grandes volúmenes de datos con frameworks como Apache Spark y Apache Hadoop. Elígela cuando el requisito sea ejecutar un flujo de procesamiento basado en esos frameworks, no solo consultar datos o crear dashboards. Amazon EMR simplifica la ejecución de frameworks de big data en AWS.; Apache Hadoop y Apache Spark son dos ejemplos de frameworks compatibles.; EMR puede procesar datos para análisis e inteligencia de negocios.; EMR puede transformar y mover grandes volúmenes de datos hacia y desde almacenes como Amazon S3 y Amazon DynamoDB.

chunks.title: Amazon EMR (Spark/Hadoop big data processing)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company has an existing Apache Spark workflow that processes a large archive of files in Amazon S3. The engineering team wants a managed cluster platform on AWS to run the workflow without replacing its processing framework. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Run the Apache Spark workflow on an Amazon EMR cluster.
