Why: The deciding requirement is to keep the existing Apache Spark workflow and run it on a managed cluster platform. Amazon EMR is designed to simplify running Spark and other big data frameworks on AWS. Athena could query data in S3, but ad-hoc SQL would not run the specified workflow.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Athena to run ad-hoc SQL queries against the S3 archive. (Athena addresses ad-hoc SQL queries, not the requirement to run the existing Spark workflow.); Use an AWS Glue crawler to discover the archive's schemas. (Schema discovery does not run the company's existing Spark processing workflow.); Load the archive into Amazon Redshift for BI queries. (A data warehouse for BI queries does not meet the requirement to run the existing Spark workflow.)

chunks.title: Amazon EMR (Spark/Hadoop big data processing)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company receives large datasets from several partners in Amazon S3. Its analysts must run an established Apache Hadoop processing workflow before the resulting data is used for reports. The company wants an AWS-managed cluster platform that supports that workflow. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Use Amazon EMR to run the Apache Hadoop workflow on a managed cluster.
Why: The reports are downstream of an established Apache Hadoop processing workflow, so querying or visualizing the input data is insufficient. Amazon EMR provides a managed cluster platform for running Hadoop at large scale. Redshift is a plausible choice for reporting queries, but it does not satisfy the stated Hadoop-processing requirement.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Athena to query the partner data directly in S3. (Direct SQL queries do not execute the established Hadoop workflow.); Use Amazon Redshift to run warehouse queries over the partner data. (Warehouse queries do not run the required Hadoop workflow.); Use Amazon Quick to create dashboards from the partner data. (Dashboards present data but do not perform the required Hadoop processing.)

chunks.title: Encryption at rest vs in transit
chunks.text:
Encryption at rest vs in transit. Identify where data needs protection. Use encryption at rest, such as encryption with AWS KMS, for stored data; use TLS with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate for data moving across a connection; use client-side encryption when data must be encrypted before it leaves the client.
When to use: Stored data must be unintelligible to unauthorized parties: choose encryption at rest.; A connection must protect data while it travels: choose TLS.; Data must be encrypted before it reaches AWS: choose client-side encryption.
Key facts: Encryption renders data unintelligible to unauthorized access.; AWS KMS is an example of a mechanism for encryption at rest.; ACM certificates used with TLS are an example of encryption in transit.; Client-side encryption acts before data is sent to AWS.
Gotchas: Encrypting stored data does not, by itself, satisfy a requirement to use TLS on a connection.; TLS on a connection does not, by itself, encrypt data in storage.; If data must be encrypted before it reaches AWS, encryption performed only after arrival is too late.
Confused with: Encryption at rest vs. TLS: Encryption at rest protects stored data; TLS protects data on a connection.; Encryption at rest vs. client-side encryption: Client-side encryption meets a requirement to encrypt data before it leaves the client.
ES: Identifica dónde se necesita proteger los datos. Usa cifrado en reposo, por ejemplo con AWS KMS, para datos almacenados; usa TLS con un certificado de AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) para datos que viajan por una conexión; usa cifrado del lado del cliente cuando los datos deban cifrarse antes de salir del cliente. El cifrado vuelve los datos ininteligibles para el acceso no autorizado.; AWS KMS es un ejemplo de mecanismo para el cifrado en reposo.; Los certificados de ACM usados con TLS son un ejemplo de cifrado en tránsito.; El cifrado del lado del cliente actúa antes de enviar los datos a AWS.

chunks.title: Encryption at rest vs in transit
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher receives manuscripts over connections that already use TLS. Its new policy requires manuscripts to be encrypted while stored in AWS, without adding encryption logic to the submission application. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use encryption at rest with AWS KMS for the stored manuscripts.
Why: The deciding requirement concerns manuscripts while they are stored, not while they travel to AWS. Encryption at rest with AWS KMS addresses that layer without adding client-side encryption logic. An ACM certificate used with TLS protects a connection, so it does not resolve the new storage requirement.
Wrong options: Use an ACM certificate with TLS for the submission connection. (TLS protects the connection, which is already covered, rather than the stored manuscripts.); Encrypt manuscripts in the submission application before sending them to AWS. (This adds the application encryption logic that the publisher wants to avoid.); Set policies governing access to encryption keys, but do not encrypt the manuscripts. (Controlling access to keys does not make unencrypted manuscripts unintelligible.)

chunks.title: Encryption at rest vs in transit
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company already encrypts customer records while they are stored in AWS. A security review finds that its public web endpoint must also protect the browser-to-endpoint connection with TLS. The company does not require encryption before data leaves the browser. Which solution meets the new requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use an ACM certificate with TLS on the public web endpoint.
Why: The records are already encrypted while stored, so the missing control is protection for data in transit. An ACM certificate used with TLS addresses the browser-to-endpoint connection. More AWS KMS encryption of the stored records targets the wrong layer, while browser-side encryption is not the TLS control requested.
Wrong options: Encrypt records in the browser before they are submitted. (Client-side encryption is not the requested TLS protection for the connection.); Change access policies for the keys protecting stored records. (Key access policies do not provide TLS for the public web endpoint.); Apply additional AWS KMS encryption to the stored customer records. (Additional storage encryption does not provide TLS for the browser connection.)

chunks.title: Event-driven architecture patterns
chunks.text:
Event-driven architecture patterns. Event-driven architectures let producers emit events that independent consumers process asynchronously. Choose this pattern when components must scale at different rates or new consumers must be added without changing the producer; reconsider it when consistent, very low latency is essential.
When to use: Incoming work is unpredictable, and downstream processing is slower than event production.; New consumers should react to events without the producer knowing about them.; An S3 upload or another service event should start a narrow Lambda task.
Key facts: Amazon S3 can invoke Lambda directly when an object is uploaded.; With an Amazon SQS event source mapping, Lambda polls the queue and invokes the function.; Amazon SQS can buffer messages between components that process at different rates.; Amazon EventBridge rules can filter and route events based on their content.; Asynchronous workflows commonly involve variable latency and eventual consistency.
Gotchas: A chain of synchronous Lambda-to-Lambda calls adds cost and complexity instead of providing loose coupling.; A function that writes to the same S3 resource whose events invoke it can create a recursive loop.; Event-driven processing is not a good default for workloads requiring consistent, extremely low latency.
Confused with: 
ES: Las arquitecturas event-driven permiten que los productores emitan eventos que consumidores independientes procesan de forma asíncrona. Elige este patrón cuando los componentes deban escalar a ritmos distintos o cuando necesites agregar consumidores sin cambiar al productor; reconsidera su uso si es indispensable una latencia muy baja y constante. Amazon S3 puede invocar Lambda directamente cuando se carga un objeto.; Con un event source mapping de Amazon SQS, Lambda consulta la cola e invoca la función.; Amazon SQS puede almacenar mensajes temporalmente entre componentes que procesan a diferentes ritmos.; Las reglas de Amazon EventBridge pueden filtrar y dirigir eventos según su contenido.; Los flujos asíncronos suelen presentar latencia variable y consistencia eventual.

chunks.title: Event-driven architecture patterns
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics platform publishes shipment status changes for internal applications. Different applications need different event types, and additional teams expect to subscribe later without requiring changes to the shipment producer. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST coupling?
Correct: Publish shipment events to Amazon EventBridge and use rules to route them by event content.
Why: The producer must remain unaware of both current and future consumers, while consumers need events selected by content. Amazon EventBridge rules provide content-based filtering and routing for this arrangement. Direct Lambda invocation can process an event, but it requires the producer to know each destination.
Wrong options: Combine the producer and current consumers into one Lambda function with separate code paths. (A single function ties consumer changes to the producer and makes future extensions harder.); Have the producer invoke each current consumer's Lambda function directly when a shipment changes. (The producer must know and be updated for each consumer, including future ones.); Have every consumer poll the shipment application for changes it needs. (Consumer polling adds integration work and does not use events to route relevant changes.)

chunks.title: Event-driven architecture patterns
chunks.text:
Scenario: A nonprofit receives donation records in bursts, but its validation task processes records at a steadier pace. Records are already being placed in an Amazon SQS queue. The team wants Lambda to run the validation task as messages become available without writing a queue-polling application. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure an Amazon SQS event source mapping for the validator Lambda function.
Why: The records are already in SQS, and the team specifically wants to avoid maintaining polling code. An SQS event source mapping lets Lambda retrieve messages and invoke the validation function. A scheduled function could inspect the queue, but it adds application-managed polling rather than using Lambda's supported integration.
Wrong options: Replace the SQS queue with direct Amazon S3 upload events that invoke the validator. (S3 events do not consume the records already buffered in the required SQS queue.); Have the donation producer invoke the validator Lambda function synchronously before placing each record in SQS. (Synchronous validation makes the producer wait and bypasses the queue's buffering role.); Schedule a Lambda function to inspect the SQS queue and invoke the validator for messages it finds. (Custom scheduled inspection adds polling logic that Lambda event source mapping already handles.)

chunks.title: Event-driven architecture patterns
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company receives unpredictable bursts of image uploads in an Amazon S3 bucket. Each new image needs a short metadata-extraction task, after which a slower cataloging service can process the metadata asynchronously. The team wants managed event integrations and must avoid a design in which the extraction function triggers itself. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Send extracted metadata to Amazon SQS and use an event source mapping for the cataloging Lambda function. + Configure S3 upload events to invoke a focused metadata-extraction Lambda function.
Why: The design needs an event when an image arrives and a buffer between fast extraction and slower cataloging. S3 can directly invoke a focused Lambda function, and an SQS event source mapping lets Lambda consume buffered metadata for cataloging. Writing extraction output to the triggering S3 resource risks a recursive loop; synchronous cataloging would instead make extraction wait.
Wrong options: Have the extraction function invoke the cataloging Lambda function synchronously for every upload. (Synchronous invocation makes extraction wait for the slower cataloging task.); Have the extraction function write its output to the same S3 location that triggers it. (Writing to its own triggering S3 resource risks recursive invocations.); Run a scheduled Lambda function that repeatedly lists the bucket to discover new uploads. (Custom discovery polling adds work when S3 can emit upload events directly.)

chunks.title: Amazon EventBridge event bus, rules, scheduler and pipes
chunks.text:
Amazon EventBridge event bus, rules, scheduler and pipes. Amazon EventBridge connects applications through events. Choose an event bus to route events from AWS services, third-party software, or custom applications to multiple targets; choose EventBridge Scheduler for managed recurring or one-time invocations.
When to use: Events from multiple sources need filtering and routing to different consumers.; A stream needs transformation or enrichment before its events reach one target, possibly an event bus.; A team wants to replace a server that runs scheduled tasks.
Key facts: An event bus can deliver an event to zero or more targets.; Event buses are suited to many-source, many-target routing and can transform events before delivery.; Each EventBridge pipe connects one source to one target and can transform or enrich events.; A pipe can send events from a DynamoDB stream to an event bus for routing to multiple targets.; EventBridge Scheduler supports cron expressions, rate expressions, and one-time invocations.
Gotchas: A pipe alone is point-to-point; use an event bus when events must reach multiple targets.; EventBridge Scheduler is the recommended managed scheduling option; scheduled rules on the default event bus can also invoke targets on a schedule.; SNS fan-out is not the deciding feature when the requirement is to route events from many AWS, third-party, and custom sources.
Confused with: Amazon SNS: SNS pushes a message to subscribers; EventBridge event buses are designed to route events from many sources to many targets.; Amazon MQ: Choose Amazon MQ for applications that must retain existing messaging protocols; choose EventBridge for event routing without that compatibility requirement.; AWS Step Functions: Step Functions orchestrates the steps and state of a workflow; EventBridge routes events to consumers.
ES: Amazon EventBridge conecta aplicaciones mediante eventos. Elige un event bus para dirigir eventos de servicios de AWS, software de terceros o aplicaciones propias a varios destinos; elige EventBridge Scheduler para invocaciones recurrentes o de una sola vez sin administrar un servidor. Un event bus puede entregar un evento a cero o más destinos.; Los event buses son adecuados para dirigir eventos de muchas fuentes a muchos destinos y pueden transformar eventos antes de entregarlos.; Cada EventBridge pipe conecta una fuente con un destino y puede transformar o enriquecer eventos.; Un pipe puede enviar eventos de un DynamoDB stream a un event bus, que después los dirige a varios destinos.; EventBridge Scheduler admite expresiones cron, expresiones rate e invocaciones de una sola vez.

chunks.title: Amazon EventBridge event bus, rules, scheduler and pipes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A property management company runs a small server solely to invoke a maintenance application every night. It also needs to schedule occasional one-time inspection reminders and wants to retire the server. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use EventBridge Scheduler for a recurring nightly invocation and one-time reminder invocations.
Why: The company needs both recurring and one-time invocations without maintaining its cron server. EventBridge Scheduler is a managed service that supports cron or rate schedules as well as one-time invocations. An event bus could route an event produced by the server, but that design fails to retire the server. SNS and SQS address message delivery rather than the stated scheduling need.
Wrong options: Place reminder messages in an SQS queue and have the maintenance application poll for due work. (A queue buffers messages but does not replace the requested managed scheduling of invocations.); Publish maintenance events to an SNS topic and ask subscribers to check whether each event is due. (SNS distributes published messages but does not meet the requirement for managed recurring and one-time schedules.); Send a daily event to an EventBridge event bus from the existing server and route it to the application. (This retains the server that the company needs to retire.)

chunks.title: Amazon EventBridge event bus, rules, scheduler and pipes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A utilities company records meter changes in a DynamoDB stream. It needs to enrich each change before routing selected events to several internal applications, and it must replace a server that invokes a separate reconciliation application on a recurring schedule. Which TWO components meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use EventBridge Scheduler to invoke the reconciliation application on a recurring schedule. + Use an EventBridge pipe to enrich stream events and deliver them to an EventBridge event bus for routing.
Why: The scenario has two distinct needs: enrich a stream before many-target routing, and replace a recurring-invocation server. A pipe can enrich DynamoDB stream events and target an event bus, which then routes events to multiple applications. EventBridge Scheduler supplies the managed recurring invocation. Sending the pipe directly to one application misses the routing requirement, while retaining the scheduling server misses the replacement requirement.
Wrong options: Keep the scheduling server and send its reconciliation events through the event bus. (Keeping the server fails the explicit requirement to replace it.); Use an EventBridge pipe to enrich stream events and deliver them directly to one internal application. (A direct pipe target does not route selected enriched events to several applications.); Use a shared SQS queue so every internal application can poll for its selected meter changes. (A shared queue does not provide the requested routing of selected events to several applications.)

chunks.title: Amazon EventBridge event bus, rules, scheduler and pipes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturing application writes equipment changes to DynamoDB, and a downstream application needs enriched change events. The team wants a managed integration from the DynamoDB stream to that one application, with enrichment before delivery. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an EventBridge pipe with the DynamoDB stream as its source, enrichment, and the application as its target.
Why: This is a point-to-point integration: one stream feeds one application, and events must be enriched before delivery. EventBridge Pipes is intended for that pattern and supports enrichment. Sending events to a bus for consumers to enrich changes the point at which enrichment occurs. Step Functions would introduce workflow orchestration that the scenario does not require.
Wrong options: Publish each stream record to an SNS topic and make the downstream application enrich it after receipt. (Enrichment after receipt misses the requirement to enrich events before delivery.); Start a Step Functions workflow for each change and track enrichment as a workflow step. (Workflow state tracking adds overhead to a stated point-to-point integration.); Send the stream records to an EventBridge event bus and have each consumer enrich its own copy. (Consumer-side enrichment does not provide the requested enrichment before delivery to the application.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "highly available" vs "fault tolerant"
chunks.text:
Exam cue: "highly available" vs "fault tolerant". Read the failure boundary before choosing a design. For a workload that must remain available when one Availability Zone fails, choose capacity across multiple AZs; if the requirement includes a Regional disruption, plan capacity and recovery across Regions.
When to use: The scenario says “highly available” and identifies an Availability Zone failure as the risk.; The scenario requires service to continue during a Regional disruption.; A proposed design concentrates all serving capacity in one AZ.
Key facts: Single points of failure undermine reliability.; Automation and proven failure-recovery processes are reliability considerations.; The architecture must match the failure scope: an AZ failure and a Regional disruption call for different placement decisions.; Backups support recovery, but a backup-only design does not provide continuously serving redundant capacity.
Gotchas: Do not select multiple instances if every instance remains in the same AZ.; Do not treat a Multi-AZ design as meeting an explicit requirement to continue through a Regional disruption.; Do not equate the ability to restore from a backup with uninterrupted service.
Confused with: 
ES: Identifica primero qué tipo de falla debe resistir la arquitectura. Si la carga debe seguir disponible cuando falla una Availability Zone, distribuye la capacidad entre varias AZ; si el requisito incluye una interrupción de una Region, planifica capacidad y recuperación entre Regions. Los puntos únicos de falla debilitan la confiabilidad.; La automatización y los procesos de recuperación probados son consideraciones de confiabilidad.; La arquitectura debe corresponder al alcance de la falla: una falla de AZ y una interrupción de Region exigen decisiones de distribución distintas.; Los backups ayudan a recuperar el servicio, pero por sí solos no aportan capacidad redundante que ya esté atendiendo solicitudes.

chunks.title: Exam cue: "highly available" vs "fault tolerant"
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company is replacing a single application instance before its next sales event. The service must remain available if one Availability Zone fails, but the company has no requirement to survive a Regional disruption. Which design meets the availability requirement without adding a second-Region deployment?
Correct: Run application capacity across multiple AZs and distribute requests across that capacity.
Why: The deciding requirement is continued availability when an AZ fails, not protection against a Regional disruption. Distributing serving capacity across multiple AZs removes the stated single-AZ dependency. Extra instances, automation, or backups confined to one AZ do not meet that requirement.
Wrong options: Keep one serving instance and automate its replacement in the same AZ. (Automated replacement in the affected AZ does not remove the AZ as a failure boundary.); Run several application instances in one AZ and keep a backup for recovery. (All serving instances would be lost to the stated AZ failure.); Keep the application in one AZ and schedule more frequent backups. (More frequent backups help recovery but do not provide serving capacity during the AZ failure.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "highly available" vs "fault tolerant"
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company runs a dispatch application across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region. Its new continuity policy requires dispatch to continue even if that entire Region becomes unavailable, rather than wait for a later restoration. Which architectural change meets this requirement?
Correct: Prepare serving capacity in another Region and a tested process to redirect service there.
Why: The new failure boundary is an entire Region, not an AZ. Serving capacity in another Region, together with a recovery process, addresses that boundary. More capacity or AZs in the original Region remain exposed to the stated event, while backups alone imply waiting for restoration.
Wrong options: Add another AZ to the existing Regional deployment and test instance replacement. (Another AZ still leaves all serving capacity in the affected Region.); Increase the number of application instances across the existing AZs. (Additional instances within the same Region do not address a Regional disruption.); Keep the current deployment and retain more frequent backups for restoration. (Backups enable recovery but do not keep dispatch serving during the disruption.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "highly available" vs "fault tolerant"
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher serves a daily news application from one Availability Zone. Editors require readers to retain access during an AZ outage, but they can accept a planned recovery process for the less likely loss of an entire Region. Which approach meets these distinct requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Serve the application across multiple AZs in one Region and maintain a tested recovery process for a Regional loss.
Why: The publisher sets different expectations for the two outage scopes: continued access for an AZ outage and recovery after a Regional loss. Multi-AZ serving capacity plus a tested Regional recovery process matches those expectations without requiring continuously serving multi-Region capacity. Backups or extra instances in a single AZ fail the immediate AZ-availability requirement.
Wrong options: Operate continuously serving deployments in multiple Regions for both outage types. (Continuously serving multi-Region capacity exceeds the stated need to recover after a Regional loss.); Serve the application from one AZ and use backups for both AZ and Regional outages. (Recovery from backups does not keep readers connected during the specified AZ outage.); Add instances within the current AZ and establish a tested Regional recovery process. (The tested recovery process does not remove the single-AZ dependency for everyday service.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "least operational overhead"
chunks.text:
Exam cue: "least operational overhead". “Least operational overhead” asks who must run and maintain the solution after deployment. When the required function is available as a purpose-built AWS managed service, prefer it over custom scripts or software your team must operate on EC2.
When to use: The scenario explicitly prioritizes “least operational overhead” or “least management effort.”; One option meets the requirement with a managed service, while another requires operating equivalent software.; A proposed design adds custom scripts or infrastructure that the requirement does not call for.
Key facts: Operational excellence covers the design, delivery, and maintenance of workloads—not just their initial deployment.; An operationally effective architecture provides insight into its status and supports efficient event response.; Operational practices should continue to improve in support of business goals.; The provided Well-Architected excerpt gives operational guidance, not a rule that a named service is always the best choice.
Gotchas: Do not choose a managed service if it does not perform the function the scenario requires.; Do not treat automated scripts as maintenance-free; the team still owns the scripts and what runs them.; Least operational overhead does not mean ignoring workload status or event response.
Confused with: 
ES: “Least operational overhead” te pide evaluar quién deberá operar y mantener la solución después del despliegue. Si un servicio administrado de AWS diseñado para esa función cumple el requisito, prefiérelo frente a scripts propios o software que tu equipo deba operar en EC2. La excelencia operativa abarca el diseño, la entrega y el mantenimiento de las cargas de trabajo, no solo su despliegue inicial.; Una arquitectura eficaz para la operación permite conocer su estado y responder eficientemente a eventos.; Las prácticas operativas deben seguir mejorando para apoyar los objetivos del negocio.; El extracto de Well-Architected ofrece orientación operativa, no una regla de que un servicio específico siempre sea la mejor opción.

chunks.title: Exam cue: "least operational overhead"
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional museum is replacing the entry point for a public REST API. The application team can update the API integration, but its small operations team does not want to maintain the software that receives and routes client requests. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use Amazon API Gateway as the managed entry point for the REST API.
Why: The deciding requirement is to provide a REST API entry point without maintaining the software that receives and routes requests. Amazon API Gateway is the managed option aligned with API creation and management. An EC2-hosted proxy could also receive requests, but the team would have to operate it, contrary to the stated priority.
Wrong options: Package an API proxy in containers and run it on team-managed EC2 instances. (Container packaging does not remove the stated responsibility for operating the proxy and its hosts.); Use scripts on EC2 instances to receive requests and forward them to the application. (The team would own both the request-routing scripts and the instances running them.); Run a reverse proxy on EC2 instances and have the team maintain its configuration. (It provides an API entry point but leaves proxy software and configuration with the operations team.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "least operational overhead"
chunks.text:
Scenario: A medical scheduling company is reviewing how its applications obtain database credentials. The team currently maintains its own credential storage and update scripts and wants to retire that custom management work. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS Secrets Manager for the application credentials.
Why: The requirement is to stop maintaining a custom system for application credentials. AWS Secrets Manager is the purpose-built managed option for that function. An EC2-hosted credential store might be workable, but it preserves the team's responsibility for operating and updating the store.
Wrong options: Build a credential-distribution application and schedule its update jobs on EC2. (It replaces one custom management process with another that the team must operate.); Run a credential store on EC2 instances and have the team manage its updates. (It moves the custom store to EC2 but keeps its operation and updates with the team.); Store credentials in application configuration files and maintain scripts to update them. (It retains the custom credential-update scripts the team wants to retire.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "least operational overhead"
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing startup is designing two separate components: a public REST API entry point and a queue to hand accepted requests to processors. The team can integrate with managed AWS services but cannot take on routine maintenance of API proxy or queue software. Which TWO components meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Amazon SQS for the request handoff to processors + Amazon API Gateway for the REST API entry point
Why: This design needs two functions, not one: a REST API entry point and a queue for handing off work. Amazon API Gateway and Amazon SQS are the corresponding managed components. An EC2 proxy or EC2-hosted queue could perform one of those functions, but each conflicts with the explicit restriction on routine software maintenance.
Wrong options: Queue software installed and maintained on EC2 instances (It addresses the queue function but leaves routine queue-software maintenance with the team.); A database table with team-maintained polling scripts for pending requests (It creates a custom handoff that requires the script maintenance the team wants to avoid.); An API proxy installed and maintained on EC2 instances (It could serve as an entry point, but the team would maintain the proxy software.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "most cost-effective"
chunks.text:
Exam cue: "most cost-effective". “Most cost-effective” means the lowest-cost design that still meets every stated functional requirement. Eliminate options that miss a requirement before comparing their costs.
When to use: The scenario asks for the lowest cost or most cost-effective solution.; Options differ in cost and in a required outcome such as retrieval time, availability, or capacity.; A cheaper option is tempting but fails one stated constraint.
Key facts: The AWS Well-Architected Cost Optimization Pillar defines a cost-optimized workload as one that meets functional requirements at the lowest possible price point.; Cost optimization includes selecting and configuring resources to achieve the required outcome.; Expenditure and usage awareness, managing demand and supply, and optimizing over time are cost-optimization practices.
Gotchas: Do not choose the cheapest option until you have checked every requirement.; Do not pay for extra capability when a less expensive option already meets the requirement.; Compare costs for the workload described, not an assumed typical workload.
Confused with: 
ES: “Most cost-effective” significa elegir el diseño de menor costo que todavía cumpla todos los requisitos funcionales. Descarta las opciones que incumplen un requisito antes de comparar costos. El Cost Optimization Pillar de AWS Well-Architected define una carga de trabajo optimizada en costos como aquella que cumple los requisitos funcionales al menor precio posible.; La optimización de costos incluye seleccionar y configurar recursos para lograr el resultado requerido.; Conocer el gasto y el uso, gestionar la demanda y el suministro, y optimizar con el tiempo son prácticas de optimización de costos.

chunks.title: Exam cue: "most cost-effective"
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company has measured the capacity and monthly cost of four Amazon EC2 deployments for its checkout service. The service must handle 8,000 checkout requests per minute and remain available if either of two Availability Zones becomes unavailable. The company validated each deployment's stated capacity under that failure condition. Which deployment meets the requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Two-AZ deployment P: $1,900 monthly; 9,000 requests per minute after either zone fails.
Why: Capacity must be assessed after a zone failure, not just during normal operation. Deployments P and S both meet the 8,000-request target under the required failure condition. P is less expensive; Q misses availability, while R misses post-failure capacity.
Wrong options: Single-AZ deployment Q: $900 monthly; 12,000 requests per minute while its zone operates. (It cannot meet the requirement to remain available after its zone becomes unavailable.); Two-AZ deployment R: $1,550 monthly; 7,000 requests per minute after either zone fails. (Its validated capacity after a zone failure is below 8,000 requests per minute.); Two-AZ deployment S: $2,450 monthly; 11,000 requests per minute after either zone fails. (It meets the requirements but costs more than deployment P.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "most cost-effective"
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company has evaluated four VPC network designs for a production workload. Its security team requires the evaluated design to keep the specified application-to-storage traffic on an approved private path, and its resilience policy requires connectivity after either Availability Zone becomes unavailable. The company's estimates include transfer and infrastructure charges for its measured traffic. Which evaluated design meets the requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Design X: $480 monthly; approved private path; connectivity survives either zone failure.
Why: This decision depends on both the approved traffic path and resilience after either zone failure. W and X meet both conditions according to the company's evaluation. X costs less; Y fails resilience, and Z fails the private-path requirement.
Wrong options: Design W: $720 monthly; approved private path; connectivity survives either zone failure. (It meets both requirements but costs more than another qualifying design.); Design Z: $310 monthly; connectivity survives either zone failure; path not approved as private. (It fails the stated security requirement despite its lower cost.); Design Y: $390 monthly; approved private path; connectivity fails if one designated zone fails. (It misses the requirement to retain connectivity after either zone fails.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "most cost-effective"
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum is choosing one Amazon S3 storage configuration for digital records and one Amazon EC2 deployment for its catalog. Staff must retrieve a record within 30 minutes, and the catalog must continue serving its measured peak load after either of two Availability Zones becomes unavailable. The museum's evaluated monthly figures include expected storage requests and compute usage; it wants the lowest-cost qualifying choice for each component. Which two choices meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
Correct: S3 configuration A: $170 monthly; tested retrieval within 20 minutes. + EC2 deployment D: $800 monthly; tested peak load continues after either zone fails.
Why: The museum needs one qualifying storage choice and one qualifying compute choice. For storage, A and C meet the 30-minute limit, and A is cheaper; B misses the limit. For compute, D maintains the measured peak load after either zone fails, while cheaper E does not. Select A and D.
Wrong options: S3 configuration B: $95 monthly; tested retrieval within two hours. (Its retrieval time exceeds the 30-minute limit.); EC2 deployment E: $540 monthly; tested peak load continues only while both zones operate. (It does not meet the peak-load requirement after a zone failure.); S3 configuration C: $260 monthly; tested retrieval within two minutes. (It meets the retrieval limit but costs more than storage configuration A.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: performance, latency and throughput wording
chunks.text:
Exam cue: performance, latency and throughput wording. Performance wording tells you where to investigate the bottleneck, not which service guarantees a latency target. Match repeated reads to caching, distant users to edge delivery, and sustained data-access demand to data-store selection and capacity planning.
When to use: Repeated requests for the same data dominate a read-latency problem.; Users in distant locations experience slow delivery of shared content.; A workload needs a primary data store that can accommodate growing request volume.
Key facts: AWS Well-Architected treats performance efficiency as an architectural concern, not just a compute-sizing concern.; Its performance focus areas include architecture selection, data management, and networking and content delivery.; The exam task statements identify caching, database access patterns, database capacity planning, and edge networking as separate performance decisions.; A workload's stated latency or throughput target is a requirement to evaluate; it is not a performance guarantee from a named service.
Gotchas: Do not select edge delivery for a bottleneck caused by repeated database reads within the application.; Do not treat a cache as an unquestioned replacement for a required primary data store.; Do not assume that scaling compute addresses a data-access or content-delivery bottleneck.
Confused with: 
ES: El lenguaje de performance te indica dónde investigar el cuello de botella, no qué servicio garantiza una meta de latencia. Relaciona las lecturas repetidas con caching, los usuarios distantes con edge delivery y la demanda sostenida de acceso a datos con la selección y planificación de capacidad del almacén de datos. AWS Well-Architected considera Performance Efficiency una cuestión de arquitectura, no solo de dimensionamiento de cómputo.; Sus áreas de enfoque de performance incluyen selección de arquitectura, gestión de datos y redes y entrega de contenido.; Los enunciados de tareas del examen distinguen caching, patrones de acceso a bases de datos, planificación de capacidad de bases de datos y redes de edge como decisiones de performance.; La meta de latencia o throughput de una carga de trabajo es un requisito que debes evaluar; no es una garantía de performance de un servicio.

chunks.title: Exam cue: performance, latency and throughput wording
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum publishes the same exhibit images to visitors in several continents. Its application and database respond quickly, but visitors far from the content's current location report slow image delivery. The museum wants to improve delivery of these shared images without redesigning its database. Which solution best addresses the stated performance problem?
Correct: Evaluate Amazon CloudFront for delivering the shared images.
Why: The slow step is delivering shared images to geographically dispersed visitors, not querying records or processing application requests. Amazon CloudFront is the edge-delivery choice to evaluate for that requirement. Adding a database cache or read replica would optimize components the scenario says are already responding quickly.
Wrong options: Add Amazon ElastiCache for exhibit-record lookups. (Caching database lookups targets a component that is not the measured bottleneck.); Add an Amazon Aurora read replica for exhibit records. (The database is responding quickly, so a read replica does not address image delivery.); Increase Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling capacity for the application. (The application responds quickly, so additional application capacity misses the stated issue.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: performance, latency and throughput wording
chunks.text:
Scenario: A travel site has two measured performance issues: customers worldwide wait for shared destination images, and itinerary pages repeatedly read the same reference records from a database. The application tier has spare capacity, and the database must remain the primary store for those records. The team wants to address each bottleneck without replacing its existing application or database. Which two approaches should it evaluate? (Choose two.)
Correct: Evaluate Amazon CloudFront for the shared destination images. + Evaluate Amazon ElastiCache for the repeated reference-record reads.
Why: This scenario identifies two distinct bottlenecks, so the design should address both rather than scaling an unrelated tier. Evaluate Amazon CloudFront for delivery of shared images to worldwide users and Amazon ElastiCache for repeated reads of reference records. An Application Load Balancer or more application capacity misses the measured issues, and a read replica cannot replace the required primary database.
Wrong options: Add an Application Load Balancer for the spare-capacity application tier. (Distributing application requests does not directly address the identified image-delivery and repeated-read issues.); Increase Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling capacity for the application tier. (The application tier has spare capacity, so scaling it does not target either measured bottleneck.); Replace the existing database with an Amazon Aurora read replica. (The database must remain the primary store, which a read replica cannot replace.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "most secure" and least privilege
chunks.text:
Exam cue: "most secure" and least privilege. For a “most secure” IAM decision, prefer temporary credentials from roles over long-term access keys, then grant only the actions needed on the required resources under appropriate conditions. For workforce access, use federation; for workloads on AWS compute, use IAM roles.
When to use: People need access to AWS accounts without maintaining IAM user access keys.; An application on AWS compute needs credentials to call AWS services.; A policy grants more actions or resources than a task requires.; Multiple accounts need organization-wide permissions guardrails.
Key facts: Federated human users can assume roles and receive temporary credentials; IAM Identity Center is recommended for centralized workforce access.; AWS compute services such as EC2 and Lambda deliver temporary IAM role credentials to workloads.; Least privilege limits actions, resources, and, where appropriate, the conditions under which access is allowed.; IAM Access Analyzer can generate fine-grained policies from access activity logged in CloudTrail; test generated policies before deployment.; SCPs set permissions guardrails across accounts but do not grant permissions.
Gotchas: Rotating long-term access keys does not make them preferable when temporary role credentials work.; An AWS managed policy may be broader than a particular workload needs.; An SCP cannot replace the identity-based or resource-based policy needed to grant access.
Confused with: 
ES: Para una decisión de IAM que pida la opción “most secure”, prefiere credenciales temporales mediante roles en vez de access keys de larga duración y concede solo las acciones necesarias sobre los recursos requeridos, con condiciones cuando corresponda. Para el personal, usa federación; para cargas de trabajo en servicios de cómputo de AWS, usa IAM roles. Los usuarios federados pueden asumir roles y recibir credenciales temporales; se recomienda IAM Identity Center para centralizar el acceso del personal.; Los servicios de cómputo de AWS, como EC2 y Lambda, entregan credenciales temporales de IAM roles a las cargas de trabajo.; Least privilege limita acciones, recursos y, cuando corresponde, las condiciones de acceso.; IAM Access Analyzer puede generar políticas detalladas a partir de la actividad registrada en CloudTrail; prueba las políticas generadas antes de implementarlas.; Los SCP establecen límites de permisos entre cuentas, pero no conceden permisos.

chunks.title: Exam cue: "most secure" and least privilege
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare organization operates workloads in several AWS accounts managed with AWS Organizations. It wants a permissions guardrail that applies across the accounts, while each workload receives only the access needed for its task. The team must not rely on a guardrail to grant access. Which TWO actions meet these requirements MOST securely? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use AWS Organizations SCPs to establish permissions guardrails across the accounts. + Grant each workload's required actions through narrowly scoped IAM role policies.
Why: The scenario calls for both an organization-wide guardrail and actual least-privilege grants to workloads. SCPs establish guardrails across accounts, but they grant no permissions. Narrowly scoped IAM role policies provide the task-specific permissions, with temporary credentials for workloads. Using an SCP alone would leave the workloads without the grants they need.
Wrong options: Give every workload the same broad AWS managed policy to simplify administration. (A broad common policy does not limit each workload to the access its task requires.); Create IAM users with long-term access keys for every workload. (Workloads should use temporary role credentials where possible, rather than long-term keys.); Use SCPs as the only policies for workloads that need access to AWS resources. (SCPs do not grant permissions and cannot be the only source of workload access.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "most secure" and least privilege
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company runs a processing application on Amazon EC2. The application must read objects from one S3 bucket and does not need access to other buckets. The team wants to avoid distributing long-term credentials. Which solution meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Assign an IAM role to the EC2 instance with permission to read objects from the required bucket.
Why: The deciding requirements are temporary credentials and read access limited to one bucket. An IAM role provides temporary credentials to an EC2 workload, while a narrowly scoped policy limits what it can do. Rotating IAM user keys does not remove the need to distribute long-term credentials. A role with broad S3 permissions solves the credential problem but not the least-privilege problem.
Wrong options: Create an IAM user with read access to all S3 buckets and place its access keys on the instance. (Long-term keys must be distributed, and access to all buckets exceeds the stated need.); Create an IAM user with read access to the required bucket and rotate its access keys regularly. (The bucket scope is appropriate, but the solution still distributes long-term keys unnecessarily.); Assign an IAM role to the EC2 instance with an AWS managed policy granting broad S3 access. (The role avoids long-term keys, but broad S3 access does not meet the least-privilege requirement.)

chunks.title: Exam cue: "most secure" and least privilege
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company lets developers create IAM roles for projects within one AWS account. Each project needs different permissions, but the security team must ensure that no developer-created role can exceed an approved maximum. Developers must still be able to grant the permissions their projects require within that maximum. Which solution meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Set a permissions boundary for developer-created roles and use identity-based policies to grant each project's needed permissions.
Why: The security team needs a maximum for permissions delegated within one account, while individual roles still need project-specific grants. A permissions boundary sets that maximum; identity-based policies supply the permissions a role can use. A boundary by itself grants nothing. An SCP can provide a broader account guardrail, but it also cannot serve as the sole grant for these roles.
Wrong options: Attach the same broad AWS managed policy to every role developers create. (A broad shared policy does not enforce project-specific least privilege.); Attach only a permissions boundary to each role and omit its identity-based policies. (A permissions boundary sets a maximum but grants no permissions on its own.); Use an AWS Organizations SCP as the only policy for developer-created roles. (An SCP can act as a guardrail but cannot grant the permissions projects require.)

chunks.title: AWS Fargate serverless containers
chunks.text:
AWS Fargate serverless containers. AWS Fargate runs containers with Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS without requiring you to provision or manage EC2 hosts. Choose it when an existing container workload needs the least operational overhead; choose Fargate Spot for ECS tasks that can tolerate interruption.
When to use: A team must run containers but does not want to manage EC2 instances or cluster capacity.; A containerized application needs task-level resource and network settings.; Interruption-tolerant ECS tasks need a lower-cost capacity option.
Key facts: Fargate works with both Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS; each ECS task or Kubernetes pod has a dedicated network interface.; For an ECS service on Fargate using a load balancer, the target group uses the ip target type, not instance.; Fargate Spot uses spare capacity for interruption-tolerant ECS tasks; AWS gives a two-minute warning when it needs the capacity back.; Fargate ephemeral storage is erased when the workload stops. Amazon EFS can provide persistent storage.; GPU workloads are not supported on Fargate; use Amazon EC2 when a GPU is required.
Gotchas: Fargate removes host management, not the need to specify task CPU, memory, networking, and IAM policies.; Fargate Spot is not a fit for tasks that cannot tolerate interruption.; Increasing ephemeral storage does not make data survive a stopped task.
Confused with: Amazon ECS on EC2: ECS on EC2 provides greater instance control but requires managing EC2 capacity; Fargate removes that work.; Amazon EKS: EKS is Kubernetes orchestration and can also use Fargate; choosing Fargate does not require choosing Kubernetes.; AWS Batch: Batch addresses managed scheduling for queued batch jobs; Fargate is the serverless compute option for containers.
ES: AWS Fargate ejecuta contenedores con Amazon ECS o Amazon EKS sin que tengas que aprovisionar ni administrar hosts EC2. Elígelo cuando una carga de trabajo en contenedores requiera least operational overhead; usa Fargate Spot para tareas de ECS que toleren interrupciones. Fargate funciona con Amazon ECS y Amazon EKS; cada tarea de ECS o pod de Kubernetes tiene una interfaz de red dedicada.; Para un servicio ECS en Fargate con balanceador de carga, el target group usa el target type ip, no instance.; Fargate Spot usa capacidad disponible para tareas de ECS que toleran interrupciones; AWS avisa con dos minutos de anticipación cuando necesita recuperar la capacidad.; El almacenamiento efímero de Fargate se borra al detenerse la carga de trabajo. Amazon EFS puede proporcionar almacenamiento persistente.; Fargate no admite cargas de trabajo con GPU; usa Amazon EC2 si necesitas una GPU.

chunks.title: AWS Fargate serverless containers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer has packaged its checkout API into containers. The API must accept HTTPS traffic through a load balancer, remain available without planned capacity interruptions, and run without the team managing EC2 instances. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Run an Amazon ECS service on Fargate and use an Application Load Balancer with an ip target group.
Why: The deciding requirements are container hosting without EC2 management and an HTTPS-facing load balancer. An ECS service on Fargate removes host provisioning, and an Application Load Balancer supports HTTP/HTTPS traffic with ip targets for Fargate tasks. An instance target group is incompatible with this Fargate service. Fargate Spot misses the requirement to avoid planned capacity interruptions.
Wrong options: Run an Amazon ECS service on EC2 instances and use an Application Load Balancer with an instance target group. (This can serve HTTPS traffic but requires the team to manage EC2 capacity.); Run an Amazon ECS service on Fargate and use an Application Load Balancer with an instance target group. (Fargate tasks require an ip target group rather than an instance target group.); Run an Amazon ECS service on Fargate Spot and use an Application Load Balancer with an ip target group. (Fargate Spot tasks can be interrupted when AWS needs the spare capacity back.)

chunks.title: AWS Fargate serverless containers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A sports venue has containerized a UDP telemetry receiver. It needs a load balancer in front of an Amazon ECS service, cannot manage EC2 hosts, and will deploy the tasks on Fargate platform version 1.4. Which configuration meets these requirements?
Correct: Use a Network Load Balancer with an ip target group for the Fargate service.
Why: UDP traffic points to a Network Load Balancer rather than an Application Load Balancer. Fargate services use ip target groups, and UDP routing through a Network Load Balancer is supported on Fargate platform version 1.4 or later. An instance target group misses the Fargate networking requirement. Running ECS on EC2 would reintroduce host management.
Wrong options: Use a Network Load Balancer with an instance target group for the Fargate service. (Although a Network Load Balancer supports UDP, the Fargate service needs ip rather than instance targets.); Use an Application Load Balancer with an ip target group for the Fargate service. (An Application Load Balancer routes HTTP/HTTPS traffic, not the required UDP traffic.); Use a Network Load Balancer with an ip target group, but run the ECS service on EC2 instances. (This provides UDP routing but violates the requirement not to manage EC2 hosts.)

chunks.title: AWS Fargate serverless containers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher operates two containerized ECS workloads: an overnight indexing task that can be retried after an interruption, and a customer-facing subscription service that must not depend on reclaimable spare capacity. The team will not manage EC2 hosts and wants the lowest-cost suitable capacity choice for each workload. Which TWO configurations meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)
Correct: Run the subscription service on standard Fargate capacity. + Run the overnight indexing tasks on Fargate Spot.
Why: The two workloads have different interruption requirements, but neither may require EC2 host management. Fargate Spot is the discounted fit for retryable ECS indexing tasks. Standard Fargate is the suitable choice for the subscription service because it does not rely on Fargate Spot spare capacity. EC2 Spot violates the operational constraint, while Spot for the subscription service violates its capacity constraint.
Wrong options: Run the overnight indexing tasks on ECS with EC2 Spot Instances. (This would require managing EC2 hosts, which the team has ruled out.); Run the subscription service on Fargate Spot. (Fargate Spot depends on spare capacity that AWS can reclaim, contrary to the service requirement.); Run the overnight indexing tasks on standard Fargate capacity. (Standard Fargate avoids host management but forgoes the discounted Spot option suitable for these retryable tasks.)

chunks.title: AWS Firewall Manager
chunks.text:
AWS Firewall Manager. AWS Firewall Manager centrally administers protections across accounts and resources in an AWS Organizations organization. Choose it when the decision is how to apply and maintain policies organization-wide, especially as accounts or resources are added.
When to use: Apply AWS WAF protections consistently across multiple accounts and newly added resources.; Subscribe in-scope member accounts, including new ones, to AWS Shield Advanced.; Apply security group rules to all member accounts or selected subsets.
Key facts: Firewall Manager supports protections including AWS WAF, AWS Shield Advanced, VPC security groups and network ACLs, AWS Network Firewall, and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall.; Policies can protect resources by type or by tag.; Protections can automatically apply to newly added accounts and resources.; Firewall Manager provides centralized monitoring of DDoS attacks across an organization.
Gotchas: Configuring AWS WAF on individual resources does not provide Firewall Manager’s organization-wide policy administration.; An AWS Network Firewall policy is not a substitute for a requirement to apply security group rules.; A policy scoped to every member account does not meet a requirement limited to selected accounts.
Confused with: waf: AWS WAF provides web protections; Firewall Manager centrally applies and maintains protections such as WAF across accounts and resources.; shield: Shield Advanced is a protection; Firewall Manager can subscribe in-scope organization accounts to it, including newly joined accounts.; network-firewall: AWS Network Firewall is a supported protection; Firewall Manager centrally administers its policies across accounts and resources.
ES: AWS Firewall Manager administra protecciones de forma centralizada en las cuentas y los recursos de una organización de AWS Organizations. Elígelo cuando debas aplicar y mantener políticas en toda la organización, especialmente al agregar cuentas o recursos. Firewall Manager admite protecciones como AWS WAF, AWS Shield Advanced, VPC security groups y network ACLs, AWS Network Firewall y Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall.; Puedes definir el alcance de las políticas por tipo de recurso o por etiqueta.; Las protecciones pueden aplicarse automáticamente a cuentas y recursos nuevos.; Firewall Manager ofrece monitoreo centralizado de ataques DDoS en una organización.

chunks.title: AWS Firewall Manager
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company runs customer-facing applications in multiple accounts in an AWS Organizations organization. Its security team wants the same AWS WAF protection on every CloudFront distribution, including distributions created later. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an AWS Firewall Manager policy for AWS WAF that covers CloudFront distributions across the organization.
Why: The deciding requirements are consistent AWS WAF protection across accounts and automatic coverage of future CloudFront distributions. Firewall Manager can target all resources of a type and automatically apply protections as resources are added. Configuring WAF distribution by distribution misses the operational-overhead requirement. The other Firewall Manager policies administer different protections.
Wrong options: Configure AWS WAF protection separately on each CloudFront distribution and repeat the process for new distributions. (This requires ongoing per-resource administration instead of automatically protecting new distributions.); Create an AWS Firewall Manager policy for AWS Network Firewall across the organization's accounts. (A Network Firewall policy does not provide the requested AWS WAF protection for CloudFront distributions.); Create an AWS Firewall Manager security group policy for the organization's member accounts. (A security group policy does not apply the requested AWS WAF protection to CloudFront distributions.)

chunks.title: AWS Firewall Manager
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company uses AWS Shield Advanced for member accounts in its AWS Organizations organization. It regularly creates accounts for new events and wants every new in-scope account subscribed without a separate enrollment task. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS Firewall Manager to subscribe in-scope organization accounts to AWS Shield Advanced.
Why: The requirement is automatic Shield Advanced subscription when in-scope accounts join the organization. Firewall Manager explicitly supports both subscribing member accounts and automatically subscribing new in-scope accounts. Enrolling accounts one at a time misses the operational requirement. WAF and Network Firewall policies address different protections.
Wrong options: Subscribe each member account to AWS Shield Advanced when the account is created. (Manual enrollment creates the separate task the company wants to eliminate.); Maintain an AWS WAF policy in AWS Firewall Manager for the organization's accounts. (A WAF policy does not perform the requested Shield Advanced account subscriptions.); Maintain an AWS Network Firewall policy in AWS Firewall Manager for new member accounts. (A Network Firewall policy does not subscribe accounts to Shield Advanced.)

chunks.title: Amazon FSx for Lustre
chunks.text:
Amazon FSx for Lustre. Amazon FSx for Lustre is a managed, high-performance file system for Linux-based HPC and ML workloads. Choose it when compute needs fast file access to large datasets, especially when those datasets are in Amazon S3; then choose scratch or persistent based on whether file-server failure can cause data loss.
When to use: Linux HPC, ML, or video-processing jobs need a shared POSIX file system with very low latency and high throughput.; Jobs need S3 objects presented as files and may need to write processed data back to S3.; A short-lived processing job can tolerate loss of file-system data, or a longer-running job needs replicated file-system data.
Key facts: FSx for Lustre provides sub-millisecond latencies, up to multiple TBps of throughput, and up to millions of IOPS.; An S3-linked file system presents S3 objects as files and can write file-system data back to S3.; Scratch file systems do not replicate data; data does not persist if a file server fails.; Persistent file systems replicate data and replace failed file servers.; The SSD storage class provides consistent sub-millisecond access across the full dataset.
Gotchas: An S3-linked file system is not the same as having an application access S3 objects directly: Lustre supplies a native file-system interface.; Do not choose scratch when data must remain available after a file-server failure.; Do not assume every Lustre storage class gives consistent sub-millisecond access to the full dataset.
Confused with: Amazon EFS: EFS supplies elastic shared NFS storage; FSx for Lustre targets high-performance HPC/ML processing and can present linked S3 objects as files.; Amazon S3: S3 is object storage; FSx for Lustre gives Linux applications a native file-system interface to a linked S3 dataset.; EC2 instance store: Instance store is ephemeral storage attached to an instance, rather than a Lustre file system shared by compute workers.
ES: Amazon FSx for Lustre es un sistema de archivos administrado de alto rendimiento para cargas HPC y ML basadas en Linux. Elígelo cuando el cómputo necesite acceso rápido a archivos de grandes conjuntos de datos, especialmente si están en Amazon S3; después, elige scratch o persistent según si se puede tolerar la pérdida de datos ante una falla del servidor de archivos. FSx for Lustre ofrece latencias inferiores a un milisegundo, hasta varios TBps de rendimiento y hasta millones de IOPS.; Un sistema de archivos vinculado con S3 presenta los objetos de S3 como archivos y puede escribir datos del sistema de archivos de vuelta en S3.; Los sistemas de archivos scratch no replican los datos; estos no persisten si falla un servidor de archivos.; Los sistemas de archivos persistent replican los datos y reemplazan los servidores de archivos que fallan.; La clase de almacenamiento SSD ofrece acceso constante con latencia inferior a un milisegundo a todo el conjunto de datos.

chunks.title: Amazon FSx for Lustre
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab runs short-lived simulations on Linux EC2 instances. Input data is in Amazon S3, but the existing application expects files and directories; the lab can rerun a simulation if its temporary working data is lost when a file server fails. Which storage solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use a scratch Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to the S3 bucket.
Why: The application requires a file-system interface to data held in S3, and the working data is disposable. An S3-linked FSx for Lustre file system presents objects as files; scratch is intended for temporary, shorter-term processing. Persistent Lustre would also supply the interface, but replication does not address a requirement in this scenario.
Wrong options: Use an Amazon EFS file system for the workers and copy the S3 input into it before each run. (EFS provides shared file access, but copying the input adds a preparation step instead of presenting linked S3 objects as files.); Use a persistent Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to the S3 bucket. (It meets the file-access requirement, but its replicated deployment is unnecessary for data the lab can recreate.); Have each worker read the input directly from Amazon S3 using object requests. (Direct object requests do not provide the files-and-directories interface expected by the existing application.)

chunks.title: Amazon FSx for Lustre
chunks.text:
Scenario: A genomics team has a Linux analysis application that makes small, random file reads throughout its active dataset. The team has selected Amazon FSx for Lustre but requires consistent sub-millisecond access to the entire dataset, not just frequently accessed files. Which storage configuration meets this requirement?
Correct: Choose the FSx for Lustre SSD storage class.
Why: The requirement applies to small, random reads across the entire dataset, rather than only its frequently accessed portion. FSx for Lustre SSD is the class documented to provide consistent sub-millisecond access to the full dataset. Intelligent-Tiering can provide that latency for frequently accessed data, while HDD is described with consistent single-digit-millisecond access.
Wrong options: Choose the FSx for Lustre Intelligent-Tiering storage class with an SSD read cache. (Intelligent-Tiering offers sub-millisecond access to frequently accessed data but is not intended for consistent low latency across the full dataset.); Choose the FSx for Lustre HDD storage class with an SSD read cache. (The HDD class is described as providing consistent single-digit-millisecond access to the full dataset, not sub-millisecond access.); Store the dataset as Amazon S3 objects and have the application retrieve each object directly. (Direct object retrieval does not meet the Linux application's file-access requirement or the specified Lustre storage-class decision.)

chunks.title: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS
chunks.text:
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS. Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is the managed choice for migrating NetApp workloads that need ONTAP capabilities or access through NFS, SMB, and iSCSI. Choose Amazon FSx for OpenZFS when moving a ZFS or Linux-based file server and retaining familiar OpenZFS features through NFS access.
When to use: An on-premises NetApp application must move to AWS without changing its code or data-management practices.; One workload needs NFS, SMB, and iSCSI access to storage.; A ZFS-based file server must move to managed storage while retaining snapshots and data cloning.
Key facts: FSx for ONTAP supports file access (NFS, SMB) and block access (iSCSI, NVMe) in one file system, plus NetApp tools and API operations.; FSx for ONTAP supports SnapMirror replication and automatically tiers infrequently accessed data to lower-cost storage.; FSx for OpenZFS provides NFS access from Linux, Windows, and macOS clients; its documented NFS versions are v3, v4.0, v4.1, and v4.2.; FSx for OpenZFS supports OpenZFS snapshots and data cloning.; FSx for OpenZFS offers Multi-AZ (HA), Single-AZ (HA), and Single-AZ (non-HA) deployments; its Intelligent-Tiering storage class is elastic.
Gotchas: A Windows client does not automatically imply SMB: FSx for OpenZFS is accessible from Windows clients through NFS.; Snapshots and cloning alone do not distinguish the two services; both offer them. Look for ONTAP or OpenZFS migration requirements.; Single-AZ (HA) for OpenZFS provides failover within one Availability Zone, not across Availability Zones.
Confused with: Amazon EFS: For a migration requiring ONTAP tools or native OpenZFS capabilities, choose the matching FSx file system rather than a general shared NFS file system.; Amazon FSx for Windows File Server: SMB alone may point to Windows File Server; combined NFS, SMB, and iSCSI access with NetApp continuity points to FSx for ONTAP.
ES: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP es la opción administrada para migrar cargas de NetApp que necesitan capacidades de ONTAP o acceso mediante NFS, SMB e iSCSI. Elige Amazon FSx for OpenZFS al migrar un servidor de archivos ZFS o Linux y conservar funciones conocidas de OpenZFS mediante NFS. FSx for ONTAP admite acceso a archivos (NFS, SMB) y a bloques (iSCSI, NVMe) en un mismo file system, además de herramientas y API de NetApp.; FSx for ONTAP admite la replicación con SnapMirror y mueve automáticamente los datos de acceso poco frecuente a almacenamiento de menor costo.; FSx for OpenZFS permite el acceso por NFS desde clientes Linux, Windows y macOS; las versiones documentadas son v3, v4.0, v4.1 y v4.2.; FSx for OpenZFS admite snapshots de OpenZFS y clonación de datos.; FSx for OpenZFS ofrece implementaciones Multi-AZ (HA), Single-AZ (HA) y Single-AZ (non-HA); su clase de almacenamiento Intelligent-Tiering es elástica.

chunks.title: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media team is moving its ZFS-based NFS file server to AWS. Its dataset grows unpredictably, so the team does not want to specify a fixed file-system size, and the service must remain available if an Availability Zone fails. The team also needs to retain its OpenZFS snapshot and cloning workflow. Which configuration meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy FSx for OpenZFS as Multi-AZ (HA) with Intelligent-Tiering storage.
Why: The configuration must satisfy three requirements together: OpenZFS capabilities, elastic storage without a specified file-system size, and availability across AZs. FSx for OpenZFS Multi-AZ (HA) provides cross-AZ replication and failover, while its Intelligent-Tiering storage class is elastic and does not require a file-system size. Single-AZ (HA) can fail over only within its AZ, so its HA label does not meet the AZ-failure requirement. ONTAP's tiering and Multi-AZ options do not make it an OpenZFS file system.
Wrong options: Deploy FSx for OpenZFS as Single-AZ (non-HA) with Intelligent-Tiering storage. (Intelligent-Tiering addresses variable storage needs, but Single-AZ (non-HA) does not provide cross-AZ failover.); Deploy FSx for NetApp ONTAP as Multi-AZ with automatic data tiering. (ONTAP offers Multi-AZ deployment and tiering, but it does not retain the required OpenZFS workflow.); Deploy FSx for OpenZFS as Single-AZ (HA) with SSD storage. (Single-AZ (HA) fails over within one AZ, and SSD storage requires a specified file-system size.)

chunks.title: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company is moving an on-premises NetApp ONTAP application to AWS. Its Linux editors use NFS, its Windows editors use SMB, and a processing component requires iSCSI access to the same storage environment. The company wants to keep its existing application code and NetApp management practices. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and connect each component using its required protocol.
Why: The deciding requirement is the combination of NetApp continuity and three access protocols: NFS, SMB, and iSCSI. FSx for ONTAP supports all three and lets customers migrate on-premises ONTAP applications without changing application code or data-management practices. FSx for OpenZFS is also fully managed, but its documented client access is through NFS, so it misses two required protocols.
Wrong options: Deploy Amazon FSx for OpenZFS and connect all components to its NFS endpoints. (FSx for OpenZFS provides NFS access but does not provide the required SMB and iSCSI access or ONTAP management continuity.); Deploy Amazon EFS and connect the editors and processing component through NFS. (An NFS file system does not provide the required SMB and iSCSI access or preserve ONTAP management practices.); Deploy Amazon FSx for Windows File Server and connect the editors through SMB. (An SMB-focused file system does not meet the stated NFS, iSCSI, and NetApp continuity requirements.)

chunks.title: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
chunks.text:
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed Windows file shares over SMB, with Microsoft Active Directory authentication and Windows file and folder ACLs. Choose it when Windows applications must retain these behaviors; choose Multi-AZ when the share must remain available through an Availability Zone failure.
When to use: Windows applications need shared SMB file access without managing file servers.; Users must authenticate through Microsoft Active Directory and retain file- and folder-level Windows ACLs.; A Windows file share needs failover across Availability Zones.
Key facts: Clients access shares over SMB; a file system includes a default share named \share.; Users are authenticated with Microsoft Active Directory, and Windows ACLs control access to files and folders.; Multi-AZ maintains a standby file server in a separate Availability Zone; Single-AZ addresses component failures within one Availability Zone.; FSx manages Windows software updates, hardware failure detection and remediation, and backups.; HDD suits workloads such as home directories and departmental shares; SSD suits more latency-sensitive workloads.
Gotchas: A shared file service is not automatically a Windows-compatible SMB file service.; Single-AZ component protection does not provide failover across Availability Zones.; IAM policies control FSx API access; Windows ACLs control access to files and folders.
Confused with: Amazon EFS: EFS is a shared NFS file system; FSx for Windows supplies native Windows SMB shares and Windows ACLs.; Amazon S3: S3 stores objects, whereas FSx for Windows presents network file shares over SMB.; Amazon EBS: EBS provides block volumes, not managed SMB shares with Active Directory authentication.
ES: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server ofrece recursos compartidos de Windows totalmente administrados mediante SMB, con autenticación de Microsoft Active Directory y Windows ACLs para archivos y carpetas. Elígelo cuando las aplicaciones de Windows deban conservar estas funciones; elige Multi-AZ cuando el recurso deba seguir disponible ante una falla de una Availability Zone. Los clientes acceden a los recursos compartidos mediante SMB; cada sistema de archivos incluye uno predeterminado llamado \share.; Microsoft Active Directory autentica a los usuarios y Windows ACLs controla el acceso a archivos y carpetas.; Multi-AZ mantiene un servidor de archivos en espera en otra Availability Zone; Single-AZ atiende fallas de componentes dentro de una sola Availability Zone.; FSx administra las actualizaciones de Windows, la detección y resolución de fallas de hardware y los respaldos.; HDD es adecuado para directorios personales y recursos departamentales; SSD es adecuado para cargas más sensibles a la latencia.

chunks.title: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
chunks.text:
Scenario: A legal services firm is moving a document application to Windows EC2 instances. Its staff must keep using shared SMB paths, and existing permissions must remain enforceable at the file and folder level through Microsoft Active Directory. Which storage solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server joined to Microsoft Active Directory.
Why: The deciding requirements are shared SMB paths and Windows file and folder permissions authenticated through Microsoft Active Directory. FSx for Windows File Server supplies those features as a fully managed service. EFS is also managed shared file storage, but its NFS interface does not meet this application's Windows compatibility requirements.
Wrong options: Store the documents in Amazon S3 and grant users access with bucket policies. (S3 bucket policies do not provide the required SMB shares and Windows file and folder ACLs.); Attach an Amazon EBS volume to an application instance and store the documents there. (An EBS block volume does not itself provide a managed SMB share with Active Directory authentication.); Create an Amazon EFS file system and mount it on the application instances. (EFS uses NFS rather than the required native Windows SMB shares and ACLs.)

chunks.title: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media agency is replacing a departmental Windows file server used for home directories and shared project folders. Users will continue to access the folders over SMB, but the workload is not latency-sensitive and the agency wants to avoid paying for performance it does not need. Which managed storage choice is MOST cost-effective for these requirements?
Correct: Use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with HDD storage.
