Para un usuario o rol de IAM que accede a un recurso de la misma cuenta, los permisos basados en identidad y en recursos forman una unión; un allow en cualquiera de ellos puede permitir la acción.; Un explicit deny en una política basada en identidad o en recursos prevalece sobre un allow.; Para un usuario, los permisos basados en identidad y un permissions boundary forman una intersección; agregar el boundary puede reducir los permisos.; Para un usuario de una organización que accede a un recurso sin una política basada en recursos, las políticas del usuario, los SCP y los RCP forman una intersección. Un explicit deny en cualquiera de ellos prevalece sobre un allow.

chunks.title: IAM policy evaluation logic (explicit deny wins)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company is reviewing same-account access to two resources. For each request, an IAM role's identity-based policy allows the action; no permissions boundary or AWS Organizations policy applies. The security team must identify policy changes that would make a request fail despite its identity-based allow. Which changes would do so? (Choose two.)
Correct: Add an explicit deny for the action to the resource-based policy. + Add an explicit deny for the action to the role's identity-based policy.
Why: The question asks which changes defeat an existing identity-based allow. An explicit deny in either the identity-based or resource-based policy does so. Removing a resource-based allow does not have the same effect here: for same-account access, the role's identity-based allow can still permit the request.
Wrong options: Add a second identity-based policy that allows the same action. (An additional allow does not negate the existing allow.); Add a resource-based policy that allows the action for the role. (Another allow does not make an already allowed request fail.); Remove a resource-based allow while retaining the role's identity-based allow. (For same-account access, the remaining identity-based allow can still permit the request.)

chunks.title: IAM policy evaluation logic (explicit deny wins)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab gives an IAM user an identity-based policy that allows two AWS API actions. A permissions boundary attached to the user allows only the first action, and neither policy contains an explicit deny. No resource-based policy applies to the requests. Which result should the lab expect?
Correct: Only the first action is permitted, because the user's identity-based policy and boundary intersect.
Why: The requirement is to evaluate a user's identity-based permissions together with a permissions boundary. Their resulting permissions are the intersection, so the first action remains permitted and the second does not. An identity-based allow alone is not enough for the second action, even though the boundary contains no explicit deny.
Wrong options: Both actions are permitted, because the identity-based policy allows both. (The boundary limits the user's effective identity-based permissions.); Both actions are permitted, because the boundary has no explicit deny. (The second action is outside the boundary's allowed permissions.); Neither action is permitted, because a boundary replaces the identity-based policy. (The boundary intersects with, rather than replaces, the identity-based permissions.)

chunks.title: IAM roles for EC2 (instance profiles), Lambda and ECS tasks
chunks.text:
IAM roles for EC2 (instance profiles), Lambda and ECS tasks. Give applications AWS permissions through workload roles rather than access keys stored in code or configuration. For EC2, pass a role to the instance through an instance profile; for ECS workloads that need different permissions, use distinct task roles instead of relying on one shared EC2 instance role.
When to use: An application on EC2 must call AWS APIs without distributing long-term access keys.; Several ECS tasks on the same EC2 instance need different AWS permissions.; An application on EC2 must access resources in another AWS account.
Key facts: An EC2 instance profile contains a role and makes its temporary credentials available to applications on the instance.; Only one role can be assigned to an EC2 instance at a time; applications on that instance share its permissions.; ECS task roles can be distinct from the role of the EC2 instance hosting the tasks.; With the AWS CLI or API, create the EC2 role and instance profile separately, then specify the instance profile when launching the instance.; A role can be attached to an already running EC2 instance through an instance profile.; Launching an EC2 instance with a role requires permission to launch the instance and permission to pass that role.
Gotchas: Creating an EC2 role through the CLI or API does not, by itself, create the instance profile needed to pass it to an instance.; An EC2 instance role does not give different applications on the same instance separate sets of permissions.; Broad iam:PassRole permission can let a user launch an instance with a role that grants more access than intended.
Confused with: 
ES: Otorga permisos de AWS a las aplicaciones mediante roles de la carga de trabajo, en lugar de guardar access keys en el código o la configuración. Para EC2, pasa el rol mediante un instance profile; si las tareas de ECS necesitan permisos distintos, usa roles de tarea separados en vez de depender de un único rol compartido de la instancia. Un instance profile de EC2 contiene un rol y pone sus credenciales temporales a disposición de las aplicaciones de la instancia.; Solo se puede asignar un rol a una instancia EC2 a la vez; las aplicaciones de esa instancia comparten sus permisos.; Los roles de tarea de ECS pueden ser distintos del rol de la instancia EC2 que aloja las tareas.; Con AWS CLI o AWS API, creas por separado el rol y el instance profile de EC2; al iniciar la instancia, especificas el instance profile.; Puedes asociar un rol a una instancia EC2 que ya está en ejecución mediante un instance profile.; Para iniciar una instancia EC2 con un rol, necesitas permiso para iniciar la instancia y para pasar ese rol.

chunks.title: IAM roles for EC2 (instance profiles), Lambda and ECS tasks
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company runs two ECS tasks on the same EC2 host. One task reads a reports bucket; the other writes to a fulfillment bucket, and neither should receive the other's permissions. The team also wants to avoid application access keys. Which design meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Assign each ECS task its own role granting only that task's required bucket actions.
Why: The tasks need separate permissions while running on the same EC2 host. ECS task roles can be distinguished from the host's EC2 role, allowing each task to receive only its required access without application keys. A single host role would share permissions across applications, and an instance profile cannot contain two roles.
Wrong options: Give each task an IAM user's access keys limited to its bucket actions. (Separate IAM users could distinguish permissions, but they would place long-term keys in the applications.); Put two IAM roles into the host's instance profile and have each task select its own role. (An instance profile can contain only one IAM role.); Attach one EC2 instance role granting both sets of bucket actions and have both tasks use it. (Applications using the same EC2 instance role share its permissions, so the tasks would not be separated.)

chunks.title: IAM roles for EC2 (instance profiles), Lambda and ECS tasks
chunks.text:
Scenario: A conservation nonprofit has a fleet of running EC2 instances whose applications read field reports from S3 using access keys in configuration files. The team wants to remove those keys without rebuilding the instances and minimize ongoing credential maintenance. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure the applications to use an AWS SDK credential provider for the instance profile rather than reading keys from configuration files. + Create an EC2-trusted role with the required S3 access in an instance profile and associate the profile with the running instances.
Why: The fleet must keep running, stop using stored keys, and avoid routine credential replacement. An instance profile can be associated with a running EC2 instance, and an SDK credential provider can manage the role's automatically updated temporary credentials. Replacing or narrowing IAM user keys leaves keys on the instances, while adding a second role to each instance is not supported.
Wrong options: Replace the stored keys with a new IAM user's keys and schedule regular key updates. (Rotating IAM user keys still leaves long-term credentials on the instances and requires maintenance.); Keep the current access keys in the configuration files and restrict the keys to read-only S3 actions. (Narrower permissions do not remove the stored access keys or their maintenance burden.); Place one application role in an instance profile and a second application role directly on each EC2 instance. (An EC2 instance can have only one assigned role, so this does not provide a second independent instance role.)

chunks.title: IAM roles for EC2 (instance profiles), Lambda and ECS tasks
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher deploys an image-processing application to new EC2 instances using the AWS CLI. The application must read one S3 bucket, and the deployment must not place access keys on the instances. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST credential-management overhead?
Correct: Create an EC2-trusted IAM role with read access to the bucket, add it to an instance profile, and specify that profile when launching instances.
Why: The deciding requirements are CLI-based deployment and no access keys on the instances. An EC2 role supplies temporary credentials, but with the CLI the role must be added to an instance profile that is specified at launch. Creating only the role misses that separate CLI configuration step; IAM user keys add credential-management work.
Wrong options: Create an IAM user with read access to the bucket and periodically replace its access keys in each instance's configuration. (Periodic key replacement still requires distributing and managing long-term credentials on the instances.); Create an IAM user with read access to the bucket and copy its access keys to each instance during deployment. (The application would use long-term keys that must be distributed and managed on every instance.); Create an EC2-trusted IAM role with read access to the bucket and specify the role name directly when launching instances with the CLI. (CLI-based EC2 launches specify an instance profile, which must be created separately from the role.)

chunks.title: IAM users, groups and roles
chunks.text:
IAM users, groups and roles. IAM users represent individual people or applications, groups collect IAM users, and roles provide permissions to principals that assume them. Prefer roles when temporary credentials are possible; use an IAM user with long-term credentials only when the use case cannot use the preferred approach.
When to use: Use a role for a workload, federated identity, or cross-account principal that needs temporary access.; Use a group to assign the same permissions to a collection of IAM users.; Consider an IAM user when a client cannot use federation or roles.
Key facts: A role has no standard long-term password or access keys; assuming it provides temporary security credentials.; An IAM group is a collection of IAM users, not a principal that assumes a role.; Federated identities from an external identity provider assume IAM roles to access AWS resources.; For cross-account role delegation, the role's trust policy identifies who can assume it, while its permissions policy defines what it can do.; IAM users with long-term access keys are an exception for workloads or third-party clients that cannot use roles or supported federation.
Gotchas: Giving every workload its own IAM user and access key does not meet a requirement to avoid long-term credentials.; A group simplifies permissions for IAM users but does not replace a role for federated or service access.; A role's permissions policy alone does not establish which cross-account principal may assume it.
Confused with: IAM user group: A group collects IAM users for permissions; a role is assumed and supplies temporary credentials.; IAM user: A user is associated with a specific person or application; a role can be assumed by trusted principals.
ES: Los IAM users representan a personas o aplicaciones individuales, los IAM groups reúnen IAM users y los IAM roles otorgan permisos a quienes los asumen. Prefiere roles cuando puedas usar credenciales temporales; usa un IAM user con credenciales de largo plazo solo cuando el caso no admita el enfoque preferido. Un IAM role no tiene contraseña ni access keys estándar de largo plazo; al asumirlo obtienes credenciales de seguridad temporales.; Un IAM group reúne IAM users; no es un principal que asume un rol.; Las identidades federadas de un proveedor de identidad externo asumen IAM roles para acceder a recursos de AWS.; Para delegar acceso entre cuentas mediante un rol, su trust policy identifica quién puede asumirlo y su permissions policy define qué puede hacer.; Los IAM users con access keys de largo plazo son una excepción para cargas de trabajo o clientes de terceros que no pueden usar roles ni federación compatible.

chunks.title: IAM users, groups and roles
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company runs an application on Amazon EC2 that needs to write reports to an S3 bucket. Security requires that the application not store long-term AWS access keys. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Assign an IAM role with the required S3 permissions to the EC2 workload.
Why: The deciding requirement is that the EC2 application must not store long-term access keys. A role can be assumed by an AWS service and supplies temporary credentials with the permissions the workload needs. An IAM user, whether used alone or placed in a group, would require the proposed long-term keys.
Wrong options: Create one IAM user for the fleet and distribute its access keys to each instance. (Distributing a user's long-term keys conflicts with the requirement not to store them.); Create an IAM user for the application and store its access keys on the instance. (Storing the user's long-term keys violates the stated security requirement.); Add an IAM user for each instance to a group with the required S3 permissions. (The group can share permissions, but the application would still need IAM user credentials.)

chunks.title: IAM users, groups and roles
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company keeps its audit resources in one AWS account and its internal auditors' IAM users in another. Auditors need temporary access to perform specific audit actions in the resources account, without receiving IAM users or long-term keys in that account. Which TWO configurations are needed for IAM role-based cross-account delegation? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure the role's trust policy to allow the intended principals from the auditors' account to assume it. + Create a role in the resources account with a permissions policy for the specific audit actions.
Why: The auditors need role-based access across accounts, with temporary credentials and only specific audit permissions. Create the role in the resources account: its permissions policy defines the allowed audit actions, and its trust policy identifies the principals allowed to assume it. A permissions policy without trust is insufficient, while creating users and keys in the resources account violates the stated constraints.
Wrong options: Attach only a permissions policy to the role and allow any auditor to assume it without defining trust. (A role needs a trust policy identifying principals allowed to assume it.); Create IAM users in the resources account and give their access keys to the auditors. (This provides long-term credentials and additional users in the resources account, both of which are prohibited.); Create an IAM group in the resources account and add the auditors' IAM users from the other account. (A group is a collection of IAM users and is not the cross-account role the auditors need to assume.)

chunks.title: IAM users, groups and roles
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum has created IAM users for its cataloging staff. Every cataloger needs the same permissions on the museum's AWS resources, and administrators want to change those permissions for the entire team in one place. Which approach meets the requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Place the catalogers' IAM users in an IAM group and attach the permissions policy to the group.
Why: The staff already have individual IAM users and all need the same permissions. An IAM group is the identity designed to collect users, so attaching the shared policy to the group gives administrators one place to update it. Individual user policies or separate roles would require managing multiple copies.
Wrong options: Attach a separate copy of the permissions policy to each cataloger's IAM user. (Administrators would have to update the users individually rather than manage the team's permissions in one place.); Create one IAM user with the cataloging permissions and share its credentials with the staff. (One shared user does not preserve the existing individual IAM user identities.); Create a separate IAM role with the cataloging permissions for each staff member. (Separate roles do not provide the requested single place to change permissions for the existing IAM users.)

chunks.title: Identity federation with SAML 2.0 and OIDC
chunks.text:
Identity federation with SAML 2.0 and OIDC. Federate an existing IdP to IAM roles when external identities need access to AWS resources without individual IAM users or long-term credentials. For a small-scale, single-account deployment, choose SAML 2.0 for a corporate SAML IdP or OIDC for a compatible external application; for centralized workforce access across multiple accounts, prefer IAM Identity Center.
When to use: A corporate SAML IdP already authenticates employees who need access to one AWS account.; An external application with an OIDC-compatible IdP needs AWS access without stored access keys.; The requirement calls for temporary credentials and permissions defined by IAM roles.
Key facts: IAM federation supports SAML 2.0 and OIDC identity providers.; SAML federation can provide AWS Management Console SSO or AWS API access without creating an IAM user for each employee.; For SAML API access, AWS STS AssumeRoleWithSAML exchanges a SAML assertion for temporary security credentials.; A SAML role's trust policy names the SAML provider; its permissions policy defines allowed AWS actions.; A SAML provider referenced in a role trust policy must be in the same AWS account as that role.
Gotchas: Creating IAM users for every employee defeats the stated goal of using an existing IdP without individual AWS identities.; A role permissions policy alone does not establish trust with a SAML IdP.; IAM Identity Center is the better fit when the main requirement is centralized workforce access across multiple AWS accounts.
Confused with: iam-identity-center-sso: Choose IAM Identity Center for centralized workforce access across multiple AWS accounts; direct IAM federation fits a small-scale, single-account deployment.; cognito-user-pools: User pools add sign-up and sign-in to an application; they are not the direct IAM role-federation path for corporate AWS access.; cognito-identity-pools: Identity pools give application users temporary IAM credentials; direct IAM federation connects an external IdP to roles in an AWS account.
ES: Federa un IdP existente con roles de IAM cuando las identidades externas necesitan acceso a recursos de AWS sin crear usuarios de IAM individuales ni usar credenciales de larga duración. Para una implementación pequeña en una sola cuenta, elige SAML 2.0 si el IdP corporativo usa SAML u OIDC si una aplicación externa usa un IdP compatible; para acceso centralizado del personal a varias cuentas, prefiere IAM Identity Center. La federación con IAM admite proveedores de identidad SAML 2.0 y OIDC.; La federación SAML puede dar acceso SSO a AWS Management Console o acceso a las API de AWS sin crear un usuario de IAM por empleado.; Para acceso a API mediante SAML, AWS STS AssumeRoleWithSAML intercambia una aserción SAML por credenciales de seguridad temporales.; La trust policy de un rol SAML identifica al proveedor SAML; su permissions policy define las acciones de AWS permitidas.; El proveedor SAML indicado en la trust policy de un rol debe estar en la misma cuenta de AWS que el rol.

chunks.title: Identity federation with SAML 2.0 and OIDC
chunks.text:
Scenario: A software company runs build workflows in GitHub Actions and publishes artifacts to an S3 bucket in one AWS account. The workflows must use their existing OIDC identity and must not store AWS access keys. Which solution meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Configure the OIDC provider in IAM and grant the workflows access through an IAM role.
Why: The workflows already have an OIDC identity and cannot store AWS access keys. IAM supports an OIDC IdP trust relationship for external applications such as GitHub Actions to access AWS through roles. An IAM user with stored keys violates the credential constraint; SAML assumes a different identity-provider protocol.
Wrong options: Create a Cognito user pool and have each workflow sign in as an application user. (A user pool addresses application-user sign-in rather than the workflows' existing OIDC identity.); Configure a SAML provider in IAM and require the workflows to submit SAML assertions. (The stated external identity is OIDC, not a SAML assertion source.); Create an IAM user for the workflows and store its access keys in GitHub Actions secrets. (Stored access keys directly violate the requirement to avoid AWS access keys.)

chunks.title: Identity federation with SAML 2.0 and OIDC
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio has one standalone AWS account and an existing corporate SAML 2.0 portal. A small group of employees needs AWS Management Console access through that portal for a short-term project, without separate IAM users. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure the SAML IdP as an IAM identity provider and map employees to IAM roles for console access.
Why: The deciding constraints are the existing SAML portal, one AWS account, and no individual IAM users. IAM SAML federation maps the portal's users to roles and supports console SSO. Creating IAM users misses the identity requirement, while introducing another directory adds work without addressing it.
Wrong options: Create IAM users for the employees and link to the AWS sign-in page from the portal. (The employees would still need separate IAM users rather than using federated identities.); Deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD and create a new directory for the project. (A new directory does not use the existing SAML portal and adds unnecessary identity infrastructure.); Create a Cognito user pool and enroll the employees for application sign-in. (A user pool provides application sign-in, not the requested direct federation to AWS console roles.)

chunks.title: Immutable infrastructure and blue/green deployments
chunks.text:
Immutable infrastructure and blue/green deployments. Blue/green deployment runs two otherwise identical environments with different application versions and shifts traffic between them. Choose it when a release must avoid replacing the running version in place and preserve a path to send traffic back if the new version fails.
When to use: A release must minimize downtime and support a fast traffic rollback.; The team can prepare a separate environment before directing production traffic to it.; A server-based application needs a replacement deployment instead of patches applied to running servers.
Key facts: The blue and green environments run different application versions.; A release occurs by shifting traffic between the environments.; The approach can mitigate deployment downtime and improve rollback capability.; The data tier needs separate consideration; switching application traffic does not, by itself, reverse data changes.
Gotchas: Changing every live server in place does not preserve the previous environment for a traffic rollback.; Removing the old environment immediately weakens the rollback plan.; Do not assume an application traffic switch also restores the previous state of a database.
Confused with: 
ES: Un despliegue blue/green ejecuta dos entornos por lo demás idénticos con distintas versiones de la aplicación y cambia el tráfico entre ellos. Elígelo cuando debas evitar modificar la versión en ejecución y conservar la opción de devolverle el tráfico si falla la nueva versión. Los entornos blue y green ejecutan distintas versiones de la aplicación.; El lanzamiento se realiza al cambiar el tráfico entre los entornos.; Este enfoque puede reducir el riesgo de interrupciones y facilitar la reversión.; Debes considerar el nivel de datos por separado; cambiar el tráfico de la aplicación no revierte por sí solo los cambios en los datos.

chunks.title: Immutable infrastructure and blue/green deployments
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional news publisher has shifted reader traffic from its old application environment to a new one. Monitoring now shows errors in the new version, and the previous environment is still running. The publisher needs to restore service without first repairing or redeploying the new version. Which action best meets this requirement?
Correct: Shift reader traffic back to the previous environment and investigate the new version separately.
Why: The previous environment is still running, so the publisher can use the rollback capability of blue/green deployment: shift traffic back. This satisfies the requirement to restore service without first fixing or redeploying the new version. Patching the failing environment makes recovery depend on a successful repair.
Wrong options: Remove the previous environment and redeploy its version onto the new environment. (Redeployment adds a prerequisite even though the previous environment is already running.); Replace the instances in the previous environment with the new version, then redirect traffic there. (This removes the working previous version before readers can use it.); Patch the new environment until errors stop, leaving reader traffic routed to it. (This makes restoration depend on first repairing the failing version.)

chunks.title: Immutable infrastructure and blue/green deployments
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics startup is preparing a new version of its parcel-tracking site. The team wants to check it before production use, then release it with a way to return visitors to the current version if errors appear. Which TWO steps support this blue/green release plan? (Choose two.)
Correct: Prepare and check a separate environment running the new version. + Shift visitor traffic to the new environment while retaining the current one for a possible return.
Why: The startup needs both pre-release checks and a way to return traffic to the current version. Preparing a separate new-version environment supports the checks; shifting traffic while retaining the old environment supports rollback. Installing over the running site or shutting it down defeats the requested return path.
Wrong options: Keep a copy of the old deployment package instead of the running old environment. (A package alone cannot receive redirected visitors if the new version fails.); Install the new version over the running site before performing release checks. (An in-place installation removes the separate previous environment required for this rollback plan.); Shut down the current environment before directing visitors to the new one. (Shutting it down removes the ready destination for a traffic rollback.)

chunks.title: Infrastructure as code with AWS CloudFormation
chunks.text:
Infrastructure as code with AWS CloudFormation. AWS CloudFormation provisions and configures resources from a template, making an environment repeatable. Use a stack for a collection of resources; use StackSets when the same template must be deployed across multiple accounts and Regions.
When to use: Recreate an application environment consistently, including in a disaster recovery Region.; Provision or update stacks across multiple accounts and Regions with a single operation.; Check whether deployed StackSet resources have drifted from their intended configuration.
Key facts: A CloudFormation template describes resources and their properties; a stack manages the resulting resources as a unit.; The same template can be reused to provision resources in multiple Regions.; StackSets creates, updates, or deletes stacks in selected accounts and Regions with a single operation.; CloudFormation documentation includes drift detection for StackSets.
Gotchas: A template describes infrastructure; merely storing it does not provision resources in a recovery Region.; A stack is not the same as a StackSet operation targeting multiple accounts and Regions.; Recreating infrastructure does not, by itself, establish application data replication or failover.
Confused with: 
ES: AWS CloudFormation aprovisiona y configura recursos a partir de una plantilla para que puedas repetir un entorno de forma consistente. Usa un stack para administrar un conjunto de recursos; usa StackSets cuando debas desplegar la misma plantilla en varias cuentas y Regions. Una plantilla de CloudFormation describe los recursos y sus propiedades; un stack administra los recursos resultantes como una unidad.; Puedes reutilizar la misma plantilla para aprovisionar recursos en varias Regions.; StackSets crea, actualiza o elimina stacks en las cuentas y Regions seleccionadas con una sola operación.; La documentación de CloudFormation incluye detección de drift para StackSets.

chunks.title: Infrastructure as code with AWS CloudFormation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer has application accounts for separate business units and has selected a primary and recovery Region for each account. Its platform team maintains one approved template for the infrastructure in every selected account and Region. The team needs to roll out template updates to all those targets with a single operation. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use CloudFormation StackSets to manage stacks in the selected accounts and Regions from the approved template.
Why: The requirement is an update across multiple accounts and Regions in a single operation. CloudFormation StackSets extends stacks to create, update, or delete them across selected targets in that way. Updating ordinary stacks separately can use the same template, but it misses the operational requirement.
Wrong options: Use the approved template to update a stack in each account and Region in separate operations. (Individual stack updates do not meet the single-operation requirement.); Keep identical template copies for each business unit and have each unit update its own stacks. (Delegating separate updates does not provide one operation across all selected targets.); Create a stack from the template in one account and each primary Region, then document its settings for recovery Regions. (Documenting settings does not update stacks in the selected recovery Regions.)

chunks.title: Infrastructure as code with AWS CloudFormation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization deployed a standard set of resources to several accounts and Regions from one CloudFormation template. An audit now needs to check whether the deployed stack resources have drifted from their intended configuration. The organization also wants to keep managing deployments across those accounts and Regions centrally. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Manage the deployments with CloudFormation StackSets and perform drift detection on the StackSets deployments.
Why: The audit asks about deployed resources, not just changes to template text. CloudFormation StackSets supports managing stacks across accounts and Regions, and its documentation includes drift detection. Comparing template versions is useful for tracking edits to the template, but an unchanged template does not answer whether deployments have drifted.
Wrong options: Create a new stack from the template in one Region and use its successful creation to verify the existing deployments. (Creating another stack does not check existing deployed resources for drift across the targets.); Inspect resource settings in each account and Region manually, then maintain separate stacks for future updates. (Manual inspections and separate updates add overhead instead of retaining central cross-account and cross-Region management.); Compare versions of the template in source control and treat unchanged template text as proof that deployed resources have not drifted. (Template version history tracks template changes, not whether deployed resources have drifted.)

chunks.title: Amazon Inspector vulnerability scanning
chunks.text:
Amazon Inspector vulnerability scanning. Amazon Inspector automatically discovers eligible EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions, then continually scans them for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. Choose it when the requirement is to find and track vulnerabilities in workloads, rather than detect malicious activity or aggregate findings.
When to use: Continuously assess EC2 instances, ECR images, or Lambda functions for vulnerabilities.; Identify unintended network exposure and receive findings with remediation recommendations.; Manage vulnerability scanning and findings across AWS Organizations accounts.
Key facts: Inspector automatically discovers eligible resources; you do not manually schedule assessment scans.; It rescans in response to changes such as EC2 package updates, patches, or newly published relevant CVEs.; Findings include details about the issue and affected resource, plus remediation recommendations.; Inspector can automatically close a finding after it detects appropriate remediation.; A delegated administrator can manage Inspector findings and certain scan settings across member accounts.; Inspector publishes finding events to Amazon EventBridge and, when activated, findings to AWS Security Hub CSPM.
Gotchas: Security Hub CSPM can provide a broader view of findings, but it does not replace enabling Inspector to scan workloads.; GuardDuty-style threat detection is not the same requirement as scanning software for vulnerabilities.; Inspector reports unintended network exposure; it is not the service chosen to filter VPC traffic.
Confused with: Amazon GuardDuty: Choose Inspector for workload vulnerability scanning, not detection of malicious activity.; AWS Security Hub CSPM: Inspector produces vulnerability findings; Security Hub CSPM helps view findings within broader security-posture analysis.; AWS Network Firewall: Inspector identifies exposure; Network Firewall inspects and filters VPC traffic.
ES: Amazon Inspector descubre automáticamente instancias EC2, imágenes de contenedor en ECR y funciones Lambda elegibles, y las analiza continuamente para detectar vulnerabilidades de software y exposición de red no deseada. Elígelo cuando necesites identificar y dar seguimiento a vulnerabilidades en cargas de trabajo, no detectar actividad maliciosa ni solo reunir hallazgos. Inspector descubre automáticamente los recursos elegibles; no tienes que programar análisis de evaluación manualmente.; Vuelve a analizar los recursos ante cambios como paquetes nuevos en EC2, parches o la publicación de CVE relevantes.; Los hallazgos incluyen detalles del problema y del recurso afectado, además de recomendaciones de corrección.; Inspector puede cerrar automáticamente un hallazgo cuando detecta que se corrigió adecuadamente.; Una cuenta de administrador delegado puede administrar hallazgos y ciertas opciones de análisis de Inspector en las cuentas miembro.; Inspector publica eventos de hallazgos en Amazon EventBridge y, si está activado, también publica hallazgos en AWS Security Hub CSPM.

chunks.title: Amazon Inspector vulnerability scanning
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company runs video-processing workers on EC2 and distributes their container images through Amazon ECR. Security staff need to discover software vulnerabilities when packages change or a relevant CVE is published, without scheduling repeated assessments. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable Amazon Inspector scanning for the EC2 instances and ECR images.
Why: The deciding requirement is continuous vulnerability assessment of EC2 instances and ECR images without scheduled scans. Amazon Inspector discovers eligible resources and rescans when changes or newly published relevant CVEs can affect them. GuardDuty addresses malicious activity instead, while Security Hub CSPM provides a broader view of security posture rather than performing the requested Inspector scans.
Wrong options: Enable Amazon GuardDuty to detect suspicious activity affecting the workers. (Detecting suspicious activity does not meet the requirement to continually scan packages and images for vulnerabilities.); Enable AWS Security Hub CSPM to review the company's security posture. (A broader view of security posture does not replace the requested vulnerability scanning.); Enable Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in the company's S3 buckets. (Discovering sensitive S3 data does not assess EC2 packages or ECR images for vulnerabilities.)

chunks.title: Amazon Inspector vulnerability scanning
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer deploys Lambda functions and stores container images in Amazon ECR. The security team needs continuous vulnerability findings for both resource types and wants new findings routed to an Amazon SNS topic in near-real time for its existing workflow. Which TWO actions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use Amazon EventBridge to route Inspector finding events to the Amazon SNS topic. + Enable Amazon Inspector scanning for Lambda functions and ECR images.
Why: There are two distinct requirements: continually scan Lambda functions and ECR images, then route new findings to SNS in near-real time. Amazon Inspector performs the scans and publishes finding events to EventBridge, which can route them to an SNS topic. Security Hub CSPM can receive Inspector findings, but treating it as the scanning service leaves the first requirement unmet.
Wrong options: Enable Amazon GuardDuty to detect malicious activity in the AWS environment. (Malicious-activity detection does not provide the requested vulnerability scans of Lambda functions and ECR images.); Enable Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in Amazon S3. (Sensitive-data discovery in S3 meets neither the workload-scanning nor the finding-routing requirement.); Activate AWS Security Hub CSPM and use its broader security-posture view as the scanning service. (Security Hub CSPM can receive Inspector findings but does not replace Inspector scanning.)

chunks.title: EC2 instance store (ephemeral block storage)
chunks.text:
EC2 instance store (ephemeral block storage). EC2 instance store provides temporary block storage on disks physically attached to the host. Choose it for frequently changing caches, scratch data, or replicated data that can be rebuilt—not for data that must remain available after an instance stops or terminates.
When to use: An EC2 workload needs local block storage for temporary, frequently changing data.; A cache, scratch file, or replicated dataset can be recreated if the instance goes away.; The workload can use an instance type with instance store and benefits from storage included in the instance usage cost.
Key facts: Instance store volumes are exposed to an EC2 instance as block devices.; The disks are physically attached to the host computer.; Not every instance type provides instance store; available capacity and device count vary by type and size.; Instance store volumes have no additional charge beyond the instance usage cost.
Gotchas: Do not place the only copy of important data on instance store; it is temporary storage.; Do not assume an existing EC2 instance type has instance store volumes.; Local block storage does not provide a shared file system for multiple instances.
Confused with: Amazon EBS: Choose EBS when the block data must persist beyond an instance stop; instance store is temporary.; Amazon EFS: EFS provides a shared file system; instance store provides local block devices.; Amazon S3: S3 stores objects; instance store supplies temporary block storage to an EC2 instance.
ES: EC2 instance store ofrece almacenamiento de bloques temporal en discos conectados físicamente al host. Elígelo para cachés, datos de trabajo o datos replicados que puedas reconstruir, no para datos que deban seguir disponibles después de detener o terminar una instancia. Los volúmenes de instance store se presentan a una instancia EC2 como dispositivos de bloques.; Los discos están conectados físicamente al host.; No todos los tipos de instancia ofrecen instance store; la capacidad y la cantidad de dispositivos varían según el tipo y el tamaño.; Los volúmenes de instance store no tienen un cargo adicional al costo de uso de la instancia.

chunks.title: EC2 instance store (ephemeral block storage)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A game studio runs EC2 workers that use two datasets: intermediate files created during asset builds and a local index replicated across the worker fleet. Both datasets change frequently, can be recreated, and must be placed on local temporary block devices included in the instance usage cost. Which two placements meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Place the replicated index on instance store volumes of the workers. + Place the build intermediates on instance store volumes of the workers.
Why: Both datasets can be recreated, so temporary storage is acceptable. Instance store supplies local block devices included in the EC2 instance usage cost for both scratch data and replicated fleet data. EBS is a plausible block-storage distractor, but the question specifically requires volumes included with the instance; S3 and EFS also miss the local block-device requirement.
Wrong options: Place the replicated index on Amazon EBS volumes attached to the workers. (EBS is block storage, but it does not satisfy the requirement for temporary volumes included in instance usage cost.); Place the replicated index in an Amazon EFS file system. (EFS is a shared file system rather than local block storage included with each instance.); Place the build intermediates in Amazon S3 objects. (S3 objects do not provide local temporary block devices to the workers.)

chunks.title: EC2 instance store (ephemeral block storage)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company runs video-processing workers on EC2. Each worker repeatedly rewrites intermediate files, while the input files and finished videos are stored separately and any intermediate file can be recreated. The company wants local block storage included in the instance usage cost. Which storage choice meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Choose EC2 workers with instance store volumes and place the intermediate files there.
Why: The intermediate files are rebuildable, so they do not need persistent storage. Instance store is temporary block storage on disks attached to the EC2 host, and its volumes are included in the instance usage cost. EBS is a plausible block-storage choice, but it does not match the stated preference for storage included with the instance.
Wrong options: Store the intermediate files as Amazon S3 objects. (S3 is object storage, not the requested local block storage for frequently rewritten intermediate files.); Mount an Amazon EFS file system on every worker for the intermediate files. (EFS provides a shared file system rather than the requested local block devices.); Use Amazon EBS volumes for the intermediate files on each worker. (EBS provides block storage, but instance store specifically meets the requirement for temporary local storage included in the instance usage cost.)

chunks.title: Amazon Keyspaces (Apache Cassandra compatible)
chunks.text:
Amazon Keyspaces (Apache Cassandra compatible). Amazon Keyspaces is a serverless, managed Apache Cassandra–compatible wide-column database. Choose it when a workload must keep using Cassandra application code and developer tools without managing database servers.
When to use: Move an existing Apache Cassandra workload to AWS while retaining its application code and developer tools.; Run Cassandra-compatible tables without provisioning, patching, or managing servers.; Let tables scale automatically as application traffic changes.
Key facts: Amazon Keyspaces is a managed, highly available Apache Cassandra–compatible database service.; Existing Cassandra workloads can use the same application code and developer tools.; The service is serverless; tables scale up and down in response to application traffic.; You pay for only the resources that you use.; You can create keyspaces and tables without deploying infrastructure or installing software.
Gotchas: Serverless NoSQL alone does not make DynamoDB the best fit when retaining Cassandra code and tools is a requirement.; A managed database is not necessarily Cassandra-compatible; check the existing workload’s required interface.; Do not assume that moving to Keyspaces requires provisioning Cassandra servers.
Confused with: Amazon DynamoDB: DynamoDB is a serverless key-value/document option; Keyspaces fits the requirement to retain Cassandra application code and developer tools.; Amazon DocumentDB: DocumentDB targets MongoDB-compatible document workloads, not the stated Cassandra workload.; Amazon Neptune: Neptune fits graph relationships; Keyspaces fits a Cassandra-compatible wide-column workload.
ES: Amazon Keyspaces es una base de datos de columnas anchas, administrada, serverless y compatible con Apache Cassandra. Elígela cuando debas conservar el código y las herramientas de una aplicación Cassandra sin administrar servidores de base de datos. Amazon Keyspaces es un servicio de base de datos administrado, de alta disponibilidad y compatible con Apache Cassandra.; Las cargas existentes de Cassandra pueden usar el mismo código y las mismas herramientas de desarrollo.; El servicio es serverless y sus tablas escalan hacia arriba o hacia abajo según el tráfico.; Pagas solo por los recursos que usas.; Puedes crear keyspaces y tablas sin desplegar infraestructura ni instalar software.

chunks.title: Amazon Keyspaces (Apache Cassandra compatible)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing platform stores event activity in Apache Cassandra tables. Traffic rises during ticket releases and falls between events, but the platform must continue running its existing Cassandra workload. The team wants tables that adjust automatically to traffic and a serverless service where it pays only for resources used. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use Amazon Keyspaces for the Cassandra tables and let them scale with traffic.
Why: The platform needs both Cassandra compatibility and serverless scaling as traffic changes. Amazon Keyspaces scales tables up and down with application traffic, and customers pay for the resources they use. Running Cassandra on EC2 preserves the workload but fails the serverless requirement; changing to another database does not preserve the existing Cassandra workload.
Wrong options: Run Apache Cassandra on Amazon EC2 and adjust server capacity for each release. (Adjusting EC2 capacity requires server management rather than the requested serverless service.); Use Amazon DynamoDB and redesign activity storage around its keys and items. (Redesigning storage for DynamoDB does not meet the requirement to continue the existing Cassandra workload.); Use Amazon Aurora Serverless and move the activity data into relational tables. (Moving to relational tables does not preserve the existing Cassandra workload.)

chunks.title: Amazon Keyspaces (Apache Cassandra compatible)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company runs an Apache Cassandra application that records package scans. It wants to move the workload to AWS while keeping its existing Cassandra application code and developer tools. The database team does not want to provision or patch servers. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Move the Cassandra workload to Amazon Keyspaces and continue using its existing code and tools.
Why: The deciding constraints are continued use of Cassandra application code and tools and no server provisioning or patching. Amazon Keyspaces is a managed, Cassandra-compatible service that meets both. DynamoDB is a plausible serverless alternative, but the proposed migration requires adapting the application.
Wrong options: Run Apache Cassandra on Amazon EC2 instances and retain the current application. (This retains the application but leaves the team responsible for managing the servers.); Move the scan records to Amazon DynamoDB and adapt the application to its data model. (Adapting the application does not meet the requirement to keep its Cassandra code and tools.); Move the scan records to Amazon DocumentDB and adapt the application for document access. (A document-oriented migration does not preserve the stated Cassandra application interface.)

chunks.title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (shards, retention, ordering)
chunks.text:
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (shards, retention, ordering). Amazon Kinesis Data Streams ingests records for real-time processing by multiple independent applications. Choose it when consumers need custom processing, ordered reads within shards, or access to retained records rather than only managed delivery to a destination.
When to use: Several applications must independently process the same incoming records.; Producers need continuous ingestion for custom, real-time analytics or alerts.; Consumers need to read retained records again after a processing change.; Records from one entity must be routed together for ordered processing within a shard.
Key facts: A shard is the base throughput unit and contains a sequence of records; consumers can read records in the order stored in that shard.; A producer supplies a partition key to route records to shards. Using an entity ID as the key routes that entity's records together.; Multiple applications can consume the same stream independently.; Shared fan-out consumers share a shard's read throughput; an enhanced fan-out consumer receives its own read-throughput allotment.; On-demand Standard automatically manages capacity; provisioned mode lets you manage throughput yourself.; Records are available until they expire. Extended retention can keep data beyond 24 hours.
Gotchas: Per-shard ordering does not promise one global order across the entire stream.; A single partition key for every entity can concentrate traffic on one shard.; Multiple shared fan-out consumers still compete for a shard's shared read throughput.; If the only goal is managed delivery into a destination, a custom stream-processing application may be unnecessary.
Confused with: data-firehose: Data Firehose is the managed-delivery choice; Data Streams is the retained stream for independent, custom consumers.; amazon-msk: Choose MSK when Apache Kafka compatibility is a requirement, rather than introducing Kafka for a new Data Streams workload.; Amazon SQS: SQS supports per-message queue processing, not independent consumers rereading the same retained stream.
ES: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams ingiere registros para que varias aplicaciones independientes los procesen en tiempo real. Elígelo cuando los consumidores necesiten procesamiento personalizado, lecturas ordenadas dentro de cada shard o acceso a registros retenidos, y no solo entrega administrada a un destino. Un shard es la unidad básica de capacidad y contiene una secuencia de registros; los consumidores pueden leerlos en el orden en que se almacenaron en ese shard.; El productor proporciona una partition key para dirigir registros a shards. Usar el ID de la entidad como clave dirige juntos sus registros.; Varias aplicaciones pueden consumir el mismo stream de forma independiente.; Los consumidores con shared fan-out comparten la capacidad de lectura de un shard; cada consumidor con enhanced fan-out recibe su propia asignación.; On-demand Standard administra la capacidad automáticamente; provisioned mode te permite administrarla.; Los registros están disponibles hasta que vencen. Extended retention puede conservar datos durante más de 24 horas.

chunks.title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (shards, retention, ordering)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer sends temperature and vibration events from many machines to a Kinesis data stream. A custom consumer must process each machine's events in their stored order, while the producer should distribute different machines across shards rather than route all events together. Which producer configuration BEST meets these requirements?
Correct: Use the machine ID as the partition key when publishing each event to Kinesis Data Streams.
Why: The requirement is ordering for each machine, not a global order across all machines. Kinesis Data Streams uses the producer-supplied partition key to route records to shards, whose records consumers can read in stored order. Using the machine ID keeps a machine's records together while allowing different IDs to be routed across shards. A random key per event loses that grouping, whereas one universal key defeats the requested distribution.
Wrong options: Generate a new random partition key for each event from every machine. (Changing keys for one machine can route its events to different shards, undermining the requested per-machine ordering.); Use one fixed partition key for all events from all machines. (A single key routes the machines' records together instead of distributing different machines across shards.); Send events directly to Amazon Data Firehose and use the machine ID as a field in the delivered records. (A field in delivered records does not establish partition-key routing for the requested custom shard consumer.)

chunks.title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (shards, retention, ordering)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A city transit system has several applications reading the same Kinesis data stream to update arrival estimates and trigger service alerts. As more applications are added, their shared reads contend for a shard's read throughput. Each application still needs to receive the stream independently with high performance. Which change BEST addresses the read contention?
Correct: Register the applications as enhanced fan-out consumers and use SubscribeToShard.
Why: The bottleneck is competition among applications reading the same shard, not an inability to ingest events. Shared fan-out consumers share a shard's read throughput, while enhanced fan-out provides each registered consumer a separate allotment. Those consumers use SubscribeToShard to retrieve records. Moving applications to a queue or delivered S3 objects would change the required independent stream-consumption pattern.
Wrong options: Deliver the stream to Amazon S3 with Data Firehose and have applications read delivered objects. (Reading delivered objects replaces independent, high-performance stream consumption rather than resolving its read contention.); Replace the stream with a single Amazon SQS queue polled by all applications. (A single queue does not provide the required independent consumption of the same stream.); Keep all applications as shared fan-out consumers using GetRecords. (Shared fan-out consumers continue to share the shard's read-throughput allotment.)

chunks.title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (shards, retention, ordering)
chunks.text:
Scenario: An online learning platform receives a continuous stream of lesson interactions. A custom application must update engagement metrics as events arrive, and analysts must be able to revisit retained events after revising that logic. The platform also wants managed delivery of the same source events to Amazon S3 for an archive, without writing an archive-delivery application. Which TWO components together meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use Amazon Data Firehose to deliver data from Kinesis Data Streams to Amazon S3. + Ingest interactions into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for the custom application to consume.
Why: The custom metrics application and its need to revisit retained events call for Kinesis Data Streams as the source. Its prebuilt integration with Data Firehose can deliver records to S3 without a separately written archive application. Using Data Firehose alone loses the requested retained-stream design for the live consumer. Introducing a second platform does not meet the same-source, low-overhead archive requirement.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Data Firehose as the only ingestion point and deliver events directly to Amazon S3. (Direct delivery alone does not supply the retained stream needed by the custom live consumer.); Introduce Amazon MSK as a second ingestion platform for the archive workflow. (A second streaming platform does not provide the requested low-overhead managed S3 delivery from the same source stream.); Put interactions in one Amazon SQS queue for both the metrics application and archive workflow. (One queue does not provide the requested independent reading and revisiting of a retained stream.)

chunks.title: KMS envelope encryption and data keys
chunks.text:
KMS envelope encryption and data keys. Envelope encryption encrypts data with a data key, then protects that data key with a KMS key. For large objects, choose a data key used outside AWS KMS rather than sending each object to AWS KMS for encryption.
When to use: An application must encrypt large amounts of data while protecting the encryption keys.; Encrypted data and the key needed to decrypt it must be stored together.; Data encrypted under one key must also be protected under another key without re-encrypting the large object.
Key facts: GenerateDataKey returns a plaintext data key and a copy encrypted under a specified symmetric encryption KMS key.; The application uses the plaintext data key outside AWS KMS to encrypt data, then removes it from memory as soon as possible.; The encrypted data key can be stored alongside the encrypted data.; To decrypt the data, call AWS KMS Decrypt on the encrypted data key, then use the returned plaintext data key outside AWS KMS.; AWS KMS does not store, manage, or track data keys; its cryptographic operations have per-second request quotas.
Gotchas: GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext returns only an encrypted data key; it does not provide a plaintext key for immediate encryption.; AWS KMS does not use a generated data key to encrypt your application data.; Do not retain a plaintext data key alongside encrypted data; store its encrypted copy instead.
Confused with: 
ES: Envelope encryption cifra los datos con una data key y protege esa data key con una KMS key. Para objetos grandes, elige una data key que se use fuera de AWS KMS en lugar de enviar cada objeto a AWS KMS para cifrarlo. GenerateDataKey devuelve una data key en texto sin cifrar y una copia cifrada bajo una KMS key simétrica de cifrado especificada.; La aplicación usa la data key en texto sin cifrar fuera de AWS KMS para cifrar los datos y después la elimina de la memoria lo antes posible.; La data key cifrada puede almacenarse junto a los datos cifrados.; Para descifrar los datos, llama a AWS KMS Decrypt con la data key cifrada y luego usa la data key en texto sin cifrar fuera de AWS KMS.; AWS KMS no almacena, administra ni rastrea las data keys; sus operaciones criptográficas tienen cuotas de solicitudes por segundo.

chunks.title: KMS envelope encryption and data keys
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher has encrypted a large catalog with data keys protected by one KMS key. It now needs to protect that catalog's data keys under another key while avoiding the work of encrypting every large document again. Which approach meets this requirement MOST efficiently?
Correct: Protect the existing data keys under the other key without re-encrypting the documents.
Why: The publisher needs a change in key protection, not a change to the encrypted documents. With envelope encryption, it can re-encrypt the data keys that protect large data instead of re-encrypting that data. Decrypting and encrypting every document repeats the expensive work the scenario explicitly excludes. Storing plaintext keys would not protect them under the new key.
Wrong options: Send every encrypted document to AWS KMS Decrypt and then encrypt the returned documents under the other key. (AWS KMS Decrypt can decrypt the encrypted data key, not use that data key to decrypt an entire document.); Store a plaintext copy of every data key with its document for future changes. (Plaintext copies do not provide the required protection under the other key.); Decrypt every document and encrypt it again using a newly generated data key. (This repeats encryption of the large documents, which the publisher wants to avoid.)

chunks.title: KMS envelope encryption and data keys
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company encrypts large batches of shipment records in its application. Its architects want to keep the key that protects each batch's data key in AWS KMS and avoid making an AWS KMS cryptographic request for every record. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Call GenerateDataKey with a symmetric encryption KMS key to obtain plaintext and encrypted copies of a data key. + Encrypt batch records outside AWS KMS with the plaintext data key and store its encrypted copy with the batch.
Why: The requirements call for a KMS-protected data key and encryption that does not invoke AWS KMS for every record. GenerateDataKey returns both a plaintext data key for use outside AWS KMS and an encrypted copy protected by the specified symmetric KMS key. The application can encrypt the batch records with the plaintext key and store the encrypted key with the batch. Calling AWS KMS Encrypt for each record would conflict with the request pattern the architects want to avoid; AWS KMS cryptographic operations also have per-second quotas.
Wrong options: Ask AWS KMS to store and track each plaintext data key until the batch is decrypted. (AWS KMS does not store, manage, or track generated data keys.); Call AWS KMS Encrypt separately for each shipment record. (This makes an AWS KMS cryptographic request for every record.); Call GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext and use the returned encrypted key directly for batch encryption. (An encrypted data key cannot serve as the plaintext key needed for immediate batch encryption.)

chunks.title: KMS key policies, grants and cross-account key use
chunks.text:
KMS key policies, grants and cross-account key use. A KMS key policy is the primary access control for a KMS key; an IAM allow alone cannot grant access unless the key policy permits it. For cross-account key use, the key owner's policy must permit the external account or principal, and the external account must delegate the permitted actions to its identity.
When to use: An application in one AWS account must encrypt or decrypt with a KMS key owned by another account.; An IAM role has KMS permissions but still cannot use a key.; Only a specific external role should be able to use a shared key.
Key facts: Every KMS key has exactly one key policy, and key policies are Regional.; A key policy can name an external account or specific external users or roles; the external account must also grant the applicable permissions to its identities.; The IAM policy in the external account can grant only actions and principals permitted by the key policy.; Cross-account permissions work for cryptographic operations and certain listed operations, including CreateGrant and DescribeKey, but not ScheduleKeyDeletion.; For cross-account cryptographic requests, identify the key by its key ARN or alias ARN; a bare key ID or alias name is treated as a key in the caller's account.
Gotchas: Granting an external role kms:Decrypt in IAM does not override a key policy that excludes it.; Naming an external account in the key policy does not, by itself, give every identity in that account usable access.; Do not use an unrestricted * principal in an allow statement: it can expose the key to identities in other accounts that have matching permissions.
Confused with: 
ES: La key policy es el control de acceso principal de una KMS key; un permiso de IAM por sí solo no concede acceso si la key policy no lo permite. Para usar una clave entre cuentas, la política de la cuenta propietaria debe permitir la cuenta o identidad externa, y la cuenta externa debe delegar las acciones permitidas a su identidad. Cada KMS key tiene exactamente una key policy, y las key policies son Regional.; Una key policy puede nombrar una cuenta externa o usuarios o roles externos específicos; la cuenta externa también debe conceder los permisos correspondientes a sus identidades.; La IAM policy de la cuenta externa solo puede conceder acciones a identidades permitidas por la key policy.; Los permisos entre cuentas funcionan para operaciones criptográficas y ciertas operaciones enumeradas, incluidas CreateGrant y DescribeKey, pero no ScheduleKeyDeletion.; Para operaciones criptográficas entre cuentas, identifica la clave con su key ARN o alias ARN; un key ID o alias name sin ARN se interpreta como una clave de la cuenta que hace la solicitud.

chunks.title: KMS key policies, grants and cross-account key use
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics firm has authorized a role in its reporting account to encrypt data with a KMS key in its security account. The key policy and the role's IAM policy allow the operation, but the role's application specifies only the key ID and cannot use the intended key. The team wants to keep the existing cross-account access model. Which change should the team make?
Correct: Specify the security account's key ARN in the encryption request.
Why: Both policies already provide cross-account encryption permission; the remaining problem is key identification. For a cryptographic request against a key in another account, the application can supply its key ARN or alias ARN. A bare key ID is interpreted as referring to a key in the caller's account. Adding ListKeys permission does not fix that interpretation.
Wrong options: Select the security account's key from the KMS console list in the reporting account. (The KMS console does not list keys from other accounts, even when the role can use them.); Replace the key ID with the key's alias name, without an ARN. (A bare alias name, like a bare key ID, is interpreted as a key in the caller's account.); Add kms:ListKeys to the reporting role's IAM policy. (ListKeys does not change how the encryption request resolves a bare key ID.)

chunks.title: KMS key policies, grants and cross-account key use
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research company stores encrypted analysis results in one AWS account. A processing role in a second account already has an IAM policy allowing kms:Decrypt on the KMS key ARN, but its decrypt requests are denied. The key owner's policy does not mention the second account. Which change allows only that processing role to use the key for decryption with the MOST restrictive access?
Correct: Add the processing role ARN as a principal in the key policy and allow kms:Decrypt.
Why: The deciding requirements are cross-account decryption and access limited to one role. The role already has its IAM permission, so the missing allowance belongs in the key owner's key policy. Naming the role ARN there restricts which external identity can receive the permission. Naming the entire external account would work for access but would permit broader delegation than requested.
Wrong options: Add kms:Decrypt to the processing role's existing IAM policy with a Resource of *. (A broader IAM resource does not help when the owning account's key policy does not permit the external role.); Add kms:ListKeys to the processing role's IAM policy in the second account. (ListKeys does not grant decrypt access and is not an effective cross-account permission on the owner's key.); Add the second account as a principal in the key policy and allow kms:Decrypt. (This can enable the existing role, but it also lets that account's administrators delegate the permission to other identities, missing the restriction to one role.)

chunks.title: KMS automatic and manual key rotation
chunks.text:
KMS automatic and manual key rotation. For a customer managed symmetric KMS key with AWS_KMS-generated material, use automatic rotation when new key material is needed on a recurring schedule; you can configure the rotation period. For an immediate change, consider on-demand rotation, including for eligible keys with imported material. If the key type does not support either method, create a new KMS key and switch applications or aliases to it.
When to use: A compliance rule calls for recurring rotation of an eligible customer managed key without scheduling it yourself.; New key material is needed immediately while retaining the same eligible KMS key.; An asymmetric key, HMAC key, or key in a custom key store must be rotated manually.
Key facts: Automatic rotation is supported for symmetric encryption customer managed keys with AWS_KMS-generated material; its default period is 365 days, and a custom period can be specified.; On-demand rotation is supported for symmetric encryption keys with AWS_KMS or EXTERNAL origin.; Rotation of an existing key changes its key material, not its logical KMS key; AWS KMS selects the appropriate older material when decrypting existing ciphertext.; For multi-Region keys with AWS_KMS origin, enable automatic rotation or initiate on-demand rotation on the primary key.
Gotchas: Automatic rotation is not supported for imported key material, although eligible symmetric keys with imported material support on-demand rotation.; Rotating a KMS key does not rotate data keys or re-encrypt protected data.; An on-demand rotation does not change an existing automatic rotation schedule.
Confused with: 
ES: Para una clave administrada por el cliente de tipo simétrico cuyo material genera AWS KMS, usa automatic rotation si necesitas material nuevo en un calendario recurrente; puedes configurar el período. Para un cambio inmediato, considera on-demand rotation, incluso para claves elegibles con material importado. Si el tipo de clave no admite ninguno de esos métodos, crea una clave KMS nueva y cambia las aplicaciones o los alias para que la usen. Automatic rotation se admite para claves de cifrado simétricas administradas por el cliente con material generado por AWS KMS; el período predeterminado es de 365 días y puedes especificar uno personalizado.; On-demand rotation se admite para claves de cifrado simétricas con origen AWS_KMS o EXTERNAL.; La rotación de una clave existente cambia su material, no la clave KMS lógica; AWS KMS selecciona el material anterior adecuado para descifrar ciphertext existente.; Para claves multi-Region con origen AWS_KMS, habilita automatic rotation o inicia on-demand rotation en la clave primaria.

chunks.title: KMS automatic and manual key rotation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company encrypts its archive with a customer managed symmetric KMS key whose material AWS KMS generated. Its contract requires new KMS key material on a recurring, company-defined schedule. The archive must remain readable without changing the application's key reference. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable automatic rotation on the existing key with a custom rotation period.
Why: The deciding requirements are recurring rotation on a company-defined schedule and an unchanged application key reference. Automatic rotation with a custom period rotates material within the existing logical KMS key. A one-time on-demand rotation does not create a recurring schedule. Omitting the period selects the default rather than the company's specified interval.
Wrong options: Perform one on-demand rotation on the existing key when the contract begins. (One immediate rotation does not establish recurring rotation.); Enable automatic rotation on the existing key without specifying a rotation period. (This uses the default period rather than the required company-defined schedule.); Create a new KMS key for each scheduled change and update the application to reference it. (This requires recurring application changes instead of retaining the existing key reference.)

chunks.title: KMS automatic and manual key rotation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab uses a customer managed symmetric encryption KMS key with imported key material. After a planned change to its imported material, the lab needs to initiate rotation immediately and keep the same logical KMS key for existing applications. Which approach meets these requirements?
Correct: Import the new material into the existing key and initiate on-demand rotation.
Why: The lab needs immediate rotation of imported material without replacing its logical KMS key. On-demand rotation supports symmetric encryption keys with EXTERNAL origin after the new material is imported. Automatic rotation is limited to eligible keys with AWS_KMS-generated material. Creating a replacement key would break the requirement to retain the existing logical key.
Wrong options: Create a new key and update every application to use its key ID. (A new key would not retain the existing logical KMS key required by the lab.); Wait for AWS KMS to rotate the imported material on its annual schedule. (AWS KMS does not automatically rotate imported material.); Enable automatic rotation with a custom period on the existing key. (Automatic rotation is not supported for keys with imported material.)

chunks.title: AWS KMS key types: AWS owned vs AWS managed vs customer managed
chunks.text:
AWS KMS key types: AWS owned vs AWS managed vs customer managed. Choose a customer managed KMS key when you must control its policy, lifecycle, or cross-account access. If you do not need that control, an AWS managed key avoids key administration; an AWS owned key offers even less visibility and no customer key charges.
When to use: Choose customer managed when you must edit the key policy, disable the key, or control rotation.; Choose customer managed when another account needs permission to use the key.; Choose AWS managed when an integrated service can manage the key and you only need to view its policy or audit its use.; Choose AWS owned when supported by the service and automated encryption without customer-visible key activity is acceptable.
Key facts: Customer managed keys are in your account; you can manage their policies and lifecycle and audit their use in CloudTrail.; AWS managed keys are in your account. You can view their policies and audit their use in CloudTrail, but you cannot change their policies or lifecycle.; AWS managed keys are automatically rotated every year; you cannot change that schedule.; AWS owned keys reside in an AWS service account. You cannot view their policies or audit their key activity.; Customer managed keys have a monthly fee and usage charges. AWS managed keys have no monthly fee but may incur usage charges; AWS owned keys have no customer key charges.
Gotchas: AWS managed does not mean customer-manageable: a visible key policy is not an editable key policy.; AWS managed keys are limited to use by principals in the key's account; they cannot support sharing resources encrypted under them with another account.; AWS owned and AWS managed keys both remove key administration, but only AWS managed key use is visible in your CloudTrail logs.
Confused with: kms-multi-region-keys: Multi-Region keys address use of related key material across Regions; they do not replace the decision about who controls a key's policy and lifecycle.; cloudhsm: CloudHSM is for requirements such as a single-tenant HSM and exclusive customer key control, not merely an editable KMS key policy.
ES: Elige una customer managed KMS key cuando debas controlar su política, su ciclo de vida o el acceso entre cuentas. Si no necesitas ese control, una AWS managed key evita administrar la clave; una AWS owned key ofrece aún menos visibilidad y no genera cargos por la clave al cliente. Las customer managed keys están en tu cuenta; puedes administrar sus políticas y su ciclo de vida, y auditar su uso en CloudTrail.; Las AWS managed keys están en tu cuenta. Puedes consultar sus políticas y auditar su uso en CloudTrail, pero no puedes cambiar sus políticas ni su ciclo de vida.; Las AWS managed keys rotan automáticamente cada año; no puedes modificar ese calendario.; Las AWS owned keys están en una cuenta del servicio de AWS. No puedes consultar sus políticas ni auditar la actividad de esas claves.; Las customer managed keys tienen un cargo mensual y cargos por uso. Las AWS managed keys no tienen cargo mensual, pero pueden generar cargos por uso; las AWS owned keys no generan cargos por la clave al cliente.

chunks.title: AWS KMS key types: AWS owned vs AWS managed vs customer managed
chunks.text:
Scenario: A claims platform encrypts records through an AWS service that supports customer managed KMS keys. Its security team must define which roles may use the key and must be able to disable the key immediately during an incident. Which key choice meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a customer managed KMS key and configure the service to use it.
Why: The deciding requirements are control over key permissions and the ability to disable the key. A customer managed KMS key provides both and can be selected by the integrated service. An AWS managed key is easier to adopt, but its policy and lifecycle cannot be changed by the customer. CloudHSM adds operational work that the scenario does not require.
Wrong options: Use an AWS managed key created by the service in the platform's account. (The team can view an AWS managed key's policy but cannot change it or disable the key.); Provision a CloudHSM cluster and keep the record-encryption key there. (A CloudHSM cluster adds infrastructure management when a customer managed KMS key supplies the requested controls.); Use the service's AWS owned key for the records. (AWS owned keys do not let the security team set key permissions or disable the key.)

chunks.title: AWS KMS key types: AWS owned vs AWS managed vs customer managed
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization stores encrypted datasets in an AWS account and grants a partner in a different AWS account access to selected datasets. The encryption key must permit authorized principals in the partner account to use it, and the organization must maintain the key policy. The service storing the datasets supports customer managed KMS keys. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
