Correct: Use a customer managed KMS key and configure its policy for the partner account.
Why: Cross-account key use and customer-maintained policy control determine the choice. A customer managed KMS key supports both and works with the stated service integration. Granting dataset access alone does not make an AWS managed key usable by principals in another account. CloudHSM introduces operational work that is unnecessary for these requirements.
Wrong options: Use the storage service's AWS owned key and edit its policy for the partner account. (The organization cannot view or edit the policy of an AWS owned key.); Use the storage service's AWS managed key and grant the partner access to the datasets. (Resources encrypted under an AWS managed key cannot be shared with another account using that key.); Store the encryption key in a CloudHSM cluster and manage partner permissions there. (CloudHSM adds HSM operations when a customer managed KMS key supplies the required cross-account policy control.)

chunks.title: AWS KMS key types: AWS owned vs AWS managed vs customer managed
chunks.text:
Scenario: A hospital is assigning KMS key types to several AWS-service encryption workloads. Each listed service supports customer managed KMS keys, and the hospital wants to use them only where the stated control requires them. Which TWO workload decisions correctly identify a need for a customer managed key? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use a customer managed key when security staff must be able to disable the key. + Use a customer managed key when security staff must edit the key policy.
Why: The question asks which requirements make customer control necessary, not merely useful. Editing a key policy and disabling a key both require a customer managed key. AWS managed keys already provide customer-visible policies and CloudTrail auditability, although customers cannot edit those policies. Where offered, an AWS owned key is the better match for default encryption with no customer key charges.
Wrong options: Use a customer managed key when staff must merely view the key policy. (The hospital can view an AWS managed key's policy without creating a customer managed key.); Use a customer managed key when staff need only to audit key use in CloudTrail. (AWS managed key use is also auditable in CloudTrail, so audit visibility alone does not require customer management.); Use a customer managed key when a service needs encryption by default with no customer key charges. (If the service offers one, an AWS owned key provides default encryption without customer key charges.)

chunks.title: KMS multi-Region keys
chunks.text:
KMS multi-Region keys. AWS KMS multi-Region keys are related keys in selected Regions that share key material and a key ID. Choose them when client-side encrypted data must be decrypted in another Region without re-encryption or a cross-Region KMS call.
When to use: A disaster recovery Region must decrypt client-side encrypted data from the primary Region.; An active-active application moves client-side encrypted data between Regions and needs local cryptographic operations.
Key facts: Create a multi-Region primary key, then explicitly create replicas in selected Regions within the same AWS partition.; Related primary and replica keys can decrypt one another’s ciphertext because they share key material and a key ID.; Each Regional key has its own key policy, grants, aliases, tags, and enabled or disabled state.; An existing single-Region key cannot be converted to a multi-Region key; moving existing data requires re-encryption under new multi-Region keys.; Most AWS services that integrate with KMS treat multi-Region keys as single-Region keys; Amazon S3 cross-Region replication still decrypts and re-encrypts data keys in the destination Region.
Gotchas: Multi-Region keys are not global: AWS KMS does not automatically create replicas in other Regions.; A replica does not automatically inherit later changes to the primary key’s policy or grants.; Related keys do not eliminate a service-specific replication workflow, such as S3 cross-Region replication’s handling of encrypted data keys.
Confused with: AWS managed KMS keys: AWS managed keys are always single-Region keys, so they cannot provide a related multi-Region replica.; Single-Region customer managed KMS keys: Separately created single-Region keys do not share the key material and key ID needed for interoperable decryption.; AWS CloudHSM: Multi-Region KMS keys cannot be created in a custom key store; choose related KMS keys for this cross-Region interoperability requirement.
ES: Las multi-Region keys de AWS KMS son claves relacionadas en las Regions que selecciones; comparten material de clave y key ID. Elígelas cuando necesites descifrar datos cifrados del lado del cliente en otra Region sin volver a cifrarlos ni hacer una llamada entre Regions a KMS. Creas una multi-Region primary key y luego creas explícitamente réplicas en las Regions elegidas dentro de la misma AWS partition.; Las claves principales y réplicas relacionadas pueden descifrar los datos cifrados por cualquiera de ellas porque comparten material de clave y key ID.; Cada clave regional tiene sus propias key policies, grants, aliases, tags y estado enabled o disabled.; No puedes convertir una single-Region key existente en una multi-Region key; para migrar datos existentes debes volver a cifrarlos con nuevas multi-Region keys.; La mayoría de los servicios integrados con KMS tratan las multi-Region keys como single-Region keys; Amazon S3 cross-Region replication todavía descifra y vuelve a cifrar las claves de datos en la Region de destino.

chunks.title: KMS multi-Region keys
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company encrypts archive files in its application before storing copies in two AWS Regions. If the primary Region fails, the recovery application must decrypt the existing files locally without re-encrypting them or calling KMS in the failed Region. Which key design meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a multi-Region KMS primary key and a related replica in the recovery Region.
Why: The deciding constraint is local decryption of already encrypted files during a Regional outage. A related multi-Region replica shares the primary key’s material and key ID, so the recovery application can decrypt the files in its own Region without re-encryption. Two independent Regional keys, even with matching aliases, are not interchangeable. A cross-Region call also fails because the primary Region may be unavailable.
Wrong options: Use an AWS managed KMS key in each Region and grant the recovery application access to both keys. (AWS managed keys are single-Region keys and do not form an interoperable primary-and-replica set.); Create a KMS key in the primary Region and have the recovery application call that Region to decrypt files. (Calling KMS in the primary Region violates the local-decryption requirement during its outage.); Create a customer managed single-Region KMS key in each Region and give both keys the same alias. (Matching aliases do not make independently created keys share the key material needed to decrypt existing ciphertext.)

chunks.title: KMS multi-Region keys
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research platform runs active-active analysis in two AWS Regions. Its applications encrypt datasets client-side and move the ciphertext between Regions; each Regional team must maintain its own key policy and grants. Which solution supports local decryption in either Region while preserving that independent access control?
Correct: Create a multi-Region primary key and a related replica, then set each Regional key’s policy and grants.
Why: This design needs both interchangeable decryption and separate Regional access controls. Related multi-Region keys share key material, while each key has its own policy and grants. Independently created single-Region keys can have similar policies but cannot decrypt one another’s ciphertext. A custom key store is not an alternative because multi-Region keys cannot be created in one.
Wrong options: Use the AWS managed KMS key in each Region and configure matching application permissions. (AWS managed keys are single-Region keys and cannot supply related key material across Regions.); Create separate customer managed single-Region keys and configure matching policies and grants. (Matching access settings do not make separate keys cryptographically interoperable.); Create multi-Region KMS keys in a custom key store in both Regions. (AWS KMS does not support creating multi-Region keys in a custom key store.)

chunks.title: AWS Lake Formation (data lake permissions and governance)
chunks.text:
AWS Lake Formation (data lake permissions and governance). AWS Lake Formation centrally governs access to data lake data in Amazon S3 and its metadata in AWS Glue Data Catalog. Choose it when analytics users need fine-grained permissions or when governed datasets must be shared across AWS accounts.
When to use: Different users may see different tables, columns, rows, or cells in a data lake.; Teams need centrally managed access to cataloged data across AWS accounts.; An existing data lake must adopt Lake Formation permissions incrementally.
Key facts: Lake Formation permissions augment the IAM permissions model.; Data filters can restrict access to combinations of columns and rows.; Lake Formation can share fine-grained access to Data Catalog metadata and underlying data across accounts.; LF-Tags can simplify permission management across many databases, tables, and columns.; Hybrid access mode lets selected users adopt Lake Formation permissions while other users retain existing IAM-based access.; Lake Formation provides audit logs through AWS CloudTrail for access through Lake Formation.
Gotchas: Cataloging data with an AWS Glue crawler does not, by itself, establish fine-grained access policies.; An Amazon S3 bucket policy alone does not provide Lake Formation's centralized row- and column-level controls.; Hybrid access mode is an incremental migration option, not a requirement for every Lake Formation deployment.
Confused with: AWS Glue Data Catalog: The catalog stores discoverable metadata; Lake Formation centrally governs fine-grained access to cataloged data.; IAM and Amazon S3 bucket policies: These can control AWS and S3 access, but Lake Formation adds centrally managed, granular data lake permissions.
ES: AWS Lake Formation administra de forma centralizada el acceso a los datos de un data lake en Amazon S3 y a sus metadatos en AWS Glue Data Catalog. Elígelo cuando los usuarios de análisis necesiten permisos detallados o cuando debas compartir conjuntos de datos gobernados entre cuentas de AWS. Los permisos de Lake Formation complementan el modelo de permisos de IAM.; Los data filters pueden restringir el acceso a combinaciones de columnas y filas.; Lake Formation puede compartir acceso detallado a los metadatos de Data Catalog y a los datos subyacentes entre cuentas.; Los LF-Tags pueden simplificar la administración de permisos en muchas bases de datos, tablas y columnas.; Hybrid access mode permite que usuarios seleccionados adopten permisos de Lake Formation mientras otros conservan el acceso existente basado en IAM.; Lake Formation proporciona registros de auditoría mediante AWS CloudTrail para el acceso a través de Lake Formation.

chunks.title: AWS Lake Formation (data lake permissions and governance)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company keeps shipment data in an Amazon S3 data lake with metadata in AWS Glue Data Catalog. A partner in another AWS account needs governed access to selected datasets, and compliance staff must review which identities attempted to access the data through Lake Formation and when. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use Lake Formation cross-account sharing to grant the partner fine-grained access to catalog metadata and underlying data. + Use Lake Formation audit logs in AWS CloudTrail to review access attempts through Lake Formation.
Why: The company has two distinct requirements: governed cross-account access and a reviewable access history. Lake Formation cross-account sharing addresses fine-grained access to the catalog metadata and underlying data. Lake Formation audit logs in CloudTrail provide information about access attempts through Lake Formation. A bucket policy alone misses the specified governance, and hybrid access mode is for incremental authorization adoption rather than auditing.
Wrong options: Run AWS Glue crawlers in the partner account to replace access grants on the source datasets. (Crawlers discover schemas but do not grant the partner access to the source datasets.); Enable Lake Formation hybrid access mode as the mechanism for recording the partner's access attempts. (Hybrid access mode supports incremental permissions adoption, not the requested audit history.); Give the partner access to the Amazon S3 location with a bucket policy instead of sharing governed catalog data. (S3 location access alone does not provide the requested Lake Formation governance of catalog metadata and underlying data.)

chunks.title: AWS Lake Formation (data lake permissions and governance)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company already uses IAM policies for access to its Amazon S3 data lake and AWS Glue Data Catalog. It wants to introduce Lake Formation permissions for one research team first, without interrupting the policies used by other teams' workloads. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST disruption?
Correct: Use Lake Formation hybrid access mode and selectively onboard the research team to Lake Formation permissions.
Why: The company needs an incremental permissions change, not an immediate migration for every workload. Lake Formation hybrid access mode lets administrators enable Lake Formation permissions for selected users while other existing users continue using IAM permissions. Replacing all IAM access at once misses the no-interruption constraint. Crawlers and CloudTrail serve cataloging and auditing purposes, respectively, rather than this authorization transition.
Wrong options: Enable CloudTrail auditing for the research team's datasets and leave authorization unchanged. (Auditing access does not onboard the research team to Lake Formation permissions.); Replace every team's IAM access with Lake Formation grants before onboarding the research team. (Replacing all existing access at once conflicts with the requirement to preserve other teams' workloads.); Add AWS Glue crawlers for the research team's datasets and retain IAM-only access for all teams. (Crawlers catalog datasets but do not introduce Lake Formation permissions for the research team.)

chunks.title: Lambda concurrency: reserved vs provisioned, cold starts
chunks.text:
Lambda concurrency: reserved vs provisioned, cold starts. Reserved concurrency gives a Lambda function exclusive access to a specified amount of concurrency and caps it at that amount; it does not pre-initialize environments. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes environments to reduce cold starts, so choose it when invocation latency matters enough to justify additional charges.
When to use: Reserve concurrency when a critical function must retain capacity while other functions compete for the account pool.; Reserve concurrency to cap a function that could overwhelm a downstream database.; Provision concurrency for latency-sensitive interactive requests that need environments ready before invocation.
Key facts: Concurrency is the number of in-flight requests; estimate it as average requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds.; Reserved concurrency is both an exclusive allocation and an upper bound. It has no additional configuration charge.; Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes environments and incurs additional charges; traffic beyond its allocation can use on-demand environments.; Provisioned concurrency applies to a function version or alias, not $LATEST. Requests must reach that version or alias to use its prepared environments.; If both controls are used on one function, provisioned concurrency cannot exceed reserved concurrency.
Gotchas: Reserved capacity is not warm capacity: a reserved function can still experience cold starts.; Unused reserved concurrency cannot be borrowed by other functions.; Provisioned concurrency does not make traffic beyond its allocation free of cold starts.; Configuring provisioned concurrency on an alias does not help requests sent elsewhere.
Confused with: Reserved concurrency: Guarantees and caps a function's concurrency, but does not pre-initialize environments.; Provisioned concurrency: Pre-initializes environments for low-latency invocations, but has an additional charge.
ES: Reserved concurrency asigna capacidad exclusiva a una función Lambda y limita su concurrencia a esa cantidad; no prepara entornos de ejecución con anticipación. Provisioned concurrency prepara entornos para reducir los cold starts, así que elígela cuando la latencia de invocación justifique el costo adicional. La concurrencia es la cantidad de solicitudes en curso; puedes estimarla multiplicando las solicitudes promedio por segundo por la duración promedio en segundos.; Reserved concurrency ofrece una asignación exclusiva y establece un límite superior. Configurarla no tiene un cargo adicional.; Provisioned concurrency prepara entornos y genera cargos adicionales; el tráfico que supera la cantidad configurada puede usar entornos on-demand.; Provisioned concurrency se aplica a una versión o alias, no a $LATEST. Las solicitudes deben dirigirse a esa versión o alias para usar los entornos preparados.; Si usas ambos controles en una función, provisioned concurrency no puede superar reserved concurrency.

chunks.title: Lambda concurrency: reserved vs provisioned, cold starts
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company configured provisioned concurrency on the STABLE alias of a Lambda function that processes upload events. X-Ray monitoring still shows cold starts, and the event source mapping points to the unqualified function rather than STABLE. The team wants event invocations to use the environments already allocated to STABLE. Which change meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Update the event source mapping to invoke the STABLE alias.
Why: Provisioned concurrency is attached to a specific version or alias, and the event source must invoke that target to use its prepared environments. Updating the mapping to STABLE addresses the identified routing mismatch directly. Increasing STABLE's allocation without changing the mapping leaves the mismatch in place. Reserved concurrency does not remove cold starts.
Wrong options: Move the provisioned concurrency configuration to $LATEST and keep the event source mapping unchanged. (Lambda does not support provisioned concurrency on $LATEST.); Increase provisioned concurrency on STABLE and keep the event source mapping unchanged. (Additional prepared environments on STABLE cannot help invocations that do not target STABLE.); Add reserved concurrency to the function and keep the event source mapping unchanged. (Reserved concurrency does not pre-initialize environments or route events to STABLE.)

chunks.title: Lambda concurrency: reserved vs provisioned, cold starts
chunks.text:
Scenario: A clinic invokes a Lambda function through its RELEASE alias to return interactive appointment results. The function accesses a database that can safely support at most 30 simultaneous executions, and peak traffic requires 20 environments ready to avoid cold-start delays. Other functions in the account also experience traffic spikes. Which two configurations together meet the latency and database-protection requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure 20 units of provisioned concurrency on RELEASE. + Configure 30 units of reserved concurrency for the function.
Why: The clinic needs two distinct controls: a database-safe concurrency ceiling and prepared environments for interactive traffic. Reserving 30 units caps the function while protecting its capacity from spikes in other functions. Provisioning 20 units on the invoked RELEASE alias prepares the required environments and stays within that reserved limit. Reserved concurrency alone cannot prevent cold starts, and provisioned concurrency cannot be placed on $LATEST.
Wrong options: Configure 20 units of provisioned concurrency on $LATEST. (Provisioned concurrency cannot be configured on $LATEST, and the clinic invokes RELEASE.); Configure 40 units of provisioned concurrency on RELEASE. (This allocation exceeds the database-safe concurrency target and cannot fit within a reserved concurrency setting of 30.); Configure 20 units of reserved concurrency for the function without provisioned concurrency. (Reserved concurrency alone does not prepare the 20 environments needed to avoid cold-start delays.)

chunks.title: AWS Lambda fundamentals and limits
chunks.text:
AWS Lambda fundamentals and limits. AWS Lambda Functions run independent handlers in response to events or API calls without server management. Choose them for short, variable-demand work; check execution time and memory before choosing a function instead of a container.
When to use: An S3, SQS, EventBridge, or API Gateway trigger should run code on demand.; Work is independent across invocations and does not require persistent in-memory state.; Demand varies and the team does not want to provision or patch servers.
Key facts: A standard Lambda Function invocation can run for up to 900 seconds (15 minutes). Certain AWS Lambda Managed Instances invocations have a documented 90-minute exception.; Function memory ranges from 128 MB to 10,240 MB in 1-MB increments; allocated CPU power increases with configured memory.; Lambda scales functions by creating execution environments in response to traffic; each invocation runs independently.; Execution environments can be reused, but state might not persist across invocations.; The default regional concurrent-executions quota is 1,000 and can be increased.
Gotchas: Packaging a function as a container image does not, by itself, remove the standard function timeout.; Increasing /tmp storage does not increase allocated CPU power; increasing function memory does.; A warm execution environment is not a reliable store for state needed by later invocations.
Confused with: AWS Fargate: Consider a container task when one uninterrupted job exceeds the standard Lambda Function invocation limit.; Amazon ECS on EC2: A short event handler does not need container hosts simply to respond to an AWS service trigger.; AWS Batch: A directly triggered, short handler is different from a workload that needs a managed batch-job queue and scheduler.
ES: AWS Lambda Functions ejecuta handlers independientes en respuesta a eventos o llamadas de API sin que administres servidores. Elígelo para trabajo breve con demanda variable; revisa el tiempo de ejecución y la memoria antes de optar por una función en lugar de un contenedor. Una invocación estándar de Lambda Function puede durar hasta 900 segundos (15 minutos). Ciertas invocaciones de AWS Lambda Managed Instances tienen una excepción documentada de 90 minutos.; La memoria de una función va de 128 MB a 10,240 MB en incrementos de 1 MB; la CPU asignada aumenta con la memoria configurada.; Lambda escala las funciones creando entornos de ejecución según el tráfico; cada invocación se ejecuta de forma independiente.; Los entornos de ejecución pueden reutilizarse, pero el estado podría no persistir entre invocaciones.; La cuota regional predeterminada de ejecuciones concurrentes es 1,000 y puede aumentarse.

chunks.title: AWS Lambda fundamentals and limits
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum receives image uploads in Amazon S3, with long quiet periods followed by unpredictable bursts. Each image needs an independent conversion that completes in about four minutes. The team does not want to manage servers or a container deployment. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure an AWS Lambda Function to process each S3 upload event.
Why: The deciding requirements are independent, short conversions triggered by S3 uploads and no server or container management. Lambda Functions can use S3 as a trigger and scale execution environments in response to demand. A container-based choice could process images, but it adds a deployment model the team explicitly wants to avoid.
Wrong options: Package the converter for AWS Fargate and run a container task for each upload. (The scenario does not require a container deployment, whereas a Lambda Function directly fits the event and duration requirements.); Deploy the converter as a container workload on Amazon EKS. (The scenario calls for a short event handler without a container deployment, not a Kubernetes workload.); Run the converter in containers on Amazon ECS with EC2 instances. (Managing container hosts conflicts with the requirement to avoid server management.)

chunks.title: AWS Lambda fundamentals and limits
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab processes individual instrument files with a program that must run uninterrupted for roughly 40 minutes. The lab initially plans to invoke a standard Lambda Function for each file, but does not want to split a file's processing into steps. It also wants to avoid managing compute hosts. Which approach meets these requirements?
Correct: Run each file as an AWS Fargate container task instead of a standard Lambda Function.
Why: Each file needs one uninterrupted run longer than the standard Lambda Function maximum of 15 minutes. A container task is a better fit than simply increasing a standard function's timeout, and Fargate avoids managing compute hosts. Packaging the Lambda code as a container image does not change that standard invocation limit. ECS on EC2 misses the lab's host-management constraint.
Wrong options: Deploy the program as a standard Lambda Function and set its timeout to 40 minutes. (A standard Lambda Function cannot be configured with a 40-minute invocation timeout.); Deploy a standard Lambda Function from a container image and set its timeout to 40 minutes. (Using a container image does not make a standard Lambda Function's 40-minute timeout valid.); Run each file in an Amazon ECS container on lab-managed EC2 instances. (Although this avoids the standard function timeout, managing EC2 hosts conflicts with the stated requirement.)

chunks.title: AWS Lambda fundamentals and limits
chunks.text:
Scenario: A weather service receives bursts of independent sensor files in Amazon S3. It wants each file analyzed on arrival without managing servers; tests show that each analysis completes within six minutes but needs more CPU than its current Lambda Function configuration provides. The team is reviewing changes that preserve this design. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Increase the Lambda Function's memory setting to allocate more CPU. + Configure the Lambda Function to run in response to S3 upload events.
Why: S3 upload events provide the requested on-arrival trigger, and Lambda handles the independent six-minute analyses without server management. Increasing function memory is the documented way to allocate more CPU to each invocation. Increasing /tmp addresses storage instead, while relying on execution-environment state would be unsafe across invocations. Moving to EC2-backed containers would also miss the no-host-management requirement.
Wrong options: Move the analyzer to ECS on EC2 to avoid managing compute hosts. (An EC2-backed container design conflicts with the requirement not to manage hosts.); Keep intermediate state only in the Lambda execution environment for the next file. (Invocations are independent, and execution-environment state might not persist for the next file.); Increase the function's /tmp allocation to provide more CPU per invocation. (The /tmp setting controls temporary storage rather than the function's CPU allocation.)

chunks.title: Lambda memory/timeout sizing and performance
chunks.text:
Lambda memory/timeout sizing and performance. Lambda memory is also a performance setting: increasing it allocates proportionally more CPU. For a slow function, use CloudWatch observations and tests at different memory settings to choose a configuration that meets the performance requirement.
When to use: A Lambda function is CPU-bound or its duration suggests a compute bottleneck.; A function approaches its configured memory maximum.; You need to compare memory settings against a latency target rather than assume the minimum setting is best.
Key facts: Lambda memory can be configured from 128 MB to 10,240 MB in 1-MB increments.; Lambda allocates CPU power in proportion to configured memory; at 1,769 MB, a function has the equivalent of one vCPU.; CloudWatch memory observations can identify memory-bound functions; duration can help assess CPU-bound and IO-bound functions.; AWS Lambda Power Tuning tests a function at different memory allocations and measures performance.; AWS Compute Optimizer memory recommendations support only functions using the x86_64 architecture.
Gotchas: Do not assume 128 MB is the best setting for every function; AWS recommends it only for simple functions such as event transformers and routers.; Raising a timeout does not address a CPU bottleneck by itself; memory is the setting that increases allocated CPU.; Do not assume Compute Optimizer memory recommendations are available for a function using an architecture other than x86_64.
Confused with: 
ES: La memoria de Lambda también determina el rendimiento: al aumentarla, se asigna proporcionalmente más CPU. Si una función tarda demasiado, usa observaciones de CloudWatch y pruebas con distintas configuraciones de memoria para cumplir el objetivo de rendimiento. Puedes configurar la memoria de Lambda entre 128 MB y 10,240 MB, en incrementos de 1 MB.; Lambda asigna CPU en proporción a la memoria configurada; con 1,769 MB, una función tiene el equivalente a una vCPU.; Las observaciones de memoria en CloudWatch ayudan a identificar funciones limitadas por memoria; la duración ayuda a evaluar funciones limitadas por CPU o I/O.; AWS Lambda Power Tuning prueba una función con distintas asignaciones de memoria y mide su rendimiento.; Las recomendaciones de memoria de AWS Compute Optimizer solo admiten funciones con arquitectura x86_64.

chunks.title: Lambda memory/timeout sizing and performance
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company uses a Lambda function to generate thumbnails after images arrive. The function completes successfully, but image processing frequently misses its latency target; CloudWatch shows that memory consumption remains well below the configured maximum. Which change should the team test FIRST to improve processing speed without rewriting the function?
Correct: Increase the function memory setting and measure its duration again.
Why: The function finishes but is too slow, while its memory consumption is well below the maximum. Because Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to configured memory, testing a higher memory setting directly addresses a possible compute bottleneck. Increasing the timeout would allow more time but would not add CPU.
Wrong options: Reduce the function memory setting and measure its duration again. (Reducing memory also reduces allocated CPU and does not address the suspected compute bottleneck.); Keep the memory setting and add a CloudWatch alarm for maximum memory consumption. (The alarm could help detect memory pressure, but the observations already indicate that memory capacity is not the immediate issue.); Increase the function timeout while keeping its memory setting unchanged. (A longer timeout does not increase the CPU allocated to a function that already completes.)

chunks.title: Lambda memory/timeout sizing and performance
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer is preparing a Lambda function that reads product files from Amazon S3 for a seasonal campaign. The team wants to choose a memory setting based on observed performance across several configurations, using live calls made by the function in its own AWS account. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST custom testing work?
Correct: Use AWS Lambda Power Tuning to test the function at different memory allocations.
Why: The deciding requirement is to measure performance at several memory settings while the function makes live calls in its own account. AWS Lambda Power Tuning is designed to run those comparisons. Selecting a fixed setting based solely on its vCPU equivalence skips the workload-specific measurement.
Wrong options: Set memory to 1,769 MB because that setting provides the equivalent of one vCPU. (The known CPU allocation does not establish which setting best meets this function's observed performance needs.); Set memory to 128 MB and use CloudWatch alarms to report when usage approaches that setting. (This detects memory pressure but does not compare performance across configurations.); Increase the timeout at each deployment and compare whether the function completes. (Changing the timeout does not test the effect of different memory allocations on performance.)

chunks.title: Lambda in a VPC (private resources, NAT for internet)
chunks.text:
Lambda in a VPC (private resources, NAT for internet). Attach a Lambda function to private subnets in your VPC when it must reach private resources such as Amazon RDS or Amazon ElastiCache. VPC attachment changes its network access: plan separate outbound connectivity if the function also needs the public internet or AWS APIs.
When to use: A Lambda function must connect to an RDS or ElastiCache resource in private subnets.; A VPC-connected function must also make outbound requests to the public internet.; A deployment needs the permissions required for Lambda to create its VPC network interfaces.
Key facts: Configure VPC access by selecting subnets and security groups for the function.; A VPC-connected function does not retain its default public internet access; the VPC needs an internet-access path, such as a NAT gateway for private-subnet outbound traffic.; Placing a Lambda function in a public subnet does not give it a public IP address or internet access.; Lambda creates and manages Hyperplane ENIs for VPC access. The execution role needs network-interface permissions when those interfaces are created.; Functions using the same subnet and security group combination can share a Hyperplane ENI.
Gotchas: Do not assume Lambda's default internet access continues after you attach the function to your VPC.; A public subnet is not a shortcut to outbound internet access for a VPC-connected Lambda function.; An IAM permission to call an AWS API does not, by itself, provide a network path to that API.
Confused with: 
ES: Conecta la función Lambda a subredes privadas de tu VPC cuando deba acceder a recursos privados como Amazon RDS o Amazon ElastiCache. La conexión a la VPC cambia su acceso de red: debes planear una salida adicional si también necesita internet público o AWS APIs. Para configurar el acceso a la VPC, selecciona las subredes y los security groups de la función.; Una función conectada a una VPC no conserva su acceso predeterminado a internet público; la VPC necesita una ruta de salida, como un NAT gateway para el tráfico saliente de subredes privadas.; Colocar una función Lambda en una subred pública no le da una dirección IP pública ni acceso a internet.; Lambda crea y administra Hyperplane ENIs para el acceso a la VPC. El execution role necesita permisos sobre interfaces de red cuando estas se crean.; Las funciones que usan la misma combinación de subredes y security groups pueden compartir una Hyperplane ENI.

chunks.title: Lambda in a VPC (private resources, NAT for internet)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A food distributor is building a Lambda function that writes to a private Amazon RDS instance and sends shipment updates to a public HTTPS endpoint. The function currently has default Lambda networking, and the VPC has no outbound internet path configured for its private subnets. Which two changes together provide the required connectivity? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure the function with private subnets in the database VPC and appropriate security groups. + Provide outbound internet access for the private subnets through a NAT gateway.
Why: Two separate network needs determine the answer: access to private RDS and outbound access to a public HTTPS endpoint. Configuring private subnets and security groups addresses the database connection; providing a NAT path addresses outbound internet traffic. Public-subnet attachment is not a substitute for the NAT path because it does not give Lambda a public IP address. IAM and security-group permissions alone cannot create a missing network route.
Wrong options: Allow outbound HTTPS in a security group without changing the private-subnet routing. (A security-group rule alone does not create the missing outbound internet path.); Configure the function with public subnets in the database VPC. (Public-subnet attachment does not give the function a public IP address or internet access.); Leave the function on default Lambda networking and grant it RDS access through its execution role. (An IAM permission does not provide a network connection to the private RDS instance.)

chunks.title: Lambda in a VPC (private resources, NAT for internet)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company moves a Lambda function into its VPC so it can read an Amazon ElastiCache cluster. The function is configured with a public subnet, but its calls to an external licensing API now fail. The team wants to keep ElastiCache private and restore outbound access. Which change meets these requirements?
Correct: Attach the function to private subnets with access to ElastiCache and configure outbound internet access through a NAT gateway.
Why: The function must retain access to private ElastiCache while calling a public API. Attach it to private subnets for the private resource and provide an outbound internet path through a NAT gateway. A public subnet alone does not give Lambda a public IP address or internet access. Detaching the function would sacrifice the required VPC access.
Wrong options: Keep the public subnet and allow outbound HTTPS in the function's security group. (Allowing HTTPS does not give a Lambda function in a public subnet a public IP address or internet access.); Keep the public subnet and add an internet gateway to the VPC. (An internet gateway does not make a VPC-connected Lambda function in a public subnet internet-accessible.); Detach the function from the VPC to restore its default internet access. (Detaching restores default internet access but removes its VPC connection to the private ElastiCache cluster.)

chunks.title: Improving reliability of legacy apps without code changes
chunks.text:
Improving reliability of legacy apps without code changes. When a legacy application cannot be changed, choose a reliability mechanism that matches what must survive failure. EC2 automatic recovery attempts to preserve one instance’s identity after a host-level failure; Elastic Load Balancing and EC2 Auto Scaling support traffic failover across healthy instances.
When to use: Choose EC2 automatic recovery when a supported singleton must retain its instance ID, IP addresses, and attached EBS volumes after an underlying host failure.; Choose Elastic Load Balancing with multiple EC2 instances and EC2 Auto Scaling when traffic must continue through healthy instances.
Key facts: A failed EC2 system status check indicates an underlying host problem; automatic instance recovery does not act when only the instance status check fails.; Simplified automatic recovery is enabled by default on supported instances. CloudWatch action-based recovery requires configuration.; Successful instance recovery preserves the instance ID, public and private IP addresses, attached EBS volumes, and Availability Zone.; Recovery loses data in RAM and resets operating-system uptime. CloudWatch action-based recovery also loses instance store data.; Automatic recovery protects an individual instance; it does not replace an architecture that fails traffic over to healthy instances.
Gotchas: Do not treat a failed instance status check as a trigger that EC2 automatic recovery can fix.; Do not assume automatic recovery moves the instance to another Availability Zone.; Do not use single-instance recovery as the sole answer when users must continue reaching other healthy instances.
Confused with: EC2 Auto Scaling: Auto Scaling manages instance capacity based on demand and health; EC2 automatic recovery attempts to restore an individual instance after an underlying host failure.; CloudWatch action-based recovery: It requires an alarm and recovery action, whereas simplified automatic recovery is enabled by default on supported instances.
ES: Cuando no puedes modificar una aplicación heredada, elige un mecanismo de confiabilidad según lo que debe sobrevivir a una falla. EC2 automatic recovery intenta conservar la identidad de una instancia ante una falla del host; Elastic Load Balancing y EC2 Auto Scaling permiten dirigir tráfico a instancias sanas. Una falla de EC2 system status check indica un problema del host; automatic instance recovery no actúa si solo falla instance status check.; Simplified automatic recovery viene habilitado de forma predeterminada en instancias compatibles. CloudWatch action-based recovery requiere configuración.; Una recuperación exitosa conserva instance ID, direcciones IP públicas y privadas, volúmenes EBS adjuntos y Availability Zone.; La recuperación pierde los datos en RAM y reinicia el tiempo de actividad del sistema operativo. CloudWatch action-based recovery también pierde los datos de instance store.; Automatic recovery protege una instancia individual; no sustituye una arquitectura que desvía el tráfico hacia instancias sanas.

chunks.title: Improving reliability of legacy apps without code changes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company has an older web application that can run on multiple EC2 instances without code changes. Customers must continue reaching healthy instances if one instance becomes unhealthy, including when the problem is within its operating system rather than its host. Which design meets the availability requirement?
Correct: Put multiple instances behind Elastic Load Balancing and manage their number with EC2 Auto Scaling.
Why: The key requirement is continued service through other healthy instances, including when the issue is not an underlying host failure. Elastic Load Balancing distributes incoming traffic across multiple EC2 instances, and EC2 Auto Scaling adjusts their number based on demand and health. Either form of EC2 automatic recovery focuses on an individual instance and does not operate when only its instance status check fails.
Wrong options: Run multiple instances with automatic recovery enabled, but route all customer traffic to one designated instance. (The other instances cannot keep serving customers if traffic is directed only to the unhealthy instance.); Run one instance with simplified automatic recovery and send all traffic directly to it. (Automatic recovery protects an individual instance from underlying failures but does not fail traffic over to other healthy instances.); Run one instance with CloudWatch action-based recovery and send all traffic directly to it. (Action-based recovery is still an individual-instance mechanism and does not address a failure detected only by an instance status check.)

chunks.title: Improving reliability of legacy apps without code changes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A small archive service runs on a supported EC2 instance and can tolerate a reboot, but its clients refer to the instance's current public IPv4 address. The team wants an automatic attempt to restore service after a host hardware failure without configuring alarms or adding their associated charges. Which approach is MOST cost-effective?
Correct: Use simplified automatic recovery on the instance.
Why: The instance is supported, the fault is at the host, and the team wants to avoid alarm configuration and associated charges. Simplified automatic recovery is enabled by default on supported instances, has no additional cost, and preserves the public IPv4 address if it succeeds. CloudWatch action-based recovery adds configuration and might incur charges; a stop/start can change the public IPv4 address.
Wrong options: Replace the instance through EC2 Auto Scaling after a health failure. (Replacing the instance does not preserve the original instance's public IPv4 address.); Stop and start the instance after a system status check failure. (Stopping and starting requires intervention and ordinarily changes its public IPv4 address unless it has an Elastic IP address.); Configure CloudWatch action-based recovery with a system status check alarm. (It can attempt recovery but requires alarm configuration and might incur CloudWatch charges.)

chunks.title: Local Zones and Wavelength (edge compute)
chunks.text:
Local Zones and Wavelength (edge compute). Choose AWS Local Zones to place applications near users in a metropolitan area, including workloads targeting single-digit-millisecond latency. Choose AWS Wavelength when the critical path is between an application and mobile devices on a carrier network.
When to use: Local Zones: users are concentrated around a city and need low-latency access to compute near that metro area.; Local Zones: a nearby deployment must retain low latency for a hybrid migration or meet applicable local data residency requirements.; Wavelength: mobile-device traffic needs processing at the edge of a communications service provider’s network.
Key facts: Local Zones place select compute, storage, database, and other AWS resources near population and industry centers.; Enabling Local Zones has no additional charge; deployed resources are billed and can have different prices from those in the parent Region.; A Wavelength Zone is in a carrier location, is associated with an AWS Region, and is managed by the Region’s control plane.; You can extend a VPC into a Wavelength Zone and run EC2 instances in a Wavelength subnet.; A carrier gateway allows inbound traffic from the carrier network and outbound traffic to the carrier network and internet.
Gotchas: A nearby city does not by itself imply Wavelength; look for a requirement involving mobile devices and a carrier network.; Local Zones are not the same as placing AWS infrastructure in your own data center.; Wavelength resources can communicate with services in the parent Region, but the latency-sensitive application runs in the Wavelength Zone.
Confused with: AWS Outposts: Outposts places AWS infrastructure on premises; Local Zones serve nearby metro users without requiring deployment in your data center.; ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere: These run containers on customer-managed infrastructure, such as on-premises servers or VMs, rather than placing compute at a carrier-network edge.; VMware Cloud on AWS: Choose it to retain VMware tooling during a migration, not simply to place an application near metro users.
ES: Elige AWS Local Zones para ubicar aplicaciones cerca de los usuarios de un área metropolitana, incluso si buscas una latencia de milisegundos de un solo dígito. Elige AWS Wavelength cuando la ruta crítica conecta la aplicación con dispositivos móviles en una red de un operador. Local Zones ubica determinados recursos de cómputo, almacenamiento, bases de datos y otros servicios de AWS cerca de centros poblacionales e industriales.; Habilitar Local Zones no tiene un cargo adicional; pagas por los recursos implementados, cuyos precios pueden diferir de los de la Region principal.; Una Wavelength Zone está en una ubicación del operador, está asociada con una AWS Region y se administra desde el plano de control de esa Region.; Puedes extender una VPC a una Wavelength Zone y ejecutar instancias EC2 en una subred de Wavelength.; Un carrier gateway permite tráfico entrante desde la red del operador y tráfico saliente hacia esa red e internet.

chunks.title: Local Zones and Wavelength (edge compute)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A game studio is launching an interactive event for players concentrated in one metropolitan area. Its application needs a single-digit-millisecond latency target for those users, who connect through a mix of home and mobile networks; the studio does not need to host equipment in its own facility. Which deployment best meets the latency requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy the game servers in an AWS Local Zone near the players.
Why: The deciding requirement is low-latency access for users across one metro area, not specifically for devices on a carrier network. A nearby Local Zone places compute close to those users without requiring the studio to host infrastructure. Wavelength is a tempting edge option, but its distinguishing placement is at a communications provider’s network edge.
Wrong options: Deploy the game servers with EKS Anywhere on studio-owned hardware. (Customer-owned hardware adds an on-premises deployment that the studio does not need.); Deploy the game servers in a Wavelength Zone at a carrier location. (Wavelength targets the carrier-network edge, while the requirement spans players on home and mobile networks.); Deploy the game servers on AWS Outposts in the studio’s facility. (Outposts puts infrastructure on premises, which the studio does not require for its metro-wide users.)

chunks.title: Local Zones and Wavelength (edge compute)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design firm is moving its virtual-workstation application from a city office to AWS. Its artists are concentrated in that city and still need low-latency access during the hybrid migration; the firm is willing to move the application off its own hardware and does not require VMware tooling. A nearby AWS Local Zone is available. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy the workstation application in the nearby Local Zone.
Why: The deciding constraints are low-latency access for city-based artists and a hybrid migration that need not keep the application on the firm’s hardware. Local Zones support virtual-workstation use cases and migrations to nearby AWS infrastructure. Outposts would preserve an on-premises deployment, while VMware Cloud on AWS addresses a tooling requirement the firm explicitly does not have.
Wrong options: Deploy the workstation application in a Wavelength Zone. (The firm needs proximity to artists in a city, not placement at a carrier-network edge for mobile devices.); Deploy the workstation application in VMware Cloud on AWS. (Retaining VMware tooling does not address a stated requirement, whereas nearby low-latency placement does.); Deploy the workstation application on Outposts at the city office. (Outposts retains an on-premises deployment even though the firm is willing to move the application off its hardware.)

chunks.title: Loose coupling and decoupling principles
chunks.text:
Loose coupling and decoupling principles. Loose coupling puts an intermediate layer between components so a slow, failed, or changing component does not directly disrupt its producer. For exam scenarios, choose the interaction pattern that matches the requirement: an SQS queue for asynchronous work, an SNS topic for push-based fan-out, or EventBridge for event-driven producer–consumer separation.
When to use: A producer can acknowledge a request without waiting for downstream processing.; A worker must process queued messages independently of the component that creates them.; One published message must reach multiple subscribers for parallel processing.; Event producers should not depend on direct integrations with event consumers.
Key facts: Amazon SQS queues decouple producers and consumers; consumers receive messages from the queue.; Amazon SNS topics support high-throughput, push-based, many-to-many messaging and fan-out.; Amazon EventBridge supports loosely coupled event-driven architectures by abstracting producers from consumers.; Asynchronous interaction is appropriate when an acknowledgment that work was registered is sufficient; it is not a blanket replacement for an immediate response.; Loose coupling allows components to scale or change independently and helps isolate component failures.
Gotchas: Direct API calls between tiers without failover or asynchronous processing can propagate a downstream failure.; Putting components behind separate services does not remove coupling if they still depend on shared data in a shared database.; A queue is not automatically appropriate for hard real-time requests: old requests may become stale before processing.
Confused with: Amazon SQS vs. Amazon SNS: Choose SQS to hold work for a consumer to receive; choose SNS when a publisher must push messages to multiple subscribers.; Amazon SNS vs. Amazon EventBridge: Choose SNS for push-based fan-out; choose EventBridge when the central requirement is an event-driven architecture that abstracts producers from consumers.
ES: Loose coupling coloca una capa intermedia entre componentes para que uno lento, con fallas o en proceso de cambio no afecte directamente a quien produce las solicitudes. En un escenario de examen, elige el patrón que corresponda: una cola de Amazon SQS para trabajo asíncrono, un tema de Amazon SNS para fan-out basado en push o Amazon EventBridge para separar productores y consumidores de eventos. Las colas de Amazon SQS desacoplan productores y consumidores; los consumidores reciben mensajes de la cola.; Los temas de Amazon SNS permiten mensajería many-to-many de alto rendimiento, basada en push, y fan-out.; Amazon EventBridge permite arquitecturas event-driven con loose coupling al abstraer a los productores de los consumidores.; La interacción asíncrona es adecuada cuando basta con confirmar que se registró el trabajo; no reemplaza siempre una respuesta inmediata.; Loose coupling permite escalar o cambiar componentes de forma independiente y ayuda a aislar sus fallas.

chunks.title: Loose coupling and decoupling principles
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company accepts booking requests faster than its fulfillment component can process them during event launches. Customers only need confirmation that their requests were registered; fulfillment can happen afterward. Which solution allows the two components to scale independently while minimizing the impact of fulfillment slowdowns?
Correct: Place booking requests in an Amazon SQS queue for the fulfillment component to receive and process.
Why: The deciding requirement is that booking can be acknowledged before fulfillment completes. An Amazon SQS queue provides an intermediate layer where requests can await a consumer, separating the booking and fulfillment components. A synchronous API call keeps confirmation dependent on fulfillment speed. An SNS topic addresses push-based delivery rather than the specified queue-based work pattern.
Wrong options: Have both components coordinate bookings through tables in a shared database. (Shared data can reintroduce tight coupling rather than isolating the components.); Have the booking component call the fulfillment API synchronously and wait for completion. (A slow fulfillment API would delay booking confirmations and keep the components directly dependent.); Publish every booking request to an Amazon SNS topic that pushes it to fulfillment. (Push-based messaging does not meet the stated need to hold work for fulfillment to receive as it becomes available.)

chunks.title: Loose coupling and decoupling principles
chunks.text:
Scenario: A news publisher generates a message whenever an editor releases an article. Several subscriber endpoints must receive each message through push-based delivery so they can begin separate processing in parallel. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST direct integration between the publisher and subscribers?
Correct: Publish article messages to an Amazon SNS topic with the endpoints as subscribers.
Why: The publisher needs to push the same message to multiple endpoints for parallel processing. An Amazon SNS topic provides that fan-out without a separate direct integration to every subscriber. One SQS queue addresses queued work rather than this specified many-subscriber push pattern. Direct API calls leave the publisher dependent on each subscriber.
Wrong options: Store each article message in one Amazon SQS queue for a subscriber to receive. (One queue for a consumer to receive work does not provide the requested push-based fan-out to several endpoints.); Have the publisher invoke each subscriber's API when an article is released. (Separate direct calls keep the publisher integrated with every subscriber.); Write article messages to a shared database that each subscriber reads. (Shared data can reintroduce coupling and does not provide the requested push-based delivery.)

chunks.title: Loose coupling and decoupling principles
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics platform has services that generate shipment and delivery events. Independent teams add event consumers over time, and the platform team does not want producers to integrate directly with each new consumer. Which solution BEST supports this event-driven design?
Correct: Use Amazon EventBridge to separate the services that generate events from the services that consume them.
Why: The key requirement is to add event consumers without building new direct integrations into producers. Amazon EventBridge is an event-driven option that abstracts event producers from the services consuming their events. Direct API calls would make producers aware of every new consumer. A shared database schema can also create coupling between teams.
Wrong options: Have producers and consumers exchange events through a shared database schema. (A shared schema can reintroduce tight coupling as teams change their components.); Have each producer call the API of every consumer that handles its events. (Each new consumer would require another direct producer-to-consumer integration.); Use one Amazon SQS queue as the integration point for a single consumer service. (A queue for one consumer does not address the stated need to abstract producers from independently added event consumers.)

chunks.title: Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery
chunks.text:
Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery. Amazon Macie discovers sensitive data in Amazon S3 objects and monitors S3 general purpose buckets for security and access-control issues. Choose it when a scenario requires locating PII in S3, identifying publicly accessible buckets, or reviewing bucket encryption settings.
When to use: Find PII, financial information, credentials, or organization-specific sensitive patterns in S3 objects.; Get an inventory of S3 general purpose buckets with visibility into public access and encryption settings.; Choose broad, sampled discovery across an S3 estate or a targeted discovery job for specific buckets and analysis criteria.
Key facts: Macie uses managed data identifiers, including machine learning and pattern matching, to discover sensitive data; custom data identifiers can match organization-specific patterns.; Automated sensitive data discovery continually evaluates the S3 bucket inventory and samples representative objects.; Sensitive data discovery jobs let you select buckets, sampling depth, and object-based criteria; they can run once or recur.; Macie creates sensitive data findings for detected data and policy findings for potential bucket security or privacy issues, such as public accessibility.; Macie publishes findings to Amazon EventBridge and can also publish them to AWS Security Hub CSPM.
Gotchas: Bucket monitoring and object inspection are different: an inventory showing encryption settings does not itself identify PII inside objects.; Automated discovery samples objects; choose a discovery job when the scenario specifies targeted buckets or analysis depth.; Security Hub CSPM can aggregate Macie findings, but it is not the service that inspects S3 objects for sensitive data.
Confused with: Amazon GuardDuty: GuardDuty identifies potentially malicious activity; Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 objects.; AWS Security Hub CSPM: Security Hub CSPM aggregates security findings; Macie generates sensitive data findings from S3 analysis.; Amazon Inspector: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities; Macie examines S3 data for sensitive content.
ES: Amazon Macie descubre datos sensibles en objetos de Amazon S3 y monitorea los buckets S3 de uso general para detectar problemas de seguridad y control de acceso. Elígelo cuando necesites localizar PII en S3, identificar buckets con acceso público o revisar la configuración de cifrado de los buckets. Macie usa managed data identifiers, incluidos machine learning y pattern matching; los custom data identifiers permiten buscar patrones propios de la organización.; Automated sensitive data discovery evalúa continuamente el inventario de buckets S3 y analiza una muestra de objetos representativos.; Los sensitive data discovery jobs permiten elegir buckets, profundidad de muestreo y criterios basados en propiedades de los objetos; pueden ejecutarse una vez o periódicamente.; Macie crea sensitive data findings por datos detectados y policy findings por posibles problemas de seguridad o privacidad de un bucket, como el acceso público.; Macie publica hallazgos en Amazon EventBridge y también puede publicarlos en AWS Security Hub CSPM.

chunks.title: Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare analytics company stores patient intake exports in many S3 buckets. Its security team needs to locate objects containing PII and see which buckets have become publicly accessible, without building its own object-inspection system. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable Amazon Macie and configure automated sensitive data discovery.
Why: The deciding requirement is to inspect S3 objects for PII while also monitoring buckets for public accessibility. Macie provides both sensitive data discovery and bucket security monitoring, and its automated discovery avoids building an inspection system. GuardDuty detects suspicious activity rather than classifying the contents of S3 objects.
Wrong options: Use AWS Security Hub CSPM to aggregate security findings for the buckets. (Security Hub CSPM can aggregate findings but does not perform Macie's sensitive-data inspection.); Enable Amazon GuardDuty to analyze activity associated with the S3 buckets. (GuardDuty identifies potentially malicious activity, not PII within S3 objects or Macie's bucket inventory.); Use Amazon Inspector to scan the company's workloads for vulnerabilities. (Inspector's vulnerability scanning does not classify PII in S3 objects.)

chunks.title: Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery
chunks.text:
Scenario: A financial cooperative manages S3 buckets in several AWS accounts. Its central security team must inspect member accounts' buckets for sensitive data and bring Macie findings into a broader security posture view alongside findings from other services. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure Macie to publish findings to AWS Security Hub CSPM. + Configure a designated Macie administrator for the member accounts.
Why: This scenario has two distinct needs: centrally inspecting S3 data across member accounts and combining the resulting findings with a broader security view. A designated Macie administrator can inspect member-account buckets, while publication to Security Hub CSPM makes Macie findings available for aggregation with other services' findings. GuardDuty cannot replace Macie's sensitive-data inspection, and Detective is an investigation tool rather than the requested posture view.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Detective as the central view for Macie findings and compliance checks. (Detective is for investigation, not the broader findings aggregation and posture view provided by Security Hub CSPM.); Use GuardDuty as the sole service to classify sensitive data in member accounts' S3 objects. (GuardDuty detects potentially malicious activity rather than classifying sensitive content in S3 objects.); Use Firewall Manager policies to inspect S3 object contents for sensitive patterns. (Firewall Manager policy management does not provide Macie's S3 sensitive-data inspection.)

chunks.title: Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher is preparing an audit of a small set of S3 buckets containing draft contracts. The audit team must choose those buckets, specify the sampling depth, and run the assessment once rather than maintain continuous discovery across the S3 estate. Which approach meets these requirements MOST directly?
Correct: Create a one-time Macie sensitive data discovery job for the selected buckets.
Why: The audit specifies both the buckets and the sampling depth, and it calls for a one-time assessment. A Macie sensitive data discovery job exposes those choices and can run on demand. Automated discovery is designed for broader, continual visibility using representative object samples, so it does not match the requested control as directly.
Wrong options: Send Macie bucket policy findings to AWS Security Hub CSPM. (Aggregating policy findings does not perform the specified object analysis.); Enable GuardDuty monitoring for activity involving the selected S3 buckets. (GuardDuty looks for potentially malicious activity rather than running a sensitive-data assessment with a chosen sampling depth.); Enable Macie automated sensitive data discovery across the S3 estate. (Automated discovery provides broad visibility through sampling but does not provide the requested one-time, bucket-specific analysis configuration.)

chunks.title: Managed and purpose-built services vs self-managed
chunks.text:
Managed and purpose-built services vs self-managed. When a suitable managed or purpose-built service meets the workload’s requirements, prefer it over installing and operating equivalent software on Amazon EC2 if reduced operational burden is the priority. Match the service to the component: Amazon RDS for a relational database and AWS Lambda for suitable event-driven processing.
When to use: A team needs a relational database but does not want to operate database software on EC2.; A team needs an event-driven processing component without operating worker servers.; A design has multiple components, and each can be matched to a suitable managed service.
Key facts: Operational excellence considers how a workload is designed, delivered, maintained, and operated.; AWS Well-Architected guidance calls for evaluating the benefits and risks of architectural decisions.; Choosing a managed service for one component does not require moving every other component off EC2.; A managed-service preference does not override a stated requirement that calls for control of a server.
Gotchas: Automation around self-managed EC2 software can reduce work without removing responsibility for operating that software.; Do not choose a managed service solely because it is managed; it must fit the component’s job.; Check every component in a proposed design: one self-managed database or worker can defeat a requirement to minimize operations for both.
Confused with: 
ES: Si un servicio administrado o diseñado para una tarea cumple los requisitos, prefiérelo antes que instalar y operar software equivalente en Amazon EC2 cuando la prioridad sea reducir la carga operativa. Elige según el componente: Amazon RDS para una base de datos relacional y AWS Lambda para un procesamiento basado en eventos que sea adecuado. Operational excellence considera cómo diseñas, entregas, mantienes y operas una carga de trabajo.; La guía AWS Well-Architected indica que debes evaluar los beneficios y riesgos de las decisiones de arquitectura.; Elegir un servicio administrado para un componente no exige trasladar todos los demás componentes fuera de EC2.; La preferencia por servicios administrados no anula un requisito explícito de control sobre un servidor.

chunks.title: Managed and purpose-built services vs self-managed
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company is adding a relational database and an event-driven job that updates ticket summaries. Its small operations team does not want to operate database software or worker servers. Which design meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use Amazon RDS for the database and AWS Lambda for the job.
Why: The deciding requirement applies to both components, not just one. Amazon RDS fits the relational database, while AWS Lambda fits the event-driven job without a worker server for the team to operate. A design that uses EC2 for either component leaves part of the stated operational burden in place.
Wrong options: Run the relational database on Amazon EC2 and use AWS Lambda for the job. (The team would still operate the database software on EC2.); Run the relational database and the job on separate Amazon EC2 instances. (The team would operate both database software and a worker server.); Use Amazon RDS for the database and run the job on Amazon EC2. (The team would still operate a worker server for the job.)

chunks.title: Managed and purpose-built services vs self-managed
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer has a vendor-supplied monitoring agent that must be installed on a server and given control over the server’s operating environment. The agent cannot be replaced or rewritten during this project. The team generally prefers managed services, but the deployment must satisfy the vendor requirement. Which choice meets the requirement?
Correct: Run the agent on Amazon EC2 and operate the required server environment.
Why: Reduced operational burden is a preference here, but installing the unchanged agent in a server environment is a requirement. Amazon EC2 is the appropriate choice for that component because the team must provide the environment the agent needs. Neither moving its logic to Lambda nor storing its records in RDS satisfies the installation requirement.
Wrong options: Store the monitoring records in Amazon RDS and omit the agent installation. (Storing records does not meet the requirement to install and run the vendor agent.); Move the agent’s monitoring logic into AWS Lambda instead of installing it. (Replacing the agent’s logic conflicts with the requirement to deploy it unchanged.); Use Amazon RDS to host the agent alongside its monitoring records. (A relational database service is not a substitute for the required server environment for the agent.)

chunks.title: Managed and purpose-built services vs self-managed
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional insurer is moving the relational database used by an existing application on Amazon EC2. The application must remain on EC2 without a rewrite, but the database team wants to stop operating database software on EC2. Which design meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Keep the application on EC2 and use Amazon RDS for its database.
Why: Only the database needs to move: the insurer explicitly requires the application to remain on EC2 without a rewrite. Amazon RDS addresses the database team’s operational goal while preserving that application placement. Moving the application to Lambda breaks a separate requirement, and keeping the database on EC2 does not remove the database team’s operational burden.
Wrong options: Keep the application on EC2 and run its database on a separate EC2 instance. (The team would still operate database software on EC2.); Rewrite the application for AWS Lambda and retain its database on EC2. (This both rewrites the application and leaves database software on EC2.); Rewrite the application for AWS Lambda and use Amazon RDS for its database. (RDS addresses the database requirement, but rewriting the application violates the stated constraint.)

chunks.title: Microservices design on AWS
chunks.text:
Microservices design on AWS. Microservices divide an application into small, loosely coupled services that teams can deploy and scale independently. In an exam scenario, choose service boundaries and API-driven or event-driven communication based on whether a workflow needs an immediate response or can proceed asynchronously.
When to use: Teams need to release different application capabilities independently.; Components have different scaling needs.; One service should continue responding without waiting for another service's work.
Key facts: Microservices communicate through well-defined APIs and are managed by autonomous teams.; API-driven and event-driven designs are both microservices patterns.; AWS guidance describes container-based and serverless approaches to implementing microservices.; Serverless can reduce infrastructure management and scale by unit of consumption.; Data consistency, asynchronous communication, and monitoring require attention across service boundaries.
Gotchas: Putting an entire monolith in a container does not, by itself, make its components independently deployable.; A chain of synchronous API calls can make a user-facing response depend on work that could happen asynchronously.; Microservices are not automatically preferable; weigh their complexity and costs against the application's needs.
Confused with: 
ES: Los microservicios dividen una aplicación en servicios pequeños y poco acoplados que los equipos pueden desplegar y escalar de forma independiente. En un escenario de examen, elige los límites de los servicios y la comunicación mediante API o eventos según si el flujo necesita una respuesta inmediata o puede continuar de forma asíncrona. Los microservicios se comunican mediante API bien definidas y están a cargo de equipos autónomos.; Los diseños basados en API y en eventos son patrones de microservicios.; La guía de AWS describe enfoques de microservicios basados en contenedores y en serverless.; Serverless puede reducir la administración de infraestructura y escalar por unidad de consumo.; La consistencia de datos, la comunicación asíncrona y el monitoreo requieren atención entre servicios.

chunks.title: Microservices design on AWS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing platform confirms reservations through an API and then updates audience analytics. Analytics jobs can run after confirmation, and a delay in analytics must not hold up the customer's response. The reservation and analytics teams also want to release their services independently. Which approach meets these requirements?
Correct: Keep reservation and analytics as separate services and initiate analytics through an event after reservation confirmation.
Why: Analytics is not required to complete before the customer receives confirmation. An event-driven interaction allows a separate analytics service to work after confirmation, while separate service boundaries support independent releases. A synchronous analytics API call is a plausible integration, but it introduces precisely the response dependency the scenario prohibits.
Wrong options: Place reservation and analytics in one Amazon ECS service and increase its capacity during ticket launches. (Additional capacity does not provide independent releases or remove the wait for analytics.); Keep reservation and analytics as separate services but wait for the analytics API to finish before confirming the reservation. (Waiting for analytics makes the customer response depend on a job allowed to run later.); Combine reservation and analytics in one AWS Lambda function so both operations finish in one request. (One function couples the teams' releases and keeps analytics in the response path.)

chunks.title: Microservices design on AWS
chunks.text:
Scenario: An online learning company has one application for course enrollment, video access, and certificates. Separate teams need to release certificate changes without redeploying enrollment, and certificate generation does not need to finish before an enrollment response is returned. Which design meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Implement separate enrollment and certificate services with AWS Lambda, expose the enrollment API through Amazon API Gateway, and initiate certificate work asynchronously.
Why: The deciding requirements are independent releases and no need to wait for certificate generation. Separate services meet the release requirement, while asynchronous initiation keeps certificate work out of the enrollment response path. AWS describes serverless as reducing infrastructure management, making the Lambda-based design a fit for the overhead qualifier. Separate ECS services could support independent releases, but option A unnecessarily makes enrollment wait.
Wrong options: Create separate Amazon ECS services but require enrollment to call the certificate API and wait for completion before responding. (The synchronous wait contradicts the requirement to return the enrollment response without waiting for certificate work.); Keep the application as one deployment behind Amazon API Gateway and add a certificate API route. (Separate routes do not let the certificate team deploy its code independently.); Put enrollment and certificate code in separate modules of one Amazon ECS service and scale the service for enrollment traffic. (Scaling the shared service does not make the modules independently deployable.)

chunks.title: Multi-AZ high availability design
chunks.text:
Multi-AZ high availability design. An AZ outage should not remove every healthy component of a workload. For a multi-tier application, place each required tier across at least two AZs and configure recovery or failover so traffic can use the remaining location.
When to use: The application must remain available if an AZ fails.; A scenario asks you to remove single-location dependencies from a multi-tier workload.; Recovery must occur without waiting for an operator to rebuild components.
Key facts: Fault isolation limits a failure’s impact to a defined boundary.; Running a workload across multiple fault isolation boundaries can improve resilience.; The AWS reliability guidance recommends deploying workloads to multiple locations.; For components constrained to one location, the guidance recommends automating recovery.; Bulkhead architectures limit the scope of impact, but do not by themselves place a workload in multiple locations.
Gotchas: Spreading web servers across AZs is insufficient if the required database remains in one AZ.; A second AZ does not help traffic if the design cannot stop sending requests to unhealthy targets.; Automated recovery in one location does not meet a requirement to survive the loss of that location.
Confused with: 
ES: Una interrupción de una AZ no debería eliminar todos los componentes sanos de una carga de trabajo. Para una aplicación de varias capas, coloca cada capa necesaria en al menos dos AZ y configura la recuperación o la conmutación por error para usar la ubicación restante.
