Which change should the solutions architect evaluate FIRST to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Evaluate placing the frequently communicating components closer together, while checking the placement against availability requirements.
Why: The traffic review has already identified a frequently used communication path, so the next step is to evaluate component placement as part of data transfer optimization. The proposed placement must still satisfy the workload’s availability requirement. Consolidating all instances without that check misses the constraint, and adding a hop does not target avoidable transfer.
Wrong options: Remove the metadata service’s existing network connection and rely on the processing service to retry requests. (Retries cannot replace the connectivity the two services require.); Route all communication between the services through an additional shared network hop so both services use one path. (An extra hop does not address the identified frequent traffic or demonstrate lower transfer costs.); Consolidate all application instances into one location without reviewing the workload’s availability design. (That move could violate the explicitly required availability.)

chunks.title: Network Load Balancer: TCP/UDP, static IPs, extreme performance
chunks.text:
Network Load Balancer: TCP/UDP, static IPs, extreme performance. A Network Load Balancer (NLB) distributes traffic at Layer 4 and is the fit for TCP or UDP workloads that need static IP addresses or very high throughput. In an exam scenario, choose it over an ALB when transport protocols and fixed addresses matter more than HTTP routing.
When to use: Clients send TCP or UDP traffic to multiple application targets.; Partners must allowlist fixed public IP addresses for an internet-facing load balancer.; A high-volume service needs load balancing across multiple Availability Zones.
Key facts: An NLB operates at OSI Layer 4 and can handle millions of requests per second.; Each enabled Availability Zone has a load balancer node with a static IP address.; An internet-facing NLB can optionally use one Elastic IP address per enabled subnet.; By default, a node sends traffic only to targets in its own Availability Zone; cross-zone load balancing changes this behavior.; For fault tolerance, enable multiple Availability Zones and place at least one target for each target group in every enabled Zone.
Gotchas: Static NLB addresses do not make a single-Availability-Zone deployment highly available.; An NLB does not provide the HTTP path- or host-based routing that points to an ALB.; A Gateway Load Balancer is for inline network appliances, not a substitute for an application's TCP or UDP load balancer.
Confused with: Application Load Balancer: Choose ALB for HTTP/HTTPS Layer 7 routing by path or host; choose NLB for TCP/UDP and static addresses.; Gateway Load Balancer: Choose GWLB to insert and scale inline virtual appliances such as firewalls; choose NLB to distribute application connections.
ES: Un Network Load Balancer (NLB) distribuye tráfico en la capa 4 y es adecuado para cargas TCP o UDP que necesitan direcciones IP estáticas o un volumen de tráfico muy alto. En un escenario de examen, elígelo en lugar de un ALB cuando importen más los protocolos de transporte y las direcciones fijas que el enrutamiento HTTP. Un NLB opera en la capa 4 del modelo OSI y puede manejar millones de solicitudes por segundo.; Cada Availability Zone habilitada tiene un nodo del balanceador con una dirección IP estática.; Un NLB orientado a internet puede usar opcionalmente una Elastic IP por cada subred habilitada.; De forma predeterminada, cada nodo envía tráfico solo a los destinos de su Availability Zone; cross-zone load balancing cambia este comportamiento.; Para mejorar la tolerancia a fallas, habilita varias Availability Zones y coloca al menos un destino de cada target group en cada una.

chunks.title: Network Load Balancer: TCP/UDP, static IPs, extreme performance
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab operates a TCP ingestion service behind a Network Load Balancer in two Availability Zones. Its only target group has healthy instances in one Zone but no registered targets in the other. The team wants the deployment to follow the NLB guidance for fault tolerance if a Zone becomes unavailable. Which change BEST meets this requirement?
Correct: Register at least one target from the target group in each enabled Availability Zone.
Why: Enabling two Zones alone is not the complete fault-tolerance configuration described for an NLB. AWS recommends at least one target from each target group in every enabled Availability Zone. Adding Elastic IPs changes addressing, not target placement; switching to GWLB would solve an appliance-inspection problem instead.
Wrong options: Replace the NLB with a Gateway Load Balancer and keep the existing targets in one Zone. (GWLB targets inline appliances and leaves the application without targets in the other Zone.); Keep the target placement and add host-based routing rules to the existing load balancer. (Host-based routing is an ALB feature and does not place a target in the empty Zone.); Keep the target placement and associate Elastic IP addresses with both NLB subnets. (Elastic IPs provide fixed addresses but do not add a target to the empty Zone.)

chunks.title: Network Load Balancer: TCP/UDP, static IPs, extreme performance
chunks.text:
Scenario: An agricultural monitoring platform receives UDP readings from remote stations. Network administrators at the stations must allowlist fixed public IP addresses, and the application needs a fault-tolerant deployment across two Availability Zones. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Deploy an internet-facing Network Load Balancer and associate an Elastic IP address with each enabled subnet. + Enable both Availability Zones on the NLB and register at least one target from each target group in each enabled Zone.
Why: The UDP protocol and fixed public addresses point to an internet-facing NLB with an Elastic IP for each enabled subnet. For the specified fault-tolerant deployment, enable both Zones and place at least one target from each target group in each Zone. Choosing one Zone reduces the number of addresses but fails the availability requirement; ALB host routing addresses HTTP rather than UDP.
Wrong options: Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer and register the monitoring application as inline inspection appliances. (GWLB serves inline inspection appliances rather than directly balancing this UDP application.); Deploy an Application Load Balancer and use host-based rules to distribute the UDP readings. (HTTP host-based rules do not meet the UDP traffic requirement.); Enable only one Availability Zone on the NLB so that the stations need to allowlist fewer addresses. (Using only one Zone contradicts the required two-Zone fault-tolerant deployment.)

chunks.title: Network Load Balancer: TCP/UDP, static IPs, extreme performance
chunks.text:
Scenario: A game studio receives UDP telemetry from players and distributes it to application targets in two Availability Zones. Its partners require fixed public IP addresses that they can allowlist for each enabled subnet. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use an internet-facing Network Load Balancer across both Availability Zones and associate an Elastic IP address with each enabled subnet.
Why: The deciding requirements are UDP traffic, fixed public IPs per enabled subnet, and deployment across two Availability Zones. An internet-facing NLB supports UDP and can associate one Elastic IP with each enabled subnet. An ALB's host routing does not address UDP, while a single-Zone NLB misses the stated Zone requirement.
Wrong options: Use an Application Load Balancer across both Availability Zones and route requests by host name. (Host-based HTTP routing does not meet the UDP and fixed-IP requirements.); Use an internet-facing Network Load Balancer in one Availability Zone with an Elastic IP address. (It supports UDP and a fixed address but does not meet the two-Availability-Zone requirement.); Use a Gateway Load Balancer across both Availability Zones to distribute the telemetry to inline firewalls. (A GWLB is intended for inline network appliances, not direct distribution to the telemetry application.)

chunks.title: Availability classes: production vs non-production schedules
chunks.text:
Availability classes: production vs non-production schedules. Match availability and operating hours to the workload: keep production resources available, but consider smaller, single-AZ dev/test resources that run only when needed. Instance Scheduler on AWS can start and stop tagged EC2 and RDS instances on a schedule, including across configured accounts and Regions.
When to use: Dev/test EC2 or RDS instances are needed during business hours but not overnight.; Production must remain available while non-production can tolerate scheduled downtime.; Tagged instances in multiple accounts or Regions need a common schedule.
Key facts: Instance Scheduler on AWS uses resource tags and AWS Lambda to start and stop EC2 and RDS instances on customer-defined schedules.; A stopped RDS DB instance incurs no DB instance-hour charges, but storage and backup charges continue.; An RDS DB instance can remain stopped for at most seven consecutive days before RDS automatically starts it.; Starting a stopped RDS DB instance can take minutes to hours.; An RDS DB instance cannot be stopped if it has a read replica or is itself a read replica.
Gotchas: Do not schedule a production database to stop if it must remain available; restarting RDS is not instantaneous.; Stopping RDS does not eliminate storage or backup costs.; Do not assume an RDS instance will stay stopped indefinitely or that an instance with a read replica can be stopped.
Confused with: 
ES: Ajusta la disponibilidad y el horario de operación a cada carga: mantén disponibles los recursos de producción, pero considera recursos dev/test más pequeños y de una sola AZ que funcionen solo cuando se necesiten. Instance Scheduler on AWS puede iniciar y detener instancias EC2 y RDS etiquetadas según un horario, incluso entre cuentas y Regions configuradas. Instance Scheduler on AWS usa resource tags y AWS Lambda para iniciar y detener instancias EC2 y RDS según horarios definidos por el cliente.; Una instancia de RDS detenida no genera cargos por horas de instancia de base de datos, pero siguen los cargos de almacenamiento y respaldos.; Una instancia de RDS puede permanecer detenida un máximo de siete días consecutivos; después, RDS la inicia automáticamente.; Iniciar una instancia de RDS detenida puede tardar de minutos a horas.; No puedes detener una instancia de RDS que tenga una read replica ni una que sea una read replica.

chunks.title: Availability classes: production vs non-production schedules
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer operates development EC2 instances and RDS databases in multiple AWS accounts and Regions. Development runs during business hours, while production databases must remain available; some development RDS instances have read replicas. The retailer wants automated off-hours savings without assuming that stopped databases have no costs or will stay stopped forever. Which two actions should the retailer take? (Choose two.)
Correct: Exclude RDS instances with read replicas from the stop plan, and account for ongoing storage and backup costs plus the seven-day automatic restart. + Configure Instance Scheduler on AWS for the relevant accounts and Regions, using schedule tags to select eligible development instances.
Why: The retailer needs automated scheduling across accounts and Regions, but only for resources eligible to stop. Instance Scheduler on AWS can target tagged development instances in the configured scope, while production databases remain available. RDS instances with read replicas cannot be stopped, so they must be excluded from this plan. For eligible RDS instances, storage and backup charges continue during a stop, and RDS automatically restarts an instance after seven consecutive days.
Wrong options: Include development RDS instances with read replicas in the stop schedule to capture the same savings as other development databases. (An RDS DB instance with a read replica cannot be stopped.); Apply an overnight stop tag to every RDS database, including production databases, so one schedule covers the fleet. (An overnight stop schedule would violate production's availability requirement.); Plan savings as though all RDS charges cease while an instance is stopped and it remains stopped until manually started. (Storage and backup charges continue, and RDS automatically starts the instance after seven consecutive days.)

chunks.title: Availability classes: production vs non-production schedules
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio runs development EC2 instances and RDS databases in several AWS accounts and Regions. Teams use them only during local business hours, but the production instances must remain available overnight. The studio wants one tag-based approach rather than separate scripts maintained by each team. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy Instance Scheduler on AWS for the configured accounts and Regions, and apply its schedule tag only to eligible development instances.
Why: The deciding requirements are a common tag-based schedule across accounts and Regions and uninterrupted production availability. Instance Scheduler on AWS can act on tagged EC2 and RDS instances across configured accounts and Regions, so the studio can target eligible development resources. Applying the schedule to production would violate its availability requirement. Manual actions and repeated RDS deletion and restoration also add avoidable operational work.
Wrong options: Have each team stop its development instances manually at the end of each workday and start them the next morning. (Manual actions require each team to perform the recurring work that the studio wants to avoid.); Deploy Instance Scheduler on AWS and apply the same overnight stop schedule to both development and production instances. (Stopping production instances conflicts with the requirement that they remain available overnight.); Have each team snapshot and delete its development RDS databases after work, then restore them before the next workday. (Snapshot, deletion, and restoration add recurring work when temporary RDS stopping is the more efficient fit.)

chunks.title: On-Demand Capacity Reservations
chunks.text:
On-Demand Capacity Reservations. EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserve capacity for matching instances in a specific Availability Zone. Choose an immediate-use reservation when capacity assurance matters but a fixed term does not; add a Savings Plan separately if eligible usage also needs a discount.
When to use: A disaster recovery workload must be able to use EC2 capacity in a particular Availability Zone.; An event requires short-term capacity assurance without a fixed-term commitment.; Specific workloads must have access to reserved capacity rather than sharing it with every matching instance.
Key facts: An immediate-use Capacity Reservation has no term commitment and can be modified or canceled.; Capacity Reservations provide a capacity benefit, not a billing discount; they can be combined with Savings Plans for a discount.; Instances must match the reservation's instance type, platform, Availability Zone, and tenancy.; By default, matching running and new instances can use a reservation; targeting restricts which workloads can use it.; Future-dated Capacity Reservations have a commitment duration and are intended for incremental instances, not existing running instances.
Gotchas: A Savings Plan discounts eligible usage but does not reserve capacity.; A Regional Reserved Instance does not reserve capacity; a Zonal Reserved Instance does, but requires a fixed term.; A future-dated reservation is not the no-term choice for capacity needed immediately.
Confused with: Savings Plans: Provide a billing discount, not guaranteed capacity; they can complement a Capacity Reservation.; Zonal Reserved Instances: Reserve capacity in an Availability Zone but require a one- or three-year commitment.; Spot Instances: Fit interruptible workloads, not a strict requirement for assured capacity.
ES: EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserva capacidad para instancias que coinciden con sus atributos en una Availability Zone específica. Elige una reserva de uso inmediato cuando necesitas asegurar capacidad sin un plazo fijo; agrega un Savings Plan por separado si también buscas un descuento para el uso elegible. Una Capacity Reservation de uso inmediato no exige un compromiso de plazo y puedes modificarla o cancelarla.; Capacity Reservations aporta capacidad reservada, no un descuento; puedes combinarla con Savings Plans para obtener un descuento.; Las instancias deben coincidir en tipo de instancia, plataforma, Availability Zone y tenencia.; De forma predeterminada, las instancias nuevas y en ejecución que coinciden pueden usar la reserva; puedes dirigirla a cargas específicas.; Las Capacity Reservations con fecha futura tienen un período de compromiso y están destinadas a instancias adicionales, no a instancias que ya se ejecutan.

chunks.title: On-Demand Capacity Reservations
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional publisher keeps EC2 instances running in a secondary Availability Zone so it can shift traffic during an outage. It needs to assure capacity for those existing instances in that zone, but it does not want a one-year or three-year commitment. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Create an immediate-use On-Demand Capacity Reservation with attributes matching the instances.
Why: The deciding requirements are capacity assurance for already-running instances in one Availability Zone and no fixed-term commitment. An immediate-use Capacity Reservation can match running instances by instance type, platform, Availability Zone, and tenancy. A future-dated reservation does not cover existing running instances, while a Savings Plan provides a discount rather than capacity.
Wrong options: Purchase Regional Reserved Instances matching the instances. (Regional Reserved Instances do not reserve capacity and require a fixed term.); Purchase a Compute Savings Plan covering the instances' usage. (A Savings Plan can discount eligible usage but does not reserve capacity.); Request a future-dated Capacity Reservation with attributes matching the instances. (Future-dated reservations are intended for incremental instances, not existing running instances, and include a commitment duration.)

chunks.title: On-Demand Capacity Reservations
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company expects a short surge starting tonight and must be able to launch additional EC2 instances in one specified Availability Zone. Its baseline EC2 usage is steady enough for a discount commitment, but the extra capacity is needed for only a few days. Which solution provides the required capacity assurance and a discount on eligible usage without a fixed-term capacity commitment?
Correct: Create an immediate-use On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the surge and purchase a Compute Savings Plan for eligible usage.
Why: The company needs capacity in a particular Availability Zone tonight, without committing to that extra capacity for a fixed term. An immediate-use Capacity Reservation provides that capacity assurance, and a Savings Plan can separately discount eligible usage. A Savings Plan alone does not reserve capacity, while a Zonal Reserved Instance introduces the fixed-term commitment the company wants to avoid.
Wrong options: Request a future-dated Capacity Reservation for the surge and purchase a Compute Savings Plan. (A future-dated reservation has a commitment duration and is not the immediate-use, no-term choice for capacity needed tonight.); Purchase Zonal Reserved Instances for the surge and a Compute Savings Plan for baseline usage. (Zonal Reserved Instances reserve capacity but impose a fixed one- or three-year commitment for the short surge.); Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for baseline and surge usage. (A Compute Savings Plan provides a discount but cannot assure launch capacity in the specified Availability Zone.)

chunks.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service (search and log analytics)
chunks.text:
Amazon OpenSearch Service (search and log analytics). Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed search and analytics service for full-text search, log analytics, and near-real-time exploration of indexed data. Choose it when a scenario needs searchable events and interactive OpenSearch Dashboards, rather than occasional SQL queries or business-intelligence reports.
When to use: Users need to search application content or log messages by text.; Teams need dashboards to explore incoming logs or application events.; A search workload needs a managed cluster rather than self-managed infrastructure.
Key facts: An OpenSearch Service domain is a managed OpenSearch cluster.; OpenSearch Service can load streaming data from services including Amazon Kinesis and Amazon DynamoDB; CloudWatch Logs can also stream data to it.; OpenSearch Dashboards provides data visualization.; A domain can allocate nodes across two or three Availability Zones in one Region.; UltraWarm and cold storage are cost-effective tiers for read-only data.
Gotchas: A dashboard requirement alone does not decide the service: determine whether users must search indexed events or view business-intelligence reports.; Athena is a better match for ad-hoc SQL on S3 than for an interactive, indexed log-search experience.; Managed OpenSearch Service reduces cluster-management work, but a provisioned domain still has configured nodes and storage.
Confused with: Amazon Athena: Athena runs ad-hoc SQL against S3 data; OpenSearch supports indexed search and log exploration.; Amazon Quick: Quick provides BI dashboards; OpenSearch Dashboards accompanies search and analysis of data in OpenSearch.; Amazon Redshift: Redshift fits structured warehouse analytics; OpenSearch fits text search and log analytics.
ES: Amazon OpenSearch Service es un servicio administrado de búsqueda y análisis para full-text search, análisis de logs y exploración casi en tiempo real de datos indexados. Elígelo cuando se necesiten eventos que se puedan buscar y OpenSearch Dashboards interactivos, en lugar de consultas SQL ocasionales o informes de BI. Un domain de OpenSearch Service es un clúster de OpenSearch administrado.; OpenSearch Service puede cargar datos en streaming desde servicios como Amazon Kinesis y Amazon DynamoDB; CloudWatch Logs también puede enviarle datos en streaming.; OpenSearch Dashboards permite visualizar datos.; Un domain puede distribuir nodos entre dos o tres Availability Zones de una misma Region.; UltraWarm y cold storage son niveles cost-effective para datos de solo lectura.

chunks.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service (search and log analytics)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A repair marketplace receives new listings throughout the day. Customers must search listing descriptions by text, while operators want to explore incoming search and click events in dashboards. Which service meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Amazon OpenSearch Service with OpenSearch Dashboards
Why: The deciding requirement is customer search across listing descriptions, combined with dashboards for incoming events. Amazon OpenSearch Service provides managed search and analytics, and OpenSearch Dashboards supports visualization. Athena could analyze files in S3, but ad-hoc SQL does not provide the requested indexed search experience.
Wrong options: Amazon Redshift to warehouse listings and click events (Redshift suits structured warehouse analytics rather than customer-facing text search.); Amazon Quick to build dashboards over listing data (Quick provides visualization but does not meet the customer-facing text-search requirement.); Amazon Athena to query listing and event files in Amazon S3 (Athena suits ad-hoc SQL on S3, not the requested indexed text-search experience.)

chunks.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service (search and log analytics)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional transit operator sends application logs to CloudWatch Logs. Its incident team wants to stream those logs into a searchable service, inspect messages in dashboards, and avoid maintaining search-cluster nodes themselves. The search deployment must also place nodes across Availability Zones. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Stream CloudWatch Logs to a Multi-AZ Amazon OpenSearch Service domain
Why: The team needs streamed, searchable logs and a managed deployment across Availability Zones. CloudWatch Logs can stream data to OpenSearch Service, which supports OpenSearch Dashboards and Multi-AZ node allocation. Athena is useful for ad-hoc analysis of S3 data, but exporting files for queries misses the stated streaming search workflow.
Wrong options: Process the logs on an Amazon EMR cluster and retain the output in Amazon S3 (EMR adds cluster operations without providing the requested managed search experience.); Export logs to Amazon S3 and query them with Amazon Athena (Ad-hoc queries on exported files do not meet the requested streaming, indexed log-search workflow.); Catalog the logs with an AWS Glue crawler and query the cataloged files (Schema discovery does not provide streamed log search or the requested search deployment.)

chunks.title: AWS Outposts (AWS on premises)
chunks.text:
AWS Outposts (AWS on premises). AWS Outposts places AWS-managed compute and storage capacity at a customer site. Choose it when a workload must run on premises for low-latency access to local systems or local data processing while using AWS APIs and tools.
When to use: The application must run at a customer facility, close to on-premises data or equipment.; The team wants AWS-managed infrastructure and the same programming interfaces used in AWS Regions.; A small site needs local compute but has limited space; consider an Outposts server.
Key facts: AWS operates, monitors, and manages Outpost capacity as part of an AWS Region.; Outpost subnets can host supported resources; EC2 instances are supported on both racks and servers.; Outposts racks support EBS volumes and RDS DB instances; Outposts servers do not.; An Outposts rack uses a 42U form factor; Outposts servers use a 1U or 2U form factor.; An Outpost uses a service link to communicate with its associated AWS Region.
Gotchas: Do not select a metro-area edge location when the workload must run inside the customer's own facility.; Do not assume every resource supported on an Outposts rack is supported on an Outposts server.; Check supported services for the associated Region when a scenario requires a particular service.
Confused with: Local Zones and Wavelength: They target metro-area or 5G mobile-edge latency; Outposts places AWS infrastructure at the customer site.; VMware Cloud on AWS: It fits a requirement to retain vSphere tooling; Outposts fits AWS infrastructure on premises.; ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere: They run containers on customer-owned hardware with AWS tooling; AWS owns and manages Outposts equipment.
ES: AWS Outposts coloca capacidad de cómputo y almacenamiento administrada por AWS en las instalaciones del cliente. Elígelo cuando una carga de trabajo deba ejecutarse allí para acceder con baja latencia a sistemas locales o procesar datos localmente, sin dejar de usar las API y herramientas de AWS. AWS opera, supervisa y administra la capacidad de Outposts como parte de una AWS Region.; Las subredes de Outposts pueden alojar recursos compatibles; las instancias EC2 son compatibles tanto con racks como con servers.; Los Outposts racks admiten volúmenes EBS e instancias de RDS; los Outposts servers no.; Un Outposts rack tiene un formato de 42U; los Outposts servers tienen un formato de 1U o 2U.; Un Outpost usa un service link para comunicarse con su AWS Region asociada.

chunks.title: AWS Outposts (AWS on premises)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer analyzes sensor readings alongside a control system inside its factory. The analysis application must run at the factory for low-latency access to the control system, and developers want to deploy EC2 instances using the AWS interfaces they already use. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST change to the team's deployment approach?
Correct: Deploy EC2 instances in an AWS Outposts subnet at the factory.
Why: The deciding constraint is that EC2 instances must run at the factory while developers continue using AWS interfaces. AWS Outposts extends AWS-managed infrastructure to customer premises and supports EC2 instances in Outpost subnets. A Local Zone may be closer to a metro area, but it does not satisfy the explicit requirement to run at the factory.
Wrong options: Deploy the application with ECS Anywhere on customer-owned servers at the factory. (This uses customer-owned hardware and container tooling rather than providing AWS-managed infrastructure for the requested EC2 deployment.); Deploy the application in an AWS Wavelength Zone on a carrier network. (A carrier-network edge location does not place the application beside the factory control system.); Deploy the application in a Local Zone near the factory. (A nearby metro-area location does not meet the requirement to run the application at the factory.)

chunks.title: AWS Outposts (AWS on premises)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare provider runs an application beside diagnostic equipment at its own facility. It needs locally deployed EC2 instances, EBS volumes, and an RDS DB instance, all on AWS-managed infrastructure; its associated AWS Region supports these Outposts services. Which deployment meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead for the underlying infrastructure?
Correct: Deploy EC2, EBS, and RDS on an Outposts rack at the facility.
Why: The provider needs three specific AWS resource types at its own facility, not just nearby compute. Outposts racks support EC2 instances, EBS volumes, and RDS DB instances, and AWS manages the Outpost infrastructure. An Outposts server is a tempting smaller form factor, but it does not support EBS volumes or RDS DB instances.
Wrong options: Deploy the application on VMware Cloud on AWS while retaining vSphere tooling. (Retaining vSphere tooling does not meet the requirement to place the specified AWS resources at the provider's facility.); Deploy EC2, EBS, and RDS on an Outposts server at the facility. (Outposts servers support EC2 but not EBS volumes or RDS DB instances.); Deploy the application with EKS Anywhere on customer-owned hardware at the facility. (EKS Anywhere uses customer-owned hardware and does not provide the specified Outposts-hosted EBS and RDS resources.)

chunks.title: IAM permissions boundaries
chunks.text:
IAM permissions boundaries. An IAM permissions boundary is a managed policy that caps the permissions an IAM user or role can receive through identity-based policies. Choose it when you need to delegate IAM user or role creation without letting the new identities exceed a defined maximum.
When to use: A developer may create IAM users or roles and attach permissions policies, but the resulting identities must stay within a fixed limit.; A particular user or role needs a permissions ceiling without imposing that ceiling on every principal in the account.
Key facts: For identity-based permissions, effective access is the intersection of the identity-based policy and the permissions boundary.; A permissions boundary limits permissions; it does not grant them.; Delegated user creation can be conditioned on assigning a specified permissions boundary.; The delegation design must prevent the delegate from removing the boundary or editing its managed policy.
Gotchas: Attaching a broad identity-based policy cannot grant actions outside the boundary.; An SCP is attached to an organization, OU, or account and applies to all its principals by default; targeting one user or role requires conditions such as aws:PrincipalArn, whereas a boundary is attached directly to that identity.; A boundary's implicit deny does not universally block permissions granted by resource-based policies; evaluation depends on the principal named in the resource policy.
Confused with: Identity-based policy: It grants actions to a user, group, or role; a permissions boundary caps what those grants can provide.; Service control policy (SCP): It is attached at the organization, OU, or account level (conditions can target specific principals), whereas a permissions boundary is attached directly to a specific IAM user or role.; Resource-based policy: It controls access to a particular resource rather than setting an identity-based permissions ceiling.
ES: Un IAM permissions boundary es una managed policy que limita los permisos que un usuario o rol de IAM puede recibir mediante identity-based policies. Elígelo cuando necesitas delegar la creación de usuarios o roles sin permitir que las nuevas identidades superen un máximo definido. Para los permisos basados en identidad, el acceso efectivo es la intersección de la identity-based policy y el permissions boundary.; Un permissions boundary limita permisos; no los concede.; Puedes condicionar la creación delegada de usuarios a que se asigne un permissions boundary específico.; El diseño de delegación debe impedir que la persona delegada elimine el boundary o modifique su managed policy.

chunks.title: IAM permissions boundaries
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturing team uses an IAM role for a monitoring application. Its identity-based policy allows cloudwatch:GetMetricData and s3:ListBucket, but its permissions boundary allows only Amazon S3 actions. The application must read CloudWatch metrics while retaining the existing S3 limit and without granting unrelated CloudWatch actions. Which change meets these requirements with the LEAST increase in permissions?
Correct: Add cloudwatch:GetMetricData to the role's permissions boundary.
Why: For these identity-based permissions, the role needs an allow in both its identity-based policy and its permissions boundary. The policy already allows cloudwatch:GetMetricData, so adding that action to the boundary is the narrowest sufficient change. Expanding the identity-based policy does not help while the boundary excludes CloudWatch. Allowing every CloudWatch action in the boundary would exceed the requested ceiling.
Wrong options: Add an SCP allowing cloudwatch:GetMetricData for the account. (An SCP does not grant the action or override the role's permissions boundary.); Add cloudwatch:* to the role's identity-based policy. (The boundary still excludes CloudWatch, so expanding the identity-based policy does not enable metric reads.); Add cloudwatch:* to the role's permissions boundary. (This enables the currently allowed metric read but leaves a broader CloudWatch ceiling than required.)

chunks.title: IAM permissions boundaries
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization has several workloads in one AWS account. A project team may create IAM roles and attach identity-based policies, but roles it creates must not gain identity-based access to a protected dataset. Other teams' existing roles in the same account must retain their current access. Which approach meets these requirements MOST precisely?
Correct: Require the project team to attach a managed permissions boundary to each new role that excludes the protected dataset, and prevent boundary removal or modification.
Why: The restriction must follow the roles the project team creates while leaving existing roles in the account unchanged. A required permissions boundary caps those new roles' identity-based permissions, and protections against removal or modification preserve the cap. An SCP is too broad because it applies at the account level. Restricting only the creators' own policies or sessions does not establish a maximum for the roles they create.
Wrong options: Restrict the project team's own identity-based policy to exclude the protected dataset while allowing role creation and policy attachment. (Limiting the creators' access does not set a permissions ceiling on roles they create.); Apply an SCP to the account that excludes access to the protected dataset. (An account-level SCP would also restrict other teams' roles.); Pass a session policy when project team members assume their own roles, excluding the protected dataset. (Limiting the creators' sessions does not enforce a lasting ceiling on newly created roles.)

chunks.title: AWS PrivateLink endpoint services (share a service privately)
chunks.text:
AWS PrivateLink endpoint services (share a service privately). AWS PrivateLink lets you share your own service privately with other VPCs or AWS accounts. Put a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front of the service, create an endpoint service, and have consumers connect through interface VPC endpoints—without VPC peering, even when CIDR ranges overlap.
When to use: Other accounts need private access to an application you operate, not just to an AWS service.; Consumer VPCs have overlapping CIDR ranges or must not be peered with the provider VPC.; You need to limit which AWS principals can connect to your service.
Key facts: The provider selects an NLB when creating the endpoint service configuration.; The provider grants specific AWS principals permission to connect; each consumer creates an interface VPC endpoint.; A consumer endpoint gets a network interface and private IP address in each selected subnet.; For high availability, enable the NLB in at least two Availability Zones and deploy registered targets in each.; A provider can associate a private DNS name so consumers can keep using an existing service name.
Gotchas: A consumer interface endpoint does not, by itself, publish the provider's application; the provider must create an endpoint service.; Cross-zone load balancing is not a substitute for hosting the service in multiple Availability Zones: failure of the zone hosting it can cut off access.; A NAT gateway provides outbound connectivity (a public NAT gateway to the internet, a private one only to other private networks), not private inbound access to your service.
Confused with: Gateway VPC endpoint: It privately reaches Amazon S3 or DynamoDB; it does not publish your own application.; Interface VPC endpoint: It is the consumer-side connection; the provider publishes its NLB-fronted application as an endpoint service.; NAT gateway: It supports outbound connections from private subnets, not consumer access to a provider's service.
ES: AWS PrivateLink te permite compartir tu propio servicio de forma privada con otras VPC o cuentas de AWS. Coloca un Network Load Balancer (NLB) frente al servicio, crea un endpoint service y haz que los consumidores se conecten mediante interface VPC endpoints, sin VPC peering incluso si los rangos CIDR se superponen. El proveedor selecciona un NLB al crear la configuración del endpoint service.; El proveedor concede permiso de conexión a AWS principals específicos; cada consumidor crea un interface VPC endpoint.; El endpoint del consumidor recibe una interfaz de red y una dirección IP privada en cada subred seleccionada.; Para alta disponibilidad, habilita el NLB en al menos dos Availability Zones e implementa targets registrados en cada una.; El proveedor puede asociar un private DNS name para que los consumidores sigan usando el nombre existente del servicio.

chunks.title: AWS PrivateLink endpoint services (share a service privately)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A software vendor runs a private telemetry collector in its VPC. Several customers need to send telemetry from their own VPCs to the vendor without VPC peering or an internet-facing entry point. The vendor wants a repeatable connection pattern as new customers sign up. Which two actions are required for the AWS PrivateLink design? (Choose two.)
Correct: Create an NLB in the vendor VPC and select it when creating an endpoint service configuration. + Grant the customer AWS principals permission to connect and have customers create interface VPC endpoints.
Why: This scenario needs both sides of a PrivateLink connection to a vendor-operated service. The vendor creates an NLB-backed endpoint service and grants customer AWS principals permission; customers create interface VPC endpoints. Gateway endpoints are for supported AWS services, and NAT gateways do not connect consumers to this private service. VPC peering is explicitly excluded.
Wrong options: Create VPC peering connections between the vendor VPC and each customer VPC. (Peering directly violates the stated requirement and is not needed for this PrivateLink design.); Have each customer create a gateway VPC endpoint for the collector. (Gateway endpoints do not connect to a vendor-operated endpoint service.); Give each customer a NAT gateway to reach the collector from private subnets. (A NAT gateway is an outbound access component, not the consumer connection to a PrivateLink service.)

chunks.title: AWS PrivateLink endpoint services (share a service privately)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company is moving an internal licensing service to an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service. Its partner applications already call the service using an established DNS name, and the partners will create interface VPC endpoints. The company wants the partners to keep using that name with the LEAST application changes. Which solution should the company choose?
Correct: Associate the established private DNS name with the endpoint service and have partners enable private DNS names on their interface endpoints.
Why: The deciding constraint is preserving the applications' established service name. The provider can associate that private DNS name with its endpoint service, and consumers can enable private DNS on their interface endpoints. Regional and zonal endpoint names are usable alternatives, but switching applications to those names requires changes. NAT gateways do not address endpoint-service DNS.
Wrong options: Have partners replace the established name with a zonal DNS name generated for each interface endpoint. (A zonal endpoint name changes the name used by the applications and does not meet the minimal-change requirement.); Create NAT gateways in the partner VPCs so applications can keep using the established name. (NAT gateways do not provide private DNS naming for a PrivateLink endpoint service.); Have partners replace the established name with the Regional DNS name generated for each interface endpoint. (The Regional endpoint name can reach the service but requires partner application configuration changes.)

chunks.title: Public vs private subnet segmentation
chunks.text:
Public vs private subnet segmentation. A public subnet has a direct route to an internet gateway; a private subnet does not. For an internet-facing application, place load balancer nodes in public subnets and application servers in private subnets so clients reach the servers through the load balancer rather than directly.
When to use: Users must reach an application from the internet, but must not connect directly to its servers.; Private application servers need outbound internet access.; A workload must remain available if one Availability Zone fails.
Key facts: Subnet type is determined by routing, not by its name.; A private subnet has no direct route to an internet gateway; for outbound internet access its resources use a NAT device (IPv4) or an egress-only internet gateway (IPv6).; A subnet resides entirely within one Availability Zone.; AWS's two-AZ production example places load balancer nodes and NAT gateways in public subnets, with application servers in private subnets.; In that example, server security groups allow load balancer traffic and health checks.
Gotchas: Putting servers in public subnets exposes a tier that could instead receive requests through a load balancer.; A NAT route provides outbound access for private servers; it is not the path for incoming client requests.; Security group rules do not turn a subnet without an internet-gateway route into a public subnet.
Confused with: Isolated subnet: An isolated subnet has no route to destinations outside its VPC; a private subnet can use a NAT device or an egress-only internet gateway for outbound internet access.; Security group: A security group controls traffic for associated resources, while the subnet's route table determines whether it has a direct internet-gateway route.
ES: Una public subnet tiene una ruta directa hacia un internet gateway; una private subnet no. Para una aplicación accesible desde internet, coloca los nodos del load balancer en public subnets y los servidores de aplicación en private subnets, de modo que los clientes lleguen a ellos a través del load balancer. El tipo de subnet depende de sus rutas, no de su nombre.; Una private subnet no tiene una ruta directa hacia un internet gateway; para salir a internet sus recursos usan un dispositivo NAT (IPv4) o un egress-only internet gateway (IPv6).; Cada subnet está completamente dentro de una sola Availability Zone.; El ejemplo de producción de AWS en dos Availability Zones coloca los nodos del load balancer y los NAT gateways en public subnets, y los servidores de aplicación en private subnets.; En ese ejemplo, los security groups de los servidores permiten el tráfico y los health checks del load balancer.

chunks.title: Public vs private subnet segmentation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics platform runs application servers in private subnets across two Availability Zones. The servers must download updates from the public internet without receiving direct internet traffic. Outbound access must remain available if either Availability Zone fails. Which TWO configurations meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Deploy a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone. + Route each private application's outbound internet traffic to its Availability Zone's NAT gateway, while routing the public NAT subnets to the internet gateway.
Why: The servers need internet egress, no direct internet-gateway route in their subnets, and resilience across Availability Zones. Deploying NAT gateways in public subnets in both AZs and routing each private application's outbound traffic through its AZ's NAT gateway satisfies those constraints. A single-AZ NAT deployment misses the failure requirement. Direct internet-gateway routes would make the application subnets public, while removing external routes would block downloads.
Wrong options: Deploy one NAT gateway in a public subnet in a single Availability Zone. (A NAT gateway in only one Availability Zone does not meet the stated AZ-failure requirement.); Add a direct internet-gateway route to each application subnet. (Direct internet-gateway routes would make the application subnets public.); Remove all routes to destinations outside the VPC from both application subnets. (That would prevent the servers from downloading updates from the public internet.)

chunks.title: Public vs private subnet segmentation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company is moving a public web application to EC2 in two Availability Zones. Customers must reach the application over the internet, but must not connect directly to the application instances. Which subnet layout meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Place the internet-facing Application Load Balancer in public subnets and the application instances in private subnets across both Availability Zones.
Why: The deciding constraint is public customer access without direct access to application instances. An internet-facing Application Load Balancer in public subnets can receive requests and forward them to instances in private subnets. Using subnets in both Availability Zones also protects against a single-AZ failure. Placing the instances in public subnets needlessly moves the protected tier into the internet-routed portion of the VPC.
Wrong options: Place the Application Load Balancer and application instances in private subnets across both Availability Zones. (This layout provides no public-subnet entry point for internet customers.); Place the Application Load Balancer and application instances in public subnets across both Availability Zones. (Public subnets unnecessarily place the application instances in the internet-routed tier.); Place the application instances in public subnets and the Application Load Balancer in private subnets across both Availability Zones. (It reverses the required exposure: the instances occupy the public tier while the load balancer does not.)

chunks.title: Public vs private subnet segmentation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute runs an application behind an internet-facing load balancer. Its application servers need outbound internet access for updates, but the database accepts connections only from resources inside the VPC and needs no external destinations. Which subnet design minimizes the database tier's network exposure?
Correct: Put the application servers in private subnets with a route to a NAT gateway, and put the database in isolated subnets.
Why: The application servers and database have different egress requirements. Private application subnets can route to a NAT gateway for updates, while isolated database subnets have no routes to destinations outside the VPC. A private subnet with a NAT route is more connectivity than the database requires. Reversing the placement would prevent application servers from reaching the update source.
Wrong options: Put the application servers and database in private subnets, and route both subnets to a NAT gateway. (The database does not need the outbound access supplied by a NAT route.); Put the application servers in isolated subnets, and put the database in private subnets with a route to a NAT gateway. (It denies the servers their required updates while giving the database unnecessary outbound routing.); Put the application servers and database in public subnets; restrict database traffic with a security group. (Security groups can restrict traffic, but this places a database with no external-access requirement in an internet-routed subnet.)

chunks.title: Purpose-built database selection (key-value, document, graph, wide-column, time series, ledger)
chunks.text:
Purpose-built database selection (key-value, document, graph, wide-column, time series, ledger). Choose a database by its data model and dominant query pattern, not by the application's industry. Highly connected relationships point to Amazon Neptune; MongoDB-compatible documents to Amazon DocumentDB; Cassandra workloads to Amazon Keyspaces; time-interval queries to Amazon Timestream; key-value lookups to Amazon DynamoDB; and large-scale analytics to Amazon Redshift.
When to use: Queries must navigate relationships among connected entities: choose Amazon Neptune.; An existing application needs MongoDB compatibility or Apache Cassandra compatibility: evaluate Amazon DocumentDB or Amazon Keyspaces, respectively.; Measurements arrive over time and queries use time intervals: choose Amazon Timestream.; Separate low-latency key-value application access from large-scale analytical reporting: evaluate Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Redshift for their respective workloads.
Key facts: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed key-value and document database that delivers single-digit millisecond performance at any scale.; Amazon DocumentDB is a fully managed document database with MongoDB compatibility for JSON workloads.; Amazon Neptune is a fully managed graph database for highly connected datasets and supports Property Graph and RDF models.; Amazon Keyspaces is a managed, serverless Apache Cassandra–compatible database service that supports existing Cassandra application code and developer tools.; Amazon Timestream is a serverless time series database that processes data by time intervals; Amazon Redshift is a fully managed data warehouse for large-scale analytics.
Gotchas: JSON data alone does not make MongoDB compatibility a requirement: DynamoDB also supports a document data model.; A relationship-heavy fraud investigation calls for graph traversal, not merely fast lookup by an entity's key.; Repeated measurements do not imply a wide-column database when time-interval analysis is the deciding requirement.; Amazon Redshift serves large-scale analytical workloads, not the low-latency key-value access pattern of an application database.
Confused with: Amazon DynamoDB vs. Amazon DocumentDB: Both can hold document data; choose Amazon DocumentDB when MongoDB compatibility is required, and Amazon DynamoDB for key-value access with single-digit millisecond performance.; Amazon Keyspaces vs. Amazon Timestream: Choose Amazon Keyspaces for Cassandra-compatible workloads; choose Amazon Timestream when queries analyze measurements over time intervals.; Amazon Neptune vs. Amazon Redshift: Amazon Neptune navigates highly connected graphs; Amazon Redshift supports large-scale data-warehouse analytics.
ES: Elige la base de datos según el modelo de datos y el patrón principal de consulta, no según el sector de la aplicación. Las relaciones muy conectadas apuntan a Amazon Neptune; los documentos compatibles con MongoDB, a Amazon DocumentDB; las cargas Cassandra, a Amazon Keyspaces; las consultas por intervalos de tiempo, a Amazon Timestream; las búsquedas por clave, a Amazon DynamoDB; y el análisis a gran escala, a Amazon Redshift. Amazon DynamoDB es una base de datos administrada de clave-valor y documentos que ofrece rendimiento de milisegundos de un solo dígito a cualquier escala.; Amazon DocumentDB es una base de datos de documentos administrada, compatible con MongoDB, para cargas JSON.; Amazon Neptune es una base de datos de grafos administrada para conjuntos de datos muy conectados y admite los modelos Property Graph y RDF.; Amazon Keyspaces es un servicio administrado y serverless compatible con Apache Cassandra que admite el código y las herramientas existentes de Cassandra.; Amazon Timestream es una base de datos de series temporales serverless que procesa datos por intervalos de tiempo; Amazon Redshift es un almacén de datos administrado para análisis a gran escala.

chunks.title: Purpose-built database selection (key-value, document, graph, wide-column, time series, ledger)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing platform stores article metadata and contributor profiles as JSON documents. Its existing application uses MongoDB-compatible code, which the team wants to retain while moving database operations to a managed AWS service. Which database meets these requirements with the LEAST application rework?
Correct: Amazon DocumentDB for the JSON document workload
Why: The application must retain MongoDB-compatible code while using a managed document database. Amazon DocumentDB is the purpose-built choice for that combination. DynamoDB also supports document data, but JSON alone is not the deciding clue: MongoDB compatibility is. Keyspaces offers Cassandra compatibility instead.
Wrong options: Amazon DynamoDB for the JSON document workload (DynamoDB supports document data, but the stated compatibility requirement points to a MongoDB-compatible service.); Amazon Neptune for the contributor and article data (Neptune targets graph queries and does not satisfy the stated MongoDB compatibility requirement.); Amazon Keyspaces for the document workload (Keyspaces is compatible with Apache Cassandra, not the stated MongoDB-compatible application.)

chunks.title: Purpose-built database selection (key-value, document, graph, wide-column, time series, ledger)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics provider runs a fleet-management application backed by Apache Cassandra. Developers want to continue using their Cassandra application code and tools, while the operations team wants to stop provisioning and patching database servers as traffic changes. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Move the workload to Amazon Keyspaces
Why: The existing Cassandra code and tools are the strongest selection criteria. Amazon Keyspaces supports Cassandra workloads without requiring the team to provision or patch servers, and its tables can scale with traffic. Running Cassandra on EC2 preserves the code but fails the operational-overhead requirement. DynamoDB is managed but does not meet the specified compatibility need.
Wrong options: Move the workload to Amazon Timestream (Timestream is designed for time series data, not for retaining Cassandra code and tools.); Run Apache Cassandra on Amazon EC2 instances (Self-hosting Cassandra retains server provisioning and patching responsibilities.); Move the workload to Amazon DynamoDB (DynamoDB is managed but does not provide the stated Cassandra compatibility.)

chunks.title: Purpose-built database selection (key-value, document, graph, wide-column, time series, ledger)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A gaming company is separating two workloads. Its player service must retrieve profile records by player ID with single-digit millisecond performance at scale; a reporting team must analyze large volumes of historical activity in a managed data warehouse. Which TWO databases best match the respective workloads? (Choose two.)
Correct: Amazon DynamoDB for player profile lookups + Amazon Redshift for historical activity reporting
Why: These are two different access patterns, so they need not share a database. DynamoDB matches key-based player lookups requiring single-digit millisecond performance at scale. Redshift matches the reporting team's requirement for a managed data warehouse and large-scale analytics. Timestream would be a stronger candidate if time-interval analysis, rather than warehousing, were the deciding requirement.
Wrong options: Amazon Timestream for historical activity reporting (Timestream targets time series and time-interval queries, while this team explicitly needs a data warehouse.); Amazon Neptune for player profile lookups (Neptune targets highly connected graph queries rather than the stated lookups by player ID.); Amazon DocumentDB for historical activity reporting (DocumentDB is a MongoDB-compatible document database rather than a large-scale analytical data warehouse.)

chunks.title: Amazon Quick (formerly QuickSight) BI dashboards
chunks.text:
Amazon Quick (formerly QuickSight) BI dashboards. Amazon Quick Sight, formerly QuickSight, is the interactive visualization and business intelligence feature within Amazon Quick. Choose it when business users need dashboards over connected data without provisioning dashboard infrastructure.
When to use: Business users need interactive dashboards rather than a data-processing or search tool.; An application needs embedded analytics.; An AWS organization needs to provision access through IAM Identity Center or IAM Federation with per-user subscriptions.
Key facts: Amazon Quick Sight is a feature within Amazon Quick; existing QuickSight APIs, SDKs, and integrations continue to work.; Quick Sight connects to data sources, builds dashboards, and embeds analytics in applications.; Amazon Quick is fully managed and requires no infrastructure to provision.; Organizations can provision Quick through the AWS Management Console using IAM Identity Center or IAM Federation, with per-user subscriptions.
Gotchas: Quick Sight is the BI feature; Quick Flows and Quick Automate address workflows and process automation, not dashboard creation.; Quick Index connects organizational information for grounded AI responses; it is not the dashboard feature.; A per-user subscription describes organizational access and billing; the excerpts do not establish row-level data permissions.
Confused with: Amazon Quick Index: Quick Index grounds AI responses in organizational information; Quick Sight builds interactive BI dashboards.; Amazon Quick Flows: Quick Flows automates repetitive tasks; Quick Sight provides visualization and embedded analytics.
ES: Amazon Quick Sight, antes QuickSight, es la función de visualización interactiva y business intelligence de Amazon Quick. Elígela cuando los usuarios de negocio necesiten dashboards sobre datos conectados sin aprovisionar infraestructura para ellos. Amazon Quick Sight es una función de Amazon Quick; las API, los SDK y las integraciones existentes de QuickSight siguen funcionando.; Quick Sight se conecta a fuentes de datos, crea dashboards e integra analytics en aplicaciones.; Amazon Quick es fully managed y no requiere aprovisionar infraestructura.; Puedes aprovisionar Quick para una organización desde AWS Management Console mediante IAM Identity Center o IAM Federation, con suscripciones por usuario.

chunks.title: Amazon Quick (formerly QuickSight) BI dashboards
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional retailer has prepared a structured sales dataset for its merchandising team. Managers want interactive visualizations they can revisit in a dashboard, and the IT team does not want to provision dashboard infrastructure. Which Amazon Quick feature meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Amazon Quick Sight
Why: The deciding requirement is an interactive dashboard for business users, not an automation or research outcome. Amazon Quick Sight is the visualization and BI feature of Amazon Quick. Quick is fully managed, so the team does not need to provision dashboard infrastructure. Quick Index is a plausible choice for connected information, but its purpose here would be grounding AI responses rather than building the requested dashboard.
Wrong options: Amazon Quick Research (Quick Research produces cited research reports rather than reusable interactive dashboards.); Amazon Quick Index (Quick Index grounds AI responses in connected information but is not the interactive dashboard feature.); Amazon Quick Flows (Quick Flows automates repetitive tasks rather than providing dashboards for managers.)

chunks.title: Amazon Quick (formerly QuickSight) BI dashboards
chunks.text:
Scenario: A travel company already displays booking summaries in its customer application. Product managers now want to embed interactive analytics sourced from connected company data in that application; automating booking tasks is a separate project. Which Amazon Quick feature should the architects select?
Correct: Amazon Quick Sight
Why: The company already has an application, so the decision turns on embedding analytics rather than building a new app. Amazon Quick Sight explicitly supports embedded analytics and interactive visualization. Quick Automate could address the separate booking-automation project, but it does not meet this project's analytics requirement.
Wrong options: Amazon Quick Automate (Quick Automate builds agent-driven business process automations, which does not satisfy the embedded analytics requirement.); Apps in Amazon Quick (Apps in Amazon Quick builds web applications, while the requirement is to embed analytics in an existing application.); Amazon Quick Flows (Quick Flows automates repetitive tasks rather than embedding interactive analytics in an application.)

chunks.title: RDS automated backups, snapshots and point-in-time recovery
chunks.text:
RDS automated backups, snapshots and point-in-time recovery. Amazon RDS automated backups support point-in-time recovery (PITR) within the configured retention period. Choose manual DB snapshots when a recovery copy must survive deletion of the DB instance, and copy a snapshot to another Region when the recovery copy must be there.
When to use: An RDS DB instance must be restored to a time before an accidental change.; A recovery copy must remain after the source DB instance is deleted.; A DB snapshot is needed in another AWS Region for disaster recovery.
Key facts: RDS can restore a DB instance to a point within its backup retention period, up to 35 days.; PITR creates a new DB instance; it does not modify the source.; The latest restorable time can lag behind the present: RDS uploads transaction logs every five minutes.; Manual DB snapshots are not deleted when the DB instance is deleted.; RDS supports copying automatic and manual DB snapshots to another Region.
Gotchas: A manual snapshot is not a substitute for selecting a precise restore time within the automated-backup retention period.; Deleting a DB instance deletes its automated backups unless you choose to retain them; manual snapshots are unaffected.; Do not assume that a time in the current minute is already restorable—check LatestRestorableTime.
Confused with: AWS Backup: Use it for centralized backup plans across services; native RDS automated backups directly support RDS PITR.; EBS snapshots and Data Lifecycle Manager: They manage EBS snapshots and AMIs, not native RDS point-in-time restores.; DynamoDB PITR: It restores DynamoDB tables, not RDS DB instances.
ES: Los automated backups de Amazon RDS permiten point-in-time recovery (PITR) dentro del período de retención configurado. Elige manual DB snapshots si necesitas conservar una copia después de eliminar la DB instance, y copia un snapshot a otra Region si necesitas una copia de recuperación allí. RDS puede restaurar una DB instance a un momento dentro del período de retención de backups, de hasta 35 días.; PITR crea una DB instance nueva; no modifica la de origen.; El momento más reciente disponible para restauración puede ser anterior al momento actual: RDS carga transaction logs cada cinco minutos.; Los manual DB snapshots no se eliminan cuando eliminas la DB instance.; RDS permite copiar automatic y manual DB snapshots a otra Region.

chunks.title: RDS automated backups, snapshots and point-in-time recovery
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research group will delete an Amazon RDS DB instance when a project ends. Its records must remain recoverable after deletion, but the group does not need to select an exact time for recovery. Which approach meets the requirement?
Correct: Create a manual RDS DB snapshot before deleting the instance.
Why: The group needs a recovery copy that survives deletion, not an exact point-in-time restore. Manual RDS DB snapshots are independent of automated backups and are not deleted with the DB instance. Automated backups are deleted at instance deletion unless the group explicitly chooses to retain them; increasing retention alone does not make that choice.
Wrong options: Rely on automated backups without selecting Retain automated backups when deleting the instance. (RDS deletes those automated backups with the DB instance.); Enable RDS automated backups and increase the retention period before deletion. (Changing retention alone does not preserve automated backups if the instance is deleted without choosing to retain them.); Record the instance's LatestRestorableTime before deleting it. (Recording a restore time does not retain the backup data needed for recovery.)

chunks.title: RDS automated backups, snapshots and point-in-time recovery
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional logistics company runs an Amazon RDS DB instance. It needs to recover from mistaken updates to a selected time within the past two weeks and keep a DB snapshot in another AWS Region for disaster recovery. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Create a manual RDS DB snapshot and copy it to the other Region. + Enable RDS automated backups with a retention period that covers the past two weeks.
Why: Two distinct requirements drive the design: selected-time recovery and a snapshot in another Region. RDS automated backups cover point-in-time restores within retention, while a manual DB snapshot can be copied across Regions. An EBS snapshot schedule is not RDS PITR, and a snapshot left only in the original Region misses the disaster-recovery location requirement.
Wrong options: Rely on an in-Region manual RDS DB snapshot for both selected-time recovery and recovery in the other Region. (An in-Region snapshot neither provides a selected PITR time nor places a copy in the other Region.); Enable DynamoDB PITR for the RDS DB instance's records. (DynamoDB PITR protects DynamoDB tables, not the RDS instance in this scenario.); Schedule EBS snapshots with Data Lifecycle Manager as the mechanism for RDS point-in-time restores. (An EBS snapshot schedule is not the native RDS PITR mechanism required here.)

chunks.title: RDS encryption at rest/in transit and IAM database authentication
chunks.text:
RDS encryption at rest/in transit and IAM database authentication. Amazon RDS encryption at rest uses an AWS KMS key and is selected when the DB instance is created. For an existing unencrypted instance, use an encrypted snapshot copy to create an encrypted replacement; use SSL/TLS for client connections and IAM database authentication when applications should connect without stored database passwords.
When to use: A new RDS database must encrypt storage, logs, backups, snapshots, and read replicas.; An existing unencrypted RDS database must be replaced with an encrypted one.; Applications must avoid storing database passwords and use IAM authentication tokens.
Key facts: RDS encryption at rest uses an AWS KMS key; an encrypted DB instance also has encrypted logs, automated backups, and snapshots.; If no customer managed key is specified for a new encrypted instance, RDS uses its AWS managed key.; The KMS key of an encrypted DB instance cannot be changed in place; an encrypted snapshot copy can use a different key.; IAM database authentication supports MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, subject to engine-version and Region availability.; IAM authentication tokens last 15 minutes; expiration does not affect an established session.
Gotchas: Encrypting traffic to a database does not encrypt its storage at rest.; Selecting a new KMS key does not change the key of an existing encrypted DB instance in place.; An IAM authentication token must be generated for the DB instance endpoint, not a custom Route 53 DNS name.
Confused with: 
ES: El cifrado en reposo de Amazon RDS usa una clave de AWS KMS y se selecciona al crear la instancia de base de datos. Para una instancia existente sin cifrar, usa una copia cifrada de un snapshot para crear un reemplazo cifrado; usa SSL/TLS para las conexiones de clientes e IAM database authentication cuando las aplicaciones deban conectarse sin guardar contraseñas de base de datos. El cifrado en reposo de RDS usa una clave de AWS KMS; una instancia cifrada también tiene cifrados sus registros, backups automatizados y snapshots.; Si no especificas una customer managed key para una instancia cifrada nueva, RDS usa su AWS managed key.; No puedes cambiar la clave de AWS KMS de una instancia cifrada en el mismo lugar; una copia cifrada de un snapshot puede usar otra clave.; IAM database authentication admite MariaDB, MySQL y PostgreSQL, según la disponibilidad de la versión del motor y la Región.; Los tokens de IAM authentication duran 15 minutos; su vencimiento no afecta una sesión ya establecida.

chunks.title: RDS encryption at rest/in transit and IAM database authentication
chunks.text:
Scenario: A clinic is creating a new Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance for an application. Its policy requires encryption at rest for the database and its backups, and the application must authenticate without a stored database password. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Enable RDS encryption when creating the DB instance. + Enable IAM database authentication and have the application connect using authentication tokens.
Why: The clinic has two separate requirements: encryption at rest and passwordless application authentication. Enable RDS encryption at creation to protect the instance and its automated backups, and use IAM database authentication tokens instead of a stored password, subject to engine-version and Region support. SSL/TLS is valuable for connections but cannot replace encryption at rest; IAM authentication alone cannot either.
Wrong options: Enable IAM database authentication instead of RDS encryption at rest. (IAM database authentication addresses passwords but does not encrypt database storage or backups at rest.); Use standard database authentication and rotate the application password. (Standard password authentication still requires the application to use a database password.); Require SSL/TLS for client connections instead of enabling RDS encryption at rest. (SSL/TLS protects data in transit but does not satisfy the at-rest encryption requirement.)

chunks.title: RDS encryption at rest/in transit and IAM database authentication
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company has an existing unencrypted Amazon RDS DB instance. A new policy requires the replacement database and its snapshots to be encrypted at rest, while retaining the existing data. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a manual snapshot, copy it with encryption enabled, and restore a new DB instance from the encrypted copy.
Why: The deciding requirements are to preserve the existing data and encrypt the replacement at rest. Copying a manual snapshot with encryption enabled lets the company restore an encrypted DB instance; snapshots of an encrypted instance are also encrypted. Requiring SSL/TLS is useful for data in transit but does not encrypt the existing storage.
Wrong options: Create a new encrypted DB instance and point clients to it without restoring a snapshot. (The new instance would not retain the data from the existing database.); Require SSL/TLS for client connections to the existing instance and continue using its current snapshots. (SSL/TLS protects connections, not the existing instance or its snapshots at rest.); Enable IAM database authentication on the existing instance and create a new manual snapshot. (IAM database authentication changes how clients authenticate, not whether storage and snapshots are encrypted.)

chunks.title: Amazon RDS fundamentals and engines
chunks.text:
Amazon RDS fundamentals and engines. Amazon RDS is the default managed choice for an existing relational database when its engine must be retained and the team does not need operating-system access. If operating-system access is a requirement, evaluate RDS Custom instead of standard RDS.
When to use: An application must keep its Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, MariaDB, MySQL, or PostgreSQL engine.; The team wants AWS to handle routine database administration, including backups, patching, and recovery.; The database needs relational features without a customer-managed operating system.
Key facts: A DB instance is an isolated database environment that can contain one or more user-created databases, depending on the engine.; RDS manages backups, database software patching, automatic failure detection, and recovery; customers remain responsible for query tuning.; A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment provides a synchronous standby for failover, but that standby does not serve reads.; Read replicas can increase read capacity.; General Purpose SSD storage is a cost-effective fit for development and testing; Provisioned IOPS storage targets workloads needing low I/O latency and consistent throughput.
Gotchas: Do not assume standard RDS gives you operating-system access.; Do not send read traffic to the standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment; a Multi-AZ DB cluster is different.; Managed patching does not mean AWS tunes application SQL queries.; Check engine-version and Region support rather than assuming every RDS feature is available everywhere.
Confused with: Amazon Aurora: Aurora is a separate MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible choice; it is not a drop-in choice when Oracle, SQL Server, or Db2 must be retained.; Amazon DynamoDB: DynamoDB fits key-value or document access patterns, not a requirement to keep an existing relational engine.; Amazon DocumentDB: DocumentDB targets MongoDB-compatible document workloads, not a requirement to retain an RDS relational engine.
ES: Amazon RDS es la opción administrada predeterminada para una base de datos relacional existente cuando debes conservar su motor y no necesitas acceso al sistema operativo. Si necesitas ese acceso, evalúa RDS Custom en lugar de RDS estándar. Una DB instance es un entorno de base de datos aislado que puede contener una o más bases de datos creadas por el usuario, según el motor.; RDS administra respaldos, parches del software de base de datos, detección automática de fallas y recuperación; tú sigues a cargo de optimizar las consultas.; Una implementación Multi-AZ DB instance mantiene una instancia secundaria síncrona para failover, pero esa instancia no atiende lecturas.; Las read replicas pueden aumentar la capacidad de lectura.; General Purpose SSD es una opción cost-effective para desarrollo y pruebas; Provisioned IOPS está orientado a cargas que requieren baja latencia de E/S y rendimiento constante.

chunks.title: Amazon RDS fundamentals and engines
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional shipping company is moving an order database to AWS. Its application must retain the Oracle database engine and existing SQL integrations, but the operations team wants to offload backups, patching, and failure recovery. No operating-system access is required. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use Amazon RDS for Oracle with automated backups.
Why: The deciding constraint is retaining Oracle while transferring routine administration to AWS. Amazon RDS supports Oracle and manages backups, software patching, failure detection, and recovery. Running Oracle on EC2 preserves the engine but leaves more administration with the company; the other choices do not retain Oracle.
Wrong options: Move the order data to Amazon DynamoDB and keep the existing SQL integrations. (DynamoDB does not preserve the required Oracle engine and existing relational integrations.); Move the database to Amazon Aurora and keep the application’s Oracle connections. (Aurora does not satisfy the requirement to retain the Oracle engine.); Run Oracle Database on Amazon EC2 and schedule backups and patches. (EC2 preserves the engine, but the team would still manage database backups and software patching.)

chunks.title: Amazon RDS fundamentals and engines
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research publisher runs a managed PostgreSQL database on Amazon RDS. A new reporting feature has increased CPU utilization, and queries are slowing down even when the number of requests is steady. The publisher wants more compute capacity without changing its database engine or rewriting the reporting application. Which action meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Change the RDS DB instance class to one with more compute capacity.
Why: The publisher specifically needs more compute without changing its engine or application. RDS lets the team change the DB instance class as capacity needs evolve. A read replica could help a read-heavy workload only if reads were directed to it, which this option does not do; a Multi-AZ DB instance standby cannot serve reports.
Wrong options: Create a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and run reports on its standby. (The standby in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment does not serve read traffic.); Move the reporting tables to DynamoDB and preserve the existing PostgreSQL queries.
