(Moving to DynamoDB does not meet the requirement to retain PostgreSQL queries without an application rewrite.); Add an RDS read replica and keep every reporting connection pointed at the primary. (A read replica will not relieve the primary if reporting connections continue to use it.)

chunks.title: Amazon RDS fundamentals and engines
chunks.text:
Scenario: An online ticketing company has an existing Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. It must keep automatic failover if an Availability Zone fails, and a new seat-browsing feature must read current ticket records without overloading the primary DB instance. The company wants to retain MySQL and avoid moving the workload to a different database service. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Add an RDS read replica and direct seat-browsing queries to it. + Keep the Multi-AZ DB instance deployment for standby-based failover.
Why: The company has two separate needs: failover protection and more read capacity. Keeping its Multi-AZ DB instance deployment addresses failover, while a read replica can serve the new read-heavy feature. The existing Multi-AZ standby is not a read endpoint, and replacing MySQL or removing Multi-AZ violates an explicit constraint.
Wrong options: Remove the Multi-AZ deployment after adding capacity for reads. (Removing Multi-AZ would discard the required standby-based failover.); Send seat-browsing queries to the existing Multi-AZ standby DB instance. (The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment does not serve read traffic.); Replace MySQL with DynamoDB and move seat-browsing reads there. (Replacing MySQL violates the requirement to retain the existing database engine.)

chunks.title: RDS Multi-AZ deployments (instance and cluster)
chunks.text:
RDS Multi-AZ deployments (instance and cluster). Amazon RDS has two Multi-AZ deployment types. Choose a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment when one non-readable standby is needed for failover; choose a Multi-AZ DB cluster when the application also needs readable failover targets.
When to use: The database needs failover support, but its standby must not serve read traffic: choose a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment.; The database needs high availability and additional read capacity in the same Region: consider a Multi-AZ DB cluster.
Key facts: A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment has one standby DB instance that supports failover but does not serve reads.; A Multi-AZ DB cluster has one writer and two readable DB instances in three Availability Zones in the same Region.; Multi-AZ DB clusters use semisynchronous replication: a commit requires acknowledgment from at least one reader, not confirmation that every reader has applied the change.; If a cluster writer fails, RDS manages failover to a reader DB instance.; Cluster readers can develop replica lag; CloudWatch ReplicaLag measures the difference between the writer’s latest transaction and a reader’s latest applied transaction.
Gotchas: Do not assume every RDS Multi-AZ standby can serve reports: the standby in a DB instance deployment cannot.; Do not describe Multi-AZ DB cluster replication as fully synchronous across both readers.; Do not assume two readers eliminate replica lag or its potential effect on failover.
Confused with: rds-read-replicas: A read replica addresses read capacity; the one-standby Multi-AZ DB instance deployment specifically provides a non-readable failover standby.; aurora-global-database: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster places its writer and readers across Availability Zones within one Region, not across Regions.; dynamodb-global-tables: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster has one writer and two readers, not multiple writable Regions.
ES: Amazon RDS ofrece dos tipos de despliegue Multi-AZ. Elige Multi-AZ DB instance deployment si necesitas una instancia de reserva que no atienda lecturas; elige Multi-AZ DB cluster si también necesitas instancias legibles que puedan asumir el rol de writer. Multi-AZ DB instance deployment tiene una instancia de reserva que ofrece soporte de failover, pero no atiende lecturas.; Multi-AZ DB cluster tiene un writer y dos instancias legibles en tres Availability Zones de la misma Region.; Multi-AZ DB cluster usa replicación semisíncrona: un commit requiere confirmación de al menos un reader, no que ambos hayan aplicado el cambio.; Si falla el writer de un cluster, RDS administra el failover hacia un reader.; Los readers pueden acumular replica lag; la métrica CloudWatch ReplicaLag compara la última transacción del writer con la última aplicada por un reader.

chunks.title: RDS Multi-AZ deployments (instance and cluster)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional ticketing company runs its transactional database on Amazon RDS. It wants a standby in another Availability Zone for failover, but it has no requirement to run queries on that standby. Which deployment meets these requirements without adding readable standby instances?
Correct: Configure a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment.
Why: The deciding requirement is one standby for failover with no need for standby reads. An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment has exactly that arrangement. A Multi-AZ DB cluster instead includes two readable standby instances, while backups do not supply a standby DB instance.
Wrong options: Keep a Single-AZ DB instance and add a read replica for reporting. (This addresses a reporting need the company does not have rather than selecting the requested non-readable Multi-AZ standby.); Keep a Single-AZ DB instance and rely on its automated backups. (Backups do not provide the requested standby DB instance for failover.); Configure a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment. (Its two standby instances can serve reads, adding readable standbys the company does not need.)

chunks.title: RDS Multi-AZ deployments (instance and cluster)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare scheduling application needs an RDS database with automatic writer failover. Its appointment-search queries must also run on database instances other than the writer, and the deployment must span three Availability Zones in one Region. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Use a Multi-AZ DB cluster and send searches to its reader instances.
Why: The application needs both readable non-writer instances and automatic failover across three Availability Zones. An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readers in three separate Availability Zones; the readers serve traffic and are automatic failover targets. The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment cannot serve the searches.
Wrong options: Use a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and send all searches to its primary. (It does not run the required search queries on instances other than the writer.); Use a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and send searches to its standby. (The standby in this deployment cannot serve search reads.); Use one Single-AZ DB instance and restore a snapshot when it fails. (A snapshot restore does not provide running readers or automatic writer failover.)

chunks.title: RDS Multi-AZ deployments (instance and cluster)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company is choosing an Amazon RDS deployment for a write-heavy application. It requires a writer and two readable failover targets within one Region, and it accepts a commit after at least one reader acknowledges the change rather than waiting for both readers to apply it. Which deployment matches these requirements?
Correct: A Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment with its two reader instances.
Why: The combination of two readable failover targets and acknowledgment from at least one reader identifies a Multi-AZ DB cluster. Its replication is semisynchronous: acknowledgment is needed from at least one reader, but changes need not be fully applied and committed on all replicas before the writer commits. A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment has just one non-readable standby.
Wrong options: A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with a second standby added to it. (A deployment with two standby DB instances is the Multi-AZ DB cluster type, not the DB instance type.); A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with its standby used for reads. (It has only one standby, which does not serve reads.); A Single-AZ DB instance with automated backups and point-in-time restore. (Backups do not provide the two running, readable failover targets.)

chunks.title: Amazon RDS Proxy
chunks.text:
Amazon RDS Proxy. Amazon RDS Proxy pools and reuses database connections so applications with many or unpredictable connections do not overwhelm an RDS database. Choose it when connection scaling, preserving application connections during database failover, or IAM authentication for proxy clients drives the decision.
When to use: Many Lambda functions or application instances open short-lived database connections.; Traffic surges could oversubscribe the database's available connections.; Applications need their connections preserved while the proxy reconnects to a standby DB instance.; Clients must authenticate to the proxy with IAM.
Key facts: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections; it can queue or throttle requests that the pool cannot serve immediately.; The proxy automatically connects to a standby DB instance after a database failure while preserving application connections.; Clients can use IAM authentication with the proxy; the proxy can authenticate to the database with IAM or credentials in AWS Secrets Manager.; An RDS Proxy must be in the same VPC as its database and cannot be publicly accessible.; For an RDS DB instance in a replication configuration, a proxy can be associated with the writer, not a read replica.
Gotchas: A proxy does not create unlimited database capacity: requests beyond configured limits can be rejected.; A SQL statement larger than 16 KB pins its session to a database connection, reducing opportunities to share that connection.; Configuring subnets in three Availability Zones does not make the default proxy endpoint span all three; the default endpoint is provisioned across only two.
Confused with: 
ES: Amazon RDS Proxy agrupa y reutiliza conexiones para que muchas conexiones, o aumentos impredecibles de ellas, no saturen una base de datos RDS. Elígelo cuando la decisión dependa de escalar las conexiones, conservar las conexiones de la aplicación durante un failover de la base de datos o exigir autenticación IAM a los clientes del proxy. RDS Proxy agrupa y comparte conexiones; puede poner en cola o limitar las solicitudes que el grupo no pueda atender de inmediato.; Tras una falla de la base de datos, el proxy se conecta automáticamente a una instancia en espera y conserva las conexiones de la aplicación.; Los clientes pueden usar IAM para autenticarse ante el proxy; este puede autenticarse ante la base de datos con IAM o con credenciales de AWS Secrets Manager.; RDS Proxy debe estar en la misma VPC que la base de datos y no puede tener acceso público.; En una configuración de replicación de RDS, puedes asociar el proxy con la instancia escritora, pero no con una read replica.

chunks.title: Amazon RDS Proxy
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company runs Lambda functions that write orders to an RDS for MySQL DB instance. Ticket releases cause unpredictable bursts of short-lived database connections, and opening new connections consumes database CPU and memory. The company wants to protect the database without changing most application code. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Place Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance and direct the functions to its endpoint.
Why: The deciding requirement is to absorb bursts of short-lived connections without repeatedly imposing connection-establishment costs on the database. RDS Proxy pools and reuses database connections and supports most applications without code changes. Direct connections retain the stated overhead. A proxy also cannot target a read replica or reside in a different VPC from its database.
Wrong options: Keep direct connections to the DB instance and allow each function to open a new connection per invocation. (Opening a new database connection for each invocation preserves the CPU and memory overhead the company needs to reduce.); Deploy Amazon RDS Proxy in a separate VPC from the database and direct the functions to it. (RDS Proxy must be in the same VPC as its database.); Associate Amazon RDS Proxy with a MySQL read replica and send order writes to the proxy. (A proxy cannot be associated with a read replica in an RDS replication configuration.)

chunks.title: Amazon RDS Proxy
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company is configuring an RDS Proxy for a database in a VPC with subnets in three supported Availability Zones. Its network standard requires the endpoint used by applications to be provisioned across all three selected Availability Zones, not just two. The company wants to retain RDS Proxy connection pooling. Which endpoint configuration meets these requirements?
Correct: Create an additional proxy endpoint and specify subnets in all three Availability Zones.
Why: The endpoint itself must be provisioned across all three selected Availability Zones. A proxy's default endpoint uses only two Availability Zones, even if the proxy has subnets configured in more than two. An additional endpoint is provisioned across every Availability Zone specified when it is created. Specify subnets in all three for that additional endpoint.
Wrong options: Create an additional proxy endpoint using subnets in two Availability Zones. (An additional endpoint is provisioned across the Availability Zones specified for its creation, which would omit the third.); Use the proxy's default endpoint and configure the proxy with subnets in all three Availability Zones. (The default proxy endpoint is provisioned across only two selected Availability Zones.); Create a proxy in another VPC and use its default endpoint for the applications. (A proxy must be in the database's VPC, and its default endpoint still spans only two Availability Zones.)

chunks.title: Amazon RDS Proxy
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer's application writes to an RDS DB instance with IAM database authentication enabled and a standby instance for failover. During promotions, application clients create many short-lived connections; security requires those clients to authenticate with IAM. The retailer wants to pool connections and preserve application connections during database failure. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Associate Amazon RDS Proxy with the writer DB instance and use its endpoint for application connections. + Require IAM authentication for clients connecting to the proxy and use Secrets Manager credentials for the proxy's database connection.
Why: The design must address connection pooling, failover, and IAM authentication for clients. Associate RDS Proxy with the writer and connect applications to the proxy so it can reuse database connections and preserve application connections when reconnecting to a standby. Require IAM for clients; the proxy may use Secrets Manager credentials to connect to the database. A read replica cannot be the proxy's associated target in this replication configuration, and password authentication by clients does not satisfy the IAM requirement.
Wrong options: Send application clients directly to the DB instance and open a new connection for each request. (Direct connections do not provide proxy connection pooling or preservation of application connections through proxy failover.); Allow clients to authenticate to the proxy with database passwords stored in Secrets Manager instead of IAM. (Clients of this proxy must authenticate with IAM because the RDS DB instance has IAM authentication enabled.); Associate Amazon RDS Proxy with an RDS read replica and use its endpoint for application writes. (The proxy cannot be associated with a read replica in an RDS replication configuration.)

chunks.title: RDS read replicas (in-Region and cross-Region)
chunks.text:
RDS read replicas (in-Region and cross-Region). Amazon RDS read replicas are read-only DB instances updated asynchronously from a source instance. Choose them to offload read-heavy queries or reporting; a cross-Region replica can support disaster recovery if you promote it, but it is not an automatic-failover solution.
When to use: Reporting queries are slowing down a production RDS DB instance.; An existing RDS workload needs more read capacity without moving its writes.; A disaster recovery plan can include promoting a cross-Region replica to a standalone DB instance.
Key facts: Applications send writes to the primary DB instance and can send reads to a read replica.; Replication to a read replica is asynchronous, so replica data might be stale.; Read replicas can be in the source Region or a different Region.; RDS does not automatically add or remove read replicas as read demand changes.; A read replica can be promoted to a standalone DB instance.
Gotchas: A read replica does not replace a Multi-AZ standby when the requirement is high availability with automatic failover.; A classic Multi-AZ standby cannot serve reporting reads.; Do not assume the replica always has the latest committed data.; Do not assume RDS automatically scales the number of read replicas.
Confused with: rds-multi-az: A Multi-AZ standby is synchronously replicated for high availability but cannot serve reads; a read replica serves reads through asynchronous replication.; aurora-global-database: Aurora Global Database is a different global relational database design; an existing RDS instance can instead use a cross-Region read replica when asynchronous replication and promotion are acceptable.; dynamodb-global-tables: DynamoDB global tables address multi-Region writes for a NoSQL workload, not read offloading for an existing RDS instance.
ES: Las read replicas de Amazon RDS son instancias de solo lectura que reciben actualizaciones de forma asíncrona desde una instancia de origen. Elígelas para descargar consultas intensivas o de reportes; una réplica cross-Region puede apoyar la recuperación ante desastres si la promueves, pero no proporciona failover automático. Las aplicaciones envían las escrituras a la instancia principal y pueden enviar las lecturas a una read replica.; La replicación hacia una read replica es asíncrona, por lo que sus datos pueden estar desactualizados.; Las read replicas pueden estar en la misma Region que el origen o en otra.; RDS no agrega ni elimina automáticamente read replicas cuando cambia la demanda de lectura.; Una read replica se puede promover a una instancia independiente.

chunks.title: RDS read replicas (in-Region and cross-Region)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer runs its order database on an Amazon RDS DB instance. Analysts run long read-only sales reports that compete with checkout queries, and the reports can tolerate slightly stale data. Which solution reduces the load on the primary database with the LEAST change to the application’s database platform?
Correct: Create an RDS read replica and route the reporting queries to it.
Why: The deciding requirements are read-only reports, tolerance for slightly stale data, and minimal change to the RDS platform. An RDS read replica accepts reporting reads while asynchronous replication keeps it updated from the primary. A classic Multi-AZ standby cannot serve those queries, and resizing the primary does not separate reporting from checkout traffic.
Wrong options: Increase the primary RDS instance size and keep all reporting queries on the primary. (This leaves the reports competing with checkout queries on the same instance rather than offloading them.); Move the order data to DynamoDB global tables and run the reports from another Region. (Changing database platforms does not meet the requirement for minimal change to the existing RDS workload.); Enable an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and route the reporting queries to its standby. (The Multi-AZ standby for a DB instance deployment cannot serve reporting reads.)

chunks.title: RDS read replicas (in-Region and cross-Region)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company keeps its shipment database on an RDS DB instance in one AWS Region. Its disaster recovery runbook permits an operator to activate a database in another Region after an outage, and the business accepts that asynchronous replication might leave some recent changes unavailable there. Which solution meets these requirements while retaining the existing RDS database?
Correct: Create a cross-Region RDS read replica and promote it to a standalone DB instance during recovery.
Why: The recovery database must be in another Region, and operator-driven activation with possible replication lag is acceptable. An RDS cross-Region read replica fits those constraints and can be promoted to a standalone instance. Multi-AZ does not place its standby in another Region, while a same-Region read replica misses the location requirement.
Wrong options: Enable an RDS Multi-AZ standby and promote that standby in the recovery Region. (A Multi-AZ standby is for a deployment within a Region, not a cross-Region replica to promote.); Replace the shipment database with DynamoDB global tables in both Regions. (Replacing the existing RDS database violates the requirement to retain it.); Create an RDS read replica in another Availability Zone of the source Region and promote it during recovery. (A replica in the source Region does not provide the required database in another Region.)

chunks.title: RDS read replicas (in-Region and cross-Region)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher uses an RDS DB instance for a subscription application. The team wants to add read capacity for an archive search feature, but search results must reflect every newly committed subscription change immediately. Which assessment of an RDS read replica is MOST accurate for this requirement?
Correct: It can offload searches, but searches that require the latest committed changes should use the primary.
Why: The deciding constraint is immediate visibility of every newly committed change. Read replicas can offload search reads, but asynchronous replication means their data might lag the primary. Neither same-AZ placement nor writing to the read-only replica removes that limitation.
Wrong options: It guarantees current search results because replica updates are synchronous. (RDS read replicas receive updates asynchronously and cannot guarantee immediate visibility.); It can provide current results by sending subscription writes to the replica first. (A read replica accepts read-only connections, not application writes.); It guarantees current search results if the replica is in the same Availability Zone. (Placing the replica in the same Availability Zone does not change asynchronous replication into a freshness guarantee.)

chunks.title: RDS storage types and Provisioned IOPS
chunks.text:
RDS storage types and Provisioned IOPS. For RDS OLTP workloads that need consistently low latency and sustained IOPS, choose Provisioned IOPS SSD io2 Block Express and an instance class that can use the provisioned performance. Choose gp3 when its engine-specific performance range meets the requirement and cost matters more than the lowest latency.
When to use: Choose io2 Block Express for latency-sensitive production transactions that require predictable, sustained I/O.; Consider gp3 when the workload can tolerate General Purpose SSD latency and its available IOPS and throughput meet the target.; Check the DB instance class’s IOPS limit before increasing provisioned storage IOPS.
Key facts: On AWS Nitro System-based RDS instances, io2 Block Express provides sub-millisecond average latency; RDS recommends it for I/O-intensive, latency-sensitive workloads.; For RDS MySQL and PostgreSQL, gp3 provides a 3,000-IOPS baseline below 400 GiB. At 400 GiB or more, its baseline is 12,000 IOPS and additional IOPS can be provisioned up to 64,000.; gp3 lets you customize storage performance independently of capacity, but additional IOPS are not available below the engine’s storage-size threshold, except for RDS SQL Server.; Provisioned storage IOPS do not override the DB instance class’s maximum IOPS rate.; RDS recommends combining Provisioned IOPS storage with Multi-AZ for production OLTP fault tolerance; a MySQL, MariaDB, or PostgreSQL read replica can use a different storage type from its primary.
Gotchas: Do not assume that gp3 on a small MySQL or PostgreSQL volume can provision IOPS above its 3,000-IOPS baseline.; Paying for more io2 IOPS does not remove a lower instance-class IOPS ceiling.; io1 is also Provisioned IOPS storage, but it does not offer the same documented latency characteristics as io2 Block Express.
Confused with: gp3 General Purpose SSD: gp3 can provide configurable performance within engine-specific ranges; prefer io2 Block Express when the requirement is sustained IOPS with sub-millisecond latency.; io1 Provisioned IOPS SSD: io1 is the previous generation; io2 Block Express is recommended where available for latency-sensitive workloads.
ES: Para cargas OLTP de RDS que necesitan latencia baja y constante e IOPS sostenidas, elige Provisioned IOPS SSD io2 Block Express y una clase de instancia capaz de aprovechar ese rendimiento. Elige gp3 cuando su rango de rendimiento para el motor cubra la necesidad y el costo importe más que obtener la menor latencia. En instancias de RDS basadas en AWS Nitro System, io2 Block Express ofrece una latencia promedio inferior a un milisegundo; RDS lo recomienda para cargas intensivas en I/O y sensibles a la latencia.; Para RDS MySQL y PostgreSQL, gp3 ofrece una base de 3,000 IOPS por debajo de 400 GiB. Desde 400 GiB, la base es de 12,000 IOPS y puedes provisionar IOPS adicionales hasta 64,000.; gp3 permite ajustar el rendimiento de almacenamiento independientemente de la capacidad, pero no ofrece IOPS adicionales por debajo del umbral de tamaño del motor, excepto en RDS SQL Server.; Las IOPS provisionadas del almacenamiento no superan el máximo de IOPS de la clase de instancia de base de datos.; RDS recomienda combinar Provisioned IOPS con Multi-AZ para la tolerancia a fallos de OLTP en producción; una read replica de MySQL, MariaDB o PostgreSQL puede usar un tipo de almacenamiento distinto al de su instancia primaria.

chunks.title: RDS storage types and Provisioned IOPS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare scheduling service runs production OLTP on RDS for PostgreSQL. Its primary needs predictable, low-latency writes and fault tolerance, while a read replica serves noncritical reports whose storage latency can be higher; the team wants to reduce replica storage cost. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements together? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use io2 Block Express on the primary with a suitable instance class and a Multi-AZ deployment. + Use gp3 on the read replica if its performance meets the reporting workload.
Why: The primary and replica have different performance requirements, so they need not use the same storage type. io2 Block Express with a suitable instance class serves the primary’s low-latency writes, and Multi-AZ adds fault tolerance. A gp3 read replica can reduce costs because the reporting workload tolerates different performance. Matching the primary’s io2 storage on the replica overlooks that cost requirement.
Wrong options: Use gp3 on the primary because its IOPS can be configured independently of capacity. (Configurable gp3 IOPS do not make it the recommended choice for the primary’s predictable, low-latency OLTP writes.); Use io1 on the primary with a Multi-AZ deployment to prioritize the lowest storage latency. (Multi-AZ helps fault tolerance, but io2 Block Express is the recommended Provisioned IOPS choice for latency-sensitive workloads.); Use io2 Block Express on the read replica to match the primary’s storage type. (A PostgreSQL read replica can use a different storage type, so matching io2 needlessly misses the stated replica cost objective.)

chunks.title: RDS storage types and Provisioned IOPS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics platform uses a 400 GiB RDS for MySQL database on io2 storage. Monitoring shows the selected DB instance class has a 40,000-IOPS maximum, while a new transaction feed requires 60,000 sustained IOPS; the platform must retain io2 for its latency-sensitive writes. Which change meets the new requirement?
Correct: Provision 64,000 io2 IOPS and select an instance class whose IOPS limit supports the target.
Why: The limiting resource is the DB instance class, not just the io2 volume allocation. Provisioning 64,000 io2 IOPS with a class capable of using the required 60,000 IOPS addresses both limits while retaining io2. Provisioning even more IOPS on the current class leaves the 40,000-IOPS ceiling in place. Multi-AZ addresses fault tolerance rather than this capacity bottleneck.
Wrong options: Add a Multi-AZ standby and keep the current instance class and io2 allocation. (A Multi-AZ deployment improves fault tolerance but does not remove the selected instance class’s IOPS limit.); Provision 128,000 io2 IOPS and keep the current instance class. (The current instance class still limits usable IOPS to 40,000.); Switch to gp3 with 64,000 provisioned IOPS and a higher-limit instance class. (This could address the IOPS target but violates the requirement to retain io2.)

chunks.title: Amazon Redshift data warehouse (RA3, Serverless, Spectrum)
chunks.text:
Amazon Redshift data warehouse (RA3, Serverless, Spectrum). Amazon Redshift is a managed data warehouse for SQL analysis and BI. Choose Redshift Serverless when warehouse demand is intermittent, or Redshift Spectrum when queries must include files in S3 without loading them into warehouse tables.
When to use: A team needs a managed data warehouse for SQL-based reporting and BI.; Warehouse queries are intermittent, and the team wants capacity to scale automatically without idle warehouse charges.; Analysts need to query structured or semi-structured files in S3 without loading them into Redshift tables.
Key facts: Redshift is a fully managed, petabyte-scale data warehouse service.; Redshift Serverless provisions resources automatically, scales warehouse capacity, and does not charge when the warehouse is idle.; Redshift Spectrum queries files in S3 without loading them into Redshift tables; most of the data remains in S3.; Multiple Redshift clusters can query the same S3 dataset concurrently without a separate copy for each cluster.; Provisioned Redshift clusters are available when a team prefers to manage its Redshift resources manually.
Gotchas: An S3 file does not have to be loaded into a Redshift table for Spectrum to query it.; Intermittent warehouse use points to Redshift Serverless, not automatically to a provisioned cluster.; A request for BI dashboards alone does not establish a need for a Redshift data warehouse; identify where the analytical queries will run.
Confused with: Amazon Athena: Athena fits ad-hoc SQL directly on S3; Redshift is the data warehouse choice, with Spectrum when warehouse queries also need S3 files.; AWS Glue: Glue handles ETL and schema discovery; Redshift runs warehouse analysis, while Spectrum reads S3 files without loading them into warehouse tables.; Amazon Quick: Quick provides BI dashboards and visualization; Redshift provides the data warehouse that can serve BI queries.
ES: Amazon Redshift es un data warehouse administrado para análisis con SQL y BI. Elige Redshift Serverless si el uso del data warehouse es intermitente, o Redshift Spectrum si necesitas consultar archivos en S3 sin cargarlos en tablas del data warehouse. Redshift es un servicio de data warehouse completamente administrado y de escala de petabytes.; Redshift Serverless aprovisiona recursos automáticamente, ajusta la capacidad y no genera cargos cuando el data warehouse está inactivo.; Redshift Spectrum consulta archivos en S3 sin cargarlos en tablas de Redshift; la mayor parte de los datos permanece en S3.; Varios clústeres de Redshift pueden consultar simultáneamente el mismo conjunto de datos en S3 sin crear una copia para cada uno.; Puedes usar clústeres de Redshift aprovisionados si prefieres administrar manualmente sus recursos.

chunks.title: Amazon Redshift data warehouse (RA3, Serverless, Spectrum)
chunks.text:
Scenario: An environmental agency already runs SQL reports in Amazon Redshift. It has received a large collection of structured observation files in Amazon S3 and wants to include those files in its Redshift queries without loading them into Redshift tables. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST data movement?
Correct: Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query the observation files in S3.
Why: The agency must query S3 files through its existing Redshift workflow without loading those files into warehouse tables. Redshift Spectrum is designed to query structured and semi-structured S3 files this way, with most data remaining in S3. Glue loading is a tempting approach, but it fails the explicit no-load requirement.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Athena to query only the observation files in S3. (Athena can query S3, but this option does not include the files in the agency's existing Redshift queries.); Use Amazon EMR to process the S3 observations into a separate reporting output. (A separate EMR output does not meet the requirement to query the S3 files from the existing Redshift workflow.); Use AWS Glue ETL to load the S3 observations into Redshift tables before querying. (Loading the observations into Redshift tables violates the requirement to query without loading them.)

chunks.title: Amazon Redshift data warehouse (RA3, Serverless, Spectrum)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A film distributor uses a data warehouse for SQL-based BI analysis, but its analysts work in short bursts around monthly releases. The team wants capacity provisioned and scaled automatically and does not want warehouse charges while the warehouse is idle. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use Amazon Redshift Serverless for the warehouse.
Why: The workload needs a data warehouse, but demand arrives in bursts and the team wants automatic capacity management. Redshift Serverless provisions and scales resources automatically and does not incur charges while the warehouse is idle. A provisioned Redshift cluster remains a warehouse option, but manually managing its resources misses the operational requirement.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Quick as the data warehouse for the BI queries. (Quick provides BI visualization rather than the requested warehouse query capacity.); Create an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster and manage its resources manually. (Manual management conflicts with the request for automatically provisioned capacity and the least operational overhead.); Run ad-hoc queries on S3 files with Amazon Athena instead of using a data warehouse. (This replaces the explicitly required data warehouse with an ad-hoc S3 query workflow.)

chunks.title: Amazon Redshift data warehouse (RA3, Serverless, Spectrum)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research consortium has two Amazon Redshift clusters that serve separate analyst teams. Both teams must query the same large dataset of semi-structured files in Amazon S3, and the consortium does not want to create a separate S3 data copy for each cluster. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Use Redshift Spectrum from both clusters to query the shared S3 dataset.
Why: The decisive constraint is that both Redshift clusters must query one shared S3 dataset without per-cluster copies. Redshift Spectrum supports concurrent queries of the same S3 dataset from multiple clusters. Loading the data separately into each cluster would undermine that requirement.
Wrong options: Create separate Amazon EMR processing outputs for the two analyst teams. (Separate processing outputs do not let both Redshift clusters query the same S3 dataset without copies.); Use AWS Glue ETL to generate separate S3 datasets for the two clusters. (Generating separate datasets introduces the per-cluster copies the consortium wants to avoid.); Load a separate copy of the S3 dataset into tables on each Redshift cluster. (Separate loaded copies conflict with the stated requirement to avoid duplicating the dataset for each cluster.)

chunks.title: Relational vs non-relational data models
chunks.text:
Relational vs non-relational data models. Choose the database model from the application's access patterns. Amazon RDS fits relational workloads that use SQL relationships; Amazon DynamoDB fits key-value or document workloads that need low-latency access at scale.
When to use: Choose Amazon RDS when an application depends on a relational database engine such as PostgreSQL or MySQL.; Choose Amazon DynamoDB when requests primarily retrieve or update items by key and the application needs low-latency access at scale.
Key facts: Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service that supports engines including MySQL and PostgreSQL.; Amazon RDS automates tasks including provisioning, database setup, patching, and backups.; Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed key-value and document database.; DynamoDB delivers single-digit millisecond performance at any scale.
Gotchas: High traffic alone does not decide the database model; check whether the application needs relational queries or key-based access.; A document-oriented workload does not automatically require Amazon DocumentDB; weigh access and query patterns, not just MongoDB compatibility.; Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse, not a substitute for an application's operational relational database.
Confused with: Amazon DocumentDB: DocumentDB is a managed document database with MongoDB compatibility; choose between it and DynamoDB based on access and query patterns, not compatibility alone.; Amazon Redshift: Redshift serves data warehousing; RDS serves operational relational applications.
ES: Elige el modelo de base de datos según los patrones de acceso de la aplicación. Amazon RDS se ajusta a cargas relacionales que usan relaciones SQL; Amazon DynamoDB se ajusta a cargas de clave-valor o documentos que necesitan acceso de baja latencia a escala. Amazon RDS es un servicio administrado de bases de datos relacionales que admite motores como MySQL y PostgreSQL.; Amazon RDS automatiza tareas como el aprovisionamiento, la configuración de la base de datos, la aplicación de parches y las copias de seguridad.; Amazon DynamoDB es una base de datos de clave-valor y documentos completamente administrada.; DynamoDB ofrece rendimiento de milisegundos de un solo dígito a cualquier escala.

chunks.title: Relational vs non-relational data models
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional wholesaler is moving an application that uses PostgreSQL tables for customers, orders, and invoices. Staff run SQL queries that combine those tables, and the application must continue using its PostgreSQL database engine. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST application change?
Correct: Run the application database on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.
Why: The application must retain PostgreSQL and its SQL queries across related tables. Amazon RDS supports PostgreSQL as a managed relational database, so it matches both constraints. DynamoDB may serve large-scale key-based workloads, but choosing it would not retain the required PostgreSQL engine.
Wrong options: Store customer and order documents in Amazon DocumentDB. (DocumentDB supports MongoDB workloads rather than the required PostgreSQL engine.); Load the operational tables into Amazon Redshift. (Redshift is a data warehouse and does not meet the requirement to retain the application's PostgreSQL database engine.); Store each customer's records as keyed items in Amazon DynamoDB. (DynamoDB is a key-value and document database, not the PostgreSQL relational engine the application must retain.)

chunks.title: Relational vs non-relational data models
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company has two separate applications. Its subscription application runs on PostgreSQL and uses SQL queries across subscriber, plan, and invoice tables; its new viewing app retrieves a viewer's saved settings by viewer ID and needs low-latency access as traffic grows. Which database recommendations fit the respective applications with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL for the subscription application. + Use Amazon DynamoDB for the viewing app's settings.
Why: The two applications have different access patterns and need not share a database model. RDS for PostgreSQL preserves the subscription application's relational engine and queries, while DynamoDB fits the viewing app's key-based settings lookups at scale. Using RDS for the settings is possible, but it does not match the stated access pattern as directly as DynamoDB.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Neptune for the viewing app's settings. (Neptune targets highly connected data, not the stated retrieval of settings by viewer ID.); Use Amazon DocumentDB for the subscription application's invoices. (DocumentDB serves MongoDB-compatible document workloads rather than the subscription application's PostgreSQL queries across tables.); Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL for the viewing app's settings. (RDS offers a relational model, but the viewing app's stated pattern is low-latency access to individual settings by key.)

chunks.title: Reserved Instances (standard vs convertible, zonal vs regional)
chunks.text:
Reserved Instances (standard vs convertible, zonal vs regional). An EC2 Reserved Instance (RI) is a billing discount for matching On-Demand usage, not a separate instance. For steady usage, choose Standard when the configuration is stable, Convertible when you need to exchange attributes, and zonal scope when capacity in a specific Availability Zone is required.
When to use: EC2 usage is expected to remain steady for a one-year or three-year commitment.; The workload has a predictable instance configuration, making a Standard RI suitable.; Instance attributes may change during the term, making a Convertible RI's exchange option valuable.; The workload requires capacity in a particular Availability Zone, pointing to a zonal RI.
Key facts: An RI discounts matching On-Demand usage; it is not a physical instance.; EC2 RI terms are one year or three years, and the three-year term offers a larger discount.; Standard RIs offer a larger discount but cannot be exchanged; Convertible RIs offer a lower discount and can be exchanged for different instance attributes.; RIs do not renew automatically. After expiration, the instance can keep running at On-Demand rates.; RI charges can continue during the term even when no matching instance is running.
Gotchas: Buying an RI does not launch an EC2 instance.; A Standard RI's ability to be modified does not mean it can be exchanged for different instance attributes.; No Upfront does not mean there is no payment obligation during the RI term.; An expiring RI changes billing, not the running instance's availability.
Confused with: Savings Plans: Savings Plans commit to a consistent USD-per-hour usage amount rather than a specific RI instance configuration.; On-Demand Capacity Reservations: Use a zonal RI when you want an RI term and capacity in a specific Availability Zone; a Capacity Reservation addresses the capacity requirement without an RI term.; Spot Instances: An RI discounts matching On-Demand usage; Spot is for workloads that can tolerate interruption.
ES: Una Reserved Instance (RI) de EC2 es un descuento de facturación para uso On-Demand que coincide con sus atributos; no es una instancia separada. Para uso constante, elige Standard si la configuración será estable, Convertible si necesitarás intercambiar atributos y alcance zonal si necesitas capacidad en una Availability Zone específica. Una RI descuenta el uso On-Demand que coincide con sus atributos; no es una instancia física.; Los plazos de EC2 RI son de uno o tres años; el plazo de tres años ofrece un descuento mayor.; Las Standard RIs ofrecen un descuento mayor, pero no se pueden intercambiar; las Convertible RIs ofrecen uno menor y se pueden intercambiar por RIs con otros atributos.; Las RIs no se renuevan automáticamente. Al vencer, la instancia puede seguir funcionando con tarifas On-Demand.; Los cargos de una RI pueden continuar durante el plazo aunque no haya una instancia compatible en ejecución.

chunks.title: Reserved Instances (standard vs convertible, zonal vs regional)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company runs the same EC2 instance configuration continuously for an established production service. It expects no configuration changes over the next three years and wants the largest discount available between the two EC2 Reserved Instance offering classes. Which purchase meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Purchase a matching three-year Standard Reserved Instance.
Why: The deciding constraints are an unchanged instance configuration and a three-year usage horizon. A three-year Standard RI combines the higher-discount term with the higher-discount offering class. Convertible would make sense if exchange flexibility were needed, but it offers a lower discount than Standard. An RI applies a billing benefit to matching On-Demand usage rather than replacing the running instance.
Wrong options: Purchase a matching three-year Convertible Reserved Instance. (Convertible provides unnecessary exchange flexibility at a lower discount than Standard.); Continue paying On-Demand rates for the matching EC2 instances. (On-Demand billing forgoes the RI savings available for predictable usage.); Purchase a matching one-year Standard Reserved Instance. (A one-year term does not offer the larger discount associated with the three-year term.)

chunks.title: Reserved Instances (standard vs convertible, zonal vs regional)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company is planning one-year EC2 commitments for two continuously used pools. The first pool has a fixed configuration and must have reserved capacity in its assigned Availability Zone; among RI offering classes, the company wants the larger discount for this pool. The second pool may need a different instance family during the term and must retain the ability to exchange its RI. Which purchases meet the respective requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Buy matching Convertible RIs for the second pool. + Buy matching zonal Standard RIs for the first pool.
Why: The two pools have different deciding constraints. The first needs AZ-specific capacity and the larger discount between RI classes, so a zonal Standard RI fits. The second needs to exchange its RI if the instance family changes, so it needs Convertible. A regional RI misses the first pool's capacity requirement, and Standard cannot meet the second pool's exchange requirement.
Wrong options: Buy matching regional Standard RIs for the first pool. (Regional scope does not satisfy the first pool's requirement for reserved capacity in its assigned Availability Zone.); Buy matching Standard RIs for the second pool and exchange them when its instance family changes. (Standard RIs cannot be exchanged for different instance attributes.); Buy matching zonal Convertible RIs for the first pool to obtain the larger RI-class discount. (Convertible offers a lower discount than Standard, and the first pool does not need exchange flexibility.)

chunks.title: Reserved Instances (standard vs convertible, zonal vs regional)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare analytics team runs EC2 servers around the clock and expects to keep them for a three-year term. Its software roadmap may require a different instance family during that term. The team specifically wants to retain an RI-based discount by exchanging its reservation if the instance attributes change. Which option meets these requirements?
Correct: Buy Convertible Reserved Instances and exchange them if the instance attributes change.
Why: The team explicitly requires an exchange when instance attributes change during an existing RI term. Convertible RIs support exchanges to other Convertible RIs with different attributes; Standard RIs do not. Although Standard offers a larger discount, that advantage does not satisfy the required exchange. Purchasing additional Standard RIs would leave the original purchase in place.
Wrong options: Buy matching Standard Reserved Instances after every instance-family change. (Buying another RI does not exchange the existing Standard RI or remove its term obligation.); Buy Standard Reserved Instances and exchange them if the instance family changes. (Standard RIs cannot be exchanged for different instance attributes.); Buy Standard Reserved Instances and rely on their automatic renewal after three years. (Standard RIs cannot be exchanged, and RIs do not renew automatically.)

chunks.title: Resource-based policies (S3, KMS, SQS, Lambda)
chunks.text:
Resource-based policies (S3, KMS, SQS, Lambda). An identity-based policy says what an IAM identity can do; a resource-based policy says who can access a particular resource and what they can do there. For direct cross-account resource access, check both sides: the requester needs an identity-based Allow, and the resource needs a resource-based Allow.
When to use: A principal in another account needs access to an S3 bucket, SQS queue, or KMS key.; You need to specify permitted principals and actions on a supported resource itself.; You need to troubleshoot a resource policy's explicit Deny despite an identity-based Allow.
Key facts: Resource-based policies attach to resources; identity-based policies attach to IAM users, groups, or roles.; S3 bucket policies, SQS queue policies, and KMS key policies are examples of resource-based policies.; For cross-account requests, the requester's account needs an identity-based Allow and the resource's account needs a resource-based Allow.; For requests within one account to which only permissions policies apply, an Allow in either policy type can permit the request, but an explicit Deny overrides an Allow.; Specifying a resource ARN in an identity-based policy is a resource-level permission, not a resource-based policy.
Gotchas: An identity-based Allow in the requesting account does not, by itself, complete direct cross-account access.; A resource-based Allow does not override an explicit Deny in an applicable policy.; A policy attached to a role remains identity-based even when it names one specific bucket or queue.
Confused with: iam-identity-based-policies: Attached to an IAM identity to specify its actions; a resource-based policy attaches to the resource to specify who can access it.; service-control-policies: An SCP is an account or OU permissions guardrail, not a resource-level access grant.; permissions-boundaries: A permissions boundary caps an IAM user or role's permissions; it does not grant access to a resource.
ES: Una identity-based policy indica qué puede hacer una identidad de IAM; una resource-based policy indica quién puede acceder a un recurso y qué puede hacer allí. Para el acceso directo entre cuentas, revisa ambos lados: la identidad solicitante necesita un Allow y la policy del recurso también. Las resource-based policies se adjuntan a recursos; las identity-based policies se adjuntan a usuarios, grupos o roles de IAM.; Las bucket policies de S3 y las policies de colas de SQS y claves de KMS son ejemplos de resource-based policies.; Para solicitudes entre cuentas, se requiere un Allow en la identity-based policy de la cuenta solicitante y otro en la resource-based policy de la cuenta del recurso.; En solicitudes dentro de una cuenta a las que solo se aplican permissions policies, un Allow de cualquiera de los dos tipos puede permitir la solicitud, pero un Deny explícito prevalece.; Indicar el ARN de un recurso en una identity-based policy es un permiso a nivel de recurso, no una resource-based policy.

chunks.title: Resource-based policies (S3, KMS, SQS, Lambda)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company keeps a KMS key in its archive account. An IAM role in a separate analytics account already has an identity-based policy allowing the required action on that key, but access is not yet permitted by the archive account. The company wants to name that role as an allowed principal for only the required key action. Which solution meets the cross-account access requirement?
Correct: Add a KMS key policy allowing that role the required action on the key.
Why: The role already has an identity-based Allow, but it is requesting a resource in another account. Cross-account access also requires a resource-based Allow on the resource in the archive account. A KMS key policy can name the allowed role and action; another role policy or a permissions limit does not fill that gap.
Wrong options: Add another identity-based policy for the key action to the analytics role. (Another role policy repeats the requester-side Allow without providing the archive account's resource-side Allow.); Add the key action to a permissions boundary on the analytics role. (A permissions boundary does not provide the required Allow from the archive account.); Add the key action to an SCP for the archive account. (An SCP does not grant the external role access to the key.)

chunks.title: Resource-based policies (S3, KMS, SQS, Lambda)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research group stores a dataset in an S3 bucket in its data account. A processing role in a separate compute account needs direct read access to the dataset; neither account currently has a policy allowing that cross-account read. The group wants to authorize only that role and the required read action, without changing which account owns the bucket. Which TWO policy changes are required? (Choose two.)
Correct: Attach an identity-based policy allowing the required bucket reads to the processing role. + Add a bucket policy allowing the processing role the required reads.
Why: This is direct cross-account access, and neither required Allow exists yet. The processing role needs an identity-based Allow in the compute account, and the bucket needs a resource-based Allow in the data account. A permissions boundary or SCP cannot replace either grant, while a policy for a different role does not authorize the requester.
Wrong options: Add an SCP allowing reads of the bucket to the compute account. (An SCP does not grant the processing role permission to read the bucket.); Attach a second identity-based policy allowing bucket reads to another role in the data account. (Permissions for a different role do not authorize the specified processing role.); Attach a permissions boundary allowing bucket reads to the processing role. (A permissions boundary caps role permissions but does not supply either required access grant.)

chunks.title: Resource-based policies (S3, KMS, SQS, Lambda)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company stores approved images in an S3 bucket in its production account. A partner's IAM role in another account already has an identity-based policy allowing it to read the images, but its requests still fail. The company wants to grant that role direct access to only the required bucket resources. Which change meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Add an S3 bucket policy allowing the partner role to read the required bucket resources.
Why: The deciding requirement is direct access by a role in another account when that role already has an identity-based Allow. Cross-account requests also need a resource-based Allow in the account that owns the bucket. An S3 bucket policy supplies that missing side; repeating the role's Allow does not.
Wrong options: Add another identity-based policy allowing S3 reads to the partner role. (The role already has an identity-based Allow; another one does not provide the required Allow on the resource side.); Add an SCP to the production account listing the partner role's S3 read actions. (An SCP is a permissions guardrail, not a bucket policy granting the external role access.); Add a permissions boundary to the partner role that includes the required S3 reads. (A permissions boundary limits a role's permissions rather than granting access from the bucket's account.)

chunks.title: Root user protection and MFA
chunks.text:
Root user protection and MFA. Protect the AWS account root user with MFA, avoid root access keys, and use root credentials only for tasks that require them. For everyday administration, use an administrative identity; configure MFA separately for IAM users because root MFA does not protect their sign-ins.
When to use: A team wants to secure an account’s most privileged identity without using it for routine work.; An application or administrator needs programmatic access, and someone proposes root access keys.; IAM users need MFA even though MFA is already configured for the root user.; An organization wants to prevent root sign-in to its member accounts.
Key facts: The root user has complete access to resources in its account; AWS recommends using it only for tasks that require root credentials.; AWS strongly recommends not creating root user access keys. IAM roles provide temporary credentials rather than standard long-term credentials.; Root-user MFA affects only root credentials; each IAM user has a separate MFA configuration.; A root user or IAM user can register up to eight MFA devices, and only one registered device is needed to sign in.; For AWS Organizations member accounts, centrally removing root credentials prevents root sign-in and root password recovery in those accounts.
Gotchas: Enabling root MFA does not enable MFA for IAM users.; Adding MFA to root access keys does not make those long-term keys the recommended approach.; Removing root credentials from an Organizations member account also removes its MFA; this is a distinct strategy from retaining and protecting member-account root credentials.
Confused with: 
ES: Protege al root user de la cuenta de AWS con MFA, evita sus access keys y usa sus credenciales solo para tareas que las requieran. Para la administración diaria, usa una identidad administrativa; configura MFA por separado para los IAM users, porque el MFA del root user no protege sus inicios de sesión. El root user tiene acceso completo a los recursos de su cuenta; AWS recomienda usarlo solo para tareas que requieren sus credenciales.; AWS recomienda enfáticamente no crear access keys para el root user. Los IAM roles proporcionan credenciales temporales en lugar de credenciales estándar de larga duración.; El MFA del root user solo afecta sus credenciales; cada IAM user tiene su propia configuración de MFA.; Un root user o IAM user puede registrar hasta ocho dispositivos MFA, y basta uno de los dispositivos registrados para iniciar sesión.; En member accounts de AWS Organizations, la eliminación centralizada de las credenciales del root user impide que este inicie sesión o recupere su contraseña en esas cuentas.

chunks.title: Root user protection and MFA
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company has a standalone AWS account with a root user and IAM users who access the console. The security team requires phishing-resistant MFA where possible and wants a lost MFA device not to interrupt access to a highly privileged identity. Which two actions best meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Register passkeys or security keys as MFA for the root user and for the IAM users who sign in. + Register multiple MFA devices for the highly privileged identity so another registered device can be used if one is lost.
Why: The scenario calls for both phishing resistance across the identities that sign in and resilience if a device is lost. Passkeys and security keys are the recommended phishing-resistant MFA methods, and root and IAM users need their own MFA configurations. Registering multiple devices lets the highly privileged identity use another registered device if one is unavailable. Root access keys and a shared TOTP token do not satisfy those requirements.
Wrong options: Assign one hardware TOTP token to several IAM users so they can share a backup second factor. (A user cannot authenticate with another user’s assigned TOTP device, and TOTP is not the preferred phishing-resistant method.); Give the root user access keys so administrators can regain access if its MFA device is lost. (AWS strongly recommends against root access keys, which do not replace MFA-device resilience.); Configure only the root user with a virtual TOTP authenticator and rely on it to protect IAM user sign-ins. (Root MFA does not protect IAM users, and TOTP is not the recommended phishing-resistant option.)

chunks.title: Root user protection and MFA
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company has a standalone AWS account. Its operations team signs in as the root user for routine resource changes and wants credentials for a deployment script. The company must reduce exposure of its most privileged identity while keeping routine administration and deployments possible. Which approach meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Configure MFA for the root user, reserve root sign-in for tasks requiring it, and use appropriately permitted administrative identities and temporary role credentials for other work.
Why: The deciding constraint is to reduce exposure of the account’s most privileged identity while preserving both workflows. Configure root MFA and reserve root credentials for tasks that require them; use administrative identities for ordinary work and temporary role credentials instead of root access keys for deployments. MFA alone does not make routine root use or root access keys a good choice.
Wrong options: Configure MFA for the root user, then continue using it for routine console work and create root access keys for the deployment script. (Root MFA does not address routine root use or the risk of long-term root access keys.); Create an administrative IAM user for deployments, but leave root sign-in without MFA because it will be used infrequently. (Infrequent root use does not remove the need to protect root sign-in with MFA.); Keep root credentials for console administration and use an IAM role only for the deployment script. (The script avoids root credentials, but routine console administration still unnecessarily uses the root user.)

chunks.title: Route tables and internet gateways
chunks.text:
Route tables and internet gateways. A subnet is public when its associated route table has a route to an internet gateway (IGW). To troubleshoot internet connectivity, check both the route for the traffic’s destination and whether the resource has the required public IPv4 or IPv6 address.
When to use: You need to decide whether a subnet is public or private from its associated route table.; An instance has a public IP address but cannot communicate through an IGW.; A design needs internet routing for IPv4, IPv6, or only a specified destination range.
Key facts: A route has a destination and a target; routing depends on the destination IP address.; An IGW must be attached to the VPC and used as a route target.; A route to an IGW makes its associated subnet public; without that route, the subnet is private.; An IGW route can use 0.0.0.0/0 for IPv4, ::/0 for IPv6, or a narrower destination range.; IPv4 communication through an IGW requires a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP address on the instance.; IPv6 communication requires IPv6 CIDR blocks for the VPC and subnet and an IPv6 address on the instance.
Gotchas: An attached IGW alone does not make every subnet public; inspect the subnet’s associated route table.; A public IPv4 address alone cannot overcome a missing route to the IGW.; An IPv4 route to an IGW does not provide an IPv6 route.
Confused with: 
ES: Una subred es pública cuando su tabla de rutas asociada tiene una ruta hacia un internet gateway (IGW). Para diagnosticar la conectividad a internet, revisa tanto la ruta hacia el destino como si el recurso tiene la dirección pública IPv4 o IPv6 necesaria. Una ruta tiene un destino y un objetivo; el tráfico se enruta según la dirección IP de destino.; El IGW debe estar conectado a la VPC y configurado como objetivo de una ruta.; Una ruta hacia un IGW hace pública a la subred asociada; sin esa ruta, la subred es privada.; Una ruta hacia un IGW puede usar 0.0.0.0/0 para IPv4, ::/0 para IPv6 o un rango de destinos más limitado.; Para comunicarse por IPv4 mediante un IGW, la instancia necesita una dirección IPv4 pública o una Elastic IP.; Para comunicarse por IPv6, la VPC y la subred necesitan bloques CIDR IPv6, y la instancia necesita una dirección IPv6.

chunks.title: Route tables and internet gateways
chunks.text:
Scenario: A community theater is preparing a new EC2 instance in a nondefault VPC to accept connections from visitors over the public IPv4 internet. The VPC already has an attached internet gateway, but the intended subnet’s associated route table has no route to it. The instance currently has only a private IPv4 address, and network permissions will allow the visitor traffic. Which two changes are required for internet connectivity through the gateway? (Choose two.)
Correct: Add a 0.0.0.0/0 route targeting the internet gateway to the subnet’s associated route table. + Assign a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP address to the instance.
Why: Two pieces are missing: an IGW route in the subnet’s associated route table and a public IPv4 address on the instance. Adding 0.0.0.0/0 to the IGW supplies the route; assigning a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP supplies the required instance address. IPv6 changes do not resolve an IPv4 connectivity requirement.
Wrong options: Assign an IPv6 address to the instance while leaving its IPv4 address private. (An IPv6 address does not satisfy the requirement for a public IPv4 address.); Add a ::/0 route targeting the internet gateway to the subnet’s associated route table. (An IPv6 default route does not route the requested public IPv4 traffic.); Add a 0.0.0.0/0 route targeting a NAT gateway to the subnet’s associated route table. (A NAT gateway route does not provide the required route to the IGW.)

chunks.title: Route tables and internet gateways
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum hosts a ticket-status page on an EC2 instance with a public IPv4 address. Its VPC has an attached internet gateway, but the instance’s subnet is associated with a route table whose default IPv4 route targets a NAT gateway. Network permissions already allow the requested traffic. Which change enables visitors on the internet to reach the instance?
Correct: Associate the subnet with a route table that sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway.
Why: The deciding detail is the default route in the subnet’s associated route table. For the subnet to be public, that table needs a route to the IGW, and the instance already meets the public IPv4 address requirement. Assigning an Elastic IP would not fix the route to the NAT gateway.
Wrong options: Change the default IPv4 route to target a VPC peering connection. (A peering connection does not provide the required route to the internet through the IGW.); Keep the subnet route table and add a second internet gateway to the VPC. (The VPC already has an IGW; the subnet’s associated route table still does not target it.); Keep the NAT gateway route and assign an Elastic IP address to the instance. (Replacing one form of public IPv4 address with another does not supply the missing IGW route.)

chunks.title: Route tables and internet gateways
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab has assigned an IPv6 CIDR block to its VPC and subnet and an IPv6 address to an EC2 instance. The VPC has an attached internet gateway. The subnet’s associated route table contains 0.0.0.0/0 to that gateway but no IPv6 route; network permissions allow the traffic. Which change enables the instance to communicate with IPv6 destinations on the internet?
Correct: Add ::/0 with the internet gateway as its target to the associated route table.
Why: Routes are selected using the destination IP address. The existing 0.0.0.0/0 route applies to IPv4, so it does not route traffic to IPv6 internet destinations. Because the VPC, subnet, and instance already have IPv6 addressing, adding ::/0 to the IGW supplies the missing route.
Wrong options: Add another 0.0.0.0/0 route with the internet gateway as its target. (An additional IPv4 route would not match the IPv6 destinations in this scenario.); Replace 0.0.0.0/0 with an IPv4 route to a NAT gateway. (Changing the IPv4 route does not provide a route for IPv6 destination addresses.); Assign an Elastic IP address to the instance. (An Elastic IP addresses IPv4 connectivity, while the missing route is for IPv6 destinations.)

chunks.title: Route 53 failover routing (active-passive)
chunks.text:
Route 53 failover routing (active-passive). Route 53 failover routing supports an active-passive design: send traffic to the primary resource while it is healthy and to a secondary resource when it is unhealthy. Choose it when the deciding condition is primary health, not a planned traffic split or a user's location.
When to use: A standby site should receive traffic only when the primary fails a health check.; A secondary S3 website should display a fallback page during a primary outage.; An active-passive application needs failover records in a private hosted zone.
Key facts: Failover routing directs traffic to one resource when it is healthy and a different resource when it is unhealthy.; Primary and secondary records can point to resources ranging from an S3 bucket configured as a website to a complex tree of records.; Failover routing can be used for records in a private hosted zone.
Gotchas: Weighted routing expresses a traffic split; it is not the choice when the secondary must receive traffic only after primary failure.; Latency-based routing selects by network latency, not by an active-passive health condition.; Geolocation routing selects by user location, not by whether the primary is healthy.
Confused with: route53-weighted-routing: Weighted routing is for a percentage split; failover routing is for a healthy primary and an unhealthy-primary fallback.; route53-latency-routing: Latency-based routing favors the lowest-latency Region; failover routing follows primary health.; route53-geolocation-geoproximity: Geolocation follows user location, while geoproximity uses distance and bias; neither expresses primary-then-secondary failover.
ES: Route 53 failover routing permite un diseño activo-pasivo: dirige el tráfico al recurso principal mientras está en buen estado y al secundario cuando deja de estarlo. Elígelo cuando la condición decisiva sea la salud del principal, no una distribución planificada del tráfico ni la ubicación del usuario. Failover routing dirige el tráfico a un recurso cuando está en buen estado y a otro cuando no lo está.; Los registros principales y secundarios pueden apuntar a recursos que van desde un bucket de S3 configurado como sitio web hasta un árbol complejo de registros.; Puedes usar failover routing para registros de una private hosted zone.

chunks.title: Route 53 failover routing (active-passive)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company serves its booking site from a primary application. It has prepared an S3 bucket configured as a website to display outage instructions, but customers must not see those instructions while the application is healthy. Which Route 53 routing policy meets these requirements?
Correct: Failover routing with the application as primary and the S3 website as secondary
Why: The deciding constraint is that the S3 website must remain a fallback while the application is healthy. Failover routing sends traffic to the primary resource when healthy and to a different resource when it is unhealthy. Weighted routing would implement a planned split rather than this health-dependent switch, and the location- and latency-based policies use different selection criteria.
Wrong options: Latency-based routing between the application and the S3 website (Choosing by latency does not enforce the requirement to use the S3 website only after primary failure.); Weighted routing that gives the application most traffic and the S3 website a small share (A nonzero share would expose some customers to outage instructions while the application is healthy.); Geolocation routing between the application and the S3 website (Choosing by customer location does not make application health the condition for showing the fallback page.)

chunks.title: Route 53 failover routing (active-passive)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A city museum publishes a visitor portal and has a separate S3 website with temporary-closure information. During normal operation, everyone should reach the portal, including visitors near the S3 website's location. Only an unhealthy portal should cause visitors to reach the closure page. Which DNS design meets these requirements?
Correct: Use Route 53 failover records for the portal and the S3 website
Why: The closure page is an outage destination, not local content for nearby visitors. Failover routing permits a primary portal and an S3 website secondary, with the switch determined by primary health. Geoproximity and geolocation answer location-based questions instead, while a weighted share would expose the closure page during normal operation.
Wrong options: Use geolocation routing to assign nearby visitors to the S3 website (It would show closure information to visitors based on location even while the portal is healthy.); Use weighted routing to assign a small visitor share to the S3 website (It would show closure information to some visitors during normal operation.); Use geoproximity routing and bias traffic toward the portal's location (Distance and bias do not make portal health the deciding condition.)

chunks.title: Route 53 failover routing (active-passive)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer uses a Route 53 private hosted zone for an internal inventory service. A secondary service is ready, but employees should use it only when the primary service fails its health check. Which routing policy meets the requirement without making the secondary an active destination during normal operations?
Correct: Failover routing with primary and secondary records in the private hosted zone
Why: This is an active-passive requirement within a private hosted zone. Route 53 supports failover routing there, using a secondary resource when the primary is unhealthy. A weighted allocation would deliberately send some normal traffic to the secondary; geoproximity and latency-based routing select destinations for reasons other than the primary's health.
Wrong options: Latency-based routing with records for both service locations (Routing by lowest latency could select the secondary while the primary is healthy.); Weighted routing with a small allocation to the secondary service (The allocation would make the secondary an active destination during normal operations.); Geoproximity routing with bias toward the primary service location (Distance and bias do not express the required health-dependent switch.)

chunks.title: Route 53 geolocation vs geoproximity routing
chunks.text:
Route 53 geolocation vs geoproximity routing. Route 53 geolocation routing selects resources according to the location of the DNS query, such as a country or continent. Choose geoproximity routing when the decision depends on the locations of users and resources, and you need bias to expand or shrink a resource’s geographic catchment.
When to use: Use geolocation when content or distribution rights differ by country or continent.; Use geolocation when an individual country needs a different endpoint from the rest of its continent.; Use geoproximity when users should generally reach the closest resource, but one resource should receive traffic from a larger or smaller surrounding area.
Key facts: Geolocation records can specify a continent, country, or US state; the smallest geographic region takes priority when records overlap.; A geolocation default record handles queries from unmapped IP addresses and locations without a matching record; without it, Route 53 returns no answer for those queries.; Geoproximity routes based on user and resource locations and sends traffic to the closest available resource.; A positive geoproximity bias expands a resource’s geographic catchment; a negative bias shrinks it.; Geoproximity rules identify AWS resources by Region or Local Zone Group and non-AWS resources by latitude and longitude.
Gotchas: Geolocation relies on IP-to-location mapping; even records covering every continent cannot identify every query.; Geoproximity bias adjusts geographic catchments, not a fixed percentage of traffic.; A nearby resource is not necessarily the right choice when the requirement is a specific country’s content or distribution rights.
Confused with: route53-latency-routing: Select latency-based routing for the lowest-latency Region, not a specified country’s content or a bias-adjusted geographic catchment.; route53-weighted-routing: Weighted routing specifies a traffic split; geoproximity bias changes which geographic areas route to a resource.; route53-failover-routing: Failover is for switching from a primary to a secondary endpoint after a health-check failure, not routine location-based selection.
ES: Route 53 geolocation routing selecciona recursos según la ubicación de la consulta DNS, como un país o continente. Elige geoproximity routing cuando importen tanto la ubicación del usuario como la del recurso y necesites usar bias para ampliar o reducir el área geográfica atendida. Los registros de geolocation pueden especificar un continente, país o estado de EE. UU.; si se superponen, tiene prioridad la región geográfica más pequeña.; Un registro default de geolocation atiende consultas de direcciones IP no identificadas y ubicaciones sin registro coincidente; sin él, Route 53 no devuelve una respuesta para esas consultas.; Geoproximity enruta según la ubicación de los usuarios y los recursos, hacia el recurso disponible más cercano.; Un bias positivo amplía el área geográfica atendida por un recurso; uno negativo la reduce.; Las reglas de geoproximity identifican recursos de AWS por Region o Local Zone Group, y recursos externos a AWS por latitud y longitud.

chunks.title: Route 53 geolocation vs geoproximity routing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company serves a tracking application from resources in two AWS Regions. It wants users to generally reach the closest resource, but its operations team has spare capacity at one site and wants to expand the geographic area routed there without defining a fixed traffic percentage. Which Route 53 configuration meets these requirements MOST appropriately?
Correct: Use geoproximity routing and apply a positive bias to the site with spare capacity.
Why: The company needs location-based selection with an adjustable geographic boundary. Geoproximity routes toward the closest available resource, and positive bias expands the area from which a particular resource receives traffic. Weighted routing can change a traffic split, but it does not specify the requested change to a geographic catchment.
Wrong options: Use geolocation routing and assign whole continents to the site with spare capacity. (Continental assignments do not provide the requested distance-based catchment adjustment.); Use weighted routing and increase the weight of the site with spare capacity.
