(Weights adjust the traffic split rather than expanding the site's geographic catchment.); Use latency-based routing and rely on the lowest-latency Region for each user. (Lowest-latency selection does not provide a bias to expand one site's geographic catchment.)

chunks.title: Route 53 geolocation vs geoproximity routing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A marketplace is configuring two separate DNS names. Its storefront must select country-specific catalogs and return a general catalog for queries with unmapped locations. Its delivery-status application should normally use the closest facility, but the team wants its non-AWS Johannesburg facility to serve a larger surrounding area. Which TWO Route 53 configurations meet these respective requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use country geolocation records and a default record for the storefront. + Use geoproximity records with Johannesburg's coordinates and a positive bias for that facility.
Why: The two DNS names have different location requirements. Geolocation country records with a default address the storefront’s country selection and unmapped queries. Geoproximity supports a non-AWS resource specified by latitude and longitude, with positive bias to expand the area routed to it. Weighted routing changes a traffic split, not the geographic boundary requested for the delivery-status application.
Wrong options: Use latency-based records to select the lowest-latency endpoint for the storefront. (Lowest latency does not select the catalog assigned to each country.); Use failover records to make Johannesburg the delivery-status secondary endpoint. (Failover does not provide routine closest-resource routing with an expanded catchment.); Use weighted records to increase Johannesburg's traffic percentage for delivery status. (A weighted split does not expand the geographic area served by Johannesburg.)

chunks.title: Route 53 health checks
chunks.text:
Route 53 health checks. Route 53 health checks can monitor a specified resource, the status of other health checks, or the status of a CloudWatch alarm. When multiple resources serve the same function, use a health check with DNS failover to route traffic from an unhealthy resource to a healthy one.
When to use: A reachable web server must be monitored so DNS traffic can move to a healthy alternative if it fails.; The health decision must follow an existing CloudWatch alarm rather than a direct resource check.; The health decision must depend on the status of other Route 53 health checks.
Key facts: A Route 53 health check can monitor a specified resource, such as a web server.; A health check can monitor the status of other health checks or a CloudWatch alarm.; With multiple resources performing the same function, DNS failover can route traffic from an unhealthy resource to a healthy one.; A CloudWatch alarm can notify you when a health check changes status; notification and DNS failover are separate configurations.
Gotchas: Monitoring health does not, by itself, configure DNS failover.; An alarm that notifies you of a health-check change is not a substitute for configuring DNS failover.; Choose a check of other health checks only when their statuses are the intended health signal.
Confused with: 
ES: Route 53 health checks pueden supervisar un recurso específico, el estado de otros health checks o el estado de una alarma de CloudWatch. Si varios recursos cumplen la misma función, usa un health check con DNS failover para dirigir el tráfico del recurso no saludable a uno saludable. Un Route 53 health check puede supervisar un recurso específico, como un servidor web.; Un health check puede supervisar el estado de otros health checks o de una alarma de CloudWatch.; Si varios recursos cumplen la misma función, DNS failover puede dirigir el tráfico de un recurso no saludable a uno saludable.; Una alarma de CloudWatch puede notificarte cuando cambia el estado de un health check; la notificación y DNS failover se configuran por separado.

chunks.title: Route 53 health checks
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company has two web servers that perform the same function. If either server becomes unhealthy, the company wants DNS to direct traffic to the healthy server rather than wait for an operator to respond to an alert. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create Route 53 health checks for the servers and configure DNS failover to route traffic to a healthy server.
Why: The deciding requirement is DNS routing to a healthy server without waiting for an operator. Route 53 health checks can monitor the servers, and DNS failover can route traffic away from an unhealthy resource when another resource performs the same function. CloudWatch notifications can report a status change, but notifications alone do not configure DNS failover.
Wrong options: Create Route 53 health checks for the servers and configure CloudWatch alarms to notify operators of status changes. (Notifications inform operators but do not configure the requested DNS failover.); Create a Route 53 health check that monitors the status of other health checks, but do not configure DNS failover. (Checking health without DNS failover does not provide the requested traffic routing.); Create a CloudWatch alarm for each server and use the alarms solely to notify operators when a server is unhealthy. (Operator notifications do not meet the requirement for DNS to route traffic automatically.)

chunks.title: Route 53 health checks
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company already has Route 53 health checks for several resources in a regional application. For a new routing decision, it wants the health signal to come from the status of those existing checks, not from directly checking another server or consulting a CloudWatch alarm. Which Route 53 health check type should the company use?
Correct: A health check that monitors the status of other health checks.
Why: The key constraint is that the health signal must come from existing Route 53 health checks. Route 53 supports a health check that monitors the status of other health checks. A direct resource check or CloudWatch alarm check uses a different signal, while a notification does not create the requested health check.
Wrong options: A health check that monitors the new routing target as a specified resource. (This monitors a resource directly rather than the statuses of the existing health checks.); A CloudWatch alarm that notifies operators when one existing health check changes status. (An operator notification is not a health check whose signal comes from other checks.); A health check that monitors the status of a CloudWatch alarm. (The company explicitly requires existing health checks, not an alarm, as the signal.)

chunks.title: Route 53 hosted zones, record types and alias records
chunks.text:
Route 53 hosted zones, record types and alias records. A Route 53 hosted zone contains DNS records for a domain and its subdomains. Use a public hosted zone for internet traffic and a private hosted zone for DNS within a VPC; use an alias record when a zone-apex name must point to a supported AWS resource.
When to use: An internet-facing domain apex must route to a CloudFront distribution, load balancer, or S3 static website.; Names for an application need to resolve within a VPC.; A supported AWS resource may change IP addresses, and DNS should follow it without manual record updates.
Key facts: A CNAME cannot be created at a hosted zone’s apex; an alias record generally can.; Route 53 detects changes to a supported AWS resource targeted by an alias record and updates its DNS responses.; Route 53 does not charge for alias queries to AWS resources; it charges for CNAME queries.; An alias targeting an AWS resource uses that resource’s default TTL; you cannot set the alias TTL.; A CNAME can point to a DNS record outside Route 53, while an alias is limited to supported targets.
Gotchas: An alias at the zone apex cannot target a CNAME record in the same hosted zone.; For an alias to an S3 website bucket, the bucket must be configured as a static website and its name must match the alias record name.; Private hosted zones route DNS traffic within a VPC; they are not the choice for an internet-facing name.
Confused with: 
ES: Una hosted zone de Route 53 contiene registros DNS de un dominio y sus subdominios. Usa una public hosted zone para tráfico de internet y una private hosted zone para DNS dentro de una VPC; usa un alias record cuando el zone apex deba apuntar a un recurso de AWS compatible. No puedes crear un CNAME en el zone apex de una hosted zone; por lo general, sí puedes crear un alias record.; Route 53 detecta cambios en un recurso de AWS compatible al que apunta un alias record y actualiza sus respuestas DNS.; Route 53 no cobra las consultas de alias a recursos de AWS; sí cobra las consultas de CNAME.; Si un alias apunta a un recurso de AWS, usa el TTL predeterminado del recurso y no puedes establecerlo tú.; Un CNAME puede apuntar a un registro DNS fuera de Route 53; un alias solo admite destinos compatibles.

chunks.title: Route 53 hosted zones, record types and alias records
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company uses Route 53 for the public domain tickets.example. Its vendor has supplied an external DNS name, entry.vendor.example.net, as the destination for the subdomain checkin.tickets.example; the vendor has not supplied a fixed IP address. Which record should the company create to meet the requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a CNAME record for checkin.tickets.example pointing to entry.vendor.example.net.
Why: The destination is an external DNS name, and the requested source is a subdomain rather than the zone apex. A CNAME can point to a DNS record outside Route 53 without requiring the company to maintain an IP address. An alias is not a general-purpose pointer to arbitrary external DNS names, and a CNAME for tickets.example would be at the unsupported apex.
Wrong options: Create a CNAME record for tickets.example pointing to entry.vendor.example.net. (A CNAME at the zone apex is unsupported and would not configure the requested checkin subdomain.); Create an A record for checkin.tickets.example containing the vendor destination’s IP address. (The vendor supplied a DNS name rather than the fixed IP address this configuration requires.); Create an A alias record for checkin.tickets.example pointing to entry.vendor.example.net. (A Route 53 alias cannot target an arbitrary external DNS name.)

chunks.title: Route 53 hosted zones, record types and alias records
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer is assigning names under machines.factory.example to services used by applications in an Amazon VPC. The team wants those names to direct DNS traffic within the VPC rather than serve as public internet records. Which Route 53 configuration meets this requirement?
Correct: Create a private hosted zone for factory.example and add records for the machine services.
Why: The requirement is DNS routing within an Amazon VPC, so a private hosted zone is the appropriate container for the records. A public hosted zone instead contains records specifying how to route traffic on the internet. Choosing alias or CNAME records in a public zone does not address the requirement for a private zone.
Wrong options: Create a public hosted zone and add CNAME records for the machine services. (Changing the record type to CNAME does not change a public hosted zone into a VPC-focused private zone.); Create a public hosted zone and add alias records targeting each service name. (Alias records in a public hosted zone do not make the zone a private DNS container for the VPC.); Create a public hosted zone for factory.example and add records for the machine services. (Public hosted zones contain records for routing traffic on the internet, not specifically within a VPC.)

chunks.title: Route 53 latency-based routing
chunks.text:
Route 53 latency-based routing. Route 53 latency-based routing answers a DNS query with a record for the AWS Region that offers the user the lowest latency among the Regions you configured. Choose it for a multi-Region active-active application when network latency—not a fixed geographic rule or traffic percentage—should determine the destination.
When to use: The application serves users from resources in multiple AWS Regions.; The requirement is to direct users toward the Region with the lowest network latency.; Both regional deployments can serve traffic, rather than keeping one only for failover.
Key facts: Create latency records for resources in each participating AWS Region.; Route 53 evaluates the Regions with latency records and responds with a value from a record for the lowest-latency Region.; Routing can change as network conditions and Route 53 latency data change.; Latency routing is supported for records in a private hosted zone.; AWS latency data reflects traffic between users and AWS data centers; it might not represent actual latency to resources outside an AWS Region.
Gotchas: Do not substitute the user's country for measured regional latency: the lowest-latency Region need not match a geographic assumption.; Do not choose weighted routing when the requirement is lowest latency rather than a percentage split.; Latency routing selects among configured Regions; it does not mean every query always receives the same regional answer.
Confused with: Route 53 failover routing: Failover is for a primary and secondary destination; latency routing selects a low-latency Region for an active-active application.; Route 53 geolocation routing: Geolocation applies location-based rules, such as country or continent; latency routing uses regional latency data.; Route 53 weighted routing: Weighted routing controls a traffic split; latency routing favors the lowest-latency configured Region.
ES: Route 53 latency-based routing responde una consulta DNS con un registro de la AWS Region que ofrece la menor latencia al usuario entre las Regions configuradas. Elígelo para una aplicación active-active en varias Regions cuando la latencia de red, y no una regla geográfica fija o un porcentaje de tráfico, deba determinar el destino. Creas registros de latencia para los recursos de cada AWS Region participante.; Route 53 evalúa las Regions con registros de latencia y responde con el valor de un registro de la Region con menor latencia.; El enrutamiento puede cambiar cuando cambian las condiciones de red y los datos de latencia de Route 53.; Latency routing admite registros en una private hosted zone.; Los datos de latencia de AWS reflejan el tráfico entre usuarios y centros de datos de AWS; quizá no representen la latencia real hacia recursos fuera de una AWS Region.

chunks.title: Route 53 latency-based routing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization hosts an internal analysis service on resources in three AWS Regions. Its applications resolve the service name through a Route 53 private hosted zone, and every regional deployment is active. Researchers want resolution to favor the Region with the lowest network latency rather than the Region nearest their office on a map. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Use latency records in the private hosted zone for resources in all three Regions.
Why: The private hosted zone does not rule out latency routing: Route 53 supports latency records there. With records for resources in all three Regions, Route 53 can select the Region offering the lowest latency. Geoproximity is tempting because it concerns location, but distance with bias is not the requested latency-based decision.
Wrong options: Use geolocation records in the private hosted zone, mapping each office's country to a Region. (A country-based mapping follows location rules rather than regional latency data.); Use geoproximity records in the private hosted zone, with bias toward the largest deployment. (Distance and bias do not directly meet the requirement to select the Region with the lowest network latency.); Use weighted records in the private hosted zone, with weights based on regional capacity. (Capacity-based traffic proportions do not select the lowest-latency Region for each user.)

chunks.title: Route 53 latency-based routing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company serves an interactive editing application from two AWS Regions, with both sites accepting user sessions. Its team has noticed that the Region geographically closer to a customer is not always the faster network destination. It does not need a fixed allocation of sessions between Regions. Which Route 53 policy should the company choose to improve user performance?
Correct: Latency-based routing, with a latency record for the application in each AWS Region.
Why: Both sites are active, and the company wants the faster network destination rather than the geographically nearer one. Latency-based routing uses Route 53 latency data to select among the AWS Regions for which latency records exist. Geolocation and geoproximity make location-based decisions, while weighted routing addresses a traffic split that the company does not require.
Wrong options: Geolocation routing, with each customer's country mapped to the geographically closer Region. (The scenario explicitly says geographic closeness does not reliably identify the faster destination.); Geoproximity routing, with bias adjusted to favor the Region with more editing capacity. (A distance-based policy with bias does not select by the user's lowest regional network latency.); Weighted routing, with the session split adjusted when regional demand changes. (Adjusting a traffic split does not select the lowest-latency Region for an individual user.)

chunks.title: Route 53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints for hybrid DNS
chunks.text:
Route 53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints for hybrid DNS. Route 53 VPC Resolver answers VPC DNS queries by default, including queries for associated private hosted zones. For hybrid DNS, choose the endpoint by query direction: outbound plus a forwarding rule for VPC-to-on-premises queries; inbound plus on-premises forwarding for on-premises-to-VPC queries.
When to use: A workload in a VPC must resolve a domain hosted by an on-premises DNS server.; An on-premises client must resolve a name in an AWS private hosted zone.; Both environments need to resolve names hosted in the other environment over VPN or Direct Connect.
Key facts: VPC Resolver is available by default in VPCs and answers queries for records in private hosted zones.; A VPC-to-on-premises query uses a domain-specific Resolver forwarding rule and an outbound endpoint.; An on-premises-to-VPC query uses an inbound endpoint; the on-premises DNS resolver forwards the relevant domain to it.; Resolver rules are applied to VPCs and can be shared across multiple accounts.
Gotchas: An inbound endpoint does not send VPC queries to an on-premises DNS server.; An outbound endpoint alone does not select which domain's queries to forward.; The default VPC Resolver does not, by itself, provide on-premises clients a path to private hosted zone answers.
Confused with: 
ES: Route 53 VPC Resolver responde de forma predeterminada a las consultas DNS de una VPC, incluidas las de zonas alojadas privadas asociadas. Para DNS híbrido, elige el endpoint según la dirección: outbound con una regla de reenvío para consultas de la VPC hacia on-premises; inbound con reenvío desde on-premises para consultas hacia la VPC. VPC Resolver está disponible de forma predeterminada en las VPC y responde consultas de registros en zonas alojadas privadas.; Una consulta de la VPC hacia on-premises usa una regla de reenvío de Resolver para el dominio y un outbound endpoint.; Una consulta de on-premises hacia la VPC usa un inbound endpoint; el DNS on-premises le reenvía las consultas del dominio correspondiente.; Las reglas de Resolver se aplican a las VPC y se pueden compartir entre varias cuentas.

chunks.title: Route 53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints for hybrid DNS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer runs an application on EC2 in a VPC. Its inventory service uses names in plant.example.com, which are hosted on a DNS server in the company's data center. The VPC and data center are connected by AWS Site-to-Site VPN. Which solution lets the application resolve these names with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and associate a plant.example.com forwarding rule with the VPC.
Why: The deciding requirement is that EC2 must resolve a domain whose DNS server remains on-premises. A domain-specific forwarding rule associated with the VPC directs those queries through an outbound Resolver endpoint over the private connection. An inbound endpoint handles queries traveling toward the VPC, while an outbound endpoint without a rule does not select the domain to forward.
Wrong options: Create an inbound Resolver endpoint and forward plant.example.com queries from the data-center DNS server to it. (Inbound endpoints accept queries toward the VPC, but the EC2 application needs to query names hosted in the data center.); Create a Route 53 private hosted zone for plant.example.com and rely on the default VPC Resolver. (A private hosted zone does not forward queries to the existing authoritative DNS server in the data center.); Create an outbound Resolver endpoint without a forwarding rule and continue querying the default VPC Resolver. (The endpoint alone does not tell VPC Resolver to forward plant.example.com queries to the on-premises server.)

chunks.title: Route 53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints for hybrid DNS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company is moving its editing tools into a VPC while keeping a licensing service in its data center. EC2 instances must resolve license.corp.example, hosted by data-center DNS, and data-center workstations must resolve edit.aws.example, stored in a private hosted zone associated with the VPC. The environments are connected by AWS Site-to-Site VPN. Which design provides DNS resolution in both directions?
Correct: Use an outbound endpoint with a VPC forwarding rule for corp.example; use an inbound endpoint with data-center DNS forwarding for aws.example.
Why: The scenario has two separate DNS paths: EC2 to data-center DNS for corp.example, and data-center workstations to the VPC for aws.example. The first needs a VPC forwarding rule and outbound endpoint; the second needs data-center DNS forwarding to an inbound endpoint. Merely deploying both endpoint types is insufficient if the forwarding rules send each domain in the wrong direction.
Wrong options: Use an outbound endpoint with VPC forwarding rules for both corp.example and aws.example; keep data-center DNS unchanged. (Outbound forwarding does not provide the data-center workstations a path to the VPC's private hosted zone.); Use both endpoint types, but forward corp.example from data-center DNS to the inbound endpoint and aws.example from the VPC to the outbound endpoint. (This reverses the forwarding directions needed for the two specified workloads.); Use an inbound endpoint with data-center DNS forwarding rules for both corp.example and aws.example; keep VPC DNS unchanged. (Inbound forwarding does not send the EC2 instances' corp.example queries to data-center DNS.)

chunks.title: Route 53 weighted routing
chunks.text:
Route 53 weighted routing. Route 53 weighted routing distributes DNS traffic among resources according to relative record weights. Choose it when a release or migration needs a controlled traffic share rather than routing by location, latency, or primary-site failure.
When to use: Introduce a new version to a small share of traffic.; Gradually shift traffic between old and new resources.; Keep a resource out of normal routing with a zero weight while retaining it in a weighted record group.
Key facts: Weighted records for the resources have the same name and type.; Each record's traffic share is its weight divided by the total weight of the group.; Changing weights changes the traffic balance; a weight of zero stops normal traffic to that record.; If the weighted records have health checks, Route 53 considers nonzero-weight records first. It considers zero-weight records if all nonzero-weight records are unhealthy.
Gotchas: Weights are relative shares, not percentages assigned independently to each record.; A zero-weight record is not necessarily excluded when health checks are configured and every nonzero-weight record is unhealthy.; Weighted routing does not select a destination because it is the lowest-latency Region or the user's country.
Confused with: route53-failover-routing: Failover routing selects a secondary site when the primary fails; weighted routing controls relative traffic shares.; route53-latency-routing: Latency-based routing selects by network latency, not a specified release share.; route53-geolocation-geoproximity: Geolocation uses user location, and geoproximity uses distance and bias; neither is the direct choice for a weight-based split.
ES: Route 53 weighted routing distribuye el tráfico DNS entre recursos según los pesos relativos de sus registros. Elígelo cuando un lanzamiento o una migración requiere controlar la proporción de tráfico, en vez de enrutar por ubicación, latencia o falla del sitio principal. Los registros ponderados de los recursos tienen el mismo nombre y tipo.; La proporción de tráfico de cada registro es su peso dividido entre el peso total del grupo.; Cambiar los pesos modifica la distribución; un peso de cero detiene el tráfico normal hacia ese registro.; Si los registros ponderados tienen health checks, Route 53 considera primero los de peso distinto de cero. Considera los de peso cero si todos los anteriores están unhealthy.

chunks.title: Route 53 weighted routing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research portal has two production endpoints and a recovery endpoint under one domain name. It must share normal DNS traffic between the production endpoints, send no normal traffic to recovery, and avoid answering with recovery if its own health check reports it unhealthy. Which two configurations meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Add a same-name, same-type zero-weight recovery record with its own health check. + Create same-name, same-type weighted records for the production endpoints with positive weights and health checks.
Why: The portal needs a normal weighted split plus a recovery record that stays dark while production is healthy. Positive-weight, health-checked production records provide the split; a zero-weight recovery record with its own health check satisfies the recovery conditions. A positive recovery weight admits normal traffic, while a zero-weight recovery record without a health check does not meet the requirement to avoid answering with unhealthy recovery.
Wrong options: Route production traffic by geolocation and assign recovery to an additional country. (Geolocation assigns traffic by user location rather than sharing normal traffic by weight while keeping recovery dark.); Add a zero-weight recovery record without a health check. (An unchecked zero-weight record can be answered with when all positive-weight records are unhealthy, even if recovery itself is unhealthy.); Give the recovery record a small positive weight so it is ready for an outage. (A positive weight makes recovery eligible for normal traffic.)

chunks.title: Route 53 weighted routing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company is releasing a redesigned checkout service alongside its existing service. It wants to direct a small share of DNS traffic to the redesign, then increase that share without choosing destinations by customer location or network latency. Which Route 53 routing policy meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use weighted records for the two services and adjust their weights during the release.
Why: The deciding requirement is a controllable share for a gradual release. Route 53 weighted routing distributes traffic according to relative record weights, which the company can change as the release progresses. Latency-based and geolocation routing use different selection criteria, while failover routing does not provide the requested gradual split.
Wrong options: Use geolocation records for the two services. (Geolocation routing chooses by user location rather than a controlled share of traffic.); Use failover records with the existing service as primary. (Failover routing is for switching to a secondary destination when the primary fails, not a gradual split.); Use latency-based records for the two services. (Latency-based routing chooses by latency rather than the release share the company wants to control.)

chunks.title: RPO and RTO
chunks.text:
RPO and RTO. RPO limits how much recent data can be lost; RTO limits how long service can remain unavailable after an interruption. In a disaster recovery scenario, choose a design that meets both limits, then compare the cost or operational overhead of the qualifying designs.
When to use: The business specifies a maximum period of lost data after a disaster.; The business specifies a maximum delay before service is restored.; Several recovery plans offer different tested recovery points and restoration times.
Key facts: RPO is the maximum acceptable time since the last data recovery point.; RTO is the maximum acceptable delay from service interruption to restoration.; DR objectives address recovery from events such as large-scale technical failures, attacks, or human error.; RTO is a maximum target for an event; MTTR is a mean measured across multiple availability-impacting events.
Gotchas: A short RTO does not compensate for an RPO that allows too much data loss.; A recent recovery point does not prove that service can be restored within the RTO.; A low average MTTR does not establish that a disaster recovery plan meets its RTO.
Confused with: MTTR: MTTR averages recovery times across events; RTO is the maximum acceptable recovery delay for an event.; Availability objective: Availability measures resiliency over time; DR objectives set recovery targets for a disaster event.
ES: RPO limita cuántos datos recientes se pueden perder; RTO limita cuánto tiempo puede permanecer indisponible el servicio tras una interrupción. En un escenario de disaster recovery, elige un diseño que cumpla ambos límites y luego compara el costo o la carga operativa de los diseños que califican. RPO es el tiempo máximo aceptable desde el último punto de recuperación de datos.; RTO es el retraso máximo aceptable entre la interrupción y la restauración del servicio.; Los objetivos de DR cubren la recuperación ante eventos como fallas técnicas a gran escala, ataques o errores humanos.; RTO es un objetivo máximo para un evento; MTTR es un promedio de varios eventos que afectan la disponibilidad.

chunks.title: RPO and RTO
chunks.text:
Scenario: A hospital's appointment portal must resume within 2 hours of a disaster, with no more than 15 minutes of appointment changes lost. The hospital has measured the following recovery results in regional disaster drills and wants the lowest-cost plan that meets both targets. Which plan should it select?
Correct: Warm standby: 5-minute-old recovery point, 45-minute restoration; cost tier 3.
Why: The hospital must meet both the 15-minute RPO and the 2-hour RTO. The tested warm standby plan meets both and has the lowest cost tier of the qualifying choices. The backup plan restores quickly enough but loses too many changes; the pilot light plan preserves enough data but restores too slowly. Active-active also meets the targets, but the stated cost is higher.
Wrong options: Active-active: 1-minute-old recovery point, 30-minute restoration; cost tier 5. (It meets both targets but costs more than option D.); Pilot light: 10-minute-old recovery point, 3-hour restoration; cost tier 2. (It meets the RPO but exceeds the 2-hour RTO.); Backup and restore: 12-hour-old recovery point, 90-minute restoration; cost tier 1. (It meets the RTO but loses more data than the 15-minute RPO permits.)

chunks.title: RPO and RTO
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company reports an MTTR of 25 minutes across routine service incidents. However, a regional disaster drill took 5 hours to restore sales, and the business now sets a 90-minute RTO and a 1-hour RPO for such a disaster. The team has tested the alternative plans below under the same disaster scenario. Which plan meets both DR objectives?
Correct: Use a plan that recovered from a point 40 minutes old and restored service in 65 minutes.
Why: RTO is a maximum acceptable restoration delay for an event, not an average over routine incidents. The 25-minute MTTR therefore does not establish that the current plan meets the 90-minute disaster RTO. Option C's disaster test meets both the 1-hour RPO and the 90-minute RTO. Options A and C each meet only one of those limits.
Wrong options: Use a plan that restored service in 70 minutes but recovered from a point 2 hours old. (Its restoration time meets the RTO, but its recovery point exceeds the 1-hour RPO.); Use a plan that recovered from a point 45 minutes old but restored service in 2 hours. (Its recovery point meets the RPO, but its restoration time exceeds the 90-minute RTO.); Keep the current plan because routine incidents have a 25-minute MTTR; its disaster drill restored service in 5 hours with a 20-minute-old recovery point. (Average recovery from routine incidents does not overcome the disaster drill's 5-hour restoration time.)

chunks.title: RPO and RTO
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics firm operates a shipment-tracking application in one AWS Region. It already recovers from an Availability Zone interruption within 10 minutes, but the new requirement concerns loss of the entire Region: at most 30 minutes of tracking updates may be lost, and service must return within 90 minutes. The firm tested the following proposals against a regional-loss scenario. Which proposal meets the new requirement?
Correct: Prepare recovery in another Region; its regional-loss test restores service in 80 minutes from a point 25 minutes old.
Why: The requirement is recovery from loss of the entire Region, not merely an Availability Zone interruption. Option A is tested for that event and falls within both the 30-minute RPO and 90-minute RTO. Option B's Zone test does not address the stated disaster because it has no recovery location outside the Region. Options C and D address regional loss but miss the data-loss and restoration limits, respectively.
Wrong options: Expand the existing in-Region failover; its Zone test restores service in 5 minutes with a 1-minute-old recovery point, but it has no recovery location outside the Region. (Strong results for a Zone interruption do not provide recovery when the entire Region is lost.); Prepare recovery in another Region; its regional-loss test restores service in 70 minutes from a point 50 minutes old. (Its recovery point exceeds the permitted 30 minutes of lost updates.); Prepare recovery in another Region; its regional-loss test restores service in 2 hours from a point 10 minutes old. (Its restoration time exceeds the 90-minute RTO.)

chunks.title: S3 Access Points (and Object Lambda)
chunks.text:
S3 Access Points (and Object Lambda). S3 Access Points give applications separate named endpoints for object access to a shared bucket. Choose them when each application needs its own access policy or network controls, especially an endpoint that accepts requests only from a VPC.
When to use: Many teams or applications use objects in the same bucket but need distinct permissions.; An application's S3 object-access endpoint must accept requests only from a VPC.; You want to manage an application's object-access rules separately from those of other applications.
Key facts: An access point is a named network endpoint attached to a data source such as an S3 bucket.; Each access point has its own policy and network controls for requests made through it.; An access point attached to a bucket works in conjunction with the underlying bucket policy.; An access point can be configured to accept requests only from a VPC.; Access points support object operations such as GetObject and PutObject, not bucket deletion or S3 Replication configuration.
Gotchas: An access point policy does not replace the underlying bucket policy.; VPC-only settings control requests through that access point; do not assume they automatically restrict every other route to the bucket.; An access point is not an endpoint for bucket administration.
Confused with: S3 bucket policy: A bucket policy applies to the bucket; access points give applications separate endpoints with distinct policies and network controls.; S3 presigned URL: A presigned URL provides temporary access to an object, rather than a reusable application endpoint with its own policy.; CloudFront signed URLs/cookies: These restrict content delivered through CloudFront, rather than govern application requests through S3 access points.
ES: S3 Access Points ofrece endpoints con nombre separados para que las aplicaciones accedan a objetos de un bucket compartido. Elígelo cuando cada aplicación necesite su propia política o controles de red, en especial un endpoint que solo acepte solicitudes desde una VPC. Un access point es un endpoint de red con nombre asociado a una fuente de datos, como un bucket de S3.; Cada access point tiene su propia política y controles de red para las solicitudes que pasan por él.; La política de un access point asociado a un bucket funciona junto con la política del bucket subyacente.; Puedes configurar un access point para que solo acepte solicitudes desde una VPC.; Los access points admiten operaciones sobre objetos, como GetObject y PutObject, pero no la eliminación de buckets ni la configuración de S3 Replication.

chunks.title: S3 Access Points (and Object Lambda)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company lets several production applications upload and retrieve objects from a shared S3 bucket. The architect proposes separate S3 access points so each application can have its own object-access policy. A reviewer asks whether those policies will replace the bucket policy and whether the endpoints can also be used to configure S3 Replication. Which response is correct?
Correct: The access point policies work with the bucket policy, and replication must be configured without using access points.
Why: The reviewer is testing two boundaries of S3 Access Points. For an access point attached to a bucket, its policy works in conjunction with the underlying bucket policy. Access points support object operations such as GetObject and PutObject, but cannot create S3 Replication configurations. Answers that treat the access point policy as a replacement or the endpoint as a replication-management interface fail those boundaries.
Wrong options: The access point policies replace the bucket policy, but replication must be configured through another S3 interface. (An access point policy works in conjunction with the underlying bucket policy rather than replacing it.); The access point policies work with the bucket policy, and the access points can configure replication for their applications. (Access points cannot be used to create S3 Replication configurations.); The bucket policy alone determines requests through the access points, and the access points can configure replication. (Each access point has its own enforced policy, and access points do not configure S3 Replication.)

chunks.title: S3 Access Points (and Object Lambda)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research company stores datasets for several internal applications in one S3 bucket. Each application needs a distinct policy for reading and writing objects, and one application must use an endpoint that accepts requests only from its VPC. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create an S3 access point for each application, assign distinct access point policies, and configure the required access point to accept requests only from the VPC.
Why: The deciding requirements are separate application policies and an endpoint that accepts requests only from a VPC. S3 Access Points provide distinct policies and network controls for requests through each endpoint. A single bucket policy does not provide a separate endpoint per application, while presigned URLs address temporary object access. The access point policies still work in conjunction with the bucket policy.
Wrong options: Issue a presigned URL for each object request and maintain separate URL-generation rules for each application. (Presigned URLs provide temporary object access but do not provide each application with a named endpoint and distinct network controls.); Use one bucket policy to manage every application's object permissions and network conditions. (A bucket policy can govern access but does not give applications separate endpoints with their own network controls.); Deliver the datasets through CloudFront and assign signed cookies to each application. (CloudFront signed cookies govern access to CloudFront-delivered content rather than provide VPC-only S3 object-access endpoints.)

chunks.title: S3 bucket policies, ACLs and Block Public Access
chunks.text:
S3 bucket policies, ACLs and Block Public Access. Use an S3 bucket policy for rules that apply to a bucket and its objects, such as granting a specified account access or restricting requests to a VPC endpoint. Use S3 Object Ownership with Bucket owner enforced to disable ACLs, and use S3 Block Public Access for safeguards against public exposure that override resource policies and ACLs.
When to use: A bucket owner needs to grant another AWS account access to a bucket.; Access to a bucket must depend on a request condition, such as the VPC endpoint used.; Public access must be blocked centrally across multiple AWS accounts.; The bucket owner wants to manage uploaded objects through policies instead of ACLs.
Key facts: Only the bucket owner can associate a bucket policy with the bucket.; By default, Object Ownership uses Bucket owner enforced: ACLs are disabled, the bucket owner owns all objects, and policies manage access.; S3 applies the most restrictive applicable Block Public Access settings across organization, account, bucket, and access point levels.; At the organization level, Block Public Access enables or disables all four settings together; individual settings cannot be selected.; BlockPublicAcls rejects requests that specify public ACLs; IgnorePublicAcls ignores public ACLs but does not prevent them from being submitted.
Gotchas: A bucket-level Block Public Access setting cannot relax a more restrictive organization or account setting.; Block Public Access does not remove existing public policies or ACLs; removing a protective setting can expose resources again.; RestrictPublicBuckets can block even specifically granted cross-account access when the bucket has a public policy.; A bucket policy cannot prevent deletions or transitions performed by an S3 Lifecycle rule.
Confused with: S3 presigned URLs: A presigned URL provides temporary access to an individual object; a bucket policy sets rules for bucket and object requests.; S3 Access Points: Access Points provide separate access paths and policies for applications sharing a bucket; a bucket policy can enforce a rule on direct bucket requests.; CloudFront signed URLs/cookies: These restrict content delivered through CloudFront, not general S3 bucket API access.
ES: Usa una S3 bucket policy para reglas aplicables a un bucket y sus objetos, como dar acceso a una cuenta específica o restringir solicitudes a un VPC endpoint. Usa S3 Object Ownership con Bucket owner enforced para desactivar las ACL y S3 Block Public Access para impedir la exposición pública incluso si las políticas o ACL permiten acceso. Solo el propietario del bucket puede asociarle una bucket policy.; De forma predeterminada, Object Ownership usa Bucket owner enforced: las ACL están desactivadas, el propietario del bucket posee todos los objetos y el acceso se administra con políticas.; S3 aplica la combinación más restrictiva de Block Public Access entre los niveles de organización, cuenta, bucket y access point que correspondan.; A nivel de organización, Block Public Access activa o desactiva las cuatro configuraciones juntas; no permite elegirlas individualmente.; BlockPublicAcls rechaza solicitudes que especifican ACL públicas; IgnorePublicAcls ignora las ACL públicas, pero no impide que se envíen.

chunks.title: S3 bucket policies, ACLs and Block Public Access
chunks.text:
Scenario: A financial services group has S3 buckets in several AWS accounts. Administrators want a central safeguard that blocks public access to current and future S3 resources in selected member accounts, even if a bucket owner changes a bucket-level setting. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable S3 Block Public Access through an AWS Organizations policy for the selected accounts.
Why: The requirement is centralized enforcement across selected accounts, including future resources. An AWS Organizations Block Public Access policy applies to member accounts and cannot be weakened by disabling protection at an individual bucket. Bucket-by-bucket policies or settings require ongoing coverage and do not satisfy that central enforcement requirement.
Wrong options: Add a non-public bucket policy to each existing bucket and review new buckets monthly. (Per-bucket policies and reviews do not provide the requested centrally enforced protection for future resources.); Enable S3 Block Public Access only on each bucket that currently stores financial data. (Bucket-level settings do not automatically cover future buckets or establish a central safeguard across accounts.); Require each application to access its objects through an S3 Access Point with a non-public policy. (Access point policies do not replace a centrally enforced public-access safeguard across the organization's S3 resources.)

chunks.title: S3 bucket policies, ACLs and Block Public Access
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media archive is auditing legacy clients that upload S3 objects with public ACLs. During the audit, uploads containing those ACLs must continue to succeed, but the ACLs must not grant public access. Which setting meets these requirements?
Correct: Enable IgnorePublicAcls on the bucket.
Why: The deciding constraint is that uploads carrying public ACLs must still succeed without making objects publicly accessible. IgnorePublicAcls causes S3 to ignore those ACLs without preventing them from being submitted. BlockPublicAcls would instead reject the affected PutObject requests, interrupting the legacy clients.
Wrong options: Enable BlockPublicPolicy on the bucket. (BlockPublicPolicy addresses new public bucket policies, not public access granted by object ACLs.); Enable RestrictPublicBuckets on the bucket. (RestrictPublicBuckets addresses access when a bucket or access point has a public policy, not the stated ACL behavior.); Enable BlockPublicAcls on the bucket. (BlockPublicAcls rejects PutObject requests that include a public ACL, so the legacy uploads would fail.)

chunks.title: S3 bucket policies, ACLs and Block Public Access
chunks.text:
Scenario: A software company lets a deployment team update an S3 bucket policy and upload build artifacts. Security wants S3 to reject any newly submitted public bucket policy and to reject uploads that specify public ACLs, without relying on a later audit to find them. Which TWO S3 Block Public Access settings meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: BlockPublicAcls + BlockPublicPolicy
Why: The company needs two preventive checks: one for newly submitted public bucket policies and one for uploads carrying public ACLs. BlockPublicPolicy rejects the first, and BlockPublicAcls rejects the second. IgnorePublicAcls would allow an upload with a public ACL to succeed, so it misses the explicit rejection requirement.
Wrong options: IgnorePublicAcls (IgnorePublicAcls ignores public ACLs but still permits uploads that specify them.); RestrictPublicBuckets (RestrictPublicBuckets limits access associated with a public policy but does not reject a newly submitted public bucket policy.); Bucket owner enforced (Bucket owner enforced disables ACLs but does not reject newly submitted public bucket policies.)

chunks.title: S3 encryption: SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C, client-side
chunks.text:
S3 encryption: SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C, client-side. Every new S3 object is encrypted at rest with SSE-S3 by default. Choose SSE-KMS when a scenario requires KMS key policies and auditable key usage, DSSE-KMS when it requires two independent server-side encryption layers, or SSE-C when the customer must manage the keys while S3 performs encryption.
When to use: Choose SSE-S3 when automatic encryption with no additional encryption charge is sufficient.; Choose SSE-KMS with a customer managed key when you need to control key access, audit KMS usage, or share KMS-encrypted objects across accounts.; Choose DSSE-KMS when compliance explicitly requires two independent layers of server-side encryption.; Choose SSE-C when the customer must manage the encryption keys but wants S3 to encrypt and decrypt the objects.
Key facts: SSE-S3 is the default for new object uploads; SSE-KMS and DSSE-KMS can instead be configured as bucket defaults.; SSE-KMS supports key policies and auditing KMS key usage through CloudTrail, and incurs additional KMS charges.; An SSE-KMS key must be in the same Region as its S3 bucket; cross-account sharing of SSE-KMS objects requires a customer managed key.; DSSE-KMS applies two independent AES-256 encryption layers on the server side.; Changing a bucket's default to SSE-KMS does not change existing objects; S3 Batch Operations can copy them to apply SSE-KMS.; SSE-C is disabled by default for new general purpose buckets and must be deliberately enabled for applications that need it.
Gotchas: Default SSE-S3 encryption does not provide the KMS key-policy controls or KMS usage audit required by some scenarios.; An AWS managed SSE-KMS key is not suitable when SSE-KMS objects must be shared across accounts.; A new bucket default affects new uploads, not the encryption type of objects already stored.; Do not select DSSE-KMS merely because encryption is required; its distinguishing requirement is two independent layers.
Confused with: SSE-S3 vs. SSE-KMS: Both encrypt in S3, but SSE-KMS adds KMS key controls and auditable KMS usage.; SSE-KMS vs. DSSE-KMS: DSSE-KMS provides two independent server-side encryption layers rather than one.; SSE-C vs. SSE-KMS: With SSE-C, the customer manages and provides the keys; with SSE-KMS, AWS KMS manages the keys used by S3.
ES: Cada objeto nuevo de S3 se cifra en reposo con SSE-S3 de forma predeterminada. Elige SSE-KMS si necesitas políticas de claves y auditoría del uso de AWS KMS, DSSE-KMS si necesitas dos capas independientes de cifrado del lado del servidor, o SSE-C si el cliente debe administrar las claves mientras S3 realiza el cifrado. SSE-S3 es la opción predeterminada para objetos nuevos; SSE-KMS y DSSE-KMS también pueden configurarse como opciones predeterminadas del bucket.; SSE-KMS permite usar políticas de claves y auditar el uso de claves de AWS KMS mediante CloudTrail; AWS KMS genera cargos adicionales.; La clave de SSE-KMS debe estar en la misma Region que el bucket; para compartir objetos SSE-KMS entre cuentas se necesita una customer managed key.; DSSE-KMS aplica dos capas independientes de cifrado AES-256 del lado del servidor.; Cambiar el valor predeterminado del bucket a SSE-KMS no modifica los objetos existentes; S3 Batch Operations puede copiarlos para aplicar SSE-KMS.; SSE-C está deshabilitado de forma predeterminada para los buckets nuevos de uso general y debe habilitarse deliberadamente si una aplicación lo necesita.

chunks.title: S3 encryption: SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C, client-side
chunks.text:
Scenario: A medical imaging provider stores new scans in S3 and uses AWS services to analyze them after upload. Its compliance policy explicitly requires two independent layers of encryption applied on the server side, without making the application encrypt files before upload. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Configure DSSE-KMS for the scans in the S3 bucket.
Why: The decisive constraint is that both independent encryption layers must be applied on the server side. DSSE-KMS uses a KMS data encryption key for one layer and a separate S3-managed encryption key for the other. This also preserves the described ability to use AWS services and tools to analyze data in S3. Encrypting in the application adds a layer on the client side, while SSE-KMS alone does not provide two layers.
Wrong options: Have the application encrypt each scan before upload, then store it using SSE-S3. (Application encryption before upload violates the requirement that both layers be applied on the server side.); Use SSE-S3 for the scans and restrict access through an S3 bucket policy. (SSE-S3 encrypts the scans but does not provide the required two independent server-side layers.); Use SSE-KMS with a customer managed KMS key for the scans. (Standard SSE-KMS provides KMS-backed server-side encryption but not DSSE-KMS's two independent layers.)

chunks.title: S3 encryption: SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C, client-side
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research company stores trial files in an S3 bucket. Its security team must control which application roles can use the encryption key and review cryptographic key usage in CloudTrail. A single server-side encryption layer is sufficient. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Configure SSE-KMS with a customer managed key and restrict its key policy to the application roles.
Why: The deciding requirements are control over key use and an audit trail of cryptographic operations. SSE-KMS with a customer managed key supports key policies, and CloudTrail can record KMS operations such as GenerateDataKey and Decrypt. SSE-S3 already encrypts new uploads, but its default encryption does not supply the requested KMS key controls. The scenario explicitly does not require DSSE-KMS's second layer.
Wrong options: Keep the bucket's default SSE-S3 encryption and restrict object access with a bucket policy. (A bucket policy can restrict object access, but SSE-S3 does not provide the required KMS key policy and KMS usage audit.); Use SSE-C and have the application supply its encryption key for each object request. (SSE-C lets the customer manage keys but does not meet the requirement to control and audit use of an AWS KMS key.); Configure DSSE-KMS to add a second server-side encryption layer to the files. (The second layer is not required, so DSSE-KMS adds a feature that does not address the deciding requirement better than SSE-KMS.)

chunks.title: S3 encryption: SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C, client-side
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics firm has an S3 bucket containing years of shipping records encrypted with SSE-S3. New compliance rules require both existing records and future uploads to use SSE-KMS, and the firm wants to process the old records in bulk rather than rewrite its application to upload them again. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Set the bucket default to SSE-KMS and use S3 Batch Operations to copy existing records back to the bucket.
Why: This scenario has separate requirements for future uploads and objects already stored. Setting SSE-KMS as the bucket default addresses new uploads, but it does not retroactively change old objects. S3 Batch Operations can copy existing objects back to the bucket so they are written as SSE-KMS objects. Changing only the default is the key trap because the stored SSE-S3 records remain unchanged.
Wrong options: Enable S3 Bucket Keys on the bucket and retain its SSE-S3 default encryption. (S3 Bucket Keys are for SSE-KMS cost reduction and do not change the encryption type of old or future objects to SSE-KMS by themselves.); Set the bucket default to SSE-KMS and rely on S3 to update the encryption of all stored records. (Changing default encryption does not change the encryption type of existing objects.); Keep SSE-S3 as the bucket default and use S3 Batch Operations to copy only the existing records. (Copying old records does not make future uploads use SSE-KMS while the default remains SSE-S3.)

chunks.title: S3 Event Notifications (Lambda, SQS, SNS, EventBridge)
chunks.text:
S3 Event Notifications (Lambda, SQS, SNS, EventBridge). S3 Event Notifications publish selected bucket events to Lambda, SQS, SNS, or EventBridge. For object-created processing, choose the destination that fits the workflow; use EventBridge when an S3 event must reach an SQS FIFO queue.
When to use: An object upload should trigger processing, such as thumbnail creation.; An application needs notifications for selected S3 events, such as object creation or removal.; An S3 event must reach an SQS FIFO queue.
Key facts: A bucket notification configuration specifies the events to publish and their destinations.; Supported destinations include SNS topics, SQS queues, Lambda functions, and EventBridge.; S3 event notifications are delivered at least once; they typically arrive in seconds but can take a minute or longer.; An SQS FIFO queue is not supported as a direct S3 event notification destination; EventBridge can be used to send the event to one.; A function that writes to its triggering bucket can create an execution loop.
Gotchas: Do not assume one notification means one delivery; processing must tolerate duplicate notifications.; Do not select a direct S3-to-SQS FIFO notification configuration.; Writing generated files to the same bucket can retrigger processing; limit the trigger to an incoming prefix and write output outside it, or use a separate output bucket.
Confused with: 
ES: S3 Event Notifications publica eventos seleccionados de un bucket en Lambda, SQS, SNS o EventBridge. Para procesar objetos creados, elige el destino según el flujo de trabajo; usa EventBridge si un evento de S3 debe llegar a una cola SQS FIFO. La configuración de notificaciones del bucket especifica qué eventos se publican y a qué destinos.; Los destinos admitidos incluyen temas SNS, colas SQS, funciones Lambda y EventBridge.; Las notificaciones de eventos de S3 se entregan al menos una vez; normalmente llegan en segundos, pero pueden tardar un minuto o más.; S3 no admite una cola SQS FIFO como destino directo de notificaciones; puedes usar EventBridge para enviarle el evento.; Una función que escribe en el bucket que la activa puede generar un ciclo de ejecuciones.

chunks.title: S3 Event Notifications (Lambda, SQS, SNS, EventBridge)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A small real estate site uploads listing photos to an S3 bucket. Each new photo needs a thumbnail created by an existing Lambda function, and the team does not need to retain an intermediate notification for another application. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure an S3 object-created notification with the Lambda function as its destination.
Why: The deciding requirement is to invoke an existing function for new photos with the least operational overhead. S3 supports object-created notifications with a Lambda function as the destination. SQS, SNS, and EventBridge are possible notification paths, but each introduces an intermediate component that this scenario does not call for.
Wrong options: Configure an S3 object-created notification to an SNS topic, then send the notifications to the Lambda function. (The topic adds an intermediate destination without meeting an additional stated requirement.); Send S3 events to EventBridge, then route object-created events to the Lambda function. (EventBridge adds an intermediate step when S3 can notify the function directly.); Configure an S3 object-created notification to an SQS queue, then have the Lambda function process queued notifications. (An intermediate queue adds a component when the scenario does not require one.)

chunks.title: S3 Event Notifications (Lambda, SQS, SNS, EventBridge)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company stores incoming manuscripts in S3. Its processing application already reads from an SQS FIFO queue, and the company wants notifications when manuscripts are uploaded without changing that destination. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Enable S3 events in EventBridge and send the object-created events to the SQS FIFO queue.
Why: The existing SQS FIFO queue is the constraint that decides the answer. Although S3 can notify SQS queues directly, SQS FIFO queues are not supported as direct S3 event notification destinations. The S3 documentation identifies EventBridge as the way to send an S3 event notification to an SQS FIFO queue. Switching to SNS or Lambda would not retain the required destination.
Wrong options: Set the SQS FIFO queue as the direct destination of an S3 object-created notification. (S3 does not support an SQS FIFO queue as a direct event notification destination.); Set a Lambda function as the S3 notification destination and have the application receive the Lambda invocation. (A Lambda invocation does not preserve the application's specified SQS FIFO destination.); Set an SNS topic as the S3 notification destination and have the application read notifications from the topic. (This changes the application's required SQS FIFO destination.)

chunks.title: Amazon S3 fundamentals: durability, consistency, object limits
chunks.text:
Amazon S3 fundamentals: durability, consistency, object limits. Amazon S3 is scalable object storage for data such as static content, backups, and data lakes. Choose it when an application needs durable object storage and must read or list objects immediately after a successful write, without managing file servers or a separate consistency layer.
When to use: The application stores objects rather than requiring a mounted file system or block device.; The number of objects or total stored data may grow substantially.; Readers must see a newly written or overwritten object immediately.
Key facts: S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for new objects and overwrites; list operations also reflect completed writes.; The total volume of data and number of S3 objects are unlimited.; An individual object can be up to 50 TB, but a single PUT can upload no more than 5 GB; consider multipart upload for objects larger than 100 MB.; Objects in S3 Standard are stored across multiple devices spanning at least three Availability Zones.
Gotchas: Strong consistency does not mean that every S3 storage class stores data across multiple Availability Zones; S3 One Zone-IA uses one AZ.; Do not confuse the maximum object size with the maximum size of a single PUT.; S3 object access is not a substitute for a required mounted NFS or SMB file share.
Confused with: Amazon EBS: Choose EBS for block storage attached to EC2; choose S3 for scalable object storage.; Amazon EFS: Choose EFS when multiple Linux clients need a shared NFS file system, not merely access to objects.; Amazon FSx for Windows File Server: Choose FSx for Windows when applications require SMB shares, NTFS permissions, or Active Directory integration.
ES: Amazon S3 es almacenamiento de objetos escalable para contenido estático, respaldos y data lakes. Elígelo cuando necesites almacenar objetos de forma duradera y leerlos o listarlos inmediatamente después de una escritura correcta, sin administrar servidores de archivos ni una capa de consistencia adicional. S3 ofrece strong read-after-write consistency para objetos nuevos y sobrescrituras; las operaciones de listado también reflejan las escrituras completadas.; El volumen total de datos y la cantidad de objetos en S3 son ilimitados.; Un objeto puede medir hasta 50 TB, pero un solo PUT admite como máximo 5 GB; considera multipart upload para objetos mayores de 100 MB.; Los objetos en S3 Standard se almacenan en varios dispositivos distribuidos en al menos tres Availability Zones.

chunks.title: Amazon S3 fundamentals: durability, consistency, object limits
chunks.text:
Scenario: A wildlife research group receives an unpredictable number of camera images each day. Researchers retrieve images as objects through a web application, and the group wants the stored images to span multiple Availability Zones without managing storage servers. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Store the images in an S3 Standard general purpose bucket.
Why: The images are accessed as objects, their count is unpredictable, and storage must span multiple Availability Zones. An S3 Standard general purpose bucket meets those requirements without managing storage servers. S3 One Zone-IA is still object storage, but its single-AZ placement fails the explicit resilience requirement.
Wrong options: Store the images on an Amazon EBS volume attached to an EC2 instance. (An EBS volume is block storage attached to EC2, rather than scalable, serverless object storage.); Store the images on EC2 instance store volumes. (Instance store is ephemeral and does not provide the required durable object storage.); Store the images in S3 One Zone-IA. (S3 One Zone-IA stores objects in a single Availability Zone, contrary to the stated requirement.)

chunks.title: Amazon S3 fundamentals: durability, consistency, object limits
chunks.text:
Scenario: A film preservation studio produces finished media packages of 12 TB each. It wants to retain each package as one object in its growing Amazon S3 collection so authorized clients can retrieve it by object key. Which upload approach meets these requirements?
Correct: Use S3 multipart upload to create one object for each package.
Why: Each package must remain one S3 object, and 12 TB is below the documented 50 TB maximum object size. A single PUT cannot upload it because that operation is limited to 5 GB. Multipart upload addresses the upload constraint without changing the client's one-object retrieval model.
Wrong options: Upload each package to S3 with one PUT request. (A single PUT is limited to 5 GB, below the size of a package.); Split each package into separate S3 objects and require clients to reassemble them. (Clients would no longer retrieve each complete package as one object.); Keep each package on an Amazon EBS volume and expose it through an EC2 server. (This replaces the required S3 object collection with server-managed block storage.)

chunks.title: Amazon S3 fundamentals: durability, consistency, object limits
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer uploads inspection images under object keys, sometimes replacing an image after a reviewer corrects it. A reporting job reads a corrected image and lists the bucket immediately after the replacement succeeds. The manufacturer wants the objects stored across multiple Availability Zones and does not want an additional system to track when writes become visible. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Store the images in an S3 Standard general purpose bucket. + Use S3's native strong consistency for reads and listings after completed overwrites.
Why: The storage decision must satisfy both multiple-AZ placement and immediate visibility after a successful overwrite. S3 Standard stores objects across at least three AZs, and S3's native strong consistency supports subsequent reads and listings. S3 One Zone-IA misses the placement requirement, while a separate tracking database adds operational overhead without solving an unmet consistency need.
Wrong options: Store the images on Amazon EFS and mount the file system on the reporting host. (This substitutes mounted file storage for the stated object-key and bucket-listing workflow.); Store the images in S3 One Zone-IA. (Its single-AZ storage fails the multiple-AZ requirement.); Maintain a separate database of successful S3 writes and consult it before each read. (A separate write-tracking system adds overhead that native S3 consistency makes unnecessary.)

chunks.title: S3 Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive and retrieval tiers
chunks.text:
S3 Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive and retrieval tiers. Choose the S3 Glacier storage class by how quickly a rarely accessed archive must be available: Instant Retrieval for immediate GET access, Flexible Retrieval for restores in minutes to hours, and Deep Archive when longer restores are acceptable. For objects already archived, choose the least costly retrieval option that fits the time window.
When to use: Choose S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval when a rarely accessed archive still needs millisecond access.; Choose S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval when the application can restore objects before using them, including occasional urgent restores.; Choose S3 Glacier Deep Archive when archived data rarely needs access and a restore taking up to 12 or 48 hours fits the requirement.
Key facts: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval objects are immediately available with GET; Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects require a restore first.; For S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Expedited typically takes 1–5 minutes for objects under 250 MB; Standard typically takes 3–5 hours; Bulk typically takes 5–12 hours.; For S3 Glacier Deep Archive, Standard typically finishes within 12 hours and Bulk typically finishes within 48 hours. Expedited is unavailable.; Bulk is the lowest-cost retrieval option for S3 Glacier storage classes. Bulk retrievals from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval are free.; Without provisioned capacity, Expedited retrieval requests might not be accepted during periods of high demand.
Gotchas: Do not choose Flexible Retrieval with Expedited when the application needs immediate GET access: Expedited is still a restore.; Do not choose Deep Archive with Expedited; that retrieval option is unavailable.; Do not assume Bulk fits every archive deadline merely because it has the lowest retrieval cost.
Confused with: S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA: These provide millisecond access for infrequently accessed data; the Glacier classes target rarely accessed, long-term archives, with only Instant Retrieval providing immediate access.; S3 Intelligent-Tiering: Choose it for unknown or changing access patterns; its optional asynchronous archive tiers may still require a restore.
ES: Elige la clase S3 Glacier según la rapidez con que debe estar disponible un archivo de acceso poco frecuente: Instant Retrieval para acceso inmediato mediante GET, Flexible Retrieval para restauraciones en minutos u horas y Deep Archive cuando se aceptan esperas más largas. Si los objetos ya están archivados, elige la opción de recuperación de menor costo que cumpla el plazo. Los objetos de S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval están disponibles de inmediato mediante GET; los de Flexible Retrieval y Deep Archive requieren primero una restauración.; En S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Expedited suele tardar de 1 a 5 minutos para objetos menores de 250 MB; Standard, de 3 a 5 horas; y Bulk, de 5 a 12 horas.; En S3 Glacier Deep Archive, Standard suele terminar en un máximo de 12 horas y Bulk en un máximo de 48 horas. Expedited no está disponible.; Bulk es la opción de recuperación de menor costo para las clases S3 Glacier. Las recuperaciones Bulk desde S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval son gratuitas.; Sin Provisioned Capacity, es posible que las solicitudes Expedited no se acepten durante períodos de alta demanda.

chunks.title: S3 Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive and retrieval tiers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum keeps digitized exhibit files for long-term preservation. Curators open a small selection only a few times a year, but the viewing application must serve any selected file immediately with millisecond access and cannot wait for a restore. Which storage class is designed for this archive while meeting the access requirement MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
Why: The deciding constraint is immediate millisecond access to a known, rarely accessed long-term archive. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is designed for that combination and supports immediate GET access. S3 Standard-IA also provides millisecond access, but is positioned for infrequently accessed data rather than rarely accessed archives. Flexible Retrieval and the Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access tier require restoration.
Wrong options: S3 Intelligent-Tiering with Archive Access activated (Objects in its Archive Access tier require a restore, which conflicts with immediate viewing.); S3 Standard-IA (It provides millisecond access, but Glacier Instant Retrieval is designed for long-term data that is rarely accessed and needs that speed.); S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (Its archived objects require a restore before the application can access them.)

chunks.title: S3 Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive and retrieval tiers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute already keeps historical experiment records in S3 Glacier Deep Archive. For a scheduled audit, staff can wait for restorations that typically finish within 12 hours, but not for a 48-hour retrieval. They want the lowest-cost available retrieval option that fits that window without changing the objects' storage class. Which option should they select?
Correct: Use Standard retrieval from S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Why: The records must remain in Deep Archive, and the accepted typical restore window is 12 hours rather than 48. Standard retrieval from Deep Archive typically finishes within 12 hours. Bulk is the lowest-cost retrieval option in general, but its typical Deep Archive completion time is within 48 hours, so it misses this window. Deep Archive does not offer Expedited retrieval.
Wrong options: Move the records to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and use Bulk retrieval. (It changes the objects' storage class, contrary to the stated requirement.); Use Expedited retrieval from S3 Glacier Deep Archive. (Expedited retrieval is not available for Deep Archive.); Use Bulk retrieval from S3 Glacier Deep Archive. (Bulk retrieval from Deep Archive typically finishes within 48 hours, which does not fit the stated window.)

chunks.title: S3 Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive and retrieval tiers
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer is designing storage for two independent collections. Rarely opened calibration images must be available immediately through GET, while historical compliance records can be restored when needed and their reviews can wait for retrievals that typically finish within 48 hours. Which two choices match the collections' access requirements and use an archive class or retrieval option suited to each? (Choose two.)
Correct: Store the compliance records in S3 Glacier Deep Archive and use Bulk retrieval. + Store the images in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
Why: The two collections have different access constraints, so they should not be assigned the same retrieval approach. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval keeps the rarely opened images immediately accessible by GET. S3 Glacier Deep Archive with Bulk retrieval fits records that can wait for its typical 48-hour completion time; Bulk is the lowest-cost Glacier retrieval option. Flexible Retrieval with Expedited and Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access both fail the images' immediate-access requirement.
Wrong options: Store the images in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and use Expedited retrieval. (Expedited is a restore operation and does not provide immediate GET access.); Store the compliance records in S3 Glacier Deep Archive and use Expedited retrieval. (Expedited retrieval is not available for Deep Archive.); Store the images in S3 Intelligent-Tiering with Archive Access activated. (Images moved to Archive Access would require restoration rather than immediate GET access.)

chunks.title: S3 Standard-IA vs One Zone-IA
chunks.text:
S3 Standard-IA vs One Zone-IA. S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA serve long-lived objects that are accessed infrequently but need millisecond access. Choose Standard-IA for a primary or irreplaceable copy that must survive an Availability Zone loss; choose the less expensive One Zone-IA when the data can be re-created after that loss.
When to use: Access is predictably infrequent, but objects must be available in milliseconds.; Choose Standard-IA when the objects are the only copy or cannot be re-created.; Choose One Zone-IA when objects can be re-created and loss of their Availability Zone is acceptable.
Key facts: Standard-IA stores data across multiple Availability Zones; One Zone-IA stores it in one.; Both classes charge retrieval fees and have a 30-day minimum storage duration.; Both are suited to objects larger than 128 KB; smaller objects are billed as 128 KB.; One Zone-IA costs less than Standard-IA but is not resilient to the physical loss of its Availability Zone.
Gotchas: Millisecond access alone does not distinguish Standard-IA from One Zone-IA; recoverability after an Availability Zone loss does.; Deleting, overwriting, or transitioning objects before 30 days does not avoid the minimum-duration charge.; Do not choose an archive class that requires a restore when the application needs immediate access.
Confused with: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: Use it for unknown or changing access patterns; it moves objects between access tiers automatically and has a monitoring fee but no retrieval fees.; S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval: It provides millisecond access for long-lived archive data accessed roughly once a quarter, rather than the roughly monthly access associated with the IA classes.; S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: Archived objects require a restore and are not available for immediate, real-time access.
ES: S3 Standard-IA y S3 One Zone-IA sirven para objetos de larga duración que se consultan poco, pero necesitan acceso en milisegundos. Elige Standard-IA para una copia principal o irreemplazable que deba resistir la pérdida de una Availability Zone; elige One Zone-IA, que cuesta menos, si puedes recrear los datos tras esa pérdida. Standard-IA almacena datos en varias Availability Zones; One Zone-IA los almacena en una sola.; Ambas clases cobran por recuperación y tienen una duración mínima de almacenamiento de 30 días.; Ambas son adecuadas para objetos de más de 128 KB; los objetos menores se facturan como si fueran de 128 KB.; One Zone-IA cuesta menos que Standard-IA, pero no resiste la pérdida física de su Availability Zone.

chunks.title: S3 Standard-IA vs One Zone-IA
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional museum stores digitized originals in Amazon S3. Curators retrieve each collection about once a month, but their catalog must open any image in milliseconds, and the files cannot be re-created if an Availability Zone is lost. Which storage class meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: S3 Standard-IA for the digitized originals
Why: The deciding constraints are roughly monthly reads, millisecond access, and an irreplaceable copy that must survive an Availability Zone loss. Standard-IA is designed for infrequent access and stores objects across multiple Availability Zones. One Zone-IA is less expensive but fails the resilience requirement, while Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires a restore.
