Wrong options: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for the digitized originals (Archived objects require restoration and are not available for immediate catalog access.); S3 Standard for the digitized originals (It supports immediate access, but it is designed for frequently accessed data rather than these predictably infrequent reads.); S3 One Zone-IA for the digitized originals (It provides millisecond access but cannot protect the only copy against loss of its Availability Zone.)

chunks.title: S3 Standard-IA vs One Zone-IA
chunks.text:
Scenario: A delivery platform writes route snapshots to Amazon S3 and overwrites each snapshot after ten days. Dispatchers open snapshots repeatedly throughout each day, and the platform needs millisecond access. Which storage class best fits this workload MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: S3 Standard for the route snapshots
Why: The snapshots are opened frequently and overwritten after ten days. S3 Standard supports millisecond access for frequently accessed objects and has no minimum storage duration. Both IA classes are meant for infrequent reads and impose a 30-day minimum charge, including a prorated remainder when an object is overwritten early.
Wrong options: S3 Standard-IA for the route snapshots (Frequent reads and overwrites before its 30-day minimum make this infrequent-access class a poor fit.); S3 One Zone-IA for the route snapshots (It charges for retrievals and for the remainder of its 30-day minimum when snapshots are overwritten early.); S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for the route snapshots (It is intended for rarely accessed, long-lived archives rather than snapshots opened throughout the day.)

chunks.title: S3 Standard-IA vs One Zone-IA
chunks.text:
Scenario: A biotech company has two S3 datasets retained for many months: original experiment records that cannot be re-created, and derived charts that can be regenerated from those records. Analysts open each dataset roughly once a month and require millisecond access. The company wants to minimize storage cost while preserving the originals through an Availability Zone loss; losing the charts in that event is acceptable. Which storage class assignments meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Store the original experiment records in S3 Standard-IA. + Store the derived charts in S3 One Zone-IA.
Why: Both datasets have predictable, infrequent reads and require millisecond access, so an IA class fits their access pattern. The originals cannot be re-created and must survive an Availability Zone loss, making Standard-IA the appropriate assignment. The charts can be regenerated, so the less expensive One Zone-IA meets their requirements; Glacier Flexible Retrieval would require a restore.
Wrong options: Store the derived charts in S3 Standard-IA. (It adds multi-AZ resilience that the company does not require for charts it can regenerate, rather than minimizing their storage cost.); Store the original experiment records in S3 One Zone-IA. (The only copies of the records would not be resilient to loss of the storage Availability Zone.); Store the derived charts in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval. (A restore would be required before analysts could open archived charts.)

chunks.title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
chunks.text:
S3 Intelligent-Tiering. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically adjusts the access tier of eligible objects as their access patterns change. Choose it when future access is hard to predict and you want cost optimization without managing tier transitions.
When to use: Objects may alternate between frequent and infrequent access.; The application needs low-latency access even when objects become rarely accessed.; Objects can eventually be restored asynchronously, and you want to enable optional archive tiers.
Key facts: Eligible objects move to Infrequent Access after 30 consecutive days without access and to Archive Instant Access after 90 days.; The three automatic tiers provide low-latency access; the storage class remains S3 Intelligent-Tiering as objects move between tiers.; Optional Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers support asynchronous access after a minimum of 90 and 180 days without access, respectively.; Objects smaller than 128 KB are not monitored or automatically tiered; they remain in Frequent Access.; Intelligent-Tiering has a monthly object monitoring and automation charge.
Gotchas: Do not enable optional asynchronous archive tiers when every read must remain immediately available.; Do not expect objects smaller than 128 KB to move automatically to lower-cost tiers.; SelectObjectContent resets the inactivity timer for optional archive tiers, but does not move an object back to Frequent Access.
Confused with: S3 Standard-IA and One Zone-IA: Choose Intelligent-Tiering when you need S3 to monitor changing access and move eligible objects between access tiers automatically.; S3 Glacier storage classes: Intelligent-Tiering's automatic tiers retain low-latency access; its optional asynchronous archive tiers require a restore before retrieval.
ES: S3 Intelligent-Tiering ajusta automáticamente el nivel de acceso de los objetos elegibles cuando cambia su patrón de uso. Elígelo si no puedes predecir el acceso futuro y quieres optimizar costos sin administrar las transiciones entre niveles. Los objetos elegibles pasan a Infrequent Access después de 30 días consecutivos sin acceso y a Archive Instant Access después de 90 días.; Los tres niveles automáticos ofrecen acceso de baja latencia; la clase de almacenamiento sigue siendo S3 Intelligent-Tiering al cambiar de nivel.; Los niveles opcionales Archive Access y Deep Archive Access permiten acceso asíncrono después de un mínimo de 90 y 180 días sin acceso, respectivamente.; Los objetos menores de 128 KB no se monitorean ni cambian automáticamente de nivel; permanecen en Frequent Access.; Intelligent-Tiering tiene un cargo mensual por monitoreo y automatización de objetos.

chunks.title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
chunks.text:
Scenario: A museum stores high-resolution exhibit photos in Amazon S3. Public interest is unpredictable: a photo may go unused for months and then receive many requests after a news story. Every request must receive low-latency access, and the museum does not want to manage transitions as popularity changes. Which storage choice meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Store the photos in S3 Intelligent-Tiering without enabling its optional archive tiers.
Why: Unpredictable demand and low-latency reads are the deciding requirements. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves eligible objects among three low-latency tiers and moves accessed objects in its lower automatic tiers back to Frequent Access. Enabling Deep Archive Access would introduce an asynchronous restore step for archived photos, while reviewing reports and changing classes adds operational work.
Wrong options: Move photos to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval once they have gone unused for 90 days. (That archival choice does not meet the requirement for immediate low-latency access to every photo.); Store the photos in S3 Intelligent-Tiering and enable Deep Archive Access after 180 days without access. (An object in Deep Archive Access needs restoration before it can be retrieved.); Store the photos in S3 Standard-IA and review access reports to change storage classes when popularity rises. (This requires staff to manage the changes in access pattern.)

chunks.title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design platform stores 2 MB project files and 60 KB preview thumbnails in Amazon S3. Access to project files changes unpredictably, so the team wants eligible files to change access tiers automatically. Thumbnails must remain readily available, but the team does not want its cost plan to assume they will automatically tier. Which plan meets these requirements?
Correct: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering for project files and S3 Standard for thumbnails.
Why: Object size determines whether Intelligent-Tiering can perform the expected automatic moves. The 2 MB files exceed the documented 128 KB threshold, while 60 KB thumbnails remain in Frequent Access if placed in Intelligent-Tiering. Using Intelligent-Tiering for the project files and not budgeting for automatic thumbnail tiering satisfies both requirements; enabling an archive tier does not remove the size restriction.
Wrong options: Use S3 Standard-IA for project files and S3 Intelligent-Tiering for thumbnails, forecasting automatic tiering for the thumbnails. (The plan assigns automatic tiering to the objects that are below the eligibility threshold.); Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering with Deep Archive Access enabled for both groups and forecast automatic archival of the thumbnails. (Enabling an optional archive tier does not make 60 KB objects eligible for automatic tiering.); Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering for both groups and forecast automatic lower-tier placement for both. (The 60 KB thumbnails are too small to be monitored or automatically tiered.)

chunks.title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
chunks.text:
Scenario: A travel marketplace stores 3 MB destination images and 80 KB icons in Amazon S3. Campaigns can make old images popular again without warning, and any image request must have low-latency access without a restore step. The team wants automatic storage-tier adjustments for eligible images but will not assume that the icons can tier automatically. Which two choices meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Place the 3 MB images in S3 Intelligent-Tiering to adapt to changing access. + Leave Intelligent-Tiering's optional asynchronous archive tiers disabled for the images.
Why: The large images have unpredictable demand, must remain available with low latency, and qualify for Intelligent-Tiering's automatic tier changes. Choose Intelligent-Tiering for those images and leave optional asynchronous archive tiers disabled so a newly popular image does not need restoration. The 80 KB icons cannot tier automatically, and manually changing an image's class misses the automation requirement.
Wrong options: Place the 80 KB icons in Intelligent-Tiering and budget for their automatic movement to lower tiers. (Objects smaller than 128 KB are not monitored or eligible for automatic tiering.); Place the images in S3 One Zone-IA and change their storage class manually after each campaign. (Manual changes do not satisfy the requirement for automatic adjustments to changing demand.); Enable Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access for images after 90 days of inactivity. (Images in that optional tier require restoration rather than immediate low-latency retrieval.)

chunks.title: S3 Lifecycle transitions and expiration
chunks.text:
S3 Lifecycle transitions and expiration. S3 Lifecycle rules automate storage-class transitions and object expiration for a bucket. Choose them when the decision depends on an object's age and the goal is to reduce storage costs or delete objects after a retention period without running a cleanup process.
When to use: Objects follow a predictable pattern: active first, archived later, then deleted.; Existing and future objects should follow the same age-based expiration rule.; Only objects matching a prefix, tag, or size filter should receive an action.
Key facts: Lifecycle configurations contain transition and expiration actions; rules apply to both existing and new objects.; By default, objects smaller than 128 KB do not transition to any storage class; a custom object-size filter can allow them.; S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive are not available for real-time access.; A single rule cannot schedule a transition out of a storage class before its minimum storage duration has passed.; In a versioning-enabled or versioning-suspended bucket, objects with Pending or Failed replication status cannot transition.
Gotchas: A bucket policy that denies deletion does not stop an S3 Lifecycle rule from deleting objects in a general purpose bucket.; Transitions incur request costs, which can outweigh storage savings for small objects.; A lifecycle action can occur after its eligibility date; a delay does not necessarily mean the rule failed.
Confused with: 
ES: Las reglas de S3 Lifecycle automatizan las transiciones entre clases de almacenamiento y la expiración de objetos de un bucket. Elígelas cuando la decisión dependa de la antigüedad del objeto y se busque reducir costos o eliminar objetos al terminar su período de retención sin operar un proceso de limpieza. Las configuraciones de S3 Lifecycle incluyen acciones de transición y expiración; sus reglas se aplican a objetos existentes y nuevos.; De forma predeterminada, los objetos menores de 128 KB no se transfieren a ninguna otra clase de almacenamiento; un filtro de tamaño personalizado puede permitirlo.; Los objetos en S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval y S3 Glacier Deep Archive no están disponibles para acceso en tiempo real.; Una sola regla no puede programar la salida de una clase antes de que termine su duración mínima de almacenamiento.; En un bucket con versioning habilitado o suspendido, los objetos cuyo estado de replicación sea Pending o Failed no pueden transferirse.

chunks.title: S3 Lifecycle transitions and expiration
chunks.text:
Scenario: A delivery company stores diagnostic files in an S3 bucket. Some files are already older than the required 30-day retention period, and new files arrive daily. The company must delete files once they exceed 30 days of age without maintaining a cleanup application. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Add an S3 Lifecycle expiration action for files 30 days after creation.
Why: The deciding requirements are deletion by object age and coverage of both existing and future files. An S3 Lifecycle expiration rule applies to both groups, including existing objects already past the specified age. Moving files to S3 Standard-IA preserves them rather than deleting them. A scheduled application adds operational work that the managed Lifecycle action avoids.
Wrong options: Run a scheduled application that lists the bucket and deletes files older than 30 days. (The application could delete the files but requires ongoing operation that a Lifecycle rule avoids.); Add an S3 Lifecycle transition that moves files to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days. (A transition changes the storage class but does not delete files after the retention period.); Deny access to files older than 30 days through a bucket policy. (Preventing access does not remove the files after their retention period.)

chunks.title: S3 Lifecycle transitions and expiration
chunks.text:
Scenario: An accounting firm uses one general purpose S3 bucket for temporary files under `scratch/` and records under `records/`. A bucket-wide Lifecycle rule expires objects after 90 days, but the records must remain longer; a bucket policy already denies object deletions. Which change protects the records while continuing to expire temporary files with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Scope the Lifecycle expiration rule to the `scratch/` prefix instead of the entire bucket.
Why: The requirement calls for different expiration behavior for two prefixes. Scoping the Lifecycle rule to `scratch/` retains automatic deletion of temporary files without selecting the longer-lived records. The existing bucket policy does not protect objects from Lifecycle deletion in a general purpose bucket. Replacing expiration with a transition would leave temporary files undeleted.
Wrong options: Keep the bucket-wide Lifecycle rule because the bucket policy will prevent expiration of the records. (A bucket policy cannot prevent deletions performed by an S3 Lifecycle rule.); Change the bucket-wide Lifecycle expiration action to a transition to S3 Standard-IA. (That change preserves the records but also stops the required expiration of temporary files.); Remove delete permissions from the IAM identities that upload objects under `records/`. (Changing uploader permissions does not stop the bucket-wide Lifecycle expiration action.)

chunks.title: S3 Lifecycle transitions and expiration
chunks.text:
Scenario: A video company keeps encrypted, large S3 objects in a versioning-enabled bucket. Some objects have Pending or Failed replication status. The company wants eligible objects to move from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after one year, while retaining encryption and identifying why some objects do not move. Which TWO actions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure an S3 Lifecycle transition from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after one year. + Check replication status when investigating objects that remain in S3 Standard.
Why: An S3 Lifecycle rule supplies the requested automatic, age-based move to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and objects stay encrypted throughout the transition. In a versioning-enabled bucket, objects with Pending or Failed replication status cannot transition, so checking that status is relevant when investigating objects left behind. Decrypting objects adds unnecessary work. A bucket policy cannot make an ineligible object transition.
Wrong options: Add a second Lifecycle transition from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval back to S3 Standard for objects that fail to archive. (Lifecycle cannot transition objects from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval back to S3 Standard.); Use a bucket policy to force transitions of objects with Pending or Failed replication status. (Objects with either status cannot transition in this versioning-enabled bucket, and a bucket policy cannot override that constraint.); Decrypt the objects before the Lifecycle transition and encrypt them again after archival. (Encrypted objects remain encrypted during a Lifecycle transition, so these extra operations are unnecessary.)

chunks.title: S3 Object Lock and Glacier Vault Lock (WORM)
chunks.text:
S3 Object Lock and Glacier Vault Lock (WORM). S3 Object Lock protects individual object versions against deletion or overwrite using WORM retention. Choose compliance mode when no user, including the account root user, may shorten retention or delete a protected version; choose governance mode when authorized exceptions are required.
When to use: Records must remain immutable for a required retention period, even from the root user.; An investigation requires protection that continues until an authorized user removes a legal hold.; Retention must continue for a specified duration after a future business event.
Key facts: S3 Object Lock works only in buckets with S3 Versioning enabled; retention and legal holds protect individual object versions.; Compliance-mode retention cannot be shortened, and a protected version cannot be overwritten or deleted during its retention period, even by the account root user.; Governance-mode retention can be overridden with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission and an explicit bypass request header.; A legal hold has no expiration date, is independent of retention, and remains until a user with the required permission removes it.; Variable retention can keep an event hold active and set the retain-until-date to the event-hold release time plus a specified duration.; Amazon Glacier Vault Lock applies an unchangeable compliance policy to a vault in the original standalone Amazon Glacier service, not to an S3 Glacier storage class.
Gotchas: Versioning retains versions but does not, by itself, enforce WORM retention.; Object Lock does not prevent a new version or a delete marker from being added above a protected version.; A legal hold can be removed by an authorized user; it is not a substitute for an unshortenable compliance-mode retention period.; For new archival storage, do not confuse the original standalone Amazon Glacier vault service with Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes.
Confused with: s3-versioning-mfa-delete: Versioning helps recover earlier versions; Object Lock adds WORM protection to specified versions.; s3-replication: Replication copies objects for needs such as disaster recovery; it is not the retention control that makes a version immutable.
ES: S3 Object Lock protege versiones individuales de objetos contra eliminación o sobrescritura mediante retención WORM. Elige compliance mode si nadie, ni siquiera el usuario raíz de la cuenta, puede acortar la retención o eliminar una versión protegida; elige governance mode si se requieren excepciones autorizadas. S3 Object Lock solo funciona en buckets con S3 Versioning habilitado; la retención y los legal holds protegen versiones individuales.; En compliance mode no se puede acortar la retención ni sobrescribir o eliminar una versión protegida durante ese período, ni siquiera mediante el usuario raíz.; En governance mode se puede omitir la retención con el permiso s3:BypassGovernanceRetention y el encabezado explícito de omisión.; Un legal hold no tiene fecha de vencimiento, es independiente de la retención y permanece hasta que lo retire un usuario con el permiso necesario.; Variable retention puede mantener activo un event hold y fijar la fecha de fin de retención en el momento de liberarlo más la duración especificada.; Amazon Glacier Vault Lock aplica una política de cumplimiento que no puede modificarse a un vault del servicio independiente original Amazon Glacier, no a una clase de almacenamiento S3 Glacier.

chunks.title: S3 Object Lock and Glacier Vault Lock (WORM)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A clinical research organization writes signed study reports to Amazon S3. Its regulator requires each submitted version to remain available and unaltered for a defined retention period, even if an administrator or the account root user attempts to delete it. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Enable S3 Object Lock with compliance-mode retention for the submitted versions.
Why: The deciding requirement is that even the account root user must be unable to delete a submitted version during its retention period. S3 Object Lock in compliance mode provides that protection for object versions. Governance mode permits an authorized bypass, while Versioning and replication address different protection needs.
Wrong options: Enable S3 Object Lock with governance-mode retention for the submitted versions. (An authorized user can bypass governance-mode retention, contrary to the requirement that no administrator can delete a protected version.); Enable S3 Versioning and require MFA Delete for permanent version deletions. (Versioning and MFA Delete do not provide the required compliance-mode WORM retention.); Replicate the submitted reports to an S3 bucket in another AWS Region. (A second copy does not make each submitted version undeletable for the required period.)

chunks.title: S3 Object Lock and Glacier Vault Lock (WORM)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company is an existing customer of the original standalone Amazon Glacier service and must keep using an established vault and its existing API integration. Auditors want a vault-wide WORM retention policy that cannot be edited after the company finalizes it. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Attach a Vault Lock policy to the existing Amazon Glacier vault and complete the lock.
Why: The company must retain its original standalone Amazon Glacier vault, and the policy must become unchangeable. Amazon Glacier Vault Lock is designed to enforce compliance controls on that vault; after the lock is completed, its policy cannot be changed or deleted. A vault access policy is not lockable, and an S3 Glacier storage class is not the existing vault.
Wrong options: Add a vault access policy that denies archive deletion. (A vault access policy is not the lockable compliance policy the auditors require.); Use S3 Object Lock compliance mode on an S3 Glacier storage class. (An S3 Glacier storage class is distinct from the company's existing standalone Amazon Glacier vault.); Copy the archives to a versioned S3 bucket and enable MFA Delete. (Moving to S3 changes the required vault integration and does not lock a vault-wide WORM policy.)

chunks.title: S3 performance: prefixes, multipart upload, byte-range fetches
chunks.text:
S3 performance: prefixes, multipart upload, byte-range fetches. Amazon S3 has different ways to improve performance depending on the bottleneck: distribute requests across prefixes, use multipart upload for large objects, and batch small objects when the workload permits. Identify whether the scenario needs more request throughput, faster and more resilient large uploads, or fewer individual uploads.
When to use: Reads or writes need higher request throughput: parallelize requests across multiple S3 prefixes.; Objects are 100 MB or larger, or large uploads encounter network interruptions: use multipart upload.; Many small items are consumed together and do not need separate S3 objects: batch them before upload.
Key facts: S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE or 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix; a bucket can have any number of prefixes.; Scaling to a higher request rate is gradual, and 503 Slow Down errors can occur while S3 scales.; Multipart upload sends parts independently; parts can be uploaded in parallel, and a failed part can be retried without restarting the entire object.; AWS recommends multipart upload for objects that are 100 MB or larger.; Uploaded parts continue to incur storage charges until the multipart upload is completed or stopped.
Gotchas: Multipart upload improves the transfer of an individual large object; it does not replace distributing high request volumes across prefixes.; Additional prefixes do not make S3 scaling instantaneous or eliminate every possible 503 Slow Down response.; Do not leave failed multipart uploads unfinished: a lifecycle rule can remove incomplete uploads.
Confused with: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration: Choose it for faster transport over long geographical distances, not to address request distribution across prefixes.; Amazon CloudFront: Caching can help an appropriate read workload, but it does not replace multipart upload for transferring a large object into S3.
ES: Amazon S3 ofrece distintas formas de mejorar el rendimiento según el cuello de botella: distribuir solicitudes entre prefijos, usar multipart upload para objetos grandes y agrupar objetos pequeños cuando la carga lo permita. Identifica si el escenario necesita más capacidad de solicitudes, cargas grandes más rápidas y resistentes, o menos cargas individuales. S3 admite al menos 3500 solicitudes PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE o 5500 GET/HEAD por segundo por prefijo particionado; un bucket puede tener cualquier cantidad de prefijos.; El escalado a una tasa de solicitudes más alta es gradual, y pueden aparecer errores 503 Slow Down mientras S3 escala.; Multipart upload envía las partes de forma independiente; puedes cargarlas en paralelo y reintentar una parte fallida sin reiniciar todo el objeto.; AWS recomienda multipart upload para objetos de 100 MB o más.; Las partes cargadas siguen generando cargos de almacenamiento hasta que completes o detengas el multipart upload.

chunks.title: S3 performance: prefixes, multipart upload, byte-range fetches
chunks.text:
Scenario: A field research team sends 800 MB video files to Amazon S3 from sites with intermittent connectivity. When a transfer fails, the team does not want to resend the entire file. The files must remain individual S3 objects after upload. Which approach meets these requirements MOST effectively?
Correct: Upload each video with S3 multipart upload and retry only interrupted parts.
Why: The key constraint is avoiding a full restart when a large file transfer is interrupted. Multipart upload divides one object into independently uploaded parts, so the team can retry only the affected parts and still complete one S3 object. Multiple prefixes address request throughput rather than recovery of an individual transfer. A single PUT request does not provide the required part-level retry.
Wrong options: Send each video with a single PUT request and retry the request if it fails. (Retrying the single request requires resending the video rather than only an interrupted part.); Cache completed videos with Amazon CloudFront and keep each upload as a single request. (Caching completed objects does not prevent a failed single-request upload from restarting.); Distribute video keys across multiple S3 prefixes and keep each upload as a single request. (Multiple prefixes can help request throughput but do not provide part-level recovery for an individual upload.)

chunks.title: S3 performance: prefixes, multipart upload, byte-range fetches
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer generates many tiny machine readings throughout each shift. Analysts download and process readings by completed shift; they do not need to retrieve individual readings as separate S3 objects. The manufacturer wants to reduce the number of upload requests while retaining S3 as the destination. Which approach meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Batch readings into shift-level files and upload each file as an S3 object.
Why: The deciding requirements are fewer upload requests and consumption by completed shift rather than by individual reading. Combining readings into shift-level objects avoids an individual upload for each tiny item. Spreading individual objects across prefixes may help throughput, but it does not reduce the request count. Multipart upload addresses transferring an object in parts, not consolidating separate readings.
Wrong options: Upload each reading separately and add a lifecycle rule for incomplete multipart uploads. (The lifecycle rule concerns unfinished multipart uploads and leaves the individual-reading upload count unchanged.); Use multipart upload separately for each reading and complete each as an S3 object. (Multipart upload does not consolidate the readings and introduces part-upload requests for each tiny item.); Upload each reading as its own object, distributing the keys across multiple S3 prefixes. (Prefixes can distribute request load but do not reduce the number of uploads for individual readings.)

chunks.title: S3 presigned URLs
chunks.text:
S3 presigned URLs. An S3 presigned URL grants time-limited access to a specific S3 object operation without giving the recipient AWS credentials or changing the bucket policy. Choose it when someone needs to upload or download a private object directly from S3 for a limited time.
When to use: An external recipient needs temporary access to download one private S3 object.; A client without AWS credentials needs to upload an object directly to S3.; The application can generate a URL for a specific object key and HTTP method.
Key facts: The URL uses the permissions of the IAM principal that generated it; that principal must be allowed to perform the requested operation.; A presigned URL specifies a bucket, object key, HTTP method, and expiration interval.; The URL can be used multiple times until it expires. A PUT upload replaces an existing object with the same key.; A URL expires at its configured time or when its signing credentials expire, whichever comes first.; AWS CLI and SDKs can set an expiration as high as 7 days, but temporary credentials can shorten its effective lifetime.
Gotchas: A presigned URL is a bearer token: anyone who obtains it can use it while it remains valid.; Setting a longer URL expiration does not extend the lifetime of the role session that signed it.; An explicit bucket-policy deny can still prevent access through a presigned URL.; Expiration does not make a URL single-use.
Confused with: S3 bucket policies: Bucket policies set resource-level access rules; a presigned URL grants temporary access to a specified object operation without updating the policy.; S3 Access Points: Access Points provide separate access policies for applications or teams sharing a bucket, rather than issuing a temporary link to a recipient.; CloudFront signed URLs/cookies: These restrict content served through CloudFront; an S3 presigned URL authorizes an operation directly against S3.
ES: Una S3 presigned URL concede acceso por tiempo limitado a una operación sobre un objeto específico de S3, sin dar credenciales de AWS al destinatario ni cambiar la bucket policy. Elígela cuando alguien deba subir o descargar un objeto privado directamente desde S3 durante un periodo limitado. La URL usa los permisos del principal de IAM que la genera; ese principal debe tener permiso para realizar la operación solicitada.; Una presigned URL especifica un bucket, una clave de objeto, un método HTTP y un intervalo de vencimiento.; La URL puede usarse varias veces hasta que venza. Una carga PUT reemplaza un objeto existente que tenga la misma clave.; La URL vence al llegar a la hora configurada o cuando vencen las credenciales con que se firmó, lo que ocurra primero.; AWS CLI y los SDK pueden configurar un vencimiento de hasta 7 días, pero las credenciales temporales pueden acortar su vigencia efectiva.

chunks.title: S3 presigned URLs
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research firm stores private report files in Amazon S3. Each external reviewer needs to download one assigned report for a short period, but reviewers must not receive AWS credentials and the firm does not want to change its bucket policy for each review. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Have an authorized application generate an S3 GET presigned URL for each assigned report.
Why: The deciding requirements are temporary access to one private S3 object, no reviewer AWS credentials, and no per-review bucket-policy changes. An authorized application can generate a GET presigned URL for the report. An Access Point separates access policies but is not a temporary download link, and a CloudFront signed URL applies to content served through CloudFront.
Wrong options: Serve each report through CloudFront and issue a CloudFront signed URL to its reviewer. (A CloudFront signed URL controls content served through CloudFront, while this scenario calls for temporary access to objects directly in S3 without adding a distribution.); Create an S3 Access Point for each reviewer and grant access to the assigned report. (An Access Point provides a separate access policy but does not itself issue the requested time-limited download link.); Add a bucket-policy allow statement for each reviewer, then remove it after the review period. (Per-reviewer policy changes add operational work and do not meet the requirement to avoid changing the bucket policy for each review.)

chunks.title: S3 presigned URLs
chunks.text:
Scenario: An insurance company asks customers to upload claim photos from a mobile app directly to a private S3 bucket. Customers do not have AWS credentials, and the application assigns a specific object key to each upload. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Generate a PUT presigned URL for the assigned object key using a principal allowed to upload it.
Why: The customer must upload directly to a specific S3 key without AWS credentials. A principal with the necessary permission can generate a PUT presigned URL for that key. A GET presigned URL has the wrong HTTP method, while per-customer bucket-policy or Access Point management does not provide the requested low-overhead temporary upload link.
Wrong options: Issue each customer a temporary bucket-policy allow statement for uploads to the assigned key. (Changing the bucket policy for each customer adds overhead and does not replace the need for an appropriate way to authorize a customer without AWS credentials.); Create a separate S3 Access Point for each customer to use for the upload. (An Access Point separates access policies but does not itself provide a temporary upload authorization to a customer without AWS credentials.); Generate a GET presigned URL for the assigned object key and send it to the customer. (A GET presigned URL authorizes a download, not the required upload.)

chunks.title: S3 Cross-Region and Same-Region Replication
chunks.text:
S3 Cross-Region and Same-Region Replication. S3 Replication asynchronously copies objects to another bucket. Choose Cross-Region Replication (CRR) for copies in another Region, Same-Region Replication (SRR) for copies within a Region, and S3 Batch Replication for objects that existed before live replication was configured.
When to use: A disaster recovery, compliance, or nearby-access requirement calls for object copies in another Region.; Logs or other objects must be copied between buckets or accounts within one Region.; Existing objects need a one-time replication job, or new objects need a predictable replication time.
Key facts: Live CRR and SRR automatically and asynchronously replicate new and updated objects; they do not replicate objects that existed before the rule was configured.; S3 Batch Replication copies existing objects on demand and can retry objects whose replication previously failed.; S3 Replication Time Control (S3 RTC) has an SLA to replicate 99.99% of new objects within 15 minutes; it does not apply to Batch Replication.; Replication can use buckets in different AWS accounts and can target one or multiple destination buckets.; For writes made after a Regional failover to replicate back to the original bucket, configure two-way replication rules.
Gotchas: Versioning helps recover overwritten or deleted objects, but does not by itself copy them to another bucket or Region.; S3 Object Lock addresses retention; it does not replace a replication rule.; Turning on live replication does not backfill older objects.; S3 RTC is a replication-time SLA for new objects, not a 15-minute guarantee for a Batch Replication job.
Confused with: S3 Versioning and MFA Delete: Keeps versions for recovery from accidental changes; replication makes copies in another bucket.; S3 Object Lock and Glacier Vault Lock: Provides WORM retention; replication addresses where object copies are stored.
ES: S3 Replication copia objetos de forma asíncrona a otro bucket. Elige Cross-Region Replication (CRR) para copias en otra Región, Same-Region Replication (SRR) para copias dentro de una Región y S3 Batch Replication para objetos que ya existían antes de configurar la replicación en vivo. CRR y SRR en vivo replican de forma automática y asíncrona objetos nuevos y actualizados; no copian los que existían antes de configurar la regla.; S3 Batch Replication copia objetos existentes bajo demanda y puede reintentar objetos cuya replicación falló.; S3 Replication Time Control (S3 RTC) ofrece un SLA para replicar el 99.99 % de los objetos nuevos en un máximo de 15 minutos; no se aplica a Batch Replication.; La replicación puede realizarse entre buckets de distintas cuentas de AWS y hacia uno o varios buckets de destino.; Si necesitas que las escrituras posteriores a un failover regional vuelvan al bucket original, configura reglas de replicación bidireccional.

chunks.title: S3 Cross-Region and Same-Region Replication
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media publisher uploads new images to an S3 bucket and needs copies in a second AWS Region. Its distribution agreement requires an SLA-backed replication target of 15 minutes for new objects. Which configuration meets both requirements?
Correct: Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication with S3 Replication Time Control.
Why: This scenario requires both a different-Region destination and an SLA-backed replication time for new objects. CRR meets the geographic requirement; adding S3 RTC provides an SLA to replicate 99.99% of new objects within 15 minutes. CRR alone lacks that SLA, and the S3 RTC SLA does not apply to Batch Replication.
Wrong options: Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication without S3 Replication Time Control. (CRR meets the location requirement but does not itself provide the requested 15-minute SLA.); Run S3 Batch Replication jobs to the second Region every 15 minutes. (S3 RTC's SLA does not apply to Batch Replication jobs.); Configure S3 Same-Region Replication with S3 Replication Time Control. (S3 RTC addresses timing, but SRR cannot copy to a second Region.)

chunks.title: S3 Cross-Region and Same-Region Replication
chunks.text:
Scenario: A gaming studio uses S3 buckets in two AWS Regions and plans to direct traffic to the second Region during a disruption. Players may upload new content to the second bucket during failover, and the studio needs those uploads replicated back to the original bucket. Which replication design meets this requirement?
Correct: Configure two-way S3 Cross-Region Replication rules between the buckets.
Why: The key constraint is that writes made to the second bucket during failover must return to the original bucket. Two-way replication rules provide replication in both directions between the Regions. A one-way rule from the original bucket would not replicate those failover writes back, and Versioning alone would not copy them between buckets.
Wrong options: Configure a one-way CRR rule from the original bucket to the second bucket. (One-way CRR does not replicate uploads made to the second bucket back to the original.); Configure a one-way SRR rule from the second bucket to the original bucket. (SRR cannot replicate between buckets in different Regions.); Enable S3 Versioning on both buckets without configuring replication rules. (Versioning alone does not copy failover writes between buckets.)

chunks.title: S3 Cross-Region and Same-Region Replication
chunks.text:
Scenario: A travel company stores newly uploaded itinerary files in an S3 bucket. Its recovery plan requires automatic copies in a bucket in another AWS Region so the files remain available if the source Region is disrupted. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure S3 Cross-Region Replication from the source bucket to a bucket in the recovery Region.
Why: The deciding requirement is an automatic copy of new objects in another Region. CRR is the live replication option for buckets in different Regions. Versioning does not create a second bucket copy, while SRR cannot place its destination in another Region. Batch Replication is an on-demand option rather than the least-overhead way to replicate each new upload.
Wrong options: Run S3 Batch Replication jobs to copy each day's new uploads to the recovery Region. (Batch Replication is on demand rather than automatic live replication and requires recurring jobs.); Enable S3 Versioning on the source bucket and retain previous versions there. (Versioning retains versions but does not create the required copy in another Region.); Configure S3 Same-Region Replication to a bucket in a separate account. (SRR can copy across accounts, but its destination remains in the same Region.)

chunks.title: S3 Requester Pays
chunks.text:
S3 Requester Pays. S3 Requester Pays shifts request and data-download charges from the owner of a general purpose bucket to authenticated requesters. Choose it when sharing a dataset without paying for consumers’ access; the bucket owner still pays for storage.
When to use: A dataset owner wants consumers to pay for their own S3 requests and downloads.; Consumers can authenticate and explicitly acknowledge Requester Pays charges.
Key facts: Requester Pays applies to S3 general purpose buckets.; For successful requests, the requester pays for the request and data transfer; the bucket owner pays for storage.; Anonymous requests are not allowed.; Requesters acknowledge charges with the x-amz-request-payer header, the RequestPayer parameter, or the CLI --request-payer parameter.; If a requester assumes an IAM role, the account that owns the role is charged.; For RestoreObject, the requester pays for the request, but the bucket owner pays retrieval charges.
Gotchas: Requester Pays does not transfer storage charges to consumers.; Enabling Requester Pays does not make anonymous downloads billable to anonymous users.; Having a consumer assume a role in the owner’s account does not charge the consumer’s account.
Confused with: 
ES: S3 Requester Pays traslada los cargos por solicitudes y descargas de datos del propietario de un bucket de uso general a los solicitantes autenticados. Elígelo para compartir un conjunto de datos sin pagar por el acceso de los consumidores; el propietario sigue pagando el almacenamiento. Requester Pays se aplica a los buckets de uso general de S3.; En las solicitudes exitosas, el solicitante paga la solicitud y la transferencia de datos; el propietario paga el almacenamiento.; No se permiten solicitudes anónimas.; Los solicitantes aceptan los cargos con el encabezado x-amz-request-payer, el parámetro RequestPayer o el parámetro --request-payer de CLI.; Si un solicitante asume un rol de IAM, se cobra a la cuenta a la que pertenece el rol.; Con RestoreObject, el solicitante paga la solicitud, pero el propietario del bucket paga los cargos de recuperación.

chunks.title: S3 Requester Pays
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retail consortium stores shared product images in a Requester Pays S3 bucket. Each member runs a workload in its own AWS account and uses an assumed IAM role to download images. The consortium wants each member's account, not the consortium's account, charged for successful requests and downloads. Which access design meets this requirement?
Correct: Have members assume roles in their own accounts and include the RequestPayer parameter.
Why: For a requester using an assumed IAM role, S3 charges the account that owns the role. Each member should therefore use a role in its own account and acknowledge Requester Pays charges with the RequestPayer parameter. A role in the consortium's account would put the charges on the wrong account, while omitting the acknowledgment does not meet Requester Pays request requirements.
Wrong options: Have members assume a role in the consortium's account and include the RequestPayer parameter. (The consortium's account owns the assumed role and would be charged.); Have members make anonymous requests and include the x-amz-request-payer header. (Requester Pays does not allow anonymous requests, even with a payer header.); Have members use roles in their own accounts but omit the RequestPayer parameter. (Requester Pays requests must explicitly acknowledge the charges.)

chunks.title: S3 Requester Pays
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute shares objects in a Requester Pays S3 bucket with authenticated partner labs. Partners sometimes call RestoreObject, and the institute agrees to cover retrieval charges while partners pay for their restore requests. What should the institute require of partners to meet this billing arrangement?
Correct: Include the x-amz-request-payer header in authenticated RestoreObject requests.
Why: The institute wants partners to pay for RestoreObject requests, but not the associated retrieval charges. Requester Pays supports RestoreObject when the requester acknowledges charges with the payer header or parameter; the bucket owner still pays retrieval charges. Disabling Requester Pays or using a role owned by the institute would not place the request charge on the partner's account.
Wrong options: Have partners assume an IAM role in the institute's account and include the RequestPayer parameter. (The institute's account would be charged for requests made using its role.); Submit RestoreObject requests anonymously and include the RequestPayer parameter. (Requester Pays buckets do not accept anonymous requests.); Disable Requester Pays before each RestoreObject request and re-enable it afterward. (With Requester Pays disabled, the bucket owner generally pays S3 request charges.)

chunks.title: S3 static website hosting
chunks.text:
S3 static website hosting. Amazon S3 can serve static webpages, including pages with client-side scripts. Choose S3 website hosting when an HTTP website is sufficient; for HTTPS with private S3 content, use CloudFront with an S3 bucket origin and origin access control (OAC).
When to use: A site consists of static files and does not need server-side application processing.; An HTTP-only site can be served directly from an S3 website endpoint.; Visitors need HTTPS while the S3 bucket remains private.; S3 content uses SSE-KMS and must be served through CloudFront.
Key facts: S3 static website hosting supports an index document and a custom error document.; An S3 website endpoint does not provide HTTPS.; CloudFront can serve static content stored in S3 over HTTPS.; For an SSE-KMS-encrypted S3 website served through CloudFront, use OAC; origin access identity (OAI) does not support SSE-KMS.; AWS recommends Amplify Hosting for a fully managed deployment of static S3 content to a CloudFront-powered CDN with a public HTTPS URL.
Gotchas: Do not choose a direct S3 website endpoint when visitors require HTTPS.; Do not treat an S3 website endpoint as the private S3 bucket origin protected by CloudFront OAC.; For SSE-KMS content, replacing OAC with OAI does not meet the encryption requirement.
Confused with: AWS Amplify Hosting: Amplify manages deployment to a CloudFront-powered CDN and provides a public HTTPS URL; direct S3 website hosting does not provide HTTPS.; CloudFront OAI: For an S3 origin with SSE-KMS-encrypted objects, use OAC rather than OAI.
ES: Amazon S3 puede servir páginas estáticas, incluso con scripts del lado del cliente. Elige S3 website hosting si basta HTTP; para HTTPS con contenido privado en S3, usa CloudFront con un origen de bucket S3 y origin access control (OAC). S3 static website hosting admite un documento de índice y un documento de error personalizado.; Un S3 website endpoint no proporciona HTTPS.; CloudFront puede servir contenido estático almacenado en S3 mediante HTTPS.; Para un sitio en S3 cifrado con SSE-KMS y servido mediante CloudFront, usa OAC; origin access identity (OAI) no admite SSE-KMS.; AWS recomienda Amplify Hosting para implementar contenido estático de S3 en un CDN administrado basado en CloudFront, con una URL pública HTTPS.

chunks.title: S3 static website hosting
chunks.text:
Scenario: A neighborhood association publishes meeting notes as HTML pages with a small amount of client-side JavaScript. Its existing link uses HTTP, HTTPS is not required, and the association does not need a CDN. Which solution serves the site with the LEAST configuration?
Correct: Enable static website hosting on an S3 bucket and configure an index document.
Why: The pages are static, HTTP is acceptable, and the association does not need a CDN. S3 static website hosting can serve the files directly, with an index document for the site's entry page. Amplify Hosting and both CloudFront designs introduce a CDN that this scenario does not call for.
Wrong options: Create a CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 website endpoint as its origin. (The CloudFront distribution adds configuration despite the stated lack of a CDN requirement.); Deploy the files through AWS Amplify Hosting to its managed CDN. (Amplify adds a managed CDN deployment that the association does not need.); Create a CloudFront distribution with an S3 bucket origin and OAC. (CloudFront and OAC add configuration when neither HTTPS nor private-origin access is required.)

chunks.title: S3 static website hosting
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research nonprofit stores its static publication site in an S3 bucket and requires SSE-KMS encryption for the files. Visitors must use HTTPS, and the bucket must not grant anonymous public access. Which design meets these requirements?
Correct: Use a CloudFront distribution with an S3 bucket origin and OAC.
Why: The deciding constraints are HTTPS, a bucket without anonymous public access, and SSE-KMS-encrypted files. CloudFront with an S3 bucket origin and OAC addresses those constraints. A direct S3 website endpoint cannot provide HTTPS, and a public website origin fails the access requirement. OAI is also unsuitable because it does not support SSE-KMS.
Wrong options: Enable S3 website hosting and grant public read access to the encrypted files. (A direct website endpoint does not provide HTTPS, and public read access violates the bucket requirement.); Use a CloudFront distribution with an S3 bucket origin and OAI. (OAI does not support the required SSE-KMS-encrypted origin content.); Put CloudFront in front of the S3 website endpoint and allow public access to the bucket. (Although CloudFront can provide HTTPS to visitors, this design leaves the bucket publicly accessible.)

chunks.title: S3 storage classes overview
chunks.text:
S3 storage classes overview. Choose an S3 storage class by how often objects are accessed, how quickly they must be retrieved, how long they will be kept, and whether they must survive the loss of an Availability Zone. The cheapest-looking infrequent-access option is not suitable if it misses a retrieval, retention, or resilience requirement.
When to use: Choose S3 Standard-IA for infrequently accessed, long-lived objects that need millisecond access and resilience to the loss of an Availability Zone.; Choose S3 One Zone-IA when infrequently accessed objects can be re-created after an Availability Zone loss.; Choose S3 Intelligent-Tiering when access patterns are unknown or change and automatic tiering is needed.; Choose a S3 Glacier class for rarely accessed data, according to whether retrieval must take milliseconds, minutes to hours, or hours.
Key facts: S3 Standard is the default class for frequently accessed objects.; S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA have a 30-day minimum storage duration and retrieval fees; only S3 Standard-IA is resilient to an Availability Zone loss.; S3 Intelligent-Tiering has a monitoring and automation fee but no retrieval fees. Objects smaller than 128 KB remain in its Frequent Access tier.; S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval provides millisecond access with a 90-day minimum storage duration.; S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires restoration, supports retrieval in minutes to hours, and has a 90-day minimum; S3 Glacier Deep Archive requires restoration, supports retrieval in hours, and has a 180-day minimum.
Gotchas: S3 One Zone-IA's durability does not mean it survives the physical loss of its Availability Zone.; S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive cannot serve real-time reads without restoration.; S3 Intelligent-Tiering's optional Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers also require restoration.; Deleting or transitioning Standard-IA or One Zone-IA objects before 30 days incurs a charge for the remaining minimum duration.
Confused with: 
ES: Elige una clase de almacenamiento de S3 según la frecuencia de acceso, el tiempo de recuperación, cuánto tiempo conservarás los objetos y si deben resistir la pérdida de una Availability Zone. Una opción de menor costo para accesos poco frecuentes no sirve si incumple un requisito de recuperación, retención o resiliencia. S3 Standard es la clase predeterminada para objetos de acceso frecuente.; S3 Standard-IA y S3 One Zone-IA tienen una duración mínima de almacenamiento de 30 días y cargos por recuperación; solo S3 Standard-IA resiste la pérdida de una Availability Zone.; S3 Intelligent-Tiering cobra por monitoreo y automatización, pero no por recuperación. Los objetos menores de 128 KB permanecen en su nivel Frequent Access.; S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval ofrece acceso en milisegundos y tiene una duración mínima de almacenamiento de 90 días.; S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval requiere restauración, permite recuperar en minutos a horas y tiene un mínimo de 90 días; S3 Glacier Deep Archive requiere restauración, permite recuperar en horas y tiene un mínimo de 180 días.

chunks.title: S3 storage classes overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: A medical imaging company retains the only copy of completed scans in Amazon S3 for several years. Clinicians open a scan about once a month and require millisecond access; the scans must remain available if an Availability Zone is lost. Which storage class meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: S3 Standard-IA
Why: Monthly reads and millisecond access point to an infrequent-access class, while the only-copy and AZ-loss requirements rule out S3 One Zone-IA. S3 Standard-IA is designed for long-lived, infrequently accessed data and stores objects across multiple Availability Zones. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval requires restoration instead of providing real-time access.
Wrong options: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (Archived objects must be restored before access, so it cannot provide the required millisecond reads.); S3 Standard (It provides millisecond access and multi-AZ resilience, but is intended for frequently accessed data rather than these monthly reads.); S3 One Zone-IA (It cannot meet the requirement to keep the only copy available after its Availability Zone is lost.)

chunks.title: S3 storage classes overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: A news publisher stores S3 articles whose popularity changes unpredictably after publication. Most objects are larger than 128 KB, readers may request any article without a restoration step, and the team does not want to revise lifecycle rules as trends change. Which storage class meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering with its automatic low-latency access tiers
Why: Unpredictable demand and a desire to avoid adjusting lifecycle rules favor S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Its automatic low-latency tiers accommodate changing access patterns without a performance impact. Activating an optional asynchronous archive tier would introduce a restoration step for archived articles, violating the reader-access requirement.
Wrong options: S3 Intelligent-Tiering with Deep Archive Access activated for every eligible article (Articles moved to this optional archive tier must be restored before readers can access them.); S3 Standard-IA for every article (It does not automatically adapt to articles that become frequently accessed and charges for retrievals.); S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for every article (Articles in this class require restoration and are unavailable for immediate reader requests.)

chunks.title: S3 storage classes overview
chunks.text:
Scenario: An architecture firm keeps completed project packages in S3 for several years. Auditors open a package about once per quarter, but when they do, the download must begin with millisecond access and no restoration request. Which storage class best fits this archive workload MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
Why: Quarterly archive reads paired with a strict millisecond-access requirement match S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. Unlike S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive, it provides real-time access without first restoring an object. S3 Standard-IA also provides millisecond reads, but is designed for more frequent access.
Wrong options: S3 Glacier Deep Archive (It requires restoration and supports retrieval in hours, not immediate access.); S3 Standard-IA (It provides millisecond access but is intended for more frequent, approximately monthly access rather than this quarterly archive workload.); S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (It requires restoration and is not available for real-time access.)

chunks.title: S3 Transfer Acceleration
chunks.text:
S3 Transfer Acceleration. S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance transfers into a general purpose S3 bucket by routing data through globally distributed edge locations. Choose it when geographically dispersed clients upload to one bucket and upload performance—not content delivery or application failover—is the requirement.
When to use: Customers around the world upload to one centralized general purpose S3 bucket.; Regular cross-continent uploads cannot use all available internet bandwidth.
Key facts: Transfer Acceleration is enabled on the bucket and uses an optimized network path from an edge location to S3.; Accelerated requests use bucket-name.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com; the dual-stack variant supports IPv6.; The bucket name must be DNS-compliant and contain no periods, and requests must use virtual-hosted style.; The speed increase can take up to 20 minutes after enabling the feature.; Additional data transfer charges might apply.
Gotchas: Enabling the feature does not make requests to regular S3 endpoints use the accelerated path.; A bucket name containing periods cannot be used with Transfer Acceleration.; CloudFront uses edge locations too, but edge caching is not the same requirement as accelerating uploads into S3.
Confused with: cloudfront-fundamentals: Choose CloudFront for edge caching of delivered content; choose S3 Transfer Acceleration for long-distance transfers into a bucket.; global-accelerator: Choose Global Accelerator for static anycast IPs, non-HTTP TCP/UDP applications, or fast Regional failover—not accelerated S3 bucket uploads.
ES: S3 Transfer Acceleration acelera las transferencias de larga distancia hacia un bucket de S3 de propósito general mediante ubicaciones de borde distribuidas globalmente. Elígelo cuando clientes dispersos geográficamente suben archivos a un solo bucket y el requisito es mejorar las cargas, no distribuir contenido ni proporcionar conmutación por error de aplicaciones. Transfer Acceleration se habilita en el bucket y usa una ruta de red optimizada desde una ubicación de borde hasta S3.; Las solicitudes aceleradas usan bucket-name.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com; la variante dual-stack admite IPv6.; El nombre del bucket debe cumplir con DNS y no contener puntos; las solicitudes deben usar virtual-hosted style.; La mejora de velocidad puede tardar hasta 20 minutos después de habilitar la función.; Podrían aplicarse cargos adicionales por transferencia de datos.

chunks.title: S3 Transfer Acceleration
chunks.text:
Scenario: A nonprofit has enabled S3 Transfer Acceleration on its general purpose bucket for volunteers who upload media from distant countries. A new volunteer application must connect to the bucket over IPv6 while using the accelerated path. The bucket name meets the feature's naming requirements. Which endpoint should the application use?
Correct: The bucket-name.s3-accelerate.dualstack.amazonaws.com endpoint.
Why: The application needs both IPv6 connectivity and S3's accelerated transfer path. The documented endpoint for connecting to an enabled bucket over IPv6 is the accelerate dual-stack endpoint. A regular S3 endpoint does not provide accelerated transfers, even if it meets the connectivity requirement. The non-dual-stack accelerate endpoint is not the documented IPv6 choice.
Wrong options: A CloudFront distribution endpoint with the bucket configured as its origin. (A CloudFront distribution does not give this upload application the requested S3 accelerated path.); A regular S3 endpoint for the bucket with IPv6 connectivity. (A regular S3 endpoint can be used for standard transfers but does not use the accelerated path.); The bucket-name.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com endpoint. (For the stated IPv6 requirement, the documented accelerate option is the dual-stack endpoint.)

chunks.title: S3 Transfer Acceleration
chunks.text:
Scenario: An online marketplace receives product videos from sellers across continents into a single general purpose S3 bucket. Its DNS-compliant bucket name has no periods, and sellers make virtual-hosted style requests. The marketplace wants those requests to use the S3 accelerated transfer path rather than standard transfers. Which two actions meet this requirement? (Choose two.)
Correct: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket. + Send uploads to the bucket's s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com endpoint.
Why: The bucket already meets the stated naming and request-style requirements. To use Transfer Acceleration, the marketplace must enable it on the bucket and direct sellers to the bucket's accelerate endpoint. Sending requests to the regular S3 endpoint instead keeps them on standard transfers. CloudFront and Global Accelerator address different edge or application requirements and do not replace these two steps.
Wrong options: Create a CloudFront distribution with the bucket as its origin. (A CloudFront distribution does not enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the sellers' uploads.); Route the upload clients through AWS Global Accelerator. (Global Accelerator addresses application connectivity rather than enabling accelerated transfers to this S3 bucket.); Send uploads to the bucket's regular S3 endpoint. (Regular endpoint requests continue to use standard data transfer.)

chunks.title: S3 Versioning and MFA Delete
chunks.text:
S3 Versioning and MFA Delete. S3 Versioning keeps multiple versions of an object so you can recover from accidental overwrites and deletes. Add MFA Delete when permanently deleting a version or changing the bucket’s versioning state must require an MFA code.
When to use: Users might overwrite an object and need to restore an earlier version.; An accidental delete must be reversible.; Permanent version deletion or a versioning-state change must require MFA.
Key facts: Versioning is disabled by default and is enabled at the bucket level.; In a versioning-enabled bucket, an overwrite creates a new version; an ordinary delete inserts a delete marker rather than permanently removing the object.; MFA Delete requires additional authentication to permanently delete an object version or change the bucket’s versioning state.; Only the bucket owner’s root account can enable MFA Delete, using the AWS CLI or API—not the AWS Management Console.; Each stored version is a full object and incurs normal S3 storage charges.
Gotchas: MFA Delete does not require MFA for an ordinary delete that inserts a delete marker.; MFA Delete cannot be used with lifecycle configurations.; Enabling versioning does not change objects already in the bucket; future modifications receive versions.
Confused with: S3 Object Lock: Choose Object Lock for WORM retention, not merely to recover from an accidental overwrite or delete.; S3 Replication: Replication copies objects to another destination; Versioning preserves earlier variants in the bucket for recovery.
ES: S3 Versioning conserva varias versiones de un objeto para que puedas recuperarte de sobrescrituras y eliminaciones accidentales. Agrega MFA Delete cuando la eliminación permanente de una versión o un cambio en el estado de versionado del bucket deba requerir un código MFA. Versioning está deshabilitado de forma predeterminada y se habilita a nivel de bucket.; En un bucket con Versioning habilitado, una sobrescritura crea una versión nueva; una eliminación normal inserta un delete marker en lugar de quitar el objeto permanentemente.; MFA Delete exige autenticación adicional para eliminar permanentemente una versión de objeto o cambiar el estado de versionado del bucket.; Solo la cuenta raíz del propietario del bucket puede habilitar MFA Delete mediante AWS CLI o la API, no mediante AWS Management Console.; Cada versión almacenada es un objeto completo y genera los cargos normales de almacenamiento de S3.

chunks.title: S3 Versioning and MFA Delete
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design agency stores client deliverables in an S3 bucket. Staff sometimes overwrite the wrong file or delete one by mistake, and the security team wants an additional authentication factor before anyone permanently removes a stored version. The agency has no WORM retention requirement. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable S3 Versioning and MFA Delete on the bucket.
Why: The deciding combination is recovery from accidental overwrites and deletes plus MFA before permanent version deletion. S3 Versioning retains earlier variants and uses a delete marker for an ordinary delete; MFA Delete adds authentication when a version is permanently deleted. Versioning alone misses the MFA requirement, while Object Lock compliance mode addresses WORM retention that the agency does not need.
Wrong options: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket without MFA Delete. (Versioning supports recovery but does not add the required MFA check for permanent version deletion.); Apply S3 Object Lock compliance-mode retention to the deliverables. (WORM retention addresses a different requirement and does not provide the requested MFA-gated deletion of versions.); Configure S3 Replication to copy deliverables to another bucket. (Replication does not satisfy the requirement to require MFA before permanently deleting a version.)

chunks.title: S3 Versioning and MFA Delete
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company wants to restore S3 objects after accidental overwrites. To control storage costs, it also needs an automated policy that eventually removes noncurrent versions; no MFA approval is required for those removals. Which configuration meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Enable S3 Versioning and configure S3 Lifecycle expiration for noncurrent versions.
Why: The company needs both recoverable prior versions and automated removal of noncurrent versions to control their storage cost. S3 Versioning provides the former, and a noncurrent expiration configuration provides the latter. MFA Delete is a tempting extra protection, but it cannot be used with lifecycle configurations and is not required here. Expiring only current objects does not address the specified noncurrent versions.
Wrong options: Enable S3 Versioning and MFA Delete, then configure S3 Lifecycle expiration for noncurrent versions. (MFA Delete cannot be used with lifecycle configurations.); Configure S3 Replication and expire objects in the source bucket. (Replication does not replace a noncurrent-version expiration policy in the bucket.); Enable S3 Versioning and configure S3 Lifecycle expiration only for current objects. (Expiration for current objects does not provide the requested management of noncurrent versions.)

chunks.title: S3 Versioning and MFA Delete
chunks.text:
Scenario: An engineering firm already has Versioning enabled on an S3 bucket. Its security policy now requires an MFA code to change the bucket’s versioning state or permanently delete a version. An IAM administrator offers to enable the feature in the AWS Management Console. Which implementation meets the policy?
Correct: Have the bucket owner’s root account enable MFA Delete using the AWS CLI or API.
Why: The policy identifies the two operations protected by MFA Delete: changing the versioning state and permanently deleting a version. Only the bucket owner’s root account can enable MFA Delete, and enablement requires the AWS CLI or API. The proposed IAM administrator lacks that ability; switching to the root account but staying in the console would still fail.
Wrong options: Have the bucket owner’s root account enable MFA Delete in the AWS Management Console. (The root account is the right actor, but MFA Delete cannot be enabled in the console.); Have the IAM administrator enable MFA Delete using the AWS CLI or API. (The CLI or API is the right interface, but an IAM administrator cannot enable MFA Delete.); Have the IAM administrator enable MFA Delete in the AWS Management Console. (Neither the IAM administrator nor the console can enable MFA Delete.)

chunks.title: Amazon SageMaker AI (custom ML models)
chunks.text:
Amazon SageMaker AI (custom ML models). Amazon SageMaker AI is a fully managed service for building, training, and deploying custom ML models. Choose it when a scenario requires a broader proprietary prediction model trained on the organization's data, rather than a pre-trained AI capability.
When to use: The team must train a proprietary prediction model using its own labeled examples.; A custom model must be deployed in a hosted environment.; Pre-trained text, speech, image, or document capabilities do not meet the requirement.
Key facts: SageMaker AI supports building, training, and deploying ML models.; It provides a production-ready hosted environment for deployed models.; It supports bring-your-own algorithms and frameworks.; It offers distributed training options and can deploy models into a secure, scalable environment.
Gotchas: A text task does not automatically call for Comprehend, but custom training alone does not rule it out: Comprehend supports custom classifiers and entity recognizers.; Extracting fields from a document is different from training a model to predict an outcome from those fields.; Image input alone does not decide the service; look for a requirement to build and train a specialized model.
Confused with: Comprehend and other language services: Use a language service for its supported tasks; Comprehend also trains custom classifiers and entity recognizers. Choose SageMaker AI for broader proprietary prediction models.; Rekognition: Rekognition addresses image and video analysis tasks; SageMaker AI fits a requirement to build and train a custom model.; Textract: Textract extracts text, forms, and tables from documents; SageMaker AI can train a custom model to make predictions from data.
ES: Amazon SageMaker AI es un servicio totalmente administrado para crear, entrenar y desplegar modelos de ML personalizados. Elígelo cuando el escenario requiera un modelo de predicción propio más amplio, entrenado con datos de la organización, en lugar de una capacidad de AI preentrenada. SageMaker AI permite crear, entrenar y desplegar modelos de ML.; Proporciona un entorno alojado listo para producción para los modelos desplegados.; Admite algoritmos y frameworks propios.; Ofrece opciones de entrenamiento distribuido y permite desplegar modelos en un entorno seguro y escalable.

chunks.title: Amazon SageMaker AI (custom ML models)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional insurer has years of labeled claim records and adjuster notes. Its data science team needs to train a proprietary model that predicts which new claims need specialist review, then deploy that model for application requests. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Train the claim-review model in Amazon SageMaker AI and deploy it in a hosted environment.
Why: The deciding requirement is to train a proprietary predictor from labeled records and host it for application use. SageMaker AI provides managed tools for building, training, and deploying that model. Comprehend can identify entities in text, but entity identification is not the requested claim-review prediction. Self-managed servers add operational work that the scenario asks to minimize.
Wrong options: Build the claim-review model on self-managed servers and host it on those servers. (Self-managed training and hosting could support a custom model but do not meet the least-operational-overhead requirement.); Use Amazon Comprehend to identify entities in the adjuster notes and use those entities as the review decision. (Entity identification does not fulfill the requirement to train and deploy the insurer's proprietary prediction model.); Use Amazon Textract to extract fields from claim documents and use the extracted fields as the review decision. (Field extraction does not train a model to predict whether a claim needs specialist review.)

chunks.title: Amazon SageMaker AI (custom ML models)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer photographs components under a microscope and has labeled historical images with its own defect-severity scores. Engineers need to train a model using those labels and deploy it to score incoming images; identifying objects in a photo alone is not sufficient. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Train the labeled-image severity model with Amazon SageMaker AI and deploy it in a hosted environment.
Why: The manufacturer needs predictions based on its own labeled severity scores, not general image labels. SageMaker AI supports training a custom model and deploying it to a managed hosted environment. Rekognition addresses image analysis, but the proposed object labels do not provide the specified severity scoring. Self-managed compute can host a model but misses the operational-overhead qualifier.
Wrong options: Train a severity model on self-managed compute and host it on self-managed servers. (This could meet the custom-model requirement but adds management work compared with a managed ML service.); Use Amazon Rekognition to identify objects in the component images and report those labels as severity scores. (Object labels do not satisfy the requirement to learn the manufacturer's severity scores from labeled images.); Use Amazon Textract to extract text from the component images and report the extracted text as severity scores. (Text extraction does not train a model on the labeled defect-severity examples.)

chunks.title: Savings Plans (Compute vs EC2 Instance)
chunks.text:
Savings Plans (Compute vs EC2 Instance). Savings Plans lower eligible usage costs in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment measured in $/hour. Choose Compute Savings Plans when usage may move across EC2 families or Regions, or to Fargate or Lambda; choose EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the lowest prices when usage will stay in one EC2 family and Region.
When to use: A steady hourly compute baseline is expected, but its EC2 family, Region, or service may change: consider Compute Savings Plans.; Steady EC2 usage will remain in one instance family and Region, and the priority is the lowest price: consider EC2 Instance Savings Plans.; A workload needs both discounted usage and guaranteed EC2 capacity: pair an applicable Savings Plan with an On-Demand Capacity Reservation.
Key facts: Savings Plans require a $/hour usage commitment for one or three years; usage beyond the commitment is charged at On-Demand rates.; Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2 regardless of family, size, operating system, tenancy, or Region, and also apply to Fargate and Lambda.; EC2 Instance Savings Plans cover a selected EC2 family in a selected Region, regardless of Availability Zone, size, operating system, or tenancy.; EC2 Instance Savings Plans offer the lowest prices of the two types; Compute Savings Plans offer more flexibility.; Savings Plans do not reserve EC2 capacity.
Gotchas: Changing size or Availability Zone within the chosen family and Region does not, by itself, require a Compute Savings Plan.; An EC2 Instance Savings Plan does not extend its discount to Fargate, Lambda, another EC2 family, or another Region.; A discounted usage commitment is not a capacity guarantee.; Do not commit to a variable peak merely because a steady baseline exists; usage beyond the commitment can remain On-Demand.
Confused with: Reserved Instances: EC2 Reserved Instances can discount steady EC2 usage, but Compute Savings Plans also follow eligible usage across EC2 families and Regions, Fargate, and Lambda.; Spot Instances: Spot suits interruptible work; a Savings Plan discounts eligible usage without making the workload interruptible.; On-Demand Capacity Reservations: A Capacity Reservation addresses capacity availability; a Savings Plan addresses eligible usage pricing and does not reserve capacity.
ES: Savings Plans reducen el costo del uso elegible a cambio de un compromiso de uno o tres años medido en $/hora. Elige Compute Savings Plans si el uso puede cambiar de familia o Region de EC2, o pasar a Fargate o Lambda; elige EC2 Instance Savings Plans para obtener el precio más bajo si el uso permanecerá en una familia y Region de EC2.
