Savings Plans requieren un compromiso de uso en $/hora durante uno o tres años; el uso que exceda el compromiso se cobra a tarifa On-Demand.; Compute Savings Plans se aplican a EC2 sin importar la familia, el tamaño, el sistema operativo, la tenencia o la Region; también se aplican a Fargate y Lambda.; EC2 Instance Savings Plans cubren una familia de EC2 en una Region seleccionada, sin importar la Availability Zone, el tamaño, el sistema operativo o la tenencia.; EC2 Instance Savings Plans ofrecen los precios más bajos de los dos tipos; Compute Savings Plans ofrecen mayor flexibilidad.; Savings Plans no reservan capacidad de EC2.

chunks.title: Savings Plans (Compute vs EC2 Instance)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A hospital must keep EC2 capacity available in a particular Availability Zone for a continuously running application. Its EC2 family and Region will remain unchanged, and it also wants the lowest Savings Plans price on its predictable usage. The purchasing approach must address capacity availability and usage cost separately. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the application's family and Region. + Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation in the required Availability Zone.
Why: This scenario has two separate requirements: discounted predictable usage and available capacity in a specific Availability Zone. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan offers the lowest Savings Plans prices for the unchanged family and Region. An On-Demand Capacity Reservation addresses the Availability Zone capacity requirement and can be paired with a Savings Plan. Neither type of Savings Plan reserves capacity on its own.
Wrong options: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan instead of reserving capacity. (A Compute Savings Plan does not reserve capacity and is not the lowest-priced Savings Plans type for this fixed family and Region.); Use a Dedicated Host instead of a capacity reservation and Savings Plan. (A Dedicated Host addresses dedicated-host needs rather than the requested combination of reserved capacity and a Savings Plans discount.); Use Spot Instances to ensure capacity is available in the required Availability Zone. (Spot is an interruptible purchasing option, not a capacity guarantee.)

chunks.title: Savings Plans (Compute vs EC2 Instance)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization uses consolidated billing for separate application accounts. One account has steady EC2 usage, while another has steady Lambda usage; both teams may change their compute mix during the next year. The finance team wants a single hourly commitment whose discount can apply to eligible usage across the accounts by default. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST commitment management?
Correct: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan within the consolidated billing family.
Why: The commitment must cover two eligible compute services and work across accounts under consolidated billing. A Compute Savings Plan applies to EC2 and Lambda, and Savings Plans benefits apply across accounts in a consolidated billing family by default. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan and EC2 Reserved Instances do not cover Lambda. A Capacity Reservation addresses EC2 capacity rather than this pricing requirement.
Wrong options: Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances for the EC2 account and use them for both accounts' compute usage. (EC2 Reserved Instances do not cover the Lambda usage specified in the scenario.); Purchase an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the EC2 account and share its benefit across both accounts. (A capacity reservation does not provide the requested discount for eligible EC2 and Lambda usage.); Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the EC2 account's current family and Region. (It does not discount the other account's Lambda usage or follow a change away from the selected EC2 family and Region.)

chunks.title: Savings Plans (Compute vs EC2 Instance)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer runs a predictable EC2 workload in one instance family and one AWS Region. It sometimes changes instance sizes and Availability Zones, but will not change families or Regions or move the workload to another compute service during its planned commitment. It wants the lowest Savings Plans price for this usage. Which option meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the chosen family and Region.
Why: The workload's family and Region remain fixed, so it does not need the broader coverage of a Compute Savings Plan. EC2 Instance Savings Plans offer the lowest prices for usage in a selected family and Region. Changing size or Availability Zone within those boundaries does not prevent the plan from applying. A Capacity Reservation would address a different requirement.
Wrong options: Keep the workload entirely on On-Demand EC2 pricing. (On-Demand pricing forgoes the Savings Plans discount on the predictable usage.); Use an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the selected instance family. (A capacity reservation addresses capacity availability, not the requested Savings Plans price.); Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for the workload's hourly usage. (It provides flexibility the workload does not need, while EC2 Instance Savings Plans offer lower prices.)

chunks.title: Choosing scaling metrics and conditions
chunks.text:
Choosing scaling metrics and conditions. Choose a scaling metric that reflects the work each instance must handle. For an SQS worker fleet, use backlog per InService instance rather than raw queue length; set its target from acceptable queue latency and average message-processing time.
When to use: An EC2 Auto Scaling group processes messages from an SQS queue.; The workload specifies an acceptable queue delay.; Queue activity changes, and worker capacity should adjust with demand.
Key facts: Calculate backlog per instance by dividing the queue's ApproximateNumberOfMessages attribute by the Auto Scaling group's InService instance count.; Calculate the acceptable backlog-per-instance target by dividing acceptable latency by average processing time per message.; Raw visible-message count is not necessarily proportional to the worker capacity required.; Metric math can avoid the cost and effort of publishing a custom backlog-per-instance metric.; EC2 instance usage metrics, including CPU, are in the AWS/EC2 CloudWatch namespace.
Gotchas: A growing queue does not, by itself, tell you how many workers are needed; processing time and acceptable delay also matter.; Do not divide backlog by instances that are not InService.; Backlog-based scaling does not, by itself, protect an instance processing a long-running task from scale-in termination.
Confused with: 
ES: Elige una métrica de escalado que refleje el trabajo que debe atender cada instancia. Para una flota que procesa mensajes de SQS, usa la cantidad de mensajes pendientes por instancia InService en vez del tamaño total de la cola; fija el objetivo según la latencia aceptable y el tiempo promedio de procesamiento. Calcula los mensajes pendientes por instancia dividiendo el atributo ApproximateNumberOfMessages de la cola entre las instancias InService del grupo.; Calcula el objetivo de mensajes pendientes por instancia dividiendo la latencia aceptable entre el tiempo promedio de procesamiento por mensaje.; La cantidad total de mensajes visibles no necesariamente es proporcional a la capacidad de trabajadores requerida.; Metric math puede evitar el costo y el esfuerzo de publicar una métrica personalizada de mensajes pendientes por instancia.; Las métricas de uso de instancias EC2, incluida CPU, están en el espacio de nombres AWS/EC2 de CloudWatch.

chunks.title: Choosing scaling metrics and conditions
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company has an EC2 Auto Scaling group whose instances process reservations from an SQS queue. During releases, both the number of waiting reservations and the number of InService workers change. Architects need a target tracking policy tied to acceptable queue delay rather than a fixed total queue size. Which two choices establish the appropriate metric and target? (Choose two.)
Correct: Divide the queue's ApproximateNumberOfMessages attribute by the group's InService instance count. + Divide acceptable queue latency by average per-instance processing time for one message to set the target.
Why: The policy must represent waiting work per active worker and translate the delay limit into a target. Calculate backlog per instance from ApproximateNumberOfMessages divided by InService capacity, then calculate its target from acceptable latency divided by average message-processing time. A raw visible-message count misses the changing relationship between queue size and worker capacity. Including instances that are not InService also misstates the documented per-instance calculation.
Wrong options: Set the target to the total number of reservations the company expects during a release. (An expected total does not derive the acceptable work per instance from the queue-delay requirement.); Divide the queue's ApproximateNumberOfMessages attribute by every instance in the group, regardless of state. (The documented calculation divides by instances in the InService state, not every instance.); Track the queue's visible-message count directly as the target tracking metric. (Total queue length might not change proportionally to the size of the group processing it.)

chunks.title: Choosing scaling metrics and conditions
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research portal runs its interactive application on one EC2 Auto Scaling group and processes submitted datasets from SQS on a separate worker group. The portal team monitors EC2 CPU usage for its application, while worker processing times and queue wait times determine how much worker capacity is needed. Each group must scale independently according to its own load. Which metric selection best meets these requirements?
Correct: Use EC2 CPU usage for the application group and SQS backlog per InService instance for the worker group.
Why: The two groups have different sources of load and must scale independently. EC2 CPU usage is the metric the team monitors for its interactive application; the SQS workers need backlog per InService instance because processing time and acceptable delay determine their required capacity. Using CPU for both groups ignores the worker queue requirement. Using raw queue length for workers does not account for changes in active worker capacity.
Wrong options: Use EC2 CPU usage for both groups. (For the worker group, CPU usage does not capture the stated queue-delay and message-processing requirements.); Use SQS backlog per InService instance for the application group and EC2 CPU usage for the worker group. (It assigns the queue-work metric to the group that does not process queue messages.); Use EC2 CPU usage for the application group and total SQS visible-message count for the worker group. (The worker metric omits the changing number of instances available to process the messages.)

chunks.title: AWS Secrets Manager (with rotation)
chunks.text:
AWS Secrets Manager (with rotation). AWS Secrets Manager stores credentials and API keys for applications to retrieve at runtime. Choose it when secrets must rotate automatically without changing and redeploying application code.
When to use: Database credentials, application credentials, OAuth tokens, or API keys need automatic rotation.; Applications must retrieve credentials dynamically instead of storing them in source code.; Rotation must update both the stored secret and the database or service that accepts it.
Key facts: Secrets Manager supports configurable automatic rotation schedules.; Rotation updates credentials in both the secret and the database or service.; Managed rotation is available for most managed secrets; the service configures and manages it without a Lambda function.; For other types of secrets, rotation uses a Lambda function.; Secrets Manager charges for usage; Lambda-based rotation can also incur Lambda charges.
Gotchas: Changing only the stored value is not sufficient: the database or service must accept the new credential.; Do not assume every rotation requires a Lambda function; managed rotation does not.; A SecureString in Parameter Store does not provide built-in automatic rotation.
Confused with: Systems Manager Parameter Store: Use Parameter Store for configuration or SecureString values when built-in automatic rotation is not required; choose Secrets Manager when it is.
ES: AWS Secrets Manager almacena credenciales y API keys para que tus aplicaciones las recuperen en tiempo de ejecución. Elígelo cuando los secretos deban rotar automáticamente sin cambiar ni volver a desplegar el código. Secrets Manager permite configurar una programación de automatic rotation.; La rotación actualiza las credenciales tanto en el secreto como en la base de datos o el servicio.; Managed rotation está disponible para la mayoría de los secretos administrados; el servicio la configura y gestiona sin una función Lambda.; Para otros tipos de secretos, la rotación usa una función Lambda.; Secrets Manager cobra por uso; la rotación basada en Lambda también puede generar cargos de Lambda.

chunks.title: AWS Secrets Manager (with rotation)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer is replacing a hard-coded API key used by several applications to call an external service. The key is not a managed secret or a secret held by a Secrets Manager partner. Security requires scheduled changes, and a new key must be accepted by the external service without redeploying the applications. Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Store the key in Secrets Manager and have the applications retrieve it at runtime. + Configure Secrets Manager rotation by Lambda function to update the secret and the external service.
Why: Two distinct requirements decide the design: applications need the current key without redeployment, and rotation must update the external service as well as the stored secret. Runtime retrieval from Secrets Manager satisfies the first; Lambda-based rotation satisfies the second for this non-managed case. Replacing only the stored value misses the external-service update. Parameter Store SecureString does not offer built-in automatic rotation.
Wrong options: Embed the current Secrets Manager secret value in each application's next deployment. (Embedding the value would require application deployments to propagate later changes.); Configure a scheduled process that replaces only the value stored in Secrets Manager. (Replacing only the stored value does not ensure the external service accepts the new key.); Store the key in Parameter Store SecureString and rely on built-in automatic rotation. (Parameter Store SecureString does not provide built-in automatic rotation.)

chunks.title: AWS Secrets Manager (with rotation)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company stores a database password in its application source code. Security requires scheduled credential changes, and the team cannot redeploy the application each time the password changes. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Store the credential in Secrets Manager, configure automatic rotation, and have the application retrieve it at runtime.
Why: The deciding requirements are scheduled changes and no application redeployment. Secrets Manager supports automatic rotation, and the application can retrieve the current credential at runtime. Parameter Store SecureString addresses storage but lacks built-in automatic rotation. Storing a secret without enabling rotation likewise misses the scheduled-change requirement.
Wrong options: Store the credential as a Parameter Store SecureString and have the application retrieve it at runtime. (Runtime retrieval removes the hard-coded value, but Parameter Store does not provide built-in automatic rotation.); Keep the credential in the source code and deploy a new application version whenever the password changes. (Each password change would still require the redeployment the company cannot perform.); Store the credential in Secrets Manager and have the application retrieve it at runtime, without configuring rotation. (This removes the hard-coded credential but does not meet the scheduled-rotation requirement.)

chunks.title: AWS Secrets Manager (with rotation)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media platform uses an API key to call a service outside AWS. The key is not a managed secret or a secret held by a Secrets Manager partner, and the external service requires an update when the key changes. The platform needs scheduled rotation that keeps the stored key and the external service synchronized. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Put the key in Secrets Manager and configure Lambda-based rotation to update the secret and the external service.
Why: Rotation must change both the stored key and the service that accepts it. For a secret outside the managed-rotation cases described, Secrets Manager uses a Lambda function to perform rotation. Simply changing the stored value would break synchronization with the external service. Parameter Store retrieval also does not supply built-in automatic rotation.
Wrong options: Put the key in Secrets Manager and enable managed rotation without a rotation function. (The scenario excludes the managed-secret and partner-held cases described for rotation without Lambda.); Put the key in Secrets Manager and replace only the stored value on a schedule. (Updating only the stored value leaves it out of sync with the external service.); Put the key in Parameter Store SecureString and configure clients to retrieve it for each request. (Client retrieval does not provide built-in rotation or update the external service.)

chunks.title: Securing ingestion access points and data lakes
chunks.text:
Securing ingestion access points and data lakes. Secure ingestion by matching each control to the risk: an interface VPC endpoint keeps VPC-to-Kinesis traffic on the Amazon network, IAM and endpoint policies constrain access, and KMS server-side encryption protects Kinesis data at rest. For an S3 data lake, include bucket policies in the access-control design.
When to use: VPC-based producers must send records to Kinesis without traffic leaving the Amazon network.; Producers must access only an approved stream, or only through a specified VPC endpoint.; Ingested Kinesis records require encryption at rest.
Key facts: Kinesis Data Streams supports interface VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink.; A Kinesis interface endpoint does not require an internet gateway or NAT device for VPC-to-Kinesis traffic.; Endpoint policies can restrict which streams are accessible through an endpoint; IAM policies can restrict access to a stream to a specified endpoint.; Kinesis server-side encryption uses AWS KMS keys to encrypt data at rest.
Gotchas: A private network path does not, by itself, restrict a producer to one stream.; KMS encryption at rest does not replace controls on who can access a stream.; An endpoint policy alone is not the same as requiring every request to use that endpoint; the documented IAM policy pattern can impose that requirement.
Confused with: 
ES: Protege la ingesta según el riesgo: un interface VPC endpoint mantiene el tráfico entre la VPC y Kinesis dentro de la red de Amazon; IAM y endpoint policies limitan el acceso; y el cifrado del lado del servidor con AWS KMS protege los datos de Kinesis en reposo. Para un data lake en S3, incluye bucket policies en el diseño de control de acceso. Kinesis Data Streams admite interface VPC endpoints mediante AWS PrivateLink.; Un interface endpoint de Kinesis no requiere internet gateway ni NAT device para el tráfico entre la VPC y Kinesis.; Las endpoint policies pueden limitar los streams accesibles mediante un endpoint; las IAM policies pueden exigir que el acceso a un stream ocurra mediante un endpoint específico.; El cifrado del lado del servidor de Kinesis usa claves de AWS KMS para cifrar los datos en reposo.

chunks.title: Securing ingestion access points and data lakes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A food distributor runs telemetry producers in a VPC and sends their records to a Kinesis data stream. The network team will not provide an internet gateway or NAT device, and traffic to Kinesis must not leave the Amazon network. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a Kinesis Data Streams interface VPC endpoint for the producers' VPC.
Why: The deciding constraint is network access from a VPC without an internet gateway or NAT device. A Kinesis Data Streams interface VPC endpoint provides a private path that keeps this traffic on the Amazon network. KMS encryption and IAM permissions address different security requirements and do not create that path.
Wrong options: Configure a restrictive VPC endpoint policy but do not create a Kinesis interface endpoint. (An endpoint policy cannot supply the required private path when there is no interface endpoint.); Enable KMS server-side encryption on the stream and leave the producers' network configuration unchanged. (KMS server-side encryption protects records at rest but does not provide the required network path.); Attach an IAM policy that allows the producers to write only to the destination stream. (Limiting stream permissions does not provide a network path without internet or NAT access.)

chunks.title: Securing ingestion access points and data lakes
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab ingests instrument readings into Kinesis Data Streams before storing curated files in an S3 data lake. Its producers already use a Kinesis interface VPC endpoint, but a new policy requires encryption of streaming records at rest and access controls for the lake bucket. Which design meets both requirements?
Correct: Enable Kinesis server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys and apply an S3 bucket policy for lake access.
Why: The scenario names two distinct resources and controls: streaming records need encryption at rest, and the S3 lake needs bucket access control. Kinesis server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys addresses the first; an S3 bucket policy addresses the second. Endpoint restrictions are useful for Kinesis access but do not replace either requested control.
Wrong options: Restrict the Kinesis endpoint policy to the stream and apply an S3 bucket policy for lake access. (These policies constrain access but do not provide the required Kinesis encryption at rest.); Require producers to use the Kinesis interface endpoint and rely on that endpoint for both controls. (The interface endpoint addresses the VPC-to-Kinesis network path, not stream encryption at rest or bucket access.); Enable Kinesis server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys and rely on the Kinesis endpoint policy for lake access. (Kinesis encryption covers the stream, but a Kinesis endpoint policy is not an access policy for the S3 bucket.)

chunks.title: Security groups (stateful instance firewall)
chunks.text:
Security groups (stateful instance firewall). A security group is an allow-only, stateful firewall for an associated resource such as an EC2 instance. Choose it when access should follow a workload, especially when one tier should accept traffic only from another tier's security group.
When to use: Restrict inbound traffic to an EC2 workload by source, protocol, and port.; Allow an application tier to reach a database tier without listing application instance IP addresses.; Keep access rules tied to workloads that share a subnet with other workloads.
Key facts: Security groups control allowed inbound and outbound traffic for associated resources.; Inbound rules specify a source, port range, and protocol; outbound rules specify a destination, port range, and protocol.; Rules allow traffic; a security group does not provide a deny rule for a specific IP address.; Security groups are stateful: responses to allowed traffic do not require separate rules for the return direction.; A security group rule can reference another security group as its source, allowing access to follow the referenced workload group.
Gotchas: An outbound rule on the application security group does not replace the database security group's required inbound rule.; Do not add security group rules solely to allow response traffic for an already permitted connection.; For an explicit deny of a source IP at the subnet boundary, use a network ACL instead of a security group.
Confused with: network-acls: A network ACL filters at the subnet boundary, supports allow and deny rules, and is stateless; a security group filters associated resources with allow-only, stateful rules.
ES: Un security group es un firewall stateful que solo permite tráfico para un recurso asociado, como una instancia EC2. Elígelo cuando el acceso deba seguir a una carga de trabajo, especialmente si una capa debe aceptar tráfico solo desde el security group de otra capa. Los security groups controlan el tráfico entrante y saliente permitido de los recursos asociados.; Las reglas entrantes especifican origen, rango de puertos y protocolo; las salientes especifican destino, rango de puertos y protocolo.; Sus reglas permiten tráfico; un security group no ofrece una regla deny para una dirección IP específica.; Los security groups son stateful: las respuestas al tráfico permitido no necesitan reglas independientes para el sentido de retorno.; Una regla de un security group puede referenciar otro security group como origen para que el acceso siga al grupo de cargas de trabajo referenciado.

chunks.title: Security groups (stateful instance firewall)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization allows partner networks to reach an EC2 service on TCP port 443. An incident team identifies one hostile source IP address within an otherwise approved partner CIDR range and must block that address at the subnet boundary while retaining access for the rest of the range. Which change meets these requirements MOST securely?
Correct: Add a network ACL deny rule for the hostile IP address before the broader allow rule for the partner CIDR.
Why: The decisive constraint is an explicit block of one IP at the subnet boundary, without blocking other partner addresses. A network ACL supports deny rules and evaluates them in rule-number order, so the specific deny must precede the broader allow. A security group has allow rules only and cannot express this exception. Removing the entire partner CIDR would violate the requirement to retain access.
Wrong options: Add a security group rule allowing TCP 443 from the partner CIDR with a higher priority than other rules. (An allow rule cannot block the hostile address, and security group rules are not ordered deny rules.); Add a deny rule for the hostile IP address to the EC2 instance's security group. (Security groups do not support deny rules.); Remove the partner CIDR from the security group and allow only the hostile IP address in the subnet's network ACL. (This would not retain access for the rest of the approved partner range.)

chunks.title: Security groups (stateful instance firewall)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio places rendering and asset-management EC2 instances in the same subnet. Only the rendering instances should accept TCP connections on port 8443 from a designated processing tier; asset-management instances must not accept those connections. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Associate a security group with the rendering instances that allows inbound TCP 8443 from the processing tier's security group.
Why: Both workloads share a subnet, but only rendering instances should accept the processing tier's connections. A security group associated with the rendering instances provides that workload-specific control, and referencing the processing tier's group identifies the permitted source. A network ACL operates at the subnet boundary, so its allow rule cannot by itself separate these workloads. An outbound rule on the processing tier also does not replace the rendering tier's inbound permission.
Wrong options: Add a network ACL rule allowing TCP 8443 from the processing tier to the shared subnet. (The subnet-level rule does not distinguish rendering instances from asset-management instances.); Allow outbound TCP 8443 in the processing tier's security group, without permitting inbound TCP 8443 on the rendering instances. (An outbound rule on the source does not authorize inbound traffic at the destination.); Allow inbound TCP 8443 from the processing tier's subnet CIDR on a security group associated with both rendering and asset-management instances. (Associating that group with both workloads would also allow connections to asset-management instances.)

chunks.title: Security groups (stateful instance firewall)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company runs web, application, and database EC2 tiers in one VPC. Web instances must connect to application instances on TCP 443, and only application instances must connect to database instances on TCP 3306; other EC2 instances share their subnets. The security groups already permit the required outbound connections, and the network ACLs permit the necessary traffic in both directions. Which TWO inbound-rule changes provide the required workload isolation with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Allow inbound TCP 3306 on the database security group with the application security group as the source. + Allow inbound TCP 443 on the application security group with the web security group as the source.
Why: The requirement is to authorize two specific tier-to-tier paths while excluding unrelated instances in shared subnets. An inbound TCP 443 rule on the application group sourced from the web group provides the first path. An inbound TCP 3306 rule on the database group sourced from the application group provides the second. Subnet CIDR sources are too broad, and changing the web group's inbound database-port rule targets the wrong tier.
Wrong options: Allow inbound TCP 443 on the application security group from the entire web subnet CIDR. (Other instances in the web subnet would also be permitted as sources.); Allow inbound TCP 3306 on the database security group from the entire application subnet CIDR. (Other instances sharing the application subnet would also be permitted to connect.); Allow inbound TCP 3306 on the web security group with the application security group as the source. (This changes access to the web tier rather than permitting connections to the database tier.)

chunks.title: AWS Security Hub
chunks.text:
AWS Security Hub. AWS Security Hub CSPM brings security findings from accounts and integrated services into one view and runs checks against security standards and best practices. Choose it when the requirement is to assess overall security posture, not just consume findings from one source.
When to use: Collect findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie across accounts in one view.; Run security controls against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices or CIS.; Prioritize findings and trigger responses to specific findings.
Key facts: Security Hub CSPM receives findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and supported third-party products.; It runs continuous security checks and generates control findings.; AWS Config must be enabled and record resources for most control findings.; For full compliance with CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark security checks, enable Security Hub CSPM in all supported AWS Regions.; It processes findings only in Regions where it is enabled and does not retroactively consolidate findings generated before enablement.
Gotchas: An integrated finding source is not a substitute for Security Hub CSPM's consolidated view and standards checks.; Enabling Security Hub CSPM in one Region does not make it process findings in every Region.; Enabling Security Hub CSPM without the required AWS Config recording can leave most control findings unavailable.
Confused with: Amazon GuardDuty: GuardDuty can send findings to Security Hub CSPM; Security Hub CSPM also consolidates other providers' findings and runs standards checks.; AWS Firewall Manager: Firewall Manager centrally enforces security policies; Security Hub CSPM consolidates findings and assesses security controls.; Amazon Detective: Detective supports investigation of findings; Security Hub CSPM provides the consolidated findings and standards-check view.
ES: AWS Security Hub CSPM reúne hallazgos de cuentas y servicios integrados en una sola vista y ejecuta controles basados en estándares y prácticas recomendadas de seguridad. Elígelo cuando necesites evaluar la postura de seguridad general, no solo consultar los hallazgos de una fuente. Security Hub CSPM recibe hallazgos de GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie y productos de terceros compatibles.; Ejecuta controles de seguridad continuos y genera hallazgos de controles.; Para generar la mayoría de los hallazgos de controles, debes habilitar AWS Config y registrar recursos.; Para cumplir plenamente con los controles de CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, habilita Security Hub CSPM en todas las AWS Regions compatibles.; Solo procesa hallazgos en las Regions donde está habilitado y no consolida retroactivamente hallazgos generados antes de habilitarlo.

chunks.title: AWS Security Hub
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company wants a cross-account view of findings from its integrated security services and results from security standards checks. When a particular finding appears, it wants to trigger an automatic response without waiting for an analyst to select an action. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use Security Hub CSPM for the consolidated findings and checks, and integrate it with Amazon EventBridge to trigger responses.
Why: The company needs both Security Hub CSPM's consolidated findings and standards checks, plus an automatic response to a specific finding. Security Hub CSPM integrates with Amazon EventBridge for that response. Automation rules can modify or suppress findings, but suppressing one is not the requested response; an analyst-invoked action also fails the no-wait requirement.
Wrong options: Use Security Hub CSPM for the consolidated findings and checks, and require analysts to invoke custom actions for matching findings. (Requiring an analyst to select an action conflicts with the automatic-response requirement.); Use Amazon GuardDuty for the consolidated findings and checks, and integrate its findings with Amazon EventBridge. (GuardDuty does not provide the requested consolidated view of integrated providers and security standards checks.); Use Security Hub CSPM for the consolidated findings and checks, and rely only on automation rules to suppress matching findings. (Suppressing findings changes how they are handled but does not meet the requirement to trigger an automatic response.)

chunks.title: AWS Security Hub
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retail company has several AWS accounts. Its security team already receives findings from Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, and Amazon Macie, but reviews each source separately. The team also needs checks against AWS security best practices and a consolidated view across accounts. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable AWS Security Hub CSPM to collect the integrated findings and run security standards checks.
Why: The deciding requirements are a consolidated view across accounts and checks against security best practices. Security Hub CSPM collects findings from the named services and runs controls that generate findings. GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie are integrated finding sources, so choosing any one of them does not meet both requirements.
Wrong options: Use Amazon Macie as the central view for the existing findings and best-practice checks. (Macie can send findings to Security Hub CSPM but does not fulfill the combined aggregation and standards-check requirement.); Use Amazon GuardDuty as the central view for the existing findings and best-practice checks. (GuardDuty is a finding source, not the service described for consolidating these providers and running standards checks.); Use Amazon Inspector as the central view for the existing findings and best-practice checks. (Inspector can send findings to Security Hub CSPM but does not provide the requested consolidated standards-check view.)

chunks.title: Serverless application pattern (API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB + S3)
chunks.text:
Serverless application pattern (API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB + S3). For a variable-traffic web application that should not require server management, use a serverless multi-tier pattern: Amazon API Gateway for the API, AWS Lambda for application logic, Amazon DynamoDB for application data, and Amazon S3 for web assets. In an exam scenario, choose the complete pattern when the requirements include both a web interface and a backend API.
When to use: Traffic is variable and the team wants to avoid managing application servers.; A web interface needs an API backed by application logic and data.; The architecture should keep the web, API, logic, and data responsibilities separate.
Key facts: AWS describes API Gateway and Lambda as building blocks for serverless multi-tier architectures.; The documented examples include mobile backends and single-page applications.; AWS says these services can reduce the development and operations cycles needed to create and manage multi-tier applications.; In this pattern, S3, API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB have distinct web-asset, API, application-logic, and data roles.
Gotchas: An S3-based web interface alone does not supply the requested backend API and application logic.; A database choice alone does not provide an API for web clients.; Adding servers for the application tier conflicts with an explicit no-server-management requirement.
Confused with: 
ES: Para una aplicación web con tráfico variable que no debe requerir la administración de servidores, usa un patrón multinivel serverless: Amazon API Gateway para la API, AWS Lambda para la lógica, Amazon DynamoDB para los datos y Amazon S3 para los recursos web. En un escenario de examen, elige el patrón completo cuando se requieren tanto una interfaz web como una API de backend. AWS describe API Gateway y Lambda como componentes de arquitecturas multinivel serverless.; Los ejemplos documentados incluyen backends móviles y aplicaciones de página única.; AWS indica que estos servicios pueden reducir los ciclos de desarrollo y operación necesarios para crear y administrar aplicaciones multinivel.; En este patrón, S3, API Gateway, Lambda y DynamoDB cumplen funciones distintas para recursos web, API, lógica y datos.

chunks.title: Serverless application pattern (API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB + S3)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A travel publisher is replacing an application-server-based trip planner. Its new single-page interface needs an API for itinerary changes and a data store for saved plans; usage rises sharply during holiday promotions. The publisher wants the web, API, and logic tiers separated without managing application servers. Which design best meets these requirements?
Correct: Put web assets in Amazon S3, expose requests through Amazon API Gateway, run logic in AWS Lambda, and store plans in Amazon DynamoDB.
Why: This is a single-page application with distinct web, API, logic, and saved-data requirements. The S3, API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB design maps to those tiers without application servers. A design that keeps application servers misses the operational constraint, even if it otherwise separates the tiers.
Wrong options: Put web assets in Amazon S3, expose requests through Amazon API Gateway, and run logic in AWS Lambda without a saved-plan data store. (This omits the data store explicitly required for saved plans.); Put web assets in Amazon S3, expose requests through Amazon API Gateway, run logic on application servers, and store plans in Amazon DynamoDB. (The application servers contradict the requirement not to manage them.); Put web assets in Amazon S3 and store plans in Amazon DynamoDB, with all itinerary changes handled in the interface. (This does not provide the required API and separate application-logic tier.)

chunks.title: Serverless application pattern (API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB + S3)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A local government office has built a request-tracking web prototype with files in Amazon S3 and request records in Amazon DynamoDB. It now needs a backend API that applies status-change rules before updating records. Staffing is limited, and the office will not manage application servers. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Keep S3 and DynamoDB, add Amazon API Gateway for the backend API, and use AWS Lambda for status-change rules.
Why: The prototype already has web files and request records, so the architectural gap is the API and its status-change logic. API Gateway and Lambda supply those distinct roles in the serverless multi-tier pattern. Adding application servers would address the logic but fail the explicit staffing and operations constraint.
Wrong options: Keep S3 and DynamoDB, and make the web interface responsible for applying every status-change rule without a backend API. (This omits the required backend API and moves its rules into the interface.); Keep S3 and DynamoDB, and add AWS Lambda for the rules without providing an API for the web interface. (This adds backend logic but not the requested API.); Keep S3 and DynamoDB, add Amazon API Gateway, and run the status-change rules on application servers. (This adds the API but requires the office to manage application servers.)

chunks.title: Serverless application pattern (API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB + S3)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A sports club already stores its membership portal files in Amazon S3 and member records in Amazon DynamoDB. For occasional enrollment drives, it must add a backend API that accepts changes and applies membership rules. The club does not want to operate application servers. Which TWO additions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Add AWS Lambda to apply the membership rules. + Add Amazon API Gateway to provide the backend API.
Why: S3 and DynamoDB already cover the portal files and member records. The two missing responsibilities are the backend API and the logic that applies membership rules, supplied here by API Gateway and Lambda. More file or data storage would not fill those gaps, while application servers would violate the operations requirement.
Wrong options: Add another Amazon DynamoDB data store instead of an API layer. (An additional data store does not supply the required backend API.); Add a second Amazon S3 location to hold membership rules instead of an application-logic tier. (Another location for files does not supply the application logic needed to apply the rules.); Add application servers to apply membership rules. (Application servers conflict with the club's no-server-operations requirement.)

chunks.title: Service control policies (SCPs)
chunks.text:
Service control policies (SCPs). Service control policies (SCPs) set organization-wide permission guardrails for member accounts, including their root users. Choose an SCP when a rule must cap what accounts or OUs can do regardless of their IAM grants; use IAM or resource policies to grant access.
When to use: Apply the same permission ceiling across multiple member accounts or an OU.; Prevent member-account administrators from overriding a restriction with broad IAM permissions.; Restrict the root user of a member account as well as its IAM users and roles.
Key facts: SCPs require an AWS Organizations organization with all features enabled; consolidated billing alone is insufficient.; SCPs grant no permissions. Users and roles still need appropriate permissions from IAM or resource policies.; A member account's permissions must be permitted at every level above it in the organization.; SCPs affect member accounts, including delegated administrator accounts and their root users, but not users or roles in the management account.; SCPs do not restrict service-linked roles or directly apply to principals from outside the organization.
Gotchas: An SCP that allows an action does not grant that action to a role with no IAM permissions.; AdministratorAccess in a member account does not override an applicable SCP restriction.; Do not expect an SCP to restrict management-account principals or service-linked roles.; Test an SCP with a small number of accounts before attaching it to the organization root.
Confused with: IAM identity-based policies: They grant permissions to users and roles; SCPs cap permissions across member accounts.; Resource-based policies: They control access to a resource, including access by outside principals; an SCP does not directly restrict those outside principals.; Permissions boundaries: They cap permissions for a specific IAM user or role; an SCP caps permissions for member accounts or OUs.
ES: Las service control policies (SCPs) establecen límites de permisos para las cuentas miembro de una organización, incluidos sus usuarios root. Elige una SCP cuando debas limitar lo que pueden hacer cuentas u OUs aunque IAM les otorgue permisos amplios; usa políticas de IAM o de recursos para otorgar acceso. Las SCPs requieren que la organización de AWS Organizations tenga habilitadas todas las funciones; consolidated billing por sí solo no basta.; Las SCPs no otorgan permisos. Los usuarios y roles aún necesitan permisos adecuados mediante políticas de IAM o de recursos.; Los permisos de una cuenta miembro deben estar permitidos en todos los niveles superiores de la organización.; Las SCPs afectan a las cuentas miembro, incluidas las cuentas de administradores delegados y sus usuarios root, pero no a los usuarios o roles de la cuenta de administración.; Las SCPs no restringen los service-linked roles ni se aplican directamente a entidades externas a la organización.

chunks.title: Service control policies (SCPs)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company has production accounts in an AWS Organizations OU. Its security team must prevent IAM administrators and the root users of those member accounts from performing a specified set of actions, even when an administrator attaches AdministratorAccess to a role. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Attach an SCP that denies the actions to the production OU.
Why: The deciding requirement is a common restriction that also applies to member-account root users. An SCP on the OU sets a permission ceiling that AdministratorAccess cannot override. A permissions boundary is scoped to particular IAM identities, so attaching one to administrator roles leaves root users outside that control.
Wrong options: Replace each administrator role's identity policy with one that omits the actions. (Changing those roles' identity policies does not establish a ceiling for root users or other identities in the accounts.); Attach a permissions boundary that denies the actions to each administrator role. (A boundary on administrator roles does not restrict the member accounts' root users or every other role.); Add deny statements to the resource policies of resources used by the production accounts. (Individual resource policies do not provide the requested account-wide guardrail for the specified actions.)

chunks.title: Service control policies (SCPs)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization attaches an SCP that permits the actions needed by a new analytics team. The team's role in a member account has no IAM permission policy, and its first API request is denied. The team needs access only to its approved analytics resources. Which change meets this requirement with the LEAST additional access?
Correct: Attach an identity-based policy to the role that grants the required actions on the approved resources.
Why: The role has no IAM permission policy, and an SCP cannot grant access even when it permits an action. An identity-based policy grants the required actions on the approved resources while the SCP remains the organization guardrail. A broader SCP or a permissions boundary cannot substitute for the missing grant.
Wrong options: Move the account to an OU with fewer SCP restrictions. (Relaxing SCP restrictions does not provide the missing IAM permission grant.); Attach a broader SCP to the member account that permits all AWS actions. (A broader SCP still would not grant permissions to the role.); Attach a permissions boundary to the role that lists the required actions and resources. (A permissions boundary sets a maximum but does not grant permissions to a role without an IAM permission policy.)

chunks.title: Service quotas and throttling (including standby environments)
chunks.text:
Service quotas and throttling (including standby environments). Service quotas cap resources or operations and are generally Region-specific unless a quota says otherwise. For disaster recovery, check the applied quotas in the standby account and Region before failover; for API-heavy workflows, design request volume around operation quotas rather than assuming an increase will be immediate.
When to use: A standby environment must scale up during a regional failover.; A deployment or recovery workflow might exceed a resource or API-operation quota.; A new or lightly used account may have a lower applied quota than the published default.
Key facts: Service Quotas shows default and applied quota values and whether a quota is adjustable.; Unless otherwise noted, quotas are Region-specific; check each quota’s description to determine its scope.; Some quotas cannot be increased. AWS Support can approve, deny, or partially approve an increase, and processing can take time.; Service Quotas can be used to request increases for supported adjustable quotas; AWS SDKs include error-handling and retry functionality.
Gotchas: Capacity available under a quota in the primary Region does not establish the applied quota in the DR Region.; A published default is not proof of a particular account’s applied quota.; Submitting an increase request during failover does not make extra capacity immediately available.; Retries alone do not raise an operation quota.
Confused with: 
ES: Las service quotas limitan recursos u operaciones y, salvo que se indique lo contrario, son específicas de cada Region. Para disaster recovery, verifica las cuotas aplicadas en la cuenta y Region de standby antes del failover; si un flujo hace muchas llamadas API, ajusta el volumen de solicitudes a las cuotas de operaciones sin suponer que un aumento será inmediato. Service Quotas muestra los valores predeterminados y aplicados, e indica si una cuota es ajustable.; Salvo que se indique lo contrario, las cuotas son específicas de cada Region; revisa la descripción de cada cuota para confirmar su alcance.; Algunas cuotas no se pueden aumentar. AWS Support puede aprobar, rechazar o aprobar parcialmente una solicitud, y procesarla toma tiempo.; Puedes solicitar aumentos de cuotas ajustables compatibles mediante Service Quotas; los AWS SDK incluyen manejo de errores y reintentos.

chunks.title: Service quotas and throttling (including standby environments)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics firm is preparing a standby environment in a separate AWS account and Region. A failover would create more resources and run a burst of provisioning API calls, but recovery must not depend on quota increases being approved during the event. Which TWO actions should the firm take before its next failover test? (Choose two.)
Correct: Check the standby account’s applied resource quotas and request needed adjustable increases in advance. + Pace provisioning calls against applicable operation quotas and handle failed API calls with SDK retries.
Why: The firm faces two distinct constraints: resource capacity in the standby account and Region, and the rate of provisioning operations. Checking applied resource quotas and seeking necessary adjustable increases before the test addresses the first; pacing API calls and handling failures addresses the second. Values from the primary account or another Region do not establish standby capacity. Waiting until failover to request an increase risks a delayed, partial, or denied response.
Wrong options: Use the primary account’s applied quota values as the standby account’s recovery capacity. (The standby account and Region need their own quota assessment.); Defer quota checks until the failover test and request any increases when resource creation fails. (Increase requests are not immediate or guaranteed, so this makes recovery depend on approval during the event.); Treat all quotas as account-wide so a value checked in one Region also covers the standby Region. (Quotas are generally Region-specific unless a particular quota specifies otherwise.)

chunks.title: Service quotas and throttling (including standby environments)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research laboratory uses a recently created AWS account for disaster recovery. Its deployment planner finds that the resource quota needed for full recovery is marked non-adjustable, and the planned deployment would exceed the account’s applied value. The laboratory must make the recovery plan executable before its next test. Which action meets this requirement?
Correct: Revise the recovery deployment so its resource usage stays within the applied quota, then test the revised plan.
Why: The applied quota is below the resources the recovery plan would create, and this quota cannot be increased. The laboratory must therefore change the plan to fit the quota and validate the revised deployment. A recently created account may have an applied value below the AWS default, so planning against the default is unsafe. API retries cannot provide permission to exceed a resource quota.
Wrong options: Use the AWS default quota rather than the applied quota when sizing the recovery deployment. (The account’s applied value, not the published default, governs this deployment.); Request an increase through Service Quotas and run the existing deployment after submitting the request. (The quota is non-adjustable, and submitting a request would not make the deployment executable.); Retain the deployment plan and add SDK retries to every resource-creation call. (Retries do not change a non-adjustable resource quota that the deployment would exceed.)

chunks.title: Shared responsibility model
chunks.text:
Shared responsibility model. AWS secures the underlying cloud infrastructure; customers secure what they run and configure in it. For an EC2-based design, assign guest operating system patches, application software, and security group configuration to the customer—not AWS.
When to use: A scenario asks who patches an EC2 instance versus its underlying host.; A security plan assigns ownership of security groups, encryption, or key management.; An auditor needs to distinguish AWS-operated physical controls from customer control verification.
Key facts: AWS manages the host operating system, virtualization layer, and physical security of its facilities.; The customer manages the guest operating system, including updates and security patches, and associated application software.; The customer configures the AWS-provided security group firewall.; Responsibilities vary with the services selected and how they are integrated.; Customers can use encryption and key management to meet more stringent security or compliance requirements.
Gotchas: AWS patching the host does not mean AWS patches an EC2 guest operating system.; An AWS-provided security group still needs customer configuration.; AWS managing physical controls does not eliminate the customer's control evaluation and verification work.
Confused with: 
ES: AWS protege la infraestructura subyacente de la nube; tú proteges lo que ejecutas y configuras en ella. En una solución basada en EC2, las actualizaciones del sistema operativo invitado, el software de aplicación y la configuración de los security groups te corresponden a ti, no a AWS. AWS administra el sistema operativo del host, la capa de virtualización y la seguridad física de sus instalaciones.; Tú administras el sistema operativo invitado, incluidas sus actualizaciones y parches de seguridad, y el software de aplicación asociado.; Tú configuras el firewall de security groups proporcionado por AWS.; Las responsabilidades varían según los servicios elegidos y cómo se integran.; Puedes usar cifrado y administración de claves para cumplir requisitos de seguridad o conformidad más estrictos.

chunks.title: Shared responsibility model
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research company runs analysis software on Amazon EC2. A new contractual requirement calls for additional encryption and key management controls beyond the company's current design. The security team must assign this work without assuming that AWS's physical security satisfies the contract. Which assignment meets the requirement?
Correct: Have the customer design and manage the additional encryption and key management controls.
Why: The contract requires additional encryption and key management, not merely physical facility protection. The customer can design and manage those controls to meet its stricter requirements. AWS manages physical security and the virtualization layer, but neither responsibility substitutes for the company's specified controls.
Wrong options: Have AWS configure the security groups as the encryption control. (The customer configures security groups, and firewall configuration does not address the stated encryption and key management requirement.); Have the customer manage the virtualization layer to implement encryption. (AWS manages the virtualization layer, so this assigns the work to the wrong party.); Have AWS choose the application's encryption controls because AWS manages the facilities. (AWS's responsibility for physical facilities does not transfer the customer's additional application security requirements to AWS.)

chunks.title: Shared responsibility model
chunks.text:
Scenario: A financial services firm is evaluating IT controls for an application running on AWS. Its compliance team needs to assess controls associated with the physical infrastructure and complete its own control verification procedures. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use AWS control and compliance documentation for the team's evaluation and verification procedures.
Why: The firm must evaluate physical infrastructure controls while performing its own verification. AWS manages those infrastructure controls, and customers can use AWS control and compliance documentation in their evaluation procedures. Delegating the entire evaluation to AWS misses the firm's stated obligation; operating AWS facility controls assigns it work that belongs to AWS.
Wrong options: Substitute a review of the firm's security groups for an assessment of physical controls. (Customer-configured security groups do not replace evaluation of controls associated with physical infrastructure.); Have the firm operate physical security controls at AWS facilities and document the results. (AWS, not the customer, manages physical security of its facilities.); Assign AWS the firm's entire control evaluation because AWS manages the physical infrastructure. (AWS managing physical controls does not remove the customer's evaluation and verification procedures.)

chunks.title: AWS Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced
chunks.text:
AWS Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced. AWS Shield Standard automatically protects AWS customers against common infrastructure-layer DDoS attacks. Choose Shield Advanced for eligible critical resources when the requirement adds protection against larger attacks, near real-time incident visibility, DDoS scaling cost protection, or access to the Shield Response Team.
When to use: Rely on Shield Standard when the requirement is common layer 3/4 DDoS protection without additional cost.; Consider Shield Advanced for critical protected resources that need enhanced DDoS mitigation and incident notifications.; Choose Shield Advanced when DDoS scaling cost protection or expert incident assistance is required.
Key facts: Shield Standard protects all AWS customers against common layer 3/4 events, including SYN and UDP floods.; Shield Advanced supports protected EC2, ELB, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, and Route 53 resources.; Shield Advanced provides near real-time notifications of suspected DDoS incidents.; DDoS scaling cost protection lets customers request credits for eligible attack-related usage spikes on protected resources.; Shield Advanced customers with Business or Enterprise support can engage the Shield Response Team 24/7 for application-layer DDoS events.
Gotchas: Do not add Shield Advanced when the stated need is only the common infrastructure-layer protection already provided by Shield Standard.; Shield Standard does not provide Shield Advanced's DDoS scaling cost protection or Shield Response Team access.; For HTTP GET or POST floods, distinguish application-layer protection from Shield Standard's infrastructure-layer protection.
Confused with: AWS WAF: AWS WAF can protect against application-layer HTTP floods; Shield Standard addresses common infrastructure-layer DDoS events.; AWS Firewall Manager: Firewall Manager centrally enforces security policies across accounts; it is not a substitute for Shield Advanced's DDoS response and cost protection.
ES: AWS Shield Standard protege automáticamente a los clientes de AWS contra ataques DDoS comunes en la capa de infraestructura. Elige Shield Advanced para recursos críticos compatibles cuando se necesite protección frente a ataques mayores, visibilidad casi en tiempo real, protección de costos por escalamiento o acceso al Shield Response Team. Shield Standard protege a todos los clientes de AWS contra eventos comunes de capa 3/4, incluidos ataques SYN y UDP.; Shield Advanced admite recursos protegidos de EC2, ELB, CloudFront, Global Accelerator y Route 53.; Shield Advanced proporciona notificaciones casi en tiempo real de posibles incidentes DDoS.; La protección de costos por escalamiento permite solicitar créditos por aumentos elegibles de uso causados por un ataque en recursos protegidos.; Los clientes de Shield Advanced con Business o Enterprise support pueden contactar al Shield Response Team las 24 horas para eventos DDoS de capa de aplicación.

chunks.title: AWS Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company runs a critical application behind an Application Load Balancer and has AWS Enterprise Support. A major DDoS event could cause its protected load balancer to scale, and the company wants both help from AWS specialists during the event and a way to address eligible attack-related scaling charges. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Protect the load balancer with Shield Advanced and use the Shield Response Team when needed.
Why: The company needs two Shield Advanced capabilities: DDoS scaling cost protection for a protected load balancer and access to the Shield Response Team. Its Enterprise Support plan meets the stated support condition for engaging that team during application-layer DDoS events. Eligible scaling charges can be addressed by requesting credits through AWS Support. Shield Standard and AWS WAF alone do not supply that combination.
Wrong options: Add AWS WAF rules to the load balancer and rely on Enterprise Support for scaling cost protection. (AWS WAF rules do not provide Shield Advanced's DDoS scaling cost protection.); Use Firewall Manager to enforce security policies for the load balancer. (Central enforcement alone does not provide the requested DDoS scaling cost protection and specialist assistance.); Use Shield Standard and request DDoS scaling credits through AWS Support. (Shield Standard does not include Shield Advanced's scaling cost protection or specialist response access.)

chunks.title: AWS Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced
chunks.text:
Scenario: A nonprofit serves a registration site through Amazon CloudFront. It already relies on Shield Standard for common infrastructure-layer floods, but its new concern is a surge of malicious HTTP GET requests to registration pages. The organization does not want to enroll in Shield Advanced. Which addition best addresses the new requirement?
Correct: Use AWS WAF to protect the CloudFront-served site from HTTP GET floods.
Why: The new threat is an HTTP GET flood, which is an application-layer concern. AWS documentation identifies AWS WAF as an option for protecting against HTTP GET and POST floods. Shield Standard already addresses the organization's common infrastructure-layer concern but is not the targeted addition here. Shield Advanced has additional DDoS capabilities, yet the scenario explicitly rules out enrolling in it.
Wrong options: Continue using Shield Standard as the only protection for the HTTP GET flood. (Shield Standard's common infrastructure-layer protection does not specifically address the requested application-layer flood.); Enroll the CloudFront distribution in Shield Advanced for application-layer DDoS protection. (Shield Advanced can add application-layer protection, but enrollment violates the organization's explicit constraint.); Use Firewall Manager solely to centrally enforce security policies. (Central enforcement by itself does not specify protection against the malicious HTTP requests.)

chunks.title: AWS Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media platform delivers live-event streams through Amazon CloudFront and guarantees availability to its customers. During suspected DDoS events, its operations team needs near real-time notifications and enhanced mitigation against sophisticated attacks. It does not need a policy-management service spanning multiple accounts. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Protect the CloudFront distribution with Shield Advanced.
Why: The deciding requirements are enhanced mitigation for sophisticated attacks and near real-time notifications of suspected DDoS incidents. Shield Advanced provides both for protected CloudFront resources. Shield Standard covers common infrastructure-layer events but lacks the requested advanced capabilities. Firewall Manager addresses central policy enforcement, which the scenario specifically says is unnecessary.
Wrong options: Rely only on Shield Standard for the CloudFront distribution. (Shield Standard does not provide the requested Shield Advanced incident visibility and enhanced mitigation.); Use AWS WAF rules as the sole source of DDoS incident notifications. (WAF rules are not the Shield Advanced near real-time suspected-DDoS notification capability requested here.); Use Firewall Manager to centrally enforce security policies across accounts. (Cross-account policy enforcement is not the stated need and does not replace the requested Shield Advanced capabilities.)

chunks.title: Eliminating single points of failure
chunks.text:
Eliminating single points of failure. A highly available design must keep serving requests when a component fails. In an exam scenario, identify the component with no healthy alternative—such as an instance, Availability Zone, NAT gateway, network connection, or database—and add redundancy and a way to fail over.
When to use: A single instance or Availability Zone supports a service that must remain available.; Private-subnet egress, a network connection, or a database has only one serving path.; The requirement calls for low recovery time or automatic response to failure.
Key facts: Monitor workload components to detect failures.; Fail over to healthy resources rather than merely creating extra resources.; Automate healing across layers when low mean time to recovery matters.; Check each layer independently: redundant application instances do not remove a single network or database dependency.
Gotchas: More instances in one Availability Zone do not address loss of that Availability Zone.; A standby resource does not help promptly if traffic cannot move to it.; Backups help recovery but do not by themselves provide a serving database during a failure.
Confused with: 
ES: Un diseño highly available debe seguir atendiendo solicitudes cuando falla un componente. En un escenario de examen, identifica el componente sin una alternativa en buen estado —como una instancia, Availability Zone, NAT gateway, conexión de red o base de datos— y agrega redundancia y una forma de hacer failover. Monitorea los componentes de la carga de trabajo para detectar fallas.; Haz failover hacia recursos en buen estado; no basta con crear recursos adicionales.; Automatiza la recuperación en las distintas capas cuando importa reducir el tiempo medio de recuperación.; Revisa cada capa por separado: tener instancias de aplicación redundantes no elimina una dependencia única de red o base de datos.

chunks.title: Eliminating single points of failure
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media-processing application has workers in private subnets in two Availability Zones. Each subnet's route table sends outbound traffic through the same NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone, and workers must retain outbound connectivity if either Availability Zone fails. Which change best removes the single point of failure?
Correct: Deploy a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone and route each private subnet through the NAT gateway in its own Availability Zone.
Why: The workers already span Availability Zones, but their outbound path does not. A NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, paired with the corresponding private-subnet route, avoids making both worker groups depend on one Availability Zone for egress. Merely adding a second NAT gateway is insufficient when both route tables still use the first one. This illustrates why each component and its path must be checked for failover.
Wrong options: Deploy a second NAT gateway in the second Availability Zone but leave both private-subnet route tables pointing to the first. (The unused second NAT gateway does not provide an outbound path when the first path fails.); Move the NAT gateway to the second Availability Zone and keep both private-subnet routes pointing to it. (Moving the shared NAT gateway changes the location of the single point of failure without removing it.); Add more workers in the second Availability Zone while retaining the existing private-subnet routes. (Additional workers still depend on the single NAT gateway for outbound connectivity.)

chunks.title: Eliminating single points of failure
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer exchanges time-sensitive orders between its data center and an application in AWS through one AWS Direct Connect connection. The application runs across multiple Availability Zones, but an interruption to the Direct Connect connection would stop new orders. Which design best addresses the remaining single point of failure while preserving a private connectivity option?
Correct: Add an independent Direct Connect connection at a separate location and configure failover to the healthy connection.
Why: The application's instances are redundant, but incoming orders still rely on one Direct Connect path. An independent connection at a separate location provides an alternative, and failover makes that alternative usable when the original path fails. A second router attached to the same connection does not remove the connection as a single point of failure. Two connections at one location leave that location as a shared dependency.
Wrong options: Add a second Direct Connect connection at the same connectivity location and use only that location for both paths. (Both paths would still depend on one connectivity location.); Add application instances in another Availability Zone and keep the existing Direct Connect connection. (More application instances do not provide an alternative path from the data center.); Add a second data-center router, but connect both routers through the existing Direct Connect connection. (The existing Direct Connect connection remains the only connectivity path.)

chunks.title: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
chunks.text:
AWS Site-to-Site VPN. AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates an IPsec connection between an on-premises network and AWS. Choose it when a site needs encrypted hybrid connectivity over the internet, rather than a connection for individual remote users or between VPCs.
When to use: An on-premises network needs encrypted access to resources in a VPC.; A site needs a VPN endpoint for one VPC or for a network of multiple VPCs.; The design needs redundant VPN tunnels for availability.
Key facts: Each Site-to-Site VPN connection includes two encrypted tunnels that can be used simultaneously for high availability.; A virtual private gateway is an AWS-side VPN endpoint that attaches to a single VPC; a transit gateway can serve as the endpoint for multiple VPCs.; Configure routing so traffic passes through the VPN connection.; A standard tunnel supports 1.25 Gbps. A Large Bandwidth Tunnel supports up to 5 Gbps per tunnel on connections attached to Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN.; One VPN connection cannot carry IPv4 and IPv6 traffic simultaneously; use separate connections. VPN connections on a virtual private gateway do not support IPv6 traffic.
Gotchas: Creating a VPN connection without configuring routes does not complete the path between the networks.; The two tunnels belong to one VPN connection; you can use both for high availability.; Do not assume the 5 Gbps Large Bandwidth Tunnel is available with a virtual private gateway.; Do not choose a virtual private gateway for a requirement to carry IPv6 traffic through the VPN.
Confused with: AWS Direct Connect: Choose Site-to-Site VPN when the requirement is an IPsec connection over the internet; Direct Connect is a dedicated private connection, not an IPsec VPN by default.; AWS Client VPN: Client VPN connects individual remote users; Site-to-Site VPN connects an on-premises network through customer gateway equipment.; AWS Transit Gateway: Transit Gateway can be the AWS-side endpoint for Site-to-Site VPN and interconnect multiple VPCs; it is not itself the encrypted tunnel.
ES: AWS Site-to-Site VPN crea una conexión IPsec entre una red local y AWS. Elígela cuando una sede necesite conectividad híbrida cifrada por internet, en vez de una conexión para usuarios remotos individuales o entre VPC. Cada conexión Site-to-Site VPN incluye dos túneles cifrados que puedes usar simultáneamente para alta disponibilidad.; Un virtual private gateway es un endpoint VPN del lado de AWS que se conecta a una sola VPC; un transit gateway puede ser el endpoint para varias VPC.; Configura el enrutamiento para que el tráfico pase por la conexión VPN.; Un túnel estándar admite 1.25 Gbps. Large Bandwidth Tunnel admite hasta 5 Gbps por túnel en conexiones asociadas a Transit Gateway o Cloud WAN.; Una conexión VPN no puede transportar IPv4 e IPv6 simultáneamente; usa conexiones separadas. Las conexiones VPN en un virtual private gateway no admiten tráfico IPv6.

chunks.title: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
chunks.text:
Scenario: A community hospital needs its on-premises scheduling system to communicate with an application in one VPC using IPsec over the internet. The network team will configure its gateway device and wants the connection designed for high availability. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Configure the Site-to-Site VPN connection's two tunnels for simultaneous use. + Create a Site-to-Site VPN to a virtual private gateway on the VPC and configure routes for the hospital network.
Why: The hospital needs both a routed IPsec connection from its site and a design that uses the VPN's availability feature. For a single VPC, a virtual private gateway can be the AWS-side endpoint; configuring routes lets the scheduling traffic use the VPN. Each Site-to-Site VPN connection includes two tunnels that can be used simultaneously for high availability. Client VPN serves individual remote clients, not the hospital's site network.
Wrong options: Use a Direct Connect connection by itself as the encrypted IPsec tunnel from the hospital. (Direct Connect alone is not the requested IPsec VPN over the internet.); Create a Client VPN endpoint and install client software on hospital employees' laptops. (Laptop access does not connect the on-premises scheduling system's network to the VPC.); Create a VPC peering connection between the hospital network and the application VPC. (VPC peering connects VPCs and does not create an IPsec connection to the hospital network.)

chunks.title: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional food distributor is moving its inventory application into one VPC. Its warehouse network must reach the application through an encrypted connection over the internet, and the network team can configure its on-premises gateway device. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a Site-to-Site VPN to a virtual private gateway attached to the VPC, and configure routes through the VPN.
Why: The deciding requirements are a site-wide, encrypted connection over the internet and access to just one VPC. Site-to-Site VPN supplies the IPsec connection, while a virtual private gateway can serve as the AWS-side endpoint for that VPC. Routes must direct traffic through the connection. A transit gateway could also be a VPN endpoint, but it adds a hub the scenario does not need.
Wrong options: Create a VPC peering connection and add routes from the warehouse network to the VPC. (VPC peering connects VPCs, not the warehouse's on-premises gateway device.); Create a Site-to-Site VPN to a transit gateway attached to the VPC, and configure routes through the VPN. (This can provide VPN connectivity, but a transit hub adds an unnecessary component for the stated single-VPC requirement.); Create a Client VPN endpoint for the inventory application and give the warehouse network a client configuration. (Client VPN is intended for individual remote clients rather than a site-wide connection from the warehouse gateway.)

chunks.title: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research company has separate VPCs for data ingestion, analysis, and reporting. Its laboratory network needs an IPsec connection over the internet that can reach all three VPCs through an AWS-side network hub. Which design meets this requirement?
Correct: Attach the VPCs to a transit gateway, use it as the Site-to-Site VPN endpoint, and configure the needed routes.
Why: The company needs both an IPsec site connection and a hub for multiple VPCs. Site-to-Site VPN provides the encrypted tunnels, and a transit gateway can be its AWS-side endpoint while interconnecting the VPCs and on-premises network. Configure routing for the intended paths. A virtual private gateway is an endpoint for a single VPC, not the requested multi-VPC hub.
Wrong options: Connect the laboratory to the ingestion VPC with Direct Connect and peer that VPC with the other two. (Direct Connect alone does not satisfy the stated IPsec-over-the-internet requirement, and peering is not a transitive hub.); Peer the three VPCs and terminate a Client VPN connection at the ingestion VPC.
