(Client VPN targets remote clients, and peering does not provide a transitive path from the laboratory network.); Attach a virtual private gateway to the ingestion VPC and route traffic to the other VPCs through VPC peering. (A virtual private gateway attaches to one VPC, and VPC peering does not provide the requested transitive hub.)

chunks.title: AWS Snow Family (Snowball Edge, Snowcone)
chunks.text:
AWS Snow Family (Snowball Edge, Snowcone). AWS Snowball Edge is a shipped device for moving large datasets when an online transfer is impractical, or for running storage and compute workloads at disconnected sites. In an exam scenario, choose it for physical transport or local processing—not routine online synchronization—and check whether the customer is eligible to order it.
When to use: An existing customer must move tens of TB to PB, but available network bandwidth makes online transfer impractical.; A remote site must collect or process data locally while disconnected.; An existing customer needs to import local data into Amazon S3 or export S3 data using a shipped device.
Key facts: Snowball Edge Storage Optimized is intended for large transfers; Compute Optimized is suited to demanding local processing.; A single Storage Optimized device can transfer approximately 210 TB; larger datasets can use multiple devices.; Snowball Edge supports local data transfer through an S3-compatible endpoint or NFS file interface and can import data into Amazon S3.; Device provisioning and preparation may take up to four weeks, separate from loading, shipping, and unloading time.; Snowball Edge is available only to existing customers, not new customers.
Gotchas: Do not select Snowball Edge for a new customer merely because physical transfer sounds attractive; the supplied documentation says new customers cannot order it.; Shipping a device is not a substitute for recurring online synchronization.; Do not assume a shipped device provides immediate delivery; account for provisioning and shipping.; Do not delete the source data immediately after returning an import device; confirm successful ingestion into S3 first.
Confused with: AWS DataSync: Use DataSync for online migration or scheduled synchronization when usable network connectivity is available; Snowball Edge physically transports data.; AWS Transfer Family: Transfer Family preserves partners' SFTP, FTPS, FTP, or AS2 client workflows; it is not an offline bulk-transport device.
ES: AWS Snowball Edge es un dispositivo que se envía físicamente para mover grandes conjuntos de datos cuando la transferencia en línea no es viable, o para ejecutar almacenamiento y cómputo en sitios desconectados. En un escenario de examen, elígelo para transporte físico o procesamiento local, no para sincronización en línea habitual, y verifica si el cliente puede solicitarlo. Snowball Edge Storage Optimized está orientado a transferencias grandes; Compute Optimized es apropiado para procesamiento local exigente.; Un dispositivo Storage Optimized puede transferir aproximadamente 210 TB; para conjuntos mayores puedes usar varios dispositivos.; Snowball Edge permite copiar datos localmente mediante un endpoint compatible con S3 o una interfaz NFS, e importar datos a Amazon S3.; El aprovisionamiento y la preparación pueden tardar hasta cuatro semanas, sin contar la carga, el envío y la descarga.; Snowball Edge solo está disponible para clientes existentes, no para clientes nuevos.

chunks.title: AWS Snow Family (Snowball Edge, Snowcone)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retail chain must copy updates from its store file shares to Amazon S3 every night. The stores have reliable network connections, and the team wants scheduled online transfers rather than arranging device shipments for each update. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure AWS DataSync to transfer the file-share updates to Amazon S3 on a schedule.
Why: The requirement is recurring, scheduled transfer over reliable connections. AWS DataSync matches that online synchronization pattern. Snowball Edge addresses physical transport or edge processing, neither of which is needed for nightly updates. Transfer Family is appropriate when retaining a file-transfer client protocol is the deciding requirement, not when scheduling file-share synchronization is the goal.
Wrong options: Configure AWS Transfer Family endpoints and have each store upload updates with an SFTP client. (An SFTP endpoint does not itself provide the requested scheduled synchronization of file shares.); Send Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices to the stores for each nightly update. (Repeated physical shipments do not meet the requested scheduled online workflow.); Deploy Snowball Edge Compute Optimized devices and process each update at the stores. (Local edge processing does not address the requested scheduled online transfer.)

chunks.title: AWS Snow Family (Snowball Edge, Snowcone)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A shipping company that already uses Snowball Edge collects high-resolution sensor data aboard vessels with intermittent connectivity. Crews must run substantial analytics locally during voyages and later transfer the collected data to AWS. Which solution best meets the local processing requirement?
Correct: Use Snowball Edge Compute Optimized devices to process data aboard the vessels before transferring it to AWS.
Why: The crews need analytics during voyages, not only after data reaches AWS. Snowball Edge Compute Optimized is intended for demanding processing in locations with limited connectivity. Storage Optimized is the more natural choice when the primary task is bulk transport. Online transfers through DataSync or Transfer Family do not supply the required local processing.
Wrong options: Schedule AWS DataSync transfers from each vessel and run the analytics after the data reaches AWS. (Processing after an online transfer does not satisfy the requirement to analyze data locally during voyages.); Use AWS Transfer Family to receive uploads from the vessels, then process the data in AWS. (A managed transfer endpoint does not provide disconnected local analytics aboard the vessels.); Use Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices primarily to transport the raw data for later processing. (Transporting raw data for later processing misses the stated need for substantial processing during voyages.)

chunks.title: Amazon SNS pub/sub and SNS-to-SQS fan-out
chunks.text:
Amazon SNS pub/sub and SNS-to-SQS fan-out. Amazon SNS publishes a message to a topic and pushes it to multiple subscribers. Choose SNS-to-SQS fan-out when independent applications must each receive the event and keep their own queue for later processing.
When to use: One event must reach multiple independent subscribers.; Different applications need their own queued copy of an event for asynchronous processing.; A notification must reach endpoints such as Lambda, HTTP(S), email, or SMS.
Key facts: SNS publishers send messages to a topic; SNS delivers them to subscribed endpoints.; Fan-out replicates and pushes a published message to multiple endpoints.; SQS subscribers retain messages for applications to process later.; SNS uses push delivery; SQS consumers use a polling model.
Gotchas: A single shared SQS queue does not give every independent application its own copy of each event.; SNS delivery to a subscriber is not the same as retaining an event in that subscriber's SQS queue.; Do not choose workflow orchestration when the requirement is simply to notify independent subscribers.
Confused with: Amazon SQS: SQS buffers messages for polling consumers; SNS fans one publication out to multiple subscribers.; Amazon EventBridge: Choose EventBridge for requirements centered on AWS or SaaS events, routing rules, or schedules; choose SNS for the stated publish/subscribe fan-out.; AWS Step Functions: Step Functions coordinates steps in a workflow; SNS distributes a notification to independent subscribers.
ES: Amazon SNS publica un mensaje en un tema y lo envía mediante push a varios suscriptores. Elige fan-out de SNS a SQS cuando varias aplicaciones independientes deban recibir el evento y conservarlo en sus propias colas para procesarlo después. Los publicadores envían mensajes a un tema de SNS, que los entrega a los endpoints suscritos.; Fan-out replica y envía mediante push un mensaje publicado a varios endpoints.; Los suscriptores de SQS conservan mensajes para que las aplicaciones los procesen después.; SNS usa entrega push; los consumidores de SQS consultan la cola mediante polling.

chunks.title: Amazon SNS pub/sub and SNS-to-SQS fan-out
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company already publishes each uploaded-video notification to an SNS topic. It is adding a review application that may be unavailable during maintenance, but must later process every notification without delaying existing subscribers. Which change meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Subscribe a dedicated SQS queue for review to the existing SNS topic.
Why: The new application needs its own retained notifications while existing subscribers continue independently. Subscribing a dedicated SQS queue to the SNS topic adds an asynchronous processing path without replacing the publisher's fan-out. A shared queue fails because it does not supply a separate copy to each subscriber.
Wrong options: Replace the topic with a Step Functions workflow that runs review before other subscribers. (Running review first could delay others and does not provide review its own queue.); Have an existing subscriber forward notifications to review after it completes processing. (Review would depend on that subscriber rather than receive notifications independently.); Replace the SNS topic with a single SQS queue shared by review and the existing subscribers. (A shared queue would not give every subscriber its own copy of each notification.)

chunks.title: Amazon SNS pub/sub and SNS-to-SQS fan-out
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab publishes a new-sample event once. Its cataloging and quality-control teams run separate applications, and each must eventually process every event even if its application pauses. The lab wants managed messaging rather than application-to-application forwarding. Which two design elements meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Subscribe a separate SQS queue for each application to the topic. + Publish each new-sample event to an SNS topic.
Why: One publication must reach both applications, and each needs events available after a pause. Publish to an SNS topic and subscribe a separate SQS queue for each application. A single shared queue buffers events but does not give both applications an independent copy.
Wrong options: Make cataloging forward processed events directly to quality control. (This makes quality control dependent on cataloging and uses the forwarding the lab wants to avoid.); Use one SQS queue shared by both applications as their only event destination. (One shared queue does not give both applications their own copy of every event.); Run the applications as sequential steps of a Step Functions workflow. (Sequential steps do not meet the requirement for independent processing from each application's own retained events.)

chunks.title: Amazon SNS pub/sub and SNS-to-SQS fan-out
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company records each new reservation as one event. Its billing and analytics applications both need every event, but either application may be offline while the other continues processing. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Publish each event to an SNS topic subscribed to separate SQS queues for billing and analytics.
Why: The deciding requirement is that both applications receive every reservation and can process it independently after downtime. An SNS topic with a separate SQS subscription for each application provides fan-out plus queued messages for later processing. A single SQS queue buffers events but does not give each application its own copy.
Wrong options: Start a Step Functions workflow that runs billing before analytics. (A sequential workflow couples the two applications instead of giving each an independently retained event.); Invoke billing from the publisher, then have billing invoke analytics. (Analytics depends on billing being available and completing its work.); Send each event to one SQS queue polled by both billing and analytics. (A shared queue does not provide each application with its own copy of every event.)

chunks.title: Spot Instances, interruptions and Spot Fleet
chunks.text:
Spot Instances, interruptions and Spot Fleet. Spot Instances use spare EC2 capacity at a discount, but EC2 can interrupt them when it needs capacity back. Choose Spot for work that can be retried, resumed, or delayed—not work that must run without interruption.
When to use: Batch, analysis, or background jobs can tolerate interruptions.; Workers are stateless or can checkpoint progress and resume.; The workload can use multiple instance types and Availability Zones rather than depend on one Spot capacity pool.
Key facts: A Spot capacity pool consists of one instance type in one Availability Zone.; EC2 provides a two-minute interruption notice for termination or stopping; for hibernation, the notice arrives when hibernation begins.; An EC2 instance rebalance recommendation can signal elevated interruption risk before that notice.; An interruption can terminate, stop, or hibernate an instance, depending on the request's interruption behavior.; A persistent Spot request is resubmitted after interruption; it does not preserve the interrupted job's progress.; Savings Plans do not add a discount to Spot usage, and Spot spend does not apply toward Compute Savings Plans commitments.
Gotchas: A two-minute notice for termination or stopping is time to react, not a promise that the job will finish; hibernation has no two-minute window.; Setting a maximum Spot price can increase interruptions.; A persistent request can seek another instance, but the application must still recover its work.
Confused with: Savings Plans: A Savings Plan does not stack an additional discount on Spot Instances or count Spot spend toward a Compute Savings Plans commitment.; On-Demand Instances: On-Demand avoids Spot's capacity-reclamation interruptions; Spot suits work that can tolerate them.
ES: Las Spot Instances usan capacidad EC2 disponible a un precio reducido, pero EC2 puede interrumpirlas cuando necesita recuperar esa capacidad. Elige Spot para trabajo que puedas reintentar, reanudar o posponer, no para trabajo que deba ejecutarse sin interrupciones. Un pool de capacidad Spot corresponde a un tipo de instancia en una Availability Zone.; EC2 envía un aviso de interrupción con dos minutos de anticipación si termina o detiene la instancia; si la hiberna, el aviso llega cuando comienza la hibernación.; Una EC2 instance rebalance recommendation puede señalar un mayor riesgo antes de ese aviso.; Una interrupción puede terminar, detener o hibernar una instancia, según el comportamiento configurado en la solicitud.; Una solicitud Spot persistente se vuelve a enviar después de una interrupción; no conserva el progreso del trabajo.; Savings Plans no añade otro descuento al uso de Spot, y el gasto en Spot no cuenta para los compromisos de Compute Savings Plans.

chunks.title: Spot Instances, interruptions and Spot Fleet
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media archive distributes retryable encoding tasks among Spot workers that already use several instance types and Availability Zones. The team wants workers to respond both to early signs of interruption risk and to the final warning so that less work must be repeated. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use the two-minute interruption notice to checkpoint active tasks before the worker is interrupted. + Act on EC2 instance rebalance recommendations by shifting pending tasks to other workers.
Why: The scenario asks for responses to two distinct signals: early elevated risk and the final interruption warning. Rebalance recommendations support proactive task movement, while the two-minute notice provides a window to checkpoint active work. Neither signal guarantees that an instance will remain available. Persistent requests seek replacement capacity but do not restore in-memory task progress.
Wrong options: Rely on persistent Spot requests to restore each interrupted task's in-memory progress. (A persistent request resubmits the instance request, not the interrupted task's in-memory progress.); Set a maximum Spot price to prevent EC2 from interrupting workers for capacity. (A maximum price cannot prevent capacity interruptions and can increase interruptions.); Move all tasks to one instance type in one Availability Zone to avoid changing Spot pools. (This concentrates the workload in one Spot pool instead of addressing interruption risk or saving progress.)

chunks.title: Spot Instances, interruptions and Spot Fleet
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab runs nightly simulations that save progress periodically and can resume on another worker. Jobs may finish later if EC2 capacity becomes scarce, but the lab wants to reduce compute costs and avoid dependence on a single Spot capacity pool. Which approach meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use Spot workers across multiple instance types and Availability Zones, and checkpoint when an interruption notice arrives.
Why: The simulations can resume and have flexible completion times, so interruptions are acceptable. Spot offers discounted spare capacity, and using different instance types and Availability Zones avoids relying on just one pool. Checkpointing lets workers recover after an interruption. A single-pool design misses the explicit capacity-diversity requirement.
Wrong options: Use Spot workers of one instance type and apply a Compute Savings Plans commitment for an additional Spot discount. (Savings Plans do not add savings to Spot usage, and this design still depends on one instance type.); Use Spot workers of one instance type in one Availability Zone, and checkpoint when an interruption notice arrives. (One instance type in one Availability Zone leaves the jobs dependent on a single Spot capacity pool.); Use only On-Demand workers across multiple Availability Zones, and keep the existing checkpoints. (On-Demand does not use the discounted spare capacity that these interruptible jobs can tolerate.)

chunks.title: Spot Instances, interruptions and Spot Fleet
chunks.text:
Scenario: A mapping company runs restartable tile-generation jobs on Spot Instances. Its workers can transfer pending jobs to replacement workers, and the team wants to act before an interruption notice when EC2 detects increased risk. Which solution BEST addresses that requirement?
Correct: Use EC2 instance rebalance recommendations to start transferring jobs, and use interruption notices for final cleanup.
Why: The team specifically wants a signal before the two-minute interruption notice. EC2 instance rebalance recommendations indicate elevated interruption risk and provide an opportunity to shift work proactively. The interruption notice remains useful for final cleanup. Waiting for that notice alone misses the early-action requirement, and a persistent request does not transfer pending jobs.
Wrong options: Use persistent Spot requests and assume interrupted workers will retain their pending jobs. (Resubmitting a Spot request does not preserve application work on an interrupted worker.); Set a low maximum Spot price so that workers remain available until their jobs finish. (A specified maximum price can increase interruptions rather than ensure completion.); Wait for each two-minute interruption notice before beginning any transfer of pending jobs. (This does not act on the earlier signal of elevated interruption risk.)

chunks.title: Queue-based load leveling and scaling consumers on backlog
chunks.text:
Queue-based load leveling and scaling consumers on backlog. Put work in Amazon SQS to decouple incoming requests from consumers during bursts. For EC2 queue workers, scale on backlog per InService instance—not raw queue depth—and set the target from acceptable queue delay and processing time.
When to use: Requests arrive faster than workers can process them during unpredictable spikes.; EC2 workers must scale to meet a specified queue-delay target.; A Lambda function can process queued work without managing EC2 workers.
Key facts: Backlog per instance is the number of messages available for retrieval divided by the Auto Scaling group's InService instance count.; The acceptable backlog-per-instance target is acceptable queue latency divided by average processing time per message.; Metric math can avoid the cost and effort of publishing a custom backlog-per-instance metric.; Lambda polls SQS through an event source mapping; the queue and function must be in the same Region, but may be in different accounts.; Lambda's SQS event source mapping processes messages at least once, so function code should be idempotent.
Gotchas: Raw visible-message count alone does not account for how many EC2 workers are processing the queue.; A failed Lambda batch is retried after the visibility timeout by default, including messages that succeeded earlier in that batch.; Terminating an EC2 worker returns its unfinished messages to the queue; consider scale-in protection for long-running work.
Confused with: 
ES: Coloca el trabajo en Amazon SQS para desacoplar las solicitudes entrantes de los consumidores durante los picos. Si usas trabajadores EC2, escala según el backlog por instancia InService, no solo por la cantidad total de mensajes, y calcula el objetivo a partir de la demora aceptable y el tiempo de procesamiento. El backlog por instancia es la cantidad de mensajes disponibles para recuperar dividida entre las instancias InService del Auto Scaling group.; El objetivo de backlog aceptable por instancia es la latencia aceptable en la cola dividida entre el tiempo promedio de procesamiento por mensaje.; Metric math puede evitar el costo y el esfuerzo de publicar una métrica personalizada de backlog por instancia.; Lambda consulta SQS mediante un event source mapping; la cola y la función deben estar en la misma Región, aunque pueden estar en cuentas distintas.; El event source mapping de SQS para Lambda procesa los mensajes al menos una vez; por eso, tu función debe ser idempotente.

chunks.title: Queue-based load leveling and scaling consumers on backlog
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing platform sends reservation updates to an SQS queue, and a Lambda function processes them in batches. Occasionally one update fails after other updates in the same batch have succeeded. The team wants to avoid retrying those successful updates while continuing to process the failed one. Which change meets this requirement with the LEAST custom deletion logic?
Correct: Implement partial batch responses that identify the failed records.
Why: By default, a Lambda failure makes all messages in the SQS batch visible again after the visibility timeout. Partial batch response logic identifies failed records so successfully processed records need not be retried. Increasing the timeout merely postpones the retry; idempotency remains important because duplicate processing can still occur. Partial batch responses meet the selective-retry requirement without per-message DeleteMessage calls.
Wrong options: Reduce the Lambda batch window so the function receives records sooner. (The batch window affects when records are invoked, not which records are retried after a failure.); Keep the default batch failure behavior and make each update idempotent. (Idempotency limits duplicate side effects but does not avoid retrying successful records.); Increase the SQS visibility timeout so the entire batch stays hidden longer. (A longer visibility timeout delays retries but does not distinguish successful records from failed ones.)

chunks.title: Queue-based load leveling and scaling consumers on backlog
chunks.text:
Scenario: A document-processing company receives submissions in brief surges, but its EC2 workers take much longer to process each document than the front end takes to accept it. The company wants to buffer accepted work and scale its worker Auto Scaling group according to an acceptable queue-delay target, with minimal metric-publishing effort. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Place accepted document jobs in an SQS queue for the EC2 workers to retrieve. + Use metric math to target available messages per InService instance based on acceptable delay and average processing time.
Why: SQS separates the quick submission path from slower document processing so jobs can wait for workers during a surge. For EC2 Auto Scaling, target tracking should use backlog per InService instance; its target follows from acceptable queue delay divided by average time per document. Metric math avoids publishing that value as a custom metric. Raw visible-message count omits fleet size, while a published custom metric misses the minimal-effort requirement.
Wrong options: Set a target tracking policy directly on the queue's visible-message count. (Raw queue depth does not account for the number of workers or the acceptable delay per worker.); Publish a custom metric for available messages per InService instance. (The metric could support scaling, but publishing it adds effort that metric math can avoid.); Set the worker group's minimum capacity to the fleet size required for every surge. (A fixed surge-sized fleet does not scale capacity according to the queue-delay target.)

chunks.title: Queue-based load leveling and scaling consumers on backlog
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab's EC2 Auto Scaling group processes simulation jobs from SQS. Some jobs run for a long time, and the group must scale in when demand falls. The lab wants an active worker to finish its current job before it is selected for scale-in, while still allowing idle workers to terminate. Which approach meets these requirements?
Correct: Enable instance scale-in protection while a worker processes a job, then remove it when the worker is idle.
Why: The deciding requirement is to finish a long-running job before its worker is selected for scale-in. Instance scale-in protection can be set during processing and removed while the worker is idle. If an instance is terminated with unfinished messages, those messages return to SQS for another worker, but that does not satisfy the lab's preference to let active jobs finish. A visibility timeout does not control which EC2 instance scales in.
Wrong options: Increase the SQS visibility timeout and leave scale-in behavior unchanged. (Visibility timeout does not stop the Auto Scaling group from terminating an active worker.); Keep every worker protected from scale-in for the lifetime of the instance. (Permanent protection conflicts with the requirement to terminate idle workers.); Scale in when the queue has no visible messages, without tracking workers' active jobs. (A queue can have no available messages while workers are still processing jobs.)

chunks.title: Amazon SQS standard vs FIFO queues
chunks.text:
Amazon SQS standard vs FIFO queues. Amazon SQS buffers messages so producers and consumers can scale independently. Choose a standard queue when at-least-once delivery and high scale are acceptable; choose a FIFO queue when message order and avoidance of queue-introduced duplicates are required.
When to use: Use a standard queue to absorb traffic spikes when consumers can tolerate and handle repeated deliveries.; Use a FIFO queue when operations must be received in the order sent.; Use FIFO message groups when separate streams each need ordering within one queue.
Key facts: Standard queues support at-least-once delivery.; FIFO queues preserve the order in which messages are sent and received and do not introduce duplicates into the queue.; FIFO queues support exactly-once processing, but have a limited transactions-per-second rate; high-throughput mode can increase the transaction limit.; A consumer must delete a processed message; during its visibility timeout, the message remains in the queue but is not returned to subsequent receive requests.
Gotchas: Do not select a standard queue when the scenario requires strict message ordering or cannot tolerate queue-introduced duplicates.; Do not assume FIFO has the same throughput characteristics as a standard queue; consider FIFO high-throughput mode when both ordering and greater throughput matter.; SQS provides a queue for consumers, not topic-based distribution to multiple independent subscriber groups.
Confused with: Amazon SNS: SNS distributes a publication to multiple subscribers; SQS buffers messages for queue consumers.; Amazon MQ: Amazon MQ fits migration of applications dependent on existing broker protocols; SQS offers a queue with a simple API.; AWS Step Functions: Step Functions orchestrates workflow steps; SQS buffers work for independent consumers.
ES: Amazon SQS almacena mensajes en una cola para que productores y consumidores escalen de forma independiente. Elige una cola standard si aceptas entregas at-least-once y necesitas alta escala; elige una cola FIFO si necesitas orden y evitar duplicados introducidos por la cola. Las colas standard admiten entrega at-least-once.; Las colas FIFO conservan el orden de envío y recepción y no introducen duplicados en la cola.; Las colas FIFO admiten exactly-once processing, pero tienen una tasa limitada de transacciones por segundo; high-throughput mode puede aumentar ese límite.; El consumidor debe eliminar el mensaje procesado; durante el visibility timeout, el mensaje permanece en la cola, pero no se devuelve en solicitudes de recepción posteriores.

chunks.title: Amazon SQS standard vs FIFO queues
chunks.text:
Scenario: A laboratory sends instrument commands to a processing service through a message queue. For each instrument, commands must be received in the order submitted, and the queue must not introduce duplicate commands. Commands from different instruments may be processed independently. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue with a separate message group for each instrument.
Why: Each instrument needs its own ordered command stream, and the queue must not introduce duplicates. An SQS FIFO queue provides those properties, and message groups allow multiple ordered streams in one queue. A standard queue supports at-least-once delivery and does not satisfy the stated ordering requirement. Amazon MQ addresses broker compatibility, which the laboratory has not requested.
Wrong options: Use an Amazon SQS standard queue and attach the instrument ID to each message. (Adding an ID does not give a standard queue strict ordering or prevent queue-introduced duplicates.); Publish commands to an Amazon SNS topic with a separate subscriber for each instrument. (SNS distributes messages to subscribers rather than providing the required FIFO queue behavior.); Use an Amazon MQ broker for every instrument without changing the application's messaging API. (The scenario does not require compatibility with an existing broker protocol, which is the reason to favor Amazon MQ.)

chunks.title: Amazon SQS standard vs FIFO queues
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing platform uses an Amazon SQS standard queue to pass purchase requests from its website to workers. It is launching an event where requests must be received in the order submitted, and the queue must not introduce duplicates. The team also expects increased transaction volume and wants to retain a managed queue. Which change best meets these requirements?
Correct: Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue and consider its high-throughput mode for the increased volume.
Why: The new requirements are ordered receipt and no duplicates introduced by the queue, so a standard queue is no longer the right type. SQS FIFO provides these properties while retaining a managed queue. FIFO has a limited transactions-per-second rate, and its high-throughput mode can increase the transaction limit. Adding workers to the standard queue cannot change its delivery guarantees.
Wrong options: Replace the queue with an Amazon MQ broker to retain purchase-request order. (No existing broker protocol compatibility requirement justifies replacing SQS with Amazon MQ.); Keep the SQS standard queue and increase the number of workers. (More workers do not add FIFO ordering or prevent queue-introduced duplicates.); Replace the queue with an Amazon SNS topic to distribute requests to workers. (SNS provides subscriber distribution rather than the required ordered work queue.)

chunks.title: Amazon SQS standard vs FIFO queues
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher wants each completed manuscript to trigger two independent jobs: format an ebook and prepare a print layout. Each team needs its own durable queue so its workers can consume jobs at a different pace; neither job requires ordering. Which architecture meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Publish manuscripts to an Amazon SNS topic subscribed to by a separate Amazon SQS standard queue for each team.
Why: The deciding requirement is not simply buffering work: both teams must receive every manuscript in their own queue. An SNS topic can fan out publications to separate SQS queues, allowing each team to consume at its own pace. Because neither job needs ordering, standard queues fit. A single shared SQS queue does not give both teams an independent queue containing each manuscript.
Wrong options: Put manuscripts in one Amazon SQS standard queue and have both teams poll that queue. (A shared queue does not give each team its own copy and independent queue of every manuscript.); Put manuscripts in one Amazon SQS FIFO queue and use one message group per team. (Message groups do not distribute a copy of each manuscript to two independent consumer queues.); Publish manuscripts to one Amazon SNS topic with both teams subscribed directly. (Direct subscriptions do not provide the separate durable SQS queues explicitly required for each team.)

chunks.title: SQS visibility timeout, dead-letter queues, long polling, delay queues
chunks.text:
SQS visibility timeout, dead-letter queues, long polling, delay queues. A received SQS message stays in the queue but is temporarily invisible to other consumers. Set the visibility timeout to cover processing and deletion, extend it when work runs long, and use a dead-letter queue (DLQ) to isolate messages that repeatedly fail.
When to use: Workers need time to process messages without another worker picking them up prematurely.; Processing duration varies, so workers must extend visibility while work continues.; Repeatedly failing messages need separate inspection without circulating indefinitely in the source queue.; Consumers poll an often-empty queue; long polling can reduce empty receives.
Key facts: The default visibility timeout is 30 seconds; an undeleted message becomes visible again when its timeout expires.; ChangeMessageVisibility can adjust a received message’s timeout, but extensions cannot exceed 12 hours from its first receipt.; Delete messages after successful processing. Visibility timeout does not guarantee that a message will never be delivered more than once.; A DLQ must be in the same AWS account and Region as its source queue. The source queue’s redrive policy sets maxReceiveCount.; For a standard queue, set DLQ retention longer than source-queue retention because expiration remains based on the original enqueue timestamp.; At the standard-queue in-flight limit, long polling returns no new messages rather than an OverLimit error.
Gotchas: A visibility timeout that is too short permits premature reprocessing; one that is too long delays retries after a worker fails.; Extending visibility does not reset the 12-hour limit.; A DLQ can break the exact order required by some FIFO workflows.; Long polling does not resolve a backlog of received but undeleted messages.
Confused with: 
ES: Un mensaje recibido de SQS permanece en la cola, pero queda temporalmente invisible para otros consumidores. Ajusta el visibility timeout para cubrir el procesamiento y la eliminación, extiéndelo cuando el trabajo tarde más y usa una dead-letter queue (DLQ) para aislar mensajes que fallan repetidamente. El visibility timeout predeterminado es de 30 segundos; un mensaje no eliminado vuelve a estar visible cuando vence.; ChangeMessageVisibility permite ajustar el timeout de un mensaje recibido, pero las extensiones no pueden superar las 12 horas desde su primera recepción.; Elimina los mensajes después de procesarlos correctamente. El visibility timeout no garantiza que un mensaje nunca se entregue más de una vez.; La DLQ debe estar en la misma cuenta y AWS Region que la cola de origen. La redrive policy de la cola de origen establece maxReceiveCount.; Para una cola standard, configura una retención de la DLQ mayor que la de la cola de origen, porque la expiración sigue basándose en la marca de tiempo de envío original.; Cuando una cola standard alcanza el límite de mensajes in-flight, long polling deja de devolver mensajes nuevos en lugar de generar un error OverLimit.

chunks.title: SQS visibility timeout, dead-letter queues, long polling, delay queues
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing platform uses long polling on a busy SQS standard queue. During a surge, approximately 120,000 messages have been received but not deleted, and long-polling requests stop returning new messages without reporting OverLimit. An audit shows that workers finish processing but frequently leave completed messages in the queue. Which change should the platform make to restore deliveries MOST directly?
Correct: Delete messages promptly after successful processing and monitor the in-flight message count.
Why: The decisive constraint is the in-flight backlog, not an empty queue. At the approximate standard-queue in-flight limit, long polling returns no new messages rather than an OverLimit error. Promptly deleting successfully processed messages reduces that count; monitoring helps detect the condition before deliveries stall. Increasing the polling wait or visibility timeout does not remove completed messages from the in-flight count.
Wrong options: Extend visibility for all received messages until the long-polling requests return new messages. (Visibility extensions leave the messages in flight and do not clear the condition blocking new deliveries.); Increase the long-polling wait so each request has more time to receive a message. (A longer wait does not make new messages available while the in-flight limit is reached.); Lower maxReceiveCount so completed messages move to a DLQ sooner. (A DLQ handles messages that are not successfully processed; it does not replace deletion after successful processing.)

chunks.title: SQS visibility timeout, dead-letter queues, long polling, delay queues
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company uses an SQS queue to distribute rendering jobs among workers. Most jobs finish quickly, but some take several minutes; those longer jobs sometimes become visible to another worker before the first worker finishes. The company also wants failed workers’ jobs to become eligible for retry without an unnecessarily long delay. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Set a reasonable initial visibility timeout, extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility while a worker is still processing, and delete the message after success.
Why: The deciding requirements are variable processing time and prompt retries after worker failure. Workers can extend visibility only while they need it, then delete successfully processed messages. A uniformly long timeout would delay failed jobs from becoming visible again, while a DLQ does not solve premature visibility during active processing. Visibility timeout reduces concurrent processing but is not an absolute duplicate-delivery guarantee.
Wrong options: Set a long, fixed visibility timeout for every job and leave each message in the queue after successful processing. (A long fixed timeout can delay retries, and leaving completed messages undeleted allows them to reappear.); Increase the queue’s long-polling wait and delete each message as soon as a worker receives it. (Long polling does not extend visibility, and deleting before processing prevents a failed job from being retried.); Set a low maxReceiveCount and move jobs to a DLQ after their first unsuccessful attempt. (A DLQ isolates failures but does not keep an active long-running job invisible until its worker finishes.)

chunks.title: Systems Manager Parameter Store
chunks.text:
Systems Manager Parameter Store. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store centrally stores application configuration as named parameters, including KMS-encrypted SecureString values. Choose standard parameters for low-scale, static configuration when automatic rotation and managed deployment safeguards are not required.
When to use: Applications need centrally managed endpoint URLs, resource IDs, or approved AMI IDs.; Configuration should be organized by application and environment in hierarchical paths.; A value needs encryption, but automatic rotation is not required.; Standard-tier limits meet the need and minimizing storage cost matters.
Key facts: Parameter types are String, StringList, and SecureString; SecureString uses AWS KMS encryption.; The standard tier has no additional charge; advanced parameters and higher throughput incur charges.; Standard parameters support values up to 4 KB and up to 10,000 parameters per account and Region.; IAM policies can restrict parameter access by path and grant permission to decrypt encrypted values.; A parameter update takes effect on the next read; Parameter Store does not validate changes, gradually roll them out, or automatically revert them.
Gotchas: Parameter Store has no built-in credential rotation; AWS recommends Secrets Manager for database credentials, API keys, and other secrets.; A changed Parameter Store value injected into an ECS task environment variable is not picked up by an already-running task.; Standard parameters cannot be shared across AWS accounts; that capability requires advanced parameters.; The standard tier being free does not mean higher-throughput mode is free.
Confused with: AWS Secrets Manager: Prefer Secrets Manager for credentials and other secrets, especially when automatic rotation is required; use Parameter Store for static configuration without rotation.; AWS AppConfig: AppConfig adds validation, gradual rollout, and alarm-based rollback; a Parameter Store update simply applies on the next read.
ES: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store almacena de forma centralizada la configuración de aplicaciones como parámetros con nombre, incluidos valores SecureString cifrados con AWS KMS. Elige parámetros standard para configuración estática de baja escala cuando no necesitas rotación automática ni controles administrados para el despliegue de cambios. Los tipos de parámetros son String, StringList y SecureString; SecureString usa cifrado de AWS KMS.; El nivel standard no tiene cargo adicional; los parámetros advanced y el mayor throughput generan cargos.; Los parámetros standard admiten valores de hasta 4 KB y hasta 10 000 parámetros por cuenta y Región.; Las políticas de IAM pueden limitar el acceso por ruta y conceder permiso para descifrar valores cifrados.; Una actualización se aplica en la siguiente lectura; Parameter Store no valida los cambios, no los despliega gradualmente ni los revierte automáticamente.

chunks.title: Systems Manager Parameter Store
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer keeps a static internal service identifier in application configuration. Its security policy requires the stored value to be encrypted with AWS KMS, but the value is not a credential and does not need rotation. The application has a low request rate, and the team wants to avoid paying for capabilities it does not use. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Store the identifier as a standard SecureString parameter in Systems Manager Parameter Store.
Why: This is an encrypted configuration value, not a credential requiring rotation. Parameter Store SecureString provides AWS KMS encryption, and the standard tier is appropriate for the stated low-scale need. A plain String misses encryption; an advanced parameter or Secrets Manager adds cost without meeting an additional requirement.
Wrong options: Store the identifier as a standard String parameter in Systems Manager Parameter Store. (A String parameter is plain text and does not satisfy the encryption requirement.); Store the identifier as an advanced SecureString parameter in Systems Manager Parameter Store. (SecureString provides encryption, but the advanced tier adds charges without a stated need for advanced capabilities.); Store the identifier in AWS Secrets Manager and enable automatic rotation. (Secrets Manager adds charges and rotation is unnecessary for this static, noncredential value.)

chunks.title: Systems Manager Parameter Store
chunks.text:
Scenario: A healthcare analytics team stores production and development application settings in one AWS account. Some settings are noncredential identifiers that must be encrypted, while others are plain-text endpoint URLs. Applications need IAM access limited to their own environment, and the team does not need rotation or cross-account sharing. Which two design choices meet these requirements while retaining standard-tier parameters? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use distinct hierarchical paths for each environment and restrict application access to the relevant path with IAM. + Store identifiers as standard SecureString parameters and endpoint URLs as standard String parameters.
Why: The two decisions are how to separate access by environment and how to encrypt only the values that require it. Hierarchical paths with IAM restrictions address environment-specific access; standard SecureString and String parameters address the two value types. Plain String identifiers fail the encryption requirement, while advanced parameters solve an unneeded cross-account-sharing problem at additional cost.
Wrong options: Use standard String parameters for the identifiers to keep every setting in one parameter type. (String parameters are plain text and do not satisfy the requirement to encrypt the identifiers.); Place every setting in AWS Secrets Manager to separate development from production. (Secrets Manager is unnecessary for these configuration values and incurs charges when standard parameters meet the requirements.); Use advanced parameters for all settings to enable sharing between AWS accounts. (Cross-account sharing is not required, and advanced parameters would not retain the requested standard-tier design.)

chunks.title: Stateless vs stateful workloads and session state
chunks.text:
Stateless vs stateful workloads and session state. A stateless application does not depend on session data stored on the instance that handled a previous request. Offload session state to a shared service such as Amazon ElastiCache or Amazon DynamoDB so any instance can serve the next request and an instance can be replaced without losing the session.
When to use: Users must keep their sessions when an application instance fails or is replaced.; A web tier must scale horizontally without tying users to particular instances.; Application components need to scale independently.
Key facts: Session data persists across requests; a stateless application does not store that data locally.; Amazon ElastiCache and Amazon DynamoDB are examples of services that can hold offloaded session data.; With a stateless design, any available compute resource can serve a request.; Amazon S3 can hold large, unstructured data such as images and documents, while DynamoDB can hold information such as user profiles.
Gotchas: Sticky sessions can route a user back to the same instance, but they do not remove the dependency on that instance's local session data.; Adding instances does not fix a session design that requires each user to reach one particular instance.; Moving images or user profiles to shared storage does not help if session data remains local.
Confused with: Sticky sessions: Request affinity is a workaround for local state; offloading session state removes the need to reach a particular instance.
ES: Una aplicación sin estado no depende de los datos de sesión guardados en la instancia que atendió una solicitud anterior. Guarda el estado de sesión fuera de las instancias, por ejemplo, en Amazon ElastiCache o Amazon DynamoDB, para que cualquier instancia atienda la siguiente solicitud sin perder la sesión si se reemplaza una instancia. Los datos de sesión persisten entre solicitudes; una aplicación sin estado no los guarda localmente.; Amazon ElastiCache y Amazon DynamoDB son ejemplos de servicios donde puedes guardar los datos de sesión fuera de las instancias.; Con un diseño sin estado, cualquier recurso de cómputo disponible puede atender una solicitud.; Amazon S3 puede almacenar datos no estructurados grandes, como imágenes y documentos, mientras que DynamoDB puede almacenar información como perfiles de usuario.

chunks.title: Stateless vs stateful workloads and session state
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio serves client documents through a web application on multiple EC2 instances. Each instance holds uploaded documents and editing sessions locally; replacing an instance interrupts an active editor and makes that instance's documents unavailable. The studio wants instances to be replaceable and to scale the web tier independently of stored content. Which solution best meets these requirements?
Correct: Store documents in Amazon S3 and editing sessions in Amazon ElastiCache.
Why: Two kinds of locally stored data prevent the studio from replacing instances freely. Amazon S3 can hold large, unstructured documents, and Amazon ElastiCache can hold offloaded session data. Moving only one kind of data leaves the other dependent on an instance; sticky sessions remove neither dependency.
Wrong options: Store documents in Amazon S3 but continue storing editing sessions in instance memory. (Documents are externalized, but replacing an instance still interrupts its local editing sessions.); Use sticky sessions and add EC2 instances while keeping documents and sessions locally. (Affinity and extra instances do not remove either dependency on local data.); Store editing sessions in Amazon DynamoDB but keep uploaded documents on instance disks. (Sessions are externalized, but documents still depend on the instance that stores them.)

chunks.title: Stateless vs stateful workloads and session state
chunks.text:
Scenario: A travel agency has a web tier behind a load balancer. Each server keeps itinerary-building sessions in memory, so replacing a server forces its customers to restart; the agency wants to scale servers in and out without this disruption. Which two changes together make the web tier independent of locally stored session data? (Choose two.)
Correct: Move itinerary session data to Amazon DynamoDB. + Update the application so any server can retrieve and use a customer's stored session.
Why: The agency must both move sessions off individual servers and make the application use the shared session data. DynamoDB provides an external place for that data, and letting any server retrieve it removes the dependency on the previous server. Sticky sessions, added servers, and externalized profiles alone all leave itinerary sessions in server memory.
Wrong options: Enable sticky sessions while retaining session data in server memory. (Affinity still ties a customer's session to a replaceable server.); Move customer profiles to Amazon DynamoDB but retain itinerary sessions in server memory. (Externalizing profiles does not externalize the sessions that must survive replacement.); Add web servers while keeping sessions in each server's memory. (More servers do not remove the local-state dependency.)

chunks.title: Stateless vs stateful workloads and session state
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company runs its web application on multiple EC2 instances behind a load balancer. Each instance keeps shopping sessions in memory, and customers lose their carts when an instance is replaced. The company wants to add or remove instances as demand changes. Which solution meets these requirements while allowing any instance to handle a customer's next request?
Correct: Store session data in Amazon DynamoDB and have each instance retrieve it for incoming requests.
Why: The deciding requirement is that any instance must handle the next request without losing a cart. Offloading session data to DynamoDB removes the dependency on instance memory and supports horizontal scaling. Sticky sessions may keep requests on one instance while it is available, but do not solve session loss when that instance is replaced.
Wrong options: Store customer profiles in Amazon DynamoDB but keep active carts in instance memory. (Moving profiles does not preserve the session data that contains the carts.); Use sticky sessions on the load balancer and continue storing carts in instance memory. (Affinity still leaves a cart dependent on the original instance when that instance is replaced.); Add more EC2 instances and continue storing each customer's cart in instance memory. (Additional capacity does not make a locally stored cart available to other instances.)

chunks.title: AWS Step Functions workflow orchestration
chunks.text:
AWS Step Functions workflow orchestration. AWS Step Functions orchestrates multi-step processes as state machine workflows, with branching, retries, parallel work, and tracked execution state. Choose Standard for long-running or human-approval workflows; choose Express for high-event-rate workflows that finish within five minutes and can tolerate at-least-once execution.
When to use: A process must run tasks in sequence, choose a path based on data, or retry and handle failures.; Independent tasks must run in parallel before the process continues.; A workflow must pause for a human response and resume after a callback.
Key facts: Choice states branch on input; Retry and Catch handle task failures; Parallel states run independent branches.; A Map state applies workflow steps to each item in a dataset.; Standard workflows can run for up to one year and provide execution history and visual debugging.; Express workflows can run for up to five minutes and are suited to high-event-rate workloads.; Standard supports the wait-for-callback task-token pattern for supported integrations; Express supports only Request Response integrations.; Standard has exactly-once workflow execution; Express has at-least-once workflow execution.
Gotchas: Routing an event to a target is not the same as tracking a process through multiple dependent steps.; An Express workflow is not suitable when a task must wait for a callback.; Express steps can run more than once; do not assume exactly-once workflow execution.
Confused with: Amazon SQS: SQS buffers work for consumers; Step Functions tracks and coordinates steps in a process.; Amazon SNS: SNS fans a message out to subscribers; Step Functions controls what happens before and after each task.; Amazon EventBridge: EventBridge routes events by rules; Step Functions maintains workflow state across tasks.
ES: AWS Step Functions orquesta procesos de varios pasos mediante workflows de máquinas de estados, con ramificaciones, reintentos, trabajo paralelo y seguimiento del estado. Elige Standard para procesos largos o con aprobación humana; elige Express para muchos eventos si cada ejecución termina en cinco minutos y admite ejecución at-least-once. Choice ramifica según la entrada; Retry y Catch manejan fallas; Parallel ejecuta ramas independientes.; Map aplica pasos del workflow a cada elemento de un conjunto de datos.; Standard puede durar hasta un año y ofrece historial de ejecución y depuración visual.; Express puede durar hasta cinco minutos y se adapta a cargas con una alta tasa de eventos.; Standard admite wait-for-callback con task token para integraciones compatibles; Express solo admite Request Response.; Standard tiene ejecución de workflow exactly-once; Express tiene ejecución de workflow at-least-once.

chunks.title: AWS Step Functions workflow orchestration
chunks.text:
Scenario: A property insurer validates a claim automatically, then sends claims above a threshold to an adjuster. The adjuster may take several days to respond, and processing must resume only after that response arrives. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use a Standard Step Functions workflow with a Choice state and a task-token callback.
Why: The deciding requirements are conditional routing and waiting several days for a human response. A Standard Step Functions workflow can use Choice for the threshold and a task-token callback to pause until approval arrives. Express cannot use the callback pattern, while SNS and SQS address message distribution or buffering rather than tracking this process.
Wrong options: Place claims in an Amazon SQS queue and have workers poll for claims ready for payment. (A queue buffers claims but does not itself manage the conditional, multi-day approval workflow.); Publish each claim to Amazon SNS and use separate subscribers for validation and payment. (Fan-out does not track the claim through a conditional approval step or wait for the adjuster's response.); Use an Express Step Functions workflow with a Choice state and a task-token callback. (Express workflows do not support the wait-for-callback integration pattern.)

chunks.title: AWS Step Functions workflow orchestration
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer processes a high rate of sensor readings. For each reading, it must validate the data, choose one of two enrichment steps, and send a result; every workflow finishes within a minute. The tasks tolerate at-least-once execution, and no human response or job-completion wait is needed. Which solution is the BEST fit?
Correct: Use an Express Step Functions workflow with a Choice state.
Why: Each reading requires an ordered process with a branch, so it needs workflow orchestration rather than event routing or fan-out alone. Express is suited to high-event-rate workloads, and the stated duration and at-least-once tolerance fit its behavior. Standard could perform the steps, but its long-running, auditable strengths are not the deciding requirements here.
Wrong options: Use a Standard Step Functions workflow with a Choice state. (Standard can orchestrate the steps, but Express is the better fit for the stated high-event-rate, short-duration workload.); Publish each reading to Amazon SNS with separate enrichment subscribers. (Fan-out does not choose an enrichment step after validation and track the subsequent result.); Use Amazon EventBridge rules to route each reading directly to an enrichment target. (Routing a reading to a target does not coordinate validation, conditional enrichment, and the final result as one workflow.)

chunks.title: AWS Step Functions workflow orchestration
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab processes access requests for sensitive datasets. Two independent checks must run before a request is sent to a reviewer; a failed check should be retried, and the reviewer can take several days to respond. The request must not advance until that response arrives. Which TWO design choices meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use a Standard Step Functions workflow with a task-token callback for reviewer approval. + Use Parallel branches for the checks and Retry on the check tasks before the approval step.
Why: The workflow needs both parallel checks with retries and a pause for a human response that may take days. Parallel and Retry address the checks; a Standard workflow can then wait using a task-token callback. Express lacks that callback pattern and has a five-minute maximum duration. The SNS and EventBridge designs distribute messages or events without coordinating all of these steps.
Wrong options: Use an Express Step Functions workflow so the approval task can wait for a task-token callback. (Express does not support wait-for-callback and cannot accommodate a response that takes several days.); Use Amazon EventBridge rules to invoke both checks and route their events to the reviewer. (Event routing alone does not track both check results, retry a failed check, and wait for the response.); Publish the request to Amazon SNS so reviewer and check subscribers each advance the process when finished. (Fan-out does not enforce checks-before-review or hold the process until reviewer approval.)

chunks.title: When storage auto scaling is required (RDS storage autoscaling, EFS, EBS)
chunks.text:
When storage auto scaling is required (RDS storage autoscaling, EFS, EBS). Choose storage that matches the workload before deciding how it should grow: Amazon RDS storage autoscaling for an RDS DB instance, Amazon EFS for elastic file storage, and Amazon S3 for elastic object storage. Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes can be enlarged, but a volume modification and file-system extension are not the same as automatically growing file storage.
When to use: An RDS DB instance has unpredictable storage growth and should increase allocated storage without manual intervention.; A growing file-storage workload should avoid preallocating an EBS volume.; An existing EBS volume needs more capacity while its application continues running.
Key facts: RDS storage autoscaling increases DB instance storage when free space is at most 10% of allocated storage for at least five minutes, subject to modification conditions.; The RDS maximum storage threshold must be at least 10% above currently allocated storage; AWS recommends at least 26% above it to avoid an approaching-threshold notification.; RDS storage autoscaling cannot reduce allocated storage and is not supported for additional storage volumes.; EBS Elastic Volumes can increase volume size without detaching or restarting when the instance supports the feature; extend the file system after resizing.
Gotchas: RDS autoscaling is not a guarantee against storage-full conditions during large data loads.; A low RDS maximum storage threshold can prevent the needed increase.; EBS volume modifications increase capacity but do not provide automatic storage growth or shrinkage.
Confused with: Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes: Modify an existing EBS volume when needed; use RDS storage autoscaling when an RDS DB instance must increase storage automatically.; Amazon EFS: Choose elastic file storage for a file workload, not RDS storage autoscaling, which applies to DB instance storage.
ES: Elige primero el almacenamiento que corresponde a la carga de trabajo: Amazon RDS storage autoscaling para una instancia de base de datos RDS, Amazon EFS para almacenamiento de archivos elástico y Amazon S3 para almacenamiento de objetos elástico. Amazon EBS Elastic Volumes permite ampliar un volumen, pero modificarlo y extender su sistema de archivos no equivale a crecimiento automático del almacenamiento de archivos. RDS storage autoscaling aumenta el almacenamiento de la instancia cuando el espacio libre es como máximo el 10% del almacenamiento asignado durante al menos cinco minutos, sujeto a condiciones de modificación.; El umbral máximo de almacenamiento de RDS debe superar en al menos un 10% el almacenamiento asignado; AWS recomienda al menos un 26% para evitar una notificación de proximidad al umbral.; RDS storage autoscaling no puede reducir el almacenamiento asignado y no admite volúmenes de almacenamiento adicionales.; EBS Elastic Volumes permite aumentar el tamaño sin desconectar el volumen ni reiniciar la instancia si esta admite la función; después debes extender el sistema de archivos.

chunks.title: When storage auto scaling is required (RDS storage autoscaling, EFS, EBS)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company runs its transactional database on an Amazon RDS DB instance. Ticket releases cause unpredictable but sustained increases in stored data, and the team wants to avoid sizing the database for the largest possible release. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Enable RDS storage autoscaling on the DB instance and set an appropriate maximum storage threshold.
Why: The deciding requirements are unpredictable growth in the RDS database and minimal manual intervention. RDS storage autoscaling increases DB instance storage when its low-free-space conditions are met, subject to a configured maximum threshold. Preallocating for the largest release conflicts with the sizing goal, while manual RDS changes do not meet the operational-overhead goal.
Wrong options: Use EBS Elastic Volumes to increase an application server's attached volume as releases occur. (Increasing the application server's EBS volume does not increase the RDS DB instance's storage.); Provision the DB instance with enough storage for the largest projected release. (This avoids storage modifications but requires the advance overprovisioning the team wants to avoid.); Monitor database free space and manually increase allocated RDS storage after each release. (Manual modifications add operational work for the unpredictable growth the team wants handled automatically.)

chunks.title: When storage auto scaling is required (RDS storage autoscaling, EFS, EBS)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab keeps an application dataset on an EBS volume attached to an instance that supports Elastic Volumes. The dataset has outgrown the volume, but the application must remain running and continue using its existing block device. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST disruption?
Correct: Increase the EBS volume size with Elastic Volumes, then extend its file system.
Why: The application must keep using its existing EBS block device while it remains running. Because the instance supports Elastic Volumes, the lab can increase the volume size without detaching it or restarting the instance, then extend the file system. EFS and S3 would change the storage model, and RDS storage autoscaling does not resize an application's attached EBS volume.
Wrong options: Move the dataset to Amazon S3 and have the application use object storage. (S3 changes the storage model instead of preserving the application's existing block device.); Enable RDS storage autoscaling for the instance that runs the application. (RDS storage autoscaling applies to an RDS DB instance, not this attached EBS volume.); Move the dataset to Amazon EFS and have the application use file storage. (EFS changes the application's storage from its existing block device to file storage.)

chunks.title: Storage cost optimization (right-size, gp2->gp3, tiering, delete orphans)
chunks.text:
Storage cost optimization (right-size, gp2->gp3, tiering, delete orphans). Optimize storage for the required access pattern, not just the lowest advertised price. For EBS snapshots, archive rarely accessed, long-term recovery points; keep snapshots that need fast retrieval in the standard tier.
When to use: A snapshot must be retained long term but is rarely accessed.; A recovery plan distinguishes fast restores from infrequent historical recovery.; A proposed archive saving depends on whether snapshots remain incremental.
Key facts: New EBS snapshots are stored in the standard tier by default, where snapshots are incremental.; Archiving converts an incremental snapshot to a full snapshot.; An archived snapshot must be restored to the standard tier before it can be used.; EBS Snapshots Archive offers up to 75% lower snapshot storage costs for snapshots retained for 90 days or longer and rarely accessed.
Gotchas: Do not archive a snapshot needed for frequent or fast retrieval.; Do not assume an archived snapshot retains incremental storage characteristics.; Do not plan to use an archived snapshot directly without first restoring it to the standard tier.
Confused with: EBS Snapshot Standard tier: Standard snapshots are incremental and suit recovery points that need faster access; Archive is for rarely accessed, long-term snapshots.
ES: Optimiza el almacenamiento según el patrón de acceso requerido, no solo por el precio anunciado más bajo. Para snapshots de EBS, usa Archive para puntos de recuperación de largo plazo que rara vez se consultan; conserva en Standard los que necesitan recuperación rápida. Los snapshots nuevos de EBS se guardan de forma predeterminada en Standard, donde son incrementales.; Al archivar un snapshot incremental, este se convierte en un snapshot completo.; Debes restaurar un snapshot archivado a Standard antes de poder usarlo.; EBS Snapshots Archive ofrece costos de almacenamiento hasta un 75 % menores para snapshots que se conservan por 90 días o más y rara vez se consultan.

chunks.title: Storage cost optimization (right-size, gp2->gp3, tiering, delete orphans)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A design studio closes projects after delivery and retains one final EBS snapshot for each project for two years. Staff almost never request these snapshots, and a delayed retrieval is acceptable when they do. Which storage choice meets the retention requirement MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Move each final snapshot to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier.
Why: The deciding requirements are long retention, rare access, and tolerance for delayed retrieval. EBS Snapshots Archive is designed for this pattern and offers lower snapshot storage costs for qualifying long-term snapshots. Keeping a Standard copy as well provides faster access, but that capability is unnecessary here.
Wrong options: Keep each final snapshot in the EBS Snapshot Standard tier. (Standard retains the snapshot but does not take advantage of the archive tier intended for rarely accessed, long-term snapshots.); Delete each final snapshot when its project closes. (Deletion fails the requirement to retain a recovery point for two years.); Keep each final snapshot in Standard and create an additional archived copy. (Retaining the Standard copy adds storage for fast access that the scenario does not require.)

chunks.title: Storage cost optimization (right-size, gp2->gp3, tiering, delete orphans)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher keeps recent EBS snapshots for an operations team that needs fast recovery during releases. It also retains one year-end snapshot for several years to satisfy a historical-records policy; requests for that snapshot are rare and can wait. The publisher wants to reduce storage costs without weakening either recovery requirement. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Keep the recent release-recovery snapshots in the Standard tier. + Move the year-end snapshot to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier.
Why: The two snapshot groups have different retrieval requirements, so they should not be placed in the same tier automatically. Keep fast-recovery snapshots in Standard and move the rarely accessed, long-retained year-end snapshot to Archive. Archiving the release snapshots misses the fast-recovery requirement, while deleting the year-end snapshot misses the retention policy.
Wrong options: Retain the year-end snapshot in Standard solely to avoid a future restore step. (The publisher permits delayed access, so paying to keep this rarely accessed snapshot in Standard is unnecessary.); Archive the recent release-recovery snapshots as soon as they are created. (Archiving them conflicts with the operations team's fast-recovery requirement.); Delete the year-end snapshot after the next set of release snapshots is created. (Recent release snapshots do not remove the policy requirement to retain the year-end recovery point.)

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: S3 File Gateway
chunks.text:
Storage Gateway: S3 File Gateway. Amazon S3 File Gateway gives applications NFS or SMB file shares backed by objects in Amazon S3. Choose it when existing applications need file access to S3 data and a local cache for low-latency access.
When to use: On-premises applications must keep using NFS or SMB while storing files as S3 objects.; Frequently accessed files need low-latency access through a local cache.; AWS applications must also be able to access the stored data directly in S3.
Key facts: S3 File Gateway supports NFS versions 3 and 4.1 and SMB versions 2 and 3.; The gateway presents S3 objects as files through file share mount points.; Transparent local caching provides low-latency access; the gateway manages transfers and bandwidth consumption.; Data stored in S3 can use S3 lifecycle policies, cross-Region replication, and versioning.
Gotchas: A requirement for NFS or SMB file shares does not call for an iSCSI volume.; Local caching does not mean the full dataset must remain on premises.; A virtual tape library is for backup software that expects tapes, not applications that mount file shares.
Confused with: Storage Gateway: Volume Gateway: Volume Gateway presents iSCSI volumes; S3 File Gateway presents NFS or SMB file shares backed by S3 objects.; Storage Gateway: Tape Gateway: Tape Gateway presents a virtual tape library to backup software; S3 File Gateway presents file shares to applications.
ES: Amazon S3 File Gateway ofrece a las aplicaciones recursos compartidos NFS o SMB respaldados por objetos en Amazon S3. Elígelo cuando las aplicaciones existentes necesitan acceso a archivos almacenados en S3 y una caché local para acceder con baja latencia. S3 File Gateway admite NFS versiones 3 y 4.1, y SMB versiones 2 y 3.; El gateway presenta los objetos de S3 como archivos mediante puntos de montaje de recursos compartidos.; La caché local transparente permite acceso de baja latencia; el gateway administra las transferencias y el consumo de ancho de banda.; Los datos en S3 pueden usar políticas de ciclo de vida, replicación entre regiones y control de versiones de S3.

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: S3 File Gateway
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional newspaper has an on-premises editing application that writes photographs to an NFS share. It wants to store the photographs as S3 objects so a cloud-based publishing application can access them directly, while retaining low-latency access to frequently used files at the newsroom. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy an S3 File Gateway and present an NFS share backed by the S3 bucket.
Why: The deciding requirements are an unchanged NFS interface, S3 object storage, and low-latency access to frequently used files. S3 File Gateway provides an NFS share backed by S3 objects and uses transparent local caching. Volume Gateway's iSCSI interface and Tape Gateway's virtual tape interface do not satisfy the application's file-share requirement.
Wrong options: Deploy a Tape Gateway and direct the editing application to its virtual tape library. (A virtual tape library does not provide the NFS file share the editing application needs.); Deploy a cached Volume Gateway and present an iSCSI volume to the editing application. (An iSCSI volume does not preserve the application's required NFS share.); Deploy a stored Volume Gateway and present an iSCSI volume to the editing application. (It presents an iSCSI volume rather than the required NFS share backed by S3 objects.)

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: S3 File Gateway
chunks.text:
Scenario: A field research lab mounts an NFS share from its on-premises analysis servers. Researchers want new files available as objects to an AWS application, but the lab's network connection sometimes becomes congested. They want to retain the NFS workflow and have the storage service manage transfers and bandwidth consumption. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Deploy an S3 File Gateway with an NFS share backed by an S3 bucket.
Why: The lab needs its existing NFS mounts and direct S3 object access for an AWS application. S3 File Gateway supports that combination and manages data transfer, including buffering applications from network congestion and managing bandwidth consumption. The volume options instead present iSCSI, while Tape Gateway presents a tape-oriented interface.
Wrong options: Deploy a stored Volume Gateway with an iSCSI volume for the analysis servers. (Keeping the full dataset locally through an iSCSI volume does not provide the required NFS share backed by S3 objects.); Deploy a cached Volume Gateway with an iSCSI volume for the analysis servers. (Its iSCSI interface does not retain the lab's required NFS workflow.); Deploy a Tape Gateway with virtual tapes for the analysis servers. (Virtual tapes target tape-based backup workflows rather than NFS file access.)

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: S3 File Gateway
chunks.text:
Scenario: A nonprofit collects scanned forms through an on-premises application that mounts an SMB share. It needs AWS services to access the stored forms directly in S3 and wants S3 versioning for the objects. Its backup software does not use a tape library. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use an S3 File Gateway SMB share and enable versioning on the backing S3 bucket.
Why: The forms must remain accessible through SMB while AWS services access them as S3 objects. S3 File Gateway supplies that file interface, and its S3 data can use versioning. Tape Gateway is a poor fit because no tape-library workflow is required; the volume gateways also miss the SMB requirement.
Wrong options: Use a stored Volume Gateway iSCSI volume and keep the full form dataset on premises. (It substitutes iSCSI for SMB and does not provide the requested S3-object file share.); Use a cached Volume Gateway iSCSI volume and enable S3 versioning for the stored forms. (An iSCSI volume does not preserve the application's SMB file-share interface.); Use a Tape Gateway virtual tape library and enable S3 versioning for the stored forms. (The application needs an SMB share, and its backup software does not use a tape library.)

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: Tape Gateway
chunks.text:
Storage Gateway: Tape Gateway. Tape Gateway replaces a physical tape infrastructure with cloud-backed virtual tapes. Choose it when a backup workflow must continue using tapes while archived backup data moves to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
When to use: Existing backup software uses a tape workflow that the organization wants to retain.; The organization wants to stop provisioning and maintaining physical tapes.; Backup data must be archived in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Key facts: Tape Gateway is the tape-based option in AWS Storage Gateway.; It provides cloud-backed virtual tape storage for backup data.; It supports archiving backup data in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive.; Storage Gateway can run on premises as a supported VM or hardware appliance, or in AWS on an EC2 instance.
Gotchas: An on-premises file share requirement points to a file gateway, not virtual tapes.; An iSCSI volume requirement points to Volume Gateway, even if the data is also backed up.; Do not replace a required tape workflow with a different storage interface merely because it also uses AWS storage.
