Confused with: storage-gateway-file: S3 File Gateway provides on-premises NFS/SMB file shares backed by S3 objects; Tape Gateway provides virtual tapes.; storage-gateway-volume: Volume Gateway provides iSCSI volumes; Tape Gateway addresses a tape-based backup workflow.
ES: Tape Gateway reemplaza una infraestructura de cintas físicas por cintas virtuales respaldadas en la nube. Elígelo cuando debas conservar un flujo de respaldos basado en cintas y archivar los datos en S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval o S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Tape Gateway es la opción de AWS Storage Gateway basada en cintas.; Proporciona almacenamiento de cintas virtuales respaldado en la nube para datos de respaldo.; Permite archivar datos de respaldo en S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval o S3 Glacier Deep Archive.; Puedes ejecutar Storage Gateway de forma local como VM compatible o dispositivo de hardware, o en AWS como instancia EC2.

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: Tape Gateway
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer is planning separate storage solutions for its factory. One workload serves shared files over SMB; another maintains application data on iSCSI volumes; a third must keep its established tape-based backup workflow while retiring physical tape equipment. Which Storage Gateway option should the architect select for the third workload?
Correct: Tape Gateway, to provide cloud-backed virtual tapes for the backup workflow.
Why: The question asks about the third workload, whose distinguishing requirement is an established tape-based backup workflow. Tape Gateway provides cloud-backed virtual tapes and removes the need to maintain physical tape infrastructure. S3 File Gateway is relevant to the SMB workload, while the Volume Gateway choices are relevant to volume-based storage.
Wrong options: Cached Volume Gateway, to present iSCSI volumes with frequently accessed data cached locally. (It addresses a volume requirement rather than the required tape workflow.); S3 File Gateway, to provide an SMB share backed by S3 objects. (It fits the shared-file workload, not the tape-based backup workload.); Stored Volume Gateway, to keep the full volume dataset on premises. (It provides volumes instead of replacing the tape equipment with virtual tapes.)

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: Tape Gateway
chunks.text:
Scenario: A film studio already writes project backups through a tape-based workflow. It wants to remove the work of maintaining a growing physical tape inventory and archive completed-project backups in S3 Glacier Deep Archive without redesigning that workflow. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Use Tape Gateway to provide virtual tapes and archive backup data in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Why: The studio must preserve its tape-based workflow, eliminate physical tape maintenance, and use S3 Glacier Deep Archive for backup data. Tape Gateway is designed for cloud-backed virtual tapes and supports that archive destination. File Gateway and Volume Gateway offer different storage interfaces, so their backup designs do not satisfy the workflow constraint.
Wrong options: Use S3 File Gateway to expose a file share for completed-project backups. (A file share would replace the required tape workflow.); Use stored Volume Gateway so the complete backup dataset remains on premises as volumes. (Stored volumes do not preserve the studio's required tape-based workflow.); Use cached Volume Gateway so frequently accessed backup data stays cached locally. (A cached volume is not a virtual tape and does not meet the interface requirement.)

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: Volume Gateway cached vs stored
chunks.text:
Storage Gateway: Volume Gateway cached vs stored. Volume Gateway presents cloud-backed block volumes to on-premises servers as iSCSI devices. Choose cached volumes when the primary dataset can reside in AWS and only frequently accessed data needs to remain local; choose stored volumes when the entire dataset must remain local with asynchronous offsite snapshots.
When to use: An on-premises application requires iSCSI block volumes, not NFS or SMB file shares.; Local capacity is limited, but frequently accessed data needs low-latency access: choose cached volumes.; The entire dataset needs low-latency local access and offsite backups: choose stored volumes.
Key facts: Cached volumes store data in Amazon S3 and retain frequently accessed subsets locally.; Cached volumes reduce the need to scale on-premises primary storage.; Stored volumes keep all data on the on-premises gateway and asynchronously back up point-in-time snapshots to Amazon S3.; Stored-volume backups can be recovered to a local data center or Amazon EC2.
Gotchas: A local cache is not the same as keeping the complete dataset on-premises.; Stored volumes provide offsite snapshots, but their primary data remains local.; An application requiring iSCSI volumes is not asking for an NFS/SMB file share or a virtual tape library.
Confused with: S3 File Gateway: Provides on-premises NFS/SMB file shares backed by S3 objects, rather than iSCSI block volumes.; Tape Gateway: Provides virtual tapes for existing backup workflows, rather than mounted application volumes.
ES: Volume Gateway presenta volúmenes de bloques respaldados por la nube como dispositivos iSCSI para servidores locales. Elige cached volumes si los datos principales pueden estar en AWS y solo los datos de uso frecuente necesitan permanecer locales; elige stored volumes si todo el conjunto de datos debe permanecer local con snapshots externos asíncronos. Cached volumes almacena los datos en Amazon S3 y conserva localmente los subconjuntos de uso frecuente.; Cached volumes reduce la necesidad de ampliar el almacenamiento principal local.; Stored volumes mantiene todos los datos en el gateway local y respalda de forma asíncrona snapshots de momentos específicos en Amazon S3.; Los respaldos de stored volumes pueden recuperarse en un centro de datos local o en Amazon EC2.

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: Volume Gateway cached vs stored
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturing plant has enough local storage for its production dataset. Its on-premises servers mount iSCSI volumes, and operators need low-latency access to every record, including rarely used records. The company also wants asynchronous offsite point-in-time backups that it could recover to Amazon EC2 after a site outage. Which solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Use Volume Gateway stored volumes with asynchronous point-in-time snapshots.
Why: Operators need low-latency access to the entire dataset through iSCSI volumes, not merely to frequently used records. Volume Gateway stored volumes keep all data on the on-premises gateway and asynchronously back up point-in-time snapshots to Amazon S3. Those backups can be recovered to Amazon EC2. Cached volumes miss the full-dataset-local requirement.
Wrong options: Use Tape Gateway to create offsite virtual-tape backups. (Virtual tapes do not provide the live iSCSI volumes needed for production access.); Use Volume Gateway cached volumes with frequently accessed records held locally. (Cached volumes keep only frequently accessed subsets local, not the entire dataset required by operators.); Use S3 File Gateway with an on-premises file-share cache. (A file share does not satisfy the servers' iSCSI-volume requirement.)

chunks.title: Storage Gateway: Volume Gateway cached vs stored
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research lab runs an on-premises analysis service that expects a mounted iSCSI volume. Most of its expanding archive is accessed infrequently, but a changing set of current experiments needs low-latency access. The lab wants its primary data in AWS rather than allocating local capacity for the complete archive. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively for on-premises primary storage?
Correct: Use Volume Gateway cached volumes for the analysis service.
Why: The lab needs an iSCSI volume but does not want to provision local storage for its entire growing archive. Cached volumes place data in Amazon S3 while keeping frequently accessed subsets local for low-latency access. Stored volumes would provide iSCSI access, but their complete local dataset conflicts with the stated storage goal.
Wrong options: Use S3 File Gateway to expose the archive through an SMB share. (An SMB share does not supply the mounted iSCSI volume the analysis service expects.); Use Tape Gateway to expose the archive as virtual tapes. (Virtual tapes do not serve as the mounted iSCSI volume required for analysis.); Use Volume Gateway stored volumes for the analysis service. (Stored volumes keep the complete dataset locally, conflicting with the lab's primary-data placement and capacity goals.)

chunks.title: Storage types: object vs file vs block
chunks.text:
Storage types: object vs file vs block. Choose storage by how the application accesses data: Amazon S3 for objects, Amazon EFS for a shared Linux file system, and Amazon EBS for a persistent block volume used by an EC2 instance. If the requirement is a native Windows file system with SMB, NTFS, and Active Directory integration, consider Amazon FSx for Windows File Server instead of EFS.
When to use: Choose S3 when an application stores and retrieves objects rather than mounting a file system.; Choose EFS when multiple Linux-based workloads need a shared, standard file system interface.; Choose EBS when an EC2 workload needs a persistent, low-latency block volume.
Key facts: Amazon S3 is object storage that scales to store any amount of data.; Amazon EFS is a fully managed, elastic file system for Linux-based workloads and supports shared access from many EC2 instances.; EFS is a regional service that stores data within and across multiple Availability Zones.; Amazon EBS provides persistent block volumes for EC2; each volume is automatically replicated within its Availability Zone.; Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides shared SMB storage with Windows NTFS and Active Directory integration.
Gotchas: An S3 object is not a replacement for a required mounted file system interface.; An EBS volume meets a block-device requirement, not a requirement for a regional shared file system.; Do not choose EFS merely because a workload needs files if it specifically requires native Windows NTFS and Active Directory integration.
Confused with: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server: Choose it for native Windows shared-file requirements such as SMB, NTFS, and Active Directory integration; EFS is aimed at Linux-based workloads.
ES: Elige el almacenamiento según cómo accede la aplicación a los datos: Amazon S3 para objetos, Amazon EFS para un sistema de archivos compartido entre cargas Linux y Amazon EBS para un volumen de bloques persistente usado por una instancia EC2. Si se requiere un sistema de archivos nativo de Windows con SMB, NTFS e integración con Active Directory, considera Amazon FSx for Windows File Server en lugar de EFS. Amazon S3 es almacenamiento de objetos que puede escalar para guardar cualquier cantidad de datos.; Amazon EFS es un sistema de archivos elástico y totalmente administrado para cargas basadas en Linux; permite el acceso compartido desde muchas instancias EC2.; EFS es un servicio regional que almacena datos dentro de varias Availability Zones y entre ellas.; Amazon EBS proporciona volúmenes de bloques persistentes para EC2; cada volumen se replica automáticamente dentro de su Availability Zone.; Amazon FSx for Windows File Server proporciona almacenamiento SMB compartido con integración con Windows NTFS y Active Directory.

chunks.title: Storage types: object vs file vs block
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research team runs a Linux analysis application on EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones. Each instance must open and update files in the same directory through the application's existing file system interface, and the team does not want to administer file servers. Which storage solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Mount a shared Amazon EFS file system from the instances.
Why: The deciding requirement is shared access through the Linux application's existing file system interface across Availability Zones. Amazon EFS provides that interface, supports shared access from EC2 instances, and is fully managed. S3 is object storage, so selecting it would not preserve the required file system access. Giving each instance an EBS volume would not create one shared directory.
Wrong options: Deploy Amazon FSx for Windows File Server for the application. (FSx for Windows File Server targets native Windows shared-file workloads rather than this Linux application.); Provision an Amazon EBS volume for each instance. (Separate EBS block volumes do not provide the same shared directory to the instances.); Store the files as objects in Amazon S3. (S3 stores objects, but the application requires a shared file system interface.)

chunks.title: Storage types: object vs file vs block
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer is moving a processing service to one EC2 instance. The service expects a persistent block device for its working data and needs consistent, low-latency storage performance; it does not need to share the data with other instances. Which storage solution meets these requirements?
Correct: Attach an Amazon EBS volume to the EC2 instance.
Why: The application explicitly expects a persistent block device on an EC2 instance. Amazon EBS is designed to provide persistent block volumes for EC2 and the consistent, low-latency performance described. EFS and FSx for Windows File Server offer file system interfaces instead. S3 is object storage, so it also misses the block-device requirement.
Wrong options: Mount an Amazon EFS file system on the instance. (EFS provides a file system interface rather than a block volume.); Place the working data in an Amazon S3 bucket. (S3 provides object storage, not the block device the service expects.); Mount an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. (FSx for Windows File Server provides shared file storage, not the required block device.)

chunks.title: Storage types: object vs file vs block
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media studio has two independent storage needs. Its ingestion service stores finished assets and retrieves them as objects; separately, Linux rendering instances in multiple Availability Zones must read and update files through a shared file system interface. Which two storage choices meet these requirements while preserving each workload's access pattern? (Choose two.)
Correct: Use Amazon EFS for the rendering instances' shared files. + Use Amazon S3 for the finished assets.
Why: The two workloads have different access patterns, so they should not be forced onto the same storage family. S3 fits the finished assets that the ingestion service accesses as objects. EFS fits the Linux renderers' shared file system requirement across Availability Zones. S3 cannot serve as the requested file system interface, while separate EBS volumes would not create a single shared file system.
Wrong options: Use Amazon S3 as the rendering instances' shared file system. (S3 is object storage rather than the shared file system interface the renderers require.); Use Amazon EFS as the finished assets' object store. (EFS provides a file system interface rather than the ingestion service's object access pattern.); Give each rendering instance its own Amazon EBS volume for shared files. (Separate EBS volumes do not provide one shared file system for the renderers.)

chunks.title: AWS STS AssumeRole, role switching and cross-account access
chunks.text:
AWS STS AssumeRole, role switching and cross-account access. Use an IAM role in the resource-owning account to delegate cross-account access without creating a second set of users. The role’s trust policy identifies who may assume it, the caller needs permission to call AWS STS AssumeRole, and the role’s permissions policy limits what the resulting temporary credentials can do.
When to use: Users managed in one AWS account need limited access to resources in another account.; Sensitive permissions should be activated only for a specific task, rather than held continuously.; An application needs cross-account access without storing long-term credentials for the destination account.
Key facts: The destination account creates the role and names trusted principals in its trust policy.; The source account grants selected callers permission to call AssumeRole for that role.; AWS STS returns temporary credentials after verifying the request against the role’s trust policy.; While a user has switched to a role, the role’s permissions apply and the user’s original permissions are suspended.; A role can require MFA before a user assumes it.
Gotchas: Trusting a source account does not, by itself, grant every user there permission to assume the role.; Permission to assume a role does not grant actions omitted from the role’s permissions policy.; Creating separate users in the destination account adds credentials to manage instead of using cross-account delegation.
Confused with: A second IAM user in the destination account: A cross-account role lets an existing identity obtain temporary credentials instead of maintaining another identity and password.
ES: Usa un IAM role en la cuenta propietaria del recurso para delegar acceso entre cuentas sin crear otro conjunto de usuarios. La trust policy indica quién puede asumirlo, quien llama necesita permiso para usar AWS STS AssumeRole y la permissions policy del rol limita lo que permiten hacer las credenciales temporales. La cuenta de destino crea el rol e identifica a las entidades confiables en su trust policy.; La cuenta de origen concede a quienes corresponda permiso para llamar a AssumeRole sobre ese rol.; AWS STS devuelve credenciales temporales después de verificar la solicitud con la trust policy del rol.; Mientras un usuario tiene activo el rol, se aplican los permisos del rol y se suspenden sus permisos originales.; Un rol puede exigir MFA antes de que un usuario lo asuma.

chunks.title: AWS STS AssumeRole, role switching and cross-account access
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research institute manages analysts and reviewers in one AWS account. A role in its archive account trusts the analysts’ account and grants read access to a specific S3 bucket; analysts can switch to the role successfully. A reviewer needs the same access but receives an error when attempting to switch, and the reviewer’s group has no permission to call AssumeRole for that role. Which change grants the reviewer access without broadening the role’s resource permissions?
Correct: Grant the reviewer’s group permission to call AssumeRole for the archive role.
Why: Analysts can already switch to the role, demonstrating that its trust relationship and bucket permissions support the intended access pattern. The reviewer’s group lacks permission to call AssumeRole for that role, so granting that specific caller permission addresses the stated failure. Adding S3 actions to the role would not help someone who cannot assume it. Trusting every account would broaden trust unnecessarily and would not replace the reviewer’s missing permission.
Wrong options: Create a separate IAM user for the reviewer in the archive account with access to the bucket. (This adds a destination-account identity instead of fixing the existing cross-account role access.); Add more S3 read actions to the archive role’s permissions policy. (The failure occurs before the reviewer can use the role’s existing bucket permissions.); Replace the archive role’s trust policy so that it trusts every AWS account. (The existing trust already works for this source account, and broader trust does not supply the missing group permission.)

chunks.title: AWS STS AssumeRole, role switching and cross-account access
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer keeps its quality-control staff in a workforce AWS account and inspection reports in an S3 bucket in a separate records account. A role in the records account already has a permissions policy limited to reading that bucket, but no trust policy or caller permissions have been configured for this access. Only the quality-control group should obtain temporary access without receiving records-account users. Which two actions complete the design with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)
Correct: Grant the quality-control group permission to call AssumeRole for the records role. + Configure the records role’s trust policy to trust the workforce account.
Why: The role already defines the allowed S3 action, but cross-account delegation still needs two pieces: destination-side trust and source-side permission to assume the role. Trusting the workforce account and granting AssumeRole to the quality-control group provide those pieces without creating new users. Granting AssumeRole to every workforce user would violate the restriction to the quality-control group. S3 permission on the source group alone does not complete the role-assumption path.
Wrong options: Create records-account IAM users for the quality-control staff. (Separate destination-account users conflict with the requirement to reuse workforce identities.); Grant the quality-control group S3 read permission in the workforce account without changing the records role. (That permission does not establish the missing trust and AssumeRole authorization.); Grant every workforce-account user permission to call AssumeRole for the records role. (This would extend role-switching permission beyond the specified quality-control group.)

chunks.title: AWS STS AssumeRole, role switching and cross-account access
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company manages its release engineers in a development AWS account. During deployments, selected engineers must upload files to one S3 bucket in a production account, without receiving separate production identities or long-term production credentials. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a production role trusted by the development account with permissions limited to bucket uploads, and allow the selected engineers to call AssumeRole for it.
Why: The engineers already have identities in development and must access a resource in production without additional production credentials. A role in production can trust the development account and restrict its permissions to the bucket, while selected engineers receive permission to call AssumeRole. AWS STS then provides temporary credentials for the role. Merely configuring the role’s trust policy, as in option D, does not grant the engineers permission to assume it.
Wrong options: Grant the development engineers upload permissions in their own account and leave the production account unchanged. (Permissions in the development account alone do not establish access to the production bucket.); Create IAM users in production for the selected engineers and grant them access to the bucket. (This creates the separate production identities the company wants to avoid.); Create a production role with bucket upload permissions and trust the development account, but grant no development engineers permission to call AssumeRole. (Trusted account status alone does not give the selected engineers permission to assume the role.)

chunks.title: AWS Systems Manager: Patch Manager, Run Command, Automation
chunks.text:
AWS Systems Manager: Patch Manager, Run Command, Automation. AWS Systems Manager operates managed nodes at scale without logging into servers. Choose Patch Manager for patch compliance and installation, Run Command for remote commands, and a scheduled diagnosis and remediation runbook when nodes stop reporting as managed.
When to use: Apply approved patches and report patch compliance across a fleet.; Run administrative commands remotely without SSH or a bastion host.; Repeatedly diagnose why nodes cannot connect to Systems Manager and guide remediation.
Key facts: A managed node needs SSM Agent installed and able to communicate with Systems Manager.; Patch Manager supports Scan for reporting missing patches and Scan and install for installing them.; A Quick Setup patch policy can define patching across accounts and Regions in an organization.; Patch compliance is measured against the organization's patch baseline, not against every available patch.; Systems Manager offers a diagnosis and remediation runbook that can run on a schedule to investigate nodes that are not reporting as managed.
Gotchas: A Scan reports missing patches; it does not install them.; Quick Setup Host Management patching scans but cannot install patches.; Patch Manager does not perform major operating system version upgrades.; Patch-baseline compliance does not, by itself, mean a node is secure.
Confused with: 
ES: AWS Systems Manager permite operar nodos administrados a escala sin iniciar sesión en los servidores. Elige Patch Manager para cumplimiento e instalación de parches, Run Command para comandos remotos y un runbook programado de diagnóstico y remediación cuando los nodos dejan de aparecer como administrados. Para que un nodo sea administrado, debe tener SSM Agent instalado y poder comunicarse con Systems Manager.; Patch Manager ofrece Scan para informar sobre parches faltantes y Scan and install para instalarlos.; Una patch policy de Quick Setup puede definir el parcheo entre cuentas y Regions de una organización.; El cumplimiento de parches se mide según la patch baseline de la organización, no según todos los parches disponibles.; Systems Manager ofrece un runbook de diagnóstico y remediación que puedes programar para investigar nodos que no aparecen como administrados.

chunks.title: AWS Systems Manager: Patch Manager, Run Command, Automation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retail company has managed EC2 instances in several AWS accounts and Regions. Its operations team needs recurring scans and installation of approved patches, with patch compliance defined by the company's own rules. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure a Quick Setup patch policy with a custom patch baseline for the organization.
Why: The deciding requirements are recurring installation across several accounts and Regions, plus company-defined approval rules. A Quick Setup patch policy can cover an organization with scanning and installation schedules, and a custom patch baseline defines which patches count toward compliance. Host Management is a tempting alternative, but its patch operation only scans and reports. Maintenance windows and Patch now require separate operations for each account-Region pair.
Wrong options: Configure a separate Systems Manager maintenance window for patching in each account-Region pair. (Maintenance windows can patch nodes, but each task targets only one account-Region pair and requires more separate configurations.); Configure Quick Setup Host Management and use its patch compliance reports. (Host Management can scan and report missing patches but cannot install them.); Use Patch Manager Patch now in each account-Region pair whenever reports show missing patches. (Patch now can install patches but is on demand rather than the requested recurring, centrally configured approach.)

chunks.title: AWS Systems Manager: Patch Manager, Run Command, Automation
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company must make the same administrative configuration change on a group of managed nodes. Its security policy prohibits operators from logging into servers or opening inbound access for SSH or remote PowerShell. The change is not a patch installation. Which Systems Manager tool meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Use Systems Manager Run Command to execute the change remotely on the group.
Why: The company needs a remote administrative action across a group, not a patch operation or an interactive visit to each node. Systems Manager Run Command is the fit for running commands remotely on managed nodes without SSH, remote PowerShell, or server logins. Patch Manager Scan and install addresses patches instead. Session Manager provides node access, but interactive changes on each node create unnecessary work here.
Wrong options: Use Patch Manager Scan and install to apply the configuration change. (Patch Manager Scan and install applies missing approved patches, not the requested administrative configuration change.); Start a Session Manager session on each node and make the change interactively. (Interactive sessions add per-node work when the same change must be sent to a group.); Use Patch Manager Scan to identify nodes needing the configuration change. (Patch Manager Scan reports missing patches and does not execute the configuration change.)

chunks.title: AWS Transfer Family (SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2)
chunks.text:
AWS Transfer Family (SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2). AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP, FTPS, FTP, and AS2 file-transfer endpoints backed by Amazon S3 or Amazon EFS. Choose it when partners must keep using their existing file-transfer clients without your team running protocol servers.
When to use: Partners must upload to or download from Amazon S3 using existing SFTP or FTPS clients.; A file-transfer workflow must use Amazon EFS as its storage destination.; A B2B exchange requires AS2 without operating file-transfer server infrastructure.
Key facts: Transfer Family supports SFTP, FTPS, FTP, AS2, and browser-based transfers.; Supported storage services are Amazon S3 and Amazon EFS.; Transfer Family supplies a fully managed protocol-enabled server endpoint; you configure the endpoint, users, and access.; Managed File Transfer Workflows can automate processing of files uploaded through Transfer Family.
Gotchas: An automated storage sync is not a replacement for an endpoint used by partners' existing SFTP or FTPS clients.; FTP and FTPS are distinct protocols; an FTP endpoint does not satisfy an FTPS requirement.; Choosing Amazon S3 as the destination misses a requirement for files to reside in Amazon EFS.
Confused with: AWS DataSync: Use DataSync for automated online data migration or synchronization, not to provide partners with their existing file-transfer protocol endpoint.; AWS Snow Family: Use Snow Family for offline transfer or disconnected-site needs, not as a live SFTP, FTPS, or AS2 endpoint.
ES: AWS Transfer Family ofrece endpoints administrados de SFTP, FTPS, FTP y AS2 respaldados por Amazon S3 o Amazon EFS. Elígelo cuando tus socios deban conservar sus clientes de transferencia de archivos sin que tu equipo opere servidores de protocolo. Transfer Family admite SFTP, FTPS, FTP, AS2 y transferencias desde un navegador.; Los servicios de almacenamiento admitidos son Amazon S3 y Amazon EFS.; Transfer Family proporciona un endpoint de servidor de protocolo completamente administrado; tú configuras el endpoint, los usuarios y el acceso.; Managed File Transfer Workflows puede automatizar el procesamiento de archivos cargados mediante Transfer Family.

chunks.title: AWS Transfer Family (SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A grocery chain receives nightly inventory files from hundreds of suppliers. Each supplier already uses an SFTP client, and the chain wants the files in Amazon S3 for downstream analysis. The operations team does not want to maintain file-transfer servers. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server endpoint backed by Amazon S3.
Why: The decisive requirements are continued use of supplier SFTP clients, storage in S3, and no customer-managed transfer servers. An AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint meets all three. DataSync addresses automated data transfers rather than providing an SFTP endpoint to those clients; an EC2-based SFTP server adds the operational work the chain wants to avoid.
Wrong options: Ship AWS Snow Family devices to suppliers for delivery of files into Amazon S3. (An offline device workflow does not let suppliers keep submitting nightly files through their SFTP clients.); Use AWS DataSync to schedule transfers from supplier file systems into Amazon S3. (DataSync is suited to automated storage transfers but does not provide the SFTP endpoint the suppliers need.); Deploy an SFTP server on Amazon EC2 and write incoming files to Amazon S3. (This can retain SFTP clients but requires the team to operate the file-transfer server.)

chunks.title: AWS Transfer Family (SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A payments company is replacing a self-managed file-transfer service used for B2B settlement documents. Its partners' integrations require AS2, and the company wants incoming documents stored in Amazon S3 without operating protocol servers. The partners cannot change their transfer protocol. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Configure AWS Transfer Family for AS2 transfers into Amazon S3.
Why: The nonnegotiable requirement is AS2 for existing B2B integrations, with S3 storage and no self-managed protocol servers. AWS Transfer Family supports managed AS2 transfers into S3. A Transfer Family SFTP endpoint is still the wrong protocol, while an EC2-hosted AS2 service retains the server-operations burden.
Wrong options: Configure an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint backed by Amazon S3. (This provides managed transfers to S3 but requires partners to switch from AS2 to SFTP.); Configure AWS DataSync to transfer settlement documents into Amazon S3. (DataSync does not provide the required AS2 exchange for the partners' existing integrations.); Host an AS2 service on Amazon EC2 and store received documents in Amazon S3. (This retains AS2 but requires the company to operate the protocol servers it wants to replace.)

chunks.title: AWS Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke
chunks.text:
AWS Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke. AWS Transit Gateway is a transit hub for connecting many VPCs and on-premises networks. Choose it when a growing peering mesh needs a hub, or when different attachments need different routing policies.
When to use: Many VPCs need connectivity through a shared hub rather than a growing set of pairwise connections.; VPCs and on-premises networks need to connect through VPC, VPN, or Direct Connect gateway attachments.; Groups of attachments need separate transit gateway route tables for network segmentation.
Key facts: A transit gateway can attach VPCs, VPN connections, Direct Connect gateways, and peer transit gateways.; Each attachment is associated with exactly one transit gateway route table; a route table can have many associated attachments.; Attachments use the default route table unless you configure other associations.; A VPC needs a static route to send traffic to the transit gateway.; A transit gateway incurs hourly attachment charges and traffic-processing charges.
Gotchas: A transit gateway route does not replace the route needed in a VPC to send traffic to the gateway.; Do not assume that every attachment must use the default transit gateway route table.; Transit Gateway simplifies a many-network topology, but its attachment and processing charges still matter.
Confused with: VPC peering: Peering connects VPCs directly; Transit Gateway provides a hub with attachment-based routing policies.; AWS Site-to-Site VPN: A VPN connection can attach an on-premises network to a transit gateway; it is not itself the multi-VPC hub.; AWS Direct Connect: A Direct Connect gateway can attach to a transit gateway; Transit Gateway organizes routing among the attached networks.
ES: AWS Transit Gateway es un hub de tránsito para conectar muchas VPC y redes locales. Elígelo cuando una malla creciente de conexiones necesite un hub o cuando distintos attachments requieran políticas de enrutamiento diferentes. Puedes conectar VPC, conexiones VPN, Direct Connect gateways y otros transit gateways.; Cada attachment se asocia con exactamente una transit gateway route table; una tabla puede tener varios attachments asociados.; Los attachments usan la tabla predeterminada si no configuras otras asociaciones.; Una VPC necesita una ruta estática para enviar tráfico al transit gateway.; Transit Gateway genera cargos por hora por attachment y cargos por procesamiento de tráfico.

chunks.title: AWS Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company has a transit gateway in each of two AWS Regions and has established a peering attachment between them. Its network team has configured routes inside the VPCs, but traffic destined for the other Region has no matching route in one transit gateway route table. Which change should the team make to enable routing through the peering attachment?
Correct: Add a static route for the other Region's destination that targets the peering attachment.
Why: The missing route is in the transit gateway route table, not in the VPCs. For a transit gateway peering attachment, the team must create a static route that points to that attachment. Relying on route propagation from the peering attachment does not meet this requirement.
Wrong options: Replace the peering attachment with a Client VPN endpoint attachment. (A Client VPN endpoint attachment does not provide the requested route through the existing transit gateway peering connection.); Associate the peering attachment with both transit gateway route tables. (An attachment can be associated with exactly one route table, and association alone does not add the missing destination route.); Enable automatic route propagation from the peering attachment into the transit gateway route table. (Routes to a transit gateway peering attachment must be created as static routes.)

chunks.title: AWS Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke
chunks.text:
Scenario: A university has attached a new research VPC and an existing Site-to-Site VPN connection to a transit gateway. The on-premises router already has a return route, and a transit gateway route table already has a route to the VPN attachment. The research VPC still cannot send traffic toward the on-premises network. Which TWO configurations should the network team verify to meet the connectivity requirement? (Choose two.)
Correct: Associate the research VPC attachment with the transit gateway route table containing the route to the VPN attachment. + Add a static route in the relevant VPC route table that sends on-premises traffic to the transit gateway.
Why: This path requires routing at both the VPC and transit gateway levels. The VPC needs a static route to the transit gateway, and its attachment must be associated with a transit gateway route table that has the VPN route. VPN route propagation is not a substitute for the VPC's static route.
Wrong options: Rely on VPN route propagation to create the missing static route inside the research VPC. (VPN propagation does not remove the need to configure the VPC's route to the transit gateway.); Replace the Site-to-Site VPN attachment with a Client VPN endpoint attachment. (Replacing the existing on-premises VPN connection does not address the VPC routing and association checks.); Associate the research VPC attachment with two transit gateway route tables simultaneously. (Each attachment can be associated with only one transit gateway route table.)

chunks.title: AWS Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturing company already uses a Direct Connect gateway for its on-premises connection and is adding VPCs for new production systems. It wants the VPCs and the existing on-premises connection to participate in one hub, with different routing policies for production and development attachments. Which design meets these requirements?
Correct: Attach the VPCs and Direct Connect gateway to a Transit Gateway, using separate transit gateway route tables for the attachment groups.
Why: The company needs to incorporate its existing Direct Connect gateway into a hub for many VPCs. Transit Gateway supports both Direct Connect gateway and VPC attachments, as well as multiple route tables. A design built around individual VPC peering connections misses the shared-hub requirement.
Wrong options: Attach the Direct Connect gateway to one VPC and use VPC peering for all other VPCs. (This does not use a transit hub with separate routing policies for production and development attachments.); Peer each production VPC with each development VPC and retain the Direct Connect gateway separately. (This does not place the VPCs and on-premises connection in the requested shared hub.); Replace the Direct Connect gateway with a Site-to-Site VPN connection to each VPC. (Separate per-VPC VPN connections do not deliver the required shared hub and discard the existing connection.)

chunks.title: VMware Cloud on AWS
chunks.text:
VMware Cloud on AWS. VMware Cloud on AWS is a managed offering that combines VMware SDDC software with AWS cloud infrastructure. Choose it when the deciding requirement is moving existing VMware workloads to AWS while retaining VMware tooling, rather than moving AWS infrastructure on premises or rebuilding applications as containers.
When to use: An organization wants to move existing VMware workloads to AWS without re-platforming them.; The operations team must continue using VMware tooling after the move.; An existing customer wants to extend its VMware environment onto AWS infrastructure.
Key facts: VMware Cloud on AWS combines VMware SDDC software with AWS cloud infrastructure in a managed offering.; The service remains available to existing customers.; Since April 30, 2024, AWS and its channel partners no longer resell the service.; Broadcom has stated that customers can renew subscriptions through Broadcom or an authorized Broadcom reseller.
Gotchas: Do not choose AWS Outposts merely because the source environment is on premises; Outposts fits a requirement to run AWS infrastructure on premises.; Do not choose ECS Anywhere or EKS Anywhere when the requirement is to retain VMware tooling rather than run containers on customer-owned hardware.; Do not assume an existing customer can buy or renew a VMware Cloud on AWS subscription through AWS.
Confused with: AWS Outposts: Outposts runs AWS infrastructure on premises; VMware Cloud on AWS moves VMware workloads onto AWS infrastructure.; Local Zones and Wavelength: These address metro-area or 5G edge latency; VMware Cloud on AWS addresses retaining VMware software when moving workloads to AWS.; ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere: These run containers on customer-owned hardware; VMware Cloud on AWS is for VMware workloads on AWS.
ES: VMware Cloud on AWS es una oferta administrada que combina el software VMware SDDC con la infraestructura de nube de AWS. Elígela cuando el requisito decisivo sea trasladar cargas de trabajo VMware existentes a AWS y conservar las herramientas de VMware, en lugar de instalar infraestructura de AWS en las instalaciones o reconstruir aplicaciones como contenedores. VMware Cloud on AWS combina software VMware SDDC con infraestructura de nube de AWS en una oferta administrada.; El servicio sigue disponible para clientes existentes.; Desde el 30 de abril de 2024, AWS y sus socios de canal ya no revenden el servicio.; Broadcom ha indicado que los clientes pueden renovar sus suscripciones mediante Broadcom o un revendedor autorizado.

chunks.title: VMware Cloud on AWS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A regional insurer runs claims applications in an on-premises VMware environment. Its operations team wants to move the workloads to AWS but must continue using VMware tooling and does not have time to re-platform the applications. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Move the VMware workloads to VMware Cloud on AWS.
Why: The deciding constraints are moving existing VMware workloads to AWS, retaining VMware tooling, and avoiding re-platforming. VMware Cloud on AWS combines VMware SDDC software with AWS infrastructure in a managed offering. Outposts is a plausible hybrid choice, but its purpose here would be to put AWS infrastructure in the insurer's data center rather than move the workloads to AWS. Containerizing the applications also conflicts with the stated migration constraint.
Wrong options: Containerize the applications and run them with ECS Anywhere on the insurer's hardware. (This requires changing the application deployment model and keeps execution on customer-owned hardware.); Rebuild the applications as containers and deploy them to an AWS Local Zone. (A Local Zone addresses metro-area latency, not the requirement to retain VMware tooling without re-platforming.); Deploy AWS Outposts in the insurer's data center and move the applications onto AWS infrastructure there. (Outposts keeps AWS infrastructure on premises instead of moving the VMware workloads to AWS.)

chunks.title: VMware Cloud on AWS
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer operates a legacy scheduling system in a VMware environment at its main facility. It wants to place a second environment on AWS infrastructure as part of a disaster recovery plan, but its small team must keep using VMware software to operate the system. There is no requirement to run compute at the facility or near a particular city. Which solution best fits the target environment with the LEAST application change?
Correct: Use VMware Cloud on AWS for the second VMware environment.
Why: The disaster recovery target must be on AWS infrastructure and preserve the team's VMware operating model with little application change. VMware Cloud on AWS is the managed offering that combines VMware SDDC software with AWS infrastructure. Outposts is tempting because the original system is on premises, but the second environment is explicitly meant to be on AWS, not at the facility. The scenario supplies no metro-area latency or container requirement to justify the other choices.
Wrong options: Use EKS Anywhere on manufacturer-owned hardware for the second environment. (It targets containers on customer-owned hardware rather than the requested VMware environment on AWS.); Use AWS Outposts at the facility for the second environment. (It places AWS infrastructure at the facility, contrary to the requested AWS-based target environment.); Use an AWS Local Zone for the second environment. (Its metro-area latency purpose does not address the stated need to keep operating VMware workloads with VMware software.)

chunks.title: VPC CIDR planning, subnets and IP addressing
chunks.text:
VPC CIDR planning, subnets and IP addressing. Choose a VPC IPv4 CIDR that leaves room for growth without conflicting with networks you may connect later. Divide its address space into separate subnets for each required Availability Zone; an existing VPC CIDR cannot be resized.
When to use: A new VPC must later connect to another VPC or an on-premises network.; A workload needs address capacity in multiple Availability Zones.; An existing VPC needs more IPv4 address space.
Key facts: A VPC requires an IPv4 CIDR when created; its allowed size is /16 through /28.; An existing IPv4 CIDR cannot be enlarged or reduced. You can associate a non-overlapping secondary CIDR, subject to association restrictions and quotas.; Each subnet resides entirely in one Availability Zone; subnets cannot span Availability Zones.; A secondary VPC CIDR receives a local route in the VPC route tables.; An active peering connection permits a new VPC CIDR only if it does not overlap the peer's CIDR.
Gotchas: Do not plan to resize the primary VPC CIDR when the workload grows.; A single subnet cannot provide placement in two Availability Zones.; A subnet's public or private classification depends on its route to an internet gateway, not its CIDR size.
Confused with: 
ES: Elige un CIDR IPv4 para la VPC que permita crecer sin entrar en conflicto con redes que conectarás después. Divide el espacio en subredes distintas para cada Availability Zone requerida; no puedes cambiar el tamaño de un CIDR existente. Debes asignar un CIDR IPv4 al crear una VPC; el tamaño permitido va de /16 a /28.; No puedes ampliar ni reducir un CIDR IPv4 existente. Puedes asociar un CIDR secundario que no se superponga, sujeto a restricciones de asociación y cuotas.; Cada subred reside por completo en una sola Availability Zone; no puede abarcar varias.; Un CIDR secundario de la VPC recibe una ruta local en las tablas de rutas de la VPC.; Con una conexión de VPC peering activa, solo puedes agregar un CIDR que no se superponga con el CIDR de la VPC par.

chunks.title: VPC CIDR planning, subnets and IP addressing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A manufacturer has a VPC with primary CIDR 10.60.0.0/16 and an active peering connection to a VPC using 10.61.0.0/16. It plans to use 10.62.0.0/16 for a separate network. A new application needs additional IPv4 address space and instances in two Availability Zones, while existing instance addresses remain unchanged. Which two actions together meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Create distinct subnets, such as 10.63.0.0/24 and 10.63.1.0/24, in separate Availability Zones. + Associate 10.63.0.0/16 as a secondary CIDR of the existing VPC.
Why: The application needs both new address space and placement in two Availability Zones without changing existing addresses. Associating the non-overlapping 10.63.0.0/16 CIDR provides the space, and creating separate subnets from it provides per-zone placement. The primary CIDR cannot be enlarged; using 10.61.0.0/16 would overlap the active peer, and one subnet cannot span zones.
Wrong options: Associate 10.61.0.0/16 as a secondary CIDR of the existing VPC. (The secondary CIDR would overlap the CIDR of the actively peered VPC.); Increase the existing VPC's primary CIDR from 10.60.0.0/16 to 10.60.0.0/14. (An existing CIDR cannot be resized, and the proposed range covers the specified peer and separate network.); Create one subnet from the additional CIDR and place instances in both Availability Zones in that subnet. (One subnet cannot span two Availability Zones.)

chunks.title: VPC CIDR planning, subnets and IP addressing
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company is creating a VPC for a new service that must run in two Availability Zones. Its on-premises network uses 10.40.0.0/16, and a VPC it plans to peer with uses 10.41.0.0/16. The team wants a VPC CIDR with room to create more subnets later. Which plan meets these requirements?
Correct: Create a VPC with 10.42.0.0/16 and use 10.42.0.0/24 and 10.42.1.0/24 for subnets in separate Availability Zones.
Why: The deciding requirements are future connectivity to the named networks, deployment across two Availability Zones, and room for more subnets. The 10.42.0.0/16 plan avoids both specified ranges and assigns a distinct subnet to each zone. Choosing 10.41.0.0/16 would conflict with the planned peer, while assigning the same /24 to both subnets does not create distinct address ranges.
Wrong options: Create a VPC with 10.41.0.0/16 and use distinct /24 subnets in separate Availability Zones. (The VPC CIDR overlaps the VPC identified for future peering.); Create a VPC with 10.42.0.0/24 and assign that entire /24 to a subnet in each Availability Zone. (The two subnets would use the same CIDR instead of distinct portions of the VPC address space.); Create a VPC with 10.40.0.0/16 and separate subnets in each Availability Zone. (The VPC CIDR conflicts with the specified on-premises address range.)

chunks.title: VPC endpoint policies and aws:SourceVpce bucket policies
chunks.text:
VPC endpoint policies and aws:SourceVpce bucket policies. A VPC endpoint policy controls which principals and requests can pass through that endpoint, including which S3 buckets they can reach through it. To make an S3 bucket accessible only through a particular endpoint, use a bucket policy that denies requests unless aws:SourceVpce matches that endpoint ID.
When to use: Limit the buckets that workloads can reach through a shared S3 VPC endpoint.; Reject access to a protected bucket unless requests arrive through one specified VPC endpoint.; Apply both controls when the endpoint must reach only approved buckets and a bucket must reject other access paths.
Key facts: The default endpoint policy grants full access through the endpoint; it does not replace identity-based or bucket policies.; An S3 bucket policy can use aws:SourceVpce with the endpoint ID, not an endpoint ARN.; aws:SourceVpc identifies a VPC rather than one endpoint within that VPC.; For a gateway endpoint policy, set Principal to * and use aws:PrincipalArn to identify a particular principal.
Gotchas: An endpoint policy on one endpoint does not, by itself, prevent access to a bucket through another endpoint.; A bucket policy that denies requests not using a specified endpoint can also block console access to that bucket.; A deny based on the wrong endpoint ID can block all access to the bucket.; A deny condition does not grant access; requests still need appropriate permissions.
Confused with: aws:SourceVpc bucket condition: It restricts access by VPC, not by a particular endpoint when the VPC has multiple endpoints.; Default endpoint policy: It allows full access through the endpoint, subject to other applicable permissions; it does not limit the reachable buckets.
ES: Una VPC endpoint policy controla qué principals y solicitudes pueden pasar por ese endpoint, incluidos los buckets de S3 que pueden alcanzar a través de él. Para que un bucket de S3 solo sea accesible mediante un endpoint específico, usa una bucket policy que deniegue las solicitudes salvo cuando aws:SourceVpce coincida con el ID de ese endpoint. La endpoint policy predeterminada permite acceso completo a través del endpoint; no sustituye las identity-based policies ni las bucket policies.; Una S3 bucket policy puede usar aws:SourceVpce con el ID del endpoint, no con el ARN del endpoint.; aws:SourceVpc identifica una VPC, no un endpoint específico dentro de ella.; En una gateway endpoint policy, configura Principal como * y usa aws:PrincipalArn para identificar un principal específico.

chunks.title: VPC endpoint policies and aws:SourceVpce bucket policies
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company has two S3 VPC endpoints in one VPC and a protected shipment bucket. Workloads already have the necessary S3 permissions. Through endpoint X, workloads must reach only the shipment bucket; the shipment bucket must also reject requests that do not use endpoint X, including requests through endpoint Y. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
Correct: Add a shipment bucket policy that denies requests when aws:SourceVpce is not endpoint X's ID. + Attach a custom policy to endpoint X that permits access through it only to the shipment bucket.
Why: There are two distinct access boundaries: what can be reached through endpoint X and which paths the shipment bucket accepts. A custom endpoint policy addresses the first; a bucket policy denying requests whose aws:SourceVpce is not endpoint X addresses the second. The default endpoint policy does not restrict X's destinations. aws:SourceVpc cannot distinguish X from Y because both are in the same VPC.
Wrong options: Add a bucket policy that denies requests when aws:SourceVpc is not the company's VPC ID. (Endpoint Y is in the same VPC, so this condition does not reject its requests.); Attach a custom policy to endpoint Y that permits access only to the shipment bucket. (This would not limit endpoint X's destinations and would not make the shipment bucket reject endpoint Y.); Keep endpoint X's default endpoint policy. (The default policy does not limit endpoint X to the shipment bucket.)

chunks.title: VPC endpoint policies and aws:SourceVpce bucket policies
chunks.text:
Scenario: A media company uses one S3 VPC endpoint for applications that already have the required S3 permissions. Through this endpoint, the applications must reach two approved buckets but no other buckets, including buckets created later. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Attach a custom endpoint policy that permits access through the endpoint only to the two approved buckets.
Why: The deciding requirement is to limit all bucket destinations reachable through one endpoint, including future buckets. A custom endpoint policy can permit access through that endpoint only to the two approved buckets; the existing S3 permissions must still allow each request. Policies on the approved buckets control access to those buckets, not access through the endpoint to every other bucket. Maintaining deny policies on unapproved buckets would also require ongoing work as buckets are created.
Wrong options: Keep the default endpoint policy and add a bucket policy to each currently unapproved bucket. (New buckets would require additional policies, and the default endpoint policy does not limit bucket access.); Add aws:SourceVpc conditions to the policies of the two approved buckets. (Those conditions do not limit which other buckets requests can reach through the endpoint.); Add aws:SourceVpce conditions to the policies of the two approved buckets. (Conditions on the approved buckets do not prevent the endpoint from being used to reach other buckets.)

chunks.title: VPC endpoints: gateway (S3/DynamoDB) vs interface
chunks.text:
VPC endpoints: gateway (S3/DynamoDB) vs interface. Use a gateway VPC endpoint for private VPC access to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB when you want to avoid NAT devices and additional endpoint charges. For other supported AWS services, choose an interface endpoint, which creates private-IP network interfaces and incurs hourly and data processing charges.
When to use: Private-subnet workloads need S3 or DynamoDB access without a NAT device: associate their route tables with a gateway endpoint.; VPC workloads need private access to another AWS service that supports AWS PrivateLink: use an interface endpoint.; S3 requests arriving through an inbound Resolver endpoint need an interface endpoint with private DNS configured for inbound access.
Key facts: Gateway endpoints support S3 and DynamoDB and have no additional charge.; A gateway endpoint adds a service-prefix-list route to each selected route table; only subnets using associated route tables use that endpoint.; Gateway endpoint routes apply to the service in the current Region, not the same service in another Region.; An interface endpoint creates a private-IP endpoint network interface in each selected subnet and incurs hourly usage and data processing charges.; An interface endpoint's security group must allow the expected inbound traffic from VPC resources.
Gotchas: A gateway endpoint is not an interface endpoint: it does not create endpoint network interfaces or use AWS PrivateLink.; Creating a gateway endpoint without associating the workload subnet's route table does not route that subnet's service traffic through it.; For S3, enabling private DNS only for inbound traffic on an interface endpoint requires an S3 gateway endpoint.; A gateway endpoint cannot serve as a general private route to other AWS services.
Confused with: NAT gateway: Provides outbound access through an internet gateway; a gateway endpoint instead routes S3 or DynamoDB traffic directly through a service-specific route.; Interface endpoint: Uses private-IP endpoint network interfaces and incurs hourly and data processing charges; a gateway endpoint uses route-table entries and has no additional charge.; AWS PrivateLink endpoint service: An endpoint service exposes a service to consumers; an interface endpoint lets a VPC connect to a supported service.
ES: Usa un gateway VPC endpoint para que una VPC acceda de forma privada a Amazon S3 o DynamoDB sin dispositivos NAT ni cargos adicionales por el endpoint. Para otros servicios de AWS compatibles, elige un interface endpoint: crea interfaces de red con IP privadas y genera cargos por hora y por procesamiento de datos. Los gateway endpoints admiten S3 y DynamoDB y no tienen un cargo adicional.; Un gateway endpoint agrega una ruta hacia la prefix list del servicio a cada tabla de rutas seleccionada; solo las subredes que usan esas tablas utilizan el endpoint.; Las rutas de un gateway endpoint corresponden al servicio en la Region actual, no al mismo servicio en otra Region.; Un interface endpoint crea una endpoint network interface con IP privada en cada subred seleccionada y genera cargos por hora y por procesamiento de datos.; El security group del interface endpoint debe permitir el tráfico entrante esperado desde los recursos de la VPC.

chunks.title: VPC endpoints: gateway (S3/DynamoDB) vs interface
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publishing company runs image-processing instances in private subnets. The instances must upload files to an S3 bucket in the same Region, and the company does not want to deploy a NAT device or pay additional endpoint charges. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Create an S3 gateway endpoint and associate it with the private subnets' route tables.
Why: The deciding requirements are S3 access from private subnets, no NAT device, and no additional endpoint charge. An S3 gateway endpoint satisfies them when the instances' route tables are associated with it. An S3 interface endpoint also supports private S3 access, but its hourly and data processing charges make it a poorer fit.
Wrong options: Route the private subnets' S3 traffic through a NAT device in a public subnet. (This requires the NAT device that the company explicitly wants to avoid.); Create a DynamoDB gateway endpoint and associate it with the private subnets' route tables. (A DynamoDB gateway endpoint does not route traffic destined for S3.); Create an S3 interface endpoint with network interfaces in the private subnets. (An S3 interface endpoint can provide private connectivity but incurs hourly and data processing charges.)

chunks.title: VPC endpoints: gateway (S3/DynamoDB) vs interface
chunks.text:
Scenario: A research organization already uses an S3 gateway endpoint for workloads in its VPC. It is adding an inbound Resolver endpoint so clients connecting through its private network can resolve S3 names to private endpoint addresses, while VPC workloads continue using the gateway endpoint. Which S3 endpoint configuration meets these requirements?
Correct: Keep the S3 gateway endpoint and add an S3 interface endpoint with private DNS enabled only for the inbound endpoint.
Why: The organization needs private DNS for S3 requests arriving through an inbound Resolver endpoint while retaining gateway endpoint routing for VPC workloads. The S3 interface endpoint offers a private-DNS-only-for-inbound setting alongside the existing S3 gateway endpoint. Removing the gateway endpoint is a trap: selecting that inbound-only setting without an S3 gateway endpoint results in an error.
Wrong options: Keep only the S3 gateway endpoint and associate additional VPC route tables with it. (Gateway endpoint route-table associations alone do not provide the requested S3 interface endpoint private DNS for inbound clients.); Delete the S3 gateway endpoint and create an S3 interface endpoint with private DNS enabled only for the inbound endpoint. (The inbound-only private DNS setting requires an S3 gateway endpoint, so this configuration cannot be completed.); Replace the S3 gateway endpoint with a DynamoDB gateway endpoint and retain the inbound Resolver endpoint. (A DynamoDB gateway endpoint cannot provide endpoint routing for S3.)

chunks.title: VPC endpoints: gateway (S3/DynamoDB) vs interface
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer created an S3 gateway endpoint for its VPC and selected the route table used by one private subnet. Instances in a second private subnet use a different route table and cannot reach S3; they have no NAT route. Both subnets must use the endpoint without introducing a NAT device. What should the retailer do?
Correct: Associate the second private subnet's route table with the existing S3 gateway endpoint.
Why: Gateway endpoint routing depends on the route tables selected for the endpoint. Associating the second subnet's route table adds the service-prefix-list route, so its instances can use the existing S3 gateway endpoint. A NAT route could provide another path to S3, but it fails the explicit requirement to avoid a NAT device.
Wrong options: Create an S3 interface endpoint for the second private subnet. (This provides a different, charged endpoint type rather than making the second subnet use the existing gateway endpoint.); Add a NAT device and a default route to it for the second private subnet. (This introduces the NAT device the retailer wants to avoid and does not make the subnet use the endpoint.); Add a default route to the internet gateway in the second private subnet's route table. (A default internet-gateway route does not associate the second subnet's route table with the gateway endpoint.)

chunks.title: VPC Flow Logs
chunks.text:
VPC Flow Logs. VPC Flow Logs captures information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces in a VPC. Choose it when you need traffic records to investigate a connectivity problem; it does not capture packet contents or identify who changed an AWS resource.
When to use: Investigate whether restrictive security group rules are contributing to failed connections.; Monitor traffic reaching an instance or determine traffic direction at its network interface.; Publish network traffic records to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, or Amazon Data Firehose.
Key facts: Flow logs capture information about IP traffic to and from VPC network interfaces, including accepted and rejected traffic metadata.; You can publish records to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, or Amazon Data Firehose.; Collection occurs outside the network traffic path, so creating or deleting flow logs does not affect network throughput or latency.; Publishing flow logs incurs vended-log ingestion and archival charges.
Gotchas: Flow logs provide traffic metadata, not packet contents.; CloudWatch Logs can receive flow log records, but CloudWatch metrics alone do not provide those records.; A flow log cannot tell you which identity made an API call that changed a security group.
Confused with: AWS CloudTrail: CloudTrail answers who made an API call; VPC Flow Logs shows IP traffic information.; AWS Config: Config tracks resource configuration history and compliance; VPC Flow Logs records traffic information.; AWS X-Ray: X-Ray traces requests across services to find latency bottlenecks; VPC Flow Logs examines IP traffic at network interfaces.
ES: VPC Flow Logs captura información sobre el tráfico IP que entra y sale de las interfaces de red de una VPC. Elígelo cuando necesites registros de tráfico para investigar un problema de conectividad; no captura el contenido de los paquetes ni identifica quién cambió un recurso de AWS. Flow logs captura información sobre el tráfico IP que entra y sale de las interfaces de red de una VPC, incluidos metadatos de tráfico aceptado y rechazado.; Puedes publicar los registros en CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3 o Amazon Data Firehose.; La recopilación ocurre fuera de la ruta del tráfico, por lo que crear o eliminar flow logs no afecta el rendimiento ni la latencia de la red.; Publicar flow logs genera cargos por ingesta y archivo de vended logs.

chunks.title: VPC Flow Logs
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher's application intermittently fails to connect to an EC2 instance. The operations team suspects an overly restrictive security group rule and wants records of IP traffic reaching the instance's network interface in CloudWatch Logs. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Create a VPC flow log and publish its records to CloudWatch Logs.
Why: The deciding requirement is to see IP traffic reaching a network interface, with records delivered to CloudWatch Logs. VPC Flow Logs is designed to capture that information and can help diagnose overly restrictive security group rules. AWS Config might reveal what a rule was, but it does not provide the requested traffic records.
Wrong options: Enable AWS X-Ray and inspect traces for requests to the application. (X-Ray traces application requests rather than recording IP traffic at the network interface.); Enable AWS CloudTrail and send API activity records to CloudWatch Logs. (CloudTrail records API activity, not the IP traffic reaching the instance.); Enable AWS Config and review the instance's security group configuration history. (Config can show configuration history but not the requested traffic records.)

chunks.title: VPC Flow Logs
chunks.text:
Scenario: A delivery company sees errors in a service that runs across several application components. Its immediate question is whether traffic is reaching a particular EC2 instance's network interface; tracing application latency can wait. Which solution should the team choose to answer the immediate question?
Correct: Use VPC Flow Logs to inspect IP traffic information for the instance's network interface.
Why: The team is asking about traffic at a specific network interface, so VPC Flow Logs is the direct fit. It captures information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces and can help monitor traffic reaching an instance. X-Ray is a plausible choice for a distributed application, but its request tracing addresses the latency investigation that the team has postponed.
Wrong options: Use CloudWatch metrics to compare application performance over time. (Performance metrics do not supply records of traffic reaching a network interface.); Use AWS Config to review the instance's resource configuration history. (Configuration history cannot establish what traffic reached the interface.); Use AWS X-Ray to trace requests across the application components. (X-Ray addresses request tracing and latency, which the scenario explicitly defers.)

chunks.title: VPC peering
chunks.text:
VPC peering. VPC peering directly connects two VPCs so resources can communicate using private IP addresses. For a small number of VPCs that need direct connections, choose it over a transitive hub when the address ranges do not overlap.
When to use: Two VPCs need private connectivity, including VPCs in different accounts or Regions.; A small topology needs direct VPC-to-VPC connections rather than transitive routing.; The design should avoid a gateway or VPN connection.
Key facts: A peering connection links two VPCs and supports private IPv4 or IPv6 communication.; Peering can connect VPCs in different accounts or Regions.; Inter-Region peering traffic stays on the AWS backbone, does not traverse the public internet, and is encrypted before leaving AWS facilities.; Creating a peering connection has no charge. Data transfer within an Availability Zone is free; transfers across Availability Zones or Regions incur charges.; Peering is not transitive, and VPCs with overlapping CIDR ranges cannot be peered.
Gotchas: A–B and B–C peering connections do not give A a route to C; A and C need their own connection.; Private inter-Region connectivity does not mean free inter-Region data transfer.; Do not select peering before checking for overlapping CIDR ranges.
Confused with: transit-gateway: Transit Gateway is a transitive hub for many networks; peering directly connects two VPCs without transitive routing.; site-to-site-vpn: Site-to-Site VPN connects networks using encrypted IPsec tunnels, typically over the internet (private IP VPN can run over Direct Connect); VPC peering does not use a VPN.; client-vpn: Client VPN connects individual remote users; VPC peering connects VPCs.
ES: VPC peering conecta directamente dos VPC para que sus recursos se comuniquen mediante direcciones IP privadas. Para pocas VPC que necesitan conexiones directas, elígelo en lugar de un hub transitivo cuando los rangos de direcciones no se superponen. Una conexión de peering enlaza dos VPC y permite comunicación mediante IPv4 o IPv6 privados.; Peering puede conectar VPC de distintas cuentas o Regions.; El tráfico de peering entre Regions permanece en la red troncal de AWS, no atraviesa internet público y se cifra antes de salir de las instalaciones de AWS.; Crear una conexión de peering no tiene cargo. La transferencia dentro de una Availability Zone es gratuita; las transferencias entre Availability Zones o Regions generan cargos.; Peering no es transitivo y no permite conectar VPC con rangos CIDR superpuestos.

chunks.title: VPC peering
chunks.text:
Scenario: A publisher keeps a catalog service and a reporting service in two VPCs owned by separate AWS accounts. The services need to communicate using private IP addresses, and their traffic stays within one Availability Zone. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
Correct: Create a VPC peering connection between the accounts' VPCs.
Why: The deciding requirements are private communication between two VPCs in separate accounts and traffic that remains within one Availability Zone. VPC peering supports cross-account private IP communication, and transfer over a peering connection within an Availability Zone is free. Transit Gateway adds a hub when the scenario calls only for one direct connection.
Wrong options: Connect the VPCs through AWS Site-to-Site VPN. (A VPN is unnecessary for direct private communication between these two VPCs.); Connect each VPC to AWS Transit Gateway. (A transitive hub is unnecessary for this single VPC-to-VPC connection.); Give reporting employees AWS Client VPN access to the catalog VPC. (Client VPN addresses remote-user access, not the required connection between the services' VPCs.)

chunks.title: VPC peering
chunks.text:
Scenario: A logistics company is adding VPCs across several AWS accounts and plans to connect its office network as well. The network team wants VPCs to communicate through a central, transitive hub rather than maintain individual connections between every pair. Which solution best meets the company's planned topology?
Correct: Connect the VPCs and office network through AWS Transit Gateway.
Why: The deciding phrase is the requirement for a central, transitive hub across several VPCs and an office network. Transit Gateway fits that topology. VPC peering links pairs of VPCs but cannot route traffic transitively through an intermediate VPC.
Wrong options: Create VPC peering connections between selected pairs and route through intermediate VPCs. (Peering does not support the transitive paths required by this topology.); Establish Site-to-Site VPN only between the office and one VPC. (That single connection does not provide the requested central connectivity among the VPCs.); Give office employees Client VPN access to one VPC. (Remote-user access does not create the required transitive network hub.)

chunks.title: AWS WAF (SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting, geo)
chunks.text:
AWS WAF (SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting, geo). AWS WAF filters HTTP(S) requests to supported application resources using rules in a web ACL. Choose it when the requirement is to control application-layer requests, such as suspicious query strings, unwanted source IPs, or request floods.
When to use: Protect a CloudFront distribution, Application Load Balancer, API Gateway REST API, AppSync GraphQL API, or Cognito user pool from unwanted web requests.; Block requests associated with SQL injection or XSS patterns, specified IP addresses, or countries.; Rate-limit HTTP(S) requests that arrive too quickly.
Key facts: AWS WAF monitors HTTP(S) requests forwarded to supported protected resources.; Rules can evaluate request characteristics such as source IP address and query-string values.; A rate-based rule counts requests by configured aggregation criteria and rate-limits groups that exceed its configured limit.; A rate-based rule can use a scope-down statement to narrow which requests it tracks.; If the same rate-based rule is used in two web ACLs, AWS WAF tracks each rule instance separately.
Gotchas: DDoS protection alone is not the same decision as filtering requests for SQL injection or XSS.; Threat findings do not themselves supply a web ACL that blocks matching HTTP(S) requests.; Rate-based rules in separate web ACLs do not share one request count.
Confused with: AWS Shield: Choose AWS WAF for rules that inspect and control application-layer web requests; Shield addresses DDoS protection.; AWS Firewall Manager: Choose Firewall Manager to enforce security policies centrally across accounts, not as a substitute for WAF request-matching rules.; AWS Network Firewall: Choose Network Firewall for stateful VPC traffic inspection; choose WAF for HTTP(S) requests to supported web resources.
ES: AWS WAF filtra solicitudes HTTP(S) dirigidas a recursos de aplicación compatibles mediante reglas en una web ACL. Elígelo cuando necesites controlar solicitudes de capa de aplicación, como query strings sospechosas, direcciones IP no deseadas o ráfagas de solicitudes. AWS WAF supervisa las solicitudes HTTP(S) enviadas a recursos protegidos compatibles.; Las reglas pueden evaluar características como la dirección IP de origen y los valores de las query strings.; Una rate-based rule cuenta solicitudes según los criterios de agrupación configurados y aplica rate limiting a los grupos que superan el límite configurado.; Una rate-based rule puede usar una scope-down statement para restringir qué solicitudes contabiliza.; Si usas la misma rate-based rule en dos web ACLs, AWS WAF lleva el seguimiento de cada instancia por separado.

chunks.title: AWS WAF (SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting, geo)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A retailer serves its storefront through Amazon CloudFront. Its security team has identified malicious query-string patterns associated with SQL injection and wants matching HTTP requests blocked before they reach the application. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the CloudFront distribution and add a rule that blocks the identified query-string patterns.
Why: The deciding requirement is to block HTTP requests based on their query-string values. AWS WAF can protect a CloudFront distribution and use a web ACL rule to control requests matching those values. Shield addresses a different threat category, while GuardDuty findings and Inspector scans do not perform the requested request filtering.
Wrong options: Enable Amazon GuardDuty and use its findings to identify suspicious storefront requests. (GuardDuty produces threat findings rather than applying a request-matching rule to block these storefront requests.); Use AWS Shield to protect the distribution from DDoS traffic. (DDoS protection does not address the stated need to match SQL injection patterns in query strings.); Use Amazon Inspector to scan the storefront's application components for vulnerabilities. (Vulnerability scanning does not block incoming requests that match the identified query-string patterns.)

chunks.title: AWS WAF (SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting, geo)
chunks.text:
Scenario: A ticketing company routes checkout traffic through an Application Load Balancer. During popular releases, automated clients send too many requests to the checkout path, but the company wants normal traffic to that path and all traffic to other paths to continue. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
Correct: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the load balancer and configure a rate-based rule scoped to checkout requests.
Why: The requirement combines request-rate control with a narrow scope: checkout traffic should be limited without applying that limit to other paths.
